“European countries need to learn”: Ukrainian defense-tech CEO warns Europe against costly defense mistakes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
18:49:20 UTC
03:49:20 KST

Europe is raising its defense budgets, but a Ukrainian defense-tech executive warns against spending the money on expensive systems that prove too ineffective to stop cheap drones at a sustainable cost. That is the case Taras Bublyk, CEO of the Ukrainian electronic-warfare firm UNWAVE, made in an interview with Ukrinform.
He argued that economics decides these fights: firing a costly missile at a cheap drone every time is a defense no budget can sustain for long. Bublyk said Europe should learn from the lessons of the Russo-Ukrainian war.
Why a missile for every drone is a losing trade
Bublyk said the core problem is the price gap between a threat and the tools used to stop it. Spend an expensive missile each time to down a relatively cheap drone, and the defense cannot be sustained.
“The cost of countering must be proportionate to the cost of the threat. The countermeasures must be affordable, produced in sufficient quantity, and work as a single system,” Bublyk explained.
His answer is a layered defense that combines detection, electronic warfare, interceptor drones, physical barriers, and conventional air defense, so that where jamming or a cheaper interceptor will do, no one burns a costly missile.
Advanced weapons are not the same as being ready to use them
For Europe, that means investing not only in the technology but also in integrating it and scaling up production because owning advanced weapons does not, by itself, mean a country can use them well.
Rising European defense budgets are a good sign, he adds, but risk flowing to systems built without the lessons of the current war.
“There is a risk of investing in expensive systems that may prove insufficiently effective. European countries need to learn to integrate drones, electronic warfare and other technologies into specific combat tasks, taking Ukraine’s experience into account,” he said.
Ukraine has previously offered to teach what it has learned under constant drone attacks and jamming.
The rules that could cost Europe precious minutes
Much of Europe’s critical infrastructure is still underprepared for modern drone threats, Bublyk continued, and even sites with some protection often run systems designed without real combat experience, while Ukraine, which has that experience, is ready to help.
“European countries should use Ukraine’s experience of protecting critical infrastructure and move now from planning to building and deploying the relevant systems,” he said.
He also pointed to a regulatory gap: many European states restrict the use of electronic warfare, including in certain frequency bands, with no clear rules for switching such systems on in a real emergency.
Responsible agencies, he argued, need clear authority and fast-response mechanisms, so no one loses precious time seeking permissions once a threat has already been detected.

Eisenkot vows to use Knesset majority to repeal judicial overhaul, advance October 7 inquiry
Yashar leader calls for immediate parliamentary action before a new government is formed, including mandatory service and greater support for IDF personnel
Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot said Saturday evening that he would seek to use the parliamentary majority opposed to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to advance an October 7 state commission of inquiry, mandatory service and the repeal of judicial overhaul legislation, without waiting for a new government to be formed.
In a statement outlining his plans following Tuesday’s election, Eisenkot called for immediate steps to increase the number of Israelis serving in the IDF and improve compensation and recognition for those who serve.
“Do not let anyone mislead you: in the State of Israel, it is the Knesset that grants its confidence to the government—not the other way around,” he said.
Eisenkot charged that Netanyahu had spearheaded a “culture of lies” that divided Israel, and said the election results reflected a clear demand for change. He promised to pursue his agenda while seeking broad agreement rather than allowing “one side” to overpower the other.
Alongside the parliamentary measures, Eisenkot reiterated his intention to form the broadest possible “Zionist, state-oriented government.” He said any lawmaker willing to accept four principles would be a potential partner: recognition of Israel as Jewish, democratic, liberal and egalitarian; commitment to the Declaration of Independence; military, national or civilian service for all citizens; and recognition of Hamas as a terrorist organization whose military and governing power in Gaza must be destroyed.
He urged an extraordinary effort to avoid another election and a prolonged political crisis. Until a new government is sworn in, he added, he would support military action only in response to direct and immediate threats that could not wait.
The statement came as Eisenkot and Yair Lapid, the No. 2 on Naftali Bennett’s B’Yachad list, met Saturday evening for their first publicly acknowledged talks since the vote. The two said they discussed the results and coordinating their next moves.
Meanwhile, Yisrael Beytenu leader Avigdor Liberman said he had received several approaches regarding the Knesset speakership but had “no desire or intention” of taking the position. His statement followed Friday reports that opposition parties were seeking to replace Likud’s Amir Ohana when the new Knesset is sworn in on November 10.
Eisenkot’s parliamentary strategy faces a significant obstacle: the four parties in the anti-Netanyahu bloc hold 48 seats, with Ra’am and the Joint List accounting for another 19. Cooperation with the Arab parties would therefore be needed to secure a majority, while Liberman has opposed such cooperation and has not clarified whether he would back replacing Ohana. Lapid and Liberman were also expected to meet, according to Channel 12.

Türkiye played problem-solving role at G20 foreign ministers' meeting: Fidan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
18:38:51 UTC
03:38:51 KST

Diyar Guldogan
31 October 2026•Update: 31 October 2026
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said Saturday that Ankara put forward practical proposals to address global crises and strengthen international cooperation during a G20 foreign ministers' meeting in the US city of Atlanta, highlighting Ankara's commitment to a constructive, problem-solving foreign policy.
Speaking to Anadolu and TRT on the sidelines of the gathering, Fidan described this year's meeting as particularly timely given the growing number of global crises, including energy disruptions and mounting pressure on international supply chains.
He said the discussions and contributions from participating countries could help advance efforts to address some of the world's most pressing challenges.
The two-day meeting, hosted by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, served as part of preparations for a G20 leaders' summit set to take place in Miami in December.
Global crises, energy, and supply chains
Fidan said the foreign ministers held three main sessions focusing on global crises, energy security, and disruptions to supply chains.
He pointed to growing bottlenecks in the Black Sea, Gulf, and Red Sea, warning that disruptions in these strategically important waterways are seriously affecting global trade and supply networks.
"Global supply chains have been severely disrupted. Discussions have taken place over how we might remedy or resolve these issues, and what the international community should do in this regard."
Fidan acknowledged that discussions involving Russia and countries supporting Ukraine are "not always easy," particularly when addressing the Black Sea situation and the energy consequences of the Russia-Ukraine war.
However, he stressed that such discussions are necessary to allow countries to clearly communicate their positions and explore potential solutions.
Türkiye seeks constructive role in international crises
Fidan said Türkiye seeks to distinguish itself through meaningful contributions rather than simply taking a different position from other countries.
"Türkiye certainly attaches importance not only to our role as a mediator but also—and more importantly—to taking a stance that is distinct from that of other countries: one that is more constructive and focused on problem-solving.
"In other words, when it comes to international and regional crises, we prioritize taking a stance not for the sake of being different, but for the sake of being genuinely useful," he said.
He added that Ankara presents substantive proposals aimed not only at resolving existing problems but also at addressing structural weaknesses in the international system to prevent similar crises from recurring.
"Although there were heated debates at times, the discussions that took place were substantive. Türkiye puts forward truly serious proposals—both regarding practical solutions to existing problems and concerning the steps that need to be taken in a systemic sense to prevent such issues from recurring. This was significant."
Extensive bilateral diplomatic contacts
Alongside the main sessions, Fidan held bilateral meetings with representatives from more than half of the participating countries, according to his account.
His meetings included Rubio, as well as officials from Russia, the UK, France, Mexico, Germany, the European Union, and Saudi Arabia.
He said the discussions covered both global challenges and regional developments, calling the meetings an important opportunity to exchange views and explore ways to address ongoing crises.
Fidan also credited Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's leadership and Türkiye's diplomatic engagement with strengthening the country's international standing.
"Türkiye is an actor whose voice is needed on the international stage," he said.
Fidan said several urgent issues remain at the forefront of international discussions, particularly the ongoing diplomatic engagement between the US and Iran.
He said countries are closely watching how the negotiations progress and whether another military confrontation can be avoided.
According to Fidan, participating countries broadly share the view that renewed conflict should be prevented and that diplomacy must continue to be given an opportunity.
"Almost all countries are at the negotiating table. They have reached a consensus on preventing further conflict and ensuring that diplomacy is consistently given a chance. This is, of course, a significant point."
He stressed that the same diplomatic approach should be maintained in addressing tensions in the Black Sea and efforts to prevent Israeli "expansionism."

Ukraine hopes European partners will help fund purchase of 500 Patriot missiles – Zelensky

"We have an understanding of what we will have this winter. It is not enough. It is not enough to protect [us]... 500 missiles... We are grateful to the United States. This is a very good offer. Of course, we need to raise funds for this offer. I am confident that we will find the funding with the help of our partners, primarily European ones," he said.
Zelensky noted that deliveries of the missiles had been postponed by several years, partly due to the specifics of their production. At the same time, he said the United States was supplying, or was ready to supply, weapons from its stockpiles to Ukraine only slowly, and that this pace was insufficient to ensure adequate protection for Ukrainians. He also cited the conflict in the Middle East as another challenge affecting the allocation of all aid packages.
He noted that Ukraine continued its work on a bilateral track with Europe and other countries.
"If we were to rely only on the number coming from the United States, it would be... things are already painful for us, and they would be even more painful," he said.
At the same time, Zelensky stressed that the U.S. package remained very important.
"Several times during this war, we have done this... and in various discussions, this arrangement of swapping places in the queue has worked. I will try to do this with some partners. With that package of 500 [missiles], we could get 10, 20 or 30 [missiles] from someone else, sign the relevant guarantees and agreements that we would later replenish those supplies from the U.S. package, with some interest or perhaps without interest. So this is a major ongoing daily effort," he said.
As Ukrinform reported, the U.S. Department of State approved the possible sale to Ukraine of 500 PAC-3 MSE missiles for Patriot air defense systems, worth a total of $2.1 billion.

Police clash with masked rioters after largely peaceful protests across France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
18:23:56 UTC
03:23:56 KST

Clashes have erupted in Paris, Marseille and other cities after tens of thousands of demonstrators, some in Halloween fancy dress, marched across France in a third wave of protests over the cost of living and deteriorating public services.
About 320,000 people – down from an estimated 410,000 last weekend – took part in rallies around the country, the interior ministry said, including 70,000 in Paris who marched along boulevards on the south-eastern outskirts, avoiding the city centre.
As evening approached and the largely peaceful demonstrations came to an end, police in several cities fired teargas and stun grenades to disperse crowds joined – as on the previous Saturday – by groups of masked rioters.
France’s interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said earlier this week 70,000 police and gendarmes, including elite units, would be deployed in an effort to quell violence on the protests’ sidelines, warning that Saturday looked like “a very high risk” day.
The Paris protesters set off peacefully from the Porte de Bagnolet near the ring road, holding placards with slogans including “No need for teargas to make our future look bleak” and “Disguised as an angry citizen for Halloween”, as a helicopter flew overhead
On and around its destination, the Porte de Charenton, dozens of masked people dressed in black used hammers to pry up paving stones and hurl them at police, and at least one incendiary device was thrown at security forces, French media reported.
Police responded with teargas and baton charges. “A hardcore of several hundred rioters” was attacking police with projectiles including a molotov cocktail, the Paris police prefecture said. Officers were “manoeuvring to restore public order”, it added.
In Lyon protesters threw projectiles at police, prompting officers to fire teargas, and in Toulouse police used water cannon against an unauthorised protest that drew several thousand people, mostly young demonstrators.
The marches brought together school students, who have been calling for better conditions for a month, trade unions and gilets jaune (yellow vests) protesters united in anger at the cost of living, widening inequalities and Emmanuel Macron’s government.
“The French economy is doing badly no matter what happens, because today we’re being run by a group of incompetents who juggle billions while families are struggling with a few cents,” said one protester on the Paris march, Jérôme Rodrigues. “That’s why we’re here, to keep shouting our demands louder and louder.”
A protester in Nantes, Camille Guérin, said: “We say no to the cost of living, no to the far right, yes to high school students’ demands, yes to giving citizens a voice.”
Saturday’s rallies came two weeks after widespread street violence and looting rocked numerous French cities during a first wave of mass protest on 17 October that became one of the worst days of civil unrest in the country’s recent history.
Student protesters vowed to stage new high school and university blockades on Tuesday and Thursday. “Then we will join the 5 November demonstration called by workers and trade unions,” said Sabrine Kharbach of the Union Étudiante, a student organisation.
Protests also took place elsewhere in Europe. In Germany, police fired water cannon to disperse protesters who hurled firework and other projectiles at the end of youth-led protests organised by a group called “Gen Z regelt!” (Gen Z will sort this).
Thousands of police were deployed across the country, with tensions rising as evening fell after mostly peaceful demonstrations for “for education, health, the climate and an affordable life” in dozens of cities.
In the western city of Cologne, police fired water cannon to disperse a crowd after saying protesters had targeted officers with fireworks, and a march was also temporarily halted in Frankfurt after protesters set off fireworks.
In Berlin, protesters hurled bottles and eggs while protesters set barricades ablaze in Hamburg, and police were using pepper spray on demonstrators in some places, the newspaper Bild reported.
Police were also on alert in Barcelona after an anonymous TikTok network called Blocus urged new gatherings, and in Italy after recent clashes with protesters in Milan, Turin and Bologna.

HC nixes NIA plea, upholds bail to J&amp;K terror conspiracy accused
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
18:20:44 UTC
03:20:44 KST

NEW DELHI: 
Delhi high court
 has dismissed NIA's appeal against a trial court order granting bail to an alleged over ground worker in J&K, Mateen Ahmed Bhat, in a terror conspiracy case.
A bench of Justices Navin Chawla and Arun Bhardwaj held that the trial court had passed the order after properly considering the restrictions on grant of bail under UAPA and examining whether the accusations against Bhat were prima facie true.
The court further said neither was the bail order a final conclusion on the evidence nor did it discharge the accused. The subsequent framing of charges against Bhat was also deemed irrelevant by the bench while deciding NIA's appeal.
The case relates to an alleged larger conspiracy involving the activities of proscribed terrorist organisations and the use of online platforms and local operatives to spread unrest in J&K.
The high court observed that an appeal against the grant of bail has a limited scope and interference is warranted where the bail order is shown to be illegal, perverse, arbitrary or based on irrelevant considerations.

Authoritarianism sets in when society fears questions: Justice Bhuyan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
18:19:32 UTC
03:19:32 KST

‘Shun the binary of ‘us’ & ‘they’; adopt ‘we’ for unity in diversity,’ said Justice Bhuyan
NEW DELHI: At a time when the opposition has branded the NDA govt authoritarian, Justice Ujjal Bhuyan Saturday said authoritarianism sets in when society fears questions, and stressed people must shed the binary of 'us' and 'they' and adopt the core constitutional philosophy of 'we' to preserve the country's unity in diversity.Speaking at the convocation ceremony of University of Science and Technology Meghalaya, the SC judge said, "A society that fears questions becomes vulnerable to authoritarianism. A society that treats tradition as beyond scrutiny may fail to reform unjust practices."Highlighting Article 51A of the Constitution that casts a duty on every citizen to develop a scientific temperament, Justice Bhuyan said, "It does not merely ask us to acquire scientific knowledge. It asks us to cultivate a temperament which is based on reason. It tells us to inquire, to question, to examine and, where necessary, to reform."He said, "I believe, scientific temperament lays the foundation for the rule of law. This is because arbitrary power thrives on ignorance, fear and unexamined belief. A society that accepts claims without evidence is susceptible to superstitious beliefs and becomes vulnerable to misinformation."
Attaching great importance to debate, he said those who ask questions must also be willing to listen to a different point of view. "Willingness to reason together through a meaningful debate alone can make a society stronger," he said, adding that questions followed by meaningful and healthy debates can happen only when people have access to information.Inspired by Nobel laureate Amartya Sen's 'The Idea of Justice', which he quoted extensively during the speech, Justice Bhuyan elaborated on the difference between 'institutional democracy' and 'functional democracy' and said that a functional democracy requires public questioning and scrutiny. "Circulation of information and scrutiny by public reasoning thus becomes part of the due process by which a democratic society resonates with justice."He said preservation of diversity demands shunning false narratives and the binary of 'us' and 'they'.
"For a more just and humane society, it is important that we move away from the destructive binary of 'us' and 'they' and embrace the idea of oneness," he said."Not for nothing, the Preamble to the Constitution starts with the expression - 'We, the People of India'. The Constitution... speaks to all citizens of India as equal members of the constitutional order. Therefore, 'we' represents a larger idea of belonging in which our individual identities or group identities do not diminish our shared constitutional unity," he said.In what could be construed as indirect opposition to Uniform Civil Code, he said, "It does not require that our individual identities should get subsumed in the larger whole. Diversity, therefore, is not an impediment to the constitutional project; rather, it infuses substance and meaning to it."

Iran has no plans for US talks, conditions must be met first: Araghchi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
18:18:53 UTC
03:18:53 KST

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has said Tehran has no plans to hold talks with US officials, dismissing reports suggesting otherwise as unfounded.
Araghchi said on Saturday that Iran had carefully examined a message sent by US Vice President JD Vance to senior Iranian security official Mohsen Rezaei. The matter remains under review by the relevant authorities, according to the official Iranian news agency IRNA.
He said Iran currently sees no need for talks with Washington and that its conditions are clear, while contacts continue with Qatar and Pakistan as mediators.
A decision on whether negotiations would be direct or indirect would come after the US accepts Iran’s conditions, he added.
Araghchi nevertheless said Vance’s message, alongside US efforts to open dialogue and reach a broader understanding, could be considered a positive step.
Addressing a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days if Iran’s seven conditions are accepted, he said mediators were discussing a shorter timeframe.
“The Qatari side had requested that the time needed to implement our proposal be reduced to five days. At this stage, a proposal to shorten that period to two days is under discussion,” he said.
Prepared for all scenarios
Araghchi said Iran does not rule out the possibility of war and is prepared for all scenarios.
He said reopening the Strait of Hormuz depends on acceptance of a new transit route designated by Iran and Oman, alongside the closure of alternative routes.
Tehran also demands that Washington reinstate the waiver concerning Iranian oil sales and release all frozen Iranian assets, including those held in Qatar.
The Wall Street Journal, citing US officials, previously reported that Vance had sent a message to Rezaei at President Donald Trump’s direction to revive peace talks.
Trump denied the report, saying Vance’s role was limited to helping provide medical supplies needed by Iran.
Mediation efforts continue
Araghchi’s remarks come amid efforts by Qatar and Pakistan to revive negotiations between Washington and Tehran, with reports of progress in indirect talks in Doha.
The mediation seeks understandings on Iran’s nuclear programme, sanctions and navigation security in the Strait of Hormuz.
The US and Israel began attacks on Iran on February 28. Tehran retaliated by targeting Israel and US assets in the region before a ceasefire agreement was reached in April.
Washington and Tehran signed a framework agreement on freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz in June, but implementation stalled over disagreements concerning security in the strait.

China unveils detailed plan for manned moon landing
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
02:08:46 CST
03:08:46 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- China will adopt a "two launches, lunar orbit rendezvous" architecture for its manned lunar exploration program, a senior engineer said on Saturday, as development work for lunar landing advances steadily.
Wang Xiang, deputy chief designer of China's manned space program and chief designer of the lunar exploration program, outlined the plan at the 7th Manned Space Symposium in Beijing.
Under the scheme, two rockets would separately send the Lanyue lunar lander and Mengzhou crewed spaceship into the Earth-moon transfer orbit, and the two spacecraft would perform a rendezvous and docking in the lunar orbit. Astronauts would then transfer from the Mengzhou spaceship into the Lanyue lander for the descent to the lunar surface and subsequent scientific work.
Wang said the approach matches China's existing technical capabilities and infrastructure, and the separate development of the spaceship and lunar lander can help standardize production and support the formation of a long-term family of vehicles.
While the plan also presents considerable challenges, Wang said the new system for mobilizing resources nationwide is the fundamental advantage for addressing them.
He said the program has established system plans, technical standards and quality requirements under a single development framework, and has adopted an integrated design approach with emphasis on interface verification between subsystems.
So far, the development of the Long March-10 carrier rocket, the Mengzhou crewed spaceship and the Lanyue lunar lander has been progressing smoothly.
Major tests already completed include the Mengzhou spaceship's zero-height abort and maximum dynamic pressure escape tests, the Lanyue lander's landing and takeoff test, plus the low-altitude demonstration and validation test for the Long March-10 rocket.
Wang said future lunar exploration should follow the principle of building knowledge and capability before moving into resource utilization, with a prolonged survey phase needed to understand the moon in a steady, step-by-step manner.
He added that manned lunar landing and unmanned lunar exploration share many common elements in key technologies, infrastructure and personnel, and that achievements from the Chang'e lunar exploration program will also support the manned landing effort. ■

The session will be held in Punta Cana, the Dominican Republic. The revised timeline was approved by the IOC Executive Board at a meeting in Dakar ahead of the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games.
Brisbane 2032 will be the first Olympic Games to apply the IOC's new methodology for determining the sports program, introduced under its "Fit for the Future" reforms.
The new approach is designed to give the Olympic program greater flexibility while keeping it relevant and sustainable. Sports disciplines will be assessed against objective criteria, including athlete representation, global appeal, cost and operational complexity.
As the next step, the IOC Executive Board intends to confirm in December 2026 which existing disciplines will be automatically recommended for inclusion in Brisbane 2032, which existing and candidate disciplines will proceed to a comparative assessment, and which candidate disciplines will be excluded from further consideration.
The majority of existing disciplines are expected to be automatically recommended for inclusion in the program.
The IOC said the new methodology was developed in close collaboration with international sports federations. It will help shape decisions on sports programs for future editions of the Olympic Games, with Brisbane 2032 serving as the first test of the new system.
Working with the Brisbane 2032 Organizing Committee, the IOC will apply the methodology with flexibility, taking into account the organizers' advanced preparations and ongoing operational planning.
The Brisbane 2032 Olympic Games is scheduled to take place from July 23 to Aug. 8, 2032. ■

Can high blood sugar help immune cells fight cancer? Study offers new clues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
18:01:05 UTC
03:01:05 KST

NEW DELHI: Could the same high blood sugar that damages the body also make some immune cells better at fighting cancer? New research offers a surprising clue, finding that high blood sugar enhances the tumour-fighting ability of immune cells in mice, potentially opening a new avenue for cancer treatment.Published in The Journal of Immunology, the study examined why people with type 1 diabetes have been found to have a lower risk of certain cancers, including melanoma, breast and colon cancer. Researchers found that the answer may lie in how high blood sugar changes T cells, immune cells that help the body recognise and attack cancer cells.In experiments, tumours grew more slowly in mice with high blood sugar than in mice with normal blood sugar and diabetic mice whose blood sugar was controlled with insulin. The hyperglycaemic mice also had more T cells, which were more effective at controlling tumour growth.The researchers found that high blood sugar altered a cellular signalling pathway in these immune cells, helping enhance their cancer-fighting activity. When diabetic mice received insulin, their T cells lost this heightened ability, pointing to a possible link between blood sugar levels and immune-cell function.
The team then looked for similar changes in humans and found increased activity in the same signalling pathway in immune cells from blood samples of people with high blood sugar. This suggests the mechanism observed in mice may also be relevant to humans, although it does not establish that high blood sugar reduces cancer risk in people.
Dr Anamika Bose, assistant professor at the National Institute of Pharmaceutical Education and Research in India and senior author of the study, said the findings could help researchers develop T-cell-based immunotherapies by replicating the immune-cell changes seen in the experiments.The potential lies not in using high blood sugar as a treatment, but in understanding how it changes immune cells and whether those effects can be reproduced safely through targeted therapies.The findings remain preliminary. The tumour experiments were conducted in mice, and further research is needed to determine whether manipulating the same signalling pathway can improve cancer treatment in humans. The study does not suggest that patients should leave diabetes uncontrolled or alter insulin treatment.
Anuja Jaiswal is a Senior Assistant Editor at The Times of India, with an impressive 18-year career in narrative journalism. She specializes in health and heritage reporting, expertly simplifying complex health information to make it engaging and understandable for readers. Her deep dives into heritage topics are well-researched, resulting in captivating narratives that resonate with her audience. Over the years, she has worked in Chandigarh, Chhattisgarh and West UP, gaining diverse on-ground experience that shapes her storytelling.

Extreme liberals who rely on traditional sources are the most likely to overrate their science knowledge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
18:00:55 UTC
03:00:55 KST

Extreme liberals who relied on offline sources, such as newspapers, television, or friends and family, for scientific information were the most likely of any group to overestimate their scientific knowledge, according to an analysis of General Social Survey data. Extreme liberals who got their science information online were the least likely of any group to do so, a contrast that did not appear among extreme conservatives. The findings were published in Public Understanding of Science.
The internet has fundamentally changed how people access scientific information. It has made it easier than ever to encounter a wide range of opinions about scientific issues. Unlike traditional media, where editors and professional journalists usually decide which information reaches the public, online platforms allow almost anyone to publish their views, regardless of their scientific expertise.
As a result, people searching for scientific information encounter not only established scientific findings but also misleading claims and arguments challenging the scientific consensus. This is particularly important in the United States, where scientific issues such as climate change and the COVID-19 pandemic have become subjects of intense political disagreement and polarization.
Research suggests that political conservatives and liberals differ in their trust in mainstream scientific institutions and the sources they rely on for information. Conservatives are generally more skeptical of mainstream scientific authority, while liberals tend to place greater trust in established scientific institutions. Encountering information that challenges one’s views can affect not only what people think about science but also how confident they feel about their own scientific knowledge.
Study authors Marcus Mann of Purdue University and Cyrus Schleifer of the University of Oklahoma reasoned that the internet might therefore affect liberals and conservatives differently. Liberals who rely on offline sources may rarely encounter views that challenge mainstream science, while online they are more likely to run into such views. Conservatives skeptical of mainstream science, by contrast, may find more challenges to their views offline and more support online.
The researchers examined how political ideology and the sources people use to obtain scientific information relate to confidence in their own scientific knowledge, and how well that confidence matches what they actually know. In particular, they wanted to know whether the link between ideology and scientific confidence differs depending on whether people get scientific information mainly from the internet or from other sources.
To do so, they analyzed General Social Survey data collected between 2006 and 2018. The authors argue this period is well suited to their question because people still varied considerably in where they got scientific information: the share of respondents who named the internet as their main source rose from about 56% in 2006 to 72% in 2018.
The General Social Survey is a large national survey of U.S. adults that has been conducted since 1972 by NORC at the University of Chicago, with a new sample of respondents in each survey year. It asks participants about their attitudes, beliefs, behaviors, and social characteristics. The analysis included 7,177 respondents.
To measure perceived scientific knowledge, the researchers used a question asking how well participants felt they understood the term “scientific study” when they encountered it in news stories. Participants could say they had “a clear understanding of what it means,” “a general sense of what it means,” or “little understanding of what it means.”
To measure actual scientific knowledge, the researchers used the National Science Foundation’s science knowledge scale, which consists of 14 questions. Most are true-or-false statements, such as “The center of the Earth is very hot” and “Father’s genes decide sex of baby,” while others ask about probability and experimental design.
By comparing participants’ confidence with how they scored on the knowledge test, the researchers classified people as overconfident (which the authors call scientific arrogance), underconfident (scientific humility), or accurate in their self-assessment. Participants also reported where they would get information if they wanted to learn about scientific issues such as global warming or biotechnology.
The researchers compared those who named the internet with those who named any offline source, including newspapers, television, books, and friends or family, which the authors refer to as “old media.” The analysis also accounted for education, science coursework, religion, and demographic characteristics.
After accounting for these factors, about 37% of extremely liberal and 35% of extremely conservative participants were predicted to report having “a clear understanding” of what a scientific study is, compared with 29% of moderates. The difference for extreme conservatives, however, fell just short of statistical significance. Overall, people who got their science information online were no more or less confident than those who relied on other sources.
On the knowledge test, liberals tended to score somewhat higher than conservatives, although differences across the political spectrum amounted to no more than about 5 percentage points. Participants who primarily got their information from the internet scored slightly higher than those relying on other sources.
The source of information mattered most for extreme liberals. Among extreme liberals who relied on old media, 53% reported having “a clear understanding” of a scientific study, compared with 30% of extreme liberals who got their information online.
Extreme liberals who relied on old media were also the most overconfident of any group in the study: 39% were classified as overestimating their knowledge and 15% as underestimating it. In every other combination of political ideology and information source, about a third or fewer overestimated their knowledge.
Among extreme liberals who got their information online, only 20% were classified as overconfident, while 29% were underconfident. This contrast between the two groups of extreme liberals was the only difference between media types to reach statistical significance. Extreme conservatives who used the internet showed a small, non-significant shift toward humility, and moderates tended to overestimate rather than underestimate their knowledge regardless of where they got their information.
Additional descriptive analyses suggested that the humbling pattern among liberals was concentrated among those who went online to established outlets, such as online newspapers, magazines, and science websites, rather than social media, search engines, or other nontraditional sources. The authors speculate that such outlets expose people to information that challenges their self-perceptions without the reinforcing echo-chamber effects of social media.
The study contributes to the scientific understanding of the links between scientific knowledge and political identity. However, it should be noted that participants’ confidence in their scientific knowledge was assessed with a single question about understanding the term “scientific study,” while their actual knowledge was assessed using an unrelated set of factual questions. This makes direct comparisons between the two measures problematic, and studies comparing people’s confidence in specific scientific facts with their knowledge of those same facts might yield different results.
The data were also cross-sectional, so it is not known whether getting information online humbles extreme liberals or whether more humble liberals are drawn to online sources. Extreme liberals and extreme conservatives each made up less than 4% of the sample, the “old media” category combined very different sources, and the data end in 2018, before more recent shifts in the online information landscape.
The paper, “Does medium matter? Political orientation and variability in scientific self-perceptions,” was authored by Marcus Mann and Cyrus Schleifer.

Em-Estudio lines Mexico City bar with walls of books

Em-Estudio lines Mexico City bar with walls of books
The vintage bookstores of Mexico City‘s Roma neighbourhood influenced the interiors of this basement bar, designed by local outfit Em-Estudio.
Located below an early 20th-century house in the Mexican capital’s historic colonia, Libreria Valladolid was designed to evoke the experience of exploring old bookshops.
“It captures the thrill felt when entering these places, searching for a unique story that has patiently waited among thousands of books on all topics and from many eras,” said Em-Estudio.
Accessed from the street through an unassuming door, the entry vestibule features shelves packed with old volumes and more stacks along a wooden staircase that descends to another threshold.
Small lamps are squeezed between the spines and placed on top of the stacks, creating a moody glow that sets the scene for the bar beyond.
“The old bookstore is encountered upon entering, as you descend the stairs, and it remains behind as you cross the first threshold, where the books transform into the skin that embraces the rooms,” said the studio.
Inside the basement, dark herringbone flooring and surfaces drenched in burgundy continue the bookshop atmosphere.
The larger walls are lined entirely with shelves filled with books stacked spine inwards, so the warm beige of their pages faces the room.
Cove lighting illuminates the books, creating a dramatic contrast with the otherwise shadowy bar, while banquettes below are accompanied by circular marble tables for placing drinks.
“The pages of thousands of books resting on bookshelves that reach the ceiling shed their literal meaning, becoming a tapestry in shades of white that only time can give, bathed in a gradient of warm light,” Em-Estudio said.
Other areas such as the DJ booth, the bar and the bathrooms are highlighted with gold leaf and brass to draw the eye.
A further hidden lounge space is disguised by another bookshelf, decorated with cans and objects that “evoke a grocery-store bar”.
This room swaps burgundy for green, applied in gloss across the ceiling and appearing in a long marble table that runs through the centre.
Dark wood Van Beuren chairs with yellow upholstery are lined up along each side, parallel to more walls of books that are uplit along each shelf.
A mirror that covers the back wall visually doubles the space, extending the table and the bookshelves in the reflection.
Em-Estudio was co-founded by architect Ivan Esqueda and interior designer Gala Sánchez-Renero – a husband and wife who also operate individual practices.
Their previous collaborations include a holiday home on a steep hillside in Oaxaca, Mexico, built from coloured concrete chosen to blend into the rocky mountainside.

====================================================================================================

The government knows it has a problem, does it have a clear path forward?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

analysis
A safe bet Labor is in for a rough economic ride this Melbourne Cup Day
Forget the form guide. The closest thing to a sure bet this Melbourne Cup Day is another rate rise.
And unlike the punters at Flemington, millions of Australians won't have a say in how much it costs them.
The average household bears no responsibility for the wars, oil crisis and AI boom that are driving up inflation, but that doesn't save them from the economic pain.
It's why Labor's emphasis on these international factors is wearing thin with voters, who want workable solutions and help rather than explanations or excuses.
As pressure builds on the Albanese government, the remarkable caucus discipline of the past four years is fraying by the day.
The difficult economic outlook has been compounded by a succession of own goals, failures of process and poor consultation, which have sparked a litany of post-budget backdowns.
The accumulation has taken a toll, with many Labor MPs feeling like they have been left to defend decisions they had little say in shaping.
Internal discontent and anonymous griping are at a notably high watermark.
There are apparently plenty of people in government able to diagnose the problems, but what's lacking is articulation of a clear path forward.
All eyes on MYEFO
Markets are pricing a more than 80 per cent chance the Reserve Bank will lift the cash rate to 4.85 per cent on Tuesday, a level not seen since the global financial crisis in 2008.
As households do what they must to absorb the cost, focus on the federal government's role in the inflation fight will only sharpen.
Gone are the days of energy rebates and slashing the fuel excise, now almost all of the political debate is about how to cut public spending to help the RBA.
All this makes next month's mid-year economic and fiscal outlook (MYEFO) an unusually important moment for the government.
Having already promised savings to help ease demand in the economy, Treasurer Jim Chalmers was this week asked if the December update would result in a "net" reduction in government spending.
He pointed out that in this year's budget and the last MYEFO, net policy decisions had made a "positive contribution over the four years" of the budget.
That is true over the forwards, but when it comes to fighting inflation, it's the shorter term that really matters. And for the current and last financial year, government decisions in those two updates added about $14 billion to the overall spend.
There is no shortage of Labor MPs who believe this MYEFO must be different, with terms like "means testing" and "net savings" a constant refrain in private conversations.
Albanese heads to CHOGM
None of this is news to Chalmers, as evidenced by his own camp pointing out it is the prime minister who ultimately rules the all-powerful expenditure review committee, where such decisions are signed off.
That sparked some ministers in Albanese's corner to argue the prime minister had been prudent in reining in some of the treasurer's budget ambitions.
The apparent deterioration in the relationship between Albanese and Chalmers has started to concern some in Labor, who fear the more time spent apportioning blame for recent events, the less the government appears focused on solutions.
Chalmers caused some raised eyebrows when he this week suggested that while he "genuinely" took responsibility for some of the "hard stuff" in the budget causing political pain for Labor, it was also up to "other ministers and the prime minister how they describe their part in that".
Whether or not the treasurer is unfairly copping the bulk of the criticism, as one Labor MP noted, it "matters little" to voters who "will be just as happy to blame us all".
That is likely precisely what will happen on Tuesday when the Reserve Bank is expected to lift the cash rate.
Chalmers will be left to manage the immediate fallout at home, while Albanese lands in the Caribbean for the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM).
Those optics are not lost on the Coalition, which already started using Question Time last week to needle the prime minister about his impending absence.
The decision to attend CHOGM has puzzled many of Albanese's colleagues.
As the prime minister himself revealed, the request came directly from King Charles, and while there Albanese will hold talks with UK leader Andy Burnham and Canada's Mark Carney.
The hope is voters will understand the need for Australia to engage on the world stage, particularly when so many of the forces affecting its economy originate overseas.
But with the demands of summit season dragging Albanese abroad for almost four of the next seven weeks, expect his detractors to give the "Airbus Albo" moniker a workout.
The prime minister has ridden out plenty of political turbulence before, but this time the economic headwinds are being compounded by growing frustration within his own ranks.
Whatever happens at the Melbourne Cup, at least someone will finish the day a winner. The same can't be said for either Albanese or Chalmers.

Banks sitting on billions in savers' money as interest rates rise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Banks sitting on billions in customer savings that don't grow with interest rate hikes
In short:
The big four banks' annual reports show they are sitting on billions in customers' money that is not earning interest.
Consumer advocates fear stringent conditions attached to high-interest savings accounts contribute to a broader issue.
What's next?
Savers are being urged to be aware of the terms and conditions and shop around.
Savers with billions of dollars in Australian banks could be missing out on the benefit of rising cash interest rates as a result of onerous account conditions or because they have not opted for the right type of savings product.
Data compiled for the ABC by comparison site Canstar shows following the last RBA interest hike announcement the Commonwealth Bank, NAB, ANZ and Westpac each increased their maximum saving rates by 0.20 or 0.25 per cent.
Consumer advocates fear some of that money is sitting in high-interest savings accounts that come with strict conditions, including regular contribution amounts, and customers are falling just shy.
The competition regulator found in a 2023 retail deposits inquiry more than 70 per cent of customers never met the monthly conditions.
While each of the major banks were quick to increase the interest paid on mortgages after the September rate hike, customers with high interest savings accounts have not been finding the corresponding interest rate increases as lucrative.
Canstar said it found the rate increases were applied only to a select few of the banks' savings account products, and with strict conditions attached.
Unless savers meet those requirements they reverted to a base rate for interest that the banks have kept flat at 0.10 per cent.
That means one slip-up, for example, missing the target for the minimum monthly deposit, or forgetting about the minimum withdrawal requirements, and savers receive virtually zero in interest.
Then there are customers who do not make the most of rate hikes at all, with the big four banks sitting on hundreds of billions of dollars of customers' money in accounts that are earning no interest.
As of June, the Commonwealth Bank held nearly $122 billion of its customers money in accounts earning no interest, according to its annual report.
Westpac held nearly $82 billion as of March, while NAB held about $67 billion, and ANZ held about $61 billion in the same period.
Banks need to be more proactive
Canstar's Sally Tindall said when banks announced they were passing rate rises it was not as clear-cut as it appeared.
"Many customers will miss out, at least from time to time, because they don't meet those terms and conditions," she said.
She argued banks could be doing more to ensure their customers did not miss out.
"Alerting people with a proactive email or text message … close to the end of the month that tells you if you're not going to meet those terms and conditions,"
she said.
Melbourne saver Corey Washbourne said he did not find the conditions on his account too onerous. He adds about $50 a month to get the bonus rate.
He is thankful for the higher interest rates on his savings accounts, because it is protecting the value of his savings against inflation and gives him breathing room.
"It's just reassuring to know that you've got that interest coming into your savings account to top it up and act as that buffer, and you're not going backwards as much.
"There's that little bit of cushion and breathing room".
In a statement to the ABC, the Australian Banking Assocation's chief executive Simon Birmingham said banks supported customers to get the most out of their savings, including through app alerts and messages.
"Australia's savings market is highly competitive, with hundreds of term deposit and savings account options available to customers," he said.
Across the last financial year, Mr Birmingham said banks paid out more than $120 billion in interest to depositors.
"Product offerings from banks do vary and this choice gives customers the flexibility to choose products that best suit their personal circumstances," he said.
Billions of dollars not earning interest
On top of marginal interest repayments, many Australians are missing out on the opportunity to make a bit of extra cash each month from choosing a bank account that pays no interest.
The ACCC inquiry found only 16 per cent of consumers switched their savings account in the past three years, and only 11 per cent have switched their transaction account.
Western Sydney University associate professor of accounting and financial planning Michelle Cull said consumers should be conducting "regular checks" of their banking to ensure they were getting the best deal.
Dr Cull said, for example, by exploring the option of an offset account.
"Because you are actually going to be saving the interest rate that has just gone up for paying the mortgage,"
she said.
"Plus you're not paying tax on it [compared to interest on savings], so there's an extra saving there."
But she emphasised every situation was unique, and it was important for consumers to read the fine print.
"You really need to look carefully at your own circumstances."
Behind those shiny numbers that the banks promote on their savings products, Dr Cull said there could be several caveats.
"Remembering an introductory rate is only for a limited time," she said.
RBA meets again to discuss interest rates
The Reserve Bank will meet again next week, to decide whether interest rates will hike again, for a fifth time this year, with the goal of curbing inflation.
Earlier this month, Reserve Bank deputy governor Andrew Hauser said the inflation outlook was "materially worse" than the RBA had forecast, lifting the odds of a hike in November.
Markets are putting the chances of a rate rise at 98 per cent.
Ms Tindall said if customers were not happy with their savings account, they could "take your nest egg shopping".
"There's a huge amount of banks to pick from. There's a huge amount of options even within the same bank,"
she said.

Olivia wasn't expected to live more than a few days, now she's a movie star
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Actor Olivia Hargroder was not expected to live more than a few days after she was born. She's now 27.
She was probably not going to talk. She's a chatterbox.
She was not expected to walk very well. She dances.
In fact, Olivia dances so well that when she was cast in the lead role of feature film Boss Cat as the rhythm-lacking Sonja, it took all Olivia's acting skills to pull it off.
"Once I found out that Sonja's not the best dancer, I found that quite hard to do," Olivia tells Australian Story with a sassy giggle. "Because I'm such a good and amazing dancer myself."
Confidence is not something Olivia lacks and it's a quality her mother, Kerry Read, says has helped Olivia rise above the low expectations many impose on people with Down syndrome.
"Anyone who meets Olivia will know optimism is her key operating system," Kerry says. "She's so optimistic, she's so confident.
"It's very easy when you're constantly put down in life to actually be demotivated. Life as someone with an intellectual impairment is full of those … [who] aren't optimistic about you."
By the time Olivia consulted her school careers counsellor, she'd almost completed her final year at a mainstream school and had become so adept at public speaking that she'd addressed the United Nations (UN) in New York on World Down Syndrome Day.
She told the counsellor her next ambition was to study at the National Institute of Dramatic Arts (NIDA), one of Australia's most prestigious acting schools.
He just laughed, told her NIDA was for "the elite" and suggested she instead work in a bakery, which, Olivia quips, "is definitely very hard when you're gluten-free".
She got into NIDA. For one year, she studied with 12 budding thespians at its Open Young Actor's Studio, before undertaking other acting courses.
Then, in 2021, she started acting with Bus Stop Films, a disability-led organisation that works with about 250 young adults with intellectual disability, autism or Down syndrome to create films and equip them with skills to get jobs in the industry.
"When they asked me to audition for Boss Cat, it was actually an incredible feeling to have because I've never been a lead in a feature before," says Olivia, who lives in Redcliffe, north of Brisbane.
"It was just a dream come true."
Loading...
Olivia has other dreams. The one she's held the longest is to dance on Broadway in musicals. Her absolute biggest dream, she says, is to be a dancer on tour with her idol, Taylor Swift.
Unachievable? Don't tell Olivia that, says Kerry.
"She does have huge dreams and sometimes," Kerry says, "the most unachievable dreams she actually achieves."
'Incompatible with life'
At her routine 20-week pregnancy scan, Kerry was told her baby had a heart condition that was "apparently incompatible with life".
She was advised "very, very strongly" to have a termination.
But Kerry's desire to hold her third child in her arms for as long as she was granted — "moments, days, whatever" — overruled the experts.
When Olivia was born, Kerry, a 40-something physiotherapist at the time, knew immediately that her daughter had Down syndrome.
"She had a gap between her first and second toes which is so classic of Down syndrome," says Kerry, who had not had scans to detect the chromosomal condition.
"But it didn't matter because every moment was precious and I never really thought that her Down syndrome was a problem. It was just, 'How long was she going to live?'"
Having survived the first few days, it was hoped Olivia would make it to three months before undergoing surgery on the hole in her heart but, at nine weeks, she was deteriorating and whisked into surgery.
She had a 20 per cent chance of survival. "I always say she's a sparky kid and she is determined to hang on," Kerry says. "And hang on she did."
To Olivia, her mum is a "superwoman".
"It wasn't just the doctors and nurses who saved my life," she says. "It was my mum."
Life-changing surgery
Kerry was told Olivia would probably not be able to speak, or her speech would be delayed. So, when Olivia was four months old, Kerry started teaching her, along with her other daughters Emily and Lucy, how to sign.
Through play, she worked on improving Olivia's low muscle tone (which is characteristic of Down syndrome), exposed her to sensory stimulation and ensured Olivia made her own choices.
Says Emily: "Mum never limited her but Mum never forced her to do anything either. I think that's really important too, that it wasn't, 'We're going to defy the odds'. It was just Olivia is who she is."
And Olivia knew she was a dancer. She loved learning routines with her sisters and dancing to music videos.
But her kneecaps were badly misaligned and as she got older, she fell over a lot, injuring herself.
"I used to get a number of fractures," Olivia says, "but I always managed to bounce back. I always do."
By her mid-teens, and still at school, Olivia was desperate to have an operation to fix her knees.
She and Kerry had consulted a number of orthopaedic surgeons when Olivia was younger but the operation could not be done until her growth plates had fused. Surgeons were also concerned about her heart (which required further surgery when she was 18) and the need for intensive rehabilitation, which some doubted a young person with Down syndrome would do.
But Olivia was determined and, at 15, she sat down and wrote a letter to one of the surgeons she'd consulted, Jeremy Bartlett.
It read, in part:
"Dear Dr Bartlett, Can you please help me with these things that I want to do? I really want to stop falling over and I also want to stop breaking bones."
Dr Bartlett says he was moved by the letter and decided to operate on one knee. Olivia was so committed to her rehab and improved so well, her second knee was operated on soon after.
"It changed my life," Olivia says. "I could run, I could jump, I could dance, I can do anything I wanted … I'm so, so grateful because I am just so happy to be where I am right now and with my dancing. It's just an incredible place to be."
A star is born
Dressed in hot pink and purple all the way down to her glittering dancing shoes, Olivia's Boss Cat character Sonja is on board a bus, krumping up a storm.
Krumping, a high-energy street dance, play a big role in the film — used as an outlet for Sonja, who has special needs, to express her anger at the death of her mother and a plan by her grandmother to move her into an assisted-care home.
Genevieve Clay-Smith, the co-founder of Bus Stop Films and writer and director of Boss Cat, beams as she remembers that day of filming and how Olivia "gobbled it up".
"Basically, the brief was 'be a pop star' and own that bus," she says. "And Olivia brought the attitude; she really channelled pop star vibes that day."
Genevieve says the moment she met Olivia she had a "visceral sensation in my gut" that she had found Sonja. After a rigorous audition process, she knew she was right.
Apart from her talent, Genevieve saya, Olivia is curious, asks insightful questions about her character and listens well to direction.
"I love being in front of the camera so much," Olivia says. "It just makes my whole world look just incredible … I love the freedom."
Before filming, the duo held weekly teleconferences to run through the script and to find ways to channel the types and depth of emotions required for a scene.
To improve her range, Olivia created a coloured mood chart as a way to indicate that a scene required rage, joy or sadness, or a combination of those. It also helped protect her from being consumed by Sonja's emotions.
"Olivia has this gift of being able to feel deeply and to really invest and find her emotional truth," Genevieve says. "The chart … helped her harness the emotions rather than letting the emotions take over her."
Genevieve's hope is that Olivia will be cast in future roles because she's a great actress, not a great actress with Down syndrome.
"I hope that she gets to do more amazing performances that draw in audiences, captivate people, and that satisfy her and fulfil her as an actress," she says.
A home of her own
Olivia reckons she and Sonja are quite different but there are similarities. They both have a strong group of friends and dream of living independently.
"My dream is to hopefully live with my boyfriend one day," Olivia says. "It's always been my dream for the longest time."
She met her "handsome, gorgeous" boyfriend, Jarred, at Bus Stop Films about a year ago, and he was there to see Olivia walk the red carpet in a stunning pink gown at the movie's premiere at the Sydney Film Festival. It is set for general release on December 3, the International Day of People with a Disability.
Olivia's mother Kerry sees no reason her daughter's dream of living away from home cannot be realised.
"She manages perfectly well when I'm not here and will perfectly well manage her own household," she says.
"I think it's important that … there's not just an assumption that all people with Down syndrome will be forever someone's child. Her thoughts and her feelings are just the same as everyone else's and she's perfectly capable of taking agency over her own life."
Olivia's sister Lucy says Kerry has plans in place for when that time arrives, with Olivia needing some support "so she can be the most fulfilled that she can be".
"Olivia goes around smashing all your boxes," Lucy says. "She's just like, 'I don't fit in that box'. Smash!
"And she just keeps doing that. And as her sister, you have no choice but to go on that journey with her. And it makes you a bigger person. And it makes you a better person. And it makes you see the world differently."
For now, Olivia is happy to keep dancing, acting, working at a major supermarket, going to coffee with Jarred and zipping around in her fully enclosed mobile scooter, dubbed the Popemobile.
Throughout her life, she's met people who see disability before they see the person, but Olivia likes to see the best in people and simply asks that others do too.
"I would say, 'Give people with Down syndrome a red hot go'," Olivia says. "They always bring something special to the table that you might not know.
"I would encourage you to take that special person into your heart … because you'll never know what they'll surprise you with."

Details

A reset at the Constitutional Tribunal is necessary — numerous political parties agree on this. This was also emphasized by President Karol Nawrocki and the legitimate President of the Constitutional Tribunal, Bohdan Święczkowski

Nigeria reports two suspected Ebola cases in northeast region
JOHANNESBURG, Oct 31 - Health authorities in Nigeria are investigating two suspected Ebola cases in the country's northeast region, the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention said on Saturday.
The two individuals have been isolated while officials carry out contact identification, listing and laboratory testing, authorities said in a post on X.
The cases remain suspected and confirmation is subject to laboratory results, the post added.
Nigeria confirmed its first Ebola case in more than a decade last week in a Swiss woman who had travelled to Uganda and then returned to the capital Abuja in central Nigeria. She and her husband were evacuated to Switzerland on Monday.
The two additional cases, if confirmed, could mean that the disease has spread within Nigeria, which would be a major public health concern. Authorities did not say whether they were believed to be linked to the first case.
The centre of Africa's Ebola outbreak is in Democratic Republic of Congo, where more than 5,000 people have died since it was declared in May. Kenya and Uganda have also reported cases.
There are no approved treatments or vaccines to combat the rare Bundibugyo species, which is behind the Congo outbreak. REUTERS

Logistics robots, drink-making robots and pet-companion robots crowded the intelligent robotics area at the fair, which is being held from Oct. 15 to Nov. 4 in Guangzhou, capital of south China's Guangdong Province.
At the booth of Hangzhou Taixi Intelligent Technology Co., Ltd., buyers lined up to try out a consumer waist-assist exoskeleton. Many overseas buyers held the handrail and shuffled forward, step by step, to feel how the device relieves pressure on their lower limbs.
It is the first flagship product to integrate its human-oriented physical AI technology roadmap, said company founder Liang Linchao. The device uses waist motors and sensors to detect movement and assist lower-limb mobility. Its weight has been cut to about 2 kg, and alongside a refined appearance, algorithms and gait plans tailored to elderly people and hemiplegic patients have been added.
The cluster of cutting-edge smart equipment reflects a broader push toward industrial innovation. At this fair, 64 percent of exhibitors have integrated the industrial internet and artificial intelligence into R&D and production, and new products accounted for 23.2 percent of exhibits, marking a record high.
A visitor tries smart office supplies on display at the Canton Fair in Guangzhou, south China's Guangdong Province, Oct. 15, 2026. (Xinhua/Lu Hanxin)
 
"At today's Canton Fair, consumer electronics are the dominant category, and tech products such as new energy storage, embodied intelligence and smart healthcare are eye-catching, with many cutting-edge Chinese-made products making their debut," said Zhang Li, an official with the Ministry of Commerce.
Nearby, several European buyers closely watched the scrolling data at DSL Tech Group's booth. The AI-POOL low-chlorine intelligent pool system uses sensor probes to collect the pool's real-time indicators such as residual chlorine, pH level, turbidity and water pressure, and automatically coordinates pumps, disinfection units and sand-filter backwash systems.
Chen Meixiang, the representative of the company, demonstrated on her phone how users can receive alerts about water quality abnormalities from thousands of miles away. The system adjusts automatically, so staff no longer need to visit regularly to take samples and mix chemicals.
People visit the Smart Health exhibition area during the Canton Fair in Guangzhou, south China's Guangdong Province, Oct. 15, 2026. (Xinhua/Deng Hua)
 
"Many overseas private pools used to rely on maintenance workers visiting once a week, and water quality would easily exceed standards," Chen said. These European clients are mainly pool operation and maintenance service providers, attracted by the system's ability to cut manual maintenance costs.
These technology-driven products are also reflected in trade data. Customs statistics show that in the first three quarters of 2026, China's total imports and exports of industrial robots, electronic components, computer parts and electrical equipment exceeded 10 trillion yuan (1.49 trillion U.S. dollars), up 58.9 percent year on year, driving overall import and export growth by 11.3 percentage points.
A robot demonstrates stair climbing skills at the Canton Fair in Guangzhou, south China's Guangdong Province, Oct. 15, 2026. (Xinhua/Deng Hua)
 
Liu Chun, president of the China Chamber of Commerce for Import and Export of Machinery and Electronic Products, said that driven by technological innovation and industrial upgrading, high-tech and high-value-added products are gradually becoming the main growth engine of foreign trade, pushing "China's smart manufacturing" toward the high end of global industrial and value chains.
This service-oriented approach is visible at the booth of Shandong Linuo Paradigma Co., Ltd., where sales staff explained tailored plans to buyers from different continents.
"Africa lacks power and is windy and dusty, so we cut costs and provide solar water-heating systems that are easy to install and run without electricity," a staff member of the company said. "The Middle East wants high quality, so we match energy-saving products with high-standard certification, and South Asia emphasizes large capacity and durability, so we strengthen system adaptability."
The company has set up agent systems and localized service outlets in markets of Belt and Road partner countries, combining Chinese manufacturing, German-partnered technology and global service into a competitive edge.
Beyond individual products, the latest edition of the Canton Fair also features a batch of prefabricated new products, including space capsules, portable integrated kitchens and modular homestay houses. Chinese suppliers are moving from selling parts to selling whole houses, and integrated overseas expansion is supporting a new growth path.
"By launching prefabricated building solutions for cultural tourism camps, we have attracted buyers from Australia, Brazil, and Saudi Arabia among other countries, and more than 300 have reached preliminary agreements. We will continue to use project meetings to deliver full-chain services from planning to design, construction and operation," said Jia Xuehong, planning and design director of Chongqing SUNDON Prefabricated Construction and Technology Co., Ltd.
Overseas buyers hold talks during the 140th Canton Fair in Guangzhou, south China's Guangdong Province, Oct. 18, 2026. (Xinhua/Deng Hua)
 
More and more foreign trade companies are shifting from simply taking orders and shipping goods to building systems and exporting supporting services. At the fair, 36.5 percent of exhibitors have started a transformation of "product plus service."
For the first time, the trade services zone covers all 10 major categories of producer services, including logistics and warehousing, industrial design, overseas operation and maintenance, cross-border investment and financing and other supporting services, building a one-stop support platform for companies expanding overseas.
Yang Jie, secretary-general of the Guangdong Industrial Design Association, said that under an industrial design and R&D approach that runs through the whole life cycle and centers on consumer pain points, more and more Chinese companies are winning favor in more markets by integrating design into the early stages of development and coordinating it with technology to deliver innovative products and solutions.
Overseas buyers view a solar panel cleaner during the Canton Fair in Guangzhou, south China's Guangdong Province, Oct. 15, 2026. (Xinhua/Lu Hanxin)
 
Green products are another highlight. Amid the global energy transition, green products and low-carbon technologies have become highly sought-after in international markets. At the fair, exhibitor Xiamen HiTHIUM Energy Storage Technology focused on showcasing its flagship long-duration energy storage products, presenting stable and reliable long-duration power supply solutions to overseas buyers.
Wang Pengcheng, co-founder and CEO of the company, said more and more countries and regions are advancing energy structure transition, and the company hopes that through the Canton Fair, the "Chinese solution" for long-duration energy storage can be seen by the world, so that more countries have the option of using stable, green and affordable clean power.
China is enriching global supply with quality green and smart products and helping accelerate the global green, low-carbon and digital and intelligent transition. Over the past decade, China has provided more than 80 percent of the world's photovoltaic modules and 70 percent of its wind power equipment, effectively driving down the cost of global wind and solar power generation.
Commenting on the trend, Liang Yutian, associate dean of the Institute of International and Regional Studies, Sun Yat-sen University, said the concentrated display of new energy, energy storage equipment, green home appliances and other products reflects the global green transition forming new market demand. In the future, around the digital economy, green energy, smart manufacturing and low-carbon technologies, countries can further strengthen technological cooperation, industrial coordination and standards alignment to cultivate new international growth points.
From continuous breakthroughs in hard technology to complete solutions stepping into the spotlight, and green thinking embedded in products, the innovation vitality surging at the Canton Fair illustrates how China's foreign trade keeps cultivating new advantages and deepening its links with the world.
