How to save money
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
17:53:44 UTC
02:53:44 KST

How to save money
Small purchases, overlapping installments and annual bills can leave little money before payday. For World Savings Day, Qazinform News Agency explores how to make room for savings.
Marked on October 31, the day promotes saving and financial education. Saken Nigmashev, Bank CenterCredit’s communications director, shared practical steps for managing household spending.
Start with the money you already spend
Before setting a savings target, look through a full month of transactions. Your banking app’s spending categories can help show where the money goes.
Cash takes more effort to track. A withdrawal shows how much you took out, but not what you bought.
Nigmashev recommends recording what withdrawn money will cover before those details slip your mind. Budgeting apps can also help, provided you enter expenses consistently.
Pay particular attention to purchases that seem too small to count.
“Small daily expenses add up to substantial spending over a month,” he said.
For illustration, spending 1,500 tenge daily adds up to 45,000 tenge over 30 days. Seeing the monthly total gives you a clearer basis for deciding what to cut.
Make saving part of payday
Waiting until month-end means your savings depend on whatever survives the spending.
Nigmashev recommends moving money into savings as soon as income arrives.
“Make it your first action and your first transaction, and turn it into a habit. Call it ‘pay yourself first,’” he said.
An automatic transfer can make that habit easier to maintain. Choose an amount that leaves enough for essential bills and everyday needs.
What if saving 10% feels impossible? Start with an amount you can afford. The US Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation recommends this approach when a fixed percentage is unrealistic. Increase contributions as your budget allows.
Give annual expenses a monthly place
School supplies, birthday gifts and planned repairs may arrive outside your usual monthly routine. They still belong in the budget.
Nigmashev suggests estimating irregular expenses across a calendar year, then dividing the total by 12.
For example, expected annual costs of 240,000 tenge would require 20,000 tenge monthly. This is an illustrative calculation, rather than a recommended household budget.
He recommends keeping that money in a separate deposit account with flexible withdrawal rules.
Predictable bills also differ from emergencies. A birthday has a date; an unexpected loss of income does not.
The US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau describes emergency savings as money for unplanned financial shocks. It recommends keeping that reserve safe and accessible.
Add up installments before adding another
A small monthly payment can look manageable when viewed alone. Several payments compete for the same salary.
Nigmashev says shoppers need stable income and a clear limit for installment payments. He gives 15–20% of income as an example of a self-imposed limit.
That example is not a universal affordability rule. Rent, existing debts and essential expenses leave different households with different amounts available.
“If you are approaching your limit, avoid new purchases until you repay earlier ones,” he said.
Before taking another installment plan, total the payments you already owe each month. Then check how much income remains for other expenses and savings.
Check which purchases actually earn cashback
Nigmashev recommends reviewing card offers for different spending categories and individual retailers. These offers often change monthly, he noted.
Some customers use different banks’ cards to match purchases with available rewards.
The useful starting point is your existing shopping plan. Check which offers apply to purchases you already intended to make.
A reward on an extra purchase still leaves you spending money.
For illustration, 5% cashback on a 20,000-tenge purchase returns 1,000 tenge. You have still spent 19,000 tenge, assuming the full cashback applies.
Check recurring charges before cutting everyday pleasures
Review your statements for subscriptions, apps and services you no longer use.
Cancel unused subscriptions and set reminders before free trials end. For services you keep, check whether a cheaper plan meets your needs.
Plan grocery shopping around what you already have
Check your fridge, freezer and cupboards before making a shopping list. Plan meals around ingredients that need using soon.
Compare prices per kilogram or liter, rather than per package. Larger packs are only worthwhile if you can use or store the contents.
Plan for evenings when you have little time to cook. Keeping ingredients for a quick dinner can help you avoid ordering delivery.
Pause before making an unplanned purchase
If a purchase can wait, give yourself 24 hours before paying. For expensive items, take longer to compare options.
Add the item to a wish list and revisit it once the excitement fades.
Removing saved card details adds a pause before checkout. Turning off promotional notifications gives you fewer reasons to browse.
Break your monthly budget into weekly amounts
After setting aside money for bills and savings, calculate what remains until payday. Divide that amount across the remaining weeks, allowing for any extra days.
For example, 80,000 tenge over four weeks gives you 20,000 tenge per week.
Use this money for variable expenses, such as groceries, transportation and entertainment. Check your balance during the week, while you still have time to adjust.
Keep money for upcoming bills separate. Part of your account balance may already be committed to rent or loan payments.

Exclusive: US delegation to join Iran talks as war fears grow

The breakthrough followed more than 12 hours of negotiations in Tehran on Friday involving a Qatari mediation delegation headed by a senior adviser to Qatar's prime minister and foreign minister.

An Iranian source confirmed to The New Arab that negotiations were continuing indirectly through mediators, adding that an Iranian deputy foreign minister was in Doha to facilitate discussions with the Qatari delegation.

Countries reach COP17 deal to speed up biodiversity action, but money still short
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31

02:46:35 KST

Countries reach COP17 deal to speed up biodiversity action, but money still short
LONDON, Oct 31 - Governments at a UN conference that ended on Saturday have agreed to step up efforts to protect global biodiversity after talks ran through the night, although the finance to deliver it remains elusive.
The two-week COP17 conference in Armenia's capital came against a fractious political backdrop, and as the world prepares for fresh climate talks in Turkey starting November 9.
The talks in Yerevan oversaw the first global review of the Global Biodiversity Framework agreed in Montreal four years ago. While progress had been made, delegates agreed it was not enough, with the world off track on almost all of its targets.
After intense talks, governments adopted a decision dubbed the Yerevan Pathway, agreeing faster action on areas such as reducing harmful subsidies, increasing finance for developing countries, and aligning national spending with biodiversity goals.
They acknowledged that action so far had been insufficient, and set out priorities to accelerate efforts through to 2030.
"At a time when multilateralism is under pressure, COP17 has shown that international cooperation can still deliver," said Anita de Horde, executive director of the Finance for Biodiversity Foundation.
"The real success of COP17 will be measured by what governments implement before COP18," she said, which delegates agreed would be held in the Ecuadorean capital, Quito, in 2028.
The framework agreed in Montreal set goals including conserving 30% of land, inland waters, marine and coastal areas by 2030, restoring 30% of degraded ecosystems, reforming harmful subsidies, and mobilising $200 billion a year to help pay to preserve biodiversity.
Nearly 90% of parties to the biodiversity convention had set national targets, although fewer than half of those assessed were on track, the UN said.
REVIEW SENT 'STRONG SIGNAL'
Daudi Sumba, chief conservation officer at WWF International, said the review of progress had sent a "strong signal", but it needed to be backed up with finance.
Organisers said more than $1.8 billion in finance from governments, philanthropies and investors had been announced during the conference.
On the issue of biodiversity-harming subsidies, governments agreed to accelerate efforts towards the existing target of reducing harmful incentives by at least $500 billion a year by 2030.
Delegates also agreed to review existing funding arrangements, set criteria for a future permanent financing mechanism and voluntarily broaden the contributor base, although some said progress overall remained too slow.
"We cannot just plod on to 2030 without a course correction," said Catherine Weller, global policy director at non-profit Fauna & Flora. REUTERS

China expands, diversifies space launch infrastructure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
17:42:20 UTC
02:42:20 KST

A typical example is a commercial rocket carrying nine satellites that lifted off from a ship in the East China Sea near Shanghai in September this year. Although the densely populated economic hub has no traditional rocket launch site, sea-based launches are able to connect Shanghai to the country's growing space industry.
China's first sea launch took place in 2019, off the coast of Haiyang in east China's Shandong Province. The coastal city has since built a spaceport for rocket assembly, testing and launch operations. Teng Yao, chief engineer of the spaceport, said sea launches offer greater flexibility in choosing launch locations and trajectories, and allow rocket debris to fall into waters that are unpopulated.
Wenchang in south China's Hainan Province, which hosts a launch site tasked with missions of launching space station modules and lunar probes, has added facilities specifically for commercial rocket and satellite launches since 2024.
Meanwhile, the Dongfeng commercial space innovation pilot zone near the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China has developed launch pads tailored to private rocket makers.
Access to launch pads has been a challenge for China's commercial space sector. Wang Lifeng, a professor at Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, cited limited launch capacity, tight schedules and long distances between launch sites and rocket assembly facilities as constraints on growth.
Large satellite networks like Qianfan (or Spacesail) and GW constellations, which each have more than 10,000 satellites, further increase the need for a steady flow of launches.
Diversified facilities not only boost launch numbers but also make launch operations more efficient.
Wenchang's commercial spacecraft launch site has put its first two pads into regular service. The second pad alone can accommodate more than 20 rocket types and can be prepared for another launch in 66 hours. The third and fourth pads in the second phase are scheduled to be operational by the end of the year. Upon full commissioning, the site is able to handle about 60 launches annually.
Haiyang offers another route to greater efficiency. Peng Haomin, co-founder of Orienspace, said the private company's facilities are clustered in Haiyang's spaceport, allowing rockets to be assembled, tested and loaded onto a launch ship within 5 km.
"This has replaced usual transportation over more than 1,000 km, drastically cutting logistics time and cost," Peng said.
Dedicated facilities can also streamline rocket operations. Meng Xiangfu, deputy chief commander of Lijian-1 rocket of commercial spaceflight company CAS Space, said that with its tailored launch pad and technical facilities at the Dongfeng commercial space innovation pilot zone, the company can complete the testing and preparation of a rocket in 10 days.
The expansion of launch infrastructure not only benefits the space industry, but also helps boost local economy through investment.
With more than 30 aerospace projects landed, Haiyang has attracted 33.5 billion yuan (around 5 billion U.S. dollars) in related investment. Wenchang's space industry park hosts over 700 companies, while Shanghai is developing a commercial spaceport-related terminal to link rocket assembly with port logistics and sea launch services.
These developments fit into a broader global trend of investing in space capabilities to support the sector's growth, as the United States aims at expanding its space transportation capabilities and Russia calls for efforts to upgrade its industrial and ground-based space infrastructure.
A 2025-2027 action plan issued by the China National Space Administration calls for coordinated development of commercial space launch sites and supports new types of commercial launch systems, including sea-based launch and recovery facilities.
At the same time, China is pressing ahead with the development of heavy-lift and reusable launch vehicles to further expand launch capacity and improve cost efficiency.
Analysts note that efficient operation of these facilities could equip China's commercial space sector with the launch capacity and operational flexibility it needs.

====================================================================================================

What really killed Harry Houdini? A new theory challenges a century-old mystery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
17:40:27 UTC
02:40:27 KST

On the morning of October 22, 1926, Harry Houdini was resting on a couch in his dressing room at the Princess Theatre in Montreal. The world's most famous magician was exhausted and suffering from a fractured ankle sustained during one of his performances. 
As he read through his mail, a student named Samuel Smilovitz was sketching his portrait, after Houdini had been impressed by an earlier drawing. Two other students entered the room. One of them, Jocelyn Gordon Whitehead, wanted to test a rumor: Could Houdini really withstand a powerful punch to the stomach without feeling pain?
Houdini, who took pride in his abdominal strength, answered yes. Before he had time to prepare and tighten his muscles, Whitehead delivered several rapid punches. The magician doubled over in pain and asked him to stop. According to one account, when Smilovitz finished the portrait, Houdini remarked that the drawing made him look tired and admitted that he was indeed feeling unwell. Nine days later, Houdini was dead.
For a century, the accepted story has been that the punches caused his appendix to rupture, leading to a fatal abdominal infection. Whitehead became widely known as the man who killed one of history's greatest magicians. He was never criminally charged, partly because it was difficult to establish that the punches had caused Houdini's death, but the accusation followed him for the rest of his life.
Now, a retired surgeon from Los Angeles is challenging that account. Dr. Larrian Gillespie, 77, argues that the wrong man was blamed and that the world may have been commemorating Houdini's death on the wrong date for the past hundred years. According to Gillespie, Houdini died from an intestinal obstruction caused by a serving of chop suey, a Chinese-American dish of meat and vegetables, that he ate in the hospital. She also believes doctors and people close to Houdini altered documents to conceal what happened during his final days.
In her book Houdini: The Man Who Died Twice, published in July, Gillespie presents a medical and historical investigation drawing on death certificates, witness accounts, letters, medical textbooks from the 1920s and contemporary newspaper reports. Her claims are far-reaching, and not all Houdini historians accept them. But the controversy has renewed interest in one of the most enduring mysteries surrounding the legendary escape artist. To understand why his death still fascinates people a century later, it is worth revisiting the extraordinary life behind the handcuffs and chains.
From a poor Jewish immigrant to an international superstar
Harry Houdini was born Erik Weisz on March 24, 1874, in Budapest, Hungary, to a Jewish family. His father, Mayer Samuel Weisz, was a rabbi, and his mother, Cecilia Steiner, was a homemaker. When Erik was four, the family immigrated to the United States and settled in Appleton, Wisconsin, where his father secured a position as a rabbi.
The American dream proved elusive. Rabbi Weisz struggled to establish himself, partly because of his limited English, and eventually lost his position. The family moved to Milwaukee and later New York, living in poverty for years. Erik began working as a child to help support the family. According to his biographies, he even ran away from home at the age of 12 in search of work. By nine, he was already performing as a trapeze artist under the name "Ehrich, Prince of the Air." He showed a talent for acrobatics and enjoyed demonstrating physical feats that seemed beyond the abilities of ordinary people.
He later became fascinated by the French magician Jean Eugène Robert-Houdin. He adapted the magician's surname, adding an "i" in the mistaken belief that it meant "like Houdin" in French. The name Harry developed from his childhood nickname, Ehrie. Years later, his admiration for Robert-Houdin soured, and he accused his former idol of stealing other magicians' ideas.
Houdini initially performed with his friend Jacob Hyman and later with his brother Theodore. In 1894, he met Wilhelmina Beatrice Rahner, known as Bess, while working in entertainment. They married roughly three weeks later. Bess was Catholic and did not convert to Judaism, although the couple also had a wedding ceremony officiated by a rabbi. She became his regular stage partner, and together they traveled between circuses and modest theaters. Money was often tight, and Houdini even considered abandoning magic for more conventional work.
Eventually, he discovered the act that would make him famous. Rather than relying on conventional card tricks and disappearing objects, Houdini specialized in escaping from seemingly impossible situations. He invited police officers and prison officials to lock him in jail cells and bind him in chains. He escaped from handcuffs, locked boxes thrown into water and straitjackets while suspended upside down above crowded streets.
In his celebrated Chinese Water Torture Cell act, he was lowered headfirst into a tank of water with his ankles restrained above him, leaving audiences convinced they were watching a man about to drown. In another spectacular illusion, he made an entire elephant disappear on a New York stage. Houdini was also a master of publicity. He made danger central to his performances, cultivated an image as a man who could never be imprisoned and carefully maintained the impression that every escape might cost him his life. His name became synonymous with escaping the impossible, and he emerged as one of the world's biggest entertainment stars. Yet the seemingly fearless performer paid a physical price for his success, suffering numerous injuries throughout his career.
His Harlem home and complicated Jewish identity
In 1904, Houdini bought a four-story brownstone in Harlem, Manhattan, where he lived until his death. The building, with its decorated facade and steps leading to the entrance, still stands today. Inside, Houdini collected rare books, magic memorabilia and materials relating to supernatural phenomena.
At the time, Harlem was home to a large Jewish community, with synagogues, schools, Yiddish newspapers and Jewish-owned businesses. Around World War I, approximately 175,000 Jews lived in the neighborhood, although its character gradually changed during the 1920s. For the son of an impoverished rabbi, owning the house represented an extraordinary achievement. One account of his life describes the day he signed the purchase agreement as among his happiest.
Houdini's relationship with Judaism was complicated. He was not religiously observant, celebrated Christian holidays with his wife and even claimed to have been born in Wisconsin rather than Budapest. Yet he did not reject his Jewish origins. A visit to Russia in 1903, following the Kishinev pogrom, exposed him to antisemitism. In 1918, he founded a charitable organization of entertainers who were sons of rabbis, supporting both the war effort and Jewish institutions. Among those associated with the organization were singer and actor Al Jolson and composer Irving Berlin. According to a contemporary report, participants collectively contributed a week's earnings totaling $8,000.
But the most important person in Houdini's life was neither his rabbi father nor his wife. It was his mother. Houdini's attachment to Cecilia bordered on obsession. After his father's death, he considered himself responsible for her welfare, supported her financially and showered her with gifts and expensive clothing. He wanted to give her the comfortable life she had been unable to afford while raising her children.
When she died in 1913, while he was performing in Europe, Houdini was devastated. He mourned her for years and longed to communicate with her even after death. That longing would bring him into direct conflict with one of the most popular movements of his era.
The magician who declared war on mediums
During the early 20th century, spiritualism was booming across Europe and the United States. Mediums claimed they could communicate with the dead, and séances became increasingly popular, particularly after World War I left countless families grieving for loved ones. Houdini, who understood the mechanics of illusion better than almost anyone, believed many mediums were fraudsters exploiting people's grief for financial gain.
One of his most surprising friendships was with British author Arthur Conan Doyle, the creator of Sherlock Holmes. Although his fictional detective was famous for his powers of rational deduction, Conan Doyle himself was a committed believer in communication with the dead. In 1922, Conan Doyle's wife, Jean, offered to conduct a séance and deliver a message from Houdini's mother. She wrote down what she claimed was a communication dictated by Cecilia's spirit.
There was a problem. The message began with a Christian cross and was written in fluent English. Houdini's mother had been Jewish, married to a rabbi and barely spoke English. He found it difficult to believe that, in death, she would suddenly adopt Christian symbolism and begin writing in a language she had scarcely used while alive.
The séance contributed to the breakdown of the friendship between Houdini and Conan Doyle. Houdini subsequently devoted much of his time to exposing fraudulent mediums and even testified before the U.S. Congress in support of legislation against charging money for fortune-telling. His campaign also inspired conspiracy theories about his death. Some suggested that angry mediums had plotted to kill him, possibly sending Whitehead to deliver the punches. No convincing evidence has ever emerged to support those claims. Other theories involved deliberate poisoning, including an especially bizarre story about a group of circus dwarfs supposedly sent to poison his morning tea.
Houdini's private life also attracted attention. Biographers have found evidence of a brief affair in 1918 with Charmian London, the widow of Jack London, author of White Fang and The Call of the Wild. Her diaries contain intimate descriptions of their relationship, and she referred to Houdini as "my magic lover." According to biographer Kenneth Silverman, it was probably his only significant extramarital affair. The relationship was short-lived, and Houdini returned to his marriage with Bess. The couple had no children.
His final performance and the accepted account of his death
In October 1926, Houdini, then 52, embarked on a performance tour despite his injuries. His wife had suffered food poisoning, while he had fractured a bone in his ankle during a dangerous stunt. Instead of resting, he continued performing. Following the punches in Montreal, his abdominal pain worsened. But Houdini, accustomed to ignoring physical discomfort, did not immediately seek medical attention.
He traveled to Detroit and took the stage on October 24 despite a fever of approximately 40°C (104°F) and severe pain. Doctors warned him about his condition, but he refused to cancel the performance. At one point, he collapsed backstage, only to return to the stage. It was his final performance.
The following day, he underwent surgery at Grace Hospital. According to medical accounts from the time, doctors found that his appendix had ruptured and that a bacterial infection had spread throughout his abdomen. Today, appendicitis can generally be treated successfully. But in 1926, before antibiotics became widely available, widespread peritonitis caused by a ruptured appendix was a life-threatening condition.
The infection could lead to sepsis and septic shock, a potentially fatal reaction in which the body's response to infection disrupts circulation and damages vital organs. Doctors attempted to save Houdini, including administering an experimental serum. He also underwent a second operation. According to the accepted historical account, Harry Houdini died on October 31, 1926, at 1:26 p.m.
But the connection between the punches and his appendicitis was never conclusively established. Blunt abdominal trauma can, in rare cases, be associated with appendicitis, but determining whether an injury caused the illness or simply preceded it is difficult. Biographer Adam Begley, whose book on Houdini was published by Yale University Press in 2020, believes the illness probably developed independently. The punches may simply have drawn Houdini's attention to abdominal pain that was already developing. Alternatively, they may have distracted him from recognizing the underlying illness.
The hospital meal at the center of a new theory
Gillespie goes considerably further. She argues that the key to Houdini's death was not his appendix but a serving of chop suey he ate at the hospital on October 28. According to her reconstruction, undigested food fibers formed a mass that blocked his intestines.
An intestinal obstruction prevents food and other contents from moving normally through the digestive tract. It can cause fluids and gas to accumulate, compromise blood supply to the intestines and, in severe cases, lead to tissue death, perforation and a life-threatening infection. Masses of undigested food and fiber can cause such blockages, although this is not a common complication of an ordinary meal.
Gillespie believes Houdini required emergency surgery on October 29, during which doctors opened his intestine and removed its contents. His condition then deteriorated. His temperature reportedly rose to approximately 40.5°C (104.9°F), and he developed septic shock and lost consciousness. She claims he underwent another operation on October 30 and died that same day at 1:26 p.m., exactly 24 hours before the officially recorded date of his death.
But contemporary newspaper reports contradict crucial parts of that timeline. As early as October 25, The New York Times reported that Houdini had undergone surgery to remove his appendix. The newspaper also published a statement from four of his doctors describing a ruptured appendix and an abdominal infection. On October 29, newspapers reported a second operation to treat intestinal paralysis that had developed following the infection. Gillespie argues that the reports and official documents do not accurately reflect what happened.
Her investigation began almost by chance while she was helping develop a website for a university course about Houdini at the University of Nevada. A graduate of the University of California, Los Angeles, Gillespie had worked for 15 years in Beverly Hills. She had never previously researched Houdini and, by her own account, had no particular interest in magic. What caught her attention was his death certificate.
Examining the document from a medical perspective, she noticed erasures, incorrect names and the signature of a physician who, she says, was not present when Houdini died. She later identified what she describes as three different death certificates, including one submitted to an insurance company. She claims one document was considered invalid because it showed signs of alteration and that she found contradictions among the various records. According to Gillespie, more than a dozen people close to Houdini, including relatives and employees, were involved in a series of actions intended to conceal the true circumstances of his death.
Medical negligence, insurance money and Halloween
Why would anyone want to conceal how or when Houdini died? Gillespie suggests three possible motives.
The first is the fear of exposing medical negligence. If Houdini developed an intestinal obstruction after eating food provided by the hospital, and doctors failed to diagnose it promptly, those responsible could have faced serious questions about his treatment. For Gillespie, the absence of any reference to the second operation in the death records she examined is one indication that something may have been concealed.
The second possible motive is financial. Houdini's life insurance policy provided an increased payout in the event of accidental death. Gillespie believes the way his death was described enabled Bess to receive double compensation.
Her third proposed motive is the most unusual: Halloween. Gillespie believes those involved wanted Houdini's death to be recorded as October 31, the holiday associated with spirits, ghosts and the supernatural, thereby strengthening the mythology surrounding the magician who had spent years challenging claims of communication with the dead.
It would be difficult to imagine a more symbolically appropriate date for the death of a man who had devoted so much of his later career to exposing fraudulent mediums. But an appealing narrative is not necessarily an accurate one.
Evidence, speculation and a divided community of historians
For all the intrigue surrounding Gillespie's theory, there is an important distinction between what the documents establish and how she interprets them. Her book is not a peer-reviewed medical study. It is an independent historical investigation published by a company she owns. No autopsy was performed on Houdini, meaning there is no direct pathological evidence that could conclusively establish what happened inside his body.
Errors and alterations in death certificates also do not, by themselves, prove an attempt to conceal medical negligence, commit insurance fraud or change the official date of death. Houdini researchers are divided over Gillespie's conclusions.
Patrick Culliton, who assisted her research, believes there is substantial evidence supporting her findings, particularly her argument that Whitehead should no longer be blamed for Houdini's death. John Cox, who runs the historical website Wild About Harry and also helped the author, was impressed by the new material but remains skeptical. In his review, Cox described the book as a compelling detective story containing intriguing theories, while emphasizing that it does not provide conclusive proof for any of them. As far as he is concerned, the mystery remains unsolved.
George Hardeen, Houdini's great-nephew, also told The New York Times that he found the theory convincing. However, he acknowledged that persuading historians, magicians and devoted fans to abandon a story they have believed for generations would be difficult.
One person who paid a considerable personal price for that story was Jocelyn Gordon Whitehead. Although he was never prosecuted, the accusation that he had killed Houdini followed him throughout his life. According to Gillespie's investigation, Whitehead became increasingly reclusive, avoiding other people because of the shame associated with the incident. He died of malnutrition in 1954 at the age of 57 and was buried in Montreal without a headstone.
Gillespie decided to address what she considers a historical injustice. She located one of Whitehead's relatives, commissioned a granite headstone and traveled to Montreal for a ceremony marking its installation. Alongside his personal details, the stone bears the words "Falsely Accused No More." A relative of Whitehead and George Hardeen, a member of Houdini's family, attended the ceremony.
A century after the famous punches, the man long blamed for the magician's death finally had someone publicly defending his name.
Houdini's final escape became a Halloween tradition
Houdini's body was transported from Detroit to New York in a specially designed bronze coffin. Shortly before his death, he had used the same coffin to demonstrate how a person could remain in an enclosed space without succumbing to fear. Approximately 2,000 people attended his funeral on November 4, 1926, including two rabbis.
At his request, Houdini was buried in a Jewish cemetery in Queens beside his mother. He had left detailed instructions concerning the rabbi who should conduct the funeral and requested that a bundle of letters his mother had written to him over the years be placed beneath his head in the coffin, allowing him to rest on them forever.
Bess, his partner throughout 32 years of marriage, was not buried beside him. Although her name appears on his monument, she was laid to rest in a Catholic cemetery in New York state because the Jewish cemetery would not permit her burial there.
Before Houdini died, the couple had agreed on one final experiment. If communication with the dead were genuinely possible, Houdini would send Bess a secret message known only to the two of them. They devised a code based on the word "Rosabelle," the title of a song connected to their courtship, and a sequence of words encoding the message "Believe."
For years after his death, Bess attempted to contact him through mediums. In 1929, the medium Arthur Ford claimed to have successfully delivered the secret message. But it later emerged that the code had already been published, and Bess withdrew her belief that Houdini had actually communicated with her.
On October 31, 1936, the tenth anniversary of his officially recorded death, a widely publicized séance was held on the roof of a Hollywood hotel before hundreds of spectators and members of the press. Everyone waited for a sign from the man who had spent his life escaping from places no one else could escape. Houdini did not appear.
Bess extinguished the light that had been kept burning in his memory and announced that she would no longer wait for him. She later explained that ten years was long enough to wait for any man. His admirers, however, never stopped trying. Annual séances became a tradition, and events have been planned for October 31, 2026, marking the centennial of his officially recorded death, including gatherings at his former Harlem home on 113th Street.
If Gillespie is right, those gathering on Halloween to contact Houdini will be observing the anniversary of a man who actually died the day before. And in Montreal, a new headstone now tells a different story about the man once held responsible for his death. After a hundred years, it may be Whitehead, the little-known student who punched Houdini, who finally manages to escape the magician's shadow.

Pressure mounts on UK government to launch inquiry into Britain’s role in Gaza
Over 50,000 people in the UK have signed a petition urging the government to launch an inquiry into Britain’s role in the war in Gaza, which has been determined to be a genocide by scholars and leading rights groups.
The petition aims to garner 100,000 signatures in order to force the matter to be discussed in the House of Commons.
As of Saturday, 56,947 people have signed the petition, with many demanding a thorough investigation into Britain’s role in the war, including through sales and supply of weapons to Israel.
The petition was started by Jennifer Forbes, a former Labour parliamentary candidate for the Truro and Falmouth constituency.
Signatories of the petition have asserted that the UK has played a vital role in the genocide through providing reconnaissance aircraft and allowing the use of Royal Air Force bases.
The mounting pressure comes as dozens of MPs in recent months, including prominent members of the Labour Party, have been pushing for such an inquiry; however, the government is yet to respond.
The petition urges that the inquiry must be carried out independently of the government so that the commission of inquiry has the power to question ministers and government officials involved in the decision-making processes, particularly regarding what is believed to be British complicity in Israeli war crimes.
Those who have signed the petition have also called for clear answers on the types of weapons supplied to Israel, the reasons behind the UK’s involvement as well as disclosure of intelligence gathered during RAF sorties over Gaza amid the war.
The petition states that the investigation should also reveal details on legal advice the British government sought during its assessment of whether genocide has occurred in Gaza.
Israel’s war on Gaza, which started in October 2023, has killed over 74,000 Palestinians. The war has plunged the enclave into a deep humanitarian crisis, levelled entire neighbourhoods and displaced much of the population.
Despite an October 2025 ceasefire, Israel has continued to violate the terms of the truce and has carried out near-daily killings and demolitions.
Israel has also failed to abide by its aid obligations and has continued to restrict vital emergency aid from entering the Strip through land crossings.
Earlier this year, independent MP Jeremy Corbyn has vowed to expose Britain's complicity in Gaza and pursue accountability for Palestine after reintroducing a bill calling for an independent inquiry into the UK's role in Israel's war.
In comments made to The New Arab in June, he said his efforts were driven by a determination to avoid the delays that followed the Iraq war, when years passed before an inquiry was established and a report published detailing failures within the British government's decision-making process.

The spokesperson said the ban did not affect lawful protests in support of the Palestinian cause.

Jordan stops armed group from attempting to enter from Syria, armed forces say
Oct 31 - Jordanian border guards stopped a group of 14 armed individuals attempting to cross into the country from Syria, state news agency Petra quoted the armed forces as saying on Saturday.
They tried to infiltrate on Friday under heavy fire and direct engagement, causing numerous casualties among the group. Some fled back into Syria, the armed forces said.
The report could not be found on Petra's website later in the day. No correction had been issued by Saturday evening.
Petra did not elaborate on the identity of the 14 people.
Jordan faces persistent security challenges along its border with Syria, including drug and weapons smuggling. Networks have employed increasingly sophisticated tactics to transport narcotics across the border.
The attempted infiltration came after Jordan launched airstrikes on southern Syria on Monday, saying it targeted hideouts of militant groups it linked to a deadly attack on a church in Jordan earlier this month. It said more than 20 Islamic State militants were killed in the strikes.
Nine people were killed and at least 34 wounded when gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in the village of Hamoud, in Jordan's southern Karak governorate, on October 23.
King Abdullah ordered an "iron fisted" response by security forces to the highly unusual attack on Jordan's Christian minority, which he and other top officials blamed on "extremist terrorists".
Islamic State, which was defeated by a US-led coalition, has been trying to make a comeback in neighboring Iraq and Syria, where it once controlled large areas.
Jordan, a US partner in the fight against Islamist militant groups, is regarded as a relatively stable state in the Middle East. Its security services have foiled plots by Islamist militants in the past, including suspected Islamic State supporters.
Jordan's strikes on southern Syria created tensions between Amman and Damascus, with Syria condemning them as a violation of its sovereignty and saying they had killed seven civilians, including three children and a woman. Jordan's foreign minister expressed regret over civilian casualties and reaffirmed Amman's respect for Syria's sovereignty.
The two countries agreed to establish a joint security committee to investigate the strikes and their aftermath and strengthen intelligence sharing and coordination on the ground.
BORDER SECURITY COOPERATION
Relations between Jordan and Syria had improved following the ousting of former Syrian President Bashar al-Assad in December 2024. They stepped up cooperation on border security, trade and efforts to combat drug trafficking and militant groups.
The recent airstrikes, however, have tested that rapprochement, although both sides have sought to ease strains through renewed security coordination.
"There is a lot of cooperation with Iraq, Jordan and Lebanon in order to guarantee the security and stability of the borders. Our region is facing lots of challenges, however, with cooperation we can overcome the challenges," Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani said at the Manama Dialogue conference in Bahrain on Saturday. Araghchi: Iran has no plans for talks with US until its conditions are met
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
17:27:29 UTC
02:27:29 KST

Araghchi: Iran has no plans for talks with US until its conditions are met
TEHRAN — Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has said Iran has no plans to hold talks with the United States under the current circumstances, stressing that Tehran will consider direct or indirect negotiations only after Washington accepts its conditions.
In an interview with Al Jazeera, Araghchi discussed the latest diplomatic efforts, a message conveyed by US Vice President JD Vance, proposals put forward by regional mediators, Iran’s conditions regarding the Strait of Hormuz, and the country's military preparedness amid the possibility of renewed confrontation.
He said the message sent by Vance had been carefully reviewed and discussed at high-level meetings in Iran. Araghchi described the initiative to open a channel for dialogue as a positive development, but warned that Washington would be making another mistake if it sought to exploit the initiative to create divisions within Iran.
“The American side’s attempt to open the door to dialogue and broader understanding is a positive step,” he said, adding that if the purpose was to sow discord, it would amount to another mistake by the United States.
Araghchi rejected speculation about an imminent meeting between Iranian and American officials, saying no such meeting was currently planned and that media reports on the matter did not reflect Tehran’s position.
“We see no need to meet with the Americans at present,” he said, emphasizing that Iran’s conditions were clear and that regional mediators were continuing their consultations on the basis of those conditions.
He added that Iran would decide whether any future negotiations should be held directly or indirectly only after the United States agreed to its demands.
Mediators continue diplomatic consultations
Araghchi said regional mediators were continuing their efforts to facilitate an understanding between Tehran and Washington. He noted that Qatar and Pakistan remained involved in the consultations and that an Iranian official had traveled to Qatar to pursue discussions.
“My aide is currently in Qatar to continue consultations,” he said.
The foreign minister also referred to proposals submitted by mediators concerning Iran’s nuclear program, saying Tehran was examining them as part of the second phase of the diplomatic process.
Addressing Iran’s relations with the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), Araghchi said a considerable distance remained before cooperation with the agency could return to normal.
He stressed that Iran remains a party to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT) and is committed to fulfilling its obligations under the treaty. Iran’s position on its nuclear commitments, he indicated, should be considered separately from the current difficulties surrounding cooperation with the IAEA.
Iran sets conditions for reopening Strait of Hormuz
Araghchi also outlined Iran’s proposal concerning the Strait of Hormuz, explaining that discussions with Qatari mediators had led to a significant reduction in the proposed implementation period.
He said the Qatari side had initially suggested a five-day period for implementing the proposal, but subsequent consultations had reduced the timeframe to two days.
The Iranian proposal includes several conditions, among them the lifting of sanctions imposed following the Islamabad memorandum, a reduction in the US military presence in the region, the restoration of oil waivers and the release of all Iranian frozen assets, including those held in Qatar.
Araghchi also emphasized that reopening the strategic waterway would require recognition of a new shipping route established by Iran in coordination with Oman, as well as the closure of other routes.
He made clear that the arrangements for maritime traffic through the strait were an essential part of Iran’s proposal and that the reopening process would have to take account of the new route and the understandings reached between Iran and Oman.
The foreign minister further stressed that Tehran sought an end to the war and the cessation of hostilities across all fronts, including Lebanon. He said efforts to end the conflict should not be confined to one front while fighting continued elsewhere in the region.
Iran prepared for all possible scenarios
Turning to the prospect of renewed military confrontation, Araghchi said Iran was not ruling out the possibility of another war and was prepared for all scenarios.
“We do not rule out any possibility regarding the outbreak of war, and we are prepared for all scenarios,” he said.
He explained that Iran had used the period following the previous confrontation to strengthen its military capabilities, upgrade its equipment, address vulnerabilities and test new weapons.
Araghchi stressed that the country’s armed forces were at the highest level of readiness and that Iran was fully prepared to respond to any renewed military action.
 
He also acknowledged the impact of US economic pressure on Iran, but insisted that such pressure would not force the country to surrender or abandon its positions.
“We will continue to stand firm and resist, and we will overcome this difficult phase through our own capabilities,” he said.

Forced to eat grass, Oleshky evacuees say Russia-Ukraine truce was a ‘blessing’

CHERNIHIV, Ukraine - Evacuees from Oleshky, a bombed-out city in Russian-occupied Ukraine, told AFP that residents had to eat grass and dogs to survive and that their rescue following a humanitarian truce was a “blessing”.
US First Lady Melania Trump announced the truce on Oct 23, saying the city was “on the brink of disaster”.
Ukrainian and Russian officials visited the city together on Oct 30, delivering aid and evacuating those who wanted to leave in a rare show of cooperation between the warring sides.
Arriving in Ukraine on Oct 31 by bus, residents whom AFP interviewed painted a dire picture of life in the city.
“People were cooking grass,” said Valera, a 29-year-old former resident who did not give his last name.
“They’d grow it, as there was nothing to eat.”
He added that some residents were forced to shoot and cook dogs to survive.
“Lots of people were blown up. There were piles of bodies on the roads, loads of cars. In short, it was brutal... Terrifying,” he said.
An AFP journalist saw the residents, some draped in Ukrainian flags, disembark from buses and tearfully embrace their loved ones.
The city in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region was captured by the Russian military in 2022, and had been caught in intense fighting between the two sides that left residents starving and unable to escape.
‘They got blown up’
Yelyzaveta Paliy, who was waiting for her father to return, said she never expected him to be gone so long.
“We last saw him at the end of January 2024, when my sister, mum and I left, and he stayed behind,” the 19-year-old said.
AFP saw Paliy, her mother and sister embracing Paliy’s father in a circle.
“This is a blessing. I’ve been waiting a long time,” her father said. “There’s no life there anymore,” he said of Oleshky.
Ivan, a 70-year-old resident, said life in Oleshky had been “really bad” over the past month.
“We’ve got a vegetable garden. We grew everything we needed there. Everything ourselves, so we managed more or less. We shared with the neighbours,” he said.
“We had these specialist lads who cleared the mines themselves and set off. They drove in their cars, and they got blown up,” he said.
He said one of his relatives had lost four vehicles driving out of Oleshky.
“What else could we do? Starve to death?”
Around 2,000 residents – compared with 24,000 before Russia’s 2022 invasion – were still in Oleshky ahead of the humanitarian operation, according to Kyiv’s estimates.
Neither Moscow nor Kyiv has specified the number of people evacuated, and authorities in both countries previously indicated that many residents wished to remain in the city, even in the event of renewed fighting. AFP

Israel's election deadlock: Likud doubts unity as Eisenkot weighs a risky coalition gamble
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
17:22:43 UTC
02:22:43 KST

Two days after Israel's final election results were released, both political blocs are struggling to find a way out of the deadlock. Calls for a national unity government are growing, but forming one would require more than overcoming the deep distrust between party leaders. Both sides would have to make major political concessions, including abandoning some of their central election promises.
In Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing bloc, senior ministers say the chances of a unity government are slim. "The political concessions required of each side are so substantial that they make the prospects of such a government extremely unlikely," a senior Likud official said.
For Netanyahu, unity would mean reversing a campaign promise, breaking up his alliance with his traditional political partners and excluding at least Otzma Yehudit leader Itamar Ben-Gvir, potentially along with some of the ultra-Orthodox parties.
The opposing bloc would face an equally difficult decision. Its parties campaigned on promises not to govern with Netanyahu or the ultra-Orthodox parties, a position tied in part to their commitment to passing legislation requiring broader military conscription. Entering a unity government would force them to reconsider those commitments.
Golan, Liberman and Eisenkot caught in the middle
There is no consensus within the anti-Netanyahu bloc about what should happen next. Each of its leaders has a different idea of how to form a government.
Democrats leader Yair Golan is pushing strongly for a government that would rely on the support or abstention of the Joint List, or one that would include Mansour Abbas' Ra'am party as a coalition partner.
Yisrael Beiteinu chairman Avigdor Liberman, however, has repeatedly ruled out supporting such an arrangement. He also sought to dismiss speculation about his own political ambitions, writing in response to claims that he would demand the position of Knesset speaker: "I have absolutely no desire or intention to serve in that position."
Some figures in the anti-Netanyahu bloc believe that forming a government capable of surviving two or three years might justify the political cost of breaking an election promise. But they see little point in establishing a fragile coalition that could collapse within months and send Israel back to the polls.
While Golan and Liberman have taken firm positions on opposite sides of the debate, the other party leaders have left themselves more room to maneuver.
Gadi Eisenkot, chairman of Yashar! and leader of the largest party in the anti-Netanyahu bloc, is expected to receive the mandate to form a government following consultations with President Isaac Herzog.
On Thursday, Eisenkot told his supporters that he intended to establish a good government and deliver on the choice voters had made. He did not, however, explain how he planned to do so.
Throughout the campaign, Eisenkot said he would be willing to form a minority government if necessary. But not all his potential coalition partners are now prepared to support that approach.
His options are further complicated by United Torah Judaism, which is seeking military conscription legislation favorable to the ultra-Orthodox community. Eisenkot has repeatedly declared that if he cannot pass a fair and equitable military draft law, he would prefer another election.
Naftali Bennett, leader of the Beyachad party, is another major question mark. Bennett has not supported forming a government dependent on the backing or abstention of Arab parties, and it remains unclear how much flexibility he is prepared to give Eisenkot.
Bennett's position is closer to Liberman's. He believes a government dependent on Arab party support would be unlikely to survive and could collapse quickly, allowing Netanyahu to return to power with a substantial majority and govern for a long, stable term. As a result, Bennett is also reluctant to support this approach.
Yair Lapid, by contrast, is more open to alternatives, according to political sources. He believes that if a workable arrangement can produce a stable government capable of serving for a substantial period, it deserves consideration.
Eisenkot and Lapid met in the evening, and a statement issued on their behalf said they had "discussed the election results and coordinated their next steps, reflecting their shared commitment to carrying out the will of the voters."
A government backed by ultra-Orthodox parties carries its own risks
Another possibility Eisenkot is exploring is a minority government that would take office with the support or abstention of ultra-Orthodox parties, particularly United Torah Judaism.
If United Torah Judaism allows Eisenkot to form a government, his side would have 55 Knesset seats compared with 53 for Netanyahu's bloc.
But this possibility has also raised considerable suspicion among the parties seeking to replace Netanyahu.
Some fear the ultra-Orthodox parties could be playing both sides, using negotiations with Eisenkot to increase their bargaining power with Netanyahu while attempting to repair their political standing after a difficult parliamentary term.
"The ultra-Orthodox option is risky because it is unclear whether we could maintain a long-term partnership with them," a source in the anti-Netanyahu bloc said. "It would also force Liberman and Bennett to break a fundamental election promise. The political cost would therefore be high."
The source added: "Eisenkot is working toward that possibility, but it is far from certain that the ultra-Orthodox parties can be trusted to genuinely commit to a government not led by Netanyahu."
On Friday, Lapid published a Facebook post urging supporters to remain patient despite the uncertainty surrounding coalition negotiations.
"It wasn't a knockout victory. It was a win on points, and that counts too. A win is a win," Lapid wrote.
"Now comes the really hard part: trying to form a government. We owe it to everyone who stood in line on Tuesday, everyone who flew in especially to vote, and everyone who spent eight hours outside a polling station trying to persuade people to vote."
Lapid acknowledged that the negotiations would be difficult and that he could offer no guarantees.
"This will be hard. I can't promise anything. There is no simple formula for this. Forming a government is a complicated political process," he wrote.
"But we have something we didn't have on Monday morning: an overwhelming majority of Israelis who made clear that this is what they want."
He concluded with an appeal to his supporters: "So I need to ask you for something that is particularly difficult to ask of Israelis: patience."

====================================================================================================

A cure for Trump? Why Democratic doctors are running in the 2026 midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
17:19:44 UTC
02:19:44 KST

San Francisco, California – Three words stretch across the front page of Richard Pan’s campaign website: “Public Health Hero”.
The California paediatrician is part of a wave of public health professionals angling for a seat in the United States Congress in Tuesday's midterm elections.
The American College of Gastroenterology has estimated that as many as 25 physicians could win congressional office this election cycle, a record number that would usher in "a new generation of physician-lawmakers".
But while many of the incumbents are Republicans, experts say there has been a notable rise in the number of Democratic doctors and healthcare workers on the ballot.
Some are competing in the highest-profile races of the year. Abdul El-Sayed, a physician and former public health official, is locked in a close race for Michigan's open Senate seat.
In South Carolina, meanwhile, paediatrician Annie Andrews has turned what would normally be a safe Senate seat for Republicans into a battleground.
Experts and advocacy groups credit the growing number of Democratic doctors-turned-politicians, in part, to frustration with Republican President Donald Trump.
Democrats, they say, are tapping into public rage not only over rising healthcare costs but also Trump-era policies they see as anti-scientific.
“Scientists themselves have woken up. We cannot just abandon the public forum to all of this misinformation, disinformation,” said Eric Feigl-Ding, an epidemiologist who founded Vax PAC, a political advocacy group that backs candidates who support responsible vaccine policies.
Feigl-Ding sees the surge in political participation not as an act of partisanship but rather as a chance to advocate for responsible healthcare policies.
“It's not like public health is rolling up our sleeves and getting dirty in the pigsty,” Feigl-Ding said. “What public health is doing is immunising ourselves against politics.”
An increasingly divisive issue
While the pocketbook issues consistently rank as the top priority for American voters, healthcare remains a prevailing concern.
A Pew Research Center poll on October 8 identified healthcare as the third most important election issue for Americans, behind the economy and the future of US democracy.
Democrats, in particular, were more likely to rank healthcare high among the factors swaying their votes. Eighty-two percent said it was a very important issue, compared with 53 percent for Republicans.
The politicisation of healthcare isn’t new, but it has evolved, according to Matt Motta, a policy expert at Boston University’s School of Public Health. He describes the issue as more divisive than it has been in the past.
“Health has always been political, but health hasn’t always been partisan,” Motta told Al Jazeera. "Our health has become increasingly polarised along partisan lines."
One of the early instances of that fracture came in the 1994 midterm election cycle. In the year leading up to the race, the administration of Democratic President Bill Clinton had pushed Congress for healthcare reform.
But Republicans like Representative Newt Gingrich framed that effort as "socialism". The right-wing party ultimately flipped both chambers of Congress that year, in a midterm race dubbed the "Republican Revolution".
Another major milestone was the passage of the Affordable Care Act (ACA) in 2010, under Democratic leader Barack Obama.
Ever since, healthcare has played a defining role in nearly every midterm following the election of a new president, according to Motta.
During the 2010 midterms, for instance, Republicans ran in opposition to the newly passed Affordable Care Act. Then, in the 2018 midterms, after Trump's first election, Democrats campaigned against his efforts to roll the Affordable Care Act back.
Later, in the 2022 race, restrictions related to the COVID-19 pandemic gave Republicans fuel to attack a new Democratic leader, then-President Joe Biden.
A backlash to MAHA?
This time around, however, Trump is back in the midterm crosshairs. The news agency Reuters and the research firm Ipsos found in late October that his approval rating has slumped to a record low of 31 percent.
As a candidate for the presidency in 2024, Trump had courted voters sceptical of the American healthcare system.
Confidence in doctors and public health researchers had been on the decline since the COVID-19 pandemic. Trump tapped into that trend by recruiting vaccine sceptic Robert F Kennedy Jr to join his campaign.
Kennedy rallied supporters under the banner "Make America Healthy Again" or "MAHA" — a variation on Trump's "Make America Great Again" slogan.
In turn, Trump promised to let Kennedy "go wild on health" if he were returned to office. Shortly after his re-election, Trump announced Kennedy as his pick for health and human services secretary.
Since the start of Trump's second term, Kennedy has pushed to minimise federal vaccine guidelines, bucking scientific consensus.
He has also championed cuts to agencies such as the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the National Institutes of Health (NIH).
Trump, meanwhile, rallied Republicans to pass the One Big Beautiful Bill Act last year, which resulted in more than $1 trillion in cuts to healthcare spending.
As part of that bill, Republicans allowed health insurance subsidies to expire, resulting in higher premiums for millions of Americans.
The new crop of Democratic doctors-turned-candidates is “trying to capitalise on how frustrated most people are with these decisions", Motta said.
In South Carolina, for instance, Andrews — the paediatrician turned Democratic Senate contender — has pointed to her state's measles outbreak as evidence of the failure of Trump's health policies.
An estimated 997 cases were reported in the state between 2025 and 2026.
"We are flirting with the return of an old killer, not because the science changed, not because the virus itself changed, but because our politics did," Andrews wrote in a February column about the outbreak.
"At the highest levels of our federal government, we have watched medical expertise get shoved aside while conspiracy theories get promoted."
In Michigan, meanwhile, El-Sayed touted his health credentials by pointing to a recent uptick in cyclospora, a diarrhoea-inducing parasite that can be spread through fresh produce, such as lettuce.
"If I were elected, I would be the first Democratic doctor elected to the US Senate in nearly 50 years,” El-Sayed said at a campaign stop in September.
"If you're kind of tired of dodging lettuce in the United States of America, I think we all could agree we probably need a public health senator right about now."
He and other Democrats have blamed the parasite's spread on the federal government’s reduced capacity to inspect food, as a result of Trump's budget cuts.
'How many times in history?'
Currently, the majority of the doctors serving in Congress are Republicans, including all four physicians previously elected to the Senate.
But those party dynamics may shift. One high-profile Republican doctor, Senator Bill Cassidy, is stepping down. Others, such as Senator Roger Marshall of Kansas, are facing uncertain odds for re-election.
Meanwhile, at least five Democratic newcomers with medical degrees are aiming to join the 120th Congress after November's midterm election.
At least 10 Democratic nurses are making a bid for Congress this year too, compared to four Republicans, according to the publication Nurse.org.
Not every healthcare professional on November's ballot shares the same view on healthcare policy, though.
In South Carolina, Andrews told NewsNation that "Medicare for All" — a proposal for universal public healthcare — is an "outdated, non-pragmatic policy".
El-Sayed, by contrast, is a strong proponent of the policy, having co-written a book called Medicare for All: A Citizen's Guide.
The US has one of the costliest healthcare systems of any high-income country in the world, and affordability has been a common feature in many of the Democratic doctors' campaigns.
Andrews, for instance, has dubbed her political agenda the "Patients and Prices Platform", and she travelled around her state on a similarly named tour.
US Representative Ami Bera, a California Democrat who is also a doctor, told Al Jazeera that the country is at a key juncture to decide the future of its healthcare system.
Bera is running for re-election in the midterms, in part based on the belief that doctors and patients should be at the centre of that discussion, as opposed to mere costs.
"Let’s not talk about reimbursement. Let’s talk about why we went to medical school — we want to care for our patient,” Bera said.
“Doctors who have practised, have been in the exam room, in the OR [operating room] have a unique perspective on patient care. They bring that unique perspective to Congress.”
Bera helped form the Democratic Doctors PAC this year to help boost healthcare as an election-season cause.
Other health-inspired groups have likewise poured money and resources into the race. The pro-science advocacy group 314 Action reported in October that it had spent nearly $30m on this year's midterms.
But Bera expressed optimism that healthcare would ultimately not be seen as a single-party issue or a source of partisan divide.
“Up until this moment in time, that is what the conversation's been, right? Democrats defending the Affordable Care Act, Republicans attacking the ACA,” Bera said. “I think it's such a crisis moment that it's opened up the opportunity to think about the ‘what next'?”
Feigl-Ding, the founder of Vax PAC, also believes this midterm election cycle is a moment of opportunity.
He pointed to the recent Democratic primary victory for Amy Acton, the former director of the Ohio Department of Health, now running to be the state's governor.
Acton is leading her Republican opponent going into Tuesday's vote by 7 percentage points, according to a recent Marist University poll. Feigl-Ding described that result as historic.
“If you think about it, how many times in history does a health director run for governor and win the primary, and is now slated to potentially win the governor’s race?” Feigl-Ding asked.

Interview: South Africa eyes Chinese market as future tourism anchor: Official
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
01:18:22 CST
02:18:22 KST

JOHANNESBURG, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- South Africa sees strong potential for tourism growth from China and is working to improve travel access and broaden its offerings for Chinese visitors, a senior tourism official has said.
"We see it as a market that is actually going to be an anchor for us in the future," Nkhumeleni Victor Vele, director-general of South Africa's Department of Tourism, told Xinhua in an interview on Friday.
To attract more Chinese visitors, South Africa is working to improve aviation capacity and connectivity and promote its Electronic Travel Authorization (ETA) system, Vele said.
South Africa officially launched the ETA in August after initially piloting it for travelers from China, India, Indonesia and Mexico during its G20 presidency last year. Eligible travelers can apply online without visiting a South African embassy or visa processing center, with applications expected to be processed within 24 hours.
Vele said China leads applications through the system, describing the uptake as an encouraging sign of renewed interest in visiting South Africa.
Beyond easier access, South Africa wants Chinese visitors to discover more of the country's distinctive experiences.
Chinese travelers are "not looking for another China outside home," Vele said. "They want an experience that is uniquely authentic, which becomes a lot more memorable over time, and therefore meaningful."
While Cape Town and Kruger National Park are already popular with Chinese tourists, the country has yet to sufficiently showcase its township and village cuisine, cultural performances and storytelling traditions, he said.
Vele highlighted the Northern Cape's desert landscapes, distinctive wildlife and plants, Karoo lamb and wines, alongside the cultural traditions of Venda communities in Limpopo's rural villages.
Such experiences should form part of South Africa's tourism packages, giving visitors a fuller understanding of the country, he said.
To help Chinese tourists enjoy these experiences comfortably, South Africa has been working to train tourist guides in Mandarin and deepen their understanding of Chinese culture, Vele said.
The efforts extend beyond language to cultural practices and sensitivities. Alongside introducing South African dishes, tourism providers also need to accommodate visitors who occasionally want familiar meals, particularly during longer stays, he said.
On further cooperation, Vele said the two sides are working on a joint marketing approach to encourage Chinese tourists to celebrate the coming Chinese New Year in South Africa.
He also called for more jointly hosted festivals and events, knowledge and information sharing, and cultural and sporting exchanges. Visitors arriving for a particular activity may then discover other attractions and experiences, he said.
Vele welcomed support from Chinese counterparts in reaching the Chinese market and called for continued cooperation, saying South Africa's door is also open to China.
"We have prepared everything for them to come and enjoy and leave with pleasant and wonderful experiences," he said. ■

ZimTrade will lead the delegation comprising businesses from horticulture, manufacturing, handicrafts, leather, construction, tourism, and e-commerce at the ninth edition of the international trade exhibition to seek new buyers, establish business partnerships, and explore opportunities from China's growing demand for imported products, the organization said in its October 2026 newsletter.

Beyond agriculture, Zimbabwe's creative industries, particularly its iconic stone sculptures and handicrafts, also present strong potential to attract Chinese buyers seeking authentic African products.

Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's parliamentary commissioner for human rights, who led the Ukrainian delegation during the humanitarian mission in Oleshky, said the oldest evacuee is 94 years old while the youngest is just one year old.

NAIROBI, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- The ninth edition of the China International Import Expo (CIIE), taking place in Shanghai from Nov. 5 to 10, offers a strategic platform to advance China-Africa business ties and unlock mutual economic benefits, according to a senior banking executive.
Richard Li, deputy CEO, head of Wealth and Retail Banking (China) and group head of Global Chinese at Standard Chartered Bank, emphasized the expo's potential to inject fresh vitality into two-way Sino-African trade and investment.
"The expo is an opportunity for Kenya and other African exporters to build buyer relationships, which provides a good foundation for trade outcomes," Li said during a recent interview with Xinhua in Nairobi, the Kenyan capital.
Li noted that a key measure of the expo's success will be turning signed agreements into delivered and repeat orders, adding that Standard Chartered Bank stands ready to facilitate transactions across both markets.
African nations, including Kenya, can leverage participation at the CIIE to showcase certified, high-value and traceable agricultural products to prospective Chinese buyers, Li said.
He urged African exporters to actively track leads, finalize workable payment and delivery frameworks, and scale up capacity to fulfill incoming orders.
"That is how an initial introduction can become a lasting relationship," said Li.
"Standard Chartered can help clients align their banking arrangements with those commitments, so the timing of production, shipment and payment is considered together," he added.
From Oct. 22 to 28 this year, the bank and its partners conducted a China roadshow aimed at positioning Kenya and the broader African continent as emerging trade and investment hubs.
The roadshow also aimed to help local African enterprises expand their presence in China, strengthen their production capacity and retain greater economic value, Li said.
The bank executive noted that companies in manufacturing, agro-processing and infrastructure are pivotal to penetrating the Chinese market, emphasizing their need for reliable partners and long-term growth financing.
Li highlighted the success of the China-Kenya Trade Corridor, launched by Standard Chartered Bank in April to help local startups expand globally through tailored financing, multi-currency banking and streamlined capital management.
"The progress since then is reflected in the relationships, referrals and opportunities developed through the Kenya Investment Authority mission. These are opportunities for follow-up, rather than evidence of completed commercial transactions," Li said.
Li emphasized that the bank has served as a "super-connector," fostering dialogue between Chinese and Kenyan businesses through market expertise, tailored banking support,and the conversion of trade referrals into executed deals.
African startups and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) will be central to the long-term sustainability of commercial ties with China, making it essential to boost export volumes and enhance local value addition, Li said.
He added that African SMEs must consistently meet Chinese quality and certification standards, secure dependable logistics, and maintain reliable production and shipping pipelines.
Li observed that reliable cold chains, stringent product certifications and dependable shipping routes will be vital to the success of African agricultural exporters targeting the Chinese market.
Over the long term, technology transfer, in-country processing and expanded local manufacturing will prove essential to enhancing their global competitiveness.
Despite ongoing geopolitical shifts, the future of Sino-African trade ties remains highly promising, Li noted, pointing to product diversification, localized value addition, resilient supply chains and proactive currency risk management as key drivers of optimism.
"The opportunity is for Africa to become a stronger engine of growth within this trading relationship, with SMEs expanding exports and building the productive capacity behind them," Li said. ■

Roundup: South Africa's Parliament condemns minibus taxi violence in Western Cape
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
01:17:58 CST
02:17:58 KST

CAPE TOWN, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- South Africa's Parliament on Saturday condemned the recent taxi violence in the Western Cape province, calling on the national bodies in the taxi industry to speedily intervene.
According to a statement issued by the Parliament, fierce violence broke out on Thursday morning in Cape Town and a number of taxi operators and drivers have reportedly been killed.
"We send our deepest condolences to the families of those who have lost their lives and wish speedy recovery to all those affected," Donald Selamolela, chairperson of the Portfolio Committee on Transport in Parliament, was quoted as saying in the statement.
"This is a sad development in our country," Selamolela said, adding that the violence came at a time when the government was doing all it could to maximize support and investment in public transport. "The last thing we need is this bout of sporadic shootings that seem to be indiscriminate," he said.
"We condemn the criminality and violence that accompanies this outbreak and we call on law enforcement to ensure and maintain visibility until calm has been restored," Selamolela said, stressing that the violence should not threaten the people's expression of their wishes in the local elections scheduled for the following week.
Five men were killed and 4 others wounded in three separate shootings across Cape Town on Thursday, including one at the Delft taxi rank, according to local media reports.
The shootings came amid a wider wave of taxi-related violence across the metro, with incidents reported in recent weeks in Gugulethu, Khayelitsha, Epping and Bonteheuwel, all located within the Cape Flats region of Cape Town.
The Cape Town International Airport experienced disruptions on Friday due to ongoing taxi-related unrest.
According to a statement issued by Airports Company South Africa (ACSA) on Friday, the unrest had affected staffing levels across airport operations, resulting in extended passenger processing times and flight delays at the airport.
ACSA said that as of 13:00 on Friday, a total of 60 flight delays had been recorded at Cape Town International Airport, comprising 44 domestic departures, 11 international departures and five arrivals. "The average delay was approximately 60 minutes, with no cancellations reported," the company said.
In a separate development, the Western Cape High Court has granted an interim interdict against two taxi associations, the Cape Amalgamated Taxi Association (CATA) and the Congress of Democratic Taxi Associations (CODETA), as well as their cited office bearers, affiliated associations and members, following recent taxi violence in the province, the Western Cape government said on Friday.
The provisional order, which takes immediate effect, prohibits "violence, intimidation, road blockades, interference with public or private transport, unlawful route takeovers, damage to property and collecting money through threats." The respondents have until Nov. 20 to show why the order should not be made final, according to the provincial government.
Western Cape Mobility Minister Isaac Sileku said the department had approached the court after other efforts to stop the violence had failed. "I have a responsibility to protect residents who rely on public transport and ensure that lawful taxi operators can work without fear," he said.
In a separate regulatory action, the Western Cape Provincial Taxi Registrar has suspended the registration of the CATA Langa Inter-township Taxi Association for six months following an inquiry into unlawful operations in the Epping area, the provincial government said.
In the Parliament's statement, Selamolela also urged taxi operators to focus on their businesses and refrain from actions that could undermine the industry, saying the shooting at the Delft taxi rank on Thursday "should never have happened."
He noted that taxis remain the only affordable mode of transport in some communities. "Our attention should be focused on making the industry affordable, safe and reliable, and importantly complementary to other forms of transport and the economy," Selamolela concluded. ■
