====================================================================================================

Israel ready for another Iran war, but Trump has yet to decide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
17:07:36 UTC
02:07:36 KST

Israel's military has completed its preparations for another confrontation with Iran, both defensive and offensive, and the country's readiness is considered exceptionally high. But while Israel is increasingly prepared for renewed fighting, the decision on whether to launch another military campaign rests with Washington, not Jerusalem.
President Donald Trump faces two options. He could continue negotiating with Tehran in an effort to secure an agreement on more favorable terms for the United States, or he could resume military strikes alongside Israel. For now, he is pursuing both tracks, keeping negotiations alive while stepping up military preparations.
What remains unclear is precisely what Trump hopes to achieve through another military campaign and, more importantly, how he intends to bring it to an end. There is still no clear indication of what military objectives would justify renewed strikes, what would constitute success or how the fighting could be brought to a close.
As previously reported, Israel's political and military leadership did not want to initiate a strike before the elections, but preparations continued at an accelerated pace. Those preparations are now complete, following close coordination with the United States. American officials are already familiar with Israel's capabilities after the IDF's performance during Operation Roaring Lion, including its strikes in Iran, where it achieved complete air superiority, and its defensive operations.
The buildup is increasingly visible. Ten U.S. military transport aircraft arrived at Israeli Air Force bases this week as part of an airlift delivering military equipment to the region. Additional American forces are also being deployed. This goes beyond political rhetoric: Equipment, supplies and military capabilities are being positioned for the possibility of renewed fighting.
The Israeli Air Force has also been conducting exercises designed to demonstrate its readiness. According to foreign reports, dozens of Israeli fighter jets and refueling aircraft flew over Syria and Iraq, reaching an area near the Iranian border before returning to Israel.
The reports said Israel notified the Americans in advance that the flights were an exercise intended to demonstrate its capabilities to Tehran. Rather than routine training, the flights rehearsed a possible scenario for another strike. The Air Force reportedly conducted the exercise more than once.
US military options are taking shape, but the objectives remain unclear
According to The Wall Street Journal, U.S. Central Command chief Adm. Brad Cooper presented Trump with military options for renewed strikes against Iran. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine also attended the meeting.
The high-level discussion underscores how seriously Washington is considering military action even as diplomatic contacts continue. According to the report, however, Trump has yet to decide whether to resume the fighting.
His public statements offer another indication of his thinking. Two days ago, Trump wrote: "Everyone knows we had to strike Iran. They are not going to have nuclear weapons, and all of this is going to end very soon."
Combined with the military discussions at the White House and the buildup of forces in the region, the message suggests that Trump is preparing for the possibility of a short campaign. But there is no guarantee Iran would accept his timetable, and it remains unclear how Washington would bring such a confrontation to an end.
Both Trump and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu would enter another campaign following elections in their respective countries. Netanyahu would remain in office as caretaker prime minister. Israeli law does not prohibit a caretaker government from deciding to go to war, but such a decision requires approval from the government or an authorized security Cabinet. The prime minister cannot make it alone.
A central concern is the lack of clarity about Washington's objectives. If Trump is considering a short air campaign against Iran's nuclear infrastructure, missile systems and military capabilities, even a highly effective operation would not necessarily topple the Iranian regime.
Regime change is a broader strategic objective that cannot be guaranteed through a series of successful airstrikes. Significant military achievements do not necessarily mean Iran's leadership will fall or change its policies.
Alternatively, Trump may be seeking to use military pressure to extract better terms from Tehran at the negotiating table. If that is the objective, the details of any eventual agreement will matter as much as the pressure used to secure it. From Israel's perspective, a deal that merely postpones another confrontation without addressing Iran's principal threats would leave the underlying problem unresolved.
There is also the possibility of renewed fighting in Lebanon. Hezbollah joined the previous confrontation during Operation Roaring Lion, and another campaign against Iran could again develop into a war on two fronts.
A U.S. plan for a campaign lasting only a few days would not prevent Iran or Hezbollah from seeking to prolong it. Both could attempt to widen the conflict, target Israel and American interests in the region and extend the fighting well beyond Trump's intended timetable.
The IDF must therefore prepare for a potentially longer conflict, including the demands it would place on Israel's air defenses, interceptor stockpiles and the readiness of its forces.
Diplomatic contacts continue as Iran warns it will decide when a war ends
Meanwhile, reports suggest there may be progress in negotiations between Washington and Tehran. The Qatari newspaper Al-Araby Al-Jadeed reported a breakthrough in indirect talks and said an American delegation had joined discussions in Doha in an effort to move toward direct negotiations.
An Iranian source cited in the report said one of Iran's deputy foreign ministers was in Qatar and that the talks were being conducted through a mediator.
According to the report, discussions have focused on initial steps concerning Iran's nuclear program, the Strait of Hormuz and economic incentives for Tehran. China and Russia could also serve as guarantors of a possible agreement.
The reports do not mean a deal is imminent. They do, however, indicate that diplomacy remains active alongside the military preparations. Significant disagreements persist over three main issues: the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's nuclear program and its missiles. Trump has addressed Hormuz and the nuclear issue, while Israel is also seeking to halt Iran's military buildup.
Tehran, meanwhile, is escalating its warnings. Against the backdrop of the reported negotiations, Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei published a series of messages following a meeting with senior military officials.
"Any threat, at any level and of any kind, must be met with an immediate, significant response without geographical restrictions," he wrote.
Khamenei also warned that if strikes against Iran resume, the country's armed forces and people will decide "when and under what conditions they will end."
The contrast is clear. Trump says the confrontation will be over very soon. Khamenei insists Iran will determine when the fighting ends and on what terms. Between those competing positions lies the possibility of another war whose duration and scale neither side may be able to control.
Another important factor is Washington's view of Israel as a major operational partner. The IDF's performance during Operation Roaring Lion, in both offensive and defensive operations, and the close coordination between the two militaries have strengthened Israel's standing with the Americans.
The American airlift, military coordination and joint preparations all point to substantial cooperation. But close military cooperation does not mean the two countries necessarily share the same strategic priorities.
Trump will ultimately make decisions based on American interests. Israel must ensure that any renewed military campaign also serves its own long-term security needs.
The decision now rests with Trump. He must determine whether the military buildup is intended to pressure Tehran into accepting a new agreement or whether it is preparation for another joint military campaign.
But before either course is chosen, the central question needs an answer: What is the strategic objective, and what would constitute victory?
Another strike against Iran is not necessarily the problem. The greater risk is entering another war without a clear plan for ending it or a realistic understanding of what comes afterward.

US President Donald Trump had previously warned of fresh military action after the US holds midterm elections early next week, saying last weekend that he was weighing whether to "finish them off".
In Israel, which is coming off fresh elections, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has spoken of a "historic, one-time opportunity" to topple the Iranian government.
Polls in both countries could determine the direction of the conflict, with Israel having voted Tuesday but yet to form a new government.
"Any level or type of threat must be met with an immediate, impactful and geographically unrestricted response," Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei told top military commanders in a meeting, according to a statement.
The encounter was the first reported meeting between Khamenei and military top brass, and included armed forces chief of staff Ali Abdollahi, army chief Amir Hatami and Revolutionary Guards commander Ahmad Vahidi.
The supreme leader has not been seen publicly since before he took the helm in March after the killing of his father Ayatollah Ali Khamenei in US-Israeli strikes.
Khamenei also ordered commanders to update Iran's target list to include "all types of tangible and intangible assets belonging to the American-Zionist enemy".
Iran has previously warned it would consider severing undersea cables in the Strait of Hormuz.
Petrol prices weigh on US vote
Since the initial US-Israeli strikes in February, ordinary Iranians "have been left in a state of limbo for the past year", Fariba, a Tehran housewife, told AFP.
But other residents in the Iranian capital brushed off the possible return to full-scale conflict.
"We do not fear another war. We have been at war for 48 years now," said Ebrahim, a salesman in his forties.
Since the outbreak of the war, Tehran has restricted shipping through the strategic waterway, which normally carries around one-fifth of global oil consumption.
Watch moreTrump vs MAGA: Why his movement is splitting
The blockade has caused a spike in global energy prices, making the war unpopular among the US public ahead of midterm congressional elections Tuesday.
Gains for the opposition Democrats could restrict, to an extent, Trump's ability to enact policy.
Voting in Israel has left Netanyahu's political camp with the most seats in parliament but short of a majority, leaving the make-up of the next administration unclear.
Read more'Atmosphere of fear': Trump moves to curtail voting rights ahead of the midterms
'Flames of war'
The war began on February 28 with US-Israeli strikes on Iran. The Islamic republic swiftly responded with attacks on American assets in countries around the region.
Fresh diplomatic efforts are underway to avert any resumption of fighting, with Qatari mediators landing in Tehran on Friday, and US Vice President JD Vance sending a letter to Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei.
But Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Saturday that "currently, there are no plans for meetings with American officials".
"Iran's conditions are clear, and consultations regarding them are ongoing among mediators," he said in an interview with Al Jazeera, according to the state news agency IRNA.
Read moreAre fresh US-Israeli strikes on Iran in the pipeline?
Qatar and Pakistan have been mediating between the warring parties, but the talks have yet to produce a lasting agreement.
The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday that Vance had sent his letter to Iran's security chief at Trump's direction in a bid to revive negotiations and avert further US strikes.
Araghchi confirmed that Iran received the letter, saying, "The American side's effort to open a dialogue and reach a broader understanding is viewed as a positive step."
But the Iranian side kept firm its warnings against further attacks.
Earlier on Saturday, army spokesman Mohammad Akaraminia said that any resumption of hostilities would only expand the scope of the war.
"The flames of war will undoubtedly engulf a much wider geographical area," he said on social media, without elaborating.
Araghchi warned on X of an "Earth-shattering blow Iran's Powerful Armed Forces will deal against those who dare harm our people".
He said there would no longer be any "red lines".

China expands foreign business access at world's largest FTP
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:58:51 UTC
01:58:51 KST

Under the measures, foreign physicians legally licensed to practice medicine overseas may obtain permits to provide clinical diagnosis and treatment services in Hainan for up to three years, with extensions available in accordance with relevant regulations.
More convenient policies regarding work permits and stay and residence will also be introduced for foreign nationals.
The Hainan FTP, located in China's southernmost island province, launched island-wide special customs operations in December 2025, allowing freer entry of overseas goods, expanded zero-tariff coverage and more business-friendly measures as part of China's efforts to promote high-standard opening-up.
Overseas companies will be allowed to use bonded facilities at Hainan's liquefied natural gas (LNG) receiving terminals, while the FTP will be supported in conducting LNG futures delivery warehouse operations after LNG futures contracts are launched.
Other measures include promoting offshore trade, expanding the range of products eligible for bonded maintenance, facilitating the entry of eligible bonded remanufactured products into pilot free trade zones on the Chinese mainland, encouraging the use of the yuan in new forms of barter trade, and deepening the FTP's economic and trade cooperation with China's Hong Kong Special Administrative Region.
Bonded remanufactured products entering mainland pilot free trade zones will be subject to applicable import tariffs, import-related value-added tax and consumption tax. They must also meet all applicable technical requirements for equivalent new products and relevant regulations on remanufactured products, and be clearly labeled as such.
The circular also calls for improved insurance products and services in areas such as international transportation and bonded maintenance.
The latest measures come amid robust growth in Hainan's foreign trade. In the first three quarters of 2026, the province's goods imports and exports reached 285.44 billion yuan (about 42.5 billion U.S. dollars), up 49.8 percent year on year, while trade in services rose 11.7 percent to 56.95 billion yuan, according to data from Hainan's provincial commerce authorities.
Trade in maintenance and repair services more than doubled year on year to 3.31 billion yuan during the same period, according to the provincial commerce department. The trade mainly came from imports of aircraft materials and components and revenues from aircraft maintenance services.
The number of newly established foreign-invested enterprises in Hainan rose 38.6 percent year on year in the first half of 2026, according to the State Administration for Market Regulation.
The FTP measures are part of China's broader efforts to promote high-standard opening-up. The country has announced plans to further expand pilot opening-up programs in sectors such as value-added telecommunications, biotechnology and wholly foreign-owned hospitals, while taking steps to facilitate cross-border trade and investment.
The circular was jointly issued by the Ministry of Commerce, the National Development and Reform Commission, the Ministry of Ecology and Environment and the General Administration of Customs.

'We are not going to let you escape'

INDIA bloc holds 'public impeachment' of CEC

French police clash with some protesters again as demonstrations continue in nation's cities
French police fired tear gas and clashed with some protesters on Saturday as thousands marched across France again in largely peaceful demonstrations against soaring living costs and police violence.
Police said about 70,000 people demonstrated in Paris alone. France's interior ministry said about 320,000 people rallied nationwide.
Officers had made 27 arrests by 2:00 p.m. on Saturday, compared with 217 arrests a week ago. In the southern port city of Marseille, demonstrators clashed with police. In Lyon, France's third-largest city, people threw projectiles at police, prompting officers to fire tear gas, according to a journalist at the scene.
In the southern city of Toulouse, police used water cannon against an unauthorized protest that drew several thousand people, mostly young demonstrators, some of them in costume.
In Paris, thousands of people, some wearing costumes ranging from Spider-Man to Frankenstein, walked through eastern Paris as a helicopter circled overhead. Placards read: "No need for tear gas to make our future look bleak" and "Dressed up as an angry citizen for Halloween." Hard-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who has accused French President Emmanuel Macron's government of "taking an increasingly authoritarian turn," joined the march.
"We say no to the cost of living, no to the far right, yes to high school students' demands, yes to giving citizens a voice," Camille Guerin, 31, said in the western city of Nantes.
In the northern French city of Lille, 47-year-old Aurelie Herrmann danced at the protest.
"I dance because on television they only show damage and destruction, whereas you can perfectly well demonstrate in good spirits," she said.
An aide to Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said on Friday that police had prepared for street violence on a scale "comparable" to the unrest two weeks ago, when shops were looted and public buildings set ablaze. Nunez said authorities had detected social media calls for Halloween gatherings on Saturday evening that urged protesters to spark a "revolution."
Some shopkeepers again prepared by barricading their businesses.
"Everyone is staying home. No one is going to come and buy anything," said Wael Boubaker, a cafe employee in eastern Paris, as he covered a storefront with plywood panels.
Alain Di Crescenzo, president of France's chamber of commerce, said business owners were worried.
"Shopkeepers can't wait for Saturday to be over," Di Crescenzo told broadcaster France Inter.
Protests come as elections near
The demonstrations come in a febrile political climate, with presidential elections less than six months away and far-right leader Marine Le Pen leading the polls.
The protest movement, bringing together activists, trade unions, and high school and university students, initially focused on the rising cost of living, inequality, and deteriorating learning conditions.
Following a security clampdown and serious injuries to some protesters, the movement broadened its demands to include greater protection of civil liberties and the right to protest. This week, student protesters complained that the police did not authorize a march through the center of the French capital, and vowed to stage new blockades of high schools and universities next week.
With the eurozone's second-largest economy on the brink of recession and under pressure to rein in its debt, the government has limited scope to appease protesters through additional spending.
Similar youth-led demonstrations have been seen across Europe in recent weeks. Thousands of young Germans took to the streets nationwide on Saturday.

Iranian strikes damage 24 US military sites, adding billions to war costs: WSJ
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:50:07 UTC
01:50:07 KST

Iranian strikes have damaged hundreds of buildings at military installations hosting US forces across the Middle East, potentially adding billions of dollars to the cost of the war, The Wall Street Journal reported on Friday.
An analysis of satellite imagery found that 274 structures at 24 installations with a US military presence sustained damage during the war's first six months.
Among the hardest-hit sites was Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan, where an Iranian strike on July 17 killed three American service members and damaged at least 19 buildings, including facilities where troops sleep.
The Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies estimated that rebuilding the damaged structures alone would cost more than $4 billion, excluding the replacement of equipment and systems inside the buildings.
Meanwhile, the Pentagon has put the damage to US military bases at a minimum of $5 billion, with estimates potentially reaching $15 billion, according to US officials cited by the Journal.
These expenses come on top of the estimated $47.1 billion cost of the war as of October 16, the report said.
Beyond the financial burden, the destruction has raised concerns over the safety of military personnel, with more than 20 US servicemembers killed and over 400 wounded since the conflict began February 28.
Opposition Democrats in the US have accused the Trump administration of deliberately low-balling figures on the cost of the war, from casualties to its budgetary and wider financial costs.

MAC details stark Taiwan-China divide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:44:06 UTC
01:44:06 KST

The fifth plenum of the Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) 20th Central Committee and Taiwan’s election debates highlighted a stark contrast between China’s centralization of power and Taiwan’s democracy, Mainland Affairs Council (MAC) Deputy Minister Shen Yu-chung (沈有忠) said yesterday.
Differences in political systems are the most fundamental issue in cross-strait relations, which have nothing to do with similarities in culture, language or ethnicity, he said.
Shen made the remarks at a forum held by the Secure Taiwan Associate Corporation to discuss possible developments in China’s domestic political situation following the fifth plenum, and their implications for Taiwan.
Photo: Fang Wei-li, Taipei Times
The theme of the plenum, which concluded on Thursday last week, was “unswerving promotion of the full and rigorous party self-governance,” a move by Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) to further bolster the CCP’s leadership and consolidate his authority ahead of next year’s 21st CCP National Congress, Shen said.
The MAC’s analysis of the plenum can be summarized into four points, he said.
First, the “Xi Jinping thought on party building” was established as a political guiding principle, further consolidating Xi’s unchallengeable position as the party’s leader, Shen said.
The plenum confirmed earlier decisions to expel 33 officials from the party, including former senior military leaders Zhang Youxia (張又俠) and Liu Zhenli (劉振立), he said, adding that accusations against them, including failing to implement central policies and engaging in duplicity and disloyalty, demonstrated that anyone who is insufficiently loyal to Xi or deviates from his ideology and directives would be purged.
Second, the MAC believes that “strict party governance” aims to ensure the CCP’s long-term rule and preserve its one-party dictatorship, Shen said.
Whether it is political, organizational, integrity or work discipline, all rules must be based on monitoring and ensuring that party members and officials obey the CCP, he said, adding that the development of China’s constitutional system, and the protection of people’s rights and interests take a back seat to the goal of consolidating the CCP’s one-party rule.
Third, the promotion of “the party’s self-revolution” represents a rejection of external oversight by the public, media and civil society, Shen said.
Although the authenticity of posts that students from more than 10 Chinese universities had allegedly signed a petition calling for the abolition of the indefinite term for the president remains unverified, they signaled that the party’s leadership is not subject to any external oversight, he said.
Xi might respond to academic activities or social movements with further legal measures or intensified surveillance, he added.
The CCP has fully internalized its oversight mechanisms within the party’s disciplinary and supervisory systems, rejecting democratic checks and balances in the name of “self-correction within the party,” he said.
Fourth, moves to eliminate dissenting voices have paved the way for Xi to secure a fourth term at next year’s 21st National Congress, Shen said.
The number of Central Committee members and alternate members absent from the plenum reached a new high since the era of Mao Zedong (毛澤東), he said.
Large-scale purges of senior party, government and military officials over the past few years have removed potential political obstacles to Xi’s ambitions, ensuring he can continue on to a fourth term with the party’s full endorsement, he added.
While the plenum unfolded in Beijing, many in Taiwan were focused on the mayoral debates in Taipei and Kaohsiung, highlighting the fundamental differences between the political systems on the two sides of the Strait, Shen said.
The CCP’s fifth plenum demonstrated the consolidation of power and the growing dominance of Xi’s leadership, he said, adding that Taiwan’s lively mayoral debates would be impossible in China.
Shen urged Taiwanese to recognize these institutional differences and unite against authoritarian aggression, build a shared commitment to protecting freedom, democracy and national sovereignty to ensure that Taiwan can continue to deepen its democracy, prosperity and development amid the CCP’s multifaceted pressure campaign.
With local elections entering their final campaign phase, the government would continue to closely monitor developments within the CCP and shifts in its power structure, while preventing and exposing various forms of Chinese election interference, he said.

Wang said that seasonal winds are expected to strengthen again tomorrow and on Tuesday, then weaken on Wednesday and Thursday before another wave arrives on Friday or Saturday. Rain is likely along the northern coast and in eastern Taiwan during this time.
Photo provided by the Central Weather Administration
Although Typhoon In-fa is not forecast to directly affect Taiwan, it could create significant swells along the northern coast, eastern Taiwan and the Hengchun Peninsula (恆春半島) from today into next week, Wang added.

ANALYTICAL ENGLISH 解析英語(常春藤)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:44:02 UTC
01:44:02 KST

Many people love their dogs and spare no effort to provide them with the best food possible. However, a recent study has shed light on an often overlooked environmental issue. By analyzing nearly 1,000 commercial dog food recipes, researchers found that these diets leave a significant “carbon pawprint.” For a 20-kilogram dog, 40% of tested dog foods were found to produce more greenhouse gas emissions than __1__ from a human vegan diet.
The primary factor is the composition and format of modern dog food, particularly wet and raw diets. Products made with meat that is also commonly __2__ humans, such as chicken breast, require more resources and create more greenhouse gases. By contrast, foods containing animal byproducts or plant proteins generally have a smaller environmental impact. Compared with standard dry kibble, wet and raw products also __3__ on the environment. They often require refrigeration or freezing and involve additional packaging and transportation.
__4__ popular belief, raw diets are not always the healthiest option. They may pose health risks, including nutritional imbalances and bacterial infections. When properly formulated, plant-based diets can also meet dogs’ nutritional needs. Although these options are not yet widely used, they are gaining acceptance among veterinarians.
Photo: AdobeStock I 照片：AdobeStock
This research indicates that the environmental impact of dog food depends largely on its ingredients. Therefore, clear labels must be placed on packaging. Consumers need __5__ ingredient information to make informed choices, and such clarity would also help buyers balance nutrition with sustainability.
許多人深愛自己的狗狗，不遺餘力地盡可能為牠們提供最好的食物。然而，近期的一項研究揭示了一個往往被忽視的環境議題。透過分析近一千種市售狗糧配方，研究人員發現這些飲食留下了顯著的「碳爪跡」。以一隻二十公斤的狗而言，在接受測試的狗糧中，發現有 40% 所產生的溫室氣體排放量甚至超過了人類純素飲食的排放量。
主要的因素在於現代狗糧的成分與形式，尤其是溼食和生食。使用人類也常食用的肉類（例如雞胸肉）所製成的產品，需要消耗更多資源，也會產生更多溫室氣體。相比之下，含有動物副產品或植物蛋白的食物，通常對環境的影響較小。與普通的乾飼料相比，溼食與生食產品對環境造成的負擔也更重。這些產品往往需要冷藏或冷凍，還包含額外的包裝與運輸。
與普遍的觀念相反，生食飲食並不總是最健康的選擇。它們可能會帶來健康風險，包括營養失衡和細菌感染。在經過妥善調配的情況下，植物性飲食同樣能夠滿足狗狗的營養需求。雖然這些選項目前尚未被廣泛使用，但已逐漸獲得獸醫們的認可。
這項研究指出，狗糧對環境的影響在很大程度上取決於其成分。因此，包裝上必須貼有清楚的標籤。消費者需要公開透明的成分資訊來做出明智的選擇，而這樣的清晰度也將有助於購買者在營養與永續發展之間取得平衡。
What Did You Learn?
1. (A) which (B) these (C) what (D) those
2. (A) restricted to (B) consumed by (C) satisfied with (D) prohibited from
3. (A) make a smaller profit (B) cast a lesser shadow (C) place a heavier burden (D) score a better success
4. (A) Contrary to (B) Prior to (C) Because of (D) Short of
5. (A) eloquent (B) imaginative (C) transparent (D) predictable
答案： 1. D 2. B 3. C 4. A 5. C
Words in Use
1. carbon n. 碳
carbon pawprint （碳爪跡）是從carbon footprint（碳足跡）衍生出的環保新詞。
carbon footprint 通常是指人類活動或產品生命週期中所排放的溫室氣體總量。
carbon pawprint 則指我們飼養的寵物在生活中所產生的碳排放量，除了文中提到的寵物食品，還包括日常用品、醫療和廢棄物等。
The bike frame is made of carbon fiber, which makes it very light and strong.
這輛自行車的車架是由碳纖維製成，讓它非常輕巧又堅固。
2. overlook vt. 忽略，忽視（本文為過去分詞作形容詞用）
This small town is an often overlooked tourist destination with beautiful scenery.
這座小鎮是個景色優美卻經常被忽略的旅遊景點。
Julian overlooked the spelling mistake on the first page of the essay.
朱利安忽略了作文第一頁的拼字錯誤。
3. analyze vt. 分析
Doctors will analyze your blood sample to find out what is causing your allergy.
醫生會分析你的血液樣本，以找出導致你過敏的原因。
4. emission n. 排放物
The new hybrid bus reduces smoke emissions.
這款新型油電混合公車降低了廢氣排放物。
5. composition n. 組合成分
Scientists are studying the chemical composition of the soil on Mars.
科學家們正在研究火星土壤的化學成分。
Practical Phrases
1. spare no effort to V 不遺餘力地……
Becca spares no effort to achieve her dream of studying abroad.
貝卡不遺餘力地去實現出國留學的夢想。
2. shed light on. . . 闡明;使人明白
The discovery of the old sign sheds light on the local history of the farm.
這塊舊招牌的發現讓人們更了解這塊農田的當地歷史。
3. by contrast 相較之下（相反）
Kevin is very quiet and shy; by contrast, his sister Sarah loves to talk.
凱文非常安靜害羞；相較之下，他妹妹莎拉非常健談。
4. compared with / to. . . 與……相比
Compared with the old system, the new software is very easy to use.
與舊系統相比，新軟體非常容易使用。
5. balance A with B 在A與B間取得平衡
Rachel learned to balance her studies with her social life.
瑞秋學會在課業與社交生活間取得平衡。

Experts caution cancer cachexia an urgent issue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:44:00 UTC
01:44:00 KST

Many people might think it is normal to experience weight loss and weakness during cancer treatment, but medical experts yesterday warned that it could also be “cancer cachexia,” and that insufficient muscle mass can even cause treatment to fail.
The 3rd International Conference on Sarcopenia, organized by Taipei Medical University (TMU) and focusing on “Sarcopenia, Cachexia and Frailty” was held at the university in Taipei yesterday.
With the global population aging, sarcopenia has become a pressing health challenge that significantly impacts the well-being and quality of life of elderly people, and surveys in Taiwan estimate that more than one-third of elderly people are affected or at risk, the TMU said.
Photo courtesy fo the Taipei Medical University
Experts from the UK, Japan, South Korea and Singapore, across sectors and disciplines — covering neurology, rehabilitation, cardiology, regenerative medicine, biomarkers, genetics and more — joined the conference to address this urgent issue, it said.
Some people become increasingly thin and frail during cancer treatment and believe that it is a normal side effect, but TMU Graduate Institute of Cancer Biology and Drug Discovery chair professor Yen Yun (閻雲) said it could be a sign of “cancer cachexia.”
Cancer cachexia is a tumor-driven metabolic syndrome that is characterized by systemic inflammation, which accelerates the breakdown of muscle mass and fat tissue, he said.
People with cancer cachexia might experience extreme weight loss and exhaustion, and it could even force the patients to discontinue cancer treatments because their body is no longer strong enough to tolerate them, he added.
Studies have estimated that cancer cachexia affects about 50 percent of people with cancer, Yen said.
In his keynote speech, National Cancer Centre of Singapore deputy chief executive officer Bin Tean Teh said that muscle loss occurred in cancer patients through transcriptomics, and shared exploratory pathways for future treatments.
TMU executive vice president Liou Tsan-hon (劉燦宏), who is also TMU Shuang Ho Hospital superintendent, said preserving muscle mass has become a public issue, as in a super-aged society, “maintaining muscle strength and preventing disability” is the key to health and longevity.
As people age, inactivity causes muscle mass and strength to decline much faster, and continued muscle loss might ultimately severely impair their ability to manage daily self-care, he said.
As there is no medication that can directly cure or treat sarcopenia globally, early lifestyle interventions combining a “nutritional diet” and “resistance exercise” have become a shared focus of preventing and managing age-related muscle loss, he said.

2026 Elections: Kaohsiung debate focuses on 205th Arsenal, donations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:43:59 UTC
01:43:59 KST

A mayoral debate was on Friday evening held in Kaohsiung, with the two leading candidates — the Democratic Progressive Party’s (DPP) Lai Jui-lung (賴瑞隆) and Chinese Nationalist Party’s (KMT) Ko Chih-en (柯志恩) — focusing largely on the redevelopment of the site of the 205th Arsenal and political donations.
The relocation of the 205th Arsenal, under the Armaments Bureau, from downtown Kaohsiung to the city’s Dashu District (大樹) was completed last year. Plans for the redevelopment of the 57-hectare site have since drawn considerable public attention.
Founded in 1945, the 205th Arsenal has been responsible for producing small arms with calibers of less than 40mm for the armed forces.
Photo: CNA
The arsenal is near Asia New Bay Area, which the city has developed into a major commercial and industrial hub, Lai said, adding that the site should therefore be reserved for future industrial development.
He criticized Ko’s proposal to relocate Kaohsiung City Hall and the Kaohsiung City Council to the former arsenal site, saying that the plan would impose a heavy financial burden on the city.
Ko said Lai had no clear idea how to redevelop the vast site.
He only offered incomplete proposals without careful consideration, such as seeking to attract Nvidia Corp to the area or turning it into an artificial intelligence park, she said.
The former arsenal is in the heart of the city and a comprehensive redevelopment plan is needed, Ko said.
She suggested transforming the site into a special district similar to New York City’s Manhattan, with the ambition of making it surpass Taipei’s Xinyi (信義) commercial district.
Ko, a legislator, questioned Lai, also a legislator, over donations he had received from solar energy developers and his arrangement of legislative hearings that allegedly benefited their business interests.
Lai said he had always declared political donations according to law.
The hearings were organized to seek expert opinions from government officials, academics and business representatives on the direction of Taiwan’s energy development, rather than to promote the interests of particular companies, he said.
Lai also criticized the KMT for introducing a proposal to increase the government’s revenue allocation to Taipei by 3 percent when the legislature amended the Act Governing the Allocation of Government Revenues and Expenditures (財政收支劃分法) in 2024.
Ko said the amendment passed by the legislature contained no provision for a 3 percent increase in Taipei’s revenue allocation, accusing Lai of spreading rumors and making personal attacks against her.
Lai said Ko did not know Kaohsiung well enough, urging voters to vote for him, so he could work for the city, arguing that Kaohsiung could not afford development policies that favored northern Taiwan over the south.
He accused Ko of claiming to put Kaohsiung first while prioritizing the KMT’s interests.
Ko responded that, as a legislator-at-large, her work in politics and policy proposals covered national issues, including energy, education and school council reform.

Top diplomats from the G20 were yesterday to wrap up two days of talks in Atlanta, Georgia, without reaching a consensus on several critical global security issues due to divisions, notably over Russia’s war with Ukraine.
As a result, the group would not release a joint communique, but instead rely on a chairman’s statement summarizing the talks, which US Secretary of State Marco Rubio was to release at the conclusion, diplomats who attended said.
The meeting was still ongoing as of press time last night.
Photo: AFP
Rubio, who opened the talks with an appeal for unity, had canceled the traditional group photo of the foreign ministers on Friday after European diplomats objected to the inclusion of Russian Minister of Foreign Affairs Sergey Lavrov and threatened to boycott or walk out of the snapshot that often starts such gatherings.
Polish Minister of Foreign Affairs Radoslaw Sikorski said he was not surprised by the failure to reach a consensus.
“We have wars going on, and we have participants in those wars around the table, so it’s very difficult to agree on a common line,” he said.
Other participants in the meetings, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said all had agreed to try to overcome their differences despite the long odds and to work to make next month’s G20 leaders summit hosted by US President Donald Trump in Florida a success.
A chairman’s statement had long been the plan due to the deep differences among the attendees, including over the Russia-Ukraine conflict, the US-Israeli war against Iran, US tariffs and Chinese machinations in the South China Sea, they said.
They described the opening session as cordial, but said Russia’s position on Ukraine is unyielding — as is its opposition to Poland’s membership in the G20.
And they said the disagreements also include the Trump administration’s not inviting G20 member South Africa over the objections of others.
The US has said a top priority for the meeting is resolving differences over issues related to freedom of navigation, particularly in the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, the Black Sea and the South China Sea.
The topic was to include discussions on Iran, Russia-Ukraine and China and its smaller neighbors.

Countries commit to get nature goals back on track
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:43:48 UTC
01:43:48 KST

Nearly 200 nations on Friday struck hard-fought agreements at a UN biodiversity summit, but the outcome was accompanied by disappointment over missed opportunities to address humanity’s destructive toll on nature.
Delegates cheered as crucial texts were approved in overtime, but the celebrations were tempered by acrimonious debates and regret over limited progress on some of the most contentious issues.
The COP17 summit in Armenia sought to revive a landmark commitment to halt and reverse the destruction of nature by 2030 after global efforts to meet that goal fell short.
Photo: AFP
Over two bruising weeks in Yerevan, nations were urged to correct course to keep the pact alive and protect the plants, animals and ecosystems that sustain life on Earth.
The UN had warned that progress was insufficient to meet the goals of the 2030 target including protecting 30 percent of Earth’s land and oceans, tackling pollution and invasive species, and boosting money for conservation.
“And that’s it. Perfect,” COP17 president and Armenian Minister of Environment Hambardzum Matevosyan said as he brought down the gavel on two major texts, the final versions of which were still not available early yesterday.
However, the outcome was “not commensurate” with the crisis engulfing the natural world, French Minister of Ecological Transition Monique Barbut said.
“The progress we failed to achieve here is a series of missed opportunities to speed up our response to the loss of biodiversity,” Barbut said, adding that “nature will not wait for the pace of our negotiations.”
The final plenary stretched through Friday night and well into yesterday morning, with negotiations turning sour as the hours dragged on. Even as some delegates left to catch flights, others stayed behind to argue technical points.
UN Convention on Biological Diversity Executive Secretary Astrid Schomaker said the summit had achieved some “quite remarkable things at a moment when multilateralism is supposedly not functioning.”
“Some of these more difficult subjects, we could not expect to have strong negotiated commitments. That was never the plan,” she said.
A draft agreement said nations were urged to “accelerate” their efforts and warned that “increased action” was needed to tackle the forces driving biodiversity loss.
This “represents a positive outcome... and though there are weaknesses, particularly on harmful subsidies, it does represent a step forward,” Guido Broekhoven from WWF International said.
Tackling subsidies and other incentives that encourage activities harmful to nature — such as fossil fuels, intensive agriculture and overfishing — was one of the most politically fraught agenda items at the summit.
A rare fight over science cast a pall over the summit, with a number of countries accused of undermining efforts to approve key reports in scenes that shocked even seasoned negotiators.
“We regret the increasing instances in which scientific evidence and its uptake has been challenged or constrained” by politics, Swiss negotiator Gabriela Blatter said. “Our delegations fully respect every state’s right to safeguard national interest, but science is not negotiable.”
A separate row revolved around finding new cash sources to fund conservation efforts — another hot-button issue with public budgets under strain amid an energy crisis and conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East.
The EU led a charge for wealthy emerging economies such as China to contribute to global conservation efforts, a contentious issue at COP17.
In a sign of a possible compromise, another draft text invited countries outside the developed-country donors to voluntarily join the group.
Outstanding questions over the design of the Cali Fund — a UN mechanism that hoped to attract billions of dollars in corporate contributions, but is close to empty — were left unresolved.
The COP17 summit has decided that Ecuador would host the next biodiversity talks in 2028 after the South American nation defeated Panama in a secret vote.

Youth Olympic Games open in Senegal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:43:46 UTC
01:43:46 KST

The Youth Olympic Games opened in Senegal yesterday, bringing an Olympic event to Africa for the first time as the continent seeks a bigger role in international sporting competitions.
About 2,700 young athletes aged 14 to 17 are competing through Nov. 13 in the capital, Dakar, the nearby city of Diamniadio and the beach resort of Saly.
Hundreds of dancers were to join a spectacle at the opening ceremony — which was to start after press time last night — celebrating Senegalese and African culture, in line with the Games motto: “Africa welcomes, Dakar celebrates.”
Photo courtesy of Taiwan’s delegation to the Youth Olympic Games
“This is a first opportunity for Senegal and, by extension, for Africa, to discover new sports,” Thomas Dieme, a Senegalese student said as Dakar prepared to host the Games. “It is only natural that we should all be happy to welcome other people, other cultures.”
Among the celebrities expected at the opening ceremony was French actor Omar Sy, who has Senegalese roots and stars in the Netflix series Lupin, as well as Senegalese Italian TikTok star Khaby Lame, both ambassadors for the Games.
The mascot, Ayo, is a young lion wearing a traditional Fulani hat. Its name means “joy” in Yoruba, a language spoken in Nigeria and neighboring west African countries.
Photo: AFP
Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye was expected to declare the Games open at 6:30pm at the Diamniadio Stadium, with International Olympic Committee (IOC) president Kirsty Coventry and some heads of state in attendance.
The Youth Olympics are a smaller competition than the Summer Olympics. Singapore hosted the first summer edition in 2010. Dakar was initially due to host in 2022, but the COVID-19 pandemic delayed the event by four years.
Athletes are competing in 153 medal events across 25 sports, including athletics, swimming, 3x3 basketball and for the first time baseball5, with Taiwan starting their campaign in the compact baseball variant on Friday.
Photo: AP
Taiwan scored a commanding victory over hosts Senegal, winning 2-0 in their Group A opener.
Taiwan took the first game 11-1 and the second 10-0 to earn the nation’s first Youth Olympic victory in baseball5.
Hsu Tzu-yi collected four hits in each game, while Chen Wan-zih contributed six hits and eight RBIs across the two contests.
“I think I was a little too excited in the first game and my legs went a bit weak, but once I got into the rhythm, I played smoothly,” Hsu told Top Sporting News Agency.
Chen said that her World Cup experience had prepared her well for Senegal.
“I prepared myself before the game, so I just played freely,” she said.
Coach Feng Wei-kuo said the players had experienced opening nerves and identified details to improve despite the convincing win.
Taiwan were to play Turkey yesterday, with Cuba the other team in the group.
Taiwan’s full delegation includes 37 athletes competing across 17 sports.
Baseball5 is a five-on-five version of baseball played by mixed-gender teams without a bat or gloves on a compact field.
Other sports making their Youth Olympic debut include Wushu, a Chinese martial art, and coastal rowing beach sprint, which combines beach runs with a head-to-head rowing race.
Beach wrestling is also at the Youth Olympics for the first time, a nod to Senegalese wrestling, the country’s national sport also performed on sand.
The first refugee team at a Youth Olympics have six athletes based in Kenya and Uganda in track and field, judo and taekwondo.
The Games arrive 130 years after the modern Olympics began in Athens.
Coventry, a Zimbabwean swimming champion, became the IOC’s first African and first female president last year.
“It is time for Africa, time for Senegal,” Coventry told media upon arriving in Senegal on Tuesday.
South Africa hosted the continent’s first soccer FIFA World Cup in 2010. Morocco is to cohost the 2030 tournament with Spain and Portugal. Rwanda hosted Africa’s first road cycling world championships last year and Formula 1 is returning to Africa with a grand prix in Rwanda starting early next decade. Botswana staged the World Athletics Relays in May.
African countries increasingly see sport as “a weapon in diplomacy and a tool for development,” Dakar-based sports analyst Frederic Sohounde said.
He pointed to Morocco’s investment in sports facilities and its ability to attract repeated competitions.
However, Senegal needs reliable maintenance funding and regular events after the Games to prevent its venues from becoming expensive, unused facilities, he said.
Russia’s delegation of 13 athletes is competing under its national flag for the first time at an Olympic event since restrictions imposed following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Russians at the Paris Olympics of 2024 and this year’s Winter Olympics competed as neutral athletes without national symbols.
That follows a shift in the IOC’s approach under Coventry, who has said the Olympics should not “hold athletes accountable for the actions of their governments.”
It could be a trial run for a full Russian return at the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028.
Additional reporting by staff writer

Mocking former leader Mao — blamed by historians for millions of deaths — is taboo in China, and Mbappe’s remarks saw him become the latest foreign sports figure to anger Beijing. Dachshunds at the center of exhibition in Germany
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:43:46 UTC
01:43:46 KST

The humble dachshund is taking center stage in a new exhibition in Germany that explores the history of the sausage dog in art — and visitors are welcome to bring their four-legged friends along.
“The Dachshund: An Icon off the Leash” opened at the Kunsthalle Bremen yesterday, showcasing artwork by dachshund owners and fans including Pablo Picasso, David Hockney and Andy Warhol.
In addition to painting, drawing, photography and video, visitors can admire delights such as a wealth of stuffed toy dogs and many other dachshund-themed objects.
Photo: AP
Museum director Christoph Grunenberg believes it is the world’s first exhibition dedicated to the dachshund in art, rather than dogs in general.
“There are many artists who owned dachshunds, who were inspired by the dachshund, loved the dachshund,” Grunenberg said. “It was like a muse and there is an incredible wealth of representation of the dachshund in very different styles by significant artists.”
“We wanted to take the dachshund as an object, as an inspiration to artists, and trace it through history in all its different forms and important works of art by Picasso, Warhol and Hockney and also ephemera,” he added.
German artist Thorsten Brinkmann honored the compact dogs’ reputation as a “handbag dog” with a bronze sculpture that features a handbag on dachshund legs. He also provided the colorful “Toxie Love” installation in the exhibition’s first room, which sets a playful tone for the show.
The dachshund has “a very curious, very special form, very long — kind of too long, actually, with the short legs — and it looks already surrealistic to me,” he said.
He was helped by objects loaned by the Dachshund Museum in Regensburg, Germany.
For several hours on Thursdays and Saturdays, the museum will let dachshunds and other small dogs into three of its eight rooms for a look and a sniff.
Among the conditions: They must have a maximum shoulder height of 30cm and an online time-slot ticket. A “Dachshund Lounge” will be offered as a waiting area.
“We want to take the dog seriously as a personality and the dog can walk around, can interact, will be able to watch videos, look outside the window, smell — and of course that’s what the dog really is interested in,” Grunenberg said.
Finnish photographer Elina Brotherus’ dachshund, Marcello, already checked out the wares ahead of the opening of the exhibition, which features Brotherus’ pictures of the 13-year-old dog.
Marcello has been her model since 2013, Brotherus said.
“I did not manage to have children, so then we got him and he’s my baby,” she said. “There’s something so, like, cute and philosophical and special about these dogs.”
Business developer Kelsey Crossman explored the show with her dachshund, Leonidas, or Leo for short.
The dogs’ appeal is in “their attitudes — they’re small, but they’re very strong and a little stubborn, probably like myself,” she said.

Once opportunity, chokepoints are now a threat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:43:44 UTC
01:43:44 KST

Stand on a clear day atop Singapore’s Marina Bay Sands hotel, and you can see the city-state’s promise and peril in a single glance.
In the foreground, a flotilla of ships lies at anchor, a physical reminder of how Singapore grew rich servicing the immense volume of global trade squeezed through the chokepoint of its narrow strait. On the horizon, you can just make out the coastline of Indonesia, a country with almost 50 times Singapore’s population and 2,500 times as much land. Its proximity is a reminder of how dependent that prosperity remains on good relations with Singapore’s much larger neighbors.
Such issues are top of mind right now. For weeks, the view has been obscured by a pall of haze drifting across the water from wildfires on the Indonesian islands of Borneo and Sumatra. Singapore passed laws a decade ago to combat this recurring public-health catastrophe, but has struggled to enforce them amid intransigence from its neighbor. Just days after the city announced measures against 10 Indonesian companies over the blazes this month, Jakarta started cutting pipeline supplies of natural gas to Singapore.
The decision might have a perfectly innocent explanation. Singapore has shifted aggressively toward liquefied natural gas (LNG) and away from Malaysian and Indonesian piped energy in the past few years, anticipating that its neighbors would use more of their own supplies as their economies expand. A key link allowing Indonesia to divert gas locally was completed just weeks ago, and the affected exports represent less than 2 percent of daily demand.
However, comments from Jakarta’s energy distribution minister do not inspire confidence. He warned neighboring countries to “be careful” about annoying Indonesia if they do not want their exports cut off.
The whole episode is another unpleasant reminder of the vulnerability underlying Singapore’s prosperity. For more than two centuries, it has thrived as a free port, in a world where chokepoints to trade have been progressively dismantled. The city was established by the British to bypass the Dutch stronghold in Java, and its most important nation building projects in the 1960s and 1970s repeated the model by making it a key node of emerging commercial networks, from oil refining, to container shipping, to long-haul aviation.
However, throughout all that Singapore has remained acutely aware of the chokeholds its larger neighbors control. Political separation from Malaysia in 1965 raised fears of water supplies being cut off. A costly program of desalination, recycling, harvesting and reservoir-building would allow near-self-sufficiency in a crisis.
The same cannot be said for energy. Even LNG supplies could be severed easily by a naval blockade. Nuclear power has been considered on and off for years, but comes with its own challenges: You could fit almost the entire nation inside the 20km mandatory-evacuation zone established after the Fukushima Daiichi disaster. Plans underway to install 4 gigawatts of solar panels by 2035 could leave about 5 percent of the country under silicon, and still meet barely a tenth of electricity demand.
Separate plans to develop renewable projects and transmission lines stretching to Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia, Malaysia, Indonesia and even Australia would at least diversify electricity suppliers. However, those connections could, in theory, be cut off with the flick of a switch. Singapore’s driving role in establishing the power grid taking shape across the Association of Southeast Asian Nations can best be seen as an attempt to spread the risk across a web of mutual dependencies.
That is the hopeful vision. In a world of multilateralism, peace and trade, small maritime republics can grow fabulously wealthy as nodes for global commerce and capital. Venice, an inspiration to Singapore’s founding generation, followed that model for centuries.
The worrying part is what came afterwards. As Europe’s commercial order gave way to an age of revolution, mass armies and nationalism, Venice’s wealth proved little protection against the larger powers surrounding it. Napoleon extinguished the thousand-year republic in 1797, and it was traded back and forth like a bargaining chip between France and Austria for decades before being subsumed into the modern Italian state in 1866.
We could be entering a similar moment. The rising force in international relations is the chokepoint maximizer, looking for leverage over computer chips, critical minerals, intellectual property and trade flows to subdue its rivals. This year’s conflict over the Strait of Hormuz is a prime example. With barriers rising to commerce, migration, and capital, free ports such as Singapore are in lonely waters.
“If there were no international law and order, and big fish eat small fish and small fish eat shrimps, we wouldn’t exist,” founding father Lee Kuan Yew (李光耀) mused in a 2007 interview. “A siege? ... Control of sea lanes? We’ll just starve.”
Lee’s successors must hope the great-power conflict brewing today is a passing storm, rather than a permanent shift in the global climate.

Brazil’s chapter in the  anti-authoritarian playbook
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:43:38 UTC
01:43:38 KST

Until Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva staged a remarkable comeback to win re-election, no Brazilian presidential candidate had overturned a first-round defeat in a runoff. Lula did so with nearly 52 percent of the vote, against Flavio Bolsonaro’s 48 percent. More than 128 million Brazilians turned out — nearly three million more than in the first round.
The result matters far beyond Brazil. US President Donald Trump would be unhappy, and not just because his favored candidate lost. The outcome might also send a signal ahead of the US midterms.
It is not the first. After years in which nationalist and illiberal movements appeared ascendant, their opponents are finding ways to fight back. Former Hungarian prime minister Viktor Orban was defeated in April after 16 consecutive years in power. On the same day as Brazil’s vote, former Serbian president Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat in a snap election held after nearly two years of protests.
Illustration: Tania Chou
Hungary’s opposition was led by a former conservative insider and Serbia’s by a student-led movement. Yet their experiences suggest an emerging anti-authoritarian playbook. And Brazil, where democracy has been repeatedly tested in the past few years, might have written its most instructive chapter.
It begins in the streets. In the weeks before Brazil’s runoff, enormous crowds gathered in cities across the country. Students marched alongside workers. Artists and indigenous leaders joined pensioners, farmers and entrepreneurs. Many were motivated less by loyalty to a political party than by concern about what another Bolsonaro presidency might mean for democratic institutions and civil liberties.
There was something strikingly spontaneous about the mobilization. Lula acknowledged that he had never seen anything quite like it in five decades of political life. Much of the energy came from outside the machinery of parties and unions. Jolted into action by the first-round defeat to Bolsonaro, civil society had rediscovered its capacity to mobilize.
Brazil’s political earthquake was also digital. For much of the past decade, the far right dominated social media, exploiting its appetite for outrage and confrontation. Supporters of Bolsonaro’s father, former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro, were particularly adept at turning WhatsApp groups and online personalities into political infrastructure. The left, with its dependence on televised speeches and conventional party structures, often appeared hapless.
The turning point came partly through Andre Janones, a federal deputy with a flair for digital spectacle, and Rafael Fonteles, the 41-year-old governor of Piaui, who helped pull Lula into a world he had long resisted, even refusing to own a cellphone. On Wednesday last week, he received one from Fonteles and joined Janones’s rapidly expanding WhatsApp operation. A politician whose career began in the factories and union halls of the 1970s was introduced to memes, livestreams and algorithmic engagement.
Janones’s WhatsApp channel, dubbed Lula’s Army, attracted more than 10 million followers. Participants were encouraged to share videos, promote hashtags and generate an avalanche of online content. Each was also given a simple mission: mobilize at least three more voters.
Political humor proved especially potent. The campaign discovered that ridicule could be more effective than another earnest denunciation. In a televised debate, when Bolsonaro, arguing that crime had risen on Lula’s watch, demanded to know why 73 percent of prisoners had supposedly voted for him, Lula shot back: “I want 100 percent of them to vote for me, even your father.” (Jair Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup after he lost the 2022 election.)
The attention economy cannot be conceded to those most willing to exploit it. Digital platforms reward speed and emotional intensity. Democratic movements must understand those incentives, even as they resist the temptation to reproduce the disinformation and intimidation that corrupt so much online political debate.
Brazil’s experience also exposed and challenged the power of the digital platforms themselves. Lula’s campaign accused Meta of favoring his opponent through its algorithms and artificial intelligence tools. Meta acknowledged technical failures, but denied political bias. Brazil’s electoral court ordered the company to apply the same criteria to both campaigns. The court’s scrutiny cut both ways: at one point it briefly suspended Lula’s Army itself.
Companies such as Meta and X wield enormous influence over the world’s political conversation, yet their recommendation systems remain opaque. Democratic competition requires transparent rules that are enforced fairly by courts that also protect legitimate speech.
There was another, more symbolic shift, as the left increasingly challenged the far right’s claim to Brazil’s national colors. For years, the green-and-yellow flag had become closely associated with Bolsonaro’s movement. During the runoff, Lula posed in the national soccer team’s yellow jersey as part of a campaign called “The green and yellow is ours,” insisting that patriotism belonged to no party. His army of online supporters followed suit.
Of course, a WhatsApp channel alone does not explain the exceptional turnout that won the election. Lula also benefited from voter dissatisfaction with his opponent, a forceful performance in the campaign’s final debate, a huge late surge of social spending, and concern about democracy. His government offered concrete economic proposals. The campaign’s digital resurgence coincided with its political recovery, but the precise contribution of each is hard to measure.
Nor should the result be mistaken for a wholesale rejection of Brazil’s right. Nearly 60 million people voted for Bolsonaro. His Partido Liberal (PL) party and its allies retain considerable influence in Congress and across state governments.
Although the PL has recognized Lula’s victory, Bolsonaro remains defiant. Like his father, he responded to electoral defeat by challenging the legitimacy of the contest, pledging to organize the opposition and seek disqualification of Lula’s ticket. He also faces a money-laundering investigation, raising the personal stakes of his political survival.
The next four years might prove considerably harder than Lula’s come-from-behind victory. The Brazilian left, heavily reliant on Lula’s extraordinary personal appeal for decades, has struggled to cultivate new leaders. The country needs a politics capable of reaching people who feel alienated from government, including those whose anxiety about crime and economic insecurity make them receptive to authoritarian candidates.
Brazil’s renewed democratic confidence must be matched by institutional and structural reforms and a willingness to build coalitions beyond the left. Its leaders need to recover some of the civic spirit that animated the campaign without assuming that an election has resolved the country’s divisions.
This is where the lessons from Hungary and Serbia become relevant. Their experiences show that resistance to concentrated power can emerge from different ideological traditions. The common denominator is a public willing to organize and institutions capable of translating mobilization into political change. As more of the world looks to the Global South for political direction, Lula’s campaign might prove even more influential than the European examples.

People enter cages, animals seem free at Art Zoo museum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:43:33 UTC
01:43:33 KST

Look up as you enter Amsterdam’s new Art Zoo museum, and a 3.66m crocodile stares down at you, mouth open, ready to chomp.
The taxidermic reptile is one of hundreds of preserved creatures on display, alongside artfully arranged piles of bones, illuminated tulips encased in apothecary jars and a cabinet of grotesque fish.
While it is not a Halloween-themed museum, the show should appeal to anybody looking for something a little dark this spooky season.
Photo: AP
“It was a little creepy,” Tomas Vasko, a Slovak living in the Dutch capital, said after touring the museum.
Art Zoo is the creation of Dutch artists Jaap Sinke and Ferry van Tongeren, who draw inspiration from “wunderkammers,” or curiosity cabinets collected by wealthy Europeans in the 16th and 17th centuries to showcase objects from the natural world.
“The main thing is that we like storytelling with the animals,” Van Tongeren said. “We like to add drama. We add an attitude to the animals, where traditional taxidermists just want to mimic nature.”
Behind him, a cheetah slouched in an alcove under the watchful eye of a cassowary.
In natural history museums, animals are posed as they could be seen in the wild. At the Art Zoo, a Japanese giant spider crab stretches its 1.83m legs above a doorway beside the leg bones of a mastodon that nearly reaches the ceiling.
The duo rose to fame in 2015 after shark-pickling artist Damien Hirst purchased their entire exhibition from a London art show.
Unlike at a traditional zoo, the human visitors are confined, not the animals. The display rooms in the 17th-century canal house where the Art Zoo is located are enclosed by brooding, black metal cages.
“We really like the concept of having all the people in a cage and then all the animals free,” Van Tongeren said. “In that way, the whole building becomes one artwork.”
None of the animals in the eclectic collection were taken from the wild.
“All our animals come from zoos where they died of natural causes,” Sinke said.
However, the paperwork can be challenging, he said.
The pair primarily obtained specimens from Europe to ensure they know the history of the animals.
Sinke and Van Tongeren consider themselves an artistic trio, crediting naturalist Charles Darwin as the third contributor to their work. They pitched the concept of the museum as the return of Darwin’s wonder.
In a nod to the man who developed the first scientific theory of evolution, one wall display contains a series of Darwin busts. Sinke and Van Tongeren see an amusing irony in honoring Darwin inside a building that once housed the Biblical Museum.
Not everything in the collection is a real animal. Underneath the crocodile suspended from the ceiling is a wall of Jenny Hanivers, ray carcasses modified into grotesque creatures by 16th-century sailors who presented the macabre beasts as real sea monsters to gullible collectors.
Their misshapen faces appear to keep an eye on guests as they move from room to room.

Taiwan in Time: How five concubines became legends
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:43:33 UTC
01:43:33 KST

Nov. 2 to Nov. 8
After 41 years in exile and the enemy closing in, the Ming Dynasty’s Prince of Ningjing (寧靖王) decided to meet his end in Taiwan. So did the five women who accompanied him.
The Qing had captured Penghu in July 1683, and the Tainan-based Kingdom of Tungning appeared doomed.
Photo courtesy of Academia Sinica
According to the Taiwan Prefecture Annals (台灣府志), compiled in 1696, the prince announced his intention to his five concubines, telling them they were free to remarry or become nuns. Lady Yuan (袁氏), Lady Wang (王氏), Xiugu (秀姑), Sister Mei (梅姐) and Sister He (荷姐) replied, “If our lord lives, we live; if our lord dies, we die with him. We beg you to grant us silk cords so that we may die alongside our lord. In this way, we may at least remain faithful to one man until death.”
The prince personally buried the women. The next day, he put on his royal robes and headgear, handed his imperial seal to Kingdom of Tungning’s boy ruler, Cheng Ke-shuang (鄭克塽), and hung himself after composing a farewell poem.
A ninth-generation descendant of the Ming Dynasty’s founding emperor, Chu Shu-kui (朱術桂) was the only Ming prince-in-exile in Taiwan to choose death over surrender. The other 16 were sent back to China along with Cheng and his officials.
Photo courtesy of National Central Library
Over the centuries, the suicides of the five concubines became the focus of poems and stories lauding their loyalty and chastity far more than the prince’s own death. The Temple of the Five Concubines was built over their grave in 1746 and renovated and expanded several times, with the latest repairs starting last month and slated for completion in 2028.
In “The unbearable heaviness of widowhood: A reconsideration of the deaths of Prince Ningjing’s five concubines in the perspectives of gender and social history” (妾身敢作未亡人？明寧靖王從死五妃史事的性別與社會史分析), however, Lei Chin-hau (雷晉豪) argues that their deaths may have been romanticized over time to glorify traditional ideals of female virtue. Without discounting their sacrifice and dedication, he notes that in a patriarchal society where women had few means of supporting themselves independently, they might not have had much of a choice.
FALLEN PRINCE
Photo courtesy of Wikimedia Commons
According to the Taiwan Prefecture Annals (台灣府志), compiled in 1696, the prince, Chu Shu-kui (朱術桂), was born in 1617 in today’s Hubei Province. The invading Qing army captured his hometown in 1642, beginning his life on the run. The Ming Dynasty collapsed two years later, and Chu joined other royals in the resisting Southern Ming. Emperor Longwu bestowed him the title Prince of Ningjing and assigned him the role of military supervisor.
The Qing continued to push south, and by 1650 Chu had fled to Kinmen where he sought the protection of warlord Cheng Cheng-kung (鄭成功, Koxinga).
Koxinga drove out the Dutch from Tainan in 1662 and established the Kingdom of Tungning. His son, Cheng Ching (鄭經), invited Chu to Tainan in 1663 and built him a residence. Chu arrived with his principal wife, Lady Lo (羅氏), as well as the five concubines. His biological son died young, so he adopted a relative, Chu Yen-chen (朱儼?), as his heir. Lo died before Chu and the five concubines.
Photo courtesy of National Museum of Taiwan History
According to the Taiwan Prefecture Annals, Cheng Ching eventually discontinued the living stipend for Chu’s household. Chu turned to cultivating land in present-day Lujhu District (路竹), Kaohsiung, but the Cheng regime imposed taxes on the land as it was waging a campaign to retake China, adding to the prince’s financial difficulties.
It’s said that before Chu’s death, he gave his land to the tenant farmers. To thank him, they buried him in Lujhu along with Lady Lo and his son, and built 100 fake tombs in the area to spare it from Qing destruction. It wasn’t identified until 1937. Chu’s residence in Tainan was later converted into the Tainan Grand Matsu Temple (大天后宮).
LITERARY EVOLUTION
Most early literary works focused on Chu’s death, writes Wang Chien-kuo (王建國) in “Political narratives and historical divergence: Poems about Prince Ningjing and the Five Concubines in Qing-era Taiwan” (政治書寫與歷史衍異─清代臺灣寧靖王與五妃題詠現象及其詩作論析).
The earliest known poem dedicated solely to the five concubines appeared in the 1720 Taiwan County Annals (台灣縣誌) by Lin Chung-kui (林中桂). Lin described seeing lingering haze and glow surrounding their grave in Kuishan (魁山), just outside Tainan and much more accessible to visitors than Chu’s unmarked tomb in the countryside. Many other poems mention the grave, which had become a temple site marked by official steles commemorating the women’s deed.
In the same volume, Shih Shih-pang (施世榜) wrote, “Ordinary women know only to share a pillow in life; the Five Concubines alone were seen to share death as one.”
This idea of their act transcending gender norms continued in other poems: “Do not say that women who follow their men are merely concubines; their righteous deaths deserve the praise given to men,” wrote Ho Chieh-yi (何借宜).
Chang Mei (張湄) took it further: “Their loyalty is comparable to Tien Heng’s 500 followers,” referring to the men who committed suicide after learning of their lord’s death rather than submit to the Han Dynasty.
After the 1720s, Wang noted that works praising or mourning the five concubines greatly surpassed those of the prince. A possible factor was the 1721 Chu Yi-kuei (朱一貴) rebellion. Since Chu shared a surname with the Ming royal house, he revolted under the banner of “reviving the Ming Dynasty.”
PRACTICAL CONCERNS
Not much is known about the concubines’ backgrounds, but many modern sources describe them as “young beauties” and add expressions of affection and sorrow absent from the original text, heightening the tragedy of their deaths, Lei writes.
However, according to Chu’s biography in the Annals of the Southwest (西南記事), he married Lady Yuan and Lady Wang in 1644, which would put them at least in their mid-to-late 50s by 1683.
The fact that the family’s heir, Chu Yen-chen, was adopted also complicated matters. Under Ming custom, concubines could not manage or dispose of family property on behalf of an adopted heir, leaving their economic future uncertain amid the imminent collapse of the Kingdom of Tungning. Sources indicate that the family was already in financial difficulty, while women in their position had few ways to support themselves independently. Chu Yan-chen eventually surrendered to the Qing and was taken to China.
As for remarrying, they would have had to wait until the three-year mourning period was over. Remarriage was also frowned upon, as widows were expected to remain chaste. Becoming nuns was another unlikely option: Lei notes that there were few monks in Taiwan at the time and apparently no nunnery in the area.
These circumstances raise questions about how much freedom they had to choose another future.
Taiwan in Time, a column about Taiwan’s history that is published every Sunday, spotlights important or interesting events around the nation that either have anniversaries this week or are tied to current events.
Much attention is being paid to increasing security ties between Taiwan and the Philippines, and rightfully so. The stakes are potentially existential, as explored in “ Donovan’s Deep Dives: Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines need to face the common threat from Beijing” (Sept. 12, page 12). Getting less attention is that across the board the relationship is growing stronger, and both sides appear to be planning to put more of their eggs in each other’s baskets. Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) in August last year confirmed plans to open a second Taipei Economic and Cultural Office (TECO) representative

EDITORIAL: A tale of two debates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31

A televised debate for the main Kaohsiung mayoral candidates, Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) candidate Lai Jui-lung (賴瑞隆) and Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) candidate Ko Chih-en (柯志恩), was held on Friday evening, followed at noon yesterday by a debate in Taipei between Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) of the KMT and the DPP’s candidate, Legislator Puma Shen (沈伯洋).
Chiang and Lai have had local government experience to rely on: Shen and Ko needed to demonstrate that they have the vision and the leadership skills needed for the job.
In Taipei, Chiang has the advantage of seeking a second term in a KMT stronghold, but the underdog Shen has been snapping at his heels, and has even overtaken him in recent polls. Chiang is a major KMT figure whose plain delivery and avoidance of providing satisfactory answers in recent interviews has damaged his campaign, especially when compared with Shen’s social media-savvy “Ocean Wave” (洋流).
Chiang’s performance yesterday failed to address his body-language issues: His team had obviously worked hard on that and positive facial expressions, but he spent a large part of his time, especially during the media questions section, referring to his notes, at times reading from them.
On the other hand, Shen was clearly the better prepared with his answers, and on several occasions pointed out that Chiang had failed to answer the question put to him.
Compare that with Friday’s debate in Kaohsiung, where the DPP is historically stronger than the KMT. Lai was well-prepared, but, like Chiang, came off as wooden in his delivery. He focused on the length of his experience in Kaohsiung’s local governance and attacking Ko over her support for the KMT’s amendments to the Act Governing the Allocation of Government Revenues and Expenditures (財政收支劃分法), which he said disproportionally favored Taipei over Kaohsiung. The Kaohsiung candidates needed to show their vision on solving issues such as traffic congestion, air quality, flooding, social housing, northward drift of jobs and youth unemployment. Ko failed to show how she could deliver on the ambitious vision she offered, but wiped the floor with Lai in terms of her presentation and debating skills.
Lai and Ko referred to previous mayors: Lai spoke of former DPP mayors Frank Hsieh (謝長廷) and Chen Chu (陳菊), as well as and incumbent Kaohsiung Mayor Chen Chi-mai (陳其邁). Hsieh and Chen Chu enjoyed high approval ratings; Chen Chi-mai is polling at 71.9 percent approval. Ko said that Lai had not mentioned former Kaohsiung mayor Han Kuo-yu (韓國瑜) of the KMT, although he probably did her a favor with the omission: Kaohsiung voters recalled Han before he had served two years of his first term.
As the natural successor of these high approval ratings for DPP leadership, one would expect Lai to win handily on Nov. 28.
Nevertheless, the DPP’s position this year appears fragile. The results of an ETtoday poll released on Thursday showed Lai and Ko to be separated by a statistically negligible 0.1 percentage point. Lai has a support rating of 43.2 percent, compared with Ko’s 43.1. The race is neck-and-neck. The DPP’s core votes remain solid, with 94.2 percent of DPP supporters backing Lai and 97.6 percent of KMT supporters backing Ko. Crucially, 12.7 percent of voters remain undecided and, while 38.8 percent of independent voters said they would vote for Ko, compared with 20.6 percent for Lai, 38.5 percent were undecided. The outcome of the Kaohsiung mayoral race appears to be in the hands of a small group of swing voters.
Two other findings would make encouraging reading for Lai: 51.6 percent of respondents believe he is likely to win, compared with 36.8 percent who favor Ko; and among respondents satisfied with Chen Chi-mai’s performance, 76.4 percent said they support Lai, with only 13.1 percent supporting Ko.
With a race that tight, Lai cannot afford to ride on Chen Chi-mai’s coattails; he must prove how he can transfer his experience to having a vision and leadership qualities.
