Sri Lanka’s Tamil farmers fight to reclaim land after civil war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:43:31 UTC
01:43:31 KST

Tired but resolute, dozens of Tamil cattle farmers have held a round-the-clock vigil for almost three years in eastern Sri Lanka, protesting what they call land “theft.”
At shift change, farmers exchange news before settling beneath a tarpaulin beside photographs of the bloodied bodies of their dead cows.
“They have been shooting our cattle, threatening us, assaulting us and spraying pesticides or poison on the pasture lands where our cattle graze,” said Seenithamby Thiyagarajah, president of the local farmers’ association, detailing the push his community felt from recipients of a state-funded program that was driving them off their land.
Photo: AFP
“Over 5,700 cows have been destroyed like this. Even after complaining numerous times to the police and all relevant places, we received no resolution,” he said.
The alleged perpetrators are farmers who have benefited from the state-funded Mahaweli development scheme. Most are Sinhalese, the country’s majority ethnic group, settling on land claimed by the largely Hindu Tamil minority, which makes up about 12 percent of the population.
The government denied any forcible attempts to remove people from their land.
Sri Lanka’s 1983 to 2009 civil war between government forces and Tamil separatists killed more than 100,000 people, according to UN data.
Nearly two decades later, land disputes continue to fuel ethnic grievances.
Thiyagarajah said that settlers aided by the scheme have encroached on grazing land used by the roughly 1,000 cattle farmers he represents.
Courts have repeatedly ordered the eviction of the scheme-backed settler farmers, he said.
“Things are peaceful, for a while, but then the illegal cultivators entered again, ruining our land and destroying our cattle,” he said.
Other communities are also fighting to reclaim land.
Ambalavar Nallathambi Velayutham, 64, an indigenous community leader, wants his rice fields back.
Armed with renewed land deeds renewed with local authorities, Velayutham and neighbors in Kunjankulam returned to farming fields they had abandoned during the war.
Sri Lankan Forest Department officials told them the land was a reserve, Velayutham said.
“We said: ‘This land belonged to our ancestors.’ They replied: ‘That won’t do. You must leave,’” he added.
Fearing reprisals, most villagers abandoned their efforts.
One night, a villager spotted forestry officials’ mobile phones glowing in the darkness.
“They dug there and planted boundary stones,” Velayutham said, pointing to the markers.
Repeated appeals to local authorities, the prime minister and president have brought no result, he said.
“This land has neither been freed nor handed back to us,” he said. “If they release this farmland and we get it back from the Forest Department, I believe this will provide a great opportunity.”
Land disputes have multiplied across Sri Lanka’s Eastern Province, where Tamils are a major ethnic group.
Examples include an army barracks encroaching on a school, while government departments responsible for archeology, wildlife or forests claim farmland, temples and private property.
Officials designate land cultivated by Tamils as forest or wildlife reserves, “obstructing development or agricultural activities for them,” said Sabarathinam Sivayoganathan, 57, president of the Eastern Province Civil Society Activists Union.
The scale of these occupations is unclear, with no public statistics and residents risking intimidation by asking questions, he said.
Opposition Member of Parliament Rasamanickam R. Shanakiyan said that population figures point to a deliberate effort to change the region’s demographics.
“In the Eastern Province, the Sinhala population has increased by 700 percent since independence in 1948,” he said, compared with 200 percent nationally.
“This has happened through state-sponsored colonization,” he said, accusing the government of altering the ethnic balance of the north and east through land settlements.
Sri Lankan President Anura Kumara Dissanayake’s election in 2024 has brought little change, Shanakiyan said, despite campaign promises to the contrary.
He accused the government of failing to honor commitments in the lead up to the election that it would release land, protect minority rights and deliver wider political reforms.
“On these promises, nothing’s been delivered,” he said. “You feel a growing sense of frustration, maybe anger in the population.”
Land ownership disputes continue to fuel tensions, resentment and accusations online and on the ground between Sinhalese and Tamils across eastern Sri Lanka.
The Sri Lankan government said it has commissioned a report on changes to land records since the civil war and whether they should be corrected.
“We will never forcibly acquire people’s land,” Sri Lankan Minister of Environment Dhammika Patabendi told reporters in an e-mail.
“Based on the recommendations of this report, we believe that these issues can be resolved promptly and fairly,” he said.
However, as torrential rain drums on the tarpaulin sheltering the angry farmers, Thiyagarajah remains unconvinced.
“For 1,010 days, alongside this road and under this tent, we have been taking part day and night. Justice has still not been granted to our people,” he said. “Today, our people live in constant fear that today or tomorrow our cattle will be destroyed.”

China’s military purge reduces war risk: experts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:43:29 UTC
01:43:29 KST

Chinese President Xi Jinping’s (習近平) military purge has reduced the risks of a planned war against Taiwan, yet increased the danger of a conflict sparked by a miscalculation or accident, Taiwanese experts said yesterday.
They made the comments at a seminar on the Fifth Plenary Session of the Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) 20th Central Committee held by the research group Secure Taiwan Associate Corp (STA) in Taipei.
The wholesale sacking of Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA) officers and managers of the aerospace and defense industry is sure to set back Xi’s timetable to prepare the PLA to launch an invasion of Taiwan by next year, they said.
Photo: AP
The Chinese armed forces’ attention would most likely be fully absorbed by efforts to rebuild their organization and leadership in the next one to four years in a welcome development for Taiwan, they said.
Yet the lack of experience in the Chinese military’s most senior command levels is also a warning sign, as amateurs and sycophants are far more likely to make missteps that inadvertently lead to war, they added.
Association for Strategic Foresight researcher Chieh Chung (揭仲) said that 96 CCP Central Committee members, or 26 percent of the total membership, have departed under a cloud.
This figure is more than double the number of Central Committee officials ousted for corruption or improprieties in the 18th iteration of the Central Committee, he said.
The dismissal of Ma Xingrui (馬興瑞), Jin Zhuanglong (金壯龍), Zhao Xiaozhe (趙曉哲) and Lei Fanpei (雷凡培), among 28 formerly high-ranking defense and aerospace industry officials, would force a comprehensive re-examination of China’s defense procurement plans, he said.
The drastic changes would derail the military reform targets Xi originally planned to achieve by the 100th anniversary of the PLA’s founding next year, he said.
Xi had rolled back the theater commands’ autonomy and ability to conduct operations independently, which runs contrary to recognized principles of modern joint warfare, he said.
The disruption to PLA leadership and its cumbersome command arrangements are likely to cripple the capability of the Chinese military to project force or respond to a contingency for the next three to four years, he said.
Yet, Xi’s willingness to put ideology and politics over professionalism also means Chinese generals would be fearful of voicing disagreements or appearing weak, he said.
These flaws would make it significantly more difficult for Beijing to exercise sound judgement or de-escalate dangerous situations, increasing the risks of sparking an unwanted conflict, he said.
The most recently dismissed members and alternate members of the Central Committee included 16 PLA brass and seven high-ranking managers of China’s defense industry, National Taiwan University political science professor Chen Shih-min (陳世民) said.
The PLA’s organizational table calls for more than 40 full generals and admirals to staff the armed forces, but only six such officers are left at the helm, he said.
The arrest of former vice chairman and PLA general Zhang Youxia (張又俠) nine months ago has all but eliminated the Central Military Commission, where he previously served as one of its two vice chairmen, Chen said.
The only members left in the Chinese military’s high command are Xi and General Zhang Shengmin (張升民), a commissar with no professional training in commanding troops, he said.
National Defense University Chinese military studies professor Ma Chen-kun (馬振坤) said the PLA would be absorbed by efforts to recuperate and reorganize its internal organization for up to two years.
The Central Committee meeting elevated Zhang Shengmin, the Central Military Commission’s last remaining general, to the Politburo, without filling vacancies in the high command, he said.
The prominence of Zhang Shengmin contravened the PLA’s long-standing policy of maintaining separate tracks for commissars and professional soldiers, he said.
Zhang Shengmin’s lack of qualifications have compromised the Chinese military’s crisis management, increasing the chances of dangerous miscalculations and mishaps, Ma said.

FEATURE: The unsung heroes of snake antivenom production
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:43:27 UTC
01:43:27 KST

Taiwan is home to a rich diversity of snake species, and nearly 1,000 people are bitten by snakes each year. In emergency rooms, where every second counts, administering the right antivenom in time can mean the difference between life and death. Behind this lifesaving treatment is an unlikely group of contributors: immunized horses.
The National Immunized Horse Farm at National Pingtung University of Science and Technology covers 2.91 hectares and houses 57 horses in six stables, with four outdoor exercise fields and two horse walkers. Of the horses, 44 are involved in antivenom production, and 13 have retired.
“People often ask us if we get to ride the horses when we travel for work. We always joke, ‘No, the horses outrank us,’” Centers for Disease Control (CDC) Center for Diagnostics and Vaccine Development animal technology specialist Lee Chia-jung (李佳蓉) said with a laugh.
Photo: CNA
Unlike horses at recreational riding stables, which are trained for activities such as riding and running, immunized horses have a very different role, Lee said, adding that the horses’ primary job is to stay healthy and undergo immunization, providing the plasma needed to produce antivenom.
Temperament is the top priority when selecting horses. Neither a spirited racehorse, which might bolt at the prick of a needle, nor a massive draft horse weighing more than a tonne, which could be difficult to restrain if something went wrong, would be suitable, deputy director Hsieh Wen-chin (謝文欽) said.
Only horses with a calm, gentle temperament are suited to the work, he said.
Antivenom must be produced using venom from locally occurring snake species, Hsieh said.
The CDC supplies four types covering Taiwan’s six major venomous snake species.
Each horse produces only one type of antivenom during its lifetime, Hsieh said.
Laboratory staff inject it with one type of venom and wait to see whether it develops antibodies. If none appear within a certain period, they try another type, repeating the process until antibodies develop. Horses that fail to respond to any available type must be retired early.
Once sufficient antibodies have developed, researchers collect the horse’s plasma and separate and purify the antibodies to make antivenom, he said.
Immunization must proceed gradually to allow the horse’s immune system to build a response. Early side effects can include wounds, abscesses and granulomas, but improved formulations have reduced these risks. The farm takes precautions to protect the horses’ health, he said.
Sheep and alpacas can also produce antivenom, but horses remain the most widely used animals because of their size, relatively docile temperament and greater plasma yield, Vaccine Manufacturing Division chief Chen Chao-hung (陳昭宏) said.
Taiwan’s immunized horses mainly come from the US and the Netherlands, Hsieh said.
Imports from New Zealand were discontinued after some horses developed anhidrosis, a condition that prevents sweating and can cause their body temperatures to rise in hot weather.
After quarantine and health checks, horses undergo training to familiarize them with their surroundings and working conditions, Hsieh said.
They learn to wear a halter, follow handlers, enter and leave restraint stocks, and tolerate the smell of alcohol, protruding objects, and pressure on their necks and skin, he said, adding that this preparation reduces stress and injury risks during immunization and blood collection.
Horses typically serve for eight to 12 years, giving blood nearly 100 times over their working lives. Each kilogram of plasma can produce about 30 doses of antivenom, meaning one horse can help save thousands of snakebite victims, Hsieh said.
Taiwan began producing antivenom during the Japanese colonial period, when the mortality rate from venomous snakebites exceeded 6 percent. Today, it has fallen to 0.18 percent, and no one has died from an allergic reaction to antivenom.
A total of 195 medical institutions across Taiwan stock antivenom, while the CDC maintains 6,000 doses across four types, enough for at least 18 months.
National Health Insurance data from 2017 to 2021 show that an average of 979 people in Taiwan are bitten by snakes each year.
“Antivenom cannot wait until someone is bitten before production begins,” Hsieh said.
Finished-product stocks cover 1.5 to two years of demand, while reserve plasma typically covers more than three years, providing a double safety net.

Worthwhile policies, not partisan politics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:43:26 UTC
01:43:26 KST

On Thursday last week, Democratic Progressive Party Legislator and Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) proposed an urban stitching initiative designed to revitalize and pedestrianize the area surrounding the elevated Civic Boulevard highway, creating a cultural and arts corridor that links with commercial districts. Former Taipei mayor Ko Wen-je (柯文哲) leaped to mock the proposal as foolish to the point of being unworthy of a serious response, and the Chinese Nationalist Party’s (KMT) Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) dismissed it as wishful thinking.
On Monday, Shen responded by presenting documents from the Taipei Department of Urban Development of a similar “stitching” proposal by the Ko administration in 2020 to create a pedestrian-friendly corridor along the city’s north-south axis. When the same urban design considerations made by the previous administration are ridiculed when put forward by their political opponent, one has to wonder whether this is really a policy issue, or a political point-scoring exercise.
The Taipei Department of Urban Development’s 2020 project to improve the pedestrian environment around Jianguo Brewery and Zhongshan Girls’ High School also proposed using Civic Boulevard as an east-west axis to reconnect the areas to its north and south. It said that existing land use around the elevated highway had fragmented and under-utilized the pedestrian environment, and that landscape and connectivity improvements were needed. The findings were also included in a work report submitted to the Taipei City Council in August 2021.
Shen’s proposal for a cultural and arts corridor linked to commercial districts is not identical to the 2020 plan, and its engineering requirements, traffic impacts and costs need to be assessed. However, the idea of reconnecting fragmented urban spaces is clearly not something that has been plucked from thin air. Politicians are entitled to question its feasibility, but they should not ignore that the administration they once led looked into the same question.
KMT New Taipei City mayoral candidate Lee Shu-chuan (李四川) said that railway undergrounding has already improved the north-south divide, and that the elevated Civic Boulevard has shrunk east-west travel times. That perspective accounts for traffic engineering, but not urban design considerations. Undergrounding the railway removes a physical barrier, but how local governments design pedestrian routes and promote spatial quality activity beneath the elevated road is another matter. That vehicles can pass through quickly does not mean pedestrians can cross safely and conveniently.
As the Ko administration had already identified a direction, the immediate questions should concern what improvements have already been completed and where more work is needed.
Taipei needs continuity in governance, not the wholesale rejection of past policies each time an election rolls around. Shen should offer a comprehensive plan covering spatial design, traffic impacts, construction costs and phased implementation. Meanwhile, Chiang and Ko should explain what has already been achieved and what still needs improvement.
Urban development is a long-term undertaking, and problems do not disappear when a new mayor takes office. Political rivals might have different visions, but policy judgements must not be reduced to partisan squabbles. If the need for a pedestrian-friendly environment was recognized in 2020, today evidence-based discussions are needed around improvements. It is not the idea of reconnecting fragmented urban spaces itself that is disorientating, but how a policy line suddenly becomes unfathomable when it is proposed by someone else.
Elliot Yao is a reviewer.

European soccer’s apology to China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:43:23 UTC
01:43:23 KST

Real Madrid forward Kylian Mbappe has never been shy about politics. In June 2024, ahead of France’s snap parliamentary elections, the France captain warned that “the extremes are at the gates of power.” During this year’s FIFA World Cup, fans dressed him up online as a dictator. Last month, he told France Football the memes were less funny once you remembered “the damage that people like that have caused throughout history.” Some of them, he said, showed “a lack of political and human awareness.”
This month, a meme cost him more than any of his political statements ever had. A video from the French show The Bridge showed Mbappe laughing at a meme that pasted his face onto the body of Mao Zedong (毛澤東). He was not making a political point. He was laughing at a meme. Beijing turned it into a diplomatic affair.
On Tuesday, three Chinese companies ended their deals with him with immediate effect, with one citing “a zero-tolerance policy toward any behavior that offends national sentiments.” State broadcaster China Central Television (CCTV) dropped Spanish La Liga.
Then came the apologies. Mbappe said sorry in three languages, Mandarin included, and spoke of his deep respect for Chinese and their history. La Liga apologized. Real Madrid apologized to Chinese. On, the Swiss sportswear brand that signed him last month, welcomed his apology and spoke of its “deep respect” for China. Hublot and Dior removed posts featuring him from their Chinese social media accounts. The Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Guo Jiakun (郭嘉昆) said Beijing took the apology “seriously.” He did not say that Beijing accepted it.
Between 1959 and 1961, Mao’s Great Leap Forward caused a famine that killed tens of millions of people. Calling him a dictator is what textbooks do. Apologizing to Beijing for a meme turns a fact into an offense.
Taiwanese have seen this movie before. On Jan. 15, 2016, the eve of the presidential election, Chou Tzu-yu (周子瑜) read a statement on camera. The Taiwanese singer, 16 years old at the time, was a member of the South Korean band Twice. She said there was “only one China.” Her offense had been to hold the Republic of China flag on South Korean television, and she had just lost a Huawei advertising deal. Many Taiwanese compared the video to a hostage tape. Tsai Ing-wen (蔡英文) won the presidential election the next day.
In May, Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs Francois Wu (吳志中) spoke at the European Parliament. Wu described how Chinese vessels harass ships crossing the Taiwan Strait. He said that, their message can be interpreted as: “If you don’t want to be harassed, you must first get my consent.”
That rule now covers soccer players and running shoes as well.
Companies usually bend. In 2018, China told foreign airlines to list Taiwan as part of China on their Web sites. The White House called it “Orwellian nonsense.” By the July deadline, most airlines had complied.
US sport was an exception. In 2019, Daryl Morey, then-general manager of the Houston Rockets, tweeted his support for Hong Kong protesters. CCTV pulled NBA broadcasts. NBA commissioner Adam Silver later said Beijing had asked him to fire Morey, and that there was “no chance” of that happening. The league admitted “substantial” losses, but it survived them.
European soccer picked the other script. Real Madrid did not need to apologize to keep playing soccer. Neither did a Swiss shoe company that has not yet sold a single soccer boot.
Taiwan cannot pay clubs to be brave, but it can make bravery cheaper. It has a decade of case files, from pop singers to airlines. Taiwan’s representative offices in Europe could share them with players’ unions such as FIFPRO, while no case is running. The message would be simple: An opinion about a dead dictator is not a breach of contract.
Taiwanese companies could add a lighter touch. A Taiwanese brand willing to sign a soccer player who laughs at Mao would buy more goodwill in Europe than a year of tourism campaigns.
In Brussels, Wu also told European lawmakers that Taiwan must become a core interest of Europe. On last week’s evidence, Europe’s clubs already have a core interest — the Chinese market.

Prized Voatsiperifery pepper at risk as forests in Madagascar face destruction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:43:21 UTC
01:43:21 KST

A rare wild pepper endemic to Madagascar and prized by international chefs is facing an uncertain future, victim of its own success and the destruction of its forest habitat.
With its subtle, aromatic flavor, Voatsiperifery pepper grows on vines that reach into the canopy of the island’s natural forests, which shrank 27 percent between 1990 and last year, the UN Food and Agriculture Organization said.
To reach the peppercorns without having to climb, harvesters often tear down the vine and, in many cases, the trees supporting them, contributing to the relentless retreat of Madagascar’s forests.
Photo: AFP
“At times, I tell myself I should never have made it known,” said French chef Olivier Roellinger, who first encountered the spice 30 years ago.
“This pepper blew me away right from the start with that piperine punch that brings out a note of peat, resin, even citrus; it’s incomparable,” he said. “On a fruit salad, it’s absolutely delicious.”
Madagascar pepper sells for 150 to 200 euros (US$167 to US$223) per kilogram in France, its main export market.
Roellinger, the founder of the Epices Roellinger spice boutique, is collaborating with efforts to certify authentic pepper based on strictly regulated harvesting zones in Madagascar.
However, he said he was “under no illusions” about the risk these rules could be circumvented.
The village of Ambongamarina, Madagascar, was at the center of a rush two decades ago for the pepper, which has a characteristic woody tail, a remnant of its stem.
From a ridge on which the village sits, farmer Maminiaina Rabearison pointed into the distance.
“Until 2010 to 2012, it was still covered in natural forest,” he said. “People used to go into the forest and, for 10 to 20 weeks a year, at least 100 kilograms were sold every week at the market to a trader.”
That trader has not visited in a long time. Harvests have dropped as the forest has been consumed by bush fires, charcoal production and slash-and-burn agriculture, or torched in protests against the distant central government.
The destruction of the vines has also forced harvesters to go deeper into the forest to find the plant, which in Malagasy is called “tsiperifery,” meaning “that makes wounds not exist,” a reference to its medicinal use for generations.
Now, “you have to walk almost a full day to find pepper in the forest,” farmer Herinaina Randrianarimanga said.
There is no national system to track the distribution, harvesting and export of this precious pepper, Jacarandas cofounder Mima Chateauneuf said.
“Today, we have no idea whether the resource is becoming scarce,” she said, calling for “traceability” to determine export volumes.
In the absence of a regulatory framework, Jacarandas is turning toward organic pepper, which has grown to make up one-third of its exports.
“For organic products, traceability is mandatory,” Chateauneuf said.
As research into the Voatsiperifery plant advances, French-Malagasy entrepreneur Olivier Ramaherison has been experimenting with domestic cultivation on land inherited from his father.
Between 500 and 1,000 vines — the result of thousands of trials — grew in terraces carved into the Mandraka forest.
There are no support trees here: The plants, laden with fruit just a few weeks from maturity, cluster close to the ground.
“The idea was to try to find a solution to make it easier to pick,” said Ramaherison, head of Essentialys, a company that produces aromatic plants, essential oils, coffee and pepper.
By chance, his team discovered that cuttings taken from the horizontal branches of the vine no longer tried to climb.
“If, like at the Piper nigrum [black pepper] plantations in Vietnam or Brazil, we manage to produce hundreds of tonnes of wild pepper, it would be a real economic boon for the country,” he said.

France prepared yesterday for a third consecutive weekend of protests over living costs and education, deploying 70,000 police and gendarmes and pushing the Paris march to the capital’s edge as youth-led demonstrations spread across Europe.
French Minister of the Interior Laurent Nunez warned of a “very high risk” of disorder, especially after dark on Halloween.
Paris police banned union and Yellow Vest marches through the city center on Friday, ordering demonstrations to follow a single route along the capital’s outer boulevards, from Porte de Bagnolet to Porte de Charenton.
Photo: AFP
Unions and student groups challenged the restrictions in court.
French President Emmanuel Macron on Monday said marches would stay out of city centers to protect shops.
Police also barred entry to the Place de la Republique and Les Halles, both hit by rioting and looting on Oct. 17, from 11pm to 6am on Saturday and Sunday nights.
Unaccompanied minors face a separate 9pm curfew around the Champs-Elysees.
A Paris court on Wednesday suspended an earlier curfew on minors as a serious and illegal infringement of freedom of movement.
The movement began with high-school students protesting school conditions and broadened into anger over living costs.
Authorities counted about 550,000 marchers on Oct. 17, when rioters looted hundreds of shops, and 410,000 on Saturday last week, when protests were largely peaceful, but police made more than 1,300 arrests.
In Germany, a youth initiative called “Gen Z regelt” — roughly “Gen Z’s got this” — urged protests in about 30 cities “for education, health, climate protection and an affordable life,” and against any return of military conscription. Organizers said more than 140,000 people signed up online.
Berlin police expect about 10,000 people at the Brandenburg Gate. Some shops on the Kurfuerstendamm boulevard boarded up windows.
In Barcelona, Spain, Catalan police planned their highest-level alert after an anonymous TikTok network called Blocus urged new gatherings. Rioting there on Saturday last week led to about 130 arrests, mostly of minors.
Italian police were on alert after clashes in Milan, Turin and Bologna, and calls to protest circulated on TikTok in Belgium, the Netherlands, Austria, Switzerland and Portugal.

Taipei still feels like home
After half a century of ties to Taiwan, I still find myself looking at a Taipei streetscape and wishing it were more appealing. Yet if asked whether I would rather live here or in beautifully landscaped Singapore, I would choose Taipei.
I first lived in Taiwan from 1975 to 1977, teaching and studying at what was then Chinese Culture College, now Chinese Culture University. I returned from 1982 to 1984 with Irving Trust Co, later acquired by the Bank of New York. My Taiwan-born wife, Joyce, and I have family and friends here that make returning personal.
I have long admired the work ethic I encountered, the importance people placed on education and family, and their determination to improve their lives. As a banker, I followed Taiwan’s economic development with particular interest. Its democratic transformation has been equally impressive.
However, my fondest memories often involve smaller encounters. People have always been quick to compliment my Mandarin, sometimes generously. However, say a few words in Taiwanese, and the enthusiasm rises another notch. An ordinary transaction becomes a friendly conversation, and a foreigner feels welcome.
The food has also held up remarkably well against memory. Nostalgia can be an unfair restaurant critic, but the rolled egg crepes I bought at a roadside stall near my old college were every bit as good as I remembered.
The urban scenery prompted a more mixed response. Driving toward Keelung to visit Joyce’s brother, I noticed old, weathered housing, densely packed buildings and little greenery between them. Modern high-rises provided occasional relief. Persistent drizzle did the older buildings no favors.
These were impressions of particular stretches, not a verdict on Taiwan. A highway view cannot tell the whole story, nor does a weathered facade reveal how people live inside. Still, I wondered why such extraordinary economic progress had not brought more improvement to everyday urban surroundings.
Housing, jobs and transport understandably took priority during rapid growth. Renewing established neighborhoods is difficult. Yet more attention to older buildings, trees and ordinary streets would make a difference. Taipei has parks and attractive places; I wish more of that care extended along the routes connecting them.
Singapore’s greenery and carefully maintained public spaces deserve admiration, but family, familiarity, wonderful food and the easy friendliness I encounter keep drawing me back to Taipei.
Affection sustained over 50 years leaves room for disappointment. I want Taipei to look more appealing, because I care about it. I would welcome more trees and better-kept buildings, and happily return tomorrow for another rolled egg crepe and a conversation in Mandarin, with a few words of Taiwanese thrown in.
Michael J. Ranieri
Bonita Springs, Florida
Responsible policies needed
On Oct. 16, the opposition-controlled Legislative Yuan passed the third reading of amendments to the Senior Citizens Welfare Act (老人福利法), which would require the central government to subsidize the National Health Insurance (NHI) premiums for all people age 65 or older who meet specific income eligibility criteria. The policy appears to offer greater support for elderly people, but why expand blanket subsidies rather than prioritize resources for those with a genuine need for assistance?
The Ministry of Health and Welfare estimates that about 4.03 million elderly people across Taiwan would qualify for the subsidies, amounting to an annual cost of about NT$40 billion (US$1.23 billion). Whether funding through NHI resources or central government tax revenues, someone would have to bear the cost. Taiwan faces a declining birthrate and an aging population. The working-age population is gradually shrinking, while healthcare and long-term care expenditures continue to rise.
The income eligibility threshold is the most important issue to reconsider. Does having an income tax rate below 20 percent mean that someone lacks the means to support themselves? Some elderly people own property, have savings and receive a steady retirement income while others struggle to make ends meet. Do these two groups really need the same subsidies? If the government is committed to supporting the disadvantaged, it should take income, assets and actual living needs into account to ensure that limited public funds first go to elderly people facing financial hardship and to young families in need of support.
Older people need security, but younger generations also need a future. Young people must shoulder mortgage payments, the costs of raising children, and various taxes and fees, all while facing an increasingly heavy burden of social spending. It is easy for political parties to win applause by championing welfare policies, but having the courage to explain the long-term funding of these policies is another matter. Supporting older people is a worthy goal, but every welfare policy must take fiscal capacity and intergenerational equity into account. Today’s political gains must not become a bill young people must pay tomorrow.
Tao Huo
Taipei

‘Reading Boy’ sculpture hoped to inspire youth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:43:18 UTC
01:43:18 KST

The Sun Yat-sen Memorial Hall in Taipei on Tuesday held a plaque-unveiling ceremony for the Reading Boy bronze sculpture by artist Wang Hsiu-chi (王秀杞) on the western side of the hall’s grounds.
The Taipei Capitol Lions Club and its Japanese sister Aomori Mahoroba Lions Club had jointly commissioned the statue as a companion to Reading Girl, which the former donated to the museum a decade ago.
The statues celebrate the joy and intellectual benefits of reading as electronic devices increasingly compete for the attention of their users, the hall’s director-general Wang Lan-sheng (王蘭生) said.
Photo courtesy of the Sun Yat-sen Memorial Hall
The pair of bronze statues are also part of the memorial hall’s project to beautify its surroundings to become a more cultured space that art enjoyers can appreciate, he said.
The hall hopes that gathering such creations would make the garden around it a landmark for people in the city, Wang said.
Taipei Capitol Lions Club president Kuo Su-mei (郭素梅) said that the group hopes the new sculpture would encourage a passion for reading in Taiwanese youth amid distractions from phones, the Internet and television.
The group hopes the memorial’s visitors would to rest and read on the three granite benches placed near the statutes, which the club also donated to show its concern for the public good, she said.
Together, the club’s gifts of the Reading Boy and Reading Girl set an example that urges people to rediscover the pleasure of reading, Wang Hsiu-chi told the event.
Wang Hsiu-chi grew up in poverty, having had to walk an hour to school and help his father tend to the family orchard after returning home, with little time left for reading, the sculptor said.
“Although my father used to tell me all the time that I must have an education if I wanted to have a future, I did not study well and chose to create sculptures,” he said. “I am thankful that the organizations involved gave me the chance to contribute to the future generation by creating something beautiful.”

The administration of US President Donald Trump on Friday green-lit the sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine, the US Department of State said, but Ukraine’s president warned deliveries could take years.
The approval, which goes to the US Congress for review, comes after weeks of complaints by Ukrainian authorities that its supplies of the interceptor missiles were dwindling.
“The proposed sale will improve Ukraine’s capability to meet current and future threats by improving its integrated air and missile defense capabilities,” the department said in a statement.
Photo: Reuters
The statement did not provide an estimate for when the weapons could be delivered to Ukraine.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy in a post on X wrote that “deliveries may begin ONLY IN A FEW YEARS.”
“We are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3 interceptors,” Zelenskiy wrote, using an acronym for the weapons.
He suggested that the US and European allies could give his country missiles they have stockpiled now, which would later be replenished by this new purchase.
Patriot missiles are among the most important weapons Ukraine has to intercept Russian drones and missiles.
“This proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a partner country that is a force for political and economic stability in Europe,” the US said.

Average taxi income rises: survey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:43:16 UTC
01:43:16 KST

The Ministry of Transportation and Communications’ (MOTC) latest Taxi Business Survey showed that full-time taxi drivers’ average monthly net income rose 20.4 percent last year to NT$32,465, while multi-purpose taxis expanded to 40 percent of the nation’s taxi fleet.
The survey showed that full-time taxi drivers earned an average monthly gross income of NT$55,788, up NT$7,022, or 14.4 percent, from 2023. After deducting operating expenses, their average monthly net income was NT$32,465, an increase of NT$5,508, or 20.4 percent.
More than 76 percent of full-time taxi drivers, defined as those whose principal source of income is operating a taxi, were affiliated with taxi dispatch fleets, up 7.4 percentage points from the previous survey.
Photo: CNA
Nearly 80 percent of taxi rides were arranged through online booking platforms, radio or satellite dispatch services, while the proportion of drivers picking up passengers by cruising the streets fell to 40 percent for the first time, reflecting a shift toward digital operations in the industry.
Full-time drivers who worked at least eight hours a day earned an average monthly gross income of NT$62,822 and net income of NT$37,403, NT$7,034 and NT$4,938 more respectively than the average for all full-time taxi drivers.
Multi-purpose taxi drivers took more days off on average than other full-time drivers, but made more trips and drove longer distances on days they worked. Their average monthly gross income was NT$59,528, higher than the average for all full-time taxi drivers.
The MOTC conducts the survey every two years. From March to June, it sampled taxi operators active at the end of last year and received 9,861 valid responses, a response rate of 33 percent.
Taiwan had 92,768 taxis at the end of last year, up 1,114, or about 1.2 percent, from the previous survey. Of those, 36,023 were multi-purpose taxis, accounting for nearly 40 percent of the fleet, the survey showed.
The ministry also released the results of its Tour Bus Business Survey, which found the industry had contracted slightly as operators diversified their services. Labor shortages among companies specializing in shuttle services and tourism had eased, while overall revenue had recovered to pre-COVID-19 pandemic levels. Tour bus drivers earned an average monthly salary of NT$48,000 last year, up NT$3,686, or 8.3 percent, from the previous survey.

How is the  US-China tech war going? Ask AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:43:15 UTC
01:43:15 KST

An unmistakable moment in the US-China tech war arrived in early 2024 — via the Netherlands.
“We do not expect to get export licenses for our most advanced immersion systems — the NXT:2000 and up — for China in 2024,” executives at ASML Holding NV, the Dutch lithography giant at the heart of the global semiconductor supply chain, said on their earnings call in January that year, warning that the curbs, a result of years of US pressure, would knock 10 to 15 percent off the company’s core China equipment sales.
For global investors, this was Washington flexing its hegemonic muscle to delay a key rival’s race to the frontier of artificial intelligence (AI), just as it was becoming the defining general-purpose technology of our era. However, the disclosure raised more questions than it answered: What does a warning like ASML’s mean for investment portfolios? Who would bear the costs and reap the profits — the US, which designed the restrictions, or China, their intended target? And how are risks and returns being rewritten for companies caught in the crossfire across the world?
The investment community has some answers in Geoeconomic Pressure, a paper written by Yale School of Management finance professor Christopher Clayton and other economists. They fed more than 600,000 corporate earnings calls — spanning two decades and 22,000 listed firms worldwide, including China — to open-source large language models running on Stanford University’s computing systems. The algorithm listened for genuine causality: not merely whether CEOs mentioned flashpoints, but if state coercion actually forced them to alter prices, divert investments, or redraw supply chains.
That nuance matters because traditional keyword searches stumble over context. Even sophisticated statistical tools unleashed on a bag of words fail to do the job: A routine maintenance shutdown can get flagged as business disruption and ascribed to a tariff action. A pre-trained language model, by contrast, grasps sentence-level intent, weeding out such false positives.
Language models are just as effective against false negatives. On public calls, corporate executives are notoriously reticent, loath to linger on the fallout of government diktats — particularly those from their own political leaders. To look past this hesitation, the researchers ran the same models over equity analysts’ reports. The AI’s reading of C-suite disclosures matched independent sell-side assessments almost in lockstep.
By latching on to what corporate bosses prefer to downplay, AI captured a nuanced account of pains and gains. In the US, firms subjected to Washington’s restrictions faced lost volumes and compressed margins. Across the Pacific, the shock worked like an adrenaline shot. In about 40 percent of Chinese earnings calls flagged for export curbs, management reported ramping up research and development. Among calls detailing higher spending, two-thirds aligned with a category that AI labeled as “Core Technology Indigenization” — pouring money into homegrown chip gear to escape the US chokehold. (The algorithm did not just sort transcripts into pre-assigned slots; it coined the category names.)
Other geopolitical shocks produced similar ironies. When Western sanctions hit Russia after its 2022 invasion of Ukraine, firms in Europe and the US shouldered write-downs, asset forfeitures and higher logistics bills. The real winners were non-aligned bystanders in China and India. Freed from Western competition, they rushed into the vacuum and scooped up heavily discounted Urals crude.
Nor did US President Donald Trump’s tariff offensive last year go as intended. Foreign exporters did not “eat” the duties, as the US president had predicted. In nearly three-quarters of instances where management disclosed an effect, the impact was negative. Among those reporting outright harm, close to 60 percent pointed to inflated input bills. The rare domestic winners were those insulated from foreign supply chains. Without being saddled with the extra costs paid by their import-reliant rivals, they could still raise prices. Meanwhile, foreign producers absorbed the pressure not by slashing export prices, but by moving factories to Vietnam and Mexico.
Whether the weapon is a tariff, a sanction or a chip ban, economic statecraft is rarely a surgical strike. More often than not, it is a messy carpet bomb that leaves substantial collateral damage in its wake. Investors profit from being able to spot unintended consequences before they appear in the price. Machines reading corporate chatter might just give them the edge to bet on geopolitics before the rest of the market catches on.
Andy Mukherjee is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering industrial companies and financial services in Asia. Previously, he worked for Reuters, The Straits Times and Bloomberg News. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

MOE sets teacher protection guides
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:43:15 UTC
01:43:15 KST

The Ministry of Education (MOE) has issued guidelines to help schools prevent and handle workplace violence and harassment against teachers, including psychological abuse, online attacks and malicious complaints.
Department of Information and Technology Education official Lien Shan-li (連杉利) on Friday said that the term covers more than physical assaults, and also includes verbal abuse, psychological violence, persistent harassment and being assigned duties outside one’s job responsibilities.
The Guidelines on Preventing Workplace Violence and Harassment in Schools and Early Childhood Education and Care Facilities (各級學校及教保服務機構職場不法侵害預防指引) cover teachers at all school levels, early childhood education and care personnel, and other school staff, Lien said.
Photo: Rachel Lin, Taipei Times
The guidelines identify guardhouses, student affairs and counseling offices, meeting rooms and school entrances as places where incidents involving outsiders are more likely to occur.
High-risk periods include students’ arrival and departure times, meetings between parents and school staff, discussions over serious student misconduct or disputes, and after-school study periods.
Schools are advised to install surveillance cameras and emergency contact equipment at these locations, while avoiding excessive monitoring. Surveillance footage should not be arbitrarily made public or shared, the guidelines state.
Schools must reject anonymous complaints, those lacking specific details and cases that have already received a final decision, it added.
Complaints involving only ordinary disciplinary matters should be handled under teacher performance assessment rules, rather than triggering investigations that could lead to dismissal or non-renewal of contracts, it said.
The guidelines also advise schools not to assign work or contact teachers about parent-teacher matters outside working hours, except in cases involving campus safety, major emergencies or urgent official duties.
A task force to investigate the issues should be formed within three days of receiving a complaint and complete investigations within one month, it said.
If a principal or preschool director is implicated, an impartial third party should conduct the investigation, it said, adding that whistle-blowers or complainants must be protected against retaliation.
The guidelines also protect teachers’ right to legally discipline students, stipulating that necessary disciplinary measures in line with legal requirements should not result in punishment or adverse performance assessments.
Schools and early childhood education and care institutions with at least 100 employees must also draw up prevention plans and retain records for three years, the guidelines state.
The ministry said that the guidelines constitute administrative guidance. Cases involving workplace bullying or sexual harassment should continue to be handled primarily under relevant laws.
The National Teachers’ Association (NTA) in a statement welcomed the guidelines, but said that they lacked concrete accountability mechanisms, calling for clearer employer responsibilities.
NTA chairman Yeh Ching-chi (葉青?) said vague provisions could allow school administrators to avoid taking action.
Schools should help teachers establish the facts and provide legal and administrative support when they face pressure or retaliatory complaints from parents over lawful student discipline, rather than demanding apologies or imposing unreasonable measures, Yeh said.
The association urged the ministry to set clear criteria for identifying repeated or malicious complaints and harassment, and to include teacher representatives in workplace risk assessments and reviews of prevention measures.

Amendments to combat illegal land use pass legislature
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:43:15 UTC
01:43:15 KST

Newly passed amendments to regulations on the utilization of farmland and slopeland are aimed to combat illegal land development, the Ministry of Agriculture said on Friday.
The Legislative Yuan on Friday passed the third reading of amendments to the Agricultural Development Act (農業發展條例), the Soil and Water Conservation Act (水土保持法), and the Act for the Utilization and Transfer of Reserved Mountainous Land (山坡地保育利用條例).
The ministry said that the amendments increased penalties for illegal agricultural land filling and illegal hillside development, as well as including wildlife-related crop losses in the scope of government relief.
Photo copied by Peng Chien-li, Taipei Times
According to amendments to articles 10 and 69 of the Agricultural Development Act, illegal filling or dumping on farmland could be fined up to NT$3 million (US$92,370), it said.
Amendments to Article 60 include crop damage caused by wildlife in the scope of cash relief, subsidies or low-interest loans from the government, the ministry said, adding that it would further formulate relief measures.
According to amendments to the Soil and Water Conservation Act, unauthorized hillside land use or development that causes soil erosion or damage to soil and water conservation could be given a maximum jail term of five years with a fine of NT$25 million.
In scenarios where the violation resulted in death or severe injury, the maximum fines have been raised to NT$100 million from NT$1 million and to NT$80 million from NT$800,000.
Those who fail to make improvements for their violation of soil and water conservation regulations could be fined up to NT$3 million, up from NT$60,000.
The amendments are expected to enhance law enforcement efficiency, the ministry said.
Additional reporting by CNA

Drone firm raided over Chinese chips
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:43:12 UTC
01:43:12 KST

Three government agencies had purchased a total of 32 drones made by or linked to Align Corp (亞拓科技), the Ministry of the Interior said yesterday, after the company’s director was detained for allegedly using Chinese-made chips in military drones.
The ministry said it would act in accordance with the Government Procurement Act (政府採購法) and contractual provisions, adding that it would not rule out seeking compensation if any contraventions were found.
A preliminary review found that the National Park Service and Central Police University each purchased one drone manufactured by the company last year, the ministry said, adding that it would verify the details and handle the matter in accordance with procurement regulations.
Photo: Taipei Times
Separately, the National Immigration Agency (NIA) this year completed a public tender under the Government Procurement Act to purchase 30 drones from Suyuan Technology Co (速源科技) at a total cost of NT$2.75 million (US$84,673), the ministry said.
While Suyuan Technology had planned to supply the drones manufactured by Align, delivery has not yet taken place, it said.
The NIA would strictly enforce contractual requirements prohibiting the delivery of drones containing Chinese-made components, it said.
As government procurement standards mandate compliance with “non-red supply chain” requirements, the ministry would continue to strictly require government agencies and suppliers to follow the regulations in procurement processes, it said.
Compensation would be sought in accordance with contractual terms if contraventions were found, it added.
The ministry’s review came as the Taichung Prosecutors’ Office on Friday said that it raided Align Corp and the company’s director Tu Ta-sen (杜大森) was ordered detained and held incommunicado.
The company’s drones were purchased by the army for educational and training purposes, it said
To ensure the equipment met procurement specifications, the military conducted inspections that included dismantling the drones and discovered that chips inside the aircraft bore the letters “CN,” it said.
The procurement contracts explicitly prohibit the use of products from China, Hong Kong and Macau, it said.
The case was reported to prosecutors who found the same issue in another batch of drones purchased by the army.
Prosecutors searched locations connected to the company and summoned six people for questioning, including Tu and his wife, they said.
Investigators found that Tu allegedly used chips manufactured by Chinese companies in at least two batches of military drone procurement contracts and directed Align Corp to assemble the drones before delivering them to the military, they said.
The contracts were worth more than NT$8 million in total, they added.
Tu and others were suspected of misrepresenting the country of origin of products supplied under the contracts, they said.
They were suspected of contravening the National Security Act (國家安全法), which prohibits the delivery of products for military procurement when the supplier knows they originate in China, and also face fraud charges under the Criminal Code, they said.
Align Corp, founded in 1984, is headquartered in Taichung’s Fengyuan District (豐原), the company’s Web site showed.
The company has long secured government contracts to supply drones to the military, police and fire departments.
The Changhua County Police Department, which established a drone unit in June, purchased two M490 drones and nine M3 drones from the company.

Photo: AP
Group-stage Cup games are to be played throughout this month, all counting in the regular-season standings. Quarter-finals are scheduled for Dec. 4 and 5, with the semi-finals on Dec. 8 and 9 before the final on Dec. 11 at Hinkle Fieldhouse in Indianapolis, Indiana.

They led by 14 in the third quarter and weathered a late Knicks surge.
Photo: AFP

2026 Elections: Chiang, Shen clash in first televised mayoral debate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:43:09 UTC
01:43:09 KST

Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) of the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and his main rival, Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator Puma Shen (沈伯洋), traded barbs over public safety, city governance and food safety in their first televised debate yesterday.
One of the sharpest exchanges concerned tougher penalties for drug-impaired driving. Chiang criticized Shen for not taking part in a legislative vote on a related amendment on Friday, accusing him of placing the interests of offenders ahead of victims and their families.
Chiang said Shen’s emphasis on his expertise in criminology showed “professional arrogance,” and questioned whether he understood the suffering of families affected by impaired driving.
Photo: Fang Pin-chao, Taipei Times
Shen said that while he supported tougher penalties for drunk and drug-impaired driving, he considered the amendment disproportionate, adding that preventing such offenses was a more direct responsibility of local governments through police checks, drug-prevention education in schools and efforts to curb drug supplies.
Drawing attention to his previous work with the Association for Victims Support and recovering drug addicts, Shen said his efforts had been misrepresented.
“It now seems as though I’m being made out to be Taipei’s biggest drug dealer,” he said.
The candidates also clashed over city administration, including the accidental felling of a 40-year-old tree near Dongmen Market and the implementation of a free school-lunch program.
The two also criticized each other’s positions on child protection legislation and food safety, each accusing the other of applying double standards.
Shen questioned whether the city government had responded consistently to cases involving school food safety and alleged child abuse, while Chiang said the city government had taken action in the cases and introduced measures to improve oversight and protect children.
The two also clashed over urban renewal, with Chiang touting his record and Shen calling for greater support to overcome hurdles.
“A mayor’s job is to solve problems by addressing their root causes,” Chiang said, highlighting progress on urban renewal projects at Xinwei public housing, Nanjichang Night Market (南機場夜市), and Hulin Street since he became mayor in 2022.
During the past four years, Taipei has approved 2.4 times more urban renewal projects than before, and 1.3 times as many as the other five municipalities combined, he said.
Chiang pressed Shen on why projects in Datong (大同) and Neihu (內湖) districts had been difficult to advance in the legislature, asking him to identify the obstacles to urban renewal.
Shen did not directly address the two cases, saying that the number of approved projects actually moving forward to construction and completion was what mattered most, “rather than simply showcasing favorable statistics.”
The city government has made it easier to launch urban renewal projects, but issues such as property rights, review times, developers’ estimates and implementation can still hold up projects, Shen said.
About 70 percent of residential buildings in Taipei are more than 30 years old, so the city naturally has more urban renewal projects, but also more that have yet to be approved, he said.
The two-hour debate, held from noon to 2pm at the TVBS studio and cohosted by TVBS and SET News, was the only one that Chiang and Shen, the two frontrunners in a six-candidate field, had agreed to so far.

Cruise ship suspends global voyage due to fuel costs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:43:09 UTC
01:43:09 KST

A US cruise ship on an around-the-world voyage that touted its cabins as floating homes suspended its three-year journey in Cambodia due to fuel costs, forcing hundreds of passengers to disembark.
The MV Odyssey set sail two years ago on a voyage to the seven continents marketed as combining long-term living at sea with global travel. Its operator had offered to “make the Odyssey your permanent home,” with the purchase price of a suite for the lifetime of the vessel starting at about US$230,000.
For now, it is docked at the Cambodian port of Sihanoukville on the Gulf of Thailand, with no certain departure date.
Photo: Reuters
The ship has been carrying 203 passengers, mostly Americans, along with 156 crew members, according to Cambodian officials.
It has a 650-passenger capacity.
Its Florida-based operator, Villa Vie Residences, said monthly fuel expenses per cabin that historically averaged US$1,800 have reached an estimated US$6,000 to US$8,000 in parts of Asia due to the war in Iran.
The company said it sought to reduce fuel consumption by slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port, but was unable to offset the surging costs.
Traffic has been curtailed in the Strait of Hormuz since the war in Iran began, squeezing supplies of all kinds of petroleum-based fuels, especially in Southeast Asia, and sharply increasing prices.
“We have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses,” Villa Vie Residences said in a statement on Tuesday. “Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution. Our focus now is on supporting residents, crew, and employees” while it tries to restructure.
“The company is working with residents to coordinate disembarkation and identify temporary living arrangements,” it said.
However, some passengers said they received no support and had to make their own arrangements after being given seven hours notice on Tuesday to disembark. Some were devastated and expressed hope a new company could rescue the venture so life at sea can continue.
Paul and Lynn Montoya, a retired couple from Wyoming, said they bought a window cabin and had expected to sail for years. They boarded the ship 17 months ago in Panama.
Paul praised the concept of residential cruising, but said the shipowner lacked the expertise to make the business financially sustainable.
While rising fuel costs had been cited publicly as the reason for the suspension, he said the company had already been struggling.
Changes to the itinerary, unreliable Internet access and declining food quality had pushed many residents to leave the ship in the past few months, he said.
Lynn said that residents were repeatedly asked to contribute additional money for fuel and other expenses, including a fresh call to raise funds for fuel to get out of Cambodia.
She said the crew members were also not paid.
“We were tired of every two to four weeks being asked for money for fuel, money for everything,” she said.
“We had hopes, but they just kept sinking further and further into the hole through mismanagement,” she added.
The company could not immediately be contacted for comment.
Yet for some, even the financial and logistical turmoil could not outweigh the extraordinary experience of traveling the world and living at sea.
Carol Larson, 69, and her sister Crystal Lavering, 72, occupied separate cabins aboard the ship for 18 months. The siblings, from California, described the suspension as heartbreaking, and hoped the cruise would be resuscitated.
“I hope there is a movement for the residents to buy the ship and I am hoping that goes through because it’s a dream to live on the ship and I don’t want it to end,” Larson said.
Lavering said her health improved during her time on the ship and that she did not need to use a cane to walk anymore.
“You come to this ship to live ... it’s just sad that it’s all over,” she said.
Larson bought her cabin for US$120,000, paid in installments, in addition to monthly maintenance fees, under a plan that had promised the possibility of living aboard for up to 15 years.
She blamed US President Donald Trump for the ship’s woes as fuel costs spiked due to the Iran war, in addition to poor management.
However, she said she did not regret her investment.
“Because it was a start-up company, I believe that it was a risk. From the very first day, I said to myself that if it lasts a year, I can walk away and feel like I got my money’s worth... I still feel that way. I feel blessed to have been part of the experiment of residential cruising,” she said.

Thousands of young Germans rally over living costs, spending cuts as police make arrests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:42:54 UTC
01:42:54 KST

Thousands of young Germans have taken to the streets nationwide to protest against political leaders they accuse of ignoring their concerns, with police reporting arrests in Hamburg and unrest in Stuttgart.
Protesters gathered in Berlin, Frankfurt, Cologne and dozens of other cities on Saturday for rallies organised by “GenZ regelt!”, or “Gen Z has got this”.
Demonstrators carried signs reading “Time for resistance” and “Merz must go”, referring to conservative Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
“We’re taking to the streets for a life that everyone can afford,” said movement spokeswoman Veronika Dinter.
“Hardly anyone still believes in a better future if everything just continues as it is.”
The movement’s grievances include high living costs, poorly maintained schools, government spending cuts and insufficient climate action, alongside a broader belief that politicians disregard the younger generation.
Protesters also oppose sharply increased military spending and fear a new voluntary military service model intended to boost troop numbers could pave the way for conscription.
Arrests in Hamburg, unrest in Stuttgart
More than 10,000 people joined the march in Hamburg, where police said at least two men were arrested on Saturday afternoon.
One was apparently carrying a fake firearm in the upscale Jungfernstieg neighbourhood. Officers overpowered both men, with no immediate reports of injuries or information about their motives.
Police used tear gas and pepper spray to disperse protesters. Drones and water cannons were also deployed as part of a large-scale security operation.
In Stuttgart, police said pyrotechnics were apparently fired at officers from within the march. They also reported scattered vandalism along the route, including graffiti and burning litter bins, which officers extinguished.
The march was halted several times over masked participants and the use of pyrotechnics. At least 3,000 people took part, according to police.
Despite these incidents, demonstrations nationwide appeared mostly peaceful by early evening.
Turnout below expectations
Attendance in several cities appeared lower than organisers had hoped, after more than 170,000 people registered to participate nationwide.
Police in Cologne said turnout was significantly below the 15,000 who had registered, without providing a precise figure.
Around 2,700 people attended in Berlin, 1,800 in Munich and 1,000 in Frankfurt.
Thousands of police officers were deployed across Germany, while some shops boarded up their windows amid fears of unrest.
The German movement has drawn inspiration from similar protests in France and Italy. Demonstrations were also taking place in France for a third consecutive weekend, following some of the country’s worst rioting in years on October 17.
German authorities had feared the protests, coinciding with Halloween, could see similar violence. Berlin has been in contact with French and Italian officials amid concerns that radicals from abroad could join the demonstrations.
Before the rallies, however, authorities said they had found no evidence of concrete plans for violence.
“GenZ regelt!” explicitly rejects violence, saying extremist groups, anti-constitutional symbols, racism and hate speech have no place in its movement.
Christian Volk, a protest researcher at Berlin’s Humboldt University, said Germany had the potential for a major protest movement.
But he told AFP that France had a “completely different tradition when it comes to confrontational forms of protest”.

A minority in their homeland who have been facing discrimination and state violence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:29:02 UTC
01:29:02 KST

A minority in their homeland who have been facing discrimination and state violence
TEHRAN - “Palestinian citizens of Israel,” also known as the “Palestinians of 1948” or “Palestinians inside Israel” have been subjected to discrimination and violence at the hands of successive Israeli governments.
Making up approximately one-fifth of Israel’s population, their votes in the October 27 Knesset election could play a decisive role in determining the composition of the next Israeli government.
Envious of the 19 seats they have won in the 120-seat Knesset, Israeli Prime Minister Netanayahu, his Likud Party, and his extremist allies have launched a campaign against them, linking their high turnout in the election to Qatar, Turkey and some other countries, a claim which seems ridiculous.
The following text, published by Middle East Eye, provides a brief story of these original inhabitants of Palestine. The text, headlined “Who Are the Palestinian Citizens of Israel?”, reads below:
A minority in their homeland, Palestinian citizens of Israel have faced decades of discrimination, marginalization and violence.
They are descendants of Palestinians who survived the Nakba and remained within the de facto borders of Israel after its establishment in 1948.
Today, they number around two million, making up roughly a fifth of Israel’s population.
Although they hold Israeli citizenship, they continue to face discrimination and state repression.
Deep-rooted inequalities persist in housing, land rights, education and public services, while they struggle with high levels of violent crime and inadequate police protection.
They have also faced deadly police violence and arrests during protests in solidarity with Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and Gaza Strip.
Despite these challenges, Palestinian citizens have organized politically and contested elections in their struggle for equal civil and political rights.
So who are Palestinian citizens of Israel? What challenges do they face, and how much influence could they wield over the country’s political future?
Minority in their homeland
Palestinian Arabs made up the majority of the population of historic Palestine before 1947. The territory now comprises Israel, the occupied West Bank and the Gaza Strip.
Between 1947 and 1948, Zionist militias, and later Israeli forces, carried out the ethnic cleansing of Palestinians to make way for the creation of Israel. Palestinians call this the Nakba, or catastrophe.
In a premeditated military campaign, Zionist forces killed thousands of Palestinians, destroyed hundreds of villages and forcibly expelled 80 percent of the Palestinian population from their homeland.
The violence was formally ended in 1949, with Israel signing armistice agreements with neighboring Arab states, whose forces had entered the war to stop the takeover of Palestine.
Israel had captured 78 percent of historic Palestine. Around 150,000 Palestinians remained within the territory that became Israel.
Some survived because Israeli forces had not yet reached their areas, while others resisted attempts to expel them.
Nearly a quarter of those who remained were internally displaced.
They were barred from returning to their homes, many of which were in villages that had been destroyed.
Overnight, Palestinians who remained found themselves a minority in their own homeland.
Today, they make up around 20 percent of Israel’s population of approximately 10 million.
They live mainly in Palestinian-majority towns and cities across the Galilee in the north, the Triangle region in central Israel and the Naqab desert in the south.
Around 80 percent are Muslim, 10 percent Christian and 10 percent Druze.
Israel and much of its society commonly refer to them as “Israeli Arabs” or “Arab citizens of Israel”.
Many, however, identify as “Palestinian citizens of Israel”, “Palestinians of 1948” or “Palestinians inside Israel”.
These terms affirm their Palestinian identity alongside their status as Israeli citizens.
Military rule and resistance
Although Palestinian citizens were granted Israeli citizenship after 1948, early Israeli governments viewed them with suspicion and subjected them to state violence.
From 1948 to 1966, they lived under a military regime imposed exclusively on them, while Jewish citizens were governed by civilian law.
During this period, they faced movement restrictions, curfews, state repression and limits on their political activity.
One of the darkest episodes was the Kafr Qasim massacre.
On 29 October 1956, Israeli forces abruptly brought forward a curfew in the Palestinian village of Kafr Qasim. Hundreds of residents working outside the village were unaware of the change.
Soldiers had been given orders to shoot those who violated the curfew.
As workers returned home, troops stopped them at the village entrance and shot them at close range.
Within hours, 49 Palestinian citizens had been killed, including women and children.
Military rule finally ended in 1966.
In the years that followed, Palestinian citizens increasingly reconnected with the wider Palestinian population, particularly after Israel occupied the West Bank and Gaza Strip in 1967.
One of the most significant protests came on 30 March 1976, in response to Israeli plans to confiscate Palestinian land in the Galilee.
Israeli police violently suppressed the demonstrations, killing six Palestinian citizens and injuring hundreds.
The events became known as Land Day, commemorated annually on 30 March as a symbol of the struggle for Palestinian land and rights.
During the Second Palestinian Intifada, which began in 2000, Palestinian citizens of Israel staged mass protests against Israel’s occupation and in solidarity with Palestinians in the occupied territories.
Police responded with deadly force, killing 13 Palestinian demonstrators and arresting hundreds more.
Discrimination and crime
Beyond state violence, Palestinian citizens have faced decades of discriminatory laws and policies under successive Israeli governments.
According to Adalah, a Haifa-based legal center defending Palestinian rights, more than 65 Israeli laws enacted since 1948 explicitly or implicitly discriminate against Palestinians in Israel and the occupied territories.
These laws cover areas including land ownership, housing, public funding and family reunification.
One of the earliest examples was the Absentees’ Property Law, passed in 1950.
It classified Palestinians who had left, fled or been expelled from their homes during the 1948 Nakba as “absentees”. Their land, homes and other property were placed under state control, including assets belonging to some Palestinians who later became Israeli citizens.
In 2003, Israel passed a law restricting family reunification between Israeli citizens and spouses from the occupied West Bank and Gaza Strip.
A 2011 law empowered admissions committees in certain agricultural and community towns to assess applicants seeking to live there. Critics say the law enables discrimination against Palestinian citizens by allowing committees to reject candidates deemed incompatible with a community’s "Zionist-Jewish character”.
One of the most controversial measures came in 2018, when the Knesset passed the Basic Law: Israel as the Nation-State of the Jewish People.
The law reserves the right to national self-determination in Israel exclusively for the Jewish people. It also downgrades Arabic from an official language to one with a “special status” and declares Jewish settlement a national value that the state should promote.
Alongside legal discrimination, Palestinian communities face a deepening crisis of organized crime and violent killings.
The Abraham Initiatives, an Israeli civil society organization, has linked the crisis to what it describes as “under-policing and tense relations with the Israeli police”.
In 2023, the NGO said that 50 percent of overall violent crime in the country affects Palestinians, even though they make up only 20 percent of Israel's population.
Palestinian community representatives have accused Israeli police of turning a blind eye to the illegal arms trade, and in some cases of indirectly enabling it.
Israel denies responsibility for the crime crisis.
The Palestinian death toll has risen sharply in recent years. A total of 116 people were killed in 2022, rising to 244 in 2023. Most victims were not involved in criminal activity.
In 2025, the number of fatalities reached 252, making it the deadliest year on record.
The Abraham Initiatives’ 2024 report also highlighted a stark gap in homicide investigations. Israeli police solved fewer than 15 percent of killings in Palestinian communities, compared with a clearance rate of around 65 percent for cases in which the victims were Jewish.
Political parties
To challenge discrimination, state violence and Israel’s occupation of Palestinian territories, Palestinian citizens of Israel have long used political organization.
Political activity began as early as the 1950s, but military rule and state repression severely restricted their ability to organize and participate in public life.
By the 1970s, Palestinian citizens were building stronger parliamentary and grassroots movements.
In 1977, Hadash - the Democratic Front for Peace and Equality - was established. It remains one of the most prominent political forces among Palestinian citizens.
Other influential parties emerged in the following decades, including Balad, the National Democratic Assembly; Ta’al, the Arab Movement for Renewal; and Ra’am, the United Arab List.
In 1982, the High Follow-Up Committee for Arab Citizens of Israel was formed. It became a key umbrella body representing Palestinian citizens across political parties and local authorities.
The committee serves as a leading voice for the Palestinian minority outside parliament, linking local municipalities with national political movements.
Palestinian-led parties have contested Knesset elections since those parties began to emerge, but have largely remained outside governing coalitions.
In 2015, Hadash, Balad, Ta’al and Ra’am joined forces to form the Joint List. The alliance followed a 2014 decision to raise the electoral threshold from 2 percent to 3.25 percent, prompting concerns that smaller parties would struggle to enter parliament independently.
The Joint List won 15 seats in the March 2020 election, becoming the Knesset’s third-largest parliamentary bloc. Internal disagreements later fractured the alliance, weakening its collective influence.
For decades, cooperation with Palestinian-led parties was widely treated as a political taboo. Many Jewish Israeli voters opposed such partnerships, while Palestinian citizens themselves remained divided over whether joining a government could deliver meaningful change.
That barrier was broken in 2021, when Ra’am joined the governing coalition led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid. Its four seats helped secure the narrow parliamentary majority that ended Benjamin Netanyahu’s 12-year run as prime minister.
Ahead of the 2026 election, Hadash, Balad and Ta’al reunited under the Joint List, while Ra’am remained a separate party.
Together, the two electoral alliances are projected to win 19 seats, potentially giving Palestinian-led parties renewed leverage over coalition negotiations and the formation of Israel’s next government.
Their influence could prove decisive in determining who governs - and whether Palestinian citizens can translate parliamentary representation into meaningful political change.

Thousands rally in Berlin as Gen Z plans protests in 30 German cities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
