Thousands rally in Berlin as Gen Z plans protests in 30 German cities
Demonstrations sweeping Europe are inspiring young Germans frustrated by rising costs of living amid military spending and conscription.
Berlin, Germany – Thousands of people are gathering in Berlin and more than 30 other German cities as the nation becomes the latest European country to be hit by a wave of student protests sweeping the continent.
Gathering at the Platz des 18 Maerz, on the west side of the capital’s iconic Brandenburg Gate on a sunny but chilly Saturday afternoon, there was support for the young people within a mixed demographic crowd.
Anti-fascist activists smoking hand-rolled cigarettes and wearing keffiyehs waited patiently alongside students dressed in Halloween outfits, smartly dressed grandmothers donning “omas gegen rechts” (grandmothers against the right) badges, and camera crews, ahead of the 2pm (13:00 GMT) rally start.
The protests were organised by a loose alliance called Gen Z Regelt (Gen Z sorts it), and by Saturday morning, nearly 180,000 people across 34 cities had signed up to participate – with the main host cities including Frankfurt, Cologne, Munich and the capital Berlin.
Nearly 12,000 people had signed up to join in the German capital, and people were continuing to stream into the square well into the demonstration to listen to speakers in what was so far a calm afternoon in the capital.
However, at a rally in the western city of Cologne, scuffles broke out between protesters and police, who moved in to contain a march there.
The protest organisers had outlined six key issues that took them to the streets on Saturday, including the rising cost of living, education cuts and military conscription.
‘Political failure’ of government
Students told Al Jazeera that they are both angry and frustrated by ongoing funding cuts, even as the government invests heavily in the military.
Yet they also said they feel a sense of hope after seeing student protests in different parts of Europe in recent weeks.
Veronika Dinter travelled to Berlin on Friday night from Hannover to participate in the protest.
The 23-year-old political science student said that due to high living costs, she had to take on a part-time job to fund her studies.
“I wanted to start studying to develop critical thinking and learn something new, but I didn’t realise how much it would cost to do so. I think this is something a lot of people in my generation are experiencing right now,” she said.
“Funding for education and social services are being cut, while the cost of living keeps rising. Universities are struggling, institutes are closing, teachers are losing their jobs and education facilities are literally falling apart.
“This crisis is the political failure of our government. And instead of solving it, Chancellor Friedrich Merz and his rich friends are funding the military with billions of euros.”
This is a sentiment that Emma Heymann, a 24-year-old student living in Berlin, resonated with.
“Our generation feels very angry at the government because they are making these huge cuts that are affecting our quality of life here. And at the same time, they are spending billions on the military and spending money to fund the genocide in Gaza,” she said.
Protesters should be ‘listened to’
Phil Tziartzianis travelled eight hours from his hometown of Kassel to join his friend Jan Chrominski and other young people at the demonstration.
“It feels important for me to be here among other young people who feel the same way,” he said.
The protesters join a wave of demonstrations that have swept across Europe in recent weeks, including in France, Belgium, Italy, Spain and Serbia.
Kilian Hampel is a senior research fellow at the Future of Work Lab at the University of Konstanz. He says other demonstrations are having an impact on young Germans.
“The frustration itself has been building for years, but this is definitely part of a wave we are seeing across Europe, and young people here are feeling that they can actually take their worries and problems to the streets,” he said. “Many of their concerns, in particular around poor educational infrastructure, are legitimate, and it’s important that they are listened to.”
The Berlin demonstration is expected to last two hours, with another one organised by a different alliance, planned at 5:30pm (16:30 GMT) in a different part of the German capital.
In the past week, political figures have raised concerns about the protests turning violent.
Yet demonstrators say they see the narrative of violence distracting from the issues they want to raise.
“We urge the police to not confront our demonstrations with any kind of violence,” Dinter, the student from Hannover, said.
“We stand in solidarity with all the people around the world who are fighting for an affordable life, for more investment in the education system, and against wars and military buildup.”

El-Sayed lashes out at defeated rival over demand to condemn ‘antisemitic’ ad

Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed lashed out Friday at his defeated primary rival after she demanded that he condemn an advertisement widely denounced as antisemitic, invoking his victory over her without explicitly repudiating the ad.
Responding to Rep. Haley Stevens, El-Sayed revived grievances over the primary, boasting that his campaign had defeated what he described as $70 million in outside spending from “big corporations and AIPAC” supporting her. He accused Stevens of seeming “intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago” and urged Democrats to concentrate on defeating Republican Mike Rogers.

Binance says 90% of $6.3 billion hack losses are now covered, plans to resume withdrawals Sunday
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:06:44 UTC
01:06:44 KST

Binance said Saturday that it has covered up to 90% of the roughly $6.3 billion in token assets stolen from its hot wallets in a record crypto theft announced Thursday.
Binance said it will continue to buy the remaining relevant token assets through market and over-the-counter channels until the covered amount reaches 100% for all tokens.
"All BTC, ETH, USDT, BNB, SOL, USDC, XRP, USD1, RLUSD, and ZEC are fully backed 100%," Binance said in a statement. "Binance will absorb the financial impact of these stolen funds, not our users."
The exchange said the outstanding 10% consists of tokens outside its top 10 that are "less liquid, which means they may take longer to source in the required amounts."
Binance said it is tapping its Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU), a portion of its Futures insurance fund, and its corporate treasury to replenish the assets.
"Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident. We will continue to demonstrate this commitment through measurable progress, transparent reporting, and concrete actions," Binance said.
Its "next milestone" will be resuming withdrawal services for users by Sunday, subject to security checks, while the exchange continues its investigation into the attack, it said.
Binance declined to discuss additional details or updates on its investigation to CNBC, referring questions to its latest statement.
It still isn't clear how the attack — the largest crypto theft on record — took place.
The world's largest crypto exchange initially said the hack may involve "a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions." However, Co-CEO Richard Teng later said the attack involved a more complex process rather than the misuse of a single engineer's permissions.
It also wasn't clear who was responsible for the breach. But TRM Labs, a blockchain intelligence and AI investigations company, pointed to North Korean hackers as the potential culprits.
"Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack and the KelpDAO hack in April 2026: small Tornado Cash withdrawals funding an operator wallet, staging that began well before the theft, and signatures obtained in advance then executed in one burst," the company said.
— CNBC's Jenny Lee, Liz Napolitano and Davis Giangiulio contributed to this report.

In 2018, Mada Masr applied for a licence but received no response, and applied again in 2020 with the same result.

Animal testing in India: Why proposed new rules have sparked a fight over safeguards
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:01:25 UTC
01:01:25 KST

The rules propose a differentiated approval system based on the severity of experiments.
NEW DELHI: Animal testing remains an important part of pharmaceutical research, vaccine development and medical science in India. But a proposed overhaul of the rules governing laboratory experiments has triggered a debate over a fundamental question: Can India streamline scientific research without weakening safeguards for animals?The draft Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (Control and Supervision of Experiment, Breeding and Trading of Laboratory Animals) Rules, 2026, issued by the Committee for Control and Supervision of Experiments on Animals (CCSEA), proposes changes to how experiments are classified and approved. While it introduces a severity-based system for assessing animal suffering, animal welfare groups have raised concerns about reduced regulatory scrutiny, the use of certain animals and potential conflicts of interest in institutional approvals.The debate also comes at a time when advances in science are opening up alternatives to animal testing, including human cell-based studies, organoids, organ-on-chip technology and computer modelling. The question is whether India's regulatory framework is keeping pace with these developments.What are the proposed rules1. Severity-Based Classification: Experiments are categorized into four levels based on expected pain or distress: Mild, Moderate, Severe, Non-recovery2. Decentralized Approvals: An establishment's internal Institutional Animal Ethics Committee (IAEC) can directly approve mild and moderate experiments on any species.
The central Committee for Control and Supervision of Experiments on Animals (CCSEA) retains approval authority for severe and non-recovery procedures, specifically for animals positioned above rodents and rabbits.3. Three Rs: Replacement, Reduction and Refinement. These involve using alternatives wherever possible, limiting the number of animals to what is scientifically necessary and improving procedures and care to minimise suffering.The proposed framework also lays down requirements for the registration of establishments, institutional ethics committees, veterinary supervision, trained personnel and animal-care facilities. Experiments may be undertaken for specified purposes, including basic and applied research, drug and food safety testing, disease research, environmental protection and species conservation.The sectors that use animals for researchAnimal experimentation is not limited to pharmaceutical companies. Dr Surat, Senior Program Director, Research and Toxicology Department, Humane World for Animals India, said it is carried out across pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies, medical research institutions, universities, veterinary colleges and government laboratories.Animals are used in vaccine development and batch testing, food and feed safety assessments, disease research and studies evaluating the effectiveness of potential treatments. Tests may assess short-term and long-term toxicity, skin and eye irritation, carcinogenicity and reproductive toxicity.Mice and rats are among the most commonly used laboratory animals, followed by rabbits, guinea pigs, fish and birds. Non-human primates are also used in certain areas of research.However, the scale of animal experimentation in India remains difficult to establish. Dr Surat said that although an estimated 100 million to more than 115 million animals are used in experiments and research worldwide every year, India does not have an official national figure or a transparent public database recording annual animal use, deaths and reported violations.Dr Ramanuj Panda, founder and managing director of Gocarin, has called for a centralised reporting system that records the species used, severity of experiments, animal deaths and welfare complaints.What existing law saysAnimal experimentation in India is governed by the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960. The law provides for the CCSEA to regulate experiments and ensure that animals are not subjected to unnecessary pain or suffering.Section 17 requires the committee to ensure that animals are not subjected to unnecessary pain or suffering before, during or after experiments. Section 18 authorises inspections of facilities and examination of relevant records. Section 19 allows the committee to prohibit experiments where the rules are not being followed, subject to the prescribed process.The proposed rules would change how approval responsibilities are distributed, particularly for experiments involving mild and moderate levels of suffering.Why are animal welfare groups concerned?One of the major concerns raised by animal welfare organisations relates to provisions allowing certain experiments involving protected wild animals, wild-caught animals and stray or feral domestic animals, subject to specified conditions and permissions.PETA India has flagged these provisions, arguing that capturing, handling, transporting and confining animals not bred for laboratory use can cause distress and disrupt their natural behaviour. It has also questioned the scientific reliability of using animals whose health, genetic background and environmental histories may be unknown.The organisation has raised concerns about the possibility of community dogs and cats being exposed to laboratory use. It has also referred to a CCSEA circular issued in 2022 that allowed the use of stray dogs in certain vaccine trials. The circular was withdrawn in 2023.Dr Noopur Jain, Science and Research Policy Advisor at PETA India, said: "India should be moving towards modern, human-relevant non-animal science, not making animal experimentation easier."PETA has also argued that the severity of an experiment, rather than the size or species of the animal, should determine the level of regulatory scrutiny.Could changes to approvals weaken oversight?Beyond the use of animals, the proposed shift towards institutional approvals has raised questions about independence and potential conflicts of interest.Dr Surat said five of the nine members of an IAEC belong to the same establishment seeking approval for an experiment, raising concerns about how independent research proposals may be assessed.The concern is that institutions could approve mild and moderate experiments involving a wider range of species without prior CCSEA clearance. This makes the role of independent members, veterinary supervision and clear scientific justification particularly important.Panda said streamlining approvals should not come at the cost of animal welfare. He called for meaningful participation by independent members in IAEC decisions, mandatory veterinary supervision, documented scientific justification and external reviews for experiments involving greater levels of suffering.The draft provides for inspections by designated nominees, including a socially aware member, at least twice a year. Separately, CCSEA inspection teams can inspect facilities to verify compliance.Dr Surat said facilities also undergo physical inspections for fresh registration and five-year renewals, while yearly mid-term inspections are mandated for large-animal research facilities.Another issue is whether India could become a destination for outsourced animal research.Dr Rukmini Jonnalagadda, founder and chief scientific officer of ULQA Scientific, Hyderabad, referred to an October 2026 investigation by Irish publication The Journal, which found that Irish universities had commissioned animal experiments at overseas laboratories, including in India.The University of Galway disclosed payments of €102,174 to an Indian organisation, Presude Lifesciences, for overseas studies.Ireland's Health Products Regulatory Authority confirmed that it has no regulatory role over animal experiments conducted abroad. The investigation does not establish that the Indian studies violated local rules, but it raises questions about how institutions commissioning research overseas assess and monitor animal welfare standards.Are animal experiments always reliable predictors of human safety?Animal models can provide useful scientific information, but differences between species can limit how accurately they predict human responses. Animals and humans may process chemicals differently and have distinct genetic, metabolic, immune and physiological characteristics.Panda said animal research should not be treated as proof that a drug or treatment will be safe for people.One frequently cited example is the 2006 clinical trial of TGN1412, an antibody that had appeared safe in preclinical testing involving non-human primates. During the first human trial, all six healthy volunteers who received the antibody developed severe immune reactions.Dr Surat also pointed to gene therapy research for X-linked myotubular myopathy. Although the treatment showed promise in dog models, clinical trials in humans were associated with severe liver complications and deaths.He also cited safety concerns surrounding Sarepta Therapeutics' Elevidys gene therapy for Duchenne muscular dystrophy, which received a boxed warning from the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) over serious liver injury.These cases do not mean animal research has no scientific value. They highlight the limitations of relying on animal studies as the sole predictor of human safety, particularly in complex diseases and therapies.What alternatives are availableNew Approach Methodologies (NAMs) include cell-based tests, three-dimensional tissue cultures, organoids, organ-on-chip systems and computer-based models. These methods allow researchers to study aspects of human biology without relying on live animals at every stage of testing.Organoids are miniature structures grown from cells that mimic certain features of human organs, while organ-on-chip systems reproduce selected functions of organs. Computer models can also help predict how substances may behave in the human body.However, these methods cannot yet replicate every interaction between organs, the immune system and other biological processes in a whole organism. They are therefore being used alongside animal models in areas where complex biological interactions remain difficult to reproduce.India has taken some steps towards recognising alternatives. The New Drugs and Clinical Trials (Amendment) Rules, 2023, recognised methods such as cell-based assays, organ chips, microphysiological systems and computer modelling for relevant regulatory purposes.A government response to Parliament in 2026 highlighted support for 109 non-animal testing projects by the Indian Council of Medical Research across 71 institutions and laboratories.However, experts say wider adoption requires investment in infrastructure, training, validation and collaboration between researchers and regulators.What needs to change?Dr Surat argued that the draft rules should do more than classify experiments according to severity. India should consider stronger provisions to promote the development and validation of alternatives, including a requirement that animal procedures should not be undertaken where a recognised non-animal method is available.The proposed framework could be strengthened by requiring researchers to document their search for alternatives before seeking approval, publishing annual statistics on animal use and establishing a national centre to validate non-animal testing methods.Dr Surat also flagged ambiguity in the draft's definition of a "humane endpoint", the point at which an experiment should be stopped to prevent further suffering. The rules, the expert said, need to establish a clear and actionable response when an animal reaches that stage.Panda said experiments involving prolonged suffering should face strict scrutiny, with veterinary monitoring, appropriate pain relief and clearly defined humane endpoints. He added that a transition away from routine animal experimentation was possible in an increasing number of applications, but would require rigorous scientific validation and a clear regulatory pathway.Dr Surat also pointed to policy initiatives in the US, UK, European Union and China to advance human biology-based testing methods. India, the expert argued, would risk falling behind without comparable policy support and investment.
The challenge is not simply to reduce the number of animals used in laboratories. It is to ensure that research is scientifically justified, animals are protected wherever experiments continue, and credible alternatives are developed and adopted wherever possible.As the government considers feedback on the draft rules, the central question remains whether the proposed framework can balance scientific research with stronger safeguards while creating a clearer path towards methods that are more relevant to human health.
Priyanka Jaiswal has four years of experience in digital journalism, news agency reporting and video production. Currently with The Times of India, she covers public policy, politics and global affairs. She is particularly drawn to human-interest stories that put people at the heart of an issue, spark awareness , and contribute to meaningful conversations.

What permanent daylight saving time could mean for sleep, mood, and mental health
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:00:51 UTC
01:00:51 KST

As lawmakers across North America move to end the twice-yearly ritual of changing the clocks, three new papers highlight a complex debate over how clock shifts and permanent time systems affect health. A policy analysis published in CMAJ argues that permanent standard time would better support winter sleep, mood, and biological rhythms than permanent daylight saving time, and a review focused on people with mental illness reaches the same conclusion. A large review of studies tracking health patterns across whole populations, however, finds that seasonal clock changes and summer daylight saving time carry a mix of harms and benefits rather than being uniformly harmful.
Although major sleep societies have recommended adopting permanent standard time, North American governments eliminating the clock switch have largely chosen permanent daylight saving time instead. Yukon adopted permanent daylight saving time in 2020, followed by British Columbia in March 2026 and Alberta and the Northwest Territories in April 2026, while the United States House of Representatives passed a bill in July 2026 to make daylight saving time permanent nationwide. Public opinion does not necessarily match that legislative push: in a 2025 Gallup poll, only 19% of Americans wanted to keep switching the clocks, while 48% preferred permanent standard time and 24% favored permanent daylight saving time.
How clock time interacts with the body’s internal clock
Standard time is a timekeeping system designed so that 12:00 noon on the local clock roughly matches solar noon, the moment when the sun reaches its highest point in the sky along a time zone’s central line of longitude. Daylight saving time shifts local clocks forward by one hour in the spring and returns them to standard time in the autumn, which does not create extra daylight but moves an hour of sunlight from the morning to the evening.
Both schedules interact directly with circadian rhythms, the internal 24-hour biological cycles that regulate sleep, alertness, hormone production, and cellular activity throughout the body. These daily rhythms are coordinated by the suprachiasmatic nucleus, a tiny cluster of nerve cells in the hypothalamus at the base of the brain that acts as the body’s master pacemaker.
Because the human master clock naturally runs slightly slower than a 24-hour day, averaging about 24.2 hours per cycle, it relies on natural daylight hitting the eyes to reset itself each morning. Bright morning sunlight speeds the internal clock up so people feel alert during the day and sleepy at night, whereas evening light slows the clock down and pushes sleepiness later. Modern habits like working indoors and looking at illuminated screens at night already weaken morning light cues and strengthen evening ones, creating a mismatch known as social jet lag, where work or school schedules force people to wake up before their delayed biological clocks are ready.
Public frustration with biannual clock shifts has grown alongside evidence that changing the schedule disrupts well-being; for instance, a study covered by PsyPost earlier this year found that both seasonal transitions triggered drops in public mood, with the autumn return to standard time producing a more lasting dip than the spring shift. Beyond temporary mood dips, the authors of a 2015 review argued that chronically disrupted or shortened sleep can contribute to the development of depression.
Canada’s choice between two permanent time systems
To evaluate what happens after a jurisdiction abolishes seasonal clock changes, Raymond W. Lam of the University of British Columbia and colleagues at Simon Fraser University and Vancouver Coastal Health conducted the public health policy analysis in CMAJ. Rather than debating whether twice-yearly transitions should end, the authors examined the chronic, year-round consequences of adopting either permanent standard time or permanent daylight saving time across Canada. They calculated winter and summer sunrise and sunset times across six major Canadian cities, synthesized evidence from biological rhythm research, disease-modeling simulations, and economic border studies, and reviewed lessons from countries that previously enacted permanent daylight saving time.
Lam and colleagues showed that under permanent daylight saving time, winter sunrises would occur around or after the start of many school days across much of Canada. By early January, switching from standard time to permanent daylight saving time shifts the latest winter sunrise from 7:51 a.m. to 8:51 a.m. in Toronto, from 8:08 a.m. to 9:08 a.m. in Vancouver, from 8:27 a.m. to 9:27 a.m. in Winnipeg, and from 8:40 a.m. to 9:40 a.m. in Calgary.
The authors also noted that political time zone boundaries often distort local solar time, pointing out that while Saskatchewan officially observes year-round Central Standard Time, much of the province sits geographically closer to Mountain Time and actually experiences light schedules resembling permanent daylight saving time. Similarly, clock policies have the greatest impact in mid-latitude regions where most Canadians live, whereas high-latitude territories like Yukon have such brief winter daylight that a one-hour shift makes little practical difference.
What darker winter mornings could mean for health
According to Lam and colleagues, prolonged winter morning darkness under permanent daylight saving time would likely worsen social jet lag and seasonal mood vulnerability. Winter dips in sleep, concentration, and energy are already most prominent among youth aged 12 to 17. An estimated 1% to 3% of Canadians experience seasonal affective disorder, a form of winter depression thought to involve a delay in the body clock linked to later morning light, while up to 15% experience milder winter slumps in mood, sleep, and energy.
Geographic patterns point in the same direction, with global prevalence of seasonal affective disorder rising by 0.2 percentage points for every 1-degree increase in northern latitude. In United States county-level analyses, residents on the western edges of time zones, who experience later clock sunrises and sunsets similar to permanent daylight saving time, averaged up to 2 additional suicide deaths per 100,000 people annually compared to those on the eastern edges (the epidemiological review described below rated this study as low quality).
In addition, a 2025 modeling study simulating chronic disease prevalence across the United States indicated that while both permanent policies improved health over twice-yearly switching, the health benefits of permanent daylight saving time were one-third smaller than those of permanent standard time, especially at northern latitudes comparable to Canada.
Comparisons of places with different sunset times indicate that an hour of later sunset is associated with nearly one hour less sleep per week and about 5% lower long-run earnings, and a time-zone border study found that workers on the late-sunset side earn about 3.5% less. In Florida, an extra hour of morning sunlight before school was linked to higher adolescent math and reading scores by 0.08 and 0.06 standard deviations, a gain comparable to reducing class sizes.
Trade-offs and lessons from other countries
Although permanent daylight saving time provides brighter evenings that can support outdoor recreation and retail spending for people with flexible schedules, its dark winter mornings could disproportionately affect teenagers, shift workers, and lower-income or rural commuters traveling on poorly lit roads.
Permanent standard time has trade-offs of its own: summer sunrises would come as early as about 4 a.m. in cities such as Vancouver and Montréal, which the authors note could wake some people too early, and winter sunsets would arrive as early as about 4:10 p.m. International experience shows how these trade-offs can play out: the United States enacted permanent daylight saving time in 1974 but repealed it within a year after widespread public backlash over dark winter school commutes; Russia, which adopted permanent daylight saving time in 2011, reversed it in 2014, and Chile reversed its 2015 move after complaints.
Lam and colleagues concluded that health evidence favors permanent standard time, and that provinces choosing permanent daylight saving time should pair it with later school start times, morning indoor light interventions, pedestrian safety upgrades, and ongoing public health monitoring.
A review of 157 studies finds a more mixed picture
While the Canadian analysis examined which permanent clock system is healthier once seasonal transitions end, a systematic review published in the European Journal of Epidemiology questioned whether the existing epidemiological evidence truly justifies abolishing the twice-yearly clock shifts in the first place. Led by first author Aiste Steponenaite of the University of Kent and the University of Greenwich and senior author Philip Lewis of the University of Cologne, the researchers searched five databases through June 2025 and identified 157 human epidemiological studies across 36 countries.
Two independent reviewers rated each study’s methodological quality as low, medium, or high, giving greater weight to large registry analyses, which draw on national health records, and to studies that included placebo tests, which check whether similar health changes happen in years, dates, or neighboring regions without a clock shift.
Across the 157 studies, roughly one in five of which met high-quality standards, the researchers found that neither the seasonal transitions nor summer daylight saving time were uniformly harmful. Among 17 studies of acute myocardial infarction, commonly known as a heart attack (6 rated high quality and 10 medium quality), the evidence pointed to an elevated risk during the first one to four weeks after the spring shift, corresponding to a relative risk increase of about 4% in a 2024 meta-analysis by two of the review’s authors. Among 16 studies of fatal traffic crashes, the evidence pointed to an increase after the spring shift in some places, mainly the United States. At the same time, a high-quality nationwide United States study found that changes in all-cause mortality, or deaths from any cause, after the spring shift were not statistically significant.
Crimes involving physical harm, such as robberies and assaults, tended to drop briefly after the spring shift and rise after the autumn shift. The autumn transition back to standard time was also linked to a roughly 2.5% relative decrease in all-cause mortality and fewer workplace accidents, each based on a single high-quality study. Living under daylight saving time during the summer months was associated with an approximately 4.5% relative reduction in all-cause mortality in one high-quality United States study and with fewer traffic accidents in Chile.
Across 22 sleep duration studies, 6 circadian rhythm studies, and 15 psychiatric outcome studies, Steponenaite and colleagues found no consistent population-wide changes in sleep duration after the spring shift or in psychiatric hospital admissions and suicides after either transition, although two low-quality studies from Russia did indicate that maintaining daylight saving time through the winter shortened sleep duration. Because summer daylight saving time and the autumn shift were associated with mortality and safety benefits, the authors suggested that retaining seasonal clock transitions while using targeted preventive measures around the spring shift, such as gradual schedule adjustments for heart patients and enhanced road safety enforcement, remains a reasonable option.
Notably, the review also concluded that if transitions were abolished, the limited sleep evidence and circadian theory would favor permanent standard time over permanent daylight saving time, the same choice the CMAJ authors recommend. Where the papers part ways is on whether ending the twice-yearly changes should be the priority, a split visible in the CMAJ analysis itself, which counts the mental-health review among papers supporting an end to clock changes and the epidemiological review among those questioning that consensus.
Why people with mental illness may be especially sensitive
Why did the epidemiological review by Steponenaite and colleagues find no consistent population-level spike in psychiatric emergencies after clock changes, even though sleep loss is closely tied to mental illness? A comprehensive review published in Brain Sciences, led by Liahm Blank, Joshua Khorsandi, Jagdish Khubchandani, and Kavita Batra at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, and New Mexico State University, offers one possible explanation for this discrepancy by focusing specifically on individuals with chronic mental illness.
The authors searched four databases through February 2026 and synthesized 66 peer-reviewed studies published between 2000 and 2026, grouping them into 12 epidemiological studies that directly evaluated daylight saving time transitions, 36 observational studies linking sleep or circadian disruption to mental health symptoms, and 18 experimental studies examining biological pathways across depression, anxiety disorders, bipolar disorder, PTSD, ADHD, and psychotic disorders.
Blank and colleagues noted that while most healthy adults adjust to a one-hour clock change within two to seven days, individuals with pre-existing psychiatric conditions often have fragile circadian timing systems that may adapt slowly or incompletely. They argue that large hospital and emergency department registries mainly capture severe crises and may miss everyday symptom flare-ups, anxiety, and mood instability. For example, a Finnish nationwide analysis and a United States emergency department study found no statistically significant increase in hospital-treated manic or psychotic episodes in the two weeks after clock transitions.
Even in population registries, some specific mental health risks have emerged, including an 11% relative increase in depressive episodes after the autumn transition and a 6.25% relative increase in United States suicide rates following the spring transition. The epidemiological review rated those same depression and suicide studies as medium quality, and its psychiatric conclusion leaned more heavily on a high-quality study from Austria, Switzerland, and Sweden that found no change in suicide rates around clock changes.
Blank and colleagues also explained that because rapid eye movement sleep, the dreaming stage essential for processing emotions and consolidating memories, occurs mostly in the final hours before waking, losing an hour of morning sleep after the spring transition may selectively cut off rapid eye movement sleep even when total sleep loss seems minor.
Across specific psychiatric conditions, modest clock disruptions may interact with baseline sleep difficulties, as sleep disturbances are reported in up to 90% of people with PTSD, and wearable-tracker research in schizophrenia has found severe circadian misalignment in roughly half of clinically stable patients. Similarly, an estimated 73% to 78% of individuals with ADHD have a delayed sleep-wake cycle, and one experiment in children with ADHD found that losing one hour of nightly sleep for a week pushed attention scores from below the clinical cutoff into clinically impaired ranges.
Blank and colleagues proposed three biological pathways that may underlie this sensitivity. First, delayed morning light may alter signals from the eyes to the hypothalamus and disrupt the nighttime release of melatonin, a hormone that promotes sleep. Second, sleep loss may activate the body’s main stress-response system, raising levels of the stress hormone cortisol and of inflammatory proteins. Third, variations in clock genes, which keep time inside individual cells, may make it harder for cells in people with bipolar disorder or schizophrenia to adjust to an abrupt time shift.
Converging with the CMAJ policy analysis, Blank and colleagues favored adopting permanent standard time to protect vulnerable psychiatric populations and recommended that clinicians help high-risk patients shift their sleep schedules by 15 to 20 minutes per day over the three to four days before a transition.
Caveats and next steps
As with all research, there are some caveats to keep in mind when interpreting these three papers. Nearly all population-level findings on daylight saving time rely on observational or quasi-experimental data, which take advantage of natural events such as clock changes, rather than on randomized trials. That means researchers cannot establish direct cause and effect, and studies comparing opposite edges of time zones must assume that neighboring communities do not differ in other lifestyle or economic ways.
Each paper also has its own limitations. The CMAJ paper is a solicited policy analysis rather than a systematic review and relies partly on unpublished data for its claims about evening leisure benefits. In the systematic review of 157 epidemiological studies, roughly four out of five papers were rated as low or medium quality, and placebo tests using non-transition dates or regions made some previously publicized effects disappear, such as supposed clock-shift impacts on stock market decisions.
The mental-health paper was a narrative review, which summarizes studies without the strict search and selection rules of a systematic review, and a single author screened studies for inclusion. Only 12 of its 66 included papers directly measured outcomes during daylight saving time transitions; the rest inferred risk from broader sleep and circadian research that often relied on small clinical samples or self-reported sleep questionnaires. Because sleep disruption and mental illness influence each other in both directions, it remains difficult to separate how much the clock shift itself drives symptom changes.
Looking ahead, the CMAJ authors urged provinces such as British Columbia and Alberta to treat their policy changes as an opportunity to monitor school attendance, traffic injuries, cardiovascular events, and mental health visits over time, while the other two teams called for longer-term studies with objective sleep measures and placebo tests.
The paper, “Analysis of health impacts associated with adopting permanent standard time or permanent daylight saving time to inform policy in Canada,” was authored by Raymond W. Lam, Ralph Mistlberger, Patrick Baylis, and Alexandra Choi.
The paper, “A systematic review of epidemiological studies into daylight-saving time & health identifying beneficial & adverse effects,” was authored by Aiste Steponenaite, Jonas P. Wallraff, Ursula Wild, Lorna Brown, Ben Bullock, Gurprit S. Lall, Sally Ferguson, Russell G. Foster, Jennifer Walsh, Greg Murray, Thomas C. Erren, and Philip Lewis.
The paper, “When the Clock Shifts: A Comprehensive Review of Daylight-Saving Time (DST), Circadian Disruption, and Neuropsychological Risk in Chronic Mental Illness,” was authored by Liahm Blank, Joshua Khorsandi, Elizabeth England-Kennedy, Srikanta Banerjee, Karen Kopera-Frye, Roberto Sagaribay, Jagdish Khubchandani, and Kavita Batra.

Gen Z protests sweep cities across Germany

Gen Z protests sweep cities across Germany
Published October 31, 2026last updated October 31, 2026
What you need to know
- Thousands of young people have joined protests across Germany, with demonstrations registered in 34 cities
- Organizers said 120,000 took part, though the number has not been officially confirmed
- Demonstrators demand better-funded schools, action on living costs, greater social justice and stronger climate protection, while opposing a possible return to military conscription
- In Cologne, police canceled the planned march over covered faces and pyrotechnics; the gathering continued as a stationary rally on the Rhine riverbank
- In Stuttgart, police repeatedly halted the march, citing covered faces, pyrotechnics and participants leaving the agreed route
This is a round-up of events at the youth protests across Germany on October 31, 2026:
Minor scuffles reported as German protests wrap up
German security forces reported minor violent incidents in several cites in the wake of the Gen Z demonstrations.
In Hamburg, protesters at the city's Steintor square pelted the police with fireworks . Police used "immediate force" to clear the area, including using a water cannon.
Several police officers were injured during a similar incident in Frankfurt, according to a state interior minister.
Police also used a water cannon in Cologne, where the march was halted and turned into a stationary rally after some protesters covered their faces and used pyrotechnics.
A police officers sustained light injuries in nearby Bonn during a confrontation with a group of protesters.
In Berlin, the authorities noted a rally separate from the official event organized by the Gen Z movement. Police initially reported "isolated instances of throwing eggs and bottles" from a crowd of around 500 people. The authorities later also reported "illegal burning of pyrotechnics" and said the crowd has grown to around 3,000 participants.
Police officers injured in Frankfurt
Several police officers were injured in a clash with a group of protesters following the Gen Z demonstration in Frankfurt, authorities said.
"One officers could be injured more seriously, but this will need some more looking into," said Hesse Interior Minister Roman Poseck.
"We assume there were about 100 attackers motivated by extreme leftist ideology," the state minister said.
"They have staged a massive attack against the police by throwing bottles, stones and fireworks."
Police responded with water cannons and have the situation in hand, he said
IN PICTURES: Germany's Gen Z take to the streets
Thousands of young people took part in protests in 34 German cities on Saturday.
German Gen Z protesters called out rising living expenses, remilitarization of Germany, and declining education.
Some of the protesters also called for Germany's current chancellor, center-right Friedrich Merz, to step down.
The protests were held under the slogan Gen Z regelt (Gen Z sorts it).
Police were out in force after many politicians warned that Germany will not tolerate the kind of violence seen in France in mid-October.
Police reported incidents in which pepper spray and water cannon were used to keep crowds under control, with protesters setting off fireworks and lighting fires.
Most of the demonstrations ended peacefully.
But tensions remained high in some German cities with reports of several police officers injured.
Hamburg: Protesters set fire to barriers
In Germany's second-biggest city, Hamburg, police estimated 6,700 people taking part in the demonstration.
They reported some groups of black-clad protesters, some of whom also wore face masks, pulling apart construction site barriers and throwing them on the street. Some of the barriers were later set on fire.
Police said they pushed the crowd back and used pepper spray to break them apart. The fire was eventually put out.
Police say some 5,000 now gathered at Berlin's Brandenburg Gate
Following an initial estimate of several hundred people attending the rally in central Berlin, police said that some 5,000 people were now gathered at the Brandenburg Gate. The organizers, "Gen Z regelt" (Gen Z sorts it) gave a much higher number, saying 10,000 people were in attendance.
One of the speakers in Berlin, Kaja Schwab, decried false promises made by politicians.
The youth is being told that "we will do well if we work hard enough." In reality, the life is getting unaffordable and the young are "forced into military service," she said, in reference to Germany's renewed recruitment drive.
Youth protests draw crowds across Germany
Thousands of young people have joined the demonstrations in over 30 German cities, with police reporting largely peaceful protests.
Early police estimates included:
- Berlin: Around 650 people gathered at the historic Brandenburg Gate
- Frankfurt: More than 1,500 attended a rally near the European Central Bank.
- Munich: Around 1,000 people attending the march
- Mainz: Police counted around 1,200 participants, situation "peaceful"
- Freiburg: Around 2,500 people attended, according to police.
Hundreds also gathered in Hamburg, Erfurt, Magdeburg, Dresden, Leipzig, Nuremberg, and elsehwere.
Retailers in several city centers had boarded up shop windows, particularly along luxury shopping streets, fearing unrest. Some shops were already closed for the Reformation Day public holiday.
No nationwide turnout figure was immediately available. More than 182,100 people had expressed interest in attending the events online.
Cologne police call off march over masks and pyrotechnics
Police in Cologne called off the planned "Gen Z regelt" procession after some participants covered their faces and used pyrotechnics.
"The demonstration will continue as a stationary rally," a police spokeswoman told the DPA news agency. Participants would remain on the Rhine riverbank, she said, appealing for restraint.
Attendance remained below the 15,000 people registered for the demonstration. Based on advance registrations, Cologne's protest was expected to be the largest in North Rhine-Westphalia.
Police respond to Stuttgart protesters trying to leave route
Police repeatedly stopped a youth protest march in Stuttgart, citing participants covering their faces and leaving the agreed route.
Officers also reported smoke devices and firecrackers before the procession began. "Be loud, but remain peaceful," a police spokeswoman urged in a video.
In other German cities, police reported a largely peaceful start to demonstrations. Authorities estimated included 2,500 participants in Freiburg, more than 1,500 in Frankfurt, 1,200 in Mainz, 1,000 in Munich and 650 in Berlin.
No nationwide turnout figure was immediately available.
Researcher warns against ignoring young protesters
Politicians must involve young people in decision-making or risk the youth turning away from political institutions, education researcher Nina Kolleck warned.
Their exclusion "creates the impression that there is a policy for the old, but not for the young," the University of Potsdam professor told Germany's RBB Inforadio.
Kolleck pointed to decades of underinvestment in schools and the disproportionate impact of climate change on younger generations.
She warned that populist parties could exploit the resulting political vacuum if young people's frustrations continued to go unanswered.
Youth protest organizers reject focus on violence warnings
Organizers of Germany's nationwide youth protests have accused the media of stoking fears of violence and distracting from their demands.
A "narrative of violence" was being used "to divert attention from our core demands," spokeswoman Veronika Dinter told the German broadcaster Deutschlandfunk.
She stressed that "GenZ regelt" — roughly meaning "Gen Z takes charge" — called for peaceful demonstrations, pointing to its published principles. Anyone who shared those principles was welcome, she said.
Dinter also regretted the decision by Germany's national school student representative body to distance itself from the protests. It had cited concerns including unclear organizational structures.
The initiative is holding rallies in Berlin, Cologne, Frankfurt and Munich, with local groups organizing protests in another 30 cities. Nearly 180,000 people had pledged online to attend, although actual turnout remained unclear.
Security authorities had warned that extremist groups could try to infiltrate the demonstrations.
What are the rules governing protests in Germany?
People in Germany have the fundamental right, enshrined in the constitution or Basic Law, to assemble in public provided they remains peaceful and are unarmed.
However, several states have adopted their own assembly acts, which means some of them have additional restrictions, such as a ban on protesting on highways in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia.
Notification generally necessary
Federal law itself imposes the obligation on organizers of protests to notify the local authority entrusted with approving public assemblies at least 48 hours before they invite people publicly to take part.
This aims to allow authorities to put in place security measures and to lessen the impact of any assembly on others by, for example, instigating traffic control measures.
Spontaneous assemblies are, however, also allowed in cases where a topical issue of urgent importance is at stake, and there is no notification requirement for indoor assemblies.
Protests or other assemblies can be banned beforehand or dispersed while they are underway, but this is considered a means of last resort.
Some locations are also subject to restrictions on protests, such as the area around the Reichstag building in Berlin where the German parliament sits, and around the Federal Constitutional Court in Karlsruhe.
Demonstrations around the Reichstag are, for example, permitted only when the parliament is not in session.
Germany no stranger to big protests
Post-war Germany has seen several massive demonstrations, including one in 1983, when 250,000 people — according to police estimates — gathered in the then West German capital, Bonn, to protest against the decision by NATO to station American nuclear missiles on German territory.
That was, however, surpassed in size by a protest in Berlin in 2003 against the invasion of Iraq by US-led forces, which drew a crowd of around half a million people.
There is some more detail on the law regarding the right of assembly in this DW article.
German 'Gen Z' protests set for cities across the country
Young people are to take part in demonstrations across Germany on Saturday, following the example of their peers in France and other countries who have been calling for better educational prospects and future opportunities.
In Germany, organizers said there is also to be a focus on rejecting military conscription and on demanding more protection for the climate as the Earth warms, with potentially catastrophic effects.
Saturday's protests are being called for by the youth initiative "Gen Z regelt" ("Gen Z sorts it") through a social media campaign
The group itself will directly organize four of the protests — in Berlin, Cologne, Frankfurt and Munich —, with associated demonstrations to take place in some 30 other cities.
It has explicitly called for peaceful protests without the violence that marred recent demonstrations in France.
Focus on security fears
This has not stopped several conservative politicians, notably from Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU), from warning that similar scenes could occur.
"Gen Z regelt" has, however, criticized what it sees as a wrong focus on the possibility of violence at the protests.
"It shows that our point about not being taken seriously or being heard is right. No one wants to work with us on the issues at stake but instead always put the topic of violence on the agenda," an organizer of the Munich protest told a press conference in Cologne.
However, other lawmakers have come out in support of the protests.
The leader of the parliamentary party of the Greens, Katharina Dröge, told the DPA news agency: "Young people are rightly furious because the federal government does not take their wishes seriously enough."
The Left Party leader, Luigi Pantisano, also said it was the right time for protests as the government mulls reforms of the nursing care and pensions systems, calling them "social cruelties."
"Gen Z" broadly refers to the generation born between 1997 and 2012.
France to see fresh cost-of-living protests
As Germany gears up for a day of mass youth protests, authorities in neighboring France are also bracing for new demonstrations on Saturday amid fears that the violence seen at October 17 rallies could repeat itself.
Some 70,000 police officers have been deployed to monitor around 150 protests across the country.
In recent weeks, protests by school pupils complaining about poor school conditions morphed into wider demonstrations on multiple issues, including the rising cost of living and social inequality.
On October 17 in particular, considerable violence occurred on the sidelines of mostly peaceful protests as extremists took the opportunity to plunder, riot and damage public property.
Welcome to our coverage
Young people in Germany are taking their lead from student protests in neighboring France to call for their opinions to be heard amid multiple challenges facing society.
As seen recently in France, organizers said they will be airing grievances about a perceived neglect of education but also calling for more social equality, less surveillance and measures to curb global warming.
Some politicians, in particular far-right leader Alice Weidel from the Alternative for Germany (AfD), have warned that the protests could attract violent extremists, but the organizers themselves have rejected any form of the violence that was seen occasionally in France.
Follow the protests as they unfold in some 34 cities across Germany.

At a press conference, Lavrov criticized the Europeans for their “arrogant boycott,” while praising the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump for its willingness to “engage with Moscow.”
Plans for the traditional group photo of G20 foreign ministers were scrapped after some European officials objected to being photographed alongside Lavrov, an AFP diplomatic source said.
A U.S. official said the group photo had been canceled to avoid allowing "a ceremonial photo opportunity to become a diplomatic distraction.”
The meeting in Atlanta, held just days before the U.S. midterm elections, is laying the groundwork for the G20 leaders’ summit scheduled to take place at President Trump’s resort in Miami in December.
Instead of a final declaration, the two-day talks are expected to conclude on Saturday with a summary report prepared by the United States.
As Ukrinform reported, President Volodymyr Zelensky said he was ready to travel to the G20 summit in Miami and meet Vladimir Putin if the United States invited the Kremlin leader to attend the forum.
In April, it became known that the United States planned to invite Putin to the G20 leaders’ summit, scheduled for December 14–15 in Miami.

The financial toll of the Iran war is mounting beyond battlefield losses, with hundreds of buildings at US military installations across the Middle East damaged in Iranian strikes, potentially adding billions of dollars to the cost of the conflict, the Wall Street Journal reported Friday.

The Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies estimated that rebuilding the damaged structures alone would cost more than $4 billion, excluding the replacement of equipment and systems inside the buildings.

These expenses come on top of the estimated $47.1 billion cost of the war as of Oct. 16, the report said.

Breadcrumb
Syria mulls joining Mecca defence pact, foreign minister says
Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani confirmed on Saturday that discussions are underway to assess Syria's potential membership of the Mecca Joint Defence Pact.
The Mecca pact, signed by Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan in the Muslim holy city on 7 August, outlines a joint defence agreement which stipulates that an attack on one member state will be considered an attack on all three.
Speaking at the Pillars of Regional Security event at the IISS Manama Dialogue 2026, Shaibani emphasised that the security of the Gulf is an "integral part of Syrian regional security", and that Damascus stands with the Gulf states and their people in confronting cross-border militias.
He added that Syria has experience in confronting militias that intervened in the country and contributed to plunging it into a devastating 14-year war, expressing the possibility of transferring this experience and strengthening regional cooperation and achieving stability.
The minister provided no further details about the ongoing talks to join the Mecca pact.
Shaibani also used his speech to condemn recent missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia, affirming Damascus' solidarity with its partners in confronting these attacks, while also rejecting the use of Syrian territory to threaten neighbouring states.
He also affirmed Syria's support for Yemen's internationally recognised government in restoring its sovereignty over the country.
On Israel, Shaibani said that Damascus' position on the occupied Golan Heights remains firm, pointing to UN Security Council Resolution 497, which rejects Israel's Golan Heights law and deems the annexation of the territory to be null and void under international law.
He highlighted that Syria has been subjected to more than a thousand Israeli attacks in less than two years, resulting in dozens of deaths, asking: "How can the demand for border control and weapons confiscation be reconciled with the fact that Syrian sovereignty is violated and targeted daily?", referring to Israel's stated justification for the attacks.
Since the signing of the Mecca pact, Saudi Arabia has come under attack from Yemen's Houthi rebels, which it has resumed fighting against in Yemen, and has reignited the civil war.
Pakistan and Turkey have not announced any attacks on the Iran-backed Houthis.

Ukraine news: Oleshky evacuees reach Kyiv-held territory

What you need to know

- Ukraine claims it hit a Russian plant producing solid fuel for rockets and missiles
- Kyiv also reports strikes on military depots in occupied Ukrainian territory
- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Istanbul for talks with Turkey's Recep Tayyip Erdogan
Here is a roundup of events from Russia's war in Ukraine on Saturday, October 31:
Zelenskyy in Istanbul for talks on Black Sea shipping
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has arrived in Istanbul for talks with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, with Black Sea shipping among the issues on the agenda.
"We're working to strengthen the protection of our people, our bilateral partnership with Türkiye, and real diplomatic prospects," Zelenskyy wrote on X, using the alternative spelling for Turkey.
The Ukrainian president also plans to meet Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew, the Istanbul-based Orthodox Christian leader.
US warns Russia of a 'mass casualty' plot to attack Moscow
The US embassy in Russia warned there was "a credible threat of a mass casualty event" at a historical site in southern Moscow.
"The US government is coordinating with appropriate Russian authorities on a response," the US embassy in Moscow said in a post on X.
The alleged plot would target the Tsaritsyno Museum Reserve, a sprawling complex of palaces and gardens built under the orders of Empress Cathrine the Great in the late 18th century.
Russia's federal law enforcement agency, the FSB, said it received the warning and was doing "appropriate work" in response to it, according to Russian news agencies.
Ukraine says it hit Russian rocket fuel factory
Ukraine's military said it struck a factory producing solid rocket fuel in Russia's Rostov region, setting a warehouse ablaze and damaging four production workshops.
The attack on the Kamensky plant in Kamensk-Shakhtinsky involved drones and Neptune missiles, according to the Ukrainian account.
The military said the plant supplies fuel for ammunition used by Russia's Uragan, Smerch and Tornado-S multiple-launch rocket systems, as well as other missiles and air-launched weapons.
Ukraine also reported strikes on four Russian military supply depots in occupied parts of the Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia and Luhansk regions.
The claims have not been independently verified.
Ukraine welcomes civilians from Oleshky after complex evacuation effort
First evacuees from the Russian-occupied Oleshky have reached Ukrainian-controlled territory amid a localized ceasefire.
Oleshky, near the front line in the southern Kherson region, has been occupied by Russia since 2022. In recent weeks, the town has faced a severe humanitarian crisis.
Both sides have recently agreed to a localized ceasefire to extract the estimated 2,000 civilians still in Oleshky, down from its pre-invasion population of 24,000.
Moscow and Kyiv credited the US first lady, Melania Trump, with brokering the truce.
Residents were given a choice to go to Russia or travel via Belarus to the part of Ukraine controlled by Kyiv.
 Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said the initiative required "an enormous amount of work."
He said evacuees included a one-year-old baby and a 94-year-old resident of Oleshky. The evacuees brought pets, including dogs, cats, a parrot and a raccoon, according to Lubinets.
He expressed hope that the Oleshky arrangement can be replicated elsewhere.
The truce started on Tuesday and is due to end on Sunday night.

World Insights: Lagarde's early exit raises questions over ECB independence, policy outlook
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
23:34:22 CST
00:34:22 KST

BERLIN, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- European Central Bank (ECB) President Christine Lagarde's decision to step down nearly nine months before the end of her term has sparked debate over the implications of her early departure and raised questions about the outlook for eurozone monetary policy.
The move comes as the eurozone faces renewed inflationary pressures, mounting fiscal strains and growing political uncertainty ahead of France's 2027 presidential election.
AN EARLY FAREWELL
The ECB announced Thursday that Lagarde, 70, would leave office on Feb. 7, 2027, ahead of the scheduled end of her eight-year term in late October.
A former French finance minister and head of the International Monetary Fund, Lagarde took over the ECB presidency from Mario Draghi in November 2019.
Her tenure has spanned a succession of crises, from the COVID-19 pandemic and the energy shock following the outbreak of the Russia-Ukraine conflict to record-high inflation and, more recently, renewed price pressures stemming from the conflict in the Middle East.
Under her leadership, the ECB launched an emergency asset purchase programme to stabilize financial markets during the pandemic. It later embarked on an aggressive tightening cycle, raising its deposit rate from minus 0.5 percent to a record 4 percent in just over a year to curb soaring inflation.
As inflation eased, the bank began cutting rates in June 2024, bringing the deposit rate down to 2 percent by June 2025. Lagarde also oversaw a review of the ECB's monetary policy strategy and advanced work on a digital euro.
French President Emmanuel Macron praised her leadership on Thursday and called for an orderly and balanced process to choose her successor.
THE POLITICS OF TIMING
Lagarde told a news conference Thursday that she wanted greater freedom to speak and engage on public issues beyond monetary policy. While the ECB's independence required its president to remain politically neutral, she said she no longer felt able to stay silent on broader international issues.
Much of the attention, however, has fallen on the timing of her departure and its political implications.
France is due to hold its presidential election in spring 2027. German public broadcaster ARD reported that Lagarde's early exit would allow Macron, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and other European leaders to agree on her successor before the vote, amid concerns that gains by France's far right or other eurosceptic forces could complicate the appointment process.
Marcel Fratzscher, head of the German Institute for Economic Research (DIW), welcomed the decision, saying that Lagarde had shown a strong sense of responsibility towards Europe and the ECB.
Clemens Fuest, president of the Munich-based ifo Institute, also said her departure would allow the ECB's top post to be filled before the French election, warning of a significant risk that radical candidates could win the vote.
However, Markus Ferber, a German member of the European Parliament, questioned whether the ECB was making itself dependent on election dates in member states despite its longstanding emphasis on independence, according to ARD.
Lagarde has not said that her decision was intended to influence the choice of her successor. Her early departure has nevertheless brought questions about the ECB's independence to the forefront of the succession debate.
AN OPEN RACE
Lagarde's announcement has brought forward the contest for one of Europe's most influential economic posts.
Former Dutch central bank governor Klaas Knot and Pablo Hernandez de Cos, the former Spanish central bank chief who now heads the Bank for International Settlements, are widely seen as leading contenders. European Investment Bank President Nadia Calvino, a former Spanish economy minister, has also been mentioned as a possible candidate.
Knot, a longtime participant in ECB policymaking, has traditionally been regarded as a monetary policy hawk, while Hernandez de Cos is seen as more moderate, with extensive experience in international financial cooperation.
Lagarde's departure also comes as several other senior ECB positions, including those of an Executive Board member and the bank's chief economist, are due to become vacant in the coming months. According to the Financial Times, European leaders may seek to negotiate the appointments as a package, taking into account national representation and differences over monetary policy.
The next ECB president will also inherit a difficult economic environment.
At its latest policy meeting Thursday, the ECB kept its three key interest rates unchanged, leaving the deposit rate at 2.5 percent after two increases this year. The bank warned that rising energy prices were adding to inflation risks while weighing on the outlook for economic growth.
The renewed energy shock from the Middle East conflict has left policymakers facing a difficult trade-off. If higher energy costs feed through into broader consumer prices and wages, the ECB may have to tighten monetary policy further. But weak growth and tighter financing conditions could make additional rate increases more costly for the economy.
Fiscal pressures in some member states add another challenge. In France, the eurozone's second-largest economy, a heavy public debt burden and rising government bond yields have heightened concerns about borrowing costs and the potential for financial market strains to spread across the currency bloc.
Despite these challenges, Holger Schmieding, chief economist at German private bank Berenberg, said the leadership change itself is unlikely to bring major shifts in ECB monetary policy. He noted that key decisions were typically reached by consensus in the Governing Council rather than made by the president alone.
Lagarde's successor will nevertheless have to contain renewed inflationary pressures without further weakening growth, while safeguarding the ECB's independence amid Europe's shifting political landscape. ■

NANJING, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- Amid deafening cheers and a sea of waving flags, China's Su Super League brought its second season to a close on Saturday, with Wuxi edging Changzhou 2-1 in the final before a crowd of 62,356 at Nanjing Olympic Sports Center.
Wuxi, unbeaten throughout the regular season, capped its dominant campaign by lifting the championship trophy, while the attendance set a new record for the tournament's final at the venue, surpassing the 62,329 spectators who watched last year's inaugural-season decider.
"The atmosphere was incredible. We chartered buses and traveled all the way from Wuxi to Nanjing to cheer for our home team," said Li Tao, a Wuxi supporter.
Fans from both Wuxi and Changzhou organized bus trips to the provincial capital, turning the final into a vibrant showcase of local pride and football fervor.
Drawing playful inspiration from both the English Premier League and the Chinese Super League, the Su Super League pits teams representing Jiangsu's 13 cities against one another. What began as a grassroots competition has evolved into a regional sporting phenomenon, fueled by fierce city rivalries, dramatic matches and packed stadiums.
The league kicked off in April and featured 91 matches this season. According to official figures, the 78 regular-season games attracted a cumulative 2.59 million spectators, up 22.17 percent from the previous year.
Demand for tickets remained intense throughout the campaign. The average success rate for ticket applications stood at just 9.6 percent, falling to 2.7 percent for the final.
The championship match also drew a star-studded supporting cast, with Olympic champions Zhang Yufei and Hao Ting, Asian Games champion Wu Mengjie, along with singers and celebrities, adding to the festive atmosphere.
Beyond the competition itself, the league has become a platform for grassroots football development and a catalyst for integrating sports with culture and tourism, helping local cities turn matchday excitement into economic activity.
Host cities have rolled out a range of incentives, including free admission to scenic attractions and discounts on accommodation and dining for fans presenting match tickets.
In Wuxi, the eight home matches this season generated 19.2 billion yuan (about 2.88 billion U.S. dollars) in total consumption across the city, up 5.9 percent year-on-year, according to local authorities.
For fans unable to secure a seat in the stadium, Jiangsu established more than 600 public viewing zones, transforming plazas and shopping malls into fan venues complete with giant screens, food stalls and crowds cheering every goal.
The Su Super League's success has also inspired a wave of grassroots football competitions across China, with more than a dozen regional amateur leagues emerging nationwide.
Earlier this month, the inaugural Northeast Super League final drew 63,259 spectators, setting a new attendance record for an amateur football match in China. ■

Yemeni army captures strategic mountain range from Houthis in Al-Jawf
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
15:30:08 UTC
00:30:08 KST

Mohammed Sami, Omer Asur Cuhadar, and Rania Abushamala
31 October 2026•Update: 31 October 2026
The Yemeni army has completed its capture of a strategic mountain range in the northern province of Al-Jawf following battles with Houthi forces, a field commander said Saturday.
Col. Rabie al-Qurashi, an army field commander in Al-Jawf, told Anadolu that government forces had secured the entire Huwayshian mountain range east of Al-Hazm, the provincial capital.
He said the advance followed fighting with the Houthis and was backed by warplanes that destroyed dozens of vehicles belonging to the group. The military operation remains underway, he added.
The mountains form the first line of defense for Al-Hazm, which remains under Houthi control, al-Qurashi said.
According to local Yemeni media, capturing the high ground enables government forces to cut Houthi supply routes in the province. The mountains also overlook key Houthi positions near Al-Hazm.
Government forces seized parts of the range during clashes Friday before completing their capture Saturday, according to an Anadolu correspondent.
Al-Jawf is strategically important as it borders Saudi Arabia and lies close to the Houthi-controlled provinces of Saada, Amran, and Sanaa. It also borders the oil-producing provinces of Hadramout and Marib, which are under government control.
Control of Al-Jawf remains divided, with the Houthis holding Al-Hazm and other areas, while government forces control other parts of the province. Both sides continue to contest strategic positions.
Yemeni strikes
Separately, the Yemeni army said it had carried out 1,119 strikes against the Houthis in recent hours, claiming to have “neutralized” 427 members of the group and destroyed or damaged 142 military vehicles, pieces of equipment and means of transport.
In a statement, the army said the strikes supported army units in advancing and capturing several strategic positions and heights on fronts in Al-Jawf province.
The army also reported continued fighting in the southwestern Taiz province, where its forces, backed by the Popular Resistance, targeted Houthi movements and reinforcements with air and artillery support.
The statement did not specify the exact period covered by the reported strikes.
Fighting has intensified in recent weeks as government-aligned forces backed by the Saudi-led coalition have carried out military operations against Houthi positions in Taiz and other provinces.
The escalation comes amid renewed hostilities between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia, with both sides reporting attacks and military operations across Yemen and the wider region.

INDIA bloc 'impeaches' CEC in mock Parliament, but what will it take to remove him for real?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
15:26:54 UTC
00:26:54 KST

NEW DELHI: The opposition on Saturday unanimously passed a "resolution" to remove Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls during a "mock Parliament" organised at Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge's residence.Former Lok Sabha Speaker Meira Kumar presided over the proceedings, with several MPs and activists supporting the demand for the CEC's removal.Kharge moved the resolution seeking Kumar's removal, accusing him of centralising control over electoral rolls and acting at the behest of Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Union home minister Amit Shah. Kharge also said that SIR was initiated to remove voters opposed to Bharatiya Janata Party."The proposal we are bringing today is to safeguard the dignity of a constitutional institution. We have no personal enmity with the CEC. Our intention is that the Election Commission should function impartially in keeping with the spirit of the Constitution," Kharge said."The trust of the common man in it should remain intact. No one sitting in Delhi should be able to wrongly delete the voting rights of weaker sections, women, and youth using a computer," he added.
Meanwhile, leader of opposition in Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi delivered the closing remarks of the proceedings, describing the event as the opposition's political weapon targeting CEC Gyanesh Kumar, PM Modi and Amit Shah."This looks like a meeting of Lok Sabha MPs, Rajya Sabha MPs, and common citizens. But actually, this is a political weapon," Rahul said.In the "mock Parliament" at Kharge's residence, the opposition sailed through the resolution with a voice vote. But while the numbers may have been on its side there, would the same motion stand a chance in the real Parliament?
What will it take to remove CEC Gyanesh Kumar for real
The removal of a CEC is deliberately difficult.Article 324(5) of the Constitution states that the Chief Election Commissioner can be removed from office only "in like manner and on the like grounds as a judge of the Supreme Court.""The other Election Commissioners shall not be removed from office except on the recommendation of the Chief Election Commissioner," it further says.
The CEC can be removed by the same procedure as a Supreme Court judge and requires a majority vote from both the Houses.
Article 124(4) of the Constitution, which lays down the procedure for removing a Supreme Court judge, states that a judge can be removed only by an order of the President following an address by each House of Parliament.Such an address must be supported by a majority of the total membership of that House and by a majority of at least two-thirds of members present and voting, in the same session, on the ground of proved misbehaviour or incapacity.The process begins with a notice of motion in either House of Parliament alleging misbehaviour or incapacity. The notice must be signed by at least 100 MPs in the Lok Sabha or 50 MPs in the Rajya Sabha.The presiding officer of the concerned House can admit or refuse the motion after considering the material and information available. If the motion is admitted, an inquiry is conducted into the charges by a committee constituted for the purpose.
If the charges are established, the motion must be passed by a majority of the total membership of each House and by a two-thirds majority of members present and voting in both Houses.Once both Houses pass the motion in accordance with these requirements, an address is made to the President, who then issues the order removing the CEC.The President's role at this stage is constitutional and formal once Parliament has passed the required address.Interestingly, this is not the first time when the opposition is gearing up for introducing a resolution seeking CEC's removal.On April 7, Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla and Rajya Sabha Chairperson CP Radhakrishnan had rejected opposition notice, which was signed by 130 Lok Sabha members, 63 Rajya Sabha members, seeking the CEC's removal over alleged partisanship and arbitrariness in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.
Rohitashwa Ranjan is a digital journalist with The Times of India, where he decodes Indian politics as a carefully staged production with scripts, subtext and everything behind. His stories track elections, party dynamics and the things that often are buried beneath the headlines. When not parsing vote shares or alliances, he is usually reading between the lines, where the real story tends to reside.
