Haunted, but hardly explored: India's untapped ghost-tourism economy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
14:36:47 UTC
23:36:47 KST

India’s haunted destinations offer an untapped tourism opportunity, with paranormal experiences yet to become a mainstream travel attraction. (AI-generated image)
India's ghosts have a customer service problem.There is almost an abundance of local places which have a reputation of being haunted in each and every state.There are ghost villages where nobody is quite sure why everyone left. Forts with stories of spirits walking through them at night. Abandoned cemeteries as old as the world wars, forgotten ‘havelis’ and stretches of forest that have acquired a mythology of their own.Out of all these only a few have become tourist attractions; others survive largely through word of mouth, local lore and the occasional paranormal investigation.India's haunted places do have an audience but it somehow lacks a concrete machinery that could make ‘dark’ tourism and ‘spectral’ cities central factions of an ever growing tourist economy.
The business of the macabre
The tourism industry has a name for this particular appetite for the unsettling: dark tourism. The term broadly describes travel to places associated with death, tragedy, violence and suffering.Ghost tours, haunted heritage walks and visits to places associated with paranormal folklore occupy a more specialised corner of this spectrum, where history, local legend and the promise of an eerie experience often intersect.
It is an appetite that the tourism industry has increasingly tried to package. Turning a city's darker history into something you can book online. And its most ideal form, the ticket buys you a completely immersive tour full of storytelling with a slight hope of encountering your first paranormal spirit.
The commercial potential of dark tourism is reflected in the market estimates. Grand View Research valued the global dark tourism market at $31.8 billion in 2023 and projects it to reach $34.2 billion in 2026 and $38.6 billion by 2030, growing at a compound annual growth rate of 2.9%. MR puts the market at $32 billion in 2025, forecasting it to reach $46.8 billion by 2036.The market for ghost tourism as a separate entity is estimated to be worth $2.9 billion in 2025 and projects it to grow to $5.7 billion by 2034, at a CAGR of 7.8%, by Dataintelo. Its estimate includes guided ghost walks, cemetery and underground tours, paranormal investigations, haunted stays and virtual experiences.For India, the more immediate question may be less about capturing a share of a global market and more about whether these scattered attractions can be turned into viable profitable local experiences. With a history as rich as ours, the ghosts are not in short supply. The challenge is to turn them into profitable experiences that people can discover, book and pay for, while ensuring that the tragedy is respected and the communities living alongside these places have a stake in the business.
From a haunted reputation to a tourism product
Kuldhara, a site that Rajasthan Tourism itself promotes as a “ghost village shrouded in mystery”, is a good starting point. The official government site describes its history as a prosperous settlement abandoned in the early 19th century. The account recounts the popular legend involving the village headman's daughter and the powerful minister Salim Singh, while also identifying the ruins as a protected monument under the state archaeology department.The village, around 17km from Jaisalmer, already has the ingredients of a tourism attraction, but having a story and having a well-managed visitor experience are two different things.There are multiple accounts of litter around the site, including discarded plastic and food packaging. How can an atmosphere feel haunted when the landscape is strewn with chips and tobacco packets?And cleanliness isn’t the only issue. Talking to two people who visited the site, the common experience has been mismanaged and under researched tour which leaves most customers underwhelmed at the end of the day.
Bhangarh, in Alwar district, is often described as one of India's most haunted places. Rajasthan Tourism itself recounts the two popular legends attached to the site: one involving the ascetic Baba Balu Nath, whose warning about the shadow of the fort was allegedly ignored, and another about a sorcerer whose failed attempt to enchant Princess Ratnavati supposedly led him to curse the town.The legends have become part of the destination's appeal, drawing visitors to its ruined temples, palaces and deserted marketplace. The restriction on entry before sunrise and after sunset, imposed at the site, has only added to its mystique. But tourists who visit the site have also called it unorganised, speaking to TOI they noted that the guide also was not entirely accurate about the historical aspects of the site and the site itself needed to have better management.
The business of making a place come alive
There are already attempts to package India's haunted heritage into guided experiences. Delhi Tourism lists Haunted Heritage Walks at Malcha Mahal and Feroz Shah Kotla Monument, each lasting around 90 minutes and available on weekends on group demand. The official booking page lists a minimum group size of six and a tariff of Rs 800 plus GST per person.The Ministry of Tourism's Utsav portal has also listed a Haunted Walk at Bhuli Bhatiyari, organised by Delhi-based Enroute Indian History. The listing describes a guided heritage walk through the old hunting lodge, combining its history with the legends associated with the site.Enroute Indian History, which has been conducting the experience for around two to three years, says the walks attract a good number of bookings and are designed for adventure seekers as much as for history enthusiasts. The operator says it takes care to keep the historical information accurate, while folklore and supernatural accounts are presented as stories rather than fact-checked historical claims. This distinction is central to the format: visitors are offered a combination of documented history, local legends and the possibility of an unsettling experience.These initiatives complicate the idea that haunted tourism in India is entirely informal or absent. There are government-backed products and private operators working in the space. The question is whether they have developed the consistency, visibility and scale needed to make haunted experiences a dependable part of a destination's tourism economy.
Ghost is only part of the experience
Detailing her experience to TOI, Kriti notes that she remembers the underground setting of the haunted heritage walk she took in Edinburgh as much as the stories themselves. The interactive displays and historical details provided by the guide gave the experience a sense of depth that a conventional ghost walk might not have offered.A ghost tour can take several forms, the attraction lies as much in how visitors encounter the story as in the story itself.A 2020 study published in Cornell Hospitality Quarterly, titled Paranormal Tourism: Market Study of a Novel and Interactive Approach to Space Activation and Monetization, makes this case through examples from the United States and elsewhere. It describes how destinations such as New Orleans combine ghost stories with local histories and cultural associations, while Salem packages its reputation around witches and ghosts. These places do not necessarily sell a standalone encounter with the paranormal; they draw on identities and histories that visitors may already associate with them.The study talks in detail about Eastern State Penitentiary in Philadelphia, a former prison that closed in 1971 and subsequently fell into disuse. Limited group tours began in 1988 as part of efforts to preserve the site. A Halloween fundraiser followed in 1991, eventually developing into the annual attraction Terror Behind the Walls. By 1994, the former prison was also offering daily historical tours to generate income for preservation, followed by museum exhibits and a broader marketing campaign.The study also points to the role of participation in making these experiences engaging. The experience can continue beyond the visit itself, with reviews, photographs and word of mouth helping to draw in new audiences.
Research into British ghost walks suggests that the appeal is not necessarily dependent on visitors believing in ghosts. An ethnographic study of 14 tours across Edinburgh, York, London and Brighton found that guides use a combination of storytelling, performance and the physical environment to make history tangible.For India, that distinction could be important. A haunted experience need not rely on sensational claims. It can be built around the history of a place, the folklore that has accumulated around it and the atmosphere of encountering that story on location.
Local community cannot remain part of the backdrop
The opportunity, however, is not simply to make India's haunted sites more theatrical or commercially attractive. It is also to ensure that the people and places behind the stories are not left out of the value chain.A 2023 qualitative study of local perceptions in Kuldhara, based on 25 interviews with residents and people working in the area, found that respondents saw several economic opportunities in developing mystery and paranormal tourism. Some respondents also pointed to existing livelihood opportunities linked to visitors, including guiding, transport and the sale of local crafts.The study also recorded expectations around the restoration and preservation of the village, alongside concerns about the role of government and private bodies in developing the destination. While it offers a glimpse of how residents view the possibilities of mystery tourism, it does not quantify how much income currently reaches the community or how widely those benefits are distributed.The concerns are not unique to haunted destinations. A 2026 study of tourism in Uttarakhand, while not focused specifically on ghost tourism, raises wider questions about the state's tourism economy. It argues for stronger community participation, local supply chains, training and livelihood diversification.These concerns are relevant when considering how niche tourism experiences might develop in the hills. A haunted walk could create work for local storytellers, drivers, homestays, food vendors and artisans. But those benefits are not automatic. If an outside operator controls the bookings, supplies the guides and takes most of the revenue, the local community may remain little more than a feature of the landscape.The challenge is to move beyond treating local legends as raw material that can be packaged elsewhere. Residents may be the custodians of oral histories, but they should also have a stake in how those histories are interpreted and monetised.
India does not need to manufacture a haunted history. What it needs is a way to bring those stories to visitors without reducing them to cheap thrills or leaving the people who have preserved them out of the business.The real test of India's haunted tourism economy will not be how many people it can convince that a place is haunted, but how many people it can persuade to stay, listen, and explore.The ghosts, after all, have been doing their bit for the tourism industry for years. It is time someone took care of the guests.
Prisha Patnaik is a journalist with The Times of India, writing across geopolitics, international affairs, culture, history and internet culture. With over two years of experience in social media and digital content, she is interested in how news, politics and culture are shaped for digital audiences. She holds a master’s degree in Media and Communications from Goldsmiths, University of London.

First the radars, then the rest: Iran's methodical assault on US bases
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
14:36:26 UTC
23:36:26 KST

Iran's campaign against American military bases across the Middle East began with a calculated assault on the systems designed to detect incoming missiles and drones, before expanding to aircraft, hangars, warehouses and troop facilities, according to an Associated Press investigation that reveals extensive damage to the U.S. military's regional infrastructure.
An analysis of satellite imagery, corroborated by interviews with four regional officials familiar with the damage, found that more than 115 drone and missile strikes claimed by Iran or Iranian-backed militias had damaged or destroyed structures at 26 military bases and other sites housing American equipment through August. The strikes caused billions of dollars in equipment damage and forced significant changes to the U.S. military's deployment across the region.
Two regional officials told the AP that Washington has moved substantial military assets out of the Persian Gulf, including aircraft, air defense systems, communications equipment and other essential infrastructure. The findings raise questions about the vulnerability of America's regional bases as President Donald Trump considers renewed military action against Iran after the November 3 midterm elections, with Tehran threatening a major response.
The investigation offers a more detailed picture of the damage than the U.S. government has publicly disclosed during the eight-month conflict. From April through June alone, hundreds of buildings and other structures were damaged or destroyed. U.S. Central Command, which oversees American military operations in the Middle East, has repeatedly declined to provide detailed assessments, citing operational security, and did not comment on the AP's findings. Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell maintained that American forces remained adequately protected and fully equipped to continue operations against Iran.
Iran's first targets: the eyes of US air defenses
The sequence of attacks reveals a deliberate pattern. Rather than immediately concentrating on barracks and other buildings, Iranian forces initially targeted the radar systems responsible for detecting and tracking incoming threats. Within the first two days of the war in late February, strikes destroyed protective enclosures around American radar installations at Camp Arifjan in Kuwait and Naval Support Activity Bahrain. Portable radars at Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia and Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan were also hit.
Among the most consequential losses was a radar in Jordan reported to have been destroyed. According to manufacturer Raytheon, the U.S. Army possesses only 13 of these specialized systems worldwide, with budget documents indicating that each costs approximately $500 million. Another radar in Qatar sustained extensive damage, although investigators could not determine whether it had been destroyed. The system had been purchased as part of a $1.1 billion agreement in 2013 and appeared to be the only one of its kind in the region.
N.R. Jenzen-Jones, director of the technical intelligence consultancy Armament Research Services, said the attacks appeared designed to weaken the ability of American and allied forces to respond to subsequent strikes. By targeting expensive, difficult-to-replace early-warning equipment, Iran was striking at a critical component of the regional air defense network.
Once the initial radar attacks had been carried out, Iranian forces broadened their targets. During the first month of fighting, more than 50 successful strikes hit 18 locations containing American military equipment, with particular attention paid to areas housing aircraft. The targets eventually expanded to include fuel storage facilities, communications infrastructure, warehouses and troop accommodations.
Kuwait's bases take the heaviest damage
Kuwait suffered the greatest concentration of Iranian attacks, although American installations in Bahrain, Iraq, Jordan, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates were also hit. At Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait, at least 30 strikes damaged or destroyed 15 aircraft hangars, numerous warehouses and 10 buildings near a residential area.
Camp Buehring, another major American installation in Kuwait, sustained particularly widespread destruction. Most of its aircraft hangars were rendered inoperable, while facilities used by troops suffered extensive damage. The base's gym was destroyed in March, a store serving personnel was hit in late July, and strikes also severely damaged a garage and dining facility, according to regional officials familiar with the attacks.
The scale of destruction became clearer only months later, when high-resolution satellite images became available. Between early March and late August, more than 30 structures at Camp Buehring were damaged or destroyed. The AP identified multiple strikes on the installation during March, April, May and July.
Kuwait was also the site of the deadliest known Iranian attack on American troops during the war. On March 1, six U.S. service members were killed when a drone struck Port Shuaiba, underscoring that the attacks threatened personnel as well as expensive military equipment.
Other countries sustained significant losses. At Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia, an Iranian strike damaged the rear section of a Boeing E-3 Sentry airborne surveillance aircraft. A regional military official who visited the installation described extensive destruction, including damaged barracks, dining halls and scattered debris. The official said several other aircraft had also been hit, including two aerial refueling tankers. Another Iranian strike damaged a CIA unit at the U.S. Embassy in Riyadh.
At Al Dhafra Air Base, approximately 20 miles (32 kilometers) south of Abu Dhabi, repeated attacks early in the conflict damaged aircraft hangars, other infrastructure and equipment, including an early-warning radar and surveillance drones. A Congressional Research Service report updated in October identified 15 American aircraft damaged at regional bases.
Satellite restrictions concealed the extent of damage
Assessing the destruction has been complicated by restrictions on commercial satellite imagery. Major providers holding U.S. government contracts blocked or delayed the public release of images following requests from American officials, sometimes citing national security concerns. This limited independent scrutiny of damaged installations, with some high-resolution images becoming available only months after the attacks.
To complete its investigation, the AP obtained imagery from OneAtlas, a satellite service owned by Airbus, and compared it with other available evidence. The resulting assessment provides a broader picture of the damage than previous official disclosures, including reports from the Pentagon's inspector general, although the military has not released a comprehensive public accounting of the losses.
The findings also highlight a broader problem confronting modern militaries: the growing vulnerability of large, fixed installations to sustained attacks involving relatively inexpensive drones and missiles. Raphael Cohen, director of the National Security Program at the RAND School of Public Policy, said even heavily equipped military forces are increasingly exposed to such threats.
"This should be a wake-up call for the United States," Cohen said.
With Washington and Tehran both leaving open the possibility of renewed fighting, further damage could deepen the uncertainty surrounding America's long-term military presence in the Persian Gulf. It remains unclear whether the United States will rebuild its damaged bases and equipment once the war ends or fundamentally rethink how its forces are positioned and protected.
For Cohen, the destruction points to a lasting shift in military strategy. The era in which American forces could depend on large, permanent bases as relatively secure platforms for operations, he argued, may be coming to an end.

‘Opportunities for agricultural cooperation with Africa available’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
14:35:47 UTC
23:35:47 KST

‘Opportunities for agricultural cooperation with Africa available’
TEHRAN- Iran’s Minister of Agriculture, Gholamreza Nouri Ghezeljeh, addressed the First National Meeting on Iran-Africa Agricultural Cooperation, stressing that opportunities for joint agricultural cooperation with Africa are available and must be converted into concrete, operational, and lasting economic ties.
The meeting was attended by ambassadors, economic counselors, honorary consuls, officials from executive bodies, economic associations, entrepreneurs, investors, and more than 200 economic actors. The minister said this broad participation provided a valuable opportunity to translate the political will for expanding Iran-Africa relations into specific projects and durable economic partnerships.
Nouri Ghezeljeh thanked the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Permanent Secretariat of the Iran-Africa Cooperation Summit, and the Ministry of Agriculture for organizing the event. He said Iran’s approach to international cooperation is based on mutual respect, avoidance of unilateralism, opposition to aggression and political pressure, and recognition of the right of all nations to peace, development, and sustainable access to food. He stressed that food and people’s livelihoods must not become tools of political pressure, and that achieving food security requires cooperation, trust, and constructive interaction among countries. This, he said, should be a foundational principle for developing agricultural relations between Iran and African countries.
The minister outlined a clear message: Iran-Africa agricultural cooperation must move from introducing capacities to defining projects; from memoranda of understanding to executive contracts; and from sporadic exchanges to sustainable partnerships in production, technology, and trade. He emphasized that Iran does not view Africa merely as a market for selling goods or as a source for supplying needed products. Rather, Iran regards African countries as important partners for investment, joint production, and creating mutual economic benefits.
Nouri Ghezeljeh linked agriculture to food security, knowledge, and economic development. He argued that food security is not simply about increasing production, but about ensuring people’s sustainable access to sufficient, healthy, high-quality, and reasonably priced food. He described water and soil, seeds and inputs, production knowledge and technology, storage, transportation, and trade as interconnected links in a single chain. Weakening any link, he warned, can undermine efforts to increase production. He also pointed to complementary capacities between Iran and African countries. Iran has strengths in irrigation and water and soil management, greenhouse production, agricultural machinery, seeds, livestock and poultry breeding, vaccines and veterinary products, fisheries, processing industries, and specialized training. African countries, according to their climatic and economic conditions, have considerable capacities in crop production, tropical products, animal husbandry, fisheries, and expanding markets. Linking these capabilities can increase productivity, create jobs, and raise value added on both sides.
The minister further identified removing executive obstacles and strengthening communication among responsible institutions as a fourth priority. He said economic actors need clear procedures, reliable transportation, practical payment mechanisms, insurance and investment coverage, and predictable regulations to enter sustainable cooperation. On tariffs and trade facilitation, he called for examining the capacity of bilateral agreements and regional mechanisms with the participation of relevant bodies. He also stressed continuous follow-up: the problems of each project must be clearly identified and recorded, a responsible body must be designated, and progress must be assessed within clear time frames.
Nouri Ghezeljeh emphasized that the government should act as a facilitator while the private sector should be the driver of economic cooperation. Embassies and economic counselors, he said, can play an effective role in identifying credible opportunities, introducing reliable partners, explaining market regulations, facilitating communication among enterprises, and following up on executive obstacles. In contrast, the private sector must play a central role in defining projects and assessing them commercially and operationally. Within the Ministry of Agriculture, the Office of International Affairs, together with specialized organizations, deputies, and private-sector associations, is responsible for the secretariat of six joint Iran-Africa cooperation commissions and more than 10 joint agricultural committees with African countries. He said the goal is not to create new and numerous mechanisms, but to use existing capacities effectively, clarify responsibilities, and prevent negotiations from stalling at the stage of administrative correspondence.
The minister asked economic actors to present proposals in the form of specific and executive plans. Each plan, he said, should clearly determine the subject of cooperation, the proposed partner, the target market, required capital, legal requirements, timetable, and evaluation indicators. He urged avoiding scattered programs and suggested starting with a few limited, well-considered, and implementable projects rather than a long list of aspirations. For each project, a clear contact point on both sides, a time schedule, and a follow-up mechanism should be designated so that successful cooperation can be expanded after initial results are evaluated.
Nouri Ghezeljeh announced that the Fourth Iran-Africa Cooperation Summit will be held next month, and that the FIDC event will take place in Senegal. He expressed hope that Iran’s private sector and agricultural economic actors will participate effectively in these programs. He said the Islamic Republic of Iran seeks cooperation based on trust, respect, and mutual interests. In agriculture, these principles should lead to more sustainable production, more balanced trade, more job opportunities, knowledge transfer, and more reliable access by people to healthy and sufficient food. He stressed that success should not be measured by the number of meetings or documents signed, but by implemented contracts, projects that produce results, value added created, and benefits that ultimately reach producers and the people. The meeting, he said, should be the starting point for practical cooperation—a stage in which knowledge becomes production, production reaches markets, and friendly relations become lasting economic ties.
On political and security developments, the minister said that when Iran was attacked by Israel and the United States, some abroad welcomed it and others expected further developments. What occurred instead, he said, was Iran’s resistance, the country’s steadfastness, the people’s courage, and the continuation of government services. Addressing ambassadors, he said that despite wartime conditions, government services in various areas, including food security and the supply of public necessities, continued, and needed goods were supplied abundantly, so that wartime conditions were not felt in meeting basic needs. He criticized US actions internationally, saying the world is heavily affected by US warmongering and that the energy and food sectors face major challenges and crises. According to official statistics in some countries, food prices have risen by up to 23 percent, and poor and vulnerable groups suffer most. He said Iran and other countries have been affected by these consequences and expressed hope that the United States would take a rational path and return to the Islamabad Memorandum to pave the way for ending the war as quickly as possible, given its pressure on economies, nutrition, and global food security, especially in poor countries.
Finally, Nouri Ghezeljeh urged participants to engage actively in the specialized panels on the sidelines of the meeting, saying these panels can move cooperation from speeches and negotiations to the operational stage. He expressed hope that, with the companionship of ambassadors, the efforts of economic actors, the support of responsible institutions, and equal participation of African countries, the ground would be prepared for sustainable agricultural cooperation. He said the hoped-for results include increased food security, economic prosperity, development of shared opportunities, and stronger lasting friendship between the Iranian nation and African countries.

Iran FM says US outreach a ‘positive step’ as delegation in Qatar for talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
14:31:37 UTC
23:31:37 KST

Iran FM says US outreach a ‘positive step’ as delegation in Qatar for talks
Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi tells Al Jazeera Tehran doesn’t rule out attack, is ‘prepared for all scenarios’.
Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says a United States effort to open dialogue with Tehran is “a positive step”, but that there are currently no plans for meetings with US officials regarding the eight-month-old war.
Speaking to Al Jazeera on Saturday, Araghchi said Iran had studied a letter sent by US Vice President JD Vance in high-level meetings, and set out Tehran’s conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, which he said would pave the way for renewed negotiations with Washington.
He added that an Iranian delegation has travelled to Doha, a day after Qatari mediators were in Tehran in an apparent bid to negotiate a revival of the US-Iran ceasefire. Araghchi said one of his aides is in Qatar to continue consultations.
“The American side’s attempt to open the door to dialogue and understanding more broadly is a positive step,” the foreign minister told Al Jazeera.
However, he warned: “If Washington’s goal in sending this letter is to stir up discord, it would be yet another mistake to add to its previous ones.”
‘No need to meet with the Americans’
Araghchi played down talk of upcoming meetings between the two sides.
“What is being circulated in this regard is merely media speculation,” he said.
“We see no need to meet with the Americans at this stage. Our conditions are clear, and mediators are continuing their consultations regarding them,” he added.
Araghchi said whether Iran would hold direct or indirect talks with the US depended on Tehran’s conditions being met.
“Mediators have presented proposals concerning the nuclear dossier, which we are currently reviewing as part of the second phase,” he said.
“Qatari and Pakistani mediators are continuing consultations regarding our conditions,” he said.
Rouzbeh Parsi, an Iran analyst and affiliated researcher at Lund University’s Department of History and Human Rights Studies, told Al Jazeera that any progress in Friday’s talks in Tehran was most likely on “the sequencing of the first steps needed to establish the barest of trust – without which further bolder steps are not possible”.
Conditions for Hormuz
Araghchi said talks with Qatari mediators had shortened the time needed to implement Iran’s proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
“The Qatari side proposed shortening the implementation period of the Iranian proposal to five days. We have reached a proposal at this stage that reduces the implementation period to two days,” he said.
“Our conditions include lifting the sanctions imposed following the Islamabad memorandum and reducing US forces in the region,” he said, adding, “We demand the restoration of oil waivers and the release of all our frozen funds, including those held in Qatar.”
Iran is also demanding recognition of shipping routes through the strait that it had discussed with Oman, and the closure of other routes, he said.
Al Jazeera’s Resul Serdar Atas, reporting from Tehran, said there was “no remarkable flexibility in Iran’s position”, with Tehran insisting on the same demands while negotiations continue.
Under a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) signed between the US and Iran in June, Washington guaranteed the oil waivers and said there would be no further restrictions on Iranian oil exports, Atas said. But when the MoU collapsed months later, the US cancelled all the waivers.
Tehran is also still insisting on the release of its frozen assets, including $6bn held in Qatar, and on the lifting of sanctions, not only those on its energy and nuclear file, but also those imposed since the MoU collapsed, which are putting huge pressure on Iran’s economy, he said.
The US, for its part, wants Iran to reopen the strait, and both sides want their demands met on the ground, not only on paper, Atas added.
‘Prepared for all scenarios’
In his remarks to Al Jazeera, Araghchi said his country does not rule out the possibility of an attack against Iran.
“We are prepared for all scenarios,” he said. “We have upgraded our weaponry, addressed our vulnerabilities, and tested new arms. Our forces are at the highest level of readiness.”
This comes as Iran’s armed forces chief of staff, Major-General Ali Abdollahi, said in a statement on Saturday that Iran would respond to any attack with “immense force”, with no geographical limits, and that it would decide when any new war ends.
Abdollahi said Iran was acting on Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei’s orders.
“We have a new stockpile of enemy targets and assets, and they are on our agenda,” he said. “America and Israel will face an unimaginable response, and we are the ones who will determine the end of any new war.”
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told a press conference on Saturday that President Donald Trump has not yet made a decision on whether to resume military action against Iran. He added that he did not know whether there was a specific timeframe for Qatar-led talks aimed at resolving hostilities.
Abbas Khamayar, a former Iranian diplomat, told Al Jazeera he expects the current situation to hold until next week’s US midterm elections.

Turkey nominates former foreign minister Sinirlioglu as UN chief
Turkey has nominated its former foreign minister and UN ambassador Feridun Hadi Sinirlioglu for the position of UN secretary-general, state-media reported on Saturday. The submission was officially backed by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan who has been particularly vocal in calling for reform of the UN Security Council.
Turkey has officially nominated a former foreign minister and yearslong ambassador to the United Nations for the next UN secretary-general, state-run media reported Saturday.
The next UN chief will succeed Antonio Guterres, who has led the world body for almost 10 years. The organisation is under pressure to reform as it finds itself sidelined in wars in Iran, Ukraine and Gaza while also facing a financial crisis that has forced major cuts to humanitarian and development programs.
Feridun Sinirlioglu, a 70-year-old former Turkish foreign minister and UN diplomat, had floated his candidacy on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly’s high-level meeting in New York last month.
Read moreEmirati diplomat could become next UN chief despite human rights concerns
Sinirlioglu was Turkey's top diplomat for a few months in 2015, an interim period between elections, and its UN ambassador between 2016 and 2023. He currently serves as the secretary-general of the Vienna-based Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe. His current three-year mandate is scheduled to end in December 2027, but the top UN job would have a January 1 start date.
Ahmet Yildiz, Turkey’s current representative to the UN, told the Anadolu news agency that Sinirlioglu's name was officially submitted with backing from Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
Erdogan has been vocal in calling for reform of the UN Security Council, especially criticizing the dominance of its five permanent members. Sinirlioglu is likely to reflect the president’s agenda.
The next UN secretary-general will be decided by the 15-nation UN Security Council, especially its five veto-wielding members – the United States, Russia, China, Britain and France. The 193-member General Assembly must give final approval.
Read moreWho are the eight candidates running to succeed Antonio Guterres as UN chief?
Sinirlioglu will likely face obstacles from several corners, including Turkey's neighbor Greece, which is one of the 10 elected members of the Security Council. Pushback also would be expected from Israel, a close ally of the US.
Seven other candidates are vying to replace Guterres as he finishes his second five-year term. Under an informal regional rotation of the UN’s top job, a candidate from the Latin American and Caribbean region could be selected.

====================================================================================================

The great Indian railway upgrade: How much has really changed for passengers?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
14:21:33 UTC
23:21:33 KST

Bigger stations, better trains: Is the passenger experience keeping pace?
NEW DELHI: New trains, redeveloped stations and upgraded infrastructure are changing the face of Indian Railways. But has the passenger experience changed at the same pace?For millions of people who depend on the network every day, the real test of modernisation begins well beyond a station's new facade or a train's sleek exterior. It lies in whether platforms are manageable, toilets are clean, drinking water is safe, coaches are well maintained and trains arrive on time.While the Railways has invested heavily in modernisation, government audits continue to flag gaps in basic passenger amenities, onboard cleanliness and maintenance. The contrast raises a larger question: Is Indian Railways building a more modern network without doing enough to improve the everyday journey?The challenge now is to ensure that the transformation is felt not just in the infrastructure passengers see, but in the quality of service they experience.
A makeover on a massive scale
The Amrit Bharat Station Scheme is among the most visible parts of the railway modernisation drive. Under the scheme, 1,337 stations had been identified for redevelopment by December 2025, with work completed at 155 stations at that point, according to the ministry of railways. The programme envisages improvements to station buildings, waiting halls, toilets, seating, drinking-water facilities, platforms, foot overbridges, lifts, escalators and passenger information systems.
From station facelifts to faster trains: Inside Indian Railways' makeover
The plan also seeks to improve access to stations, connect them better with the surrounding city and integrate different modes of transport. Facilities for passengers with disabilities and spaces for local products under the One Station One Product initiative are part of the wider approach. The idea is to make stations more accessible and useful, rather than treat redevelopment as a cosmetic exercise alone.The scale of the programme matters in a network where stations serve very different kinds of traffic. A major city terminal may need to handle large crowds, multiple platforms and complex interchange movements. A smaller station may need reliable drinking water, sufficient seating, accessible toilets and a safe way to cross between platforms. A uniform-looking makeover cannot substitute for facilities suited to the number and needs of passengers using each station.Redevelopment also has to take place while trains continue to run. Railway minister Ashwini Vaishnaw has cited the difficulty of carrying out major construction without shutting down busy stations. Work near operational tracks, shifting utilities, statutory clearances and restrictions imposed to protect passengers and train movements can all affect project schedules.That is a reminder that infrastructure transformation takes time. It also raises a separate question: While construction continues, how effectively are existing facilities being maintained?
New trains, new expectations
The train itself is another important part of the modernisation story. Vande Bharat has become the most recognisable symbol of a more contemporary railway experience, with modern coaches, improved passenger amenities and a focus on faster intercity travel.The demand for these services has been substantial. The ministry of railways said nearly 3.98 crore passengers travelled on Vande Bharat Express services in 2025-26, up from 2.97 crore in 2024-25, an increase of about 34%. Since its introduction, the service had carried more than 9.1 crore passengers through approximately one lakh trips, according to a ministry statement issued in April 2026.The appeal is understandable. Modern coaches, comfortable seating and onboard amenities can make a long journey less tiring. Faster services can also help passengers who travel regularly for work, education, business or family commitments. The introduction of a sleeper version in January 2026 extended the modern-train push to overnight travel. In its first three months, the sleeper service carried 1.21 lakh passengers over 119 trips, with reported occupancy exceeding 100%.A railway official, speaking to TOI on condition of anonymity, said the introduction of newer trains was part of a broader effort to improve passenger facilities.“New trains such as Vande Bharat and Amrit Bharat are being introduced using push-pull technology, offering passengers improved facilities. The work undertaken over the past few years is gradually beginning to show results,” the official said.These figures indicate that passengers are willing to use newer services when they offer a compelling travel option. But the success of a premium service should not become the sole measure of progress across a network that serves passengers with widely differing budgets and travel needs.For a family travelling in a reserved sleeper coach, the condition of the toilets and availability of water may matter as much as the train's design. For an unreserved passenger, access to a platform without dangerous crowding may be the more immediate concern. For someone travelling with an elderly relative, working lifts and clear signage can make the difference between a manageable journey and a stressful one.The next phase of modernisation must therefore be about raising the baseline across the network, not just creating pockets of premium travel.
The basic amenities test
A Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) audit provides a sobering measure of the gap between infrastructure ambitions and everyday facilities. Its Report No. 31 of 2026, tabled in Parliament on August 12, examined passenger amenities and sanitation at non-suburban railway stations. Of the 512 stations covered, 458 had deficiencies in one or more essential passenger amenities.According to the CAG report, the deficiencies involved basic facilities such as toilets, urinals and drinking water. The audit also found E. coli contamination in water samples collected from coolers at eight locations, raising concerns about the safety of drinking water available to passengers.
Railway modernisation vs ground reality: The widening passenger amenities gap
These findings matter because the usefulness of a facility depends on more than its installation. A water cooler may appear on a station's list of amenities, but it serves little purpose if the water is unsafe or the equipment is not maintained. A newly built toilet is not a meaningful improvement if it is dirty, lacks water or is routinely out of order.The distinction between providing an amenity and delivering a functioning service is central to the passenger experience. Construction can be measured through expenditure, project completion and the number of facilities created. Maintenance is less dramatic, but it determines whether passengers can actually use those facilities on a particular day.The CAG findings do not mean every station performs poorly, nor do they erase the benefits of redevelopment. They point instead to unevenness across the network. The task is to ensure that passengers do not have to depend on a station's size, location or level of visibility to access basic services.
Cleanliness does not end at the platform
The problem extends from stations to the trains themselves. A separate CAG audit on cleanliness and sanitation in long-distance trains, covering the period from 2018-19 to 2022-23, found that more than 40% of surveyed passengers were dissatisfied with toilet cleanliness, while over half expressed dissatisfaction with onboard housekeeping.The survey covered 2,426 passengers across 96 selected trains. The audit identified issues including dirty lavatories, choked washbasins, waterlogging and unclean vestibules. It also found that 366 passengers, or about 15% of those surveyed, reported a lack of water in toilets or washbasins. More than one lakh complaints about water shortages in train toilets and washbasins were registered through Rail Madad in 2022-23.The audit also highlighted shortcomings in the deployment of cleaning staff and equipment, as well as gaps in monitoring and enforcement of contractual obligations. It mentioned that 89% of complaints related to toilet cleanliness were addressed within the stipulated timeframe. That points to a system capable of responding to complaints, but also to the need to reduce the conditions that generate them in the first place.The railway official said bio-toilets had played an important role in the effort to improve sanitation, but maintenance and passenger awareness remained challenges.“Indian Railways has taken extensive measures to improve cleanliness, with bio-toilets playing an important role in this effort. However, the key challenge lies in their adequate maintenance, due to which problems continue to arise. Lack of awareness among passengers also contributes to sanitation-related issues,” the official said.“Although the Railways is working to spread awareness through advertisements and other means, a change in public attitude towards cleanliness is still needed,” the official added.A complaint mechanism is essential. Yet a passenger should not have to repeatedly report a choked toilet or an empty water tank for routine services to be delivered. Onboard housekeeping, water refilling and regular inspections need to work as part of normal railway operations, not only after a problem has been flagged.Cleanliness is not a minor comfort issue. It affects dignity, health and the willingness of passengers to trust the service. A train can have modern coaches and advanced safety features, but if the washroom becomes unusable halfway through a long journey, the experience quickly falls short of the promise.
Punctuality: Progress, but not the whole picture
Reliability is another test of whether the passenger experience is keeping pace with infrastructure investment. A faster train is useful only if its schedule is dependable, while an upgraded station cannot compensate for a journey that routinely runs late.The ministry of railways reported that punctuality improved from 73.62% in 2023-24 to 77.12% in 2024-25, reaching 77.24% in 2025-26 up to February 2026. The ministry said the network operates around 25,000 trains a day and attributed delays to a range of factors, including fog, track and route constraints, maintenance, signalling issues, agitations and other unforeseen events.The improvement is significant, but the latest figure also shows that punctuality remains a work in progress. Railway operations involve a vast network in which a disruption in one section can affect services elsewhere. Track maintenance, signalling upgrades and other work may be necessary to improve long-term reliability, even when they cause short-term inconvenience.The railway official said the growing demand for passenger trains had put pressure on punctuality, and that infrastructure upgrades were being undertaken to address the issue.“To address this, the Railways has started operating dedicated freight corridors or undertaken work on them to provide separate tracks for goods trains. The Delhi-Mumbai Dedicated Freight Corridor is a key example,” the official said.“Major stations are also undergoing remodelling and interlocking work to reduce additional halts and delays for trains. Sections with heavy traffic are being converted to automatic signalling systems,” the official added.The official said fog and mist also affected train operations by reducing visibility. “To address this, fog signal devices have been installed in locomotives. In addition, the Railways is installing the advanced Kavach system, which not only helps improve punctuality but also plays an important role in ensuring train safety,” the official said.For passengers, however, the experience is immediate. A late train can mean a missed connection, a longer wait at a station or an uncertain arrival time. Better information about delays and platform changes can ease some of that burden, but communication cannot replace reliable operations.More dependable schedules, clear announcements, accurate digital information and prompt assistance during disruptions are as important to many travellers as the design of the coach.
Crowds are an infrastructure problem, too
Crowd management has become another part of the passenger experience that cannot be separated from station design. Wider foot overbridges, holding areas, better access points and clearer passenger information can help manage movement, but they need to be matched to actual footfall and train capacity.The New Delhi railway station witnessed a stampede in February 2025 that killed at least 18 people.In March 2026, the railway ministry announced plans for permanent holding areas at 76 identified stations, alongside measures including access control, wider foot overbridges and technology-assisted monitoring. The ministry also referred to additional ticketing facilities, drinking-water arrangements and separate toilets at New Delhi Railway Station.The railway official said satellite stations were being developed in large and industrial cities to reduce pressure on major stations during periods of heavy passenger movement.“In large and industrial cities, where passenger footfall rises sharply during holidays and other occasions, the Railways has started developing satellite stations to reduce the pressure on major stations,” the official said.
Vande Bharat sees 34% rise in passengers: Is the network ready for more?
The official also referred to the Train on Demand initiative, particularly services with high-capacity unreserved coaches, to accommodate more passengers through fewer trains.Such measures recognise that a station is not simply a building through which passengers pass. It is a space where thousands of people may arrive at the same time, often carrying luggage, travelling with children or trying to reach a platform minutes before departure.But crowd management cannot depend on temporary arrangements alone. It also requires better coordination between train schedules, platform allocation, ticketing, station staff and the movement of people inside and outside the premises. The test is whether a passenger can reach the right platform safely and without confusion, particularly during holiday rushes, festivals and other peak periods.A station's success should not be judged only by its appearance when relatively empty. Its real test comes when several trains arrive close together and thousands of passengers have to move through the same spaces.
From construction to service delivery
The larger question facing Indian Railways is how to turn a massive modernisation programme into a consistently better everyday service. The answer lies partly in investment, but also in maintenance, staffing, monitoring and accountability.The government has committed substantial resources to passenger amenities. In December 2025, the ministry said an allocation of Rs 12,118 crore had been made under the customer amenities budget head for 2025-26, with Rs 7,253 crore spent up to October that year. Such spending can create the physical conditions for better journeys. Whether it produces lasting improvement depends on how effectively facilities are operated and maintained.There is no single measure that captures the passenger experience. Station redevelopment figures tell us how much work has been undertaken. New-train numbers indicate the expansion of services. Punctuality statistics measure one aspect of reliability. Audit findings reveal whether basic facilities meet the expected standard. Together, they offer a more complete picture than any one headline figure.A meaningful assessment would ask how many station amenities remain functional, whether drinking water is safe, how often toilets are cleaned, whether complaints are resolved promptly, and how consistently trains run to schedule. It would also compare performance across stations and railway zones, so that strong results in one area do not conceal persistent gaps elsewhere.Indian Railways has good reason to invest in bigger stations, modern trains and improved infrastructure. For a country of India's size, rail travel remains essential to mobility, livelihoods and social connection. The scale of the network makes the task difficult, but it also makes the quality of everyday service especially important.
The next measure of progress should be visible not just in the station's new facade or the train's sleek exterior, but in the ordinary details of a journey: A clean washroom, safe water, a working lift, a manageable platform and a train that arrives when expected.

Syria considering entry into Mecca defence pact, says foreign minister

Syria considering entry into Mecca defence pact, says foreign minister
Damascus ‘evaluating’ whether to join the alliance that binds Turkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan.
Syria’s government is weighing whether to enter into a mutual defence pact with Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan, the country’s top diplomat says.
“Discussions are currently under way to evaluate Syria’s entry into the Mecca alliance,” Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani said at the Manama Dialogue conference in Bahrain on Saturday.
The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement was signed by Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan in the Saudi city of Mecca in August. It states that an attack on one country is to be considered an attack on all three, and has been compared to the NATO security alliance that binds the United States, Canada and 30 European countries.
Saudi Arabia, under heavy fire from Yemen’s Houthis, is a key backer of Syria’s government led by President Ahmed al-Sharaa, which came to power after the fall of former strongman Bashar al-Assad in December 2024.
Under the Mecca pact, Pakistan and Turkiye have pledged military support to Riyadh as it faces escalating attacks from the Iran-backed group. However, neither Islamabad nor Ankara has yet announced any attacks on the Houthis.
Government officials in Turkiye, where the pact’s ratification process is ongoing, have said any future military support for Riyadh would not include deploying Turkish troops to fight in Yemen or attack the Houthis.
Speaking at the conference in Bahrain, al-Shaibani said Damascus was an “integral” part of regional security and would support any framework aimed at protecting regional stability.
The minister stressed that the region was “in greater need than ever” of developing joint deterrence and defence systems.
He said Syria backs the efforts of Yemen’s Saudi-backed internationally recognised government to restore “sovereignty and stability across its entire territory” as it battles the Houthis, Syrian state media reported.
He also urged all parties to support the unity and sovereignty of states.
Separately, the minister said Israel has carried out more than 1,000 attacks on Syria in less than two years, killing dozens of people.
“How can calls for border control and placing weapons exclusively under state control be justified while Syrian sovereignty is violated and targeted on a daily basis?” he asked.

When Shimon Peres went treasure hunting for lost German WWI gold
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
14:18:17 UTC
23:18:17 KST

What could a German treasure and a chicken farmer from central Israel possibly have in common? In 1964, the answer appeared on the front page of Yedioth Ahronoth. Between reports on political infighting within the ruling Mapai party and the Olympic Games in Tokyo, readers encountered a headline that sounded as though it belonged on the cover of an adventure novel: "Document revealing German gold treasure held by Ness Ziona poultry farmer."
The farmer was Moshe Sakshidlek, a Holocaust survivor described by people in his community as "an honest and modest man." He had shown the newspaper two documents retrieved from a secret hiding place. 
The first was a hand-drawn map, colored with pencils and marked at a scale of 1:800,000. The second was a yellowed sheet of paper containing instructions typed on a German typewriter. Together, they supposedly identified the location of a hidden fortune near the Israeli-Syrian border, buried beneath the grave of a man who had never actually been buried there. It was the beginning of an extraordinary mystery that would attract soldiers, politicians, treasure hunters and entire families, each with a different idea of where the fortune had gone.
A friend from driving school
The story began in Germany in 1945, shortly after Sakshidlek was liberated from a concentration camp. He met a German man in his 70s who operated a driving school and enrolled for lessons. Between driving sessions, the two struck up a friendship. The elderly German was living in poverty, and Sakshidlek shared the food parcels and cigarettes he received from the American Jewish Joint Distribution Committee, commonly known as the Joint. In 1948, when the German learned that his Jewish friend was preparing to immigrate to Israel, he entrusted him with two documents and an extraordinary story from his own past, when he had served as a German army paymaster in Ottoman-ruled Palestine during World War I.
In the autumn of 1918, the Ottoman-German front in Palestine was collapsing. British forces under Gen. Edmund Allenby advanced on Nazareth, where a major German headquarters was located. They nearly captured the German commander, Liman von Sanders, who, according to a well-known account, escaped wearing his pajamas. At the last moment, a convoy of vehicles slipped out of Nazareth under cover of darkness. British cavalry attacked, killing most of the men. Only one vehicle managed to escape, carrying three German officers who had been ordered to protect their cargo at all costs.
Inside were four crates containing 200 kilograms (about 440 pounds) of gold coins, valued at 20,000 Turkish pounds. The money had reportedly been intended for bribes to local tribes. One of the three officers was the paymaster who would, decades later, open a driving school in Germany. The three men buried the crates in a deserted location, about 60 centimeters (2 feet) below ground. Each took roughly 20 kilograms of gold coins for himself, and they continued toward Damascus. A few kilometers later, British cavalry attacked again. Two of the officers were killed.
This is where the story begins to resemble an Indiana Jones movie rather than a conventional wartime account. The surviving paymaster hid for several days before returning to the scene of the attack, hoping to retrieve the gold left on his comrades' bodies. He found the bodies, but the coins had vanished. He dragged his dead companions back to the buried treasure and interred them nearby, placing crosses above their graves and carving their names into stones.
Then came the deception that supposedly protected the treasure for decades. The officer thrust his rifle into the ground directly above the buried crates and placed another stone there, this one engraved with his own name. To anyone discovering the site, it would appear to be the grave of a third German officer. There would be no reason to suspect that a fortune was hidden beneath it. The yellowed instructions were remarkably specific: Ten paces east of the camel caravan trail, approximately three kilometers north of the remains of the burned vehicles.
Eventually, the paymaster was captured by the British. The prevailing assumption was that Bedouins had stolen the gold and murdered the men guarding it. The officer changed his name, returned to Germany and waited for an opportunity to retrieve his treasure. But the Nazis came to power before he could return. An anti-Nazi activist, he was arrested by the SS and spent World War II in a concentration camp. After the war, he opened his driving school, where he met Sakshidlek. And so the secret of a lost World War I fortune passed from one concentration camp survivor to another.
Sakshidlek immigrated to Israel in 1949 and immediately encountered a problem: The treasure was on the wrong side of the border. In 1954, he wrote to David Ben-Gurion, Israel's prime minister, and received a surprisingly swift response. Shimon Peres, then director-general of the Defense Ministry, personally traveled to Ness Ziona to examine the documents. According to Sakshidlek, Peres was enthusiastic and asked for permission to photograph the map. But Sakshidlek refused, demanding a government guarantee that he would receive a fair share of the treasure if it was ever recovered. The negotiations went nowhere. The treasure, the 1964 newspaper article concluded, had been "waiting 46 years for someone to claim it."
A second map, a different hiding place
Thirty years later, in 1994, Yedioth Ahronoth's 7 Days magazine returned to the mystery, publishing information collected by Haviv Knaan, a former police officer under the British Mandate and a journalist for the Haaretz newspaper who had spent nearly half a century investigating the affair. His research presented an entirely different version. According to Knaan's findings, there had been not one hidden cache but two.
In the autumn of 1918, a German military engineering company was stationed near Jenin, in what is now the northern West Bank. When British artillery began shelling the area, four crates of gold were loaded onto a mule cart. A German sergeant major was ordered to transport them to Nazareth. His party came under attack, leaving him alone. He hid the crates in a hollow he discovered in the mountains. Meanwhile, the Germans concealed the remainder of their gold inside a tunnel at their military camp and then blew up the entrance. A mule cart instead of a motor vehicle. Jenin instead of the Syrian border. A hollow in the mountains instead of a false grave. The same legendary treasure now had two completely different maps.
Knaan also discovered that Sakshidlek was far from the first person to search for the missing fortune. In 1924, a group of young Germans sought permission to erect a memorial to soldiers who had fallen near Jenin. The British authorities noticed that the Germans were having considerable difficulty "deciding" where to place the monument. In the meantime, they were digging exploratory holes across extensive stretches of land. In 1933, a British man named White Thompson, a relative of the German sergeant major, wrote a letter marked "private and confidential" to the British foreign secretary. His question was simple: "To whom will the treasure be handed over, or how will it be divided, when it is found?"
The British high commissioner in Jerusalem responded with a dry observation that searches for the treasure had already been conducted in the Jenin district, and none had met with much success. That same year, a German baron named von Bolschwing, a member of the Nazi Party, arrived with a French woman who had secured an excavation permit. They found what they believed to be the remains of the demolished tunnel. Years later, the baron wrote to Knaan about his journey: "I traveled by car through Prague, Budapest, Belgrade, Sofia, Istanbul, Ankara, Iskenderun, Beirut, Damascus, Nazareth, Jenin..." Instead of gold, however, he found something rather less valuable: "A hole in the ground near Jenin, with a hyena living in it."
Beeping metal detectors in Sheikh Abreik
The 1994 article prompted readers to send in their own memories of the hunt. One letter came from Naftali Raz of Tel Aviv's Tzahala neighborhood. He recalled that in 1949 he was serving as a technical officer in the Israeli military's Signal Corps when a friend, Lt. Col. Zvi Ben-Yaakov, asked him to obtain a mine detector. There was no mine detector available, but Raz managed to find a sensitive metal detector.
Ben-Yaakov told him that a reliable source had revealed where the German gold had been buried in 1918. A few days later, a group of officers set off for the hills of Sheikh Abreik, armed with digging tools, a diagram and considerable enthusiasm. "Every now and then, the device would beep, and the guys would eagerly rush in with their digging tools," Raz recalled. "We found old, crumbling cans and barrels."
The search was hardly confined to military officers. That same year, villagers from the Tulkarm area joined young men from Baqa al-Gharbiyye in a search near the village of Dinaba. Armed with a metal detector, they dug so extensively into one hill that it was eventually described as looking "like Swiss cheese." The gold, however, remained elusive.
The grandmothers of Yafia
But the 1994 investigation also produced a story that turned the entire treasure hunt on its head. It was covered in another article in 7 Days. Michel Shehadeh, an earthworks contractor from Yafia, a village near Nazareth, had a simple explanation for why generations of treasure hunters had failed. "Everyone can keep looking for the gold for another hundred years," he said, "because it all arrived here long ago."
Shehadeh had heard the story from his two grandmothers. In the autumn of 1918, as the Ottoman-German army retreated, residents of Yafia descended into the Jezreel Valley to see what the departing soldiers had left behind. Among them was Habib Khoury, a milk merchant and one of only two people in the village who knew how to read. In the valley, the villagers came across a mule cart loaded with crates. The others were afraid to approach it, suspecting that the boxes contained ammunition. Khoury read the writing on the crates and began leading the cart back toward the village.
Other families were said to have taken part in the haul. The Abu Nasser family of Nazareth reportedly took a cart of their own. When British soldiers arrived to search the area, family members threw the gold into a well in their courtyard. The Shamshum family allegedly hid coins in flowerpots, but neighbors informed on them. "Apart from a terrible beating," Shehadeh's mother recalled, "Shamshum got nothing." Habib Khoury, meanwhile, supposedly became so wealthy that by the 1920s he was known as "the merchant of Palestine."
His son, Muin Khoury, then 77, initially denied the story before offering a correction. "It wasn't gold," he said. "It was Turkish coins, mejidies." Had the family been wealthy before 1918? "No, no. My father sold milk to the Turks, and we weren't rich."
The investigation also led to the courtyard of the Abu Nasser family in Nazareth, where the site of the old well could still be seen. The well itself had been filled with stones years earlier. An elderly member of the family was sitting on the porch, but she was reluctant to discuss the treasure. "There used to be a gate for carts here, and a courtyard for sheep, and a well," she said. "And the well had water in it, not gold. I don't know anything about the gold."
Then she stood up and went back inside.

US to deport 150 Afghan immigrants back to Afghanistan: US media
Unknown

2026-10-31

Breadcrumb
US to deport 150 Afghan immigrants back to Afghanistan: US media
President Donald Trump's administration plans to deport more than 150 Afghan immigrants back to Afghanistan via Pakistan, US media reported Friday, a move advocacy groups say could endanger their lives.
Trump last year issued travel bans for a number of countries, including Afghanistan, as part of a broad immigration crackdown, and sought to end deportation protections for Afghans, some of whom were granted special immigrant visas following the August 2021 takeover by Taliban authorities.
More than 150 Afghan immigrants are expected to be deported in the latest push, The New York Times reported, citing three unnamed US officials, and the first flight could leave as soon as Monday.
Among those expected to be deported are relatives of Afghans who assisted the US military in the country prior to the fall of Kabul, according to AfghanEvac, a group seeking to help former Afghan allies.
While the United States cannot arrange deportations directly to Afghanistan, the officials told the Times that Pakistan will oversee their expulsion to Afghanistan.
Pakistan's government earlier this year ordered law enforcement nationwide to arrest Afghan citizens without visas as part of a years-long repatriation policy that has pushed back millions of Afghans who fled their homes after the Taliban returned to power.
Relations between Pakistan and Afghanistan have been fraught since the Taliban authorities took power in 2021, and worsened after deadly border clashes last October that led to near-total closure of the border.
Clashes subsided after mediation, but the conflict intensified again in February, with Pakistan declaring "an open war" on its neighbor.
Pakistan accuses Afghanistan of harboring militants responsible for deadly attacks on its territory, an allegation the Taliban government in Afghanistan denies.
"America is about to put Afghans on a plane to the Taliban, and the administration is doing it the week the country goes to vote, hoping no one is watching," AfghanEvac President Shawn VanDiver said in a statement, referring to the US midterm elections on Tuesday.
VanDiver said some of the migrants facing removal "are the brothers and sons of men who served alongside US forces, families the Taliban already has every reason to target."
"Whatever path brought them here, the danger waiting for them is the same."
After regaining power, Taliban authorities announced a general amnesty for Afghans who worked with Western-backed forces and governments.
However, the United Nations has recorded reports of extrajudicial killings, detentions and abuses.

Pentagon facing up to $15 bn in Iran war base damages – WSJ
Iranian missile and drone strikes have inflicted up to $15 billion in damage on military installations hosting American forces across the Middle East, the Wall Street Journal reported on Friday, citing sources and its own satellite imagery analysis. The massive destruction adds to the Pentagon’s mounting war bill, which has already reached nearly $50 billion.
The newspaper’s analysis identified a total of 274 damaged structures across 24 installations with an American military presence. At least 119 buildings at 13 installations were damaged in the opening two weeks alone; the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet headquarters in Bahrain was among the hardest hit. Tehran launched a retaliatory wave of strikes following the unprovoked US-Israeli attack which started the conflict on February 28.
An unnamed US official familiar with the matter told the WSJ that the Pentagon estimated damage to bases from Iranian strikes – which became increasingly precise as the conflict escalated – at a minimum of $5 billion. Another WSJ source suggested that the number could potentially be as high as $15 billion.
Many installations are shared with Washington’s regional allies, meaning they could potentially pay for some of the damage, the report says, adding that the Pentagon may elect not to restore some infrastructure at all.
In particular, Washington is reportedly considering pulling back from its installations in Kuwait and Saudi Arabia so that its personnel would be out of reach. Tehran has previously demanded a full-scale US military withdrawal from the region as a prerequisite for sustainable peace.
Iran, meanwhile, has been rapidly restoring missile facilities and recovering buried weapons stockpiles, the report adds, noting that the military build-up comes as US President Donald Trump is considering further strikes despite shortages in American interceptor inventories.
However, US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has been dismissive about Tehran’s military potential, saying in August that “They still have some capabilities, but it’s nowhere near what it was at all.”
Meanwhile, Democratic Senator Chris Murphy, a member of the Foreign Relations Committee and the Senate Appropriations Subcommittee on Defense, accused the administration of seeking to “mask the true cost of the war” after being denied access to Qatar’s Al Udeid Air Base, where the WSJ identified at least a dozen damaged buildings. The Pentagon said that the ban was due to regional travel restrictions.
According to the Pentagon’s latest estimate provided to Congress, the Iran war has cost $47.1 billion through October 16, excluding base damage. The figure includes roughly $29 billion to replace expended munitions, $11.9 billion in operational expenses, and $6.1 billion in equipment losses.
As for the casualties, the US military now acknowledges 23 deaths linked to Iran war operations, including 11 from enemy fire, and 865 wounded.
