Study finds the “bowing effect” on attractiveness is cultural, not universal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
14:00:42 UTC
23:00:42 KST

People in Japan tend to view a face as more attractive when the person performs a traditional bow, and this boost occurs regardless of the individual’s racial appearance. Observers in the United States, on the other hand, show little or no reaction to bowing, suggesting that cultural habits rather than universal body language explain the effect. The findings, published in Japanese Psychological Research, provide evidence that social etiquette can shape how aesthetic qualities are judged.
Bowing is a physical gesture that involves lowering the head and bending the upper body forward. In Japan, it serves as a customary greeting used to show respect, express gratitude, or offer an apology. The gesture can range from a slight fifteen-degree tilt when greeting someone in passing to a thirty-degree bow of respect for a senior colleague, or a deep forty-five-degree bend reserved for heartfelt apologies or profound thanks.
The research, led by Takayuki Osugi of Yamagata University, builds on earlier findings showing that tilting an image forward to simulate a bow increases perceived facial attractiveness among Japanese raters. Psychologists suggest that this reaction occurs because bowing activates cognitive schemas, which are mental frameworks that organize knowledge and expectations. In this context, the gesture triggers cultural associations with politeness and submissiveness, or non-threatening social deference. In Japanese society, these traits encourage a favorable overall impression that spills over into aesthetic judgments, a pattern known as a halo effect.
In related work, an experiment exploring head orientation found that downward head tilts increased perceived femininity and attractiveness for female faces, whereas upward tilts increased perceived masculinity. That earlier work examined vertical head motion as an evolutionary cue related to physical height and biological sex differences. In contrast, Osugi and his team approached bowing as an intentional, culturally learned greeting intended to communicate social respect.
One competing explanation holds that lowering the head is a universal signal of submission, observed across non-human primates, which would predict that bowing boosts attractiveness in any culture. Testing American observers offered a way to distinguish that account from a culturally specific one. In addition, past studies on the bowing effect relied almost entirely on East Asian faces shown to Japanese observers. Because the raters and the faces shared the same ethnic background, it was difficult to tell whether the boost occurred because the gesture was culturally familiar or because people were observing members of their own group.
To investigate, the researchers developed three-dimensional computer-generated models representing four racial appearances: East Asian, European, South Asian, and African. Both male and female models in their twenties were created with varied hairstyles and everyday clothing. In an initial setup phase, independent groups of Japanese volunteers rated the static appearance of these faces on a scale from 0 (unattractive) to 100 (attractive) so the team could select models with average baseline attractiveness scores of roughly 42 points.
Experiment 1 focused on Japanese participants recruited through an online crowdsourcing platform. Across six sub-experiments, each testing different combinations of model gender and race, between 45 and 49 participants evaluated faces under three movement conditions: a 1.5-second long bow, an immediate short bow, and a static upright control condition. About half of the Japanese participants took part in more than one sub-experiment, though the sub-experiments ran intermittently over roughly three years. A follow-up analysis accounting for repeated participation produced the same pattern of results.
Japanese observers consistently awarded higher facial attractiveness ratings to bowing models than to standing-still models across all sub-experiments. For instance, when rating female European models, the average score was 43.2 for the static condition, 51.1 for the short bow, and 59.0 for the long bow. Across the different model types, scores rose by roughly 6 to 12 points for short bows and 15 to 28 points for long bows compared to static faces. Across all tests, holding the bow longer produced higher ratings than a brief bow, and the interaction between the motion condition and the model’s racial appearance was not statistically significant.
In Experiment 2, the researchers presented the identical video sequences and rating tasks to American participants recruited through Amazon Mechanical Turk. Between 30 and 40 American participants completed each sub-experiment. Participant overlap was minimal in this group, ranging from just one to seven participants across sub-experiments.
American participants showed minimal change in their attractiveness ratings when models bowed. Some differences did reach statistical significance, but the gaps were small, typically under three points on the 100-point scale, compared with gains of 15 points or more among Japanese raters. In female European model tests, for example, American ratings averaged 56.5 for the static pose, 57.4 for the short bow, and 56.9 for the long bow. A direct statistical comparison between the two national samples confirmed that the attractiveness boost from bowing was robust among Japanese participants but essentially absent among American participants.
The authors then conducted Experiments 3 and 4 to test whether the bowing effect generalizes across different levels of baseline physical attractiveness. These follow-up experiments also addressed a potential confound: all initial attractiveness ratings had been completed by Japanese university students, leaving it uncertain whether American raters would judge the facial aesthetics of the models similarly. In Experiment 3, 49 Japanese participants evaluated female East Asian models and 48 evaluated male East Asian models, with faces categorized as either distinctly attractive (averaging around 55 to 58 points) or less attractive (averaging around 28 to 30 points).
Bowing increased attractiveness scores for both attractive and less attractive faces among Japanese raters. For less attractive female models, scores rose from 33.3 when standing still to 42.0 for a short bow and 49.0 for a long bow. For highly attractive female models, scores rose from 48.0 when standing still to 54.3 for a short bow and 62.7 for a long bow. Holding the bow longer produced a steady enhancement regardless of baseline looks, though a brief bow provided a slightly smaller relative lift to already attractive faces.
To evaluate American aesthetic perceptions and task engagement, Experiment 4 presented the same high- and low-attractiveness models to 35 American participants for female models and 32 for male models. The participants easily distinguished between the two tiers, giving high-attractiveness female models an average score around 65 points and low-attractiveness models around 44 to 45 points. Within each tier, bowing motion produced almost no change in ratings, and though a small overall effect of motion appeared for male models, no individual comparison held up after correction. These results indicate that American viewers were paying close attention and evaluating facial aesthetics normally, yet simply did not factor the bowing motion into their judgments.
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these findings. The researchers did not record how much exposure individual American participants had previously had to Japanese culture, anime, or travel. While some participants might have had passing familiarity with bowing etiquette, measuring this background would likely have highlighted the cultural divide even further.
The authors also did not collect race-related demographic information from the American sample, meaning future studies will need to examine whether an observer’s own racial background interacts with the racial appearance of the bowing person. Additionally, participants completed the tasks on their personal computers, so screen size, resolution, and viewing distance were not standardized. Live interpersonal encounters also involve vocal tone, body posture nuances, and spontaneous eye contact that digital avatars on computer monitors cannot capture.
The study, “Effect of Bowing on Facial Attractiveness of Other Races,” was authored by Takayuki Osugi and Jun I. Kawahara.

Iran have also secured two bronze medals at the championships, with Rahman Amouzad finishing third in the 65kg division and Hassan Yazdani winning bronze in the 97kg category.
The 2026 World Wrestling Championships are being held in Astana, Kazakhstan, from Oct. 24 to Nov. 1.

Somali pirates hijack Iranian fishing vessel

2026-10-31
13:55:56 UTC
22:55:56 KST

Breadcrumb
Somali pirates hijack Iranian fishing vessel
Armed pirates have hijacked an Iranian fishing boat off the northeastern Somali coast, the European Union Naval Force and security sources in Puntland said on Saturday.
Somali piracy has seen a resurgence, with at least 15 attacks reported since April, the highest number since 2013.
The vessel, named Azini, was seized at 0900 GMT on October 29 off the Somali coast, between the coastal towns of Bandar Beyla and Xaafun in the semi-autonomous region of Puntland, according to an alert from the EU's Maritime Security Centre Indian Ocean (MSCIO).
AFP news agency reported, citing Puntland security officials that the hijacking was conducted by eight gunmen from a remote coastal area near Bandar Beyla carried out the attack.
"There were two Somali guards on-board but they were outnumbered and overpowered by the pirates," a security official said adding: "They were fishing close to shore, which made them vulnerable to a hijacking."
A second security source said 21 crew members, excluding the two Somali guards, were aboard, while the MSCIO did not specify the number, saying their safety was "unknown".
Four more gunmen later boarded the vessel, bringing the total number of pirates aboard to 12, security officials said.
"After they took the fishing boat, they went further out to sea," a Puntland security official said.
Azini is the third Iranian fishing boat to have been hijacked off the Somali coast since July.
The MSCIO warned that the vessel could be used as a "mothership" to carry out "further piracy attacks".

Eight provinces have been affected: Haut-Uele, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Bas-Uele, Tshopo, South Ubangi and North Ubangi.
The outbreak is the second-largest globally, after the 2014–2016 epidemic in West Africa.
Call for stronger measures
The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) called on Friday for stronger measures to protect frontline workers after two young Congolese doctors died from Ebola earlier in the week in North Kivu and Ituri provinces.
Gaps in early detection and contact tracing remain among the main obstacles to stopping transmission, according to health authorities.
Only about 12 percent of confirmed cases have been identified among previously known contacts, while many deaths have occurred in communities, authorities said.

Mayon, famed for its near-perfect conical shape, is one of the Philippines' most active volcanoes and has a long history of explosive eruptions that have triggered mass evacuations. ■

China's "porcelain capital" wins Global Award for Sustainable Development in Cities
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
21:51:04 CST
22:51:04 KST

FUZHOU, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- The global observance of 2026 World Cities Day was held on Saturday in east China's Fuzhou, with five cities, including China's "porcelain capital" Jingdezhen, honored with the fourth-cycle Global Award for Sustainable Development in Cities, also known as the Shanghai Award.
The event runs from Oct. 31 to Nov. 2. Apart from Jingdezhen, the other four recipients of the Shanghai Award, which recognizes cities for achievements in sustainable urban development, are Addis Ababa in Ethiopia, Santiago de Cali in Colombia, Istanbul in Türkiye, and Katowice in Poland.
The event brings together senior United Nations officials alongside representatives from national governments, local authorities, international organizations, academic institutions, the private sector, and community networks to share best practices and advance practical solutions to common urban challenges.
In December 2013, the 68th United Nations General Assembly adopted a resolution designating Oct. 31 as World Cities Day starting in 2014. It was the first international day proposed by the Chinese government at the United Nations.
Ceramic culture has long been an ideal medium for cross-civilization dialogue. As a cornerstone commodity of the ancient Silk Road, Jingdezhen porcelain was a defining cultural symbol, through which the world came to know China and China reached out to the world.
Building on this legacy, Jingdezhen has embraced a model of development that combines cultural preservation with creative renewal. Former porcelain factories have been reimagined as cultural and creative districts, old streets are lined with ceramic-themed installations, and historic neighborhoods have been carefully preserved and revitalized.
The city is home to more than 3,200 inheritors of intangible cultural heritage in ceramic craftsmanship. It has also been named in the UNESCO Creative Cities Network as a City of Crafts and Folk Art.
Jingdezhen's recognition is just one example of China's broader urban renewal efforts.
Urban renewal also holds huge potential for investment and consumption. China has set a target of renovating 1,500 old streets and factory compounds from 2026 to 2030, bringing in new industries and business models to inject fresh momentum into urban development.
"Converting old streets and factory sites into cultural and creative districts drives growth in dining, retail and entertainment," said Yan Yuejin, deputy director of the E-house China R&D Institute. ■

China Focus: Xinjiang's past and present: weighty monographs present authentic regional history
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
21:50:55 CST
22:50:55 KST

URUMQI, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- A set of books covering the general and religious histories of northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region has been praised as a landmark cultural achievement and an academic bulwark against hostile propaganda and misconceptions about the region.
Since a September launch in Beijing, libraries across Xinjiang have listed the two books as authoritative sources, while the works also drew significant attention at a major book fair in the region's Hotan Prefecture.
Compiled over more than two years by the Xinjiang Academy of Social Sciences, the books present an authentic history of Xinjiang, spanning from the Paleolithic Age to the present. Experts and scholars have praised the set of books as a comprehensive work of historical research on Xinjiang and a significant cultural project.
Wu Yiqun, dean of the School of History at Xinjiang University, said the monographs draw on solid historical materials to correct misconceptions, presenting robust academic theories based on rigorous research to build academic agreement on the subject.
The books, as primary source material, will play a key role in clarifying matters and building consensus in college and university teaching and research, Wu added.
To guarantee the books' authoritativeness, the compilation group convened more than 100 seminars, gathering experts from across the country in disciplines such as history, ethnic studies, religion, archaeology and border governance.
The books have emerged at an appropriate time as hostile forces at home and abroad constantly concoct false narratives about Xinjiang, said Li Tao, Party chief and vice president of the academy.
One of the books, focusing on the history of Xinjiang, is considered the country's first general history work on the region, covering a wide range of fields within a complete and standardized academic format.
With support from a wealth of historical records, archaeological artifacts and statistical data, the book traces central governments' administration of Xinjiang throughout history, affirming that Xinjiang has been an inseparable part of China since ancient times.
The book also vividly outlines the tremendous changes Xinjiang has undergone over more than 70 years, as it has developed from poverty into a moderately prosperous society in all respects.
The second book deals with the history of religions in Xinjiang, delineating the region's religious landscape and how it took shape.
The book presents core themes of how multiple religions, including Shamanism and other primitive religions, Buddhism, Taoism, and Islam, have developed and coexisted, as well as their adaptation to the Chinese context, said Yu Shangping, the chief editor of the book and vice president of the academy.
According to the book, the coexistence of multiple religions, with one or two predominating, has been a basic feature of Xinjiang's religious landscape. It concludes that, in the region's history, no single religion has ever existed alone.
The set of works is underpinned by abundant archaeological artifacts, historical documents and academic achievements, all aimed at presenting history as it truly happened, said Ren Hong, director of the academy's institute of religious studies.
Tian Kang, Party chief of the Xinjiang Institute of Cultural Relics and Archaeology, said the books' solid historical conclusions should be woven into exhibition hall interpretations to tell the true stories about Xinjiang. ■

Across China: Roses honoring two late women who served rural China go on sale
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
21:50:45 CST
22:50:45 KST

KUNMING, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- Two Chinese roses named after the women who died while helping rural communities went on sale in China earlier this week, following public calls to honor them with the flowers.
One is a gosling-yellow rose called "Wenxiu." The other, "Jiaolong," has soft-pink petals and a faint fragrance. Both were bred by the Flower Research Institute of the Yunnan Academy of Agricultural Sciences and have independently developed Chinese intellectual property rights.
"Wenxiu" honors Huang Wenxiu, who returned to her hometown in south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region after earning a master's degree in Beijing. She volunteered to work in Baini village of Leye County, helping residents improve their livelihoods.
In June 2019, Huang was caught in a flash flood while returning to the village. She died at 30.
The pink rose bears the name of He Jiaolong, who once served as deputy head of Zhaosu County in northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region. She became widely known in 2020 after a video of her riding a horse across snowy grasslands to promote local tourism went viral.
She later worked to help Xinjiang farmers sell their produce online. In January this year, she fell from a horse while filming promotional material for an agricultural sales campaign. She died three days later, aged 47.
Both roses were named at the suggestion of internet users. During separate online campaigns to select names in late 2025 and early 2026, "Wenxiu" and "Jiaolong" drew widespread support and were adopted by the breeders.
The institute later donated rose plants to Guangxi and Xinjiang, where the women had worked.
The flowers were developed in Yunnan, China's largest fresh-cut flower producer. The southwestern province produced 22.15 billion stems in 2025, while roughly seven in 10 fresh-cut flowers sold across China come from Yunnan.
Yunnan's flower industry also has an international reach. Its fresh-cut flower exports reached 1.22 billion yuan (about 181.7 million U.S. dollars) in 2025, with shipments reaching 64 countries and regions.
Despite the industry's scale, Chinese growers have long relied on rose varieties developed overseas.
Cai Yanfei, a researcher at the institute, said that producing a new variety takes years of crossbreeding, screening and field observation to ensure its desirable characteristics remain stable.
The two varieties went on sale through e-commerce platforms on Thursday. Initial supplies were limited, but more flowers are expected to become available in December, Cai said.
For Huang's family, the rose is more than a new commercial variety.
In March, her elder sister, Huang Aijuan, traveled to Yunnan to receive the first plants. Wearing a pale-yellow blouse, she held a blooming "Wenxiu" rose in her hands, her eyes filling with tears.
"A flower so full of life, bearing Wenxiu's name, is the best tribute to her," she said. ■

Personal data of cumulative 260 mln people compromised in Japan since April amid cyberattack surge
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
21:50:40 CST
22:50:40 KST

TOKYO, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- Personal information on a cumulative total of about 260 million people was compromised in Japan from the start of the current fiscal year in April to mid-October, according to data recently released by the Personal Information Protection Commission.
The total, roughly twice Japan's population, includes many people who were counted more than once because they were affected by multiple incidents.
The figures are based on data leak cases reported to the commission between April 1 and Oct. 16 by businesses handling personal information, excluding financial and telecommunications firms, suggesting the actual scale could be even larger.
According to the data, a total of 2,094 incidents of unauthorized access to personal information were reported during the period. Of these, six incidents each resulted in the leak of personal information on more than 10 million people.
The number of breach incidents has been on the rise, surging in October in particular. A total of 830 incidents were reported in the first half of October alone, compared with 303 in the whole of September. In fiscal 2025, a total of 1,256 incidents were reported for the entire year, according to Kyodo News.
The trend is borne out by a string of recent reports in Japanese media.
On Wednesday alone, several companies and institutions, including Sony Life Insurance Co., discount retailer Don Quijote, video game publisher Bandai Namco Entertainment Inc., and Kyushu University and its affiliated hospital, said personal data may have been compromised following unauthorized access to their websites or other systems.
On Friday, more Japanese companies reported possible leaks, including Muji brand operator Ryohin Keikaku Co., restaurant chain operator Matsuya Foods Holdings Co., and All Nippon Airways Co.
"The number of large-scale leaks is increasing rapidly, and the government is taking the situation very seriously," Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said at a press conference Friday, adding that the government will compile a package of emergency countermeasures quickly. ■

Israel voted for Israel: Why Gaza wasn’t on the ballot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
13:35:51 UTC
22:35:51 KST

Israel voted for Israel: Why Gaza wasn’t on the ballot
Despite genocide, regional war and isolation, Israel’s election revealed little appetite for political alternatives.
Israel’s parliament remains in deadlock.
After one of the highest voter turnouts in decades, neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition nor the self-styled Zionist opposition alliance secured the 61 seats required for a parliamentary majority in the October 27 polls.
Netanyahu’s camp came first, with 53 seats, five more than the main opposition bloc. The Arab parties surged to a record 19 seats but have been relegated to merely observing coalition negotiations.
Viewed from a distance, the results could appear startling.
The judicial reforms ushered in at the start of Netanyahu’s government term in 2022 provoked the largest street protests in Israel’s history, while the prime minister himself is still embroiled in a corruption trial dating back to 2019. Alleged failures ahead of the Hamas-led attacks on October 7, 2023, that triggered Israel’s genocidal war against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip have still to be reckoned with, despite overwhelming public pressure to do so. Moreover, the genocide has led to growing international isolation, while also providing the pretext for multiple attacks on countries across the region – the latest of which, undertaken with the United States on Iran in February, continues to roil energy markets around the world.
Nevertheless, roughly 2.38 million Israelis on Tuesday made the journey to the polls to back Netanyahu’s coalition, led by his Likud party, while some 2.21 million cast their ballots for the opposition alliance.
Between the two, little space was given to examine the multiple war crimes Israel stands accused of having carried out in Gaza, where Israeli attacks have killed more than 74,500 people and left much of it in ruins, or government complicity in the surging violence and pogroms in the occupied West Bank, where a United Nations commission of inquiry said on Monday that Israel had been committing crimes against humanity, including extermination, torture and rape.
Gaza did not make the ballot
Analysts said the fact that neither Gaza nor the West Bank were a deciding factor in how Israelis voted on Tuesday was largely because they already represented an area of broad agreement across both alliances.
Instead, the election was fought on largely internal issues: the power of Israel’s courts, whether members of the ultra-Orthodox minority should be exempted from military service, and whether the government’s alleged culpability in missing the warnings of the October 2023 attack should be examined.
Leading Israeli sociologist Yehouda Shenhav-Shahrabani said the issues were pitched to the Israeli public along broadly similar lines to those used by the politicians enacting the policies.
“I don’t think the problem is simply that people are uninformed or disengaged,” he told Al Jazeera.
“Many Israelis know that Gaza has been devastated, even though they are exposed to a very selective representation of that devastation. But knowing something and recognising its moral and political implications are different things,” Shenhav-Shahrabani added, providing one explanation for the absence of empathy displayed by many Israelis in the face of the widely reported suffering of Palestinians in Gaza.
“Ordinary people, who love their families, care for their friends, and consider themselves decent human beings, can participate in or acquiesce to a political order that produces immense suffering for others,” he said.
For Shenhav-Shahrabani, there has been “a powerful mechanism of denial” at work. “Not necessarily denial of the facts, but denial of their meaning,” he said.
Security on the agenda
For Netanyahu’s supporters, however, this denial could be traced to something more personal.
“The Likud is a tribe, or perhaps a cult and, as far as they are concerned, Dear Leader is always right,” Israeli analyst Ahron Bregman said of the prime minister’s base, which has sustained his rule for a cumulative 19 years – roughly a quarter of Israel’s entire existence.
“For them, the enemy, straight after the Arabs, is the left, and they would vote for Netanyahu regardless of his faults,” added Bregman, a senior teaching fellow at King’s College London.
For much of this electorate, the vote was less a judgement on the government’s conduct than a choice between competing claims to political legitimacy – or as Israeli academic Roi Zur put it, a contest over “the heart and soul of democracy” and the future of Jewish and Israeli identity.
“The most important thing, I think, for turnout among Netanyahu’s supporters is the understanding, or the belief, that the alternative coalition would be weaker on security,” said Zur, an expert on voter behaviour who teaches at Essex University.
What Netanyahu had been particularly successful in doing, he continued, was creating “this campaign of fear and the belief that he is the only one who can deal with this situation, that he is the only strong enough prime minister”.
“The idea that Netanyahu is the only and the strongest leader that can lead Israel through these recent times and the post-October 7 war.”
War and occupation, according to Shenhav-Shahrabani, were not choices to be made on the ballot paper.
Instead, they had become the prism through which, over decades, Israelis had come to view “security, citizenship, and the very meaning of democracy”.
“That is why replacing Netanyahu, important as it may be, would not by itself resolve the deeper problem.”

Union minister Hardeep Singh Puri spoke out about the lasting impact of the 1984 anti-Sikh riots, firmly stating that no justification exists for the violence inflicted upon the Sikh community
NEW DELHI: Union minister Hardeep Singh Puri on Saturday said the assassination of former Prime Minister Indira Gandhi was a profound tragedy but stressed that it could not justify the violence subsequently inflicted on the Sikh community during the 1984 anti-Sikh riots.Ahead of the 42nd anniversary of the riots on November 1, Puri said, "The assassination of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi, regardless of one’s perspective, was a profound tragedy. The collective punishment subsequently inflicted upon the Sikh community cannot be justified under any circumstances."Speaking about the scale of the violence, Puri said an official death toll of 3,325 was recorded across the country, with Delhi alone accounting for 2,733 deaths. He also described November 1 as a painful reminder for Sikh families who lost relatives and saw their homes reduced to ashes.Puri also credited senior advocate HS Phoolka for his decades-long efforts to secure justice for the victims of the 1984 anti-Sikh riots, saying he had remained committed to the legal battle despite threats and repeated delays."One individual who has dedicated over four decades to helping the victims secure justice, remaining steadfast in his resolve and, alongside their legal counsel, keeping these cases alive despite threats and persistent delays, is HS Phoolka," Puri said.
1984 anti-Sikh riotsThe anti-Sikh violence broke out across several parts of India following the assassination of then Prime Minister Indira Gandhi by two of her Sikh bodyguards on October 31, 1984.The assassination came months after Operation Blue Star, a military operation ordered by Indira Gandhi's government to remove armed militants from the Golden Temple complex in Amritsar.
The violence intensified in Delhi over the following days, with Sikh men, women and children targeted in attacks. Homes, shops and businesses belonging to members of the community were looted and set on fire. Several neighbourhoods in the national capital witnessed widespread killings and destruction.The violence also triggered allegations of organised attacks and political complicity, leading to several investigations, commissions and prolonged court battles.The demand for accountability and justice has continued for decades, with survivors and families of victims pursuing legal action against those accused of involvement in the violence.

Burnham opens door to formal apology for Britain’s slave trade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
13:19:23 UTC
22:19:23 KST

Burnham opens door to formal apology for Britain’s slave trade
The prime minister has ruled out financial reparations despite longstanding Caribbean demands ahead of Commonwealth leaders’ summit.
Britain’s prime minister has opened the door to a formal apology for its role in the transatlantic slave trade, while ruling out financial reparations.
Andy Burnham set out his position in a Guardian article on Friday, ahead of a Commonwealth leaders’ summit in Antigua and Barbuda on Sunday.
The Commonwealth comprises 56 countries, mostly former British colonies, whose Caribbean members have long pressed Britain to acknowledge slavery’s legacy and offer redress.
Burnham offered structured talks with countries and campaign groups affected by slavery, including discussions on whether Britain should issue an official state apology.
“Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process and I am open to them,” Burnham wrote.
He expressed “sorrow and regret” for the suffering of millions of enslaved people, but rejected calls for financial compensation.
“I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part,” he said.
The stance maintains the position of previous British governments, despite his willingness to discuss an apology.
Instead, he proposed an international effort to ease the debt burden on poorer nations by extending repayment periods and cutting interest rates.
Burnham also said that former British Prime Minister Gordon Brown will assist with the initiative, adding that more than 40 percent of the world’s poorest and most vulnerable countries spend more on debt interest than on healthcare.
Barbadian Prime Minister Mia Mottley welcomed the opening for talks but reiterated her government’s position on reparations.
In a statement reported by the Guardian on Saturday, she said cooperation could also cover healthcare, education, development and fairer borrowing terms.
Antigua’s Prime Minister Gaston Browne, who is hosting the summit, welcomed the debt initiative and promises of cooperation on renewable energy.
CARICOM, the regional bloc of Caribbean countries, has drawn up a 10-point plan for reparations.
Its demands go beyond payments to include an apology, support for health and education, as well as measures to address the economic and social damage left by slavery.
The dispute surfaced at the last Commonwealth summit in Samoa in 2024, when leaders called for discussions about reparations, despite opposition from then Prime Minister Keir Starmer.
King Charles III will also attend the summit. However, Buckingham Palace has said he will not issue a formal apology for slavery during his trip, despite calls from countries in the region.

Rotmans said recordings of his voice, image and facial expressions had already been made to help create the digital version.

He also expressed hope that he would be able to interact with his AI counterpart and learn from its responses.
However, the professor acknowledged the technology's limitations, including the possibility that it could generate inaccurate information or statements he would not endorse.
He said the system would undergo extensive testing before being made available.
AI expert warns of risks
Iris van Rooij, an artificial intelligence professor at Radboud University, criticized the project, describing it as an undesirable development.
She warned that people interacting with such digital models could mistakenly attribute human qualities, including emotions and intelligence, to artificial intelligence systems.
Rotmans, however, stressed that the digital twin was not intended to replace him personally but to ensure that his knowledge remained accessible to future generations.
He said he accepted the potential risks associated with the project and expected other researchers to pursue similar initiatives.

'Northern women and esotericism': Life after death explored at Finnish National Gallery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
13:10:35 UTC
22:10:35 KST

The relationship between spirit and matter, questions related to life after death and the existence of the spirit world are the key themes of the exhibition "Arcana Borealis – Northern Women and Esotericism" at Ateneum Art Museum, Finnish National Gallery.
The Latin words arcana and borealis mean "hidden knowledge" and "the north", two elements at the heart of the Finnish National Gallery's latest exhibition.
"Arcana Borealis – Northern Women and Esotericism" is the first large-scale museum show to examine how female artists from across the Nordic region and Sápmi have engaged with esotericism, spirituality and alternative systems of knowledge from the 19th century to the present day.
The exhibition brings together more than 200 works by 50 artists and features both well-known and overlooked artists, including Hilma af Klint, Tyra Kleen and Tove Jansson.
Previously the connection between modern art and esotericism, occultism and magic has been explored mainly through famous male artists, according to Dr Marja Lahelma, Chief Curator at Ateneum Art Museum and co-curator of the exhibition.
"For quite a long time art history has been dominated by narratives focusing on male artists and on this notion of the individual genius. Our focus is on women and we also draw attention to this idea of communality and working together," Dr Lahelma explained to Euronews Culture.
Art, spirituality and handicraft
"Arcana Borealis shows how the boundaries between art and spirituality, fine art and craft, object and process, individual authorship and collective making begin to blur when viewed through the lens of artist women and esotericism" added Dr Nina Kokkinen from University of Turku, co-curator of "Arcana Borealis – Northern Women and Esotericism" .
The range of materials featured in the exhibition is exceptionally wide, including textiles, ceramics, metal engravings, and traditional media from sacral art, such as stained glass and mosaics.
Handicraft involves matrilineal transmission of tradition, that is, passing down knowledge and skills from one woman to the next. Sámi duodji, the traditional Sámi craft tradition, brings together spirituality, the tacit knowledge passed on from one generation to another, and values related to nature.
Some of the artists gathered on the exhibition were saying that they were guided by some kind of non human agency whether it was angels or guiding spirits, or in some cases a source of nature.
Halloween or Kekri
"This is a perfect exhibition to visit for Halloween, or Kekri as we say in Finnish. Esotericism is about light and darkness. We can explore themes such as death in art through this esoteric theme and sometimes the hidden knowledge, the secret knowledge that esotericism is all about, can be found through exploring darkness rather than light," explained Dr Marja Lahelm.
Arcana Borealis – Northern Women and Esotericism at Ateneum Art Museum, Finnish National Gallery is on open until 28 February 2027.

A mysterious 4,000-year-old wall is rewriting North Africa’s history
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
13:09:49 UTC
22:09:49 KST

A mysterious 4,000-year-old wall is rewriting North Africa’s history
- Date:
- October 31, 2026
- Source:
- The Conversation
- Summary:
- A remarkable 4,000-year-old defensive structure discovered in Morocco is rewriting what scientists thought they knew about ancient North African civilizations. The massive fortifications reveal unexpectedly sophisticated prehistoric societies and suggest that the region played a much greater role in Mediterranean history than previously recognized.
- Share:
In the hills of north-west Morocco, overlooking the river that gives the site its name, research at Oued Beht is bringing to light a previously unknown chapter of the region’s past. The discovery of a substantial built structure suggests that, during the second millennium BC, communities in north-west Africa were actively shaping their environment. They were also engaging in broader networks of interaction across the Mediterranean world.
Previous research by the Oued Beht Archaeological Project had already brought to light what is likely the earliest and largest agricultural complex ever discovered in Africa outside the Nile Valley. It dates to around 5,400 to 4,900 years ago. New excavations carried out in 2023 – in which we took part – have now deepened our understanding of the site.
Our new study shows how we uncovered the earliest known large-scale construction of a probably defensive nature in north Africa beyond the Nile Valley. It’s about 4,000 to 3,500 years old.
It’s not known exactly what threats these wall-like structures were designed to counter. They likely relate to increasing competition over land, resources, and possibly control of movement through the landscape, rather than to “invaders”. Constructions like these suggest communities felt the need to protect themselves or assert power over strategic locations.
This discovery pushes back the evidence for organized defensive architecture in the Maghreb and suggests that societies in this region at this time were more complex and structured than previously believed.
Our study also reveals how the ridge of Oued Beht would become a focal point again in the medieval period, during the 11th to 13th centuries AD. The same defensive structure was rebuilt, a hamlet or farm was established on a nearby hilltop, and people were buried in a cemetery between the two areas.
Together these findings provide rare archaeological insights into rural communities during both prehistoric and medieval times. They help us understand how societies developed and maintained themselves in a region too often left out of the history books.
A prehistoric hub in the Maghreb
For a long time, the later prehistory of north Africa’s Maghreb region (the Mediterranean countries of Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia) has been poorly understood. Compared with neighboring areas such as Iberia in south-western Europe or Athens in the eastern Mediterranean, archaeological evidence was often fragmentary. In the last few years this has changed completely.
Excavations at Oued Beht have revealed a large concentration of human activity spread across at least ten hectares. The earliest major phase dates to the mid-fourth and early third millennia BC, or the Final Neolithic period.
Environmental evidence from plant and animal remains in the prehistoric era indicates a farming community cultivating crops such as barley and wheat. They also exploited wild plants and kept livestock.
The site was also an important center of craft production. Thousands of polished stone axes and other tools have been discovered, along with finely made pottery, sometimes decorated with painted patterns.
It’s still uncertain whether prehistoric Oued Beht functioned as a permanent village, a seasonal center, or something less familiar. But it was clearly a major focus in the landscape of north-west Morocco.
The defensive wall
The presence of potentially ancient earthworks and walls had been noted since the 1930s. The French archaeologist Armand Ruhlmann first documented a configuration of three walls, with the fourth side protected by the natural scarp of the ridge, describing a defensive éperon barré (barred spur). Their precise nature and date remained uncertain until now.
New excavations have clarified the existence of a multi-phase ditch, rampart and wall built across a narrow section of the Oued Beht ridge between the river and a ravine. This cut off and protected the ridge’s southern tip.
Radiocarbon dating of deposits associated with these structures gave us the timelines in our study.
They place its original construction at a time equivalent to the Bronze Age of the remaining western Mediterranean. This makes it the earliest confirmed defensive construction in north Africa outside Egypt.
What was this construction for?
This structure raises important questions about the society that built it. Building an embankment and ditch system required planning, coordination and the mobilization of labor. This suggests a community capable of organizing complex construction initiatives.
During the earlier Neolithic phase, activity at Oued Beht focused on the larger and more open northern area of the site. By the period of our new study, focus had shifted to the narrower, more defensible southern ridge. This may reflect a shift in settlement strategies.
Mediterranean connections
The second millennium BC was a dynamic period across the Mediterranean. In southern Iberia, Argaric societies (about 2200-1550 BC) in today’s Europe were developing complex, often hilltop settlements. They were characterized by planned architecture, advanced metallurgy (especially bronze production), and marked social hierarchies visible in burial practices. These communities often constructed fortified sites, and strategically located settlements controlling surrounding territories.
Increasing evidence suggests that communities in north-west Africa were connected to wider Mediterranean networks. This includes today’s Spain and Portugal. The discoveries at Oued Beht indicate that the Maghreb was not isolated. It participated in broader processes shaping the western Mediterranean.
The defensive system at the site may reflect wider transformations in social organization and regional interaction. There may have been growing competition over resources, control of movement, and more formalized leadership structures.
Rewriting history
The discoveries at Oued Beht highlight how much remains to be learned about the deep history of north Africa. The defensive wall shows that communities here were able to coordinate large construction projects and points to social transformations that are only very tentatively beginning to be recognized.
The medieval remains demonstrate that the ridge was used again many centuries after the prehistoric settlement had been abandoned. Oued Beht was not simply a single-period settlement but a landscape repeatedly selected by different communities across millennia.
As research continues, this location may become key to understanding how societies in the Maghreb evolved from early farming communities to the medieval rural world.
Story Source:
Materials provided by The Conversation. Original written by Giulio Lucarini, Cyprian Broodbank, and Toby C. Wilkinson. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Giulio Lucarini, Youssef Bokbot, Toby Wilkinson, Hamza Benattia, Aïcha Bigoulimen, Alessia Brucato, Marlena Cygan, Lucy Farr, Hassan Hachami, Evangelia Kiriatzi, Rafael Laoutari, Lorena Lombardi, Adelaide Marsilio, Rafael Martínez Sánchez, Ilaria Mazzini, Jacob Morales, Giulia Muti, Jacques Pelegrin, Moad Radi, Francesco Michele Rega, Cyprian Broodbank. Expanding Oued Beht: Final Neolithic, Bronze Age, medieval and later discoveries from excavation and survey in 2023. Libyan Studies, 2026; 1 DOI: 10.1017/lis.2026.10037

Single dose of psychedelic nasal spray reduced treatment-resistant depression symptoms for eight weeks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
13:00:43 UTC
22:00:43 KST

A single dose of a fast-acting psychedelic nasal spray appears to ease symptoms of hard-to-treat depression within a day, with benefits lasting up to eight weeks, according to a clinical trial published in JAMA. The medication, a synthetic formulation of the psychedelic compound mebufotenin, produced a brief psychoactive experience that allowed most patients to be assessed as ready to leave the clinic within two hours. These findings suggest that short-acting psychedelics may offer a practical way to deliver rapid antidepressant relief without the four- to twelve-hour clinic stays required for compounds like psilocybin.
Major depressive disorder is a mood condition marked by persistent sadness, loss of interest in daily activities, and trouble sleeping or concentrating, affecting about 290 million people worldwide. Roughly one-third of patients have treatment-resistant depression, meaning their symptoms do not adequately respond to at least two antidepressant trials. People with treatment-resistant depression tend to experience greater emotional distress, a lower quality of life, and a higher risk of suicide than those who respond to standard medications.
Existing options for treatment-resistant depression, such as esketamine nasal spray or magnetic brain stimulation, require frequent clinic visits. Psychedelic drugs, which alter perception and mood by activating docking sites for the chemical messenger serotonin in the brain, offer a potential alternative because a single dose can produce lasting relief. For instance, a clinical trial of patients with treatment-resistant depression found that one 25-milligram dose of psilocybin with psychological support reduced depression scores at three weeks compared to a 1-milligram control dose, though it carried side effects including suicidal thoughts.
Because classic psychedelics like psilocybin and LSD require four to twelve hours of in-clinic supervision, scientists have turned to mebufotenin, a psychedelic compound chemically known as 5-methoxy-N,N-dimethyltryptamine that is naturally found in toad venom and certain plants. Mebufotenin activates both serotonin 1A and 2A receptors in the brain and is rapidly absorbed and eliminated by the body, producing a brief psychedelic experience.
Earlier clinical trials tested mebufotenin by inhalation. In a 2026 randomized controlled trial of 81 patients with treatment-resistant depression, an inhaled formulation of mebufotenin produced a 58 percent remission rate at day 8 compared to 0 percent for placebo, and in an open-label follow-up phase allowing up to four retreatments, 87 percent of those who reached remission were still in remission at six months. Researchers have also developed a dry-powder nasal spray for intranasal absorption, and an earlier study of psychedelic-naive healthy adults showed that intranasal mebufotenin elicited emotional, bodily, and cognitive effects peaking within 8 to 15 minutes and resolving within 45 to 60 minutes.
Joint first authors David Feifel of the Kadima Neuropsychiatry Institute in La Jolla, California, and Mathieu Seynaeve of King’s College London, along with their colleagues, tested the nasal spray in patients with treatment-resistant depression.
The researchers conducted a Phase 2b, double-blind, randomized clinical trial, a mid-stage study designed to test doses and gauge effectiveness, between September 2023 and April 2025 at 38 sites in Australia, Germany, Poland, Spain, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Of 443 adults screened, 193 received treatment. Between 5 and 14 percent of each group did not complete the eight-week core study, with the highest rate in the control group and no withdrawals due to side effects. Participants were aged 18 to 75 (average age 41 years, 59.1 percent female) with moderate to severe major depressive disorder that had not responded to two to five antidepressant trials in their current episode, which had lasted an average of 2.6 years.
To test the spray as a standalone therapy, the two-thirds of participants taking antidepressants at screening tapered off their medications at least two weeks before dosing. Participants were randomly assigned to receive a single spray into one nostril of 8 milligrams of mebufotenin benzoate (46 participants), 12 milligrams (73 participants), or a 0.3-milligram comparator dose low enough that most participants would not feel its effects (74 participants), alongside structured psychological support before, during, and after dosing. Midway through recruitment, the randomization ratio was adjusted from an equal split to prioritize the 12-milligram and 0.3-milligram groups for the primary analysis.
The primary outcome was the change in depression severity from baseline to day 29 between the 12-milligram and 0.3-milligram groups on the Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale, which scores symptoms from 0 to 60, with higher scores indicating worse depression. Independent, blinded raters conducted these interviews by video call at baseline and every two weeks after dosing, including days 2, 8, 29, and 57. Staff assessed discharge readiness every 30 minutes starting 90 minutes after dosing, though participants had to stay at least four hours. Statistical models controlled for baseline depression scores, geographic region, and randomization schedule.
Baseline depression scores averaged about 32 across the three groups. The trial was designed with enough participants to detect a 6-point difference; the primary comparison at day 29 found an adjusted mean difference of 5.3 points (confidence interval 1.8 to 8.9), as scores dropped by 11.1 points in the 12-milligram group versus 5.5 points in the control group. The 8-milligram group improved by 12.5 points, an adjusted difference of 6.2 points (confidence interval 2.1 to 10.2). Whether a participant had tapered off antidepressants before the trial was not associated with the primary outcome.
Improvements appeared by day 2, when both active groups had dropped about 9 points versus 3.8 in the control group, and persisted to day 57, where active-group reductions averaged about 11 points versus 5.2. At day 29, response rates (at least a 50 percent score reduction) were about one-third in both active groups versus 12 percent in the control group; remission rates (a score of 10 or less) were 26 and 18 percent for the 8-milligram and 12-milligram groups versus 8 percent for the control group. Response and remission rates were reported descriptively, without confidence intervals or statistical tests.
Both active doses outperformed the control dose across all time points on clinician-rated illness severity and self-reported quality of life. On a self-reported depression scale, the 12-milligram group improved more than the control group at all visits, while the 8-milligram group improved more at days 2 and 8, though differences at days 29 and 57 were not statistically significant.
On day 1, the 8-milligram and 12-milligram doses produced higher scores on a 0-to-5 questionnaire measuring mystical-type experiences such as a sense of unity, transcendence of time and space, and ineffability (averaging 2.4 and 2.6, versus 0.4 in the control group). Those scores did not correlate with day 29 symptom reductions, a finding that runs against evidence from other psychedelics, which the authors note has suggested that the intensity of the subjective experience predicts therapeutic outcomes.
Most participants in the active groups (85 percent for 8 milligrams and 78 percent for 12 milligrams) met discharge readiness criteria within two hours of dosing, with two-thirds ready at 90 minutes. Those criteria required that the acute psychedelic effects had fully subsided and that vital signs, orientation, and coordination had returned to normal. This rapid turnaround is the feature the researchers argue sets the spray apart from psilocybin and LSD.
Side effects were common in all three groups, reported by roughly 73 to 85 percent of participants, and 99.7 percent of events were mild or moderate. The most frequent were headache, nausea, and pain at the spray site. Headache was about as common in the control group as in the active groups (29.5 percent overall), while nausea was far more common with the active doses (33 and 40 percent) than with the control dose (3 percent). Because the 8-milligram dose had comparable efficacy to the 12-milligram dose with fewer side effects like nausea and anxiety, the researchers selected the 8-milligram dose for Phase 3 trials, which will follow patients for longer to test how long the benefits last.
Most side effects in the active groups appeared on the day of dosing and resolved within 24 hours, though one participant in the 12-milligram group had two severe panic attacks related to the drug. Temporary increases in heart rate and blood pressure resolved within an hour. No suicidal behavior occurred during the trial. Eight drug-related reports of suicidal thoughts without intent were recorded: one in the 8-milligram group, four in the 12-milligram group, and three in the control group, all mild or moderate, and those in the active groups all occurred in participants with a history of such thoughts.
These results align with an uncontrolled, open-label study of 10 women with postpartum depression, which tested an inhaled formulation rather than a nasal spray in a different patient group, and similarly found rapid relief of depressive symptoms. The findings also parallel a 2019 observational study in which 42 people who inhaled vapor from dried toad secretion containing mebufotenin reported reduced depression and anxiety four weeks later, though that study had no control group and relied on self-reported symptoms.
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. The trial was funded by Beckley Psytech, an AtaiBeckley company that is developing the nasal spray, and several authors are company employees or hold stock or patents related to the compound. Employees of the sponsor were involved in the trial’s design, data analysis, and the decision to publish.
Statistical adjustments for multiple comparisons were applied to the primary outcome and three key secondary outcomes; the remaining comparisons were not adjusted. The smaller size of the 8-milligram group after the randomization change may also have limited statistical power to detect differences on the self-reported depression scale at later visits.
Difficulty maintaining blinding is a recognized problem across psychedelic trials, and the authors cite it as an inherent limitation, noting that most participants and on-site clinicians guessed their treatment assignment. Blinding was better preserved among the centralized remote raters who scored the primary measure; that measure is scored through an interview in which participants describe their own symptoms. Pre-treatment expectations did not correlate with day 29 outcomes, though those expectations were measured before the first preparation visit, prior to dosing and to any knowledge of group assignment; post-dose expectancy was not measured.
In addition, the two-hour discharge figure describes an assessment rather than an actual discharge. No one was discharged at two hours because the protocol required a minimum four-hour stay. Average times to readiness were just under two hours in the active groups, with the longest cases running past four.
In an editorial published alongside the trial in JAMA, Chittaranjan Andrade of the National Institute of Mental Health and Neurosciences in Bangalore, India, called two findings striking: that a single dose given on its own kept depression scores roughly a third lower for eight weeks, and that most patients were ready to leave within two hours rather than the four to twelve hours that psilocybin and LSD require.
At the same time, Andrade noted that the average patient improved only about 30 percent, and that the response and remission rates fall below those typically seen with ketamine and electroconvulsive therapy. In his reading, either the 8- to 12-milligram dose or the single-dose approach is insufficient, and he suggests testing higher or escalating doses, or a course of treatments as is standard with ketamine and electroconvulsive therapy.
Both the study authors and Andrade note that the trial population may underrepresent more severely treatment-resistant patients. Participants had failed a median of two antidepressants, which Andrade describes as not markedly refractory depression. The protocol also excluded people with PTSD, bipolar or psychotic disorders, any personality disorder, a first-degree family history of schizophrenia or bipolar disorder, suicidal ideation with intent in the prior year, or prior nonresponse to ketamine or electroconvulsive therapy. Because active suicidal intent was an exclusion, Andrade notes that the trial could not examine whether the drug reduces suicidal thinking, as ketamine and electroconvulsive therapy have been shown to do.
Other constraints affect how the findings might translate to clinical care. Participants had to discontinue antidepressants so the spray could be tested on its own, which the authors note can cause withdrawal symptoms or a return of depression and may not reflect how the drug would be used in practice. Andrade adds that the trial offers no guidance on when or how patients would transition to a conventional antidepressant afterward. In addition, the study did not evaluate how much the structured psychological support contributed to the improvements, and the trial population lacked racial and ethnic diversity, as nearly 90 percent of participants were white.
Andrade argues that psychedelic research points toward a broader rethinking of how depression is treated, not just treatment-resistant depression. He questions whether it is justifiable to put patients in severe distress through antidepressants that take four to eight weeks to work when faster-acting options exist, and notes that current Canadian guidelines do not list ketamine and esketamine as third-line treatments for depression, naming them only as second-line add-ons for difficult-to-treat depression.
He also raises a point about access: in low- and middle-income countries, where newly approved psychedelics are likely to be unavailable or unaffordable, generic ketamine can be given orally at negligible cost, though he notes the evidence base for that approach needs strengthening. Andrade has published several studies on oral ketamine and cites his own work in making this argument.
He adds that psychedelics have not yet been approved by regulators and will need to be evaluated for long-term safety, including the risk of hallucinogen persisting perception disorder, a condition in which visual disturbances continue after the drug has worn off. He also calls for more detail on what the mebufotenin experience is actually like, including difficult experiences, whether patients found it unpleasant or frightening, and whether they would undergo it again.
The study, “Single Intranasal Administration of the Psychedelic Mebufotenin for Treatment-Resistant Depression: A Randomized Clinical Trial,” was authored by David Feifel, Mathieu Seynaeve, Wiesław Jerzy Cubała, Fiona Dunbar, Gerhard Gründer, Rosa María Dueñas Herrero, Chandni Hindocha, Paul Liknaitzky, Sean M. McGuigan, Sejal Mehta, Mimi Pierce, Dimitris Repantis, Claire Roberts, Frank Wiegand, and Robert Conley.
The accompanying editorial, “Treatment Approach to Major Depressive Disorder: It’s Time for a Paradigm Shift,” was authored by Chittaranjan Andrade.

Unmanned Systems Forces could account for 40% of all Russian troops neutralized in October – Colonel Veres
Colonel Kyrylo Veres, commander of the K-2 Brigade, said this in an interview with Ukrinform.
"The USF as a branch of the military will probably account for 40% of all enemy personnel neutralized this month [October 2026]. Forty percent is a compelling argument. The most compelling one," Veres said.
He also highlighted the role played in developing the Unmanned Systems Forces by the appointment of Robert Brovdi as their commander in June 2025 and their integration with the Drone Line project.
"After the Drone Line was integrated with the USF and the new USF commander took office, we started achieving huge results. Unit commanders were given the opportunity to purchase whatever they wanted, manage their own budgets, and were simply told: do your job as well as you can. They simply stopped interfering with us and gave us the freedom to do things the way we saw fit," Veres said.
Asked about the latest changes along the line of contact, he highlighted Operation Vivaldi.
"As far as the 3rd Army Corps is concerned, there is Operation Vivaldi, and everyone can see its results. Our brigade also played a significant role in it. Of course, we cannot compare ourselves with the infantry, which did all the work – we did not take part in assault operations. But when it comes to destroying enemy personnel, our contribution to the unmanned component was very significant," the colonel said.
Veres also commented on the record losses suffered by Russian forces, which amounted to 46,230 personnel in September.
"They are sending in more troops, and more are dying. The more they advance, the more they die. And the sooner the critical moment will come when they start thinking about their losses. Sooner or later, it will come – whether at 100,000 killed, 200,000 or 46,000 – but it will come all the same," he said.
At the same time, Veres added: "If they send in even more troops, we will kill them in much greater numbers – in direct proportion. And I am confident that we are capable of not losing a single piece of territory in our area of responsibility."
As Ukrinform reported, Russian forces lost 46,230 personnel in September, the highest monthly figure in 2026. Compared with January, their losses increased by 14,520, or 45.8%.

Gulf states scramble to avert another U.S.-Israeli war on Iran they cannot stop
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

The first of two elections that many believe are the final bell before all out war is resumed against Iran is now complete. Although it seems likely that the efforts to cobble together a governing coalition in Israel, if that is even possible, will take weeks, the American midterms are expected to be the last milestone before the United States and Israel launch a massive attack on Iran.
There is no doubt that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is almost bursting with anticipation of the bloodshed to come. Donald Trump, as always, seems unsure of how to proceed, but seems very uncomfortable with the situation as it stands, while also being unwilling to make the concessions necessary to end this futile, destructive war he started for no good reason.
Iran can do little to deter an American attack, if that is what Trump decides to do. But it can retaliate with devastating consequences, which will be felt by its Gulf Arab neighbors, Israel, and the global economy.
That is why the countries of the newly created Mecca Pact—Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Türkiye—took the dramatic step of meeting Iranian officials in Tehran.
Iran trumpeted the meeting as demonstrating the seriousness with which the Sunni Muslim states take the Islamic Republic, meeting in the Iranian capital rather than in a third country.
Saudi Arabia said the meeting was aimed at mediating between the United States and Iran, but there is no evidence the United States had any part in the planning of this meeting. Indeed, the indications are the opposite; one purpose of the confab was to establish regional dialogue specifically on security matters.
Participants included Pakistan’s Chief of Army Staff Field Marshall Asim Munir, Saudi Minister of Defense Prince Khalid bin Salman, and Turkish Director of National Intelligence Ibrahim Kalin. They met with Iran’s Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council Mohsen Rezaei.
The fact that the meeting included leaders of the countries’ respective militaries indicates that the description of the meeting—that it was to deal with regional security—is likely accurate.
And, while little has been made public about the substance of the meeting, it also seems fair to say that there was little progress that could have been made on the major issues—the war with U.S. and the ongoing battles between Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni Ansar Allah.
Little room for negotiations
Regarding Ansar Allah, Saudi Arabia was feeling Iran out to see if they would intervene with the Yemeni fighters whom the Saudis have been unable to defeat.
But Iran doesn’t have much reason to do so. While they could benefit from pulling the Saudis away from the American war effort, the compromises Tehran would have to make are far too great.
Reports out of Israel state that the Saudis offered Ansar Allah $1 billion for a ceasefire. But the Yemeni group will not budge on its understandable demand that Saudi Arabia drop its air blockade of Yemen.
This is not an issue Iran can try to mediate. If they try to get Ansar Allah to compromise on the air blockade, it undermines their argument that the United States must end its sea blockade of Iran.
Iran supports Ansar Allah’s cause, but if they thought they could get concessions from the Saudis on the kingdom’s support for American military efforts, Ansar Allah might find it reasonable to agree to a temporary ceasefire to help their ally.
But they cannot compromise on the air blockade, nor would Iran want them to. As long as Saudi Arabia maintains its efforts to block air traffic in Yemen, they can’t buy their way out of Ansar Allah attacks.
On the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, the Saudis are very worried, as are all the countries of the Gulf and their neighbors. They should be, given that Trump has warned the Gulf states to get ready for a “short, intense military campaign.” Considering that the war started on February 27 was supposed to end in just a few days, or weeks at most, no one is counting on the “short” part. But it is likely to be intense, and that intensity will be felt in Iran and the Gulf Arab states.
The problem for Iran is that its interlocutors can do little to turn Trump’s mind. Even Saudi Arabia, which is in a terrible position right now if the war restarts, has few options outside of registering its reservations with Trump, which it surely has already done.
Türkiye and Pakistan have even less leverage over Trump’s decisions. If he is reckless enough to risk the consequences of restarting the war with Iran, what can they do to stop him?
And those consequences are potentially very dire.
The costs of war
Iran has made it clear that it intends to target data centers, AI hubs, and underwater fiber networks that are the backbone of the internet in addition to oil infrastructure. No one doubts they have the capability of doing so.
The amount of damage that can be inflicted on the world dwarfs anything we’ve seen until now.
That has produced fear among the Gulf states, but it has also produced tension between them and Iran. Gulf states are angry at Iran for targeting them in response to American attacks, but Iran is aggravated because the Gulf states have cooperated with Washington.
This double-edged sword was visible this week when Qatar submitted a proposal for a ceasefire and a path back to negotiations, including reciprocal but revocable steps each side could take, presumably offering each side the assurances they needed to proceed.
But at the same time, Qatar publicly supported the call for Iran to allow international traffic through the Strait of Hormuz unconditionally. That did nothing to help the case for Qatar’s proposal, which Iran eventually dismissed as a collection of random ideas rather than a serious proposal and which Trump ignored.
Vice President JD Vance, who has quietly been opposing the resumption of large-scale fighting, tried reaching out via a letter to Rezaei, but the letter reportedly offered no immediate relief from any of the pressures the U.S. is putting on Iran while demanding that any talks include the nuclear issue, which Iran insists be left to be discussed after its minimal terms are met. In other words, it was just Vance delivering Trump’s unacceptable terms in nicer language.
If that wasn’t enough to make the Vance letter a non-starter, the fact that Vance’s earlier efforts were routinely contradicted by Trump soon after empties the vice president of any credibility, even if Tehran believes he is personally sincere in his desire to avoid another round of full-scale fighting.
This leaves only one hope: that Trump, in his eternally mercurial and indecisive way, will back away from what will be a devastating conflict.
One unknown is how much Trump understands about the danger that an Iranian response presents and how certain it is that a devastating response will be coming.
Trump’s threat of a “short intense” attack would seem to imply that he is being led to believe that the United States can overwhelm Iran with devastating force. Of course, that is exactly what he tried in February, and it failed dismally. Outside of insanity, does he have any reason to think that the same action would produce a different result this time?
It could be that what the U.S. and Israel are planning is a multi-phase attack.
American planners may think the weakness of their initial strike was that they targeted Iranian leadership while devastating large areas of civilian and military infrastructure, believing that this would lead to the collapse of the Iranian government. When that failed, there was no plan B.
It may be that the idea this time is to simply start with doing as much damage to Iranian infrastructure as they can, then pinpoint where the response is coming from and take out those missile and drone launchers.
That is consistent with what Senator Chris Murphy is warning about when he says that what the Trump administration is planning is “insane.”
“It will lead to devastating escalation, and the likely destruction of our commitment to the rule of law. There’s been open reporting as to what we may be planning and the civilian infrastructure that we may be targeting,” Murphy said. “They’ve been asked by the president to develop a plan. Whether they believe it will work or not, I do not know. But the plan that they have developed will lead, in my view, to a prolongment and an escalation of this war that will be devastating for our security interests.”
The result, then, would be one of two things. If the U.S.-Israeli attack is successful, the Gulf states will suffer significant damage, but they can recover and, theoretically, come out with a weakened Iran. But that would mean that what failed in February magically works in November, and there is no evidence to support that expectation.
The other, far more likely scenario is that Iran continues to weather American and Israeli attacks and responds by devastating the Gulf states, further demolishing American positions, and inflicting a far greater degree of damage on Israel than they have in the past.
In that scenario, Gulf oil and civilian infrastructure could be damaged beyond repair. Moreover, given the region’s inherent instability—governed as it is mostly by iron-fisted dictators ruling over states of mixed and often clashing ethnicities drawn up by colonial map-makers—such a scenario could well mean the end of one or more of the Gulf states.
It is that scenario that the Mecca Pact countries are trying to avert.
They are not fools; they knew there was little that Iran could do to change the strategic playing field. Instead, they hoped that sending their top security leaders to Tehran would signal to Washington how concerned they were. They understood that the meeting, by its very existence, would give Iran a diplomatic win and, more importantly, would show that the Mecca Pact is intended to forge a new regional security system that will want to work with Iran, potentially even including it in the group someday.
The Mecca Pact countries, as well as Iran, hope that this message of the region’s strong desire to avert the oncoming catastrophe will convince Trump to back off.
Meanwhile, in Israel, Benjamin Netanyahu is even more incentivized to see the war roar back to life. With the election process in deadlock, he needs to move swiftly, before the opposition can make the case to the public that they are better suited to defeat Iran than Netanyahu.
He needs the war to make it more difficult to replace him, and he will push hard for it. He has already tried to provoke Iran into an act that would have restarted the major fighting before Trump was ready. He will surely try again before too long.
