Americans Lost Nearly $18 Billion Last Year to Cyberscams. Is Washington Doing Enough to Help Them Get It Back?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
12:30:00 UTC
21:30:00 KST

The United States government’s response to escalating cyberscams is fragmented, leaving victims with limited options to recover lost funds, according to an investigation conducted by Democrats on Congress’s Joint Economic Committee (JEC).
The investigation, led by Sen. Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire and Rep. Don Beyer of Virginia, found that federal agencies do not have a consolidated or comprehensive record of how much money has been lost to cyberfraud, how much has been seized from overseas scam compounds, or how much has been returned to victims.
The report, published Tuesday, also concludes that the government does not “incentivize” private sector actors—such as financial institutions and social media companies—to “proactively detect and address abuse of the services that they provide while also protecting user privacy.”
Online scam operations are not new, and neither is the knowledge that the issue is escalating. The FBI released an April report showing that Americans lost nearly $18 billion in 2025, amounting to more than $2 million an hour. Overall reported internet-crime losses—a broader category—reached $20.9 billion, up 26% from 2024 and roughly triple the 2021 total.
While the problem grows worse, the response to these crimes has not scaled along with it. The Congressional investigation demonstrates that only a fraction of the money lost to scams is recovered. It also points to the fact that the government fails to fully report on its existing repatriation measures.
The FBI told the committee that it returned $336 million to scam victims in 2025, and the Secret Service returned more than $770 million in seized assets to fraud victims in fiscal years 2024 and 2025—though that money had come from a range of fraud schemes, not just cyber threats.
Suzanne Sando, a fraud analyst at Javelin Strategy & Research, points out that “fragmentation” in the reporting system—including the differing time periods and fraud categories demonstrated above—complicates the government’s ability to grasp the full extent of the problem.
“Many of the groups and entities that scam victims report their losses to operate on disparate systems,” Sando says. “The fragmented nature of these reporting entities means there’s a lack of true accounting of losses—which also means that our grasp of overall scam losses is likely less than the truth of the situation.”
The Congressional report calls on the federal government to enact new legislation to address the rising issue, including the ReportScams.Gov Act, a bipartisan bill co-sponsored by Hassan and Florida Republican Sen. Rick Scott “to mandate a unified federal strategy to combat scams and establish a central location for Americans to find information and assistance regarding scams.”
A more coordinated reporting system could help researchers and advocates better assess the scale of the problem. Another benefit would be helping the public stay informed about potential schemes, allowing advocacy groups to develop preventive strategies and educational materials for at-risk populations, like senior citizens and minors.
According to the FBI’s 2025 Internet Crime Report, Americans ages 60 and older reported losses of about $7.7 billion, a 60% increase from 2024. They reported the highest total losses of any age group, the report showed.
Individuals under 18 reported nearly $13 million in losses across 13,168 internet-crime complaints in 2025, according to the same report.
But the true extent of the losses is hard to estimate, experts say. Cyberscams are underreported because victims feel embarrassed, fear judgment, and believe recovery will be impossible.
The last point is salient, because a stronger and more coordinated response—reaching some of the benchmarks outlined this week by members of the JEC—could give victims the confidence to report crimes in a timely manner, in turn making enforcement efforts more effective.
The report calls for legislation that would “hold accountable” countries that “enable or permit” scam compound operations, and advance federal cooperation with private sector entities like the financial institutions and social media companies at the center of these scams.
Experts note that this is a growing issue whose risk is only increasing as technology improves.
In alignment with the Congressional assessment, they tell TIME that a strategic, coordinated, and well-resourced response will be necessary if the government hopes to better protect Americans and help them recover funds lost to scams.
Online scams are on the rise
Data from the FBI and Congress show that transnational criminal organizations run massive compounds—and their reach is skyrocketing.
According to Sando, the growing use of artificial intelligence has been partly responsible. 
Specifically, she calls out the prevalence of abuse on social media and the increasing sophistication of deepfakes—images, voices, or videos that make people appear to say or do things they did not.
“Criminals use social media to build trust through ongoing conversations and relationships, and AI has become a major part of criminals’ ability to manipulate situations and exploit victims,” she says. “Through AI, criminals can create more convincing and polished messages, fake social media profiles, and deepfake voices and videos with less time and effort.”
The manipulation tactics at the heart of these schemes have been consistent, Sando says, but criminals now have improved tools that allow them to quickly build credibility and “commit scams at scale.”
Jake Braun, the executive director of the Cyber Policy Initiative at the University of Chicago, tells TIME that highly vulnerable populations are more exposed than ever before.
“You've got these, you know, super at-risk populations who just weren't online before, and now they are, and so the bad guys are taking advantage of that,” he says. “The idea that a kid had an iPhone and was on Facebook just wasn’t a reality until a few years ago.”
At the same time, technology gives individuals ready access to funding streams. “They've all got Apple Pay on their phones,” Braun points out.
He explains that many of these scams are run by organized criminal networks operating in Southeast Asia, where scam compounds often use trafficked workers forced to defraud people online.
Why is it so difficult to recover lost funds?
It can be difficult to recover stolen funds because the issue is diffuse and widespread—spanning multiple countries, financial institutions, and criminal enterprises—and it is being addressed by a small group of law enforcement agencies that lack centralized coordination.
Braun says investigations are complicated because they affect “millions of victims across dozens of countries” and include large numbers of cases with relatively small individual losses.
“It's just incredibly complicated,” he says. “Nobody's robbing a bank and stealing $300 million. It's $1,000 bucks from somebody's grandma here, and it's $500 bucks [there], that collectively is billions and billions. That's a really hard problem to get after.”
Braun, who also served in the White House with former President Joe Biden as the acting Principal Deputy National Cyber Director, says that there are just a hundred or so top law enforcement officials working on the issue.
“So they're going to focus on big fish, and try and take down big rings, but that just means that they just don't have the bandwidth to go track down hundreds or thousands of dollars that are stolen from individual people because they're trying to take down groups that are collectively stealing billions,” he explains.
When reporting investigations and recovery efforts are “siloed” into different agencies, there are two immediate consequences: The process is more confusing for the victim to navigate, and it makes it difficult for government entities to coordinate quickly on an investigation and take action.
The U.S. State Department told those involved with the JEC investigation that it has 60 employees in the U.S. and Asia who dedicate significant time to fighting overseas scam compounds and said that it “has the tools it needs to combat the threat internationally.”
TIME reached out to the State Department for comment.
What obstacles stand in the way of providing better protections for Americans?
Sando says that within the private sector, there is “a lack of clear ownership and responsibility,” making it difficult to provide more protection.
“Scams can span multiple platforms,” she says. “Preventing and detecting scams to protect consumers requires a coordinated group effort across multiple industries—including financial services, telcos, and social media.”
In a perfect world, Sando continues, the government would coordinate these efforts and set clear standards for private institutions. She describes its ideal role as “facilitating relevant information-sharing, tracking consistent scam attempts and losses, [reporting] recovery rates for victims, and [adding] measures that are working to reduce the effectiveness of scams.”
Social media companies, in particular, need to be incentivized to address “fraudulent ads and impersonation profiles/accounts,” she says.
Braun agrees, saying that holding the companies accountable is one of the most tangible ways that governments could more aggressively address these scams before they ever happen.
“They know everything about every click that's made on their platform,” Braun says. “This problem wouldn't exist if those platforms didn't exist.”
Braun says meaningful discussions around prevention are often buried in conversations about how to address losses in the U.S.
“We should really think through the [cyber] grants we give to state and local governments from FEMA, [and having them include] a component where they're doing education for these at-risk communities: seniors, minors, migrants,” Braun says. “We’re focused on going after the ‘bad guys,’ when maybe we need to be focused on thinking about: ‘How do you specifically protect minors in this space? How do you specifically protect senior citizens?’”
He believes that these considerations must be part of any comprehensive solution to bring down the rate of cyberscams in the U.S.
Once the government has a better understanding of how specific communities are impacted by these scams, he says, it can start to “tailor” solutions to help protect each vulnerable group.

US approves Patriot missiles sale to Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

US approves Patriot missiles sale to Ukraine
The US State Department has green-lit a $2.1 billion Patriot missile sale to Ukraine.
The announcement follows a report by CNN earlier this month that Kiev had completely exhausted its stockpile of US-made interceptors used to defend against Russian missile and drone strikes at military-related targets.
The State Department said in a statement on Friday that the Ukrainian government had requested that Washington sell it 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles and spare parts for launchers.
Kiev will pay for the interceptors with funds donated by Canada, Germany, and Norway, the State Department said. “No US funds are involved in this sale,” it added.
The principal contractor for the deal will be Lockheed Martin, according to the statement.
“There will be no adverse impact on US defense readiness as a result of this proposed sale,” the department stressed.
The US depleted much of its Patriot missile stockpile during the war with Iran, which was widely reported by American media and confirmed in a Pentagon inspector general’s report last month. A separate Congressional Budget Office assessment said that the Pentagon had consumed between one-half and two-thirds of its inventory of certain missile-defense interceptors since June 2025.
However, US President Donald Trump has downplayed the shortages, claiming that American stockpiles are virtually unlimited.
Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky reacted to the State Department announcement in a post on X, saying that he was grateful to Trump and that 500 Patriot missiles was “a substantial number.”
However, he complained that “it has been stipulated that deliveries may begin only in a few years,” while Kiev needs the interceptors “right now.”
Zelensky claimed US and European countries currently have “sufficient stocks of PAC-3 interceptors in their warehouses,” urging Washington to find a solution that would see them supplied to Ukraine immediately.
“The Russians are attacking our energy infrastructure every single day. In just these past two weeks of October, there have already been more than 30 Russian strikes on critical parts of our power grid,” he said.
On Saturday, the Defense Ministry in Moscow said that Russian forces had conducted more drone attacks against logistics and energy infrastructure supporting Ukraine’s war effort. Among other things, a heating and power plant in Kiev and workshops used for production of UAVs and weapons’ parts in Kharkov were hit, according to the ministry.
Moscow says that the strikes are being carried out in response to Ukrainian terrorist attacks on residential areas and civilian infrastructure inside Russia, to which Kiev resorts in order to compensate for setbacks on the front line.

ICOMOS continues evaluation of Masuleh’s UNESCO World Heritage nomination
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
12:28:15 UTC
21:28:15 KST

ICOMOS continues evaluation of Masuleh’s UNESCO World Heritage nomination
TEHRAN - The evaluation of Masuleh and its cultural landscape for inscription on UNESCO’s World Heritage List is continuing, with an international expert from the International Council on Monuments and Sites (ICOMOS) conducting field assessments and attending specialist meetings on the Iranian town’s architectural, archaeological, ecological and socio-economic heritage.
The ongoing assessment in Gilan province, northern Iran, examines different aspects of Masuleh and its surrounding landscape, including its physical fabric, ecological characteristics, local livelihoods, social structures and management practices, according to the Ministry of Cultural Heritage, Tourism and Handicrafts.
The program includes field inspections and discussions with university professors, researchers and heritage specialists, focusing on safeguarding the town’s Outstanding Universal Value (OUV) while ensuring its long-term conservation and sustainable development.
As part of the assessment, the ICOMOS expert visited the archaeology and anthropology museum of Rasht, where historical collections from across Gilan province, including archaeological discoveries from Old Masuleh, were presented.
Among the notable objects displayed were the Rashi silver-gilt goblet and the Toleh gold goblet from Talesh. The artefacts offer evidence of the region’s ancient history and sophisticated metalworking traditions.
Specialist sessions also examined archaeological excavations and experimental archaeology, particularly research into historical iron-production technologies. Researchers presented findings from a project involving the reconstruction and experimental operation of ancient iron smelting furnaces, shedding light on Masuleh’s industrial history.
Last year, an interdisciplinary research team successfully reconstructed a medieval iron smelting and casting complex at the Old Masuleh archaeological site, demonstrating the technological capabilities of communities that once inhabited the area.
Led by Farzad Asadi, a faculty member at Islamic Azad University, the project involved the experimental reconstruction of a four-stage furnace system documented through approximately two decades of archaeological research.
The experiment went beyond reconstructing the physical structure. Researchers examined its operational characteristics, including airflow, thermal efficiency and the production process from sponge iron to cast iron.
The reconstructed complex featured preheated air channels, permanent stone structures and a dedicated casting installation, distinguishing it from simpler, temporary bloomery furnaces. Laboratory analysis of the resulting slag and iron also indicated high material purity and considerable control over the production process.
Mostafa Pourali, director of the Masuleh World Heritage nomination dossier, has said the second, more detailed reconstruction phase had revealed technological connections with broader Iranian-type furnaces.
The findings point to Old Masuleh's potential role as a permanent iron-production centre and a place of technological exchange along historical trade routes connecting Iran with the Caucasus and Central Asia. The research is expected to be published internationally.
Beyond its archaeological significance, the furnace reconstruction has added an industrial dimension to the understanding of Masuleh's cultural landscape, demonstrating that the settlement's historical importance extends beyond its distinctive architecture and natural setting.
Other discussions during the ICOMOS assessment addressed sustainable destination management and community-based conservation. Participants examined approaches to managing the historic settlement through the active involvement of residents, while protecting its stepped residential fabric and maintaining the relationship between people, the mountainous environment and traditional livelihoods.
Ecological research and archaeobotanical studies also featured in the program. These interdisciplinary investigations aim to improve scientific documentation of the area's historical environmental conditions and the relationship between past communities and their natural surroundings.
The sessions further addressed the physical conservation of Masuleh, including construction regulations, the use of traditional building materials, appropriate restoration techniques and the management of changes in a vulnerable mountain settlement.
According to Iran's nomination dossier, Masuleh is believed to be between 800 and 1,000 years old. Its numerous cemeteries, both within and outside the settlement, are among the archaeological indications of its historical depth.
The town is particularly distinguished by its multi-storey, terraced urban layout, which follows the slope of the surrounding mountain. Its architecture is closely integrated with the natural landscape, while the arrangement of buildings allows the roofs of lower houses to function as pedestrian spaces and courtyards for those above.
The traditional architectural arrangement also reflects the importance of craftsmanship and the visual character of the settlement. With the main facades of houses directly visible to residents and visitors, local builders and artisans paid particular attention to their appearance and architectural details.
The nomination dossier describes the combination of traditional architecture and natural scenery as a potential basis for tourism development, while recognizing tourism and the preservation of local livelihoods as closely interconnected.
The latest round of assessments highlights the need to approach Masuleh as an integrated cultural landscape rather than merely an architectural attraction. Its historic buildings, traditional industries, archaeological remains, ecological setting and living community collectively contribute to its heritage significance.
The continuing ICOMOS evaluation is an important stage in the international assessment of Iran's nomination. ICOMOS serves as an advisory body to UNESCO on cultural heritage nominations, conducting expert evaluations before the World Heritage Committee considers whether a property should be inscribed on the World Heritage List.

Syrian women’s delegation participates in New York UN Security Week in first
An official Syrian women’s delegation attended the UN’s Women, Peace and Security Week in New York, reports said on Saturday, allowing the group to relay their struggles amid over a decade of war and displacement as well as their growing role in decision-making.
This is the first time a women’s delegation from Syria has attended the event, which included several bilateral meetings, events and social gatherings.
The event also included a UN Security Council open debate on women, peace and security.
Nahla Othman, the Director of Expatriate and Refugee Affairs from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, told local media that women in the country have long faced persecution, and that the new government since the fall of the Assad regime has been working to expand the role of women in state institutions.

Earlier this year, 22 women representatives were selected in the new Syrian parliament, the first to sit since the overthrow of Assad in 2024.
Their appearance at the first session of parliament in August garnered widespread conversation on the increased diversity in Syria, and changes underway.

Iran lawmakers call for withdrawal from NPT: Will we have war or peace?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
12:22:45 UTC
21:22:45 KST

Iran lawmakers call for withdrawal from NPT: Will we have war or peace?
Withdrawal from the nuclear treaty doses not mean that Iran would build a nuclear weapon, observers say.
Several Iranian lawmakers have called for the country’s withdrawal from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT), as United States President Donald Trump says the war on Iran will be “wrapped up” soon.
The lawmakers’ demands come as Qatari mediators returned to Tehran this week to mediate peace talks with the US.
Before the US and Israel’s war on Iran began on February 28, Washington and Tehran had already been engaging in indirect nuclear negotiations mediated by Oman. Iran had also stated on numerous occasions that it had no plans to develop nuclear weapons.
Trump has also repeatedly stated that Iran “cannot have a nuclear weapon”, making it a non-negotiable condition for ending the ongoing conflict and securing a permanent deal.
Iran, however, has demanded certain conditions be met before it will talk again about its nuclear programme – including an end to the US naval blockade of its ports in and around the Strait of Hormuz, the lifting of sanctions and a guarantee there will be no more attacks.
The war, which is entering its ninth month, has upended global energy and financial markets with the closure of Hormuz.
On Friday, Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi hit back at Friedrich Merz after the German chancellor said the war on Iran has added more than 100 billion euros ($112bn) to Europe’s energy costs.
In a post on X, Araghchi noted that Merz had “hailed” the US and Israel’s attacks on Iran in June of last year, when he said: “This is the dirty work Israel is doing for all of us.”
The Iranian foreign minister then warned that any renewed attacks could come at a far higher cost for Europe.
“100bn Euro is nothing compared to the Earth-shattering blow Iran’s Powerful Armed Forces will deal against those who dare harm our people,” Araghchi wrote. “Red lines are a thing of the past,” he added.
Could Iran withdraw from the NPT, and what would that mean for diplomatic efforts to end the war?
Here’s what we know:
Which Iranian lawmakers are calling for withdrawal from the NPT, and why?
On Saturday, Iranian legislator Mahmoud Nabavian called for Iran to withdraw from the NPT and change its nuclear doctrine, adding to similar demands from other lawmakers and public figures.
“Now that we have paid the heavy costs of war and sanctions, it is time for the Iranian nation to withdraw from the NPT treaty and change the nuclear doctrine,” he wrote on X.
In parliament, Ebrahim Rezaei, a member of the National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, said 10 proposals to withdraw from the treaty had been registered, and withdrawal was under consideration, according to the Fars news agency.
Mohammad Javad Haj Ali Akbari, an Iranian politician and scholar, also called for a review of Iran’s nuclear doctrine, describing it as a “national demand” during his sermon on Friday, state broadcaster IRIB reported.
He said the demand was not a hasty or emotional reaction, but reflected Iranians’ awareness of what he described as US failures to honour commitments.
Separately, in a report earlier this week, Iran’s Tasnim news agency reported calls for Iran to withdraw from the NPT and accused the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) of becoming politically aligned with the US and Israel.
Last month, an IAEA resolution expressed “grave concerns” about Iran’s “continued noncompliance” with its obligations under the NPT, to which it is a signatory.
But the IAEA has not had access to key nuclear facilities in Iran since the US and Israel launched a 12-day war against the country in June 2025, which included attacks on key Iranian nuclear sites, such as the Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan facilities.
Iran has condemned the IAEA resolution, calling it baseless and politically motivated.
What is the NPT?
The Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons is a landmark international treaty aimed at preventing the spread of nuclear weapons and promoting peaceful uses of nuclear energy.
It was opened for signature on July 1, 1968, and entered into force on March 5, 1970. The treaty was negotiated by the US, the Soviet Union and the United Kingdom.
Under the NPT, nuclear-weapon states agree not to transfer nuclear weapons or assist non-nuclear-weapon states in developing them.
Non-nuclear-weapon states also agree not to seek or acquire nuclear weapons.
The treaty views nuclear-weapon states as those which manufactured and tested a nuclear weapon or other nuclear device before January 1, 1967. Those countries are the US, UK, France, China and Russia. The treaty also paves a path for these original nuclear weapons powers to phase out their arsenals.
A total of 191 countries are now part of the treaty. Non-signatories include India, Pakistan, Israel and South Sudan.
The treaty supports the right of all signatories to access nuclear technology for peaceful purposes under safeguards overseen by the United Nations nuclear watchdog, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA).
Among the 11 articles of the treaty, one allows a country to withdraw with three months’ notice “if it decides that extraordinary events … have jeopardised the supreme interests of its country”.
Iran signed the NPT in July 1968 and ratified it in February 1970 as a nonnuclear-weapon state.
It has since stated consistently that its nuclear programme is for peaceful purposes and research only. The IAEA has conducted inspections under the treaty’s safeguards system.
Has there been any response from Iran’s leaders?
Iranian leaders have not yet responded to demands from lawmakers to withdraw from the NPT.
But on October 24, according to Iranian media reports, the Paydari Front, a hardline faction aligned with conservative groups, also called on parliament to withdraw from the NPT.
Withdrawal from the NPT would not automatically mean that Iran would build a nuclear weapon. Officially, the Iranian government’s position on not seeking nuclear arms remains unchanged.
In June, Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs noted that lawmakers are preparing a bill to withdraw Tehran from the NPT.
“In light of recent developments, we will take an appropriate decision,” ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei had said at a news conference. “[The] government has to enforce parliament bills, but such a proposal is just being prepared, and we will coordinate in the later stages with parliament.”
But Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian has said Tehran’s policies align with Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei’s longstanding religious edict against weapons of mass destruction. “The Zionist regime is the only possessor of weapons of mass destruction in the region,” Baghaei had said, referring to the Israeli government.
What has Trump said about ‘wrapping up’ the war?
The US President has repeatedly stated that Iran “cannot have a nuclear weapon” and made this a non-negotiable condition for ending the ongoing conflict and securing a permanent deal.
In a speech at Daytona Beach, Florida late on Friday, he brought up Iran several times and repeated claims about destroying its navy and air force. “We are never going to give them a nuclear weapon,” he said.
Trump also denied that the US had started the war, saying, “This was a war they started many years ago,” and “Iran has been waging war on America since 1979.″
Separately, in an interview with Kansas City radio station KCMO on Friday, he said the war is “going to get wrapped up soon” but said Washington needs “a guarantee there’ll never be a nuclear weapon”.
Mohamed Elmenshawy, a Washington-based analyst, told Al Jazeera that Trump wants to end the standoff with Iran “whether through peace or war as quickly as possible”, and may launch new attacks after the November 3 midterm elections.
“What breaks this state of stalemate, this condition of ‘no peace, no war’, is either achieving some progress in the negotiating track, or the attacks beginning anew,” Elmenshawy told Al Jazeera.
He said Trump believes “time is on his side”, pointing to “strict economic pressure” on Iran, including the US naval blockade that has curtailed Tehran’s ability to export oil as well as sanctions on Iranian aviation and land border closures by several other countries.
Elmenshawy said Tehran “must realise” Trump will not let the conflict “remain suspended like this” and that this pressure should push “the Qatari and Pakistani mediators to drive the efforts more forcefully in order to avoid the path of war”.
Trump faces “pressure from the Israeli side to launch the attacks, and opposite pressure from the Arab Gulf side to push the negotiating track”, he added, saying Trump, “whose next moves cannot be predicted”, could yield to either.
On Saturday, the spokesperson for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), Mohammad Akraminia, sent a warning to US President Donald Trump, writing on X that its armed forces are “closely monitoring America’s movements in the region”.
Akraminia said that if the US president “resorts to another adventure in the region” along with Israel, then Iran will retaliate significantly.
“There is no doubt that the flames of war will engulf a much wider area, and the end of the conflict will not be in his [Trump’s] hands,” Akraminia wrote.
“Given the US President’s track record of betraying diplomacy,” and citing Trump’s “distrustful” nature, Akraminia said the IRGC’s armed forces are “relentlessly enhancing their combat readiness”.
What was the position before the war began?
Before the US and Israel attacked Iran on February 28 this year, Tehran and Washington were in active nuclear negotiations.
At talks in Geneva, mediator Oman said both countries had made “significant progress”.
Just one day before the US-Israeli attacks started, Oman’s foreign minister said Iran had agreed to reduce its nuclear stockpiles to “the lowest level possible”. Then the war began.
Almost eight months later, the war has brought this position no further forward.
In fact, more problems, with the closure of the Strait of Hormuz upending global energy markets and most recently, the Iran-aligned Houthis and Saudi Arabia locking horns, have threatened the Middle East’s regional stability.
Furthermore, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told Al Jazeera in September that Iran no longer trusts negotiations with Washington because attacks had come during previous rounds of talks.
Christopher Featherstone, associate lecturer at the Department of Politics and International Relations at the University of York in the UK, told Al Jazeera that the war has set the potential for negotiations all the way back to square one, and it will take significant diplomatic effort to initiate any meaningful negotiations, let alone achieve success in those negotiations.
“Intermediaries will be cautious about being seen to be too close to the US if the conflict reignites, and Iran has shown a strong willingness to reject a ‘deal’ that would favour the Trump administration too heavily,” he said.
What diplomatic efforts are happening to de-escalate the war?
On Friday morning, Qatari mediators, in coordination with US officials, returned to Tehran in an apparent bid to revive the June ceasefire that quickly fell apart over control of the Strait of Hormuz.
Days earlier, they delivered a letter from US Vice President JD Vance to Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, proposing renewed peace talks, according to US media.
Iranian sources have confirmed to Al Jazeera that Tehran received a letter from the US on ending the war and suggested the Qatari delegation had come to collect Iran’s response.
The sources said a meeting to discuss a new diplomatic path could be held within a week, either in Doha or Istanbul.
Meanwhile, Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry, spokesman for Pakistan’s military, told the Reuters news agency his country is “cautiously optimistic” about mediation efforts between Iran and the US as regional countries seek to revive a ceasefire in the eight-month-old war.
He suggested on Friday that there were positive signs in attempts to de-escalate the conflict. His comments to Reuters were the first since a high-level delegation visited Tehran this week.
Ali al-Sari, a former member of Iran’s parliament, said there are positive indications from both Tehran and Washington on the diplomatic track, despite a military buildup on both sides.
“The response has not been clear so far, but there are indications on the Iranian side, and also in my view on the American side, that the signs are somewhat positive rather than negative,” al-Sari told Al Jazeera.
He said the US is reinforcing its military buildup, while Iran is strengthening its forces “in the Strait of Hormuz and along the borders”. He added that “the coincidence of this message with the Qatari mediation is significant.
“For this reason, Tehran is studying its response carefully and has not rushed, but it wants something in return, even amid a tense situation between the two parties,” he said.
He pointed to the repeated visits of the Qatari delegation, which “came, then returned, then came again”. In his view, this suggests that the Qatari mediation and other mediation efforts, including Russia’s mediation, mean coordination with the US is continuing and is a “positive sign”. Al-Sari also highlighted the US ambassador to Turkiye Tom Barrack’s recent comments that the US and Iran are “very close” to a deal to de-escalate tensions.
Is peace or renewal of war more likely after the US midterm elections?
Currently, Washington and Tehran have sent mixed signals about whether the eight-month war is heading back to full-scale attacks or towards a peace deal.
On Thursday, the head of US Central Command (CENTCOM), Admiral Brad Cooper, briefed US President Donald Trump on options for renewed attacks on Iran, The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported.
The Wall Street Journal also reported that Trump was briefed on options for renewed attacks on Thursday. On the same day, US Senator Chris Murphy said he had been briefed on the war plan and described it as “insane”.
Separately, US media reported that Washington has warned Gulf allies to prepare for potential military action after the November 3 midterm elections.
“There has been little signal from either side of a move to a formal peace, but there is the potential for another cautious temporary ceasefire,” Featherstone said.
“After the midterm elections, if Trump loses both Houses, he will be severely limited in his ability to pursue his domestic agenda. This could push him to be more active on the international stage, and the Iran conflict would likely be a focus for his attention,” he added.
“However, he has set out almost no sign of how he would measure victory or success in this war, so a path out of the conflict is incredibly unclear,” he said.
Abas Aslani, a researcher at the Center for Middle East Strategic Studies in Tehran, said a deep lack of trust lies behind Iran’s failure to respond to the US proposals it has received.
“Washington wants Iran to make concessions on the nuclear issue in advance, but Iran insists on the seven conditions,” Aslani told Al Jazeera, referring to Tehran’s seven-point plan to end the war.
“In Iran, they fear that if they commit and fulfil their obligations, the United States will not honour its obligations and will backtrack. Instead, the United States would launch another attack.”
He noted that Trump is “trying to use this potential agreement to promote it to the public and to use it for electoral purposes in the United States”, while “Iran wants an agreement that will be vital and bring peace to the region.”
Aslani said “the conditions and the sequencing” also remain in dispute.
Iran is using mediators to send a message “that its position has not changed”, he said, but Washington “also insists on its position”.
“We don’t see any tangible progress – but despite this, efforts are still ongoing,” he added.

Humanitarian hub set up to receive participants in mission to temporarily occupied Oleshky
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
12:20:00 UTC
21:20:00 KST

Humanitarian hub set up to receive participants in mission to temporarily occupied Oleshky
According to an Ukrinform correspondent, the hub is ready to receive those evacuated from the city.
1 / 12
Representatives of the Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights, medical workers, a psychological support service and volunteer organizations are on site. Mobile heating points have been set up, and hot meals are being provided. Wheelchairs are available for people with limited mobility. An area with water and food has also been prepared for pets. A separate vehicle was allocated to transport animals as part of the humanitarian mission.
A medical mission representative at the humanitarian hub, doctor Bohdan Komlevyi, told reporters that everyone arriving will first undergo a medical examination, and first aid will be provided on site if necessary.
"We have all the specialists, from surgeons to physicians. If anyone needs urgent medical assistance, we will immediately take them to a medical facility," Komlevyi said.
Yuliia Stefaniuk, a representative of World Central Kitchen in Ukraine, told reporters that dietary meals, children's food packages and pet food had been prepared for those leaving Oleshky.
"We have adapted the meals to accommodate possible dietary restrictions, including low-fat broths. We have borshch, a traditional dish associated with home. We want them to feel that they are returning to their family. We have prepared buckwheat with chicken, a dietary meal to help them regain their strength, as they still have a journey ahead. For the children, we have special packages with treats, hematogen, which is important during the autumn-winter period, fruit purees and snacks to lift their spirits. We will also give them fruit and sweet muffins for the road," Stefaniuk said.
She added that, together with the Hachiko Foundation, they had provided food, water and pet carriers for domestic animals.
Hot drinks are also being served to people waiting to welcome their family members from Oleshky.
One of the women, Zhanna, left Oleshky after Russia blew up the Kakhovka Hydroelectric Power Plant. She came to the border area after learning about the humanitarian mission to meet her husband. She brought him some salo (cured pork fat).
"He loves salo. He promised to bring me his homemade pickled tomatoes. Kherson-style pickled tomatoes and Kyiv salo – that will make a fantastic dinner. It's emotionally difficult. For three years, we communicated only by phone. Imagine what the people leaving there must be going through – it's a shock, it's grief over everything they've lost. They will need time to recover," she said.
She also said the situation in Oleshky is difficult. The humanitarian mission had now delivered food there, and recently the Ukrainian Armed Forces had also been delivering humanitarian supplies by drone.
"If the road to the villages is demined, perhaps people will be able to bring in food. My husband lived for three years on what he grew himself," Zhanna said.
Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets reported on Telegram that the participants in the humanitarian mission to Oleshky were already in Belarus.
"We'll be home soon! We are now in the Republic of Belarus – together with our people and even their pets!" Lubinets wrote.
As reported, agreements to carry out a humanitarian mission to Oleshky were officially confirmed on October 23, 2026. International humanitarian mediation was provided by U.S. First Lady Melania Trump and her team. The agreements were confirmed on the Ukrainian side by Ukraine's Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets and on the Russian side by Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova.
Lubinets headed the Ukrainian negotiating team responsible for implementing the mission, while his Russian counterpart, Lantratova, led the Russian team. As part of the mission, the ombudsmen, acting as heads of the negotiating teams, agreed to establish a ceasefire, clear transport routes to Oleshky of mines, deliver humanitarian aid, and allow anyone wishing to leave to travel either to territory controlled by the Ukrainian government or to the Russian Federation.
To enable the humanitarian mission, Ukraine and Russia agreed to observe a ceasefire in the area around temporarily occupied Oleshky from October 27 until 22:59 on November 1.

'Keep Rahul Gandhi mock PM for life': BJP's dig at INDIA bloc's 'public impeachment' of CEC

"Keep him as your mock Prime Minister for life," Sambit Patra's dig at Rahul Gandhi.

Iran warns of unfettered retaliation if attacked as mediators try for peace

Iran warns of unfettered retaliation if attacked as mediators try for peace
Iran’s supreme leader says Tehran’s potential response will not be restricted by geography.
Tehran, Iran – Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has issued a strongly worded message to the Iranian armed forces, as mediators continue to try to prevent a new breakout of war between Iran and the United States.
Senior diplomats from Qatar held extensive talks in Tehran on Friday, with further talks expected to take place on Saturday.
Iranian authorities say they are prepared to respond forcefully amid reports that the US and Israel are preparing for new strikes on Iran.
The office of Iran’s Supreme Leader, Khamenei, who has not been seen or heard from since replacing his assassinated father, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, in March, said on Saturday that he met with senior military commanders and gave them “important strategic directives”.
Khamenei required “maximum deterrence” through preparedness for “an immediate and effective response, without geographical restriction” if the country is attacked again, according to a statement released by the office.
It comes days after US Vice President JD Vance wrote a letter to Tehran, reportedly addressed to Mohsen Rezaei, the Supreme National Security Council leader who has become a central power in strategic decision-making in Iran despite failing over decades to garner enough votes for public office.
Exact details of the letter are unclear, but Vance is believed to have called for nuclear commitments from Iran, including allowing international inspectors to monitor the country’s nuclear programme and determining the fate of Iran’s highly enriched uranium, which Tehran has said will not be shipped abroad.
Talks
US President Donald Trump earlier rejected reports that he had ordered renewed peace talks, instead claiming without elaborating that the Vance letter was concerned with allowing medical supplies into Iran.
According to Iranian media, Tehran’s proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within several days in exchange for a return to the June memorandum of understanding still remains the baseline for the mediated negotiations.
Tehran’s demands include the lifting of a US maritime blockade on Iranian ports, waivers on oil sanctions, and a truce for regional conflicts, including in Lebanon where Israeli forces continue to occupy the country’s south.
Local media confirmed that Iran received the letter, although they did not say whether any official response has been given through mediators.
An Iranian state-linked Jomhouri-e Eslami (“Islamic Republic”) newspaper published an editorial on Saturday saying that even though the chances of reaching an agreement with the US were slim and fighting could break out after the US midterm elections on November 3, it was still imperative to give a positive response to negotiations and meetings over the coming days.
“We must not allow war to be accepted as the inescapable fate for Iran,” it said.
Iran and the US have kept up their attempts to assert control in the Strait of Hormuz. The IRGC has continued attacking ships and warns of a lingering threat from alleged naval mines. The US military provides guidance and cover for a shuttle system to get oil from Arab states out of the waterway.
Local authorities reported on Saturday afternoon that two fishing boats were bombed by a US drone south of Qeshm island in southern Iran, wounding several fishermen.
Iranian state television claimed late on Friday that at least six tankers, including a very large crude carrier bearing two million barrels of oil, were damaged by explosions after allegedly hitting mines in recent days while transiting “unauthorised” routes in the strait. It also released footage recorded from a small boat close to a larger vessel that was dealing with a fire.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) on Friday reported a new type of attack that occurred a day earlier. It said a tanker was approached by a small boat which attached two explosive devices to the hull above the waterline, resulting in a blast that caused a fire in the engine room and temporarily disabled the vessel northeast of Oman’s Khasab.
The maritime monitor said it recorded 155 inbound and 122 outbound transits through the Strait of Hormuz in the week ending October 28, which was 70 percent lower than pre-war levels.
In a video message on Friday, US Central Command chief Brad Cooper said he flew over the strait and saw dozens of vessels carrying cargo, crude oil and liquid natural gas while being supported by US aircraft and sea drones.
“I didn’t see the IRGC out there at all,” he said. “They patrolled the Strait of Hormuz and surrounding waters for decades, harassing and threatening and seizing commercial vessels at will. But they were not out there because Iran’s navy is all at the bottom of the sea.”
‘Red lines a thing of the past’
The rhetoric coming from Tehran has only hardened after eight months of war. In line with Khamenei’s Saturday statement, army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia warned the Trump administration against attacking Iran.
“If the US president once more embarks on adventurism in the region through threats and greed of the Zionists, the fire of war will undoubtedly engulf a wider geography,” he said, in reference to Israel.
Other senior officials took aim at Washington’s European allies, who expressed backing for both the US-Israeli offensive on February 28 and last year’s 12-day war.
After German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the costs of war had exceeded 100 billion euros for Europe over the past eight months. Iran’s security chief Rezaei said Europe was “whining” now even though it cheered the war earlier.
“When you cheered on war crimes, did you think the fallout wouldn’t hit you, too? War and terror come at a price. Now it’s your turn to pay,” he wrote on X.
Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi also reminded that Merz had celebrated Israel and the US “doing the dirty work” for Europe during last year’s war.
“100bn Euro is nothing compared to the Earth-shattering blow Iran’s Powerful Armed Forces will deal against those who dare harm our people,” he wrote. “Red lines are a thing of the past”.
US Senator Chris Murphy said earlier this week that he had a meeting with senior officials about what a short and blistering US military campaign would look like if the war resumes.
“Their plan is insane. It will lead to devastating escalation and the likely destruction of our commitment to the rule of law,” he said.
Eric Brewer, deputy vice president for the Nuclear Materials Security Program for the US-based Nuclear Threat Initiative, said it is entirely unclear what would be achieved through extensive air strikes against Iran’s infrastructure, considering that Trump earlier this week bemoaned that Iran has focused on rebuilding after earlier attacks.
“There is no military solution for remaining nuclear sites [Pickaxe, Esfahan tunnels], and the program remains generally paused. Striking energy targets is unlikely to cause Iran to capitulate to US negotiating demands,” he wrote on X, adding that Iran will also retaliate across the region if attacked.
“They will aim to make the war not just more painful for the US and its partners, but longer than we would prefer,” Brewer said. “The risks of this operation far exceed any gains.”

Abuse survivors look to Pope Leo for accountability, lasting reform
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
12:13:00 UTC
21:13:00 KST

As Pope Leo prepares for his return to South America, Peruvian abuse survivor Pedro Salinas reflects on the hope and lingering doubts surrounding the pontiff’s efforts to confront sexual abuse within the Catholic Church.
For a decade, Salinas followed the Church’s investigation into Sodalitium Christianae Vitae, a Peru-founded Catholic movement he helped expose over allegations of sexual, physical and psychological abuse.
The effort culminated in the final days of Pope Francis’ papacy last year, when the Vatican dissolved the group and its affiliated branches.
“What was achieved, nobody, absolutely nobody, could even have imagined. It was inconceivable. But it happened,” said Salinas, 63, a journalist and former member whose reporting played a key role in bringing the allegations to light.
Robert Prevost, now Pope Leo, quietly supported survivors and advocates during his time as a bishop in Peru and later as a Vatican cardinal, Salinas said.
He attended meetings, helped gather information and maintained contact with those involved through WhatsApp and email.
“Without him, the needle didn't move,” Salinas said.
The first U.S.-born pope will travel through Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from Nov. 6 to 17, spending the final six days in Peru, where he arrived as a missionary in the 1980s and later became a citizen and served as bishop of Chiclayo. The Vatican said he will meet with clergy abuse survivors there, as he has done on other recent trips.
Survivors say they wonder whether Leo's approach in Peru, which they credit with helping bring about the rare step of dissolving a Catholic community, can translate into broader change across a Church where accountability remains uneven.
“What is lacking are bishops everywhere in the world committed to this issue,” Salinas said.
Peru is preparing for a tourism boom during Leo's visit. José Enrique Escardó, 56, president of a Peruvian survivors network, views the excitement from a different perspective.
While Escardó acknowledged that some survivors credit Leo with helping dissolve Sodalitium, he said the Church's actions have not delivered sufficient justice, accountability or reparations.
“Survivors have grown tired of being told things, of being promised things, but nothing being done,” Escardo said. “We feel more abandoned. We feel deceived.”
He wants survivors to have a role in shaping Church policy and believes reparations should include psychological care and education.
The Vatican did not respond to a request for comment.
Francis, the first Latin American pope, left a complicated legacy, survivors say.
Juan Carlos Cruz, a survivor whose case became central to Francis' 2018 reckoning with abuse in Chile, credits the former pope with introducing changes that included revisions to canon law, the removal of the pontifical secret, the Church's highest level of confidentiality, from abuse cases, and the introduction of Vos Estis Lux Mundi, a Vatican framework for addressing allegations of abuse or cover-ups involving bishops.
“We're still at the tip of the iceberg,” said Cruz, whom Francis appointed in 2021 to the Pontifical Commission for the Protection of Minors. “The commission has been working for years on universal safeguarding guidelines, and those standards need to be applied around the world.”
Anne Barrett Doyle, co-director of the watchdog group BishopAccountability.org, which tracks Catholic Church abuse allegations worldwide, called Vos Estis the most significant action Francis took on abuse. But she said the Vatican rarely makes clear whether an accused bishop's resignation represents punishment.
“The public is left in the dark,” she said.
Barrett Doyle said the Vatican has not released global disciplinary data comparable to figures it provided to a United Nations committee in 2014. Her group relies on public records, media reports and investigations by prosecutors, governments and commissions to track cases.
She wants Leo to make permanent removal from ministry the universal rule for priests found under canon law to have sexually abused children, extending worldwide a policy adopted by U.S. bishops in 2002.
“To say that no child molesters should be out to practice as priests is just such a no-brainer,” she said. “It's a step that Leo could take now.”
Vatican officials have previously cited the difficulty of creating a single abuse reporting law across all countries and argued that removing priests can put them beyond Church supervision.
Angela Walker, executive director of the U.S.-based Survivors Network of those Abused by Priests, said survivors increasingly turn to civil authorities because of the Church's “incredible failure” to police itself.
“There needs to be more transparency, more openness and more accountability,” she said. “I will believe it when I see it.”
In Mexico, survivors pressed the Vatican on clerical abuse decades before it became a defining crisis across Latin America. Among the most notorious cases was that of Marcial Maciel, the Mexican priest who founded the Legion of Christ order and whose accusers took their allegations to the Vatican in the 1990s. The Vatican ordered Maciel in 2006 to withdraw from public ministry. He died in 2008 without ever facing his accusers.
The scale of his abuse became clearer after his death. In 2019, the Legion reported that Maciel had abused at least 60 minors, among 175 instances of child abuse the order documented involving 33 priests over eight decades.
Jose de Jesus Barba Martin, 87, alleged that Maciel abused him while he was studying for the priesthood in the 1950s. He recalled survivors struggling to be heard by Church and state authorities in the late 1990s and said an appeal he sent to Pope John Paul II went unanswered.
Decades later, that experience has left him with little expectation that another appeal to Rome would bring change.
“The Church is made up of two types of men: good and bad, courageous and cowardly,” he said. “It will take a long time, and the issue will not be addressed under this pope nor the next.”
Alberto Athie, 72, a former Mexican priest who pursued clerical abuse cases from inside the Church before leaving the priesthood in 2003, sees Leo's visit as another opportunity to push for transparency.
pedr
“I do have hope,” he said. “But my hope fades just the same ... Things have to be fixed within the Church.”
Abuse survivor Sebastian Cuattromo said the Argentine Church should have been “at the international forefront” of confronting abuse under Argentine Pope Francis but fell short of what he had hoped to see.
“There is a major outstanding debt,” Cuattromo said.
Argentina's Episcopal Conference declined to comment.

UN wraps up 3-decade-long mission in conflict-hit Somalia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
12:11:00 UTC
21:11:00 KST

The United Nations political mission in Somalia officially ended Saturday following a two-year transition, bringing to a close more than three decades of U.N. political and peacebuilding operations in the East African country.
Established by the U.N. Security Council in 2013, the United Nations Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNSOM) supported Somali authorities in efforts to strengthen democratic governance, uphold the rule of law and rebuild state institutions after more than two decades of conflict involving militias, terrorist groups and criminal gangs.
The mission traces its origins to 1995, when the U.N. established the United Nations Political Office for Somalia (UNPOS).
In May 2024, Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud requested the mission's closure ahead of the expiration of its mandate in October that year.
He later revised the request, proposing a two-year transition period to allow for an orderly handover.
During the transition, UNSOM was replaced by the U.N. Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNTMIS).
"Today is not an end to the partnership between the United Nations and Somalia. Rather, it marks the conclusion of one chapter and the beginning of another," said Raisedon Zenenga, UNTMIS officer-in-charge and the U.N. secretary-general's deputy special representative for Somalia, in a statement.
"While significant challenges remain, the closure of UNTMIS comes after considerable progress by Somalia since the early years of international efforts to support the country's recovery," he added.
The mission's responsibilities have been transferred to Somali institutions or the U.N. country team.
The transition comes as Al-Qaeda-linked Al-Shabaab, which has fought the Somali government for two decades, continues to control large swaths of central Somalia despite a major international military campaign against the group.
The fight against Al-Shabaab faces growing pressure from international funding cuts, particularly after the United States withdrew all funding for a key U.N. logistics mission, raising questions about the future of military operations.
Somalia is scheduled to hold parliamentary and presidential elections next May, but persistent insecurity and disputes between the government and opposition threaten the electoral process.

- ‘I don’t believe that saying something is brave. I don’t believe that saying something is courageous. I believe that saying something is human’
- ‘I think Ed Sheeran was probably quite surprised by the backlash that he received, but I think it really shows that the tide is turning on this issue,’ says attendee
- Ben performed on stage in custom "Free Marwan" shirt. The bold garment served as high-profile demonstration of solidarity with Marwan Barghouti, highly influential Palestinian political leader who has been held in Israeli prison since 2002
US rapper Macklemore performed to a sold-out crowd at London’s OVO Arena Wembley on Friday night, bringing his three-city European “Free Palestine Tour” to a close with a lineup of musicians, activists and speakers expressing solidarity with Palestinians.
The concert, which followed previous stops in Dublin and Paris, featured performances by British singer Paloma Faith, alternative hip-hop group Cure for Paranoia, political hip-hop duo Dead Prez, and Palestinian and Arab artists Nemahsis, Lina Makoul, Shadia Mansour and Dana Salah.
Aja Monet and DJ Habibeat also joined the lineup.
The event combined musical performances with political speeches and messages of solidarity, featuring Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg, Holocaust survivor Stephen Kapos and Palestinian activist Arab Barghouthi.
The evening also included a screening of a short film by Palestinian journalist Bisan Owda and contributions from Nadia Greenspan.
 
‘Those children in Gaza are our children’
Macklemore was welcomed by loud cheers and chants of “Free Palestine” before performing “Hind’s Hall,” his protest song released in response to the war in Gaza.
Addressing the audience, the rapper explained why he had decided to speak publicly about the conflict.
“I was scrolling, scrolling, scrolling and seeing the horrific, unimaginable catastrophe that was happening in front of our eyes,” he said.
“And at a certain point, it was more uncomfortable for me to stay silent than to say something.
“And I just want to say, I don’t believe that saying something is brave. I don’t believe that saying something is courageous. I believe that saying something is human.
“And those children in Gaza are our children. There is no separation. We have bought into this idea, this insane notion that we are separate. We inherited borders, we inherited fences, we inherited walls.
“My question is: what are we doing as a global community to tear them down?”
He also thanked concertgoers for attending and praised the sense of togetherness inside the arena.
‘Palestine is moving toward its South African moment’
Macklemore performed on stage wearing a custom “Free Marwan” shirt. The garment served as a demonstration of solidarity with Marwan Barghouti, an influential Palestinian political leader who has been held in an Israeli prison since 2002.
Marwan Barghouti’s son, Arab Barghouthi, joined the rapper on stage during the London concert.
Addressing the crowd at OVO Arena Wembley, Arab Barghouthi spoke about his father’s longstanding imprisonment.
He drew parallels with the global solidarity movement that helped bring down the apartheid regime in South Africa, stating that “Palestine is moving towards its South African moment.”
‘Gaza is so much more than the devastation we see on our screens’
Thunberg, who addressed the audience during the event, highlighted Palestinian culture and resilience beyond the destruction and suffering shown in media coverage.
“Gaza is so much more than the devastation we see on our screens,” Thunberg said. “It is a place of extraordinary people, culture, history, love and joy, and tonight we honor not only what Palestinians have endured, but everything they continue to preserve.”
The concert was organized by Macklemore following his removal from a planned support slot on Ed Sheeran’s US tour in September, after venues reportedly objected to his pro-Palestinian remarks.
All proceeds from the Wembley event were directed toward humanitarian aid organizations, including Medical Aid for Palestinians, UNRWA USA, the Gaza Soup Kitchen and HEAL Palestine.
‘Macklemore gives us a bit of hope’
Speaking to Anadolu, attendees highlighted the importance of public figures and celebrities showing support for Palestinians, saying their voices offer hope and encourage continued awareness of the situation.
Salem, a British-Palestinian concertgoer whose parents were displaced during the 1948 Nakba, said: “He’s done a fantastic job for the Palestinians. […] But people like Macklemore give us a bit of hope, give us a glimmer of hope that we can change things around a bit.”
Another attendee, Sheila, described the concert as an important demonstration of solidarity, praising Macklemore for continuing to express support for Palestine despite criticism and pressure.
“We are here today in Wembley, where Macklemore is performing his Free Palestine concert. It is absolutely an amazing show of solidarity,” she said.
“It is so important that we have figures like Macklemore in the entertainment industry who have not backed down in the face of repression and attempts to silence them. He has been steadfast in his solidarity with Palestine.”
“I think Ed Sheeran was probably quite surprised by the backlash that he received, but I think it really shows that the tide is turning on this issue,” she underlined.
Anne, another concert attendee, said she had come to support both Macklemore and the Palestinian people, stressing the importance of speaking out against injustice.
Pointing to her earrings bearing the message “No justice, no peace,” she said people must continue raising their voices in support of those suffering.
“We have to treat everybody correctly, and we have to raise our voices and say what is happening, and not be put down by other people’s feelings,” she said.
“There is a genocide going on. There are children dying. There are people in pain, and we have to stand up for that and say: You are not alone. We support you in any way we possibly can.”

Evacuees from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in Ukraine's southern Kherson region arrived in Ukraine on Saturday after travelling through Belarus amid a humanitarian truce between Kyiv and Moscow.
Video footage shared on social media by Dmytro Lubinets, the Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights, showed some of the evacuated residents stepping off a bus draped in Ukrainian flags and embracing loved ones after crossing the border.
"The moment we had all been waiting for: residents of Oleshky have crossed the border — the humanitarian mission has been successfully completed!" Lubinets wrote alongside the clip, while also thanking US First Lady Melania Trump for her help brokering the deal.
"This entire mission was successfully carried out thanks to her involvement," he said.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the evacuees had crossed into Ukraine in the Chernihiv region in the north of the country and that they would now "receive the assistance they need."
They had earlier touched down in Gomel in southeastern Belarus before continuing their journey.
Melania, who helped broker the localised ceasefire, said on Friday that a convoy was ready to evacuate more than 750 people "who voluntarily choose to leave Oleshky."
"It includes 25 buses, 50 medical professionals, and ambulances," she said.
The ceasefire is due to last until Sunday evening.
Russian strikes on Ukraine
It comes as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said around 280,000 Ukrainian households had been left without power after Russian strikes overnight.
"Russian strikes have created a difficult situation with electricity supplies across our regions," Zelenskyy wrote in a post on X.
He said around 200,000 households in Dnipro and the wider region were without electricity while a further 80,000 or more in the Kyiv region were also without power.
"Repair crews are working to deal with the aftermath of the strikes and doing everything they can to restore electricity supplies," he said, adding that Russian forces had hit a "combined heat and power plant" in Kyiv on Friday night as well as four electrical substations in the eastern Dnipro region, among other targets.

Fitch revises France's IDRs outlook to negative

21:01:29 KST

PARIS, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- Fitch Ratings said Friday that it has revised France's long-term issuer default ratings (IDRs) outlook to negative from stable while affirming the country's rating at "A+".
The negative outlook reflects weaker economic growth, higher borrowing costs and a wider budget deficit since its August 2026 review, which together have worsened France's debt dynamics from an already weak starting point, it said.
Persistent political fragmentation and a challenging social environment have made it more difficult for France to achieve sustained fiscal consolidation, noted the report, adding that however, the country's rating remains supported by its large, wealthy and diversified economy, strong institutions, membership in the euro area and resilient banking sector.
Fitch forecasts France's public debt-to-GDP ratio to rise from 115.7 percent in 2025 to around 124 percent in 2028, up from its previous forecast of 122.7 percent. It noted that a large share of public spending is politically difficult to reduce, while the already high tax burden leaves little room for further revenue increases.
The agency also noted that the French government projected in late September that the budget deficit would reach 6.4 percent of GDP in 2027 without additional consolidation measures, up from its previous projection of 5.9 percent. The draft 2027 budget targets a deficit of 5.0 percent of GDP and includes politically difficult measures.
Fitch lowered its forecasts for France's real GDP growth to 0.5 percent in 2026 and 0.9 percent in 2027, from previous estimates of 0.8 percent and 1.1 percent, respectively, citing weaker economic data in the first half of 2026.
France's GDP contracted 0.1 percent in the third quarter of 2026, according to preliminary data released Friday by the French National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies. Fitch said the figure in the third quarter further highlights downside risks to its growth forecast. ■

====================================================================================================

Analysis of FDA reports finds Prozac’s sexual side effects vary widely, with some emerging years into treatment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
12:00:39 UTC
21:00:39 KST

A recent study published in Progress in Neuropsychopharmacology & Biological Psychiatry suggests that sexual side effects associated with the antidepressant fluoxetine are highly varied, involving severe sensory disruptions alongside changes in libido. Using computer modeling, the researchers found that the drug may interfere with immune and cellular stress proteins, offering clues about the biological mechanisms behind these symptoms.
Fluoxetine is a widely prescribed medication used to treat depression and anxiety. It belongs to a class of drugs called selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or SSRIs. These medications work by increasing the availability of serotonin, a chemical messenger in the brain that helps regulate mood. While effective for mental health conditions, these drugs frequently produce unwanted sexual side effects.
Lead authors Jun Li and Xing Wang, along with corresponding author Honglin Hu from Nanchang University in China, initiated the investigation to better understand these adverse reactions. Previous research pointed to serotonin as the primary culprit, as heightened serotonin activity can suppress other brain chemicals like dopamine, which drives sexual arousal. The research team suspected that other biological networks, such as inflammation and cell survival pathways, might also be involved in these side effects. They combined real-world patient reports with advanced computer simulations to explore this hypothesis.
The scientists began by extracting data from the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System. This public database collects voluntary reports of adverse drug reactions from patients and healthcare professionals. The team filtered the records from 2004 to 2025 to isolate cases where fluoxetine was listed as the primary suspected drug. They analyzed 997 reports related to sexual dysfunction to see if certain side effects were disproportionately associated with the medication.
The analysis revealed strong statistical signals for a wide range of sexual problems. Common issues like erectile dysfunction and decreased libido appeared frequently in the patient reports. However, the researchers observed the strongest reporting intensities for highly specific conditions. Symptoms such as a total inability to climax, decreased orgasmic sensation, and genital numbness showed unusually high reporting rates compared to traditional measures of sexual dysfunction.
Following the database analysis, the team calculated the time it took for these symptoms to appear after a patient started taking the medication. They only included reports that contained complete date information for both the start of treatment and the onset of the side effect. They used statistical distribution models to map out the timing patterns for different symptoms across the patient population.
The timing of the side effects varied greatly depending on the specific symptom. Some conditions, such as prolonged and painful erections or persistent genital arousal, emerged within the first few days of treatment. Issues related to sexual desire, such as a loss of libido, tended to surface after about four to five months. The most delayed side effects involved sensory and orgasmic disruptions, with reports of genital numbness and an inability to climax often appearing after more than two years of continuous medication use.
To understand the biological roots of these symptoms, the researchers turned to network toxicology. This computational approach maps out how drugs interact with the body by cross-referencing vast genetic and protein databases. The team first compiled a list of human proteins known to interact with fluoxetine. They then created a separate list of proteins and genes associated with human sexual dysfunction.
By comparing the two lists, the scientists identified 56 overlapping genetic targets. These shared targets operate within networks that control brain chemistry, including both serotonin and dopamine pathways. The overlapping targets were also heavily concentrated in biological pathways that regulate inflammation, immune responses, and cellular death.
The researchers built a digital map to visualize how these 56 targets interact with one another inside the body. This mapping process identified two core hub proteins that act like major intersections in a city traffic grid, handling a high volume of biological signals. The first is IL10, a protein that helps regulate the body’s inflammatory and immune responses. The second is TP53, a protein that responds to cellular stress and helps control when a damaged cell undergoes programmed death.
To see if the drug could physically influence these proteins, the team used a technique called molecular docking. This computer simulation predicts how a small drug molecule might fit into the three-dimensional structure of a larger protein. It operates much like a simulation of a key entering a lock.
The simulations showed that the fluoxetine molecule fits neatly into the structural pockets of both the TP53 and IL10 proteins. The binding affinity was notably strong for the IL10 protein. This physical compatibility suggests that the drug might directly attach to and alter the function of these proteins in the human body. The researchers suspect that fluoxetine might contribute to sexual side effects by triggering low-level inflammation or cellular stress in nerve and reproductive tissues.
Because the FDA database relies on voluntary submissions, it cannot capture the true frequency of these side effects in the general population. The reporting system also lacks complete information on drug dosages, the duration of treatment, and the patients’ other medications. These missing details prevent researchers from determining exactly how much of the drug is required to trigger a specific symptom.
The database does not track the severity of a patient’s underlying depression. Since depression itself is associated with bodily inflammation, it is difficult to isolate the medication as the sole driver of the immune system changes observed in the data. The underlying mental health condition may be contributing to the same biological pathways highlighted in the computer models.
The computer models used to predict protein interactions are entirely theoretical. While molecular docking shows that a physical bond is possible, it does not confirm how the drug behaves inside a living human body. Physical laboratory experiments and clinical trials are necessary to verify these biological mechanisms.
The study, “Deciphering the molecular mechanisms of fluoxetine-induced sexual dysfunction: Evidence from pharmacovigilance, network toxicology, and molecular docking,” was authored by Jun Li, Xing Wang, Yunfeng Zhang, Penglin Zhang, Zhenfa Tan, Ruizhen Huang, Zuhuan Xu, Zhiyu Zhou, and Honglin Hu.

Why You Shouldn't Toss Your Old Halloween Pumpkins In The Trash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
12:00:03 UTC
21:00:03 KST

The only thing scarier than Halloween? Getting rid of a sad looking jack-o’-lantern when it's over.
When confronted with a rotting, deflating carved pumpkin, your first instinct might be to beeline to the trash as quickly as possible. But experts caution against doing so—warning that trashing pumpkins, and thus sending them to landfill, can release harmful greenhouse gases into the atmosphere.
“Everybody throws them out from Halloween to right after Thanksgiving,” says Kay McKeen, executive director at Scarce, an environmental education non-profit. “It's a huge burst of methane gas that's going into the landfill all at one time.”
Why shouldn’t you trash your pumpkin?
When pumpkins are sent to landfill, they release methane, a potent greenhouse gas that, over a 20 year period, is around 80 times more powerful at trapping heat in the atmosphere when compared to carbon dioxide.
The lack of oxygen in landfills causes pumpkins to rot “anaerobically,” which releases methane. They are also full of water, and when they mix with waste and moisture it creates leachate, a toxic sludge that can pollute the environment.
Though a single pumpkin might not do much damage, if you consider how many pumpkins are trashed each autumn, it adds up.
“Maybe if we had a handful of pumpkins going into that waste stream, that might be one thing,” says Chris Enroth, horticulture educator with the University of of Illinois Extension, which organizes annual “Pumpkin Smash” events to help people recycle and compost old jack-o'-lanterns and pumpkins. “But we have millions of people who buy multiple pumpkins. We're talking about hundreds of millions of pumpkins that need to be disposed of post Halloween, and it's just a massive amount of organic material that goes into the landfill system.”
How do I get rid of my pumpkin?
Composting sidesteps many of the harms that come with sending food waste, like pumpkins, to landfill.
“When we compost something, it's really a whole system that we're creating that introduces both water and oxygen, [and uses] microbes, bacteria, fungi, all the little decomposers,” says Enroth. “When we introduce those things, we get that aerobic composting process, so we don't produce methane, and we're able to turn those pumpkins back into organic matter that has nutrients and can be put back out into the garden.”
What’s the best way to compost? If you have a curbside compost bin or designated compost for your apartment building, you can throw it there. If not, see if there are any drop-off composting sites near you. Some areas even organize dedicated events for residents to drop off old pumpkins. Since starting “pumpkin smashes” in 2014, Scarce and Illinois Extension have saved over 1,600 tons of pumpkins from landfill.
Don’t leave your pumpkin out for animals to eat or dump it in a park—they can be harmful to wildlife. While pumpkins are generally safe for most wildlife to eat, some small animals, like hedgehogs, can become sick, different animal species congregating together could increase the risk of disease, and it can attract predators to residential areas.
As you’re thinking about composting, keep in mind that it’s not just pumpkins that are compostable. Food is the single most common material sent to landfills in the U.S.—and wasted food is responsible for 58% of landfill methane emissions. If you’ve been thinking about starting your own home compost, now is the best time to do it, says Enroth. “We often recommend to folks thinking about starting a compost pile, to try it in the fall because we usually have leaves, grass clippings, things to get that pile started. And you could incorporate that pumpkin into that compost pile,” he says. “It's a really good combination of materials for you to get compost out of it next year.”
