How to ‘fall back’ this weekend without losing your mind
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
11:19:23 UTC
20:19:23 KST

At 2 A.M. on Sunday, most of the U.S. will set the clocks back by an hour. With the switch to standard time, we’ll get earlier sunshine and darker evenings—and an extra hour of sleep.
Research suggests standard time better aligns with our circadian rhythm, or internal clock, and reduces the risk of health complications. But changing to standard time comes with some risks, too, experts say.
Between “falling back” to standard time in November and “springing forward” to daylight saving time (DST) in March, experts say the switch to DST is the bigger disruption. In the days after the March time change, scientists have measured higher rates of lost sleep and an uptick in heart attacks. After the time change in November, however, those risks are lower.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Some research suggests rates of stroke go up around both spring and fall clock changes, although the risk of death is higher in the spring, says Beth Malow, a professor of neurology and pediatrics at Vanderbilt University.
On standard time, early risers get the benefit of a little more morning sunlight. Morning light is “one of the strongest forces” that aligns our bodies’ circadian rhythm with the outside world, Malow says. That alignment helps us wake up in the morning and drift off at night more easily.
After the fall time change, you might wake up well after the sun comes up—but that poses less of a risk than cutting off your body’s internal clock early, says Jamie Zeitzer, a professor and a sleep scientist at Stanford University. “You’re basically sleeping in,” he adds.
In fact, given the overall benefits of standard time, top medical organizations, including the American Medical Association, Sleep Research Society and American Academy of Sleep Medicine have fought efforts to make DST permanent—a frequent hobbyhorse in Congress.
A major downside to standard time, however, is less time spent outdoors. Some studies also suggest moving commuting times nearer to dusk in the fall increases the risk of vehicle collisions with deer and other wildlife, which are more active around sunset.
There are certain steps you can take to ensure a more smooth transition, experts say.
Number one, don’t go into a clock change while sleep-deprived, Malow says. And try to get as much exposure to morning light as possible throughout the season. (If you’re able to access one, a light box can be helpful for this on dark mornings in the spring.) Stay alert during dark commutes, when visibility may be limited, whether they’re on a spring morning or a fall evening, Malow adds. And if you’re consistently struggling with sleep, consider seeing a doctor.
In the fall, you may need to take extra care to get regular evening exercise in. And if you, like many Americans, aren’t getting enough shut-eye on most nights, consider using the clock change to set a new sleep habit, Malow says.
If your usual bedtime is 11 P.M., for instance, try going to bed when you’re tired instead—after the time change, that will be when the clocks read about 10 P.M.—and try to stick to the new schedule. “Take advantage of the fact that your body’s now going to be ready to go to bed earlier,” she says.
If nothing else, relish “sleeping in,” Zeitzer says. “Enjoy the extra hour of sleep.”

How your brain can turn your own reflection into something unrecognizable
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
11:19:02 UTC
20:19:02 KST

It’s Halloween night. Someone has dared you to turn off the lights and stand in front of the mirror. The rules are simple, stare into your reflection and say her name three times.
Bloody Mary. Bloody Mary. Bloody Mary.
According to the creepy urban legend, a terrifying figure will appear in the glass. Depending on which version of the story you follow, she might be a bloodied woman, a witch or a ghost seeking revenge. Sometimes, she simply appears behind you. In more sinister versions, she reaches out of the mirror.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Most of us encountered some variation of this story as children. Those brave enough to have tried it may even swear they saw a monstrous face appear in the mirror before them.
As tempting as it might be to believe that the monster you saw in mirror was something supernatural, the real explanation is perhaps even stranger. Your brain is perfectly capable of turning your own reflection into something you barely recognize.
The monster in the mirror
In 2010, Italian psychologist Giovanni Caputo published a study with the intriguing title Strange-face-in-the-mirror illusion. He asked 66 volunteers to sit approximately 40 centimeters from a mirror in a dimly lit room and look at their own faces for one minute.
Around two-thirds reported significant distortions of their faces. More than a quarter described seeing an unfamiliar person, while others reported fantastical beings, animals or the faces of relatives – sometimes deceased. Some changes began after less than a minute.
The participants weren’t being asked to summon ghosts. They were simply looking at themselves. So why would something as familiar as our own face suddenly become strange?
The explanation partly lies in the 1804 work done by Swiss physician Ignaz Paul Vital Troxler who described a curious phenomenon. When we fix our gaze on one point, objects elsewhere in our visual field can gradually fade from awareness. This is now known as the Troxler effect, or Troxler fading.
This effect happens partly because sensory neurons, which detect and transmit information about what we see, adapt to relatively constant stimulation. Our visual system is particularly interested in change: movement, shifting contrast and anything that might require our attention.
Normally, we hardly notice this process. Even when we believe we’re staring steadily, our eyes make tiny movements that continually refresh visual information. But prolonged fixation can allow relatively stable features, particularly those away from the centre of our gaze, to become less distinct.
Now imagine applying this to your face. When you stare at your own eyes in a mirror, the surrounding features remain relatively stationary. The contours of your cheeks, the edges of your nose and the outline of your mouth provide a fairly constant pattern of information.
But in dim light, those features are already harder to distinguish—so the Troxler effect alone cannot explain why someone might see an entirely different face. For that, we need to consider how the brain recognizes faces.
Human beings are extraordinarily sensitive to faces. We can recognize familiar people from surprisingly little visual information and detect subtle changes in expression.
This ability involves a network of brain regions, including the fusiform face area, which responds particularly strongly to faces. Rather than analyzing every feature independently, our visual system processes the relationships between them—including the distance between the eyes, the position of the nose and the arrangement of facial features.
When you look into a mirror, your brain isn’t simply recording what is in front of you. It interprets visual information using previous experience and expectations—and there’s perhaps no face you know better than your own. But under dim lighting, the information arriving from your eyes becomes less reliable. Shadows obscure features, contrast diminishes and the relationships between parts of the face become harder to resolve.
The brain must continue interpreting this increasingly ambiguous information. Sometimes the result is a distorted version of your own face. Sometimes it resembles another person altogether.
The mechanisms behind these illusions are still under investigation. But what makes the experience disturbing is that the reflection remains recognizably human while no longer appearing to belong to you.
Haunted mirrors
Long before children began summoning Bloody Mary, reflective surfaces were associated with spirits, prophecy and the dead.
The ancient practice of catoptromancy involved divination using mirrors. Related traditions of scrying involved gazing into reflective surfaces in the hope of seeing visions or messages hidden from ordinary sight.
Mirrors also acquired significance in mourning traditions. In some communities, they were covered following a death because of the belief they could trap the soul or reveal the dead. Other traditions have different explanations for covering mirrors – including setting aside concerns about personal appearance during mourning.
We cannot conclude that visual illusions gave rise to these customs. But it’s intriguing that prolonged staring, low illumination and the expectation of seeing something unusual feature in both supernatural mirror rituals and experiments producing perceptual distortions.
The Bloody Mary ritual adds another ingredient: anticipation. You expect something frightening, and that expectation may influence how you interpret ambiguous shadows and unfamiliar features.
In this way, the ritual creates the very conditions in which something unsettling might appear. The legend tells you what to expect, and your visual system may provide something that seems to confirm it. So, this Halloween, remember that you don’t need to believe in ghosts for something strange to happen.

Citing an Iranian source, Al-Araby Al-Jadeed said the delegation was in the Qatari capital, Doha, "to facilitate engagement with the Qatari mediator."

The discussions also paved the way for the Iranian negotiating team to accompany the Qatari delegation on its return trip to Doha, according to the report.
"Negotiations with the US side are taking place indirectly through the mediator, not directly," the Iranian source told the newspaper.
 
- US delegation expected to join talks
Sources close to Qatar- and Pakistan-led mediation efforts also told Al-Araby Al-Jadeed that an American delegation was expected to join the diplomatic process in Doha.
The sources said the US delegation could hold direct talks with Iranian negotiators in the Qatari capital.
The reported developments could pave the way for Washington and Tehran to resume negotiations following an agreement on initial measures addressing Iran's nuclear program, navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and financial incentives for Tehran.
The potential arrangement would also involve China and Russia as guarantors, according to the newspaper.

Advanced new naval anti-air missiles to arrive later this year
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
11:14:06 GMT
20:14:06 KST

Deliveries of new Aster Block 1 missiles will begin later this year, and considerable progress has been made over the past twelve months in upgrading the existing stock to the same standard, though the number converted so far is being withheld on security grounds, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked what progress has been made on upgrading all Royal Navy Aster missiles to Block 1 standard through Sea Viper Evolution Capability 1.
Luke Pollard, Minister of State for Defence, said: “The upgrading of missiles to Aster Block 1 standard is being undertaken through the Aster Mid-Life Refresh programme. The exact number of missiles upgraded to date cannot be disclosed owing to security concerns, however considerable progress has been made over the last 12 months. Additional deliveries of new Aster Block 1 missiles will commence later this year.”
Aster is the missile family behind Sea Viper, the air defence system carried by the six Type 45 destroyers, and the Block 1 standard brings an improved capability against ballistic missiles as well as aircraft and cruise missiles. Sea Viper Evolution is the wider upgrade programme announced after HMS Diamond and HMS Richmond spent months intercepting Houthi drones and missiles in the Red Sea, where the Royal Navy fired Aster in anger for the first time.
Stock depth has been the question hanging over that capability since those engagements, because a destroyer carries forty-eight cells and an intercept uses one missile or two. Replacing what was expended and raising the standard of what remains are the two halves of the same problem, and the department has consistently declined to put numbers on either.
Aster is produced by MBDA, with final assembly in France and significant British content including the Sampson radar and the command and control system from BAE Systems. The Defence Investment Plan commits £6 billion to munitions this Parliament, including £1.5 billion for an always on production pipeline.

Patriot sale to Ukraine approved, but first missiles may be years away
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
11:11:42 UTC
20:11:42 KST

- President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said deliveries of 500 U.S.-approved PAC-3 MSE interceptors may begin only in several years, too late for this winter.
- He asked the United States for 100 Patriot interceptors a month from existing stocks, replenished later by the newly approved production.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says the 500 Patriot PAC-3 MSE interceptors the United States cleared for sale to Ukraine on Oct. 30 will not help this winter, because deliveries may not begin for several years. He asked Washington to send interceptors from existing U.S. and allied stocks now and replace them later from the new production run.
The U.S. State Department notified Congress of the possible $2.1 billion sale on Oct. 30. It is funded by donations from Canada, Germany and Norway through the JUMPSTART mechanism and by Ukrainian national funds drawn from the European Union’s Ukraine Support Loan, with no U.S. money involved. The notification gave no delivery schedule.
“Five hundred PAC-3 interceptors is a substantial number, and very soon – this winter – they COULD make for a highly effective defense package. However, it has been stipulated that deliveries may begin ONLY IN A FEW YEARS,” Zelenskyy wrote on X.
Alex Raufoglu, a correspondent for Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, reported that the 500 are new-build missiles and that, according to his sources, deliveries are not expected until after 2030. Neither the State Department nor Lockheed Martin has published a delivery date.
Lockheed Martin built 620 PAC-3 MSE interceptors in 2025, and in January it signed a seven-year framework agreement with the U.S. Department of War to raise annual output from about 600 to roughly 2,000. New Foreign Military Sales orders join a queue that already includes U.S. Army replenishment and earlier buys by Poland, Germany, Japan, Gulf states and other operators. A new case also has to clear congressional review, be turned into a signed letter of offer and acceptance, and be placed on contract before the missiles enter that queue.
Zelenskyy asked instead for a winter package of 100 interceptors a month from existing stocks, which would deliver the equivalent of the 500 approved missiles in about five months, with partners’ arsenals replenished later by the production Ukraine and its allies have already paid for.
“The United States, our European partners, and other partners around the world have sufficient stocks of PAC-3 interceptors in their warehouses. Providing them to Ukraine right now – in the winter of 2026–2027 – and replenishing our partners’ arsenals LATER, in THE FOLLOWING YEARS, through this production already contracted and paid for by Ukraine and our partners would be the right approach,” Zelenskyy wrote.
On Oct. 27, Zelenskyy told journalists that Ukraine had received an average of 12 Patriot interceptors a month from the United States in 2026, a fraction of the 100 a month he is now requesting, while Russia fires roughly 150 ballistic missiles a month that need intercepting. In his post, he said Russia had made more than 30 strikes on critical parts of Ukraine’s power grid in the past two weeks of October alone, targeting electricity, heating and water supplies before winter began.
PAC-3 MSE is the Patriot interceptor Ukraine relies on against ballistic missiles: it destroys its target by direct impact, and its two-pulse motor extends range and altitude against maneuvering threats such as Russia’s Iskander and Kinzhal. Ukraine also uses older PAC-2 interceptors, but Ukrainian officials have repeatedly described PAC-3 as their only effective defense against Russian ballistic missiles. Shortages have pushed Ukrainian crews to engage some ballistic targets with a single interceptor instead of the usual two or more.
In April, Zelenskyy said U.S. deliveries under NATO’s PURL program had not stopped but that Ukraine’s interceptor shortage remained critical. In August, CNN was given access to a Ukrainian Patriot battery that had not fired in six weeks because its launchers had no interceptors to load. On Oct. 19, Ukrainian officials told the Kyiv Independent that U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth had not approved the transfer of a significant batch of Patriot interceptors that Ukraine’s allies had already paid for, and suggested the delay was meant to pressure Kyiv. A U.S. government official called those claims “not true.” The Washington Post reported the same day that the Trump administration had not approved transfers of interceptors from partner countries.
Asked about the delayed transfers, Hegseth said on Oct. 20 that Washington’s posture toward Ukraine had not changed, but that the U.S. military wanted to keep as many interceptors as possible for its own forces. U.S. inventories have been drawn down by the war with Iran that began in February; the Center for Strategic and International Studies has estimated that U.S. stocks of Patriot and other interceptors fell by about half during that conflict. The Hill reported this week that President Donald Trump is weighing new military strikes on Iran after the Nov. 3 midterm elections. U.S. officials have not publicly linked that decision to the interceptor transfers.
Citing NATO sources, Euronews reported that allies were pessimistic about Ukraine receiving more interceptors before the midterms, and that NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte had asked Greece and Spain to hand over some of their own interceptors without success.
In September, the European Commission approved €6.1 billion in defense procurement for Ukraine, including PAC-3 interceptors bought under a special exception to the EU loan’s preference for European-made weapons, though it did not disclose how much went to Patriot missiles.
“We are asking for decisions that can guarantee the protection of lives not the day after tomorrow or sometime later, but at the very moment the threat is there – when Russia is killing and destroying,” Zelenskyy wrote.
Zelenskyy thanked President Donald Trump, the State Department and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, with whom he said he had recently discussed PAC-3 interceptors. Washington has not responded publicly to his request for interim deliveries, and the delivery schedule for the 500 missiles approved on Oct. 30 remains undisclosed.

Persian language proficiency test held for 200 international students
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
11:11:09 UTC
20:11:09 KST

Persian language proficiency test held for 200 international students
TEHRAN – Around 200 international students took the second Persian language proficiency test on Friday at examination centers in Iran and abroad, demonstrating growing interest in learning the language.
Organized by the Organization of Student Affairs, the test was held at four centers, namely Ferdowsi University in Mashhad, Razi University in Kermanshah, Allameh Tabataba’i University in Tehran, and the University of Tehran’s international campus in Baghdad, Iraq, IRNA reported.
“International students who are interested in majoring in Iranian universities are required to complete 480 hours of Persian instruction under the supervision of professional and expert instructors in preparation for the Persian language proficiency test,” IRNA quoted Saeed Habiba, the head of the Organization of Student Affairs, as saying.
More than 50 Persian language teaching centers are operating in Iranian universities, he added.
The goal is to make sure international students have mastered essential skills required for studying in Iranian universities, and they are enabled to better benefit from educational materials within their respective fields of study, Habiba further noted.
The first Persian language proficiency test for international students was held on February 12 in Tehran.
On January 24, Abbas Qanbari-Baghestan, an official with the Organization of Student Affairs, said attaining a specified score in learning the Persian language will be a key requirement for foreign students to be admitted to Iranian universities from the next academic year, which will start in fall 2026.
The test includes listening, speaking, and writing sections, he added.
Highlighting the importance of providing quality education for international students, the official said Persian language teaching centers play a key role in attracting foreign students and preparing them to major in universities. So, they should do their best to employ experienced professors to provide the best educational courses to help foreign students learn the Persian language.
Nearly 60,000 foreign students are currently studying in Iranian universities, compared with 35,000 students in the past Iranian academic year, which started on September 22, 2024.
Despite existing challenges, Iran has managed to attract students from 101 countries, Saeed Habiba, the head of the Organization of Student Affairs, said in October 2025.
The scientific capacity of the country’s universities and their positive record in international cooperation are a valuable opportunity that must be seized to transform the presence of foreign students into a national discourse and strategic planning, the official said, adding that the students are mainly from Afghanistan, India, Iraq, and Pakistan.
Attracting 320,000 intl. students by 2028 on agenda
According to the Seventh National Development Plan (2023-2028), the country is projected to increase the number of international students to 320,000 from currently around 60,000.
To this end, the higher education system needs to adopt some institutional and developmental approaches in organizations associated with foreign students, Mehr news agency reported.
In this regard, the parliament research center has evaluated Iran’s situation in attracting international students and measures that need to be taken into account.
According to the report, the number of foreign students in the country has grown from 13,767 in Iranian year 1394 (2015 – 2016) to 68,563 in 1403 (2024 -2025). The number of educational institutions that are allowed to accept foreign students has noticeably increased from 45 to 206 over the past decade.
The report also shows that 13 acts, such as providing short-time sabbaticals, granting visas, establishing a center for foreign student graduates, and holding remedial courses, have been developed and officially accepted by the parliament as part of educational charter for foreign students; however, they have not been implemented in time.
Also major organizations and institutions of the country have no participation in planning cultural programs for foreign students.
A lack of strategic comprehensive marketing skills, and bureaucratic and time-consuming correspondence were among other recognized problems.
The parliament research center has put forward some proposals to help attract more international students. The most important one highlights adopting an approach that focuses on generating income, soft cultural power, and expanding science.
The other suggestion emphasizes the importance of boosting south-south international relations, that is developing political and economic interactions with highly populated countries like Pakistan, India, Egypt and some countries in Central Asia.
Ongoing evaluation of other countries’ policies in attracting students, developing software and hardware infrastructures, stable and secure network, as well as increasing the number of scholarships are among other suggested solutions.

Baghdad seeks to beef up pharmaceutical partnerships with Tehran
TEHRAN – Iraq has called for expanded pharmaceutical cooperation and joint investment in healthcare infrastructure with Iran, highlighting opportunities to strengthen bilateral ties in the health sector.
Iraqi Health Minister Abdul-Hussein Aziz Al-Mousawi, accompanied by his deputy ministers, visited Iranian pavilions at Health Expo Iraq, held from October 28 to 31 at the Baghdad International Fair, Mehr News Agency reported.
During the visit, the Iranian delegation briefed the Iraqi officials on the participation of around 30 Iranian companies, which showcased more than 40 product brands across various sectors, including pharmaceuticals, dietary supplements, raw materials, machinery, technology transfer, medical equipment, condensed milk, cosmetics, and hygiene products.
On the sidelines of the visit, Al-Mousawi highlighted the importance of deepening collaborations with Iran, including developing joint pharmaceutical industries, establishing joint forums and specialized interaction platforms in the health sector, and expanding manufacturing infrastructure with the participation of Iranian companies.
The sixth edition of Health Expo Iraq, the country’s annual international health exhibition and congress, offered Iranian health-sector manufacturers a valuable opportunity to enter the Iraqi market and expand their business in the neighboring country.
The expo featured a wide range of products and services, including medical equipment, laboratory devices, pharmaceuticals, hospital supplies, and healthcare services. The expo also hosted seminars, workshops, and panel discussions that encouraged industry professionals to share knowledge and experiences and build new business connections.
The Iranian delegation set up their pavilions to feature the products and achievements of the Iranian knowledge-based firms, establish connections between Iranian and Iraqi experts and stakeholders, hold B2B meetings, and identify the needs of the Iraqi market in the field of health.
With a population of over 46 million and the pharmaceutical market valued at 4 billion dollars, Iraq is one of the biggest health markets in West Asia. The country is planning to meet 70 percent of its pharmaceutical needs through domestic production by 2027.
Iraq seeks broader scientific ties with Iran
In October, Iraqi Ambassador to Iran Yasser Abdulzahra Al-Hajjaj stressed that scientific cooperation between the two countries should extend beyond student recruitment to include joint research projects, exchanges of professors and researchers, and stronger technological ties.
Universities are not merely educational institutions; they also serve as bridges for dialogue and the exchange of expertise among scientists from different countries, particularly Iran and Iraq, IRNA reported.
He made the remarks while addressing a national festival held at the Iran University of Science and Technology on October 20.
Referring to the significant progress achieved in bilateral scientific relations, Al-Hajjaj said today that thousands of Iraqi students are studying in more than 80 Iranian universities, majoring in medical and non-medical fields, across the country.
The past two Iran-Iraq science weeks brought together over 70 and 80 university chancellors of the two nations, and more than 250 memoranda of understanding (MOUs) were signed, indicating a good experience in expanding scientific collaborations.
The official said that the establishment of a branch of Tehran University of Medical Sciences in Iraq promoted and stabilized academic relations between Iran and Iraq more than ever.
He went on to say that a branch of University of Tehran will be inaugurated in Karbala and Najaf in the near future. He expressed hope that a branch of Sharif University of Technology and Iran University of Science and Technology would be launched in Iraq as well.
According to the official, Iraq is expanding its educational and research infrastructures, and with the increase in the number of domestic universities, the majority of Iraqi students would tend to study at home.
Given that 85 percent of Iraqi students in Iran are employees who, based on the new legislation in Iraq, will have problems studying abroad, the official suggested considering the situation as an opportunity rather than a threat to revise the model of scientific interactions between the two sides. Otherwise, the probable decrease in the number of Iraqi students in Iran would give rise to new challenges.
The Iraqi official called for the implementation of joint research projects in medical, agricultural, sand and dust, oil, gas and emerging technologies like artificial intelligence.
Developing joint educational courses and co-supervising theses were among other issues highlighted by Al-Hajjaj.
On October 18, Iran’s scientific counselor in Iraq, Mohammad-Javad Najafi, and Iraqi Deputy Minister of Higher Education and Scientific Research, Haider Abd Dahed, discussed ways to strengthen academic cooperation between universities in the two countries, with a focus on problem-solving approaches and addressing domestic and regional needs.
Collaboration on problem-oriented research, the provision of scholarships, the facilitation of educational issues for students, and preparation for the ‘Third Iran-Iraq Science Week’ were the key topics discussed during the meeting, IRNA reported.
The officials also discussed conducting collaborative research projects, supervising joint dissertations for postgraduate degrees, and publishing joint scientific articles in globally reputable magazines.
Addressing the challenges and educational problems faced by the students in reciprocal countries was the other issue raised by the two sides.

DRC Ebola outbreak kills over 5,000, raises fears of wider spread
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
11:06:00 UTC
20:06:00 KST

Deaths from an Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo have surpassed 5,000, with the disease continuing to spread despite containment efforts and cases being reported in other African countries, according to the latest government data released Saturday.
Figures from the Congolese Ministry of Health showed that 5,026 people have died among 10,351 confirmed and suspected cases, putting the fatality rate at nearly 50%. The rising death toll has heightened concerns among health experts over the authorities' ability to bring the outbreak under control.
The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo virus, was declared in mid-May, catching health authorities off guard and presenting major challenges to efforts to contain its spread. Since then, the disease has continued to claim lives as infections have extended beyond Congo's borders.
It has become the second-deadliest Ebola outbreak on record, surpassed only by the 2014-2016 West African epidemic, which killed approximately 11,000 people across several countries over two years.
"It is a very tragic milestone because it is just not a number," said Dr. Patrick Otim, a program area manager with the World Health Organization. "It is families and communities that have been devastated by this outbreak. The number also shows the severity of this outbreak."
A total of 2,788 people have recovered from the virus so far. The Bundibugyo virus has no known vaccine or specific treatment, but health workers provide supportive care based on patients' symptoms.
Since May, the disease has spread to 67 of the country's 178 health zones in eight of its 26 provinces. Fifty of the 67 affected health zones have active cases.
The virus has been concentrated in eastern Congo, particularly in Ituri and North Kivu provinces, which have recorded a combined 9,782 confirmed cases and 4,792 deaths.
Authorities are still struggling with contact tracing and testing, key components of efforts to curb the outbreak.
According to the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, about 80% of new cases are being detected outside monitored chains of transmission, meaning health authorities cannot trace the infections to previously identified contacts.
One-third of recorded deaths have involved people who died outside treatment centers before being tested for Ebola, WHO's Otim said. Health officials say these challenges contribute to community transmission beyond the immediate reach of health workers and make it harder to ensure patients receive appropriate care.
"These are people we never had opportunity to try to save, and it is one of the biggest concerns for us in this outbreak. How do we try to reach people early to get them to come to health facilities to get a fighting chance to survive?" Otim said.
The surge in infections in Congo comes amid a series of challenges that have hampered efforts to contain the outbreak.
Eastern Congo, where the outbreak is concentrated, is also the scene of conflict between government forces and several armed groups, most prominently the Rwanda-backed M23 rebel group. An Islamist insurgency along the border with Uganda, where the Allied Democratic Forces carry out attacks, has also restricted the movement and reach of health workers.
Widespread distrust among local communities has further complicated the response, contributing to attacks on health workers and medical facilities. A nurse was killed while responding to an Ebola alert last week, and a politician from the ruling party was killed in September after advocating health measures on the radio.
Health workers have also staged multiple strikes, shutting down facilities treating infected people over prolonged delays in government payments.
On Friday, workers at an Ebola treatment center in Tchomia, Ituri province, stopped working to demand four months of unpaid wages. The center currently has five confirmed Ebola patients and 10 suspected cases under care.
"We are tired of requesting our salaries. If they want to pay us, they will. ... Today, being able to feed our families has become a real problem," Moise Mugenyi, one of the striking workers, told The Associated Press.
Dr. Justin Mukonkole, acting head of response operations in Ituri, said workers should be patient as the government addresses their demands.
Similar situations have unfolded in other health zones, including Beni in North Kivu province, where services at some treatment centers have ground to a halt. Alain Siwako, an elected public official in Beni, said cases were spiraling because of a lack of fuel and financial resources from the central government.
"Across Ituri and North Kivu, this outbreak is stretching everyone responding to it, including the communities themselves," said Rose Tchwenko, country director for the Democratic Republic of Congo at Prosper Global, formerly Mercy Corps.
In October, Kenya and Nigeria both confirmed Ebola cases. Kenya reported eight cases and two deaths, while Nigeria's only confirmed patient was evacuated to Switzerland.
The cases in Kenya and Nigeria, following an earlier outbreak in Uganda, made the latest epidemic the first recorded across three African regions and the continent's most geographically widespread Ebola outbreak.

France deployed 70,000 police officers on Saturday to contain expected unrest during the latest wave of nationwide protests. Authorities are also alert to the possibility that rioters could use Halloween masks to conceal their identities. Nunez noted that existing laws already allow police to ban face coverings when public order is at risk.
The U.S. Embassy in France advised travelers to avoid areas where demonstrations or large gatherings are planned. The protests gained momentum in late September as President Emmanuel Macron's minority government began negotiations over the 2027 budget.
The French government's promises to reform the education system and ease fuel costs have failed to calm public anger. "When I was little, I was told young people were the future," said Aaron Berthier de Grandry, a 15-year-old high school student from the Paris suburb of Nogent-sur-Marne who plans to join his third consecutive weekend of protests. "Well, if we, as the future of France, lack resources, that means France will end up collapsing."
According to estimates from the Chamber of Commerce, damage to retailers has exceeded 1 billion euros. Other estimates put the total at twice that amount when uninsured damage and lost revenue are taken into account.
Meanwhile, the French government is advancing a controversial law that would make rioters liable for up to 10,000 euros in damages caused either by themselves or by groups they are deemed to belong to. Human rights organizations and some lawyers have warned that the legislation could undermine the right to peaceful protest.
The unrest in France has also inspired youth-led protests elsewhere in Europe, with demonstrations planned Saturday in more than 30 German cities.

COP17's marathon talks yield Yerevan Pathway to speed up biodiversity action

Representatives hold small-group discussions during the closing plenary for the 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17) in Yerevan, Armenia, Oct. 31, 2026. YEREVAN, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- Over 100 countries reached agreements at the 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17) in Yerevan, Armenia's capital, after marathon negotiations spanning roughly 12 hours from Friday night through Saturday morning.
The closing plenary marked a breakthrough in efforts to halt and reverse nature loss by 2030, even as divisions over biodiversity finance, harmful subsidies and scientific evidence persisted.
Delegates burst into applause when COP17 President Hambardzum Matevosyan, Armenia's environment minister, banged the gavel to adopt key decisions on the first global biodiversity progress review and resource mobilization.
The outcome renews momentum for the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, which was adopted in 2022 with 23 targets to halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030. With four years remaining, governments face mounting pressure to turn international commitments into measurable action, echoing the theme of COP17: Taking Action for Nature.
"I think we've achieved more than we could have expected in terms of the diversity of the agenda items, in terms of the importance of those items for many countries and parties, and in terms of the items that were anticipated for a long time that have managed to be approved and adopted," Matevosyan said.
"It is wonderful that we have faced up to the gaps identified in the global report. We have adopted the Yerevan Pathway, and now we need to follow this pathway towards 2030," said Astrid Schomaker, executive secretary of the secretariat of the Convention on Biological Diversity.
The Yerevan Pathway became central to discussions on accelerating biodiversity action from 2026 to 2030. Developed through the global review process, it prioritizes stronger national biodiversity strategies, improved monitoring, increased financing, technology transfer and capacity-building.
It also emphasizes whole-of-government coordination and meaningful participation by Indigenous Peoples, local communities, women and young people.
The conference also voted to hold COP18 in Quito, capital of Ecuador, in 2028.
COP17 began on Oct. 19 and was scheduled to conclude on Friday, but proceedings continued into Saturday. ■

75,000-year-old Neanderthal may have been killed by a spear aimed at the heart
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
11:05:20 UTC
20:05:20 KST

75,000-year-old Neanderthal may have been killed by a spear aimed at the heart
- Date:
- October 31, 2026
- Source:
- University of Cambridge
- Summary:
- A Neanderthal who died 75,000 years ago may have been killed by a wooden spear deliberately aimed at the heart, revealing rare evidence of prehistoric violence. A circular hole in the shoulder blade suggests the weapon pierced the chest and caused a rapidly fatal injury. Surprisingly, the same individual had survived an earlier devastating facial injury, suggesting other Neanderthals provided care and support.
- Share:
A small, circular hole in a 75,000-year-old Neanderthal shoulder blade may reveal one of the earliest known cases of deadly violence involving a wooden spear. The remarkable discovery, made in a cave in Iraqi Kurdistan, suggests that the individual was struck by a sharpened wooden weapon that passed through the chest, potentially in a deliberate attack aimed at the heart.
Researchers believe the wound could represent the oldest evidence in the hominin fossil record of fatal interpersonal violence involving a wooden spear.
The shoulder blade (scapula) is an unusually delicate bone, with some areas so thin that light can pass through them. Despite its fragile structure, the Neanderthal's bone survived for approximately 75,000 years beneath seven and a half meters of rock and sediment. Almost the entire bone remained intact, except for a remarkably precise circular opening measuring 15 millimeters across.
A Deadly Spear Wound Reveals a Neanderthal's Violent Death
Archaeologists from the University of Cambridge, who led the excavation, believe the hole was created by a spear with a sharpened wooden point. Its rounded shape is an important clue because weapons tipped with flint or stone generally produce openings with flatter or more angular edges.
Their reconstruction suggests that the spear entered the front of the Neanderthal's left chest, passed through a lung and probably major blood vessels, and continued until it pierced the shoulder blade from behind. Such a severe injury would have caused rapid death. The researchers suspect the blow may have been an intentional "heart shot."
The physical evidence offers additional clues about how the attack occurred. The opening has beveled edges, a feature commonly associated with an exit wound. Small bone fragments displaced during the impact indicate that the weapon likely entered from above and traveled downward through the body.
Using these fragments, the scientists were able to partially reconstruct the damaged area. Subtle ridges left by muscle attachments helped them determine where the pieces originally belonged.
"It's extraordinary to have a perfectly preserved scapula from 75,000 years ago. These bones are so thin that you often don't get complete scapulae from modern burials," said Dr. Emma Pomeroy, study lead author from Cambridge's Department of Archaeology. "We were able to lift it out in one piece from under almost eight meters of rock and sediment."
The remains have been named Shanidar A after the cave where they were uncovered. The findings were published in the journal Scientific Reports.
Ancient Wooden Spears Were Sophisticated Hunting Weapons
Although sharpened wooden weapons were used hundreds of thousands of years ago, relatively few examples have survived. Wood usually decays over time, making it exceptionally difficult for archaeologists to recover evidence of ancient woodworking and weapon technology.
One important discovery occurred in the 1990s at Schöningen, Germany, where researchers uncovered wooden spears preserved in waterlogged conditions. Dating back roughly 200,000 years, these weapons were made during a period when early Neanderthals inhabited Europe.
Some measured more than two meters in length. Their makers carefully selected the wood and shaped the spears to achieve a balance suitable for throwing, much like modern javelins. Archaeologists believe they were probably used to hunt large animals.
Even older evidence comes from Clacton-on-Sea in the United Kingdom. In 1911, a pointed wooden fragment was recovered from the shoreline and later identified as part of a spear more than 400,000 years old. Only its tip had survived, making it the earliest known example of a rounded wooden spear.
The Cambridge researchers believe comparable weapons could have been responsible for Shanidar A's death. If their interpretation is correct, the injury may provide the first evidence that sharpened wooden spears were used in the prehistoric Middle East.
"Holes left by recreations of spears from this time are an excellent fit for the one we found in the Neanderthal scapula," said Pomeroy, a fellow at Newnham College, Cambridge. "That early technology absolutely works for this wound."
"What evidence we have suggests that Neanderthals and their ancestors developed woodworking and weapon-making skills many thousands of years before the death of Shanidar A. This package of capabilities could have spanned the full range of Neanderthal homelands, from Wales to Siberia."
Was the Neanderthal Deliberately Killed?
The discovery raises a difficult question: Was Shanidar A the victim of a deliberate attack, or did a hunting accident cause the fatal injury?
Pomeroy acknowledges that accidents involving wooden spears would have been possible, particularly when Neanderthals hunted large, dangerous animals at close range.
"Animals such as mammoths may have been hunted up close with thrusting spears, so it's easy to imagine lethal injuries."
Nevertheless, certain features of the wound suggest that the blow may have been intentional rather than accidental.
"The position of the wound and the force required to push it right through the Neanderthal's body bear the hallmarks of an intended kill shot directed towards the heart."
The researchers cannot determine exactly what happened or who wielded the weapon. It is also impossible to establish whether modern humans played any role. However, they consider violence between Neanderthals the simplest explanation consistent with the available evidence.
"All we can ever know about the end of this Neanderthal's life is that it was violent, and came at the end of a wooden spear," said Prof Graeme Barker, fellow of St. John's College, Cambridge, who leads the Shanidar Cave excavations.
"Evidence of systematic violence is extremely rare in deep prehistory. The vast majority comes from periods of settled farming communities thousands of years after hunter-gather societies like our Neanderthals."
A Shattered Tooth Reveals a Surprising Story of Compassion
Although Shanidar A appears to have died violently, other evidence suggests this individual received considerable care earlier in life.
Alongside the shoulder blade, archaeologists recovered a nearly complete right hand, two ribs from the left side, a fragment of a right rib, and seven teeth. Together, these are the surviving remains of an adult Neanderthal believed to have been approximately 45 years old at death.
One tooth provides particularly revealing evidence about the individual's life. An incisor from the front of the lower jaw had been split vertically, leaving just half of the tooth intact. Neighboring teeth had also been forced inward.
Researchers believe the damage resulted from a powerful blow to the face. The surviving half of the incisor had accumulated substantial tartar (dental calculus) along its exposed root canal, indicating that the damaged tooth remained in the mouth for an extended period after the injury.
This buildup suggests that Shanidar A survived the original trauma rather than dying immediately. Such extensive facial damage would likely have made eating and communicating extremely painful and difficult.
"Surviving a blow that splits a tooth in this fashion, then continuing to live and eat for a period of at least a year and maybe more, would have required care and support from other Neanderthals," said Pomeroy.
The researchers suggest that other members of the group may have helped Shanidar A survive by providing softer foods. Earlier studies of sediments from Shanidar Cave found evidence that Neanderthals were soaking plant foods before cooking them around this period.
This method of food preparation could have made meals easier for someone suffering from severe facial injuries.
"There's no doubt that Shanidar A would have had difficulty communicating and been in absolute agony for a long period of time."
For the scientists, these findings reveal two seemingly opposite aspects of Neanderthal behavior in the life of a single individual.
"The remains of Shanidar A reflect the dual nature of so much of what we recognize as human. On the one hand, we have evidence of a terribly violent end. On the other, this was clearly an individual who was cared for during their lifetime."
Prof Barker said: "It is fascinating to have evidence for both compassion and violence amongst Neanderthals, our closest evolutionary cousins, embodied in this one individual."
Shanidar Cave Is Transforming Our Understanding of Neanderthals
Shanidar Cave, situated in the foothills of Iraqi Kurdistan, has played a major role in changing scientific views of Neanderthal behavior.
During the 1950s, excavations led by archaeologist Ralph Solecki uncovered the remains of ten Neanderthals. Four individuals were found grouped together in the same location, even though they had died at different times.
Their placement suggested that Neanderthals may have repeatedly returned to a particular part of the cave to bury their dead.
Another remarkable discovery from a different section of the cave involved a Neanderthal who lived thousands of years later. This individual had experienced serious physical disabilities, including a paralyzed arm, arthritis, hearing loss, and partial blindness.
Despite these conditions, the individual survived to an advanced age, suggesting that other members of the community provided assistance and care.
Discoveries like these helped overturn the image of Neanderthals that prevailed during the Victorian era, when they were often portrayed as primitive, brutish, and less than fully human.
Subsequent research has revealed increasingly sophisticated behavior, including cave art and jewelry. Genetic studies have also established that Neanderthals interbred with modern humans, leaving traces of their DNA in populations alive today.
Evidence Suggests Neanderthals Returned to Bury Their Dead
Shanidar A, excavated in 2020, adds another important piece to this growing picture of Neanderthal society.
Since 2015, the Cambridge-led archaeological team has identified three additional Neanderthals within the cave's previously known cluster of remains. These discoveries bring the number of individuals in that particular burial area to five, consisting of four adults and one infant.
All five were found within an extraordinarily confined space measuring approximately 1.5 meters long, one meter wide, and one meter deep.
The location lies immediately behind a large upright boulder that researchers describe as a "prominent marker." Thin layers of sediment separate the individual sets of remains, indicating that the bodies were deposited at different times.
Shanidar A was discovered at the greatest depth within the cluster and may have been the first individual placed there. The body was positioned on its back, with the head pointing east. The Neanderthal found directly above it had been arranged in a similar position.
These patterns suggest that the cave's occupants were not simply leaving bodies wherever space was available. Instead, they may have deliberately chosen a particular location and returned to it repeatedly to lay deceased members of their community to rest.
"The best explanation is intentional and symbolic funerary behavior," said Pomeroy. "These Neanderthals returned to the same place to lay their dead to rest. Some were deposited before the earlier body had fully decomposed, so this was happening within years or decades."
Taken together, the discoveries at Shanidar Cave paint a complex picture of Neanderthal life 75,000 years ago. The same individual who may have died in a deliberate spear attack had apparently survived a devastating earlier injury with the help of others and was eventually placed in a location that may have held special significance for the community.
Far from fitting the outdated stereotype of Neanderthals as simple, brutal creatures, Shanidar A provides rare physical evidence of a society capable of both deadly violence and sustained compassion.

Journal Reference:

Evidence for funerary behaviour and lethal trauma in a new Neanderthal individual from Shanidar Cave. Scientific Reports, 2026; 16 (1) DOI: 10.1038/s41598-026-69193-z

Iran proposes joint peace and friendship park with Armenia for biodiversity protection

Unknown Publisher

Iran proposes joint peace and friendship park with Armenia for biodiversity protection
TEHRAN - Iran has proposed establishing a joint peace and friendship park with Armenia to strengthen cross-border cooperation on biodiversity conservation and wildlife protection in the Caucasus region.
Hamid Zohrabi, deputy head of Iran’s Department of Environment (DOE), met with his Armenian counterpart, Aram Meymaryan, on the sidelines of the 17th Conference of the Parties (COP17), held in Armenia from October 19 to 30, IRNA reported.
The proposed transboundary park would promote joint efforts to conserve biodiversity in northwestern Iran and the Caucasus region, while safeguarding critical wildlife corridors, including those used by the Persian leopard.
The two officials also discussed ways to expand environmental cooperation and address shared challenges, including the protection of the Aras River.
Meymaryan welcomed the proposal and praised the active participation of the Iranian delegation in COP17.
The officials agreed to establish a working group to follow up on the agreements reached after the conclusion of the summit.
COP17 was held in two stages: technical-level discussions followed by the ministerial segment.
The leaders’ summit took place on October 16, featuring an address by President Masoud Pezeshkian. It marked the first time a president of the Islamic Republic of Iran had attended a Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity.
Addressing the summit, Pezeshkian called for “peace diplomacy” to protect biodiversity, condemning the devastating environmental impact of wars of aggression as ecocide and urging the international community to establish effective, transparent and enforceable mechanisms to safeguard natural heritage during wartime.
Shina Ansari, the head of the Department of Environment, also addressed the meeting, saying that environmental diplomacy can become an instrument of peace diplomacy, while the relationship between biodiversity, peace, and security should be viewed as a two-way relationship.
Ansari added the link between biodiversity and peace was not merely an ethical or political issue, but a fundamental concern in environmental governance, international law, and human security.
Under the Convention on Biological Diversity, she said, the main drivers of biodiversity loss are generally understood to include land-use change, habitat destruction, pollution, unsustainable exploitation of natural resources, and climate change.
The Iranian delegation also held a meeting with Vivek Menon, chair of the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Species Survival Commission (SSC), and discussed ways to strengthen cooperation in developing management and conservation programs for endangered species.
The talks particularly focused on conservation and restoration programs for the Asiatic cheetah, the great bustard, and the Persian zebra, onager, their respective habitats, as well as the reintroduction of the Persian fallow deer into its natural habitats.
The two sides also discussed enhancing technical and scientific cooperation and providing funding under sanctions.
Menon expressed hope that ongoing collaboration between IUCN officials and Iranian experts would guarantee the survival of endangered species, such as the Asiatic cheetah, in Iran.
During this year’s summit, Iran officially joined the Coalition of Action to Recover Endangered Species (CARES), which aims to strengthen international cooperation to preserve and restore the country’s wildlife.
The CARES was unveiled at COP17 in Yerevan on October 16. Colombia and Armenia launched the initiative with 17 founding participating governments: Armenia, Belize, Brazil, Canada, China, Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Fiji, Indonesia, Madagascar, Mexico, Panama, Papua New Guinea, Peru, United Kingdom, and Vanuatu. Iran has become a member of the coalition as the 18th country.
The coalition is supported by the Reverse the Red Action partnership as secretariat. The membership document was signed by Zohrabi, on October 26.
Speaking at a meeting on this occasion, Zohrabi underlined the need for equitable distribution of resources and technology to save endangered species.
Iran’s name will be listed on the website of the coalition as a country that has developed action plans for the conservation of 40 wildlife species to benefit from technical, scientific, and financial support from CARES.

Does a forest matter more than a foreigner? That’s where cultures disagree most.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
11:00:36 UTC
20:00:36 KST

People around the world tend to rank their moral obligations toward others in a remarkably similar order, placing family and friends at the top and violent criminals at the bottom, according to a new study published in European Journal of Social Psychology. An analysis of university students across 41 cultural groups indicates that this general moral pecking order holds up across a wide range of societies, especially in nations culturally similar to the United States. At the same time, cultures and individuals frequently diverge when deciding whether distant humans deserve more moral consideration than animals and the natural environment.
Moral concern refers to the personal obligation people feel to care for the welfare and interests of another being or object. Psychologists and philosophers often picture this concept as a “moral circle” made up of concentric rings, where entities placed in the innermost ring receive the highest level of protection and personal responsibility, while those left outside the boundary receive none at all. Where those entities sit inside a person’s moral circle shapes everyday choices, from donating to an animal sanctuary to supporting aid for foreign refugees or favoring laws that protect old-growth forests.
To map these priorities systematically, psychologists created the Moral Expansiveness Scale, which asks people to sort 30 human and non-human entities into four rings of moral standing. When several of the same researchers first tested this tool in a 2016 study of American adults, they observed a consistent hierarchy: family and friends came first, followed by community members, then revered figures like charity workers and marginalized people at nearly identical levels, then foreign citizens and political opponents, animals and ecosystems, plants, and finally violent criminals.
Later research linked the overall size of a person’s moral circle to real-world generosity, with a 2024 global study of charitable donors showing that people who pledged at least 10 percent of their income to charity had wider moral circles and greater open-mindedness than typical citizens.
Even within Western societies, however, not everyone follows the exact same ordering when weighing human needs against the natural world. For example, a 2021 study of American adults indicated that although most participants prioritized distant or marginalized humans over animals and ecosystems, roughly one-third reversed that pattern and valued nature above people outside their own social groups. Broader social environments also shape moral boundaries, as a 2022 study across 36 countries, drawn from the same dataset by several of the same researchers, found that high perceived economic inequality and low social trust were associated with smaller moral circles overall.
What remained uncertain was whether the specific hierarchy of who matters most was a widespread feature of human psychology or largely a byproduct of Western, educated, industrialized, rich, and democratic societies, since earlier tests of the ranking itself relied almost exclusively on participants from the United States, the United Kingdom, and Australia.
To examine whether this moral ordering holds up across diverse societies and individuals, study co-lead authors Işıl Ayça Akkuş and Bastian Jaeger of the Department of Social Psychology at Tilburg University in the Netherlands, along with their colleagues, analyzed moral rankings across 41 cultural groups.
“There have been quite a lot of studies recently on mapping people’s moral hierarchy, that is, how much concern people show for the welfare and interests of different humans, non-human animals, ecosystems, AI systems, and other entities,” Jaeger told PsyPost. “Most people showed a very similar ranking, and I had the feeling that researchers were starting to treat this pattern as an established fact of how people think about the moral standing of others. But almost all research on this topic was conducted in the US or other Western countries. We wanted to test how often the same, or at least a very similar pattern actually shows up in countries across the world.”
The researchers examined survey responses from 6,561 university students across 41 cultural groups, originally collected in 2018 and 2019, with all but four groups reaching the target of at least 100 students. These groups spanned countries across Asia, Africa, Europe, North and South America, and Oceania, and separated culturally distinct regions within the same nation, such as English-speaking and French-speaking Canada as well as the Northern and Southern United States. The participants had an average age of 21.6 years, and roughly 63 percent were women, 30 percent were men, and less than 1 percent identified as another gender. On average, the student participants leaned slightly toward the political left and rated religion as slightly below moderate importance in their daily lives.
All participants completed the Moral Expansiveness Scale by assigning 30 specific entities into four concentric rings scored from 0 to 3. Placing an entity in the inner circle (3) meant the participant felt a strong moral obligation and personal responsibility to ensure its welfare, whereas the outer circle (2) reflected moderate concern with reduced personal obligation, the fringes (1) indicated minimal moral standing, and the area outside the boundary (0) meant the entity deserved no moral concern at all. The 30 entities were grouped into 10 broader categories of three items each.
Six categories covered humans: family and friends (family member, close friend, partner or spouse); ingroup members from one’s own community (fellow citizen, neighbor, co-worker); revered figures (elected leader, soldier, charity worker); stigmatized individuals (refugee, lesbian, gay, bisexual, or transgender person, mentally challenged person); outgroup members outside one’s national, political, or religious group (foreign citizen, political opponent, person with different religious beliefs); and villains (murderer, terrorist, child molester).
The other four covered non-human nature: high-sentience animals widely seen as having complex minds and feelings (chimpanzee, dolphin, cow); the environment (national park, old-growth forest, coral reef); low-sentience animals viewed as having simpler mental capacities (chicken, bee, fish); and plants (redwood tree, apple tree, rose bush).
To evaluate how closely each cultural group and each individual matched the typical Western hierarchy, the authors focused on 13 pairwise comparisons between categories that had consistently differed in prior Western studies, such as prioritizing family and friends over ingroup members or plants over villains. Category pairs that had historically received nearly identical scores in Western samples, such as revered versus stigmatized humans or high-sentience animals versus the environment, were left out of the 13 core comparisons.
For 26 of the cultural groups with available data, the authors also compared the group rankings against a cultural distance index, which combines nearly 200 survey and institutional indicators to measure how much a society’s broader values, beliefs, and norms differ from those of the United States. The study was not preregistered, and the authors describe their approach as primarily descriptive, intended to map patterns that future work can test directly rather than to confirm specific predictions.
At the cultural group level, the results pointed to substantial cross-cultural similarity in how people organize their moral circles. Across the 41 cultural groups, a median of 11 out of the 13 expected rankings replicated, with an average of 11.32 rankings matching the typical pattern. Twelve cultural groups matched all 13 rankings: the Northern United States, Australia, English-speaking Canada, Northern Ireland, Scotland, Wales, Belgium, Japan, the Netherlands, Portugal, Singapore, and Ukraine. Most of the remaining groups fell close behind, and even the most divergent kept the majority of the hierarchy intact, with Malaysia matching 8 of 13 and French-speaking Canada, Chile, Germany, and Poland each matching 9.
Family and friends occupied the highest position in every single cultural group, receiving an average rating of 2.89 out of 3.00 across all samples. At the bottom of the hierarchy, villains received the lowest moral concern in 38 of the 41 cultural groups, with an overall average score of 0.58 out of 3.00; the only exceptions were Hong Kong, Thailand, and Uganda, where criminals received scores similar to or slightly higher than plants and low-sentience animals. Three specific rankings held true in all 41 cultural groups without exception: family and friends were always ranked above ingroup members, and the natural environment was always ranked above both low-sentience animals and plants.
“Although we found some evidence for cultural differences, what really stood out to me was how similar the results were, even across countries that differ a lot from each other,” Jaeger said. “Participants from Australia, New Zealand, and the Netherlands showed a hierarchy that was very similar to the US hierarchy. These countries are all relatively similar to the US, but we also found similar patterns in Japan, Ukraine, South Africa, and Türkiye.”
Where cultures differed most was in how they weighed distant humans against non-human nature. Prioritizing human outgroup members over the natural environment was the least consistent pattern globally, appearing in only 21 of the 41 cultural groups, while prioritizing human outgroup members over high-sentience animals occurred in 26 of the 41 groups. A multilevel statistical model estimating the sources of variation at the group level indicated that 40.73 percent of the variation in whether a typical ranking held up was explained by which two categories were being compared, whereas only 13.36 percent was explained by which cultural group was being examined.
Comparing the 26 cultural groups with available cultural distance scores showed a moderate negative correlation (-0.46) between a society’s cultural distance from the United States and the number of moral rankings that matched the standard hierarchy. In other words, societies whose general values, beliefs, and social norms were closer to those of the United States tended to display a moral hierarchy more closely aligned with the pattern originally observed in American studies.
Examining individual participants rather than group averages uncovered far greater variation from person to person. Across all 6,561 students, the median individual matched 7 out of the 13 typical rankings, with an average of 6.85 rankings (or 52.75 percent across all comparisons). Only 38.25 percent of individuals placed human outgroup members above the environment, 44.72 percent placed human outgroup members above high-sentience animals, and 31.81 percent rated high-sentience animals higher than low-sentience animals. By contrast, 91.38 percent of individual participants placed family and friends above ingroup members, the most consistent ranking in the entire dataset.
“Researchers usually focus on finding differences, but I think it is also important to recognize that for some issues, people’s views are actually very similar,” Jaeger explained. “This can be an important thing to highlight in very polarized societies like the US, where many people (often mistakenly) think that others’ beliefs and values are completely different from their own. For example, privileging family above all else is usually framed as a conservative value. Our results show that, even though political differences exist, this is a view that is held by a wide majority of people in general no matter their political orientation.”
Identical group-level rankings can also hide disagreement among people within the same country. Both the Netherlands and Ukraine matched all 13 rankings at the group average level, yet 84.25 percent of Dutch students prioritized ingroup members over stigmatized individuals compared to 55.66 percent of Ukrainian students, whereas 44.34 percent of Ukrainian students prioritized high-sentience over low-sentience animals compared to 26.03 percent of Dutch students. In a statistical model analyzing all 85,293 individual comparisons, the pair of categories being compared accounted for 13.82 percent of the variation, differences between individual participants accounted for 1.30 percent, and the participant’s home country accounted for just 0.2 percent.
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these findings. Although the dataset spanned 41 cultural groups, all of the participants were university students, who tend to be younger, more educated, from higher socioeconomic backgrounds, and more politically liberal than the general public in their home countries. Relying on student samples may have made the cultural groups appear more alike than they actually are, and future studies using nationally representative samples could uncover wider cultural differences.
“It is possible that nationally representative samples would lead to more cultural differences, but based on our results, we concluded that there are only modest cultural differences in people’s moral hierarchy,” Jaeger noted.
The high degree of variability among individual participants may also stem in part from how the categories were measured, as each of the 10 groups was represented by just three specific examples: chimpanzees, dolphins, and cows for high-sentience animals, and chickens, bees, and fish for low-sentience animals. The authors suggest that people may downplay the moral standing of cows to justify meat consumption and grant higher moral concern to bees because of their perceived usefulness, which could explain why fewer than a third of individuals rated the high-sentience group above the low-sentience group. Future research using a larger assortment of entities within each category could help separate genuine personal philosophies from measurement noise.
Finally, some of the specific groups on the questionnaire, such as refugees, sexual and gender minorities, and people with intellectual disabilities, were originally selected because they represent stigmatized populations in Western societies, and those social labels may not translate identically across every culture. Statistical checks of measurement invariance, which test whether people in different cultures interpret and use a survey scale in the exact same way, indicated that comparing raw average scores between nations remains challenging, though the researchers avoided this pitfall by comparing relative rankings within each culture rather than raw totals across borders.
Looking ahead, the researchers plan to examine why individuals differ so sharply when weighing human strangers against the natural world. “Although most people show maximum concern for family members, and very little concern for murderers and other deviants, concern for some other entities was more variable,” Jaeger added. “Many people were more concerned about human strangers than the rainforest and other ecosystems, but many also showed the opposite pattern. I’m curious which traits and beliefs can explain these differences in who people prioritize in their moral hierarchy.”
The study, “Exploring Cultural and Individual Differences in the Hierarchy of Moral Concern: Evidence From Student Samples Across 41 Cultural Groups,” was authored by Işıl Ayça Akkuş, Charlie R. Crimston, Kelly Kirkland, Brock Bastian, and Bastian Jaeger.
