Boo! See the universe’s spookiest sights in time for Halloween
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
10:26:35 UTC
19:26:35 KST

As ghosts, skeletons and spiders roam the streets trick-or-treating on Halloween night, they’ll have cosmic company. Throughout outer space lie stars and galaxies that resemble creepy creatures, spooky skulls and galactic ghouls. And while there’s no candy in outer space (though there is sugar), these colorful images are a treat in and of themselves.
Skeletons and disembodied heads are a hallmark of Halloween, but this phantasmic apparition, called the exposed cranium nebula, lurks above us all year long. Its brainlike appearance stems from the different phases of star death. First, the dying star ejects a bunch of hydrogen, which forms the white outer bubble, then heavier material, which creates the orange “brain” within.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The name of this nebula sounds like the title of a scary story. Called “the Ghost of Cassiopea,” its gas and dust glows like a haunted spirit because of hydrogen interacting with ultraviolet radiation from a star in the constellation Cassiopeia the Queen. When the two mix, the gas glows red, and the blue haze comes from light reflecting off space dust.
This nebula, called the Red Spider Nebula, is scuttling around space while its central star, glowing bright red in the middle, ejects bursts of gas and dust. These filaments, made up mostly of hydrogen, form the spider’s “legs.”
We all know the stories about black cats on Halloween, but what about space cats? The Cat’s Head Nebula is a collection of gas and young stars sitting within the Carina Nebula. Although the shape will someday dissipate, for now it resembles a cat turned to the right, with a glowing red eye that’s likely a young star.
The aptly named Phantom galaxy lies 32 million light-years away in the Pisces constellation. It’s called that because it has low surface brightness and is difficult to spot—but with a head-on spiral view that resembles a portal to another dimension, it certainly lives up to its haunted name.

‘Paycheck to paycheck’: Texas border voters shed parties amid economic woes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
10:24:21 UTC
19:24:21 KST

‘Paycheck to paycheck’: Texas border voters shed parties amid economic woes
Voters reassess 2024 swing towards Trump as Republicans and Democrats grapple for Rio Grande Valley votes.
Rio Grande Valley, Texas – Jesus Robles sells mechanical bulls.
Mainstays of bars and dance halls, once used to train rodeo riders, the bucking behemoths point to the Rio Grande Valley’s history, where Mexican and Texan Ranchero culture have long intertwined.
But the business has also been a nagging reminder of Robles’s 2024 vote, when he cast his ballot for US President Donald Trump, expecting an economic boost that would allow the company to flourish.
“I have lost tonnes of business due to our president right now,” he said, blaming Trump’s tariffs and rising fuel prices. “I ship a lot. The price of freight has doubled…. Some of my clients have been affected by immigration raids.”
Voters like Robles in 2024 helped reinforce the notion that the Rio Grande Valley, a Latino-dominated area long seen as reliably Democratic, was shifting Republican, bucking liberal hopes the ever-growing demographic would finally turn Texas blue.
His about-face in 2026, he said, underscored that no party should take voters in the region for granted.
“We focus on other countries. We focus on taxes,” said Robles, who cast his ballot on the final day of early voting in Alamo, Texas, about 50km (30 miles) from the US-Mexico border.
“But at the end of the day, I don’t feel none of these governments really help us, the people,” he added. “Because trust me, we work hard, the middle-class people work hard, and we’re the ones that get screwed the most.”
‘I did vote for Trump’
The Rio Grande Valley has become a battleground within a battleground this election season, with Republicans eyeing Trump’s 2024 gains – in which he won 14 of the 18 counties along the US-Mexico border – as evidence of a wider red shift.
They have set their sights on flipping at least two Democratic-controlled seats along the border, currently held by Representatives Vicente Gonzalez and Henry Cuellar, while holding onto a third, held by Republican Monica de la Cruz.
Democrats, riding on Trump’s high disapproval ratings among Latinos, who account for about 40 percent of the state’s population, are hoping to elect the first member of the party to statewide office in Texas since 1994. Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico is running against Republican state Attorney General Ken Paxton. Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa, meanwhile, is seeking to unseat Republican incumbent Greg Abbott.
While once considered a Democratic workhorse, the Rio Grande Valley has found itself increasingly out of step with both political parties, according to Alvaro Corral, an assistant professor of politics at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley.
Many have drifted away from a Democratic Party once embodied in figures like former President Bill Clinton, who captured “a mixture of traditional working-class economic platform that we associate with the Democratic Party, the New Deal Democrat sort of style, mixed with a little bit of, like, social conservatism, and being quite law-and-order focused”, Corral explained.
Some voters, in turn, found common ground in the religiously-dominated economic populism of Trump’s Republican Party, Corral said, only to find themselves alienated by his administration’s aggressive domestic immigration enforcement and a lack of pocketbook relief.
At the Alamo polling site, 40-year-old Natalie, an education worker who declined to give her last name out of professional concern, grimaced when she recounted her 2024 vote.
“I did vote for Trump,” she said. “It was immigration and the economy.”
But seeing her students grapple with family separation from Trump’s mass deportation drive, and watching the price of diesel to fuel her truck continue to tick up amid the US-Israel war on Iran, made her come to regret her vote.
“I just want people with empathy,” she said.
Voter Gabriel Ruiz pointed to the high cost of housing as a unifying issue, noting houses can cost between $400,000 and $500,000, a rate previously unheard of in the valley.
He said it has become common for voters to think beyond a party.
“It’s always going to be about the economy, job growth, being able to keep jobs here, and for the American people to flourish on their own and be able to afford housing, healthcare,” the 24-year-old said.
‘Paycheck to paycheck here’
Michael Mireles, the director of civil engagement at La Union Del Pueblo Entero (LUPE), a local organisation that works to turn out Latino voters, said 2024 was, in part, a result of Democrats failing to conduct meaningful outreach in the Rio Grande Valley.
Only about 40 percent of registered voters cast ballots that year.
“Democrats in the last cycle, they were not trying to reach new voters. They were not trying to talk to people who are typically left out of Valley politics, which I think is a huge mistake,” he said.
“Because the work that needs to happen is with the people who have not been activated politically.”
Advocates believe the region is ripe for that kind of engagement.
The poverty level in the Rio Grande Valley hovers around 21 percent, the highest rate in the state and twice the national rate. It has remained nearly unchanged for a decade. As of 2023, about 37 percent of Rio Grande Valley residents did not have health insurance.
The Rio Grande Valley also has the highest concentration of so-called “colonias” of any part of the state. Colonias began as informal settlements in the 1950s, with the majority of modern residents US citizens.
About 1,200 colonias in the area are typically unincorporated neighbourhoods, meaning they do not fall under local jurisdictions and can lack basic infrastructure.
LUPE is among the groups that do voter outreach and education in those neighbourhoods.
Speaking to Al Jazeera from her home on the Erling colonia in Donna, Texas, 36-year-old Angeles Arguelles recounted not taking her sick children to the doctor recently because she could not afford the medication. Her husband works two jobs as a dishwasher, and the family has no insurance.
Despite being a US citizen, she said she has never voted.
“It just feels corrupt,” she said. “I just keep to myself and my family.”
At a nearby colonia in the city of Edinburg, 52-year-old Mario Hernandez, a restaurant worker, said his neighbourhood has become increasingly politically engaged.
“I’m not a Republican. I’m not Democrat. But it depends on who it is,” he said.
Hernandez said he had cast his ballot for all Democrats this year, motivated in part by concerns for his neighbours without health insurance.
“A lot of elderly can’t survive on their income,” he said. “Most of us live paycheck to paycheck here.”

Interview: Namibian media executive eyes AI cooperation, stronger Global South voice at World Media Summit
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
18:13:07 CST
19:13:07 KST

WINDHOEK, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- Global South media must unite to dismantle persistent stereotypes and adopt artificial intelligence (AI) wisely, a senior Namibian news executive has said ahead of the World Media Summit in Beijing, China.
In an interview with Xinhua recently, Confidence Musariri, Acting Manager for Editorial and Operations at the Namibia Press Agency (NAMPA), said his agency is already using AI to cut production costs, speed up delivery and widen its audience, and that Global South news agencies should share content directly with one another rather than relying on Western gatekeepers.
Musariri addressed the need for Global South media to come together to challenge and dismantle enduring stereotypes while also exploring the practical application of artificial intelligence in newsrooms.
Specifically focusing on the stereotypes surrounding Africa, Musariri highlighted how Namibia, like many other African countries, is often subject to these generalized views.
He noted that most African countries are put under the blanket as "one Africa" rather than recognized as individual sovereign nations; hence, he said this is where the issue of war, of poverty, of corruption, all these stereotypes come out from.
He said such stereotypes hurt investment and the image of a country, and that the media must evolve and embrace social media to counter that.
"I believe we must adopt the usage of social media where every content creator tells the story the way they see it. It is outside the boundaries of conventional media now. I think social media is playing a bigger role in demystifying the stereotypes and false narratives," he said.
Musariri called on the Global South to unite and embrace the emerging momentum generated by social media.
According to NAMPA, media organizations have failed to fully utilize existing political agreements and distribution channels, continuing to rely on Western news agencies to verify and gatekeep content.
"There is a need for us now to also boost the cooperative news exchange agencies. There has to be exchanges within the agencies within the Global South for us to share the content directly with one another," he noted.
Musariri said NAMPA is integrating AI and its applications to cut costs, speed up delivery of content, and expand its audience reach.
He expects to secure hands-on skills exchange that goes beyond traditional reporting training, focusing instead on educating journalists to effectively adopt and adapt to rapidly evolving AI tools in the newsroom.
The goal is to leverage the World Media Summit to learn how newsrooms can integrate and automate data processes and digital convergence, ensuring AI analytics are deployed effectively to maximize results, Musariri noted.
"We are looking forward to striking cooperation deals, cooperation agreements with different media stakeholders at the media summit, and learning also how they are adopting the new forms of media," he said.
As Namibia formulates its national AI policy, he added, newsrooms need forward-looking technology rather than outdated tools, expressing hope that the summit will help identify next-generation AI solutions designed to support journalists over the next three to five years.
Musariri, who has travelled four times to China in a professional and personal capacity, meanwhile, said the upcoming summit carries special significance because he covered the 2008 Olympic Games as a journalist.
"It's interesting that this summit is taking place in the very same district where I stayed while covering the Olympics in 2008. That's almost 18 years ago. So, I'm basically going to a place where things have changed," he noted.
Musariri said that NAMPA will use its Global South network and partner entities to report on the summit, ensuring that media colleagues across Namibia and the broader continent have direct access to its key outcomes.
The 7th World Media Summit, hosted by Xinhua News Agency under the theme "Media's Mission and Cooperative Action amid Intelligent Transformation," will be held in Beijing from Nov. 5 to Nov. 9, 2026. ■

UK PM opens door to slavery apology but rules out reparations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
10:12:00 UTC
19:12:00 KST

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said his government is open to formally apologizing for Britain's role in the trans-Atlantic slave trade but ruled out financial reparations, ahead of a Commonwealth summit where Caribbean and African leaders are expected to renew demands for historical justice.
In an article published Saturday in The Guardian, Burnham said Britain was prepared to begin a structured dialogue with countries and communities affected by slavery, acknowledging that its failure to confront the past had damaged relations within the Commonwealth.
"For years, those members of the Commonwealth affected by the slave trade have asked for an honest conversation about the legacies of slavery," he wrote. "By sticking our heads in the sand, we have damaged the ability of the Commonwealth to function."
Burnham said listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state would be an important part of the proposed discussions, adding that he was open to such a step.
"The trans-Atlantic slave trade was a brutal and barbaric violation of those people," he said, expressing sorrow and regret for the suffering of millions of enslaved Africans and acknowledging the lasting impact of slavery on the modern world.
However, the prime minister firmly rejected demands for Britain to pay reparations, arguing that people living in the country today should not be held financially responsible for historical crimes in which they had no personal involvement.
"I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part," he wrote.
His position sets the stage for potentially difficult discussions at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, scheduled for Nov. 1-4 in Antigua and Barbuda, where reparations are expected to feature prominently.
The trans-Atlantic slave trade saw at least 12.5 million Africans abducted and transported across the ocean between the 15th and 19th centuries, according to the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database. Britain transported an estimated 3.2 million of them, building considerable wealth through the forced labor of enslaved people in its colonies.
Britain passed legislation abolishing the slave trade in 1807 before outlawing slavery throughout most of its empire in 1833. Successive governments have traditionally emphasized the country's role in ending the trade, while avoiding a formal acknowledgment of its responsibility for the suffering and wealth generated by slavery.
Burnham said Britain needed to recognize both sides of that history, arguing that acknowledging its participation was essential to rebuilding trust with Commonwealth members.
The issue has gained renewed attention during King Charles III's Caribbean tour, which precedes the summit. The monarch has faced calls for Britain to apologize and pay reparations for its colonial past.
Speaking in Nassau, the capital of the Bahamas, on Tuesday, Charles acknowledged "the great suffering and injustices of the past," but stopped short of issuing an apology. As a constitutional monarch, he speaks on behalf of the elected government and has traditionally been bound by its position on the issue.
The king is due to address Commonwealth leaders during the meeting in St. John's, the capital of Antigua and Barbuda.
Caribbean nations have increasingly framed reparatory justice as a broader effort to address the lasting economic and social consequences of slavery. Their demands include debt relief, development financing, investment in education and health care, and assistance with climate resilience.
Burnham sought to redirect part of the discussion toward those present-day challenges, proposing a new debt-relief initiative to help vulnerable developing countries repay loans over longer periods and at lower interest rates.
He said he would work with other wealthy nations and investors to advance the proposal, with former British Prime Minister Gordon Brown, a longtime advocate of debt relief for developing countries, expected to attend the Commonwealth gathering.
Antigua and Barbuda Prime Minister Gaston Browne welcomed Burnham's willingness to consider an apology and his proposals for practical assistance. However, he made clear that the Caribbean's position on reparations had not changed.
"The Caribbean's longstanding position on reparatory justice remains unchanged," Browne wrote in a Facebook post.
Burnham's remarks also come amid growing pressure within Britain to confront its colonial legacy. In 2020, protesters in Bristol pulled down a statue of Edward Colston, a 17th-century merchant and politician who played a prominent role in the Royal African Company, which transported thousands of enslaved Africans to English colonies in the Americas.
The incident intensified debate over how Britain commemorates figures who accumulated wealth through slavery.
Some institutions and families connected to the trade have already acknowledged their historical involvement and offered apologies or compensation. The Guardian's owner, for example, has previously apologized for the newspaper's historical links to slavery.

US campaign for control of Congress enters final weekend
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

US campaign enters final weekend as Alaska, California ballot fights heat up
WASHINGTON/ANCHORAGE, Oct 31 - The Trump administration pressed a criminal investigation into Alaska’s pivotal US Senate race and said on Saturday it would likely take its fight over thousands of California mail-in ballots to the Supreme Court, as the midterm campaign for control of Congress entered its final weekend.
In Alaska, federal prosecutors are investigating whether aides to Democratic challenger Mary Peltola helped to recruit a retired schoolteacher, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., to run because he shares a name with the Republican incumbent, Senator Dan S. Sullivan. The closely contested race is seen as crucial to Democrats’ hopes of taking the Senate in Tuesday’s vote.
It is one of 35 Senate races, along with all 435 House seats, that will decide whether Trump’s Republicans keep control of Congress for his final two years in office.
Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate majority and a narrow edge in the House. Losing either chamber would let Democrats block Trump’s agenda and launch investigations of an administration that has until now faced largely compliant Republican majorities.
Early voting has set a record. More than 51 million Americans have already cast ballots in person or by mail, according to the University of Florida’s Election Lab, up from nearly 46 million who voted before Election Day at the last midterms in 2022.
In California, a federal appeals court earlier this week ruled 2-1 that the Justice Department had failed to justify its emergency bid to force the state to set aside mail ballots from more than 20,000 registered voters it alleges are likely noncitizens.
“I hesitate to give a final answer, but I think probably the Supreme Court’s next on this one,” acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter told Fox News on Saturday, adding that any request for Supreme Court consideration would come before Tuesday’s election.
Trump has been on a campaign blitz in multiple states over the past month but is spending Saturday at his Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach, Florida. He returns to the campaign trail on Sunday in Kansas and Iowa.
ALASKA PROBE INTENSIFIES
The US Justice Department's top prosecutor in Alaska, US Attorney Michael Heyman, said at a Friday press conference that a recent New York Times article saying there had been an effort to recruit Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. had driven a "surge" of FBI resources onto the case.
Heyman said he had assigned several prosecutors to it and that investigative steps were taking place "intensely and swiftly."
The New York Times reported on Wednesday that Peltola aides worked with staff at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee to recruit Sullivan Jr.
Heyman called him a “sham candidate” but declined to say what crime may have been committed.
Peltola and the campaign committee have denied involvement in any effort to recruit the second Sullivan. The retired teacher has denied coordinating with Peltola's campaign.
The department had already filed its civil action but, Heyman said, "when the New York Times article hit, that's additional information that accelerated what we've been doing."
MICHIGAN RIFT
In Michigan, where Democrat Abdul El-Sayed faces Republican Mike Rogers in another closely watched Senate race, El-Sayed’s feud with the rival he beat in the primary, US Representative Haley Stevens, flared again.
El-Sayed’s campaign asked Stevens to skip his events through Election Day so as “not to distract from the central issues of the campaign,” a person familiar with the matter said. Stevens has backed El-Sayed but demanded he condemn an outside group’s ad blaming Israel for high grocery prices and apologize for past rhetoric about Israel.
“It’s certainly unhelpful to the El-Sayed campaign to have continued visible division within the party just before Election Day,” said Matt Grossmann, a political scientist at Michigan State University. Polls show El-Sayed has largely consolidated Democratic support.
TRUMP’S PRESSURE CAMPAIGN ON STATES
The administration, beyond its bid to block counting of ballots from more than 20,000 California voters it alleges could be noncitizens, has sued roughly 30 states and the District of Columbia seeking unredacted voter rolls.
The legal maneuvers have alarmed state election officials. Under the Constitution, states have primary authority over how elections are run.
On Friday, a federal judge ordered the Justice Department to stop threatening to prosecute California election officials who defy its directives.
Sean Morales-Doyle of the Brennan Center for Justice said the efforts, while unlikely to win in court, aim at “creating uncertainty, sowing fear, distrust, chaos,” in hopes of pressuring officials such as Alaska’s lieutenant governor “to do something that they’re not supposed to do.”
Even so, 76% of US voters are confident their ballots will be counted accurately, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted from September 30 to October 5, with confidence about equally high among Republicans and Democrats. REUTERS

Australia: Italian Technology at the Heart of a New Green Steel Hub
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
11:07:54 CET
19:07:54 KST

Italian technology is at the forefront of Australia’s first new steel plant in over 35 years. The project, valued at 850 million Australian dollars, will be built in Collie, Western Australia, and will be developed by the Australian company Generation Steel with the participation of two major Italian groups: Danieli and Webuild, through its subsidiary Clough.
                                    
The Italian Ambassador to Australia, Nicola Lener, accompanied by the Consul in Perth, Sergio Federico Nicolaci, and the President of SACE, Guglielmo Picchi, attended the signing ceremony for the industrial agreements on October 29.
                                    
Danieli will supply the steelmaking technologies, including an innovative electric arc furnace, while Clough will handle the design and construction planning for the facility, in preparation for the subsequent awarding of the construction contract. Powered entirely by renewable energy, the new facility will transform Australian scrap iron into 450,000 metric tons of low-emission steel annually, contributing to the country’s industrial diversification and energy transition.
                                    
During the visit, Ambassador Lener, together with Consul Nicolaci and President Picchi, also met with Vikas Rambal, President of Perdaman, to discuss the group’s major investments. These include the Ceres project for urea production in the Pilbara, valued at approximately 6.5 billion Australian dollars, carried out with the decisive contribution of Saipem and Clough (Webuild), and the proposal for a new fuel refinery, currently under study, which could offer further opportunities for Italian companies.
                                    
“These investments are concrete examples of the contribution of Italian technology and know-how to Australia’s industrial diversification, within the framework of an increasingly strategic bilateral economic partnership,” commented Ambassador Lener.
                                    
The strengthening of industrial cooperation was further solidified by the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding between SACE and the Government of Western Australia, aimed at promoting new investment and collaboration opportunities across the critical minerals supply chains—from extraction to refining, through to advanced manufacturing and recycling, with a particular focus on technologies for the energy transition.
                                    
The agreement follows up on the joint declaration signed on August 6 in Perth, during the “Calcio Italiano” event, as part of the economic forum “Beyond the Pitch: Connecting Western Australia and Italy,” organized by the state government in collaboration with the Italian Consulate. The initiative, attended by Premier Roger Cook and SACE President Guglielmo Picchi, laid the groundwork for closer cooperation on critical raw materials and supply chain security.
                                    
The agreement is part of Italy’s broader strategy to diversify supply sources and strengthen industrial security—including in strategic sectors such as defense—amid growing attention to the resilience of production chains. These initiatives confirm Western Australia’s growing importance as a strategic partner for Italy in the Indo-Pacific, highlighting the complementarity between Australian resources, industrial capabilities, and Italian technologies, and translating institutional dialogue into new, concrete prospects for economic cooperation.

Indo-Pacific Quad ministers work on supply chains, denounce arbitrary export restrictions
ATLANTA, Oct 31 - Foreign ministers from the US, Australia, India and Japan on Saturday pledged to work on building reliable global supply chains and expressed grave concerns about what they called "economic coercion" through export restrictions and non-market practices, but stopped short of calling out China.
The joint statement by the foreign ministers of the Indo-Pacific "Quad" came at a time when Japan has been extremely critical of Beijing over its restrictions on critical mineral exports, and the US has been assembling a coalition aimed at uniting G20 countries concerned about China's dominance in rare earths and other critical minerals.
The meeting was held shortly before US Secretary of State Marco Rubio hosted the final session of a meeting in Atlanta of foreign ministers from the broader Group of 20 major economies, which includes China.
The Quad ministers reiterated their support for a free and open Indo-Pacific, underscoring the importance of economic security in maintaining global stability and prosperity, including through reliable and open global supply chains.
"They expressed grave concerns regarding economic coercion, including through arbitrary export restrictions, as well as non-market policies and practices that result in overcapacity to disrupt global supply chains in critical industries," the joint statement said.
The ministers also emphasized the "absolute necessity to protect and preserve navigational rights and freedoms in the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait," the statement said.
The group pledged more than $85 million in assistance to support trusted artificial intelligence technologies across the Indo-Pacific region and said it would launch a new effort to identify vulnerabilities in semiconductor and related supply chains before they cause disruptions.
It was the third meeting of the Quad foreign ministers this year, with plans taking shape for US President Donald Trump to attend his first formal meeting of the leaders of the four countries next month in Manila during a conference of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.
Rubio told reporters that a Quad leaders meeting in Manila would "hopefully" be announced very soon, but gave no further details.
He said the Quad was not "an anti-China or anti-anybody coalition," adding that the joint statement was raising concerns about behaviors and activities that he said were "coming repetitively from one country."
He said the US had invested a lot of time in the Quad group and wanted to continue to build on its work on specific projects and initiatives, including a $20 million project in Palau aimed at improving its digital infrastructure.
Rubio said the four countries had already made substantial progress in ensuring they could pool resources in the event of a humanitarian crisis or national disaster, and also planned to set up a business forum so that businesses in all four nations could find new opportunities to work together. Abuse survivors to press Church on accountability during pope's trip to South America
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
10:06:46 UTC
19:06:46 KST

Abuse survivors to press Church on accountability during pope's trip to South America
MEXICO CITY/LIMA, Oct 31 - As Pope Leo prepares to return to South America, Peruvian abuse survivor Pedro Salinas sees reason for both hope and unease in the pope’s record confronting clerical abuse.
For a decade, Salinas watched as the Catholic Church investigated Sodalitium Christianae Vitae, the Peru-founded Catholic community he helped expose. Then, in the final days of Pope Francis' papacy last year, the Vatican dissolved the group and its branches.
"What was achieved, nobody, absolutely nobody, could even have imagined. It was inconceivable. But it happened," said Salinas, 63, a journalist and former member whose reporting helped expose allegations of sexual, physical and psychological abuse inside the group.
Robert Prevost, as Leo was known when he was a bishop in Peru and later a Vatican cardinal, quietly worked with survivors and advocates, Salinas said, attending meetings, gathering information and communicating by WhatsApp and email.
"Without him, the needle didn't move," Salinas said.
The first US-born pope will travel through Uruguay, Argentina and Peru November 6 to 17, ending with six days in Peru, where he arrived as a missionary in the 1980s and later became a citizen and served as bishop of Chiclayo. The Vatican said he will meet clergy abuse survivors there, as he has done on other recent trips.
Survivors say they wonder whether Leo's approach in Peru, which they credit with helping bring about the rare step of dissolving a Catholic community, can translate into broader change across a Church where they say accountability is uneven.
“What is lacking are bishops everywhere in the world committed to this issue," Salinas said.
Peru is preparing for a tourism bonanza during Leo's visit. José Enrique Escardó, 56, president of a Peruvian survivors network, views the excitement from a different perspective.
While Escardó acknowledged that some survivors credit Leo with helping dissolve Sodalitium, he said the Church's actions have not delivered sufficient justice, accountability or reparations.
“Survivors have grown tired of being told things, of being promised things, but nothing being done,” Escardó said. “We feel more abandoned. We feel deceived.”
He wants survivors to become involved in shaping Church policy and wants reparations to include psychological care and education.
The Vatican did not respond to a request for comment for this story.
'TIP OF THE ICEBERG'
Francis, the first Latin American pope, left a complicated legacy, survivors say. Juan Carlos Cruz, the survivor whose case became central to Francis' 2018 reckoning with abuse in Chile, credits Francis with changes including revisions to canon law, removal of the pontifical secret — the Church's highest level of confidentiality — surrounding abuse cases and Vos Estis Lux Mundi, a Vatican framework for bishops accused of abuse or cover-up.
"We're still at the tip of the iceberg," said Cruz, whom Francis appointed in 2021 to the Pontifical Commission for the Protection of Minors. "The commission has been working for years on universal safeguarding guidelines and those standards need to be applied around the world."
Anne Barrett Doyle, co-director of the watchdog group BishopAccountability.org, which tracks Catholic Church abuse allegations worldwide, called Vos Estis the most significant action Francis took on abuse. But she said the Vatican rarely makes clear whether an accused bishop's resignation represents punishment.
“The public is left in the dark,” she said.
Barrett Doyle said the Vatican has not released global disciplinary data comparable with figures it provided to a United Nations committee in 2014. Her group relies on public records, media reports and investigations by prosecutors, governments and commissions to track cases.
She wants Leo to make permanent removal from ministry the universal rule for priests found under canon law to have sexually abused children, extending worldwide a policy adopted by US bishops in 2002.
"To say that no child molesters should be out to practice as priests is just such a no-brainer," she said. “It's a step that Leo could take now.”
Vatican officials have previously cited the difficulty of creating a single abuse reporting law across all countries and argued that removing priests can put them beyond Church supervision.
Angela Walker, executive director of the US-based Survivors Network of those Abused by Priests, said survivors increasingly turn to civil authorities because of the Church's "incredible failure" to police itself.
"There needs to be more transparency, more openness, and more accountability," she said. "I will believe it when I see it."
SURVIVORS' LONG WAIT
In Mexico, survivors pressed the Vatican on clerical abuse decades before it became a defining crisis across Latin America. Among the most notorious cases was that of Marcial Maciel, the Mexican priest who founded the Legion of Christ order and whose accusers took allegations to the Vatican in the 1990s. The Vatican ordered Maciel in 2006 to withdraw from public ministry. He died in 2008, without ever facing his accusers.
The scale of his abuse became clearer after his death. In 2019, the Legion reported that Maciel had abused at least 60 minors, among 175 instances of child abuse the order documented involving 33 priests over eight decades.
José de Jesús Barba Martin, 87, alleged Maciel abused him when he was studying for the priesthood in the 1950s. He recalled survivors struggling to be heard by Church and state authorities in the late 1990s and said an appeal he sent Pope John Paul II went unanswered.
Decades later, that experience has left him with little expectation that another appeal to Rome would bring change.
“The Church is made up of two types of men: good and bad, courageous and cowardly," he said. "It will take a long time, and the issue will not be addressed under this pope nor the next."
Alberto Athié, 72, a former Mexican priest who pursued clerical abuse cases from inside the Church before leaving the priesthood in 2003, sees Leo's visit as another opportunity to push for transparency.
“I do have hope,” he said. “But my hope fades just the same ... Things have to be fixed within the Church."
Abuse survivor Sebastian Cuattromo said the Argentine Church should have been “at the international forefront” of confronting abuse under Argentine Pope Francis, but fell short of what he had hoped to see.
"There is a major outstanding debt," Cuattromo said.
Argentina's Episcopal Conference declined to comment. REUTERS

Africa suffering in ‘strongmen’ era, says governance watchdog

Africa suffering in ‘strongmen’ era, says governance watchdog
‘If you’re an African leader and you see all those strong people rising everywhere … you say, why not me too? I can get away with it’
Democracy and rights are declining in Africa as leaders take their cues from the rise of strongmen in other parts of the world, the head of a governance monitor told AFP.
Mo Ibrahim, 80, is a Sudanese-British billionaire who made a fortune in telecoms and ploughed it into monitoring and encouraging better governance across Africa.
The Mo Ibrahim Foundation’s latest report, finds broad progress on economic opportunity and human development over the past decade, but also steep declines in security, human rights and public participation at a time when Africa has suffered multiple military coups and devastating wars.
Ibrahim highlighted elections over the past year in Tanzania, where security forces were accused of killing thousands of protesters, and Uganda, where opposition leader Bobi Wine was “hunted and physically attacked”.

Leader’s message in meeting with senior cmdrs. to be released
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
10:06:10 UTC
19:06:10 KST

The Leader of the Islamic Revolution, who is also the Commander-in-Chief of the Iranian Armed Forces, made the remarks in a message issued during a meeting with senior commanders of the country’s Armed Forces.
The full text of the Leader's message is read as follows as shared on his Telegram channel:
During the meeting, the Commander-in-Chief stressed that intelligent combat readiness for a powerful confrontation with enemies is a fundamental prerequisite for achieving maximum deterrence.
The Leader decreed that any level or type of threat must be met with an immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response.
Seyyed Mojtaba Hosseini Khamenei stated that should Iran’s enemies resume military or terrorist attacks, it will be the Armed Forces of the Islamic Republic and the Iranian nation that will determine when and under what conditions those attacks will end.
The Commander-in-Chief further underscored the need to strengthen military intelligence architecture, deepen indigenous defense capabilities in both "doctrine" and "tactics," and enhance modernized defense and security capacities through the utilization of emerging technologies.
He also highlighted the importance of strengthening spiritual foundations and the spirit of jihad, alongside unremitting efforts to meet the livelihood needs of Armed Forces personnel and provide them with the necessary support.
In another directive, the Commander-in-Chief ordered the comprehensive updating of the military target database to ensure that all physical and non-physical assets of the US-Zionist enemy are brought within the reach of the Armed Forces.
He described nationwide support for the powerful Armed Forces as one of the pillars of deterrence against anti-Iranian foreign powers and their domestic mercenaries. He added that the eight-month presence of a nation that has risen up in Iran’s public squares is a continuation of the Eight-Year Sacred Defense, which, alongside the steadfastness of the military, police, and Basij forces, has protected, and will continue to protect, the territorial integrity of Iran and the Islamic system.
The Leader of the Islamic Revolution expressed his appreciation for the intelligent steadfastness of the Resistance Front in various countries. He described the "unity of operational domains" as a decisive factor with a strategic impact on shaping the new political and security order in West Asia. He further expressed hope that this new order will increasingly lay the groundwork for unity among Muslim nations and governments and the formation of the New Islamic Civilization.
During the meeting with the Commander-in-Chief, Chief of the Joint Staff of Iran’s Armed Forces Major General Ali Abdollahi, Commander-in-Chief of the Army Major General Amir Hatami, and Commander-in-Chief of the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) Major General Ahmad Vahidi, presented comprehensive reports on the high readiness status of the country’s defenders along the Persian Gulf coast, in the operational areas of the Strait of Hormuz and the Sea of Oman, and along the country’s northwestern and southeastern borders. They also briefed the Leader of the Islamic Revolution on the multi-fold increase in the production of various types of key munitions and reconnaissance, support, and combat weapons.
Expressing his satisfaction with the measures taken, the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces asked the senior military commanders to convey his gratitude and profound appreciation to all military, police, and Basij forces, the personnel of these organizations, and the dedicated staff of the Ministry of Defense and their esteemed families.

Europe's fears, Ramallah's hopes and Trump's dilemma: World braces for Israel's political deadlock
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
10:05:32 UTC
19:05:32 KST

Israel's election for the 26th Knesset ended without a clear winner, but the political deadlock is already drawing reactions in Washington, Europe and the Middle East. As Benjamin Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot seek a path to forming a government, world leaders and diplomatic officials are assessing how the results could affect the war with Iran, the future of the Gaza Strip and relations with the Palestinians.
U.S. President Donald Trump has already indicated that he would not rule out becoming involved in efforts to establish a unity government, Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas has proposed resuming peace negotiations, and Germany has warned that urgent humanitarian measures in Gaza must not be delayed until coalition talks are completed.
Netanyahu's bloc won 53 seats, the Jewish parties in the bloc opposed to him secured 48, while Ra'am and the Joint List together won 19 seats, an unprecedented achievement for the Arab parties. Neither bloc holds the majority needed to form a government, and President Isaac Herzog will have to task one of the candidates with doing so. In the meantime, until a new government is established, Netanyahu will continue to lead a caretaker government that may face significant security and diplomatic decisions.
Trump weighs whether to intervene
One of the leaders closely following developments in Jerusalem is President Trump, who publicly endorsed Netanyahu ahead of the election and subsequently claimed that his support helped the prime minister achieve a better-than-expected result. Although Likud remains the largest party, Netanyahu's bloc lost the majority it held in the outgoing Knesset, and his ability to remain in office now depends on negotiations with parties that ran against him.
Asked in a post-election interview with Axios whether he intended to intervene in efforts to form a Netanyahu-led unity government, Trump said he had not yet considered the possibility but added, "I'll look at it." Reuters noted that a broad government led by Netanyahu could serve the American interest in political stability in Israel, while stressing that neither side currently appears willing to reach such an arrangement.
The central issue for Washington is Iran. Trump and Netanyahu have recently raised the possibility of renewing strikes against the Islamic Republic amid the prolonged conflict and the prospect of further escalation after the U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday, Nov. 3. Reuters noted that Israel's political uncertainty comes at a sensitive time for the U.S. administration, which is also grappling with the economic consequences of the war and the stalemate in diplomatic efforts over Gaza. However, replacing Netanyahu would not necessarily bring a fundamental change in Israel's security position toward Iran. Jonathan Panikoff, a former senior U.S. intelligence official who is now a researcher at the Atlantic Council, told Reuters that a different Israeli leadership would also likely support escalation against Iran if Trump decided to resume strikes.
Meanwhile, Tehran is also preparing for the possibility of renewed fighting. A report published Friday by the French newspaper "Le Monde" said Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian had instructed government ministries and executive agencies to remain on alert in light of regional developments. At the same time, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi is continuing talks with mediating countries in an effort to prevent escalation. An Iranian analyst who spoke to the newspaper assessed that Tehran believes renewed strikes could serve Netanyahu's political interests, because another military confrontation could shift the public debate in Israel away from the coalition crisis and toward security issues, potentially encouraging the formation of a unity government.
Europe: 'We cannot wait for a new government'
Europe is also closely watching Israel's political developments, although reactions have varied. On Wednesday, the European Union issued a measured diplomatic statement congratulating Israeli citizens on the high voter turnout, describing it as a sign of the vitality of Israeli democracy. The EU expressed its willingness to work with the next government while maintaining open dialogue on cooperation, areas of disagreement and efforts to promote regional stability and peace.
France, meanwhile, made clear that even a change of government would not alter its policy toward Israel and the Palestinians. Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot was asked in an interview with France 2 whether an Eisenkot victory could improve relations between the two countries. He replied that French policy would remain unchanged. France, he said, would continue working to ensure Israel's security while also promoting a two-state solution. Barrot also addressed the Arab parties' electoral gains, saying their increased strength in the Knesset could influence the next government's decisions. However, he stressed that Paris would not wait for political change in Jerusalem before continuing to pursue its positions, including measures to restrict trade with settlements in the West Bank.
In Germany, concerns are growing over the consequences of prolonged coalition negotiations. A report published Friday by Deutsche Welle (DW) said the government in Berlin was avoiding expressing a preference for a particular coalition but wanted to ensure that Israel's political crisis would not delay urgent measures in Gaza. German Development Minister Reem Alabali-Radovan warned that the approaching winter was likely to worsen the humanitarian situation in the territory and called for aid organizations to be allowed to expand their operations without waiting for the conclusion of political negotiations in Israel. She also addressed settler violence in the West Bank, saying it must be stopped even during the caretaker government's term.
Meanwhile, Jürgen Hardt, a foreign policy expert from Germany's Christian Democratic Union (CDU), told DW that he would prefer an Israeli government closer to the political center. He said the Arab parties' electoral gains could open new coalition possibilities, including a minority government led by Eisenkot that would rely on their external support. However, he emphasized that the decision ultimately rests with Israel's elected representatives.
Concerns about the consequences of a prolonged caretaker government have also been raised by European think tanks. Beth Oppenheim, a researcher at the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR), warned in an analysis published Thursday that Netanyahu could exploit the period of political uncertainty to resume the military campaign against Iran or expand military operations in the West Bank. She argued that European countries should act now, together with the United States and Arab states, to prevent further escalation and advance the Gaza ceasefire plan.
Abbas proposes peace talks: 'We hope we can begin a dialogue'
The election produced a different outcome from the one some Palestinian leaders in Ramallah had hoped for. Nevertheless, Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas chose to publicly express his willingness to resume negotiations. During a visit to Cyprus on Thursday, where he met President Nikos Christodoulides, Abbas expressed hope that the formation of a new Israeli government would allow the sides to return to the negotiating table.
"For many years, we have extended our hand to the Israeli side to achieve peace, so that Israel and Palestine can live in security, stability and peace," Abbas said. He added, "We hope that immediately after a new Israeli government is formed, we can open a dialogue together."
Abbas also asked Cyprus to help mediate between the sides, explaining that its good relations with both Israel and the Palestinians could enable it to play a meaningful role. The Cypriot president, for his part, expressed his willingness to help advance regional stability. It is important to note that despite Abbas' remarks, Eisenkot also opposes the establishment of a Palestinian state, although he advocates a different policy toward the Palestinian Authority and supports action against settler violence.
Arab states remain skeptical
A sharper response came from Qatar following allegations that it had interfered in the Israeli election. Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesperson Majed Al-Ansari strongly denied Thursday that Doha had financed activities intended to influence the vote. He accused political and media figures in Israel of trying to drag Qatar into the country's internal political struggles. "These accusations are both ridiculous and dangerous," Al-Ansari said. He added that if all the allegations made in recent years about Qatar's political influence in Israel were true, Doha "would already control the entire country."
The spokesperson stressed that Qatar does not interfere in Israel's political competition and would continue its role as a regional mediator. He called on the next Israeli government to respect international law, advance a resolution to the Palestinian issue and recognize the Palestinians' right to self-determination and an independent state along the 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital. Meanwhile, Israel's Central Elections Committee clarified that allegations of systematic election irregularities were unfounded and that the security investigation into suspected foreign interference would not change the election results.
Other Arab countries have shown little enthusiasm for the possibility of a change in Israel's leadership. An analysis published Wednesday by Germany's DW noted that even a more moderate Israeli government would be unlikely to bring a rapid change in Israel's position on Palestinian statehood or its military presence in Lebanon and Syria. However, experts interviewed by the network said a government that did not include Netanyahu's far-right partners could make it easier to advance regional security arrangements, including the possibility of renewed negotiations on a security agreement with Syria and progress in talks on an Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon.
One of the region's most significant questions concerns the future of normalization with Saudi Arabia. Riyadh has repeatedly made clear that it will not move toward normalization without progress on the Palestinian issue. According to experts quoted by DW, even a change in the composition of Israel's government would not guarantee a breakthrough, although it could make it easier for Arab countries to engage in diplomatic and security talks with Jerusalem.
'Netanyahu and Eisenkot are not the same'
The debate over the significance of Israel's election has also reached the opinion pages of the European press. In an article published Friday in "Le Monde," French columnist Alain Frachon argued that despite similarities between Netanyahu and Eisenkot on several major security issues, their differences could have significant implications for Israel's future and its relations with the world. Frachon noted that both leaders oppose the establishment of a Palestinian state but emphasized their differing approaches to the Palestinian Authority, settlements, Trump's Gaza plan and the status of Israel's democratic institutions.
He argued that the outgoing government's policies had contributed to Israel's international isolation, while Eisenkot was presenting an approach that could allow for some restoration of relations with Israel's Western partners.
This analysis does not necessarily reflect the position of the French government, which, as noted, has made clear that its policy will not change according to the identity of Israel's next prime minister. It does illustrate, however, that the debate in European capitals is focused not only on who will lead the next government but also on the nature of the coalition that emerges and the policies it adopts.
For now, Israel's political deadlock has left its international partners in a state of uncertainty. Washington faces decisions concerning Iran and Gaza, Europe fears further escalation and delays in advancing humanitarian measures, and Ramallah hopes the next government might make it possible to resume negotiations. The question of who can secure 61 Knesset seats remains unanswered, but it is already clear that the political outcome in Jerusalem will shape not only Israel's future but also its relations with the world in the years ahead.

Iran's Khamenei orders unrestricted response to threats

Breadcrumb
Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has warned the United States and Israel against resuming attacks, ordering the country's armed forces to prepare for any renewed conflict and bring all US and Israeli assets within striking range.
The warnings come amid continuing tensions between Tehran and Washington, with diplomatic efforts to secure an agreement ongoing.
Other updates:
Iran's supreme leader on Saturday warned the United States and Israel against launching new attacks on the country following their threats to resume their strikes after crucial elections, as fears mount over a return to fighting.
The declaration came as the Islamic republic's top diplomat said there were no plans to hold talks with the United States, as indirect mediation via Qatar continues.
President Donald Trump has warned of fresh military action after the United States holds midterm elections early next week, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio saying on Saturday "we can achieve military objectives if we seek to".
In Israel, which is coming off fresh elections, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has spoken of a "historic, one-time opportunity" to topple the Iranian government.
Polls in both countries could determine the direction of the conflict, with Israel having voted Tuesday but yet to form a new government.
"Any level or type of threat must be met with an immediate, impactful and geographically unrestricted response," Iran's supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei told top military commanders in a meeting, according to a statement.
The encounter was the first reported meeting between Khamenei and military top brass, and included armed forces chief of staff Ali Abdollahi, army chief Amir Hatami and Revolutionary Guards commander Ahmad Vahidi.
The supreme leader has not been seen publicly since before he took the helm in March after the killing of his father Ayatollah Ali Khamenei in US-Israeli strikes.
Khamenei also ordered commanders to update Iran's target list to include "all types of tangible and intangible assets belonging to the American-Zionist enemy".
Iran has previously warned it would consider severing undersea cables in the Strait of Hormuz.
The United Nations on Saturday condemned the "heartbreaking" death of one of its employees in Yemen under custody of the Houthis and demanded an inquiry.
Mohammad al-Shami, a staff member of the UN Human Rights Office in Yemen, had been "arbitrarily held" by the Houthis since June 2024, the organisation said in a statement.
It cited his family as saying he had died more than a month ago but that his relatives had only been recently informed.
The UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Turk, said in the statement that no explanation had been given for the "heartbreaking loss".
The Iran-aligned Houthis are fighting against Yemen's internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia.
The statement said Turk "demanded full transparency from the Houthi authorities and an urgent, independent and thorough investigation into his death".
Iran is debating whether to maintain its longstanding ban on nuclear weapons in the event that hostilities resume, although no decision on any changes has been taken, security chief Mohsen Rezaei told state TV on Saturday.
British police on Saturday arrested at least 139 Palestine Action supporters, who protested in London and Edinburgh days ahead of a court appeal over the government's contentious ban of the group.
London's Metropolitan Police began detaining people shortly after hundreds started a lunchtime "mass action" outside the US Embassy, according to reports.
The force said in an evening update that officers were "continuing to make arrests" as they confirmed that 139 had already been detained.
Police have arrested more than 4,000 people on suspicion of showing support for Palestine Action, according to campaigners, after the British government outlawed it under anti-terror laws in July 2025.
Many of those arrested, including senior citizens and Holocaust survivors, have displayed signs at rallies reading: "I oppose genocide. I support Palestine Action."
In July, hearings related to more than 2,000 of those cases were postponed until later this year.
"It is truly dystopian that there have now been over 4,000 arrests under terror laws for peaceful vigils," Protest organisers Defend Our Juries said in a statement.
Regional leaders called for calm Saturday as fears of a new escalation between the US, Israel and Iran grow.
On Saturday, Saudi Arabia's vice minister of foreign affairs said the message from the region is that it wants a return to peace. Speaking at a security forum in Bahrain, Waleed ElKhereiji told the audience that efforts were being made to prevent a military escalation and reach an agreement that ends the crisis with Iran.
“If you look at … the efforts that everybody is trying to do, the message is very clear. People in this part of the world want to bring peace back to the region," he said. But he said no one can predict the outcome of the efforts.
Concerns are rising about a return to an all-out Iran war.
Speaking at the same event, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said an escalation in the region would be extremely destructive.
“We are very confident that … the second round will be more dangerous, more destructive, and it will lead to nowhere,” he said.
Syria's Foreign Minister said Saturday that border security is a shared responsibility between his country and Jordan and that a high-level meeting is expected next month to discuss arrangements.
Speaking Saturday at the security forum in Bahrain, Assad al-Shibani said there are no “skirmishes” between the countries.
The announcement came after Jordanian strikes in Syria raised tensions between the neighbors.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has said Tehran is prepared to reopen the Strait of Hormuz on its own terms, arguing that an agreement over the strategic waterway could pave the way for renewed negotiations with Washington.
Speaking to Al Jazeera, Araghchi said Iran was demanding international recognition of a new shipping route agreed with Oman, alongside the closure of other routes through the strait.
He said Tehran's conditions also included lifting sanctions imposed after the Islamabad memorandum of understanding and reducing US military forces in the region.
Araghchi described Iran's proposal as the only plan currently on the table to restore shipping through the waterway, which has been heavily disrupted since the US-Israeli war on Iran began.
He added that mediators had presented proposals on the nuclear issue, which Tehran was reviewing.
While describing Washington's efforts to establish broader dialogue with Iran as a positive step, Araghchi said there were currently no plans to meet US officials.
He added that Tehran would decide whether future negotiations would be direct or indirect once Washington accepted its conditions.
Yemen's Foreign Minister Afrah Al-Zuba has condemned the Houthis' siege of Taiz as a war crime, accusing the group of exploiting residents' need for food, medicine and fuel to exert political pressure and blackmail, state news agency Saba reported.
Al-Zuba called for the immediate lifting of the siege and the permanent and safe reopening of roads leading into and out of the city.
Speaking during the third plenary session of the Manama Dialogue 2026 in Bahrain, the minister said ending the Houthis' attempted “coup” and restoring Yemen's state institutions was a collective responsibility shared by members of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC).
She stressed that lasting regional security could not be achieved without a safe and stable Yemen.
“The repercussions of the coup against the state have extended beyond Yemen’s borders, affecting the security of neighbouring countries, navigation, and international interests,” Al-Zuba said in her speech.
“This necessitates translating solidarity into practical steps to address the source of threats and to establish sustainable stability.”
Al-Zuba made history in July 2026 when she became Yemen's first female foreign minister.
Iran said two fishermen it had reported missing on Saturday have now been found, following what it called a US attack on a vessel in the Strait of Hormuz.
"Two fishermen from Qeshm, who had gone missing following an attack by the American enemy on their fishing boat this morning, have been found," state television said.
Earlier, state TV had cited a provincial official as saying that two fishermen had gone missing and two others were wounded in what he called an attack by the United States on their vessel in the crucial Hormuz waterway.
Jordanian border guards stopped a group of 14 armed individuals attempting to cross into northern Jordan from Syria, the armed forces said in a statement on Saturday.
The group tried to infiltrate on Friday under heavy fire and direct engagement, causing numerous casualties among the armed group, while the remaining members fled back into Syria, the armed forces said.
Oman said Friday it had rescued 25 sailors from a merchant ship set ablaze in an attack.
Muscat's navy "carried out an evacuation operation for 25 crew members of the merchant ship RITI, flying the Panamanian flag, after it was targeted, which led to a fire breaking out on board," Oman's Maritime Security Centre said in a statement.
The crew members were provided with medical care, the Omani statement said, without giving details.
Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has warned the United States against resuming military attacks, saying Tehran will determine the timing and terms of any future conflict if its enemies launch further strikes.
In a statement, Khamenei also ordered Iran's armed forces to update their target list to bring “all US and Israeli assets, tangible and intangible” within striking range.
He said Iran would decide how and when any new conflict would end if its enemies resumed military or terrorist attacks.
He also called on the military to strengthen its intelligence capabilities and develop domestic defence capabilities, while ordering an increase in the production of ammunition and weapons for reconnaissance, support and combat operations.
Khamenei said Iran would decide how and when any new conflict would end if its enemies resumed military or terrorist attacks.
Iran's army warned Saturday that any new US attack would only spread their war wider, following threats by America and Israel of further military action as they hold crucial elections.
The Iranian warning comes with fresh diplomatic efforts underway to avert a resumption of fighting, with Qatari mediators in Tehran and US Vice President JD Vance reportedly sending a letter to Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei.
"If the US president once again embarks on more regional adventurism under pressure from, and in an attempt to appease, the Zionists, the flames of war will undoubtedly engulf a much wider geographical area," Iranian army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia said in a post on X, without elaborating.
Two fishermen were missing and two others injured in an attack on two boats in the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday, an official said, blaming the United States for the incident.
"An attack by the American enemy occurred around 11:30 (0800 GMT) today on two fishing boats, each carrying two people, near Qeshm Island," said Ahmad Nafisi, deputy provincial governor of Hormozgan province, according to state TV.
"Two of those were transported to Qeshm and the other two remain missing while search and rescue operations are currently underway to locate them," he added.
Turkey has officially nominated a former foreign minister and yearslong ambassador to the United Nations for the next UN secretary-general, state-run media reported Saturday.
The next UN chief will succeed António Guterres, who has led the world body for almost 10 years. The organization is under pressure to reform as it finds itself sidelined in wars in Iran, Ukraine and Gaza while also facing a financial crisis that has forced major cuts to humanitarian and development programs.
Feridun Sinirlioglu, a 70-year-old former Turkish foreign minister and UN diplomat, had floated his candidacy on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly’s high-level meeting in New York last month.
Sinirlioglu was Turkey's top diplomat for a few months in 2015, an interim period between elections, and its UN ambassador between 2016 and 2023. He currently serves as the secretary-general of the Vienna-based Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe.
His current three-year mandate is scheduled to end in December 2027, but the top UN job would have a Jan. 1 start date.
Ahmet Yildiz, Turkey’s current representative to the UN, told the Anadolu news agency that Sinirlioglu's name was officially submitted with backing from Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
Erdogan has been vocal in calling for reform of the UN Security Council, especially criticizing the dominance of its five permanent members. Sinirlioglu is likely to reflect the president’s agenda.
The next U.N. secretary-general will be decided by the 15-nation UN Security Council, especially its five veto-wielding members — the United States, Russia, China, Britain and France. The 193-member General Assembly must give final approval.
Syria's top diplomat on Saturday said Damascus was considering whether to join the Mecca alliance that binds Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan in a Nato-style defence pact.
"Discussions are currently underway to evaluate Syria's entry into the Mecca alliance," Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani said during the IISS Manama Dialogue event in Bahrain.
Iranian state broadcaster IRIB, citing a Hormozgan province official, said on Saturday that the US attacked two fishing boats near Qeshm Island, leaving two fishermen missing and one wounded.
There was no immediate US confirmation of the attack.
Iran has warned of major retaliation if attacked again, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi threatening an “earth-shattering blow” as tensions across the region continue to escalate.
The latest warnings come amid renewed diplomatic efforts to secure a deal between Tehran and Washington, with Qatari mediators returning to Iran and Egypt voicing concern over another escalation.
Meanwhile, drone attacks have been reported off Iran’s Qeshm Island, while Saudi Arabia says it intercepted drones over Riyadh and several other regions.
Follow The New Arab for the latest developments as the Iran war continues to threaten regional stability.

Beyond Western narratives: What the Russia-Africa Media Forum delivered
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
10:01:02 UTC
19:01:02 KST

Beyond Western narratives: What the Russia-Africa Media Forum delivered
Western broadcasters have long interpreted Africa for the world and, too often, for Africans themselves, while promoting negative portrayals of Russia, speakers at the Russia-Africa Media Forum argued.
Organized by RT in cooperation with Sputnik and TASS, the forum ran in Moscow from October 26 to 29 alongside the third Russia-Africa Summit. It brought calls for greater local control over the continent’s stories and direct exchanges that bypass Western interpretations.
More than 200 participants from 46 African countries attended the media gathering, which produced partnerships covering reporting, professional training, and broadcasting technology. The main Summit drew delegations from 48 African countries, including 21 leaders.
“In Ghana we are overly dependent on Western assessments of international affairs,” Ghana Broadcasting Corporation Director General Amin Alhassan said, explaining his organization’s cooperation with Russian media. Access to another perspective would help make its reporting more balanced, he argued.
The discussions unfolded amid competing accusations of interference. Moscow accused Western governments of obstructing its exchanges with African journalists, while France alleged that Russia was manipulating public opinion on the continent.
Who gets to tell Africa’s story?
African Union of Broadcasting Director General Grégoire Ndjaka urged Russia to support African journalists in producing their own accounts of events, including through training and cooperation on news 
content. 
“We do not want our history to be written for us and then sent back to Africa,” he told a Wednesday session examining the influence of media from countries of the global majority.
Ndjaka criticized what he described as an overwhelmingly one-way flow of information from the West to Africa. He said that the broadcasting union had established a center to produce news about the continent and wanted partnerships that would help African perspectives reach wider audiences.
Sebastian Maganga, head of content at Tanzania’s Clouds Media Group, similarly highlighted the value of exchanging stories directly. Such gatherings, he told RT, give African outlets opportunities to share their perspectives internationally while obtaining material from Russia and elsewhere.
Western media dominance under scrutiny
TASS Director General Andrey Kondrashov argued that the era of Western media hegemony had ended, attributing the shift to declining trust, double standards, and the suppression of inconvenient information.
For decades, he said, a small group of Western media companies had exercised disproportionate influence over which events became international news and how countries were portrayed. African journalists were increasingly challenging that arrangement by reporting on their societies themselves.
“The world is becoming multipolar, and the information space is becoming multipolar with it,” Kondrashov said, advocating a wider range of perspectives in international reporting.
Mayya Nikolskaya, head of a research program at MGIMO University’s Institute for International Studies, accused major Western broadcasters of increasingly prioritizing criticism of Russia over coverage of development.
“They [Western media] used to focus more on development projects, now they’re talking mostly just about how Russia is bad,” she told RT.
Nikolskaya named CNN, the BBC, RFI, and France 24, arguing that African countries now had greater freedom to choose partners according to their own priorities.
Pressure and competing allegations
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova told African journalists on Tuesday that Western countries were trying to obstruct direct communication between Russia and Africa. 
“We must push back against this collectively... not individually, but by acting together,” she said. Zakharova alleged that some participants had faced intimidation or been offered competing events to discourage them from traveling to Moscow. She linked this to broader efforts to restrict African cooperation with Russia, including through pressure involving financing and political support.
Separately, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot accused Russia on Tuesday of manipulating public opinion in sovereign African countries to damage French interests. He said that he would seek EU sanctions against those responsible for an alleged interference operation targeting several countries, particularly Cameroon and the Republic of Congo. Barrot accused Moscow of trying to “colonize minds.”
His allegations come as France’s influence in Africa has dwindled, particularly in the Sahel, where governments have expelled French troops, citing their failure to help combat jihadist violence. Russian media organizations have expanded partnerships with African broadcasters despite restrictions in Western countries. In March 2022, the EU suspended broadcasting by RT and Sputnik, accusing them of 
spreading disinformation and manipulating information.
In July, RT became the first international partner of Tafouk TV, the joint television channel of the Alliance of Sahel States, comprising Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger. Their memorandum covers exchanges of content and expertise, alongside joint coverage of developments in Russia and the three countries.
From discussions to newsroom partnerships
The forum also produced practical cooperation commitments. RT Editor-in-Chief Margarita Simonyan said that the network signed agreements with African outlets representing Ghana, Tanzania, Zimbabwe, Libya, and other countries. Cooperation would include exchanges of experience, training, skills development, and media technologies.

Examples included RT Arabic’s partnership with Mauritania’s Radio and Television Broadcasting Corporation. The Mauritanian organization said that the protocol would support exchanges of technical expertise and improvements in broadcasting operations.
TASS reported signing seven cooperation agreements on Monday with news agencies from Burundi, Guinea, Cameroon, Mali, Niger, Seychelles, and Tanzania. The agency also said it already supplied Arabic- and French-language news services free of charge to more than 300 African media outlets.
Other examples included Rossiya Segodnya’s partnerships with outlets in Algeria, Chad, Morocco, Ghana, and Zimbabwe. These covered content exchanges and expanded existing cooperation. Memorandums with Ethiopia’s Debre Markos University and Niger’s Higher School of Journalism and Communication provided for professional dialogue and joint events, with participants also highlighting training in 
artificial intelligence.
Liberation’s legacy and changing perceptions
Thursday’s RT session, “Forging Independence: Lessons from the Founders of African Nations,” brought descendants of liberation leaders into the discussion about Africa’s place in the world.
Samia Nkrumah, daughter of Ghana’s first president Kwame Nkrumah, connected their presence in Moscow to Russian support for African independence movements.
“We are the descendants of African liberation leaders and we are all here in Russia for a reason,” she said, adding: “That is because Russians helped us during our long and sometimes violent independence struggle all over the continent.”
Musata Kaunda Ndhlovu, granddaughter of Zambia’s first president Kenneth Kaunda, described liberation as an ongoing responsibility. Ndileka Mandela, granddaughter of South Africa’s Nelson Mandela, recalled first meeting him through a prison window on Robben Island in 1981, aged 16.
The question of how personal experience challenges outside narratives also featured in RT’s interview with Ghanaian YouTuber Wode Maya, whose videos challenge negative narratives about Africa and reach more than two million subscribers.
Maya told RT that fears about traveling to Russia had initially made him reluctant to attend the forum. “You won’t believe that I fell for the propaganda,” he said, describing how his reception in Moscow had changed his expectations.
Maya also welcomed the opportunity for Africans to speak for themselves and challenge stereotypes about their continent.
