Nearly 90% of voters now expect their candidate to win. The math doesn’t work.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
10:00:36 UTC
19:00:36 KST

Nearly 90 percent of American voters who name a preferred presidential candidate now expect that candidate to win, up from roughly 70 percent a few decades ago. New research published in Political Behavior suggests this surge in optimism is linked to growing hostility toward the opposing party. When those high hopes are dashed, losing voters who expected to win tend to stay more hostile toward the other side than losers who saw defeat coming.
In almost every democratic election, far more people predict that their favored candidate will win than the final vote tally can support. Political scientists call this pattern wishful electoral thinking, a phenomenon in which a person’s desire for an outcome directly shapes what they expect to happen. Optimistic predictions may help voters avoid mental discomfort and cope with an uncertain future.
Social scientists have documented how stubbornly these biases resist correction. For instance, a 1997 study of voters in a Jerusalem mayoral election found that citizens overwhelmingly predicted their favored candidate would win, even when they knew the latest polls or were offered cash for accurate forecasts. Media coverage can also shape expectations: two 2018 experiments on news consumption found that when partisan outlets covered viewers’ own party as winning the race, viewers became more likely to predict a win, and when coverage showed their side losing, they lowered their predictions.
Over the past few decades, the United States has also experienced a steep rise in partisan animosity, often called affective polarization, which refers to Democrats and Republicans viewing the opposing party with deep dislike and distrust. Some research suggests that many voters today are driven more by dislike of the other party than by affection for their own, though others dispute how common this is. Preliminary evidence from a 2022 working paper based on an online survey, which has not been peer reviewed, suggested that disliking the opposing party predicts expecting an election victory more strongly than feeling warmly toward one’s own party.
Hostility toward political opponents shapes how citizens process election results as well. For example, a survey of voters surrounding the 2020 presidential election found that while most Americans overestimated their emotional reactions to the outcome, people with deeply negative views of the opposing candidate experienced more intense emotions than anticipated. Building on this line of research, study author Seth Warner of the University of Connecticut examined whether partisan animosity has driven the surge in electoral optimism, and whether those high hopes leave losing voters more resentful when their candidate falls short.
“I think, initially, this started when I noticed how news outlets whose audiences lean left or right run stories that suggest that the ‘other side’ is about to fall apart,” Warner told PsyPost. “Reading the New York Times, for example, it sometimes seems like Donald Trump is always in trouble, Republicans are about to turn on him, or his supporters are beginning to question things. You see much the same thing in reverse in right-leaning media.”
“I know from personal experience — and it’s backed up by a lot of psychology — that people react badly when things don’t turn out the way they expect,” Warner added. “So my original thought was that when people expect their party to win and then lose, they might come away from the election feeling even more hostile toward the other side. That’s part of what I found, but the bigger discovery was just how stratospherically high Americans’ expectations of victory have become.”
In the first of two studies, Warner tracked how election predictions have changed using the American National Election Study, a long-running national survey of American adults conducted around each presidential election, drawing on its cumulative file from 1952 to 2020 plus survey data from 2024. Before each presidential election, participants answered who they thought would win in November, allowing Warner to measure whether voters predicted a victory for their preferred candidate (among the 71 percent expressing a vote intention) or for their party’s nominee. To account for objective race conditions, he matched each interview date to a seven-day rolling average of national polls from Gallup (before 2004) and RealClearPolitics (2004 to 2024).
Warner then analyzed survey waves from 1980 to 2020 to test which individual traits explained the rise in poll-adjusted optimism. He examined party loyalty in voting, party attachment strength, policy alignment, campaign news interest, living in a state and congressional district dominated by one’s party, and political knowledge (knowing which party controlled the U.S. House of Representatives). He also measured attitudes on a 0-to-100 “feeling thermometer” scale, where 0 represents very cold feelings and 100 represents very warm feelings, defining ratings above 75 for one’s own candidate as warm feelings and ratings below 25 for the opposing party as high partisan animosity.
The historical data showed that the share of voters expecting their preferred candidate to win hovered around 70 percent for decades, rose into the high 70s in the 2000s, and reached the high 80s from 2012 onward. Polls mattered: each additional percentage point of polling lead was associated with about a 7 percent increase in the odds of expecting victory. But polling could not explain the recent surge. Even after accounting for polling margins and how close each race was, the odds of expecting one’s side to win stayed within a fairly narrow band for decades and then climbed sharply from 2012 onward.
“The big takeaway is that elections these days are close, and nobody really knows in advance who’s going to win,” Warner explained. “Polling the public has gotten quite hard, and although we can usually get results within 5 percentage points, most pivotal elections these days are decided by less! You wouldn’t know that to talk to most Americans, though. In the last election, about 90% of people now expect their preferred candidate to win, so we’re seeing a big disconnect between expectations and reality.”
When Warner calculated how much each trait contributed to the 17.6-percentage-point linear rise in expectations of an in-party win between 1980 and 2020 (a statistical accounting rather than proof of cause), two factors stood out. Party loyalty in voting rose by 8 percentage points and accounted for 24.9 percent of the rise in optimistic predictions, while the share of voters with high partisan animosity jumped by 47 percentage points over those four decades and accounted for 22.0 percent of the increase.
Disliking the opposing party had almost no link to electoral optimism in 1980 but became a reliable predictor by 2020, whereas strong party identity (3.0 percent), candidate ratings (2.8 percent), and news interest (2.2 percent) explained very little of the shift. Taken together, the measured traits accounted for roughly half of the overall increase in optimism, leaving about half unexplained.
In a second study, Warner examined whether changes in an individual’s partisan hostility over time correspond with changes in their election predictions. He analyzed data from the American National Election Study’s 2016, 2020, and 2024 multi-wave panel survey, which tracked the exact same partisans and independent leaners across three presidential elections (providing over 5,100 observations). Partisan animosity was measured continuously from 0 to 100 by reversing each respondent’s feeling thermometer rating of the opposing party, and statistical models isolated changes within the same person from one election cycle to the next.
Across these within-person models, rising hostility toward the opposing party reliably predicted higher expectations of victory, though the link was stronger among Democrats; among Republicans it pointed the same way but was not statistically significant. Controlling only for polling margins, a one-standard-deviation increase in animosity (roughly the typical spread of scores on the scale) corresponded with an 8.0- to 8.9-percentage-point increase in the probability of expecting one’s party to win.
After controlling for candidate ratings, party attachment strength, ideology, news interest, and geographic sorting, a one-standard-deviation rise in animosity still corresponded with a 3.3- to 3.7-percentage-point increase in the probability of predicting a win. Warm feelings toward the in-party candidate had the largest direct relationship (a 17.4- to 18.0-percentage-point increase per standard deviation), while news interest and geographic sorting were not statistically significant.
Using a statistical technique that maps how different attitudes feed into one another over time, Warner also traced how attitudes among 1,912 panel participants in 2016 related to their views in 2020 and subsequently predicted expectations in 2024. This analysis indicated that 2016 partisan animosity was linked to 2024 victory predictions indirectly, through its connections with other attitudes measured in 2020, even though its direct link to 2024 expectations was small and not statistically significant. The model also suggested a two-way relationship: expecting a win in 2016 predicted higher animosity in 2020, though this reverse effect was weaker than the path from animosity to expectations.
Next, Warner tested what happens after Election Day when hopeful voters see their party lose. He analyzed pre- and post-election interviews with 22,313 respondents from American National Election Study surveys across presidential elections from 1996 to 2024 (excluding 2000, when post-election party ratings were omitted). Comparing pre-election feeling thermometer ratings of the opposing party with post-election like-or-dislike ratings, both rescaled from 0 to 1, he tested how pre-election predictions interacted with election loss while controlling for pre-election animosity, candidate ratings, party identity strength, ideology, demographics, and election year.
The results suggest that losing usually takes some of the edge off partisan hostility, but not for voters who expected to win. After accounting for their pre-election views, losing voters who had anticipated defeat ended up about 2 points less hostile toward the other party than winners, on a 100-point scale. Losing voters who had expected to win showed no such drop, scoring about 3.1 points higher than losers who had braced for defeat. The effect pointed the same way in every election studied and reached statistical significance in 2004, 2016, 2020, and 2024, with the largest estimates in the three elections Donald Trump contested.
Among Republicans who expected to win in 2020, the added hostility was still detectable in 2024, while Democrats’ disappointment from 2016 had faded by 2020. Warner cautions that the 2020 aftermath, which included Trump’s unfounded claims of mass voter fraud, was an unusual case, and that the 2016 result calls for caution about how long such effects typically last.
Warner sees this effect as small next to the rise in optimism itself. “The ‘dashed hopes’ effect that I found on post-election animosity is more modest, about three points on a 100-point scale,” he noted. “But it occurs at a particularly sensitive moment for democracy, when one side has to accept defeat and the other prepares to take power. Even relatively small changes in political hostility could matter at that moment.”
These findings stand in tension with an earlier study of American partisans across the 2022 midterm election cycle, which found that hostility toward the opposing party and support for democratic norm violations stayed persistently high after the election, leaving winners and losers equally polarized.
Both studies evaluated post-election partisan animosity among winners and losers, though Warner’s analysis spanned multiple presidential cycles and separated voters by their pre-election expectations, whereas the earlier study tracked overall shifts across a single midterm election without distinguishing between hopeful and realistic voters. Warner suggests his findings may help reconcile the two: if nearly everyone on the losing side expected to win, the usual post-election cooling may not show up.
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. Because the study relies on observational survey data rather than an experiment that randomly alters political preferences, it cannot establish strict cause and effect. Unmeasured factors could simultaneously boost both a voter’s dislike of the opposing party and their optimism, and high expectations can also feed back into greater animosity over time. In addition, pre-election animosity was measured on a 0-to-100 feeling thermometer and post-election animosity on an 11-point like-or-dislike scale, making the before-and-after comparison approximate.
National surveys are also limited in how well they can separate internal psychological desires from partisan information bubbles. Although Warner accounted for campaign news interest and geographic sorting, these measures do not capture a person’s exact media diet or social networks. Future research using experimental designs could help isolate how much of electoral optimism stems from an emotional desire to see the opposing party lose versus exposure to partisan commentators who repeatedly predict victory. Warner suggests that tempering these unrealistic expectations could help support democratic stability during post-election transitions, when unprepared voters may be especially vulnerable to anger and false claims of election fraud.
“To speak a little more normatively, it’s important for people to remember that democracy involves winning and losing,” Warner said. “In a competitive two-party system, your side is going to lose about half the time, and some degree of intellectual humility is important for democracy to work properly. That means being willing to consider what a good-faith person might find lacking in the way your side has made its case, so that parties can be self-improving, as opposed to just negatively defined by who their opponents are.”
“Of course, there are big moral issues in American politics that are genuinely difficult to find agreement on, and we shouldn’t pretend otherwise,” he added. “But there are also plenty of pragmatic issues where everybody holds a similar goal — like good jobs and schools, low crime, and national security — and it’s just the approaches that differ. For better or worse, those are often the most important ones to the swing voters who decide elections.”
The study, “Partisan Wishful Thinking in Polarized Times,” was authored by Seth Warner.

Education under fire: Gaza’s children face death on their way to school

Education under fire: Gaza’s children face death on their way to school
Children have faced Israeli bombs and sniper fire since school resumed in Gaza for the first time in years.
Gaza City— Mohammed Hamad, 14, was on his way home from school in Deir el-Balah on October 17 when an Israeli strike targeted the road he was travelling along.
He had finished classes at the makeshift school and was walking home through the al-Baraka neighbourhood with his 10-year-old brother, Abdullah. Mohammed was killed in the strike along with another man. Abdullah survived.
Mohammed was Riyad Hamad’s third child, an eighth-grade student among the top pupils in his class. His loss is difficult for the 44-year-old father to comprehend.
“He was not just my son, he was my friend,” Hamad told Al Jazeera from his family tent in Deir el-Balah. “He was doing so well. May God have mercy on him.”
The family has struggled to come to terms with the death of a boy whose schoolwork and achievements had been a source of pride.
“Mohammed used to ask me: ‘How am I with you?’ I swear, I never asked him for anything more,” he said.
The loss has also left a deep mark on Abdullah, who now fears losing his father, too.
“He has become very afraid of going to school. They used to go together every day and come back together. Now he cannot come to terms with having to go on his own,” Hamad said.
“We are living in fear. When I go out into the streets, I swear I am afraid. Even when I am walking or sitting in a car, my heart is filled with fear … Why should our children have to live with this constant fear and anxiety, even until the last moment?
“Enough is enough. The child is supposed to bury his father, not the father bury his child. They have turned the order of things upside down.”
The gradual return of children to school – even in makeshift classrooms and tents – had offered families in Gaza some hope of restoring a sense of normality after years of disruptions.
But Israeli air raids and sniper fire have continued, despite a ceasefire being established last October for Gaza. Since then, Israel has killed at least 1,574 Palestinians and injured 5,687 in Gaza, according to the enclave’s Ministry of Health.
The academic year resumed in Gaza on September 19, after nearly three years of disruptions caused by Israel’s war – and with it came more Israeli strikes.
Ten children aged from six to 16 and a teacher were killed between October 18 and 24. In a statement last Sunday, the Ministry of Education said that two girls were wounded during morning assembly at Muradiya School in Jabalia on October 21. Five students were also injured, some critically, in an attack on the Islamic University campus in Gaza City on Sunday.
The ministry called for urgent international action to protect students, schools and universities in Gaza.
The risks are particularly high for schools located near the so-called “Yellow Line”, a point that divided Gaza’s territory between Israeli and Palestinian control as part of the October 2025 “ceasefire” agreement. The line has moved westward to give Israel control of more than 65 percent of Gaza, according to the United Nations, up from the 53 percent agreed upon a year ago
At least 66 Palestinian children have been killed close to the Yellow Line, and pupils and teachers travelling near this zone remain in mortal danger from Israeli snipers and bombs.
On October 21, Suad Abd Rabbo, a fourth-grade student, went to school carrying her bag and books. Not long afterwards, her older sister rushed home shouting that Suad had been shot.
“I ran out barefoot,” Suad’s mother, Aliaa Abd Rabbo, recalled. “When I saw her, I was confused. I didn’t know what to do. She was bleeding, crying and screaming.”
The bullet struck Suad above the knee and lodged in a sensitive area close to her nerves and tendons. She was rushed to hospital, where doctors warned that trying to remove it could cause paralysis. They operated on Suad but were still unable to extract the bullet, which remains in her leg.
Abd Rabbo remembers when Suad came round from the anaesthesia after surgery and started reciting a passage she had been preparing for a school dictation exercise.
“‘O symbol of generosity and resilience … When I feel tired, I sit under an olive tree in the yard of our home, and feel rested after the exhaustion,” her mother recalled her saying.
Suad has since been discharged from hospital and has returned to her tent, where she remains unable to walk or move around. She needs surgery abroad to fully recover, but with Israel tightly controlling exit and entry from Gaza, her prospects of proper treatment are remote.
“Suad is now deeply frustrated. She cries and asks: ‘Why did this happen to me? Why was I targeted? What did I do?’” Abd Rabbo said.
Israeli tanks, military vehicles and cranes regularly open fire close to their tent in northern Gaza, particularly after sunset. Families often have to lie flat on the ground for hours to avoid the stray bullets that ricochet through the camp.
“My heart hurts when I send the girls to school. I told my husband I regret coming back from the south,” Abd Rabbo said about their return home to Jabalia after fleeing to Deir el-Balah during the war.
Another girl was also injured on the same day as Suad as students at Muradiya School were preparing for assembly at about 10:30am, Naim Aloush, the school’s principal, said.
“The girls had formed two lines … one suddenly screamed and fell to the ground … another girl standing nearby was struck by a bullet in her side,” she told Al Jazeera.
Teachers rushed to the girls and found that Suad had been shot while the second pupil, Amina Khader, a fifth-grade student, sustained a minor injury to her abdomen.
Aloush said the shooting sent fear through the school, with parents rushing to collect their children.
Pupils who had witnessed the incident were left terrified, and the school saw a marked increase in absenteeism in the days that followed.
The principal sees this incident as part of wider dangers facing the school in the al-Ghubari area, west of Jabalia al-Balad, consisting of 20 educational tents and serving about 1,000 pupils in the surrounding community, close to the Yellow Line.
Aloush said stray bullets or projectiles – from Israeli artillery, quadcopter drones and snipers – still regularly hit the school.
“Education is under fire, and our whole lives are under fire. At any moment, there can be gunfire. It is not light … it comes down like rain,” she told Al Jazeera.
“Every day, I come to school with my hand over my heart, afraid that one of my pupils or a member of the teaching staff might be hit.”
Amina, the other child injured along with Suad, has been left deeply traumatised by the incident, her father, Khaled Khader, said.
Khader said he rushed to the school after hearing that Amina had been injured and carried his daughter to a nearby clinic.
“There was terror, absolute terror. My daughter was in shock. She broke down, started screaming and collapsed,” Khader told Al Jazeera.
“Thank God she is safe … but the psychological impact of what happened will take years to overcome.”
Amina has since been afraid to return to school. Her family tried taking her back once, but she left early, unable to bear the sound of the gunfire.
“She is now afraid of the school itself. She keeps dreaming about her classmate lying there with blood running from her,” Khader said.
He said the incident had also left him afraid for the rest of his children and his wife, with Israeli air raids, random gunfire and shelling continuing to affect streets near the school.
“We are confused about what to do. Do we keep our children away from school and deprive them of their education, or do we send them out, knowing that they could be targeted at any moment?” Khader said. “A student needs stability to be able to learn. But we have no stability, and there are no alternatives.”

Fran Luin Beijing
In ancient China, without electricity, how did people stay cosy at home during freezing winters? The answer lies in warming baskets, which have been used for more than 2,000 years.
A traditional warming basket featured a charcoal brazier beneath a bamboo cover. One of the earliest written references to the device dates back to the Qin and Han dynasties (221 BC–220).
At first, the basket served as a stove to keep a room warm. Later, people added incense to the brazier and placed a basin of water beneath the basket. This allowed it to double as a garment steamer, drying clothes while infusing them with fragrance.

An AI Agent Injected Drugs Into a Live Mouse’s Brain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

If you give an AI agent a robotic arm, an injector, and a live mouse, it might just perform brain surgery.
Biotech founder Gabriel Ocana Santero recently did that using an agent to successfully carry out a brain injection procedure on a living mouse. Though it required some extra steps, it offers a glimpse into how AI could eventually become an active participant in laboratory research.
Santero posted about the experiment on social media and tells WIRED he was interested in exploring what happens when AI agents are given direct access to lab equipment, rather than simply being asked to design experiments or analyze results.
“We’ve realized that we need to connect these agents to a lab to get the maximum value from them,” he says. Santero is the CEO and cofounder of Exin Therapeutics, a San Francisco–based startup using AI to analyze brain activity to develop drugs for epilepsy and neurodegenerative diseases.
AI models are trained primarily on published scientific literature. That means they may miss important information about the research process, including failed experiments, unexpected observations, and decisions scientists make in real time. Integrating AI models with real-world experiments can make the models more reliable, Santero says.
It’s why his team decided to connect an AI agent to a custom-built surgical setup used for performing brain injections on mice. The rig included a motorized device used to immobilize a mouse and a camera that allowed the agent to observe the procedure, move an injection needle, and control the delivery of a compound. For the experiment, his team was testing a gene therapy to see whether it could reduce seizures in a mouse with epilepsy.
They asked the AI model to choose a treatment from 19 options in a spreadsheet. A veterinary surgeon first performed a craniotomy on the mouse while the AI agent observed. The agent selected the therapy, brain region, and injection coordinates, then controlled the robotic arms and injector needle, as well as all the parameters, such as volume and speed.
The team initially tested Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 model, but it refused to guide the needle into the mouse’s brain, suggesting it might stop midway through the surgery, which could endanger the animal.
“He did the experimental planning, but when it was time to inject, he said, ‘something on my output is telling me I shouldn't do this,’” Santero says, referring to the agent. “That was very interesting.”
The team switched to using Claude Sonnet 5, which agreed to proceed. Opus is a heavy-reasoning intelligence specialist best for complex multistep problem-solving, according to Anthropic, while Sonnet is better suited for everyday tasks, though it may be a stretch to call mouse brain surgery a common chore. (Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment.)
Frontier labs have been planning for more widespread physical manifestations of AI, and researchers have already begun enlisting agents to do other things in the physical world. In August, Anthropic put out a framework for how its models can interact with the real world. More recently, AI engineers put GPT, Claude, and Grok in charge of a car to pick up lunch at In-N-Out Burger. Only one of the models succeeded.
The brain injection procedure wasn’t without hiccups either. The researchers had established safeguards, including requiring the AI to propose an injection plan for human approval and installing an emergency button a human could hit that would disconnect the rig’s motors. They also restricted the agent's access to the underlying equipment code to prevent it from modifying its own operating rules.
However, a technical glitch disrupted the equipment's coordinate system. Although the agent correctly recognized that the calculated injection position was wrong, it refused to modify the code to correct the problem because its instructions explicitly prohibited doing so.
The team resolved the issue by using a separate AI agent on Opus 5 to make the necessary code changes, but they didn’t tell the agent that a live surgery was happening. The resulting back and forth delayed the procedure, Santero says: A typical brain injection surgery like this takes about 45 minutes, while this experiment lasted slightly longer than an hour. They’re now waiting for the therapy to take effect before assessing its impact on seizures.
Despite those glitches, Santero and his team were impressed by the agent’s performance. They’re testing Grok and other models next to figure out whether one model performs better. The company is also experimenting with agent-controlled craniotomies—a much more complicated task—but wants to be absolutely sure of their safety before moving to live surgeries.
“A mistake at that stage could seriously harm the mouse,” he says.
Santero thinks AI agents will increasingly work alongside human scientists, with direct access to lab equipment. For now, he says human oversight is key, particularly when experiments involve living animals. And it’s far too soon to unleash an AI agent on a human brain.
As for the mouse, Santero reports it’s recovering well.

A historically paralyzed Congress faces its voters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

A historically paralyzed Congress faces its voters
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Just 10% of Americans approve of Congress’ job performance.
- Critics say Speaker Mike Johnson has ceded congressional authority to the executive branch.
WASHINGTON — Next week’s elections are widely seen as a referendum on President Trump, his team and his party, with most voters telling pollsters they seek a check on his power. But the midterms will also serve as a reckoning for one of the least productive sessions of Congress in a century.
A stunningly low 10% of Americans approve of the job performance of Congress, which has passed fewer bills and conducted less oversight than any of its predecessors in modern history, according to scholars of the legislative branch.
The biggest achievement of unified Republican control has also become one of its biggest liabilities. Deeply unpopular when signed, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act has only grown more controversial, with most Americans still unclear on what’s in it — and those who do know largely disapproving of the law, which cut taxes for businesses and billionaires while adding trillions to the national debt.
A summer Politico poll found that just 8% of Americans believe the law has improved their bottom line. The bill cut billions of dollars for food stamps and over a trillion in health programs and Medicaid.
Two veteran Republican incumbents are battling for a solidly red congressional seat in Orange and Riverside counties in an election that could be swayed by Democratic and independent voters.
Two other significant bills passed by this Congress — the Epstein Files Transparency Act and a housing reform package targeting corporate purchases of single-family homes — ultimately became law over Trump’s opposition, leaving Republicans little credit for bipartisan wins.
“It’s not a partisan statement to say that the current Congress will go down in history as one of the most ineffective in history,” said Charles Stewart III, director of the Election Data and Science Lab at MIT. “It may not be the most ineffective, but it’s down there.”
Norman Ornstein, an emeritus scholar at the conservative American Enterprise Institute, said that congressional performance can be measured by several criteria, including the quantity and quality of legislation, its oversight of the executive branch, investigations of government and private-sector failures, and its defense of congressional powers and ethical standards.
By all accounts, he said, “the 119th Congress is an abysmal failure, perhaps the worst I have seen in well over five decades of immersion in the legislative branch.”
A recent Fox News poll found that government corruption is voters’ top concern this year, surpassing even the economy. Yet the Republican-controlled Congress has failed to deliver meaningful oversight. The enrichment of Trump, his family, allies and aides has gone uninvestigated, while Senate Republicans continue to block legislation targeting insider trading by members of Congress.
It has been a running theme from Democrats working to unseat Republican incumbents, with Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York — slated to become speaker of the House if Democrats win control of the chamber — repeatedly characterizing the current session as a “do-nothing” Congress.
In Alaska, Mary Peltola, the Democratic nominee for Senate, accused her GOP opponent, Sen. Dan Sullivan, of doing nothing to stop Trump’s tariff policies or his war with Iran. Democrat Sherrod Brown in Ohio has attacked the Republican incumbent Jon Husted for his procedural attempts to end debate over legislation on the Epstein files. And Democrat Adam Hamilton has targeted Republican Sen. Roger Marshall of Kansas for voting for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act that jeopardized funding to rural hospitals.
Defending the record of his majority, House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) has highlighted a decline in prescription drug prices, the elimination of “wasteful spending” on various federal programs and bipartisan housing reform. Only so much can be accomplished with a razor-thin majority in the chamber, Johnson has said.
California’s general election takes place on Novemer 3. Learn about L.A.’s city and county races as well races for state office.
Trump has vowed on the campaign trail that, if kept in power, a Republican Congress would pass a $5,000 dividend to each American, despite its thin record to date.
Critics of the speaker say Johnson’s deference to Trump — and relinquishing of congressional authority to the executive branch — has unilaterally ceded power, souring voters on unified government.
But Stewart, who also co-directs a voting technology project with Caltech, said Congress’ problems run deeper than its current record.
“Not only is Congress not pushing back against the administration, or even innovating in policy, but its members also don’t seem especially interested in serving their constituents on the small-ball aspects of representation,” Stewart said.
“It’s hard to say members of this Congress are connecting with their constituents as they did in decades past,” he added. “We’ll see if that lack of constituency connection will have an impact on the results.”

Proposed billionaire tax could impact California sports teams
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Proposed billionaire tax could impact California sports teams
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- The proposed billionaire tax on California’s November ballot could slap a one-time 5% levy on wealthy residents, including sports team owners, to raise healthcare funds.
- Opponents warn professional sports teams owned by wealthy Californians could face higher costs, resulting in job losses, as well as increases to the cost of tickets, parking and concessions.
- Supporters argue billionaire team owners should pay their fair share after benefiting from Trump-era tax cuts.
The billionaires targeted by the wealth tax on the November ballot include owners of some of California’s top sports teams and, among them, there will be winners and losers if voters approve the measure.
Which owners would be ensnared by the proposed tax on billionaires’ assets remains unclear, since it’s largely dependent on whether they are declared official California residents, at least for state tax purposes. And that’s before lawyers and accountants get involved, an almost certain bet if the ballot measure is approved by California voters.
So it’s possible that the majority owner of the Los Angeles Chargers, Dean Spanos, would have to pay the the wealth tax while the owner of the Los Angeles Rams, San Kroenke, would not — even though both their teams are playing on the same home field at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood. It all depends on whether the state considers Spanos or Kroenke official California residents and how their assets are tallied.
Other wealthy team owners or co-owners who have residences in California and could be subject to the tax include the Golden State Warriors’ Joe Lacob and Peter Guber, the San Diego Padres’ José E. Feliciano and Kwanza Jones, the San Jose Sharks’ Hasso Plattner and the Anaheim Ducks’ Henry Samueli.
Among those who appear to live out of state, according to news reports, and may not be impacted: the San Francisco 49ers’ Denise DeBartolo York and John York, the Los Angeles Clippers’ Steve Ballmer, the San Francisco Giants’ Charles Johnson, the L.A. Kings’ and the L.A. Galaxy’s Philip Anschutz.
In August, embattled billionaire Mark Walter agreed to sell the L.A. Lakers to former Disney chief executive Bob Iger and venture capitalist Joshua Kushner. The proposed billionaire tax would apply to Iger, who lives in California, but not Kushner, who lives in New York. A spokesperson for Iger declined comment. Walter, who also owns the Dodgers and has been under federal investigation, told the California Post on Wednesday that he has no plans to sell the team.
There is uncertainty and disagreement about how the tax would be levied on sports team owners, and how their ownership stakes would be evaluated by the state when assessing their assets.
Representatives of the Warriors and Chargers, declined comment. Spokespeople for the Kings, Padres, Sharks and Ducks did not respond to requests for comment, nor did representatives of Kroenke or Sun Microsystems co-founder Vinod Khosla, who lives in California and whose $9.6-billion purchase of the Seattle Seahawks was finalized in September.
Legendary sports agent Leigh Steinberg warned that the proposed tax would have unintended consequences. “It creates an uneven playing field,” he said. “Out-of-state owners get an advantage over in-state residents.”
Steinberg, who has represented more than 300 professional athletes including Troy Aikman, Drew Bledsoe, Michael Vick and Oscar De La Hoya, said the increased tax could be passed on to fans if voters approve Proposition 40 on Nov. 3.
“Ticket prices are high enough anyway, and somewhat prohibitive to a working person or young person attending a game live,” Steinberg said. “The last thing in the world positive for the growth of sports is passing on that surcharge.”
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% levy on many of the assets of billionaires, including their holdings in companies. It was crafted by a healthcare union to compensate for federal healthcare cuts signed by President Trump last year that will cost California an estimated $100 billion, impacting the state’s most vulnerable residents.
David Gamage, a tax law and policy professor at the University of Missouri’s law school, countered that consumers would be far more hurt by the impacts of the impending federal healthcare funding cuts than by potentially higher prices at sporting events.
“The billionaire wealth tax would address the healthcare crisis caused by the Trump administration slashing Medicaid and other healthcare funding. Passing the billionaire wealth tax would be expected to reduce healthcare costs and thereby keep the prices of hot dogs and other consumer goods lower,” Gamage said. “Trying to fool voters by implying otherwise is shameful.”
More than 200 billionaires live in California, some of whom moved themselves or their businesses out of the state because of the proposed tax. Facebook creator Mark Zuckerberg, the chief executive of social media giant Meta, told company leaders that he planned to leave the state to avoid his control over the company being substantially diluted by being forced to sell enough stock to pay the proposed levy. Last week, the company announced the creation of a new nonvoting type of stock that would allow Zuckerberg to sell enough shares to pay the proposed tax while retaining his voting power in exchange for him agreeing to remain in the state for eight years.
Proposition 40 supporters say that billionaire sports team owners have benefited from Trump’s tax cuts — dividends they didn’t share with the fans who spend hard-earned money to bring their families to games — and that they need to pay their fair share.
Opponents argue that professional sports are among myriad California economic engines that will suffer if voters approve the proposition, in part because owners based in the state would be subject to the tax while those who reside in other parts of the country would be exempt.
The measure “will also drive up the cost of operating a sports team in California, increasing the price of tickets, concessions and merchandise,” said Rob Lapsley, president of the California Business Roundtable. “This is just one of many ways Proposition 40 will cost Californians.”
A poll by UC Berkeley’s Institute of Governmental Studies released Thursdayshowed public sentiment had turned against the billionaire tax, with half of likely voters opposing it and 42% supporting it.
More than $404 million has been donated to efforts supporting and opposing the wealth tax, according to the California Secretary of State’s Office. Proponents of the ballot measure had raised $36.5 million as of Thursday, while opponents received nearly $368 million.
The upheaval underscores how L.A. franchises have become billion-dollar assets in a high-stakes arms race, in which owners chase media money, luxury arenas and global clout as fiercely as championships.
The residency of billionaires is often difficult to ascertain, given that many have multiple properties across the nation and around the world. It is not solely based on where the person is registered to vote.
Among the “facts and circumstances” the California Franchise Tax Board considers are the person’s employer, their spouse’s and childrens’ locations, where mail is delivered, and the location of doctors, accountants, lawyers, country club memberships and houses of worship. The number of days spent in California also is factored into the board’s assessment of residency.
Los Angeles Times owner Dr. Patrick Soon-Shiong, a billionaire, owns 4% of the Lakers and recently became a co-owner of a new women’s professional volleyball team in Los Angeles expected to start competing next year.
Soon-Shiong noted that it’s not only wealthy Californians who oppose the tax. Teachers, firefighters and other groups oppose Proposition 40 because of concerns about long-term impacts on the state. And, as a businessman with stakes in sports teams, he predicted bad effects on pro sports.
“It’s really, really expensive to bring a family to watch a professional game, whatever that game may be,” he said during an interview in September. “All those costs will go up, and for sure, it’ll be passed down to the cost of the ticket.”
Times Library Director Cary Schneider contributed to this report.

From pagan shadows to Soviet nightmares: Inside Russia’s unique thousand-year horror story
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
09:57:39 UTC
18:57:39 KST

In Russian culture, fear has never been just an emotion – it’s a way of making sense of the world. Where Western horror often pits the individual against some invading evil – the ghost, the vampire, the creature in the dark – Russian horror sees evil as something earned, deserved, or even necessary. The monster doesn’t come from the outside. It’s sent as punishment, or reminder.
The Russian language is full of proverbs about fear: “Fear has big eyes,” “The eyes fear but the hands keep working,” “Two deaths can’t happen, but one is inevitable.” Fear, in these sayings, is not paralysis but duty – an emotion to be mastered, not escaped.
And when Russians choose to be frightened on purpose – in stories, films, or urban legends – they rarely chase the adrenaline of terror. What they seek instead is moral clarity. From pagan spirits lurking in the bathhouse to Pushkin’s cursed gamblers and modern tales of serial killers, Russian horror has always been less about screaming in the dark and more about understanding why the dark exists in the first place.
Before Russians had psychology or theology, they had the forest. And the forest had rules. Fear in ancient Rus’ wasn’t about the unknown; it was about forgetting what you were supposed to know. A farmer who worked at noon, a woman who bathed on the wrong day, a hunter who mocked the spirits – all risked punishment. The early Russian imagination didn’t invent chaos, but personified discipline.
The creatures of Slavic folklore were never purely evil. The Bannik, a hairy old man who lurked in the bathhouse, might scald you alive – but only if you broke his rules. The Poludnitsa, a pale woman with a sickle who appeared at midday, punished those who labored too long in the sun. Likho, the one-eyed hag of misfortune, followed the greedy and the proud. Even the devilish Chort could be tricked into serving a clever peasant.
Each monster embodied a kind of social control. Every story whispered the same warning: don’t be arrogant, don’t be careless, don’t try to outsmart the world. Fear, in this early form, was a survival strategy.
When Christianity took root, these creatures didn’t disappear; they were baptized into the moral order. Pagan dread merged with Christian guilt, and terror found its theology. Evil was no longer a misstep in ritual – it became sin. Yet the core remained: fear was not rebellion against the divine but recognition of it.
That is why, even today, Russian horror rarely celebrates the act of resistance. The earliest demons taught a simpler lesson: fear keeps the world from falling apart.
If the early spirits of Russian folklore punished mistakes, their successors punished intentions. The next generation of monsters acquired faces, motives, even philosophies. They no longer embodied the rage of nature – they tested the soul.
Two of them – Baba Yaga and Koschey the Deathless – survived every cultural upheaval. They’re Russia’s oldest recurring villains and, paradoxically, its first moral teachers.
Koschey, the skeletal sorcerer who hides his soul inside a needle, the needle inside an egg, the egg inside a duck, the duck inside a chest, is less a character than a warning. His elaborate chain of protection isn’t about immortality – it’s about denial. He’s the prototype of a man who thinks he can postpone judgment. In Russian folklore, that’s the ultimate sin: trying to cheat fate rather than accept it.
Baba Yaga is harder to categorize. She lives in a hut on chicken legs that spins with the wind, an image of restlessness itself. Sometimes she devours travelers; sometimes she rescues them. She scolds, tests, bargains – a trickster grandmother who decides who deserves to live. Her evil always has a reason.
Together, they form the moral spine of Slavic horror: the idea that punishment isn’t arbitrary. Even a witch obeys rules. And every curse, like every miracle, has its logic. In this world, a strange moral mechanism that rewards humility and punishes arrogance.
And as stories evolved, the monsters began to fade, leaving only the rules behind. The next figures to inherit this world were no longer witches or demons but people – heroes who suffered under the same invisible laws.
In the bylinas, the epic songs of early Rus’, terror moved from the forest into the heart.
Ilya Muromets, paralyzed for thirty three years, gains strength from holy wanderers – only to face trials that leave his loved ones dead and his faith shaken. Dunai Ivanovich, the warrior-lover, kills his own bride by accident and discovers her unborn child inside her. From his blood, the Danube begins to flow – a river born of guilt.
The moral of these stories – every gift carries its punishment. And where Western knights slayed dragons, Russian heroes struggled against inevitability.
Even the great disasters of history followed the same logic.
When the Mongol invasion burned cities and annihilated entire regions, chroniclers saw it not as chaos but as correction – a divine punishment for collective sin.
By the end of the Middle Ages, Russian fear had completed its transformation. What began as terror of the forest had become awe before the moral universe – fear not of monsters, but of meaning itself.
By the nineteenth century, Russian fear had grown up. What once punished the sinner in the bathhouse now punished him in his conscience. Horror did not live in the forest anymore, but in the mind.
The Enlightenment had promised reason and progress, but the Russian soul wasn’t so easily tamed. Rational optimism soon cracked under its own contradictions. What filled the gap was mysticism – polite, urban, and deeply anxious.
The salons of Saint Petersburg began hosting séances. Aristocrats flirted with Freemasonry and spiritualism. Even Emperor Alexander I, haunted by the chaos of the Napoleonic wars, found solace in prophecy and divine visions.
From that world of candlelit parlors and nervous faith came the first masterpieces of Russian horror. A prime example is Pushkin’s story ‘The Queen of Spades’, one of the first pieces of Russian literature that became famous in Western Europe. In the story, a card player is haunted by a ghost that reveals winning cards to him. Ultimately, he betrays the ghost’s trust and becomes insane.
The supernatural was only a mirror; the real horror was greed, isolation, the inability to stop. A striking illustration of this is Nikolay Gogol’s story ‘Viy’. In that story, three students from a seminary venture into a village, where they encounter witchcraft and evil spirits. They manage to fend off the witches but soon face Viy – a Slavic demon who cannot open his eyes on his own, but whose gaze kills. One of the students succumbs to his curiosity and looks into the demon’s eyes, dying just before the final crow of a rooster that drives away all evil. The sin is not disbelief, but the desire to see beyond belief.
‘Viy’ became very popular, embedding itself in Russian culture and inspiring multiple screen adaptations. For some time, Russian writers continued to explore themes of mysticism and evil spirits, often setting the stories in rural areas. This influence extended to music as well, exemplified by Mussorgsky’s ‘Night on Bald Mountain’, inspired by traditional witches’ sabbaths on “bald mountains.”
These stories terrified readers not because they described demons, but because they suggested that demons might be right. They blurred the line between guilt and destiny – between punishment and justice.
The shift from folklore to literature was the shift from fate to conscience.
Dostoevsky’s murderers and madmen inherit the logic of ancient Rus’: every crime carries its own retribution, every secret a sickness that must reveal itself. In his novels, there are no ghosts left to fear – only the unbearable weight of being alive.
Russian horror thus became something unique: not a genre, but a diagnosis.
The Soviet project promised to banish fear by erasing its causes. No God, no demons, no uncertainty – only progress. Officially, there was nothing left to be afraid of. The future was planned, the present under control. Horror, as a genre, simply didn’t fit.
And yet, the attempt to build a world without fear created one steeped in it. The state itself became the unseen monster: secret, omnipresent, impossible to confront. It didn’t stalk people in the dark – it rang their doorbells.
Censorship kept horror films off screens, but the atmosphere often did the job better than fiction. The whispering neighbors, the midnight knock, the vanishing of friends – these were everyday Gothic tropes dressed in bureaucratic gray.
Only in the late Soviet and post-Soviet years did the genre return – not from the studios, but from the streets. Real horror had escaped fiction. Serial killers appeared in headlines: Vladimir Ionesyan, nicknamed ‘MosGas’, tricked his way into apartments by posing as a gas worker; Sergey Golovkin, “the Fisher,” raped and murdered boys near Moscow. The last was executed in 1996 – the final death sentence in Russia’s history.
The myths changed too. When information censorship collapsed, fear turned into rumor. People whispered about AIDS-infected needles hidden in cinema seats, about alien autopsies under Moscow State University, about a secret subway system built for the Kremlin elite. If folklore once kept villagers from wandering into the forest, urban legends now kept city dwellers from touching escalator rails.
The new demons wore human faces – policemen, criminals, doctors, strangers. Their motives were senseless, their violence random. For the first time in centuries, Russians faced horror with no moral explanation, no cosmic order, no promise of redemption.
Modern Russia no longer trembles. It scrolls. The ancient monsters have become mascots and memes; witches sell herbal tea on Instagram, and Koschey stars in children’s cartoons. Fear has been commercialized, softened, stripped of transcendence.
In cinema, horror never reached blockbuster status. A few cult directors revived folk motifs, but audiences treated them as fantasy, not warning. The real horror migrated elsewhere: into true-crime documentaries, political thrillers, and nightly news.
Psychopaths replaced phantoms, and headlines replaced folklore. Yet the emotional undertone remains the same – that dread of something vast and inevitable, only now without a name or a purpose. The Russians who once feared God, fate, or history now fear the absence of all three.
Information wars have taught Russians skepticism and irony. Every rumor is suspect, every catastrophe half-believed. Fear doesn’t paralyze, it exhausts. What began a thousand years ago as superstition has ended as fatigue.
And yet, somewhere in that fatigue lies continuity. Russians may not fear demons anymore, but they still live with the feeling that the world is ruled by forces beyond them – whether cosmic, political, or digital.
The monsters have gone, but the logic remains: that fear is not chaos, but proof of order – a faint reminder that the universe is still watching.

Britain’s most powerful nuclear sub enters final build phase
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
09:50:31 GMT
18:50:31 KST

The Dreadnought programme has entered a phase that will take the first boat through the completion of her build, sea trials and certification before she enters service in the early 2030s, while the second submarine progresses to sea trials of her own, according to an answer given in Parliament.
James MacCleary, the Liberal Democrat member for Lewes, asked what progress has been made on the Dreadnought programme in the context of the delivery confidence assessments for Government Major Project Portfolio defence projects.
Luke Pollard, Minister of State for Defence, said: “Good progress is being made on the Dreadnought programme. In July, we announced Delivery Phase 4 (DP4), the latest phase of the programme, which will enable the first-in-class submarine, Dreadnought, to complete her build, sea trials and certification, ahead of entering service in the early 2030s. During this phase, the second boat will progress to sea trials, while the third and fourth boats will achieve key construction milestones.”
Delivery Phase 4 is the funding and contracting step that carries the programme from construction into the trials and certification work needed before a ballistic missile submarine can take on operational patrols. Dreadnought, Valiant, Warspite and King George VI will replace the four Vanguard boats that have maintained continuous at sea deterrence since 1969, and the oldest of those, HMS Vanguard, commissioned in 1993 against a design life of twenty-five years.
Stretching the Vanguard class beyond that design life has produced the longest deterrent patrols in Royal Navy history, including a 204-day patrol completed by HMS Vanguard, and the Defence Committee has examined the strain that places on crews and on the maintenance cycle. The programme’s schedule matters for that reason as much as for the capability itself.
Construction runs at Barrow-in-Furness, where BAE Systems is expanding the yard to build Dreadnought and SSN-AUKUS alongside each other, and Rolls-Royce Submarines in Derby supplies the reactor cores. Major facility upgrades needed for Dreadnought core production have been delivered, with work now focused on commissioning and manufacture.
The Defence Investment Plan commits £63 billion over four years to the nuclear enterprise, taking in the submarines, a new sovereign warhead and the infrastructure at Barrow, Derby, Faslane, Coulport and Aldermaston.

Rwanda has released at least 533 people convicted of crimes during the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi after they completed their prison sentences, the country’s foreign minister said Friday.

Rwanda's National Unity and Civic Engagement Minister Jean Damascene Bizimana said the group underwent rehabilitation training before their release to prepare them for reintegration into society.
He warned those released against promoting genocide ideology, fueling ethnic divisions or committing other offenses that could lead to their return to prison.
Over 100,000 convicted over 1994 genocide
More than 100,000 people were convicted of crimes committed during the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda.
Over 1 million people, mainly ethnic Tutsis and moderate Hutus, were killed during the massacres, which lasted approximately 100 days.
The Rwandan government used traditional Gacaca courts to prosecute crimes committed during the genocide.
Established in 2002, approximately 12,000 grassroots tribunals operated across the country, adjudicating roughly 1.9 million cases.
The genocide followed the downing of a plane carrying Rwandan President Juvenal Habyarimana and Burundian President Cyprien Ntaryamira on April 6, 1994.
The aircraft was struck by a rocket, killing everyone on board.
The incident triggered mass killings carried out by Hutu extremists.

AI generated
CHERNIHIV REGION, Ukraine – Starved and exhausted residents from the Russian-controlled town of Oleshky crossed into Ukraine on Oct 31, in a major return of civilians under the first humanitarian truce of its kind in more than four years of the war.
The six-day local ceasefire in Oleshky was reached after mediation efforts by US first lady Melania Trump and with the pope’s involvement.
It is the longest local pause in fighting since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022.
“As of now, Ukrainian citizens from Oleshky have crossed the Ukrainian border in the Chernihiv region. All of them will receive the assistance they need,” said President Volodymyr Zelensky, thanking the US and Melania Trump for mediation.
Ukrainian officials greeted the evacuees with posters “You’re not alone” and “We embrace with our hearts.”
One elderly woman said that they had escaped from hell as she exited a bus. She was greeted by another woman wrapped in Ukraine’s national blue and yellow flag. Both cried.
An elderly man in a wheelchair told Reuters that he had lost 20kg over the past year, becoming so weak that he required hospital treatment.
Another resident, Svitlana Yermakova, said that they had to eat grass to survive food shortages.
“We chopped grass and squash... just to hold on,” she said, adding that she risked riding by bicycle through minefields to a nearby village to get food for herself and her dog, Manila.
To reach Ukrainian-held territory, Oleshky residents had to take a complicated route to leave the devastated town just a few kilometres away from the front line.
They first travelled by bus via Crimea to the Russian town of Anapa, before flying to Belarus from where they continued to Ukraine.
A video shared by Ukraine’s ombudsman showed dozens of Oleshky residents slowly disembarking from a plane at a Belarusian airfield. Many people were elderly. Some required help to walk, and a few were carried on stretchers or in wheelchairs. They carried minimal luggage – only a bag or two. Dogs were unloaded from the plane in cages.
Buses with evacuees cross into Ukraine
As several big buses crossed into Ukraine’s northern Chernihiv region from Belarus, the residents were greeted by relatives. Ambulances lined the street and several large military tents were erected where hot meals, tea and medical aid were provided.
Pet food and water bottles were piled up on several tables.
“We have come a complicated way: from negotiations and agreeing on a ceasefire to delivering humanitarian aid directly to Oleshky and organising the evacuation of civilians,” said Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman.
The ceasefire has been holding since Oct 27 without violations, according to both Ukrainian and Russian officials. It has allowed them to de-mine the roads and bring food, medicines and other supplies into the town.
Supply routes to Oleshky were disrupted by fighting and drones. According to some residents, food deliveries were stopped in May, pushing hundreds of people into starvation.
The ceasefire will end on Nov 1.
Lubinets said that the oldest returning resident was 94, while the youngest was a baby just over one. He gave no exact numbers on how many people returned to Ukraine.
Some residents decided to go to Russia, while others elected to remain in Oleshky, despite the lack of gas, electricity and running water.
Oleshky had a pre-war population of about 24,000. Before the evacuation, an estimated 1,700 remained. The town has been under Russian occupation since the first days of the invasion. It was devastated after the destruction of the Kakhovka Dam in 2023 and the flooding of the nearby areas.
Fighting rages on other parts of the front
Despite the ceasefire on the southern Kherson front, fighting raged on in other parts of the front. Both Russia and Ukraine also kept up their drone attacks on each other.
Zelensky said that Russia attacked Ukrainian energy infrastructure, hitting electricity substations, thermal power plants and gas infrastructure.
Ukraine’s military said that it hit a major Russian producer of missile fuel in the Rostov region.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that Ukrainian and Russian ombudsmen had a good dialogue and had gradually begun to trust each other as they worked together during the Oleshky ceasefire, Russia’s Vedomosti reported.
But the Kremlin said on Oct 31 that it was an isolated situation, which was difficult to extrapolate to the broader peace process.
Negotiators from Ukraine, Russia and the US are due to resume talks in Abu Dhabi in early November after discussions were suspended in February following the outbreak of the war in Iran. REUTERS

UK prime minister open to slavery apology, rejects financial reparations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
09:42:37 UTC
18:42:37 KST

Ayhan Şimşek
31 October 2026•Update: 31 October 2026
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he was open to a formal state apology for Britain's role in the transatlantic slave trade but rejected financial reparations.
In an opinion piece for The Guardian published ahead of next week's Commonwealth heads of government meeting, Burnham expressed "sorrow and regret" over the suffering of millions of people subjected to slavery.
"The transatlantic slave trade was a brutal and barbaric violation of those people. They were denied their humanity," he wrote.
"They were separated from their families, treated as property and worked to their deaths. I want to express my sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering of so many millions of people, and to recognize the way it still shapes our world today."
Burnham, who is preparing to attend the Commonwealth summit in the Caribbean next week, said Britain would offer structured dialogue with affected countries and campaign groups.
"Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process and I am open to them," he wrote.
Rejects financial reparations
Despite expressing openness to a formal apology, Burnham ruled out financial compensation for Britain's historical involvement in slavery.
"I do not believe that is the right answer," he wrote.
"I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, which happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part."
Instead, Burnham announced an initiative to restructure the debt of the poorest Commonwealth countries.
The initiative would be led by former British Prime Minister Gordon Brown and is expected to involve international organizations, he said.
Burnham noted that debt-servicing costs for these countries had reached their highest levels in more than 25 years.
More than 40% of the poorest Commonwealth countries now spend more on interest repayments than on health, according to the figures he cited.
"The Britain I believe in is confident, decent and brave," Burnham wrote.
"We led the world in abolishing slavery – and we can show leadership again today."

India's roads kill quietly while crashes in the sky make headlines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
09:41:16 UTC
18:41:16 KST

Six people were killed on Friday when a Trans Bharat Aviation helicopter flying from Badrinath to Dehradun crashed near Chai village in Uttarakhand's Chamoli district. The operator's fleet has been grounded and the cause is under investigation.The crash takes this year's toll in smaller civilian aircraft accidents to 22 deaths in six fatal accidents, the highest annual figure in a TOI compilation covering January 2021 to October 2026.Yet these deaths are a small part of India's transport toll. Roads kill more than 500 people every day. Major train accidents have fallen sharply, but thousands still die on railway tracks and premises. Scattered across individual incidents, many of these deaths receive little attention compared with major disasters.
Roads: A death every three minutes
Road accidents killed 1,83,434 people in 2025, up 3.5% from 1,77,175 in 2024, according to provisional figures the road transport ministry gave Parliament. There were 5,13,474 crashes, about 1,407 a day. On average, 503 people died every day, nearly 21 every hour. The figures come from the government's Electronic Detailed Accident Report (e-DAR) portal as of July 27, 2026.Road deaths have risen every year since 2021, when 1,53,972 people were killed.
The toll is up about 19% in four years. Crashes have also grown deadlier over the long term. Accident severity, measured as deaths per 100 reported accidents, rose from 21.6 in 2005 to 36.3 in 2024. Provisional figures indicate a slight dip to 35.7 in 2025.National highways make up only 2.1% of India's road network but accounted for 36.6% of road deaths in 2024, or 64,772 lives. Provisional figures show that highway deaths fell 4.1% to 62,122 in 2025, even as overall road fatalities rose.
India's deadly roads: Over 500 lives lost every day
Uttar Pradesh recorded the most deaths in 2025 (27,547) and Tamil Nadu the most accidents (71,195). India has committed to halving road traffic deaths and injuries by 2030. The government has also announced a new rating system for national highways that will assess road conditions, safety and user experience.
Railways: Fewer train crashes, thousands still die on tracks
Consequential train accidents, which include collisions, derailments, fires and level-crossing accidents, fell from 135 in 2014-15 to 31 in 2024-25 and 16 in 2025-26, an 88% drop over 11 years. They killed 17 people in 2025-26, against 18 the year before.A single disaster can still be devastating. The Balasore triple-train collision in Odisha on June 2, 2023, killed 296 people and injured more than 1,200. Investigators identified signalling and interlocking lapses linked to the crash.The overall trend, however, is downward. Accidents per million train-kilometres fell from 0.11 to 0.01 between 2014-15 and 2025-26. The government credits improvements in signalling, track maintenance, rolling stock and safety technology, including the Kavach automatic train protection system. Spending and budget allocations for railway safety rose from Rs 39,200 crore in 2013-14 to Rs 1,17,693 crore in 2025-26.But far more people die around the railway network than in major train accidents.The National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) recorded 22,413 deaths on railway tracks and premises in 2024, and another 1,888 at railway crossings, a total of 24,301. Of the 22,413 deaths on tracks and premises, 17,029 involved people falling from trains or being struck on the tracks. Maharashtra recorded the most deaths on railway tracks and premises in 2024 (3,587), followed by Uttar Pradesh (3,538). Separately, Government Railway Police data recorded 2,468 deaths on Mumbai's suburban railway network that year, down from 2,590 in 2023.
Aviation: 60 deaths in smaller aircraft since 2021
Air crashes kill far fewer people overall. A July 2025 parliamentary reply counted 18 accidents involving Indian-registered scheduled aircraft since 2015. But a single disaster can claim hundreds. The Air India AI171 crash in Ahmedabad on June 12, 2025, killed 260 people: 241 aboard and 19 on the ground.Smaller aircraft are counted separately. A TOI review of accident reports, government records and news reports finds at least 60 deaths in 19 fatal accidents involving smaller civilian aircraft between January 2021 and October 2026. These involved helicopters, chartered aircraft, training planes, air ambulances and small regional passenger aircraft. The compilation excludes military aircraft and large commercial airliners.The annual toll was one death in 2021, 14 in 2022, four in 2023, five in 2024, 14 in 2025 and 22 so far in 2026. Helicopters accounted for 37 of the 60 deaths and fixed-wing aircraft for 23.
22 lives lost: Small aircraft crashes hit 6-year high
This year's accidents span different kinds of operations. A passenger died after an IndiaOne Air aircraft made a forced landing near Rourkela in January. Later that month, a Learjet crash at Baramati killed five, including Maharashtra deputy chief minister Ajit Pawar.In February, seven died in an air-ambulance crash in Jharkhand's Chatra district, and another passenger died after a Pawan Hans helicopter crash near Mayabunder in the Andamans. A training-aircraft crash near Kanpur killed two in August, followed by Friday's six deaths near Joshimath.The Baramati, Chatra and Joshimath crashes alone accounted for 18 of this year's 22 deaths.
Uttarakhand's helicopter toll
Uttarakhand accounted for 21 of the 30 helicopter-accident deaths in India during the preceding five years, or 70%, according to a July 2025 government reply in the Rajya Sabha. In TOI's compilation, 27 of the 60 deaths are linked to pilgrimage helicopter flights.The AAIB's final report on the June 2025 Gaurikund crash in Uttarakhand, which killed seven, cited rapidly descending clouds, delayed flight-path decisions and limited experience in the Kedarnath valley. It recommended 50 hours of supervised hill flying before pilots undertake single-pilot operations in the valley for the first time.Nationally, the helicopter accident rate rose from 0.33 per 10,000 flying hours in 2024 to 0.53 in 2025, although four accidents in 2025 are too few to establish a sustained deterioration in safety.Investigators also found visibility below the minimum for visual flying and faded runway markings at Baramati, and inadequate flight-data-monitoring records at the Kanpur flying school.These findings point to operational weaknesses, but they do not establish that smaller aircraft are inherently more dangerous than commercial airliners.
The daily toll that draws less attention
At the 2025 average, India's roads claimed roughly as many lives every 12½ hours as the 260 people killed in the AI171 crash. A single average day's road toll was nearly 30 times the number killed in consequential train accidents in all of 2025-26. Air and train disasters bring immediate investigations and extensive coverage. Road deaths, spread across lakhs of crashes, rarely receive the same sustained attention.
The railways show that sustained investment and safety measures can coincide with a sharp fall in major operational accidents. The challenge is to bring similar attention to road safety, deaths around railway tracks and the oversight of smaller aircraft, areas where prevention rarely draws the attention that disasters do.
