'Atmosphere of fear': Trump moves to curtail voting rights ahead of the midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
09:40:54 UTC
18:40:54 KST

'Atmosphere of fear': Trump moves to curtail voting rights ahead of the midterms
Americans vote on November 3 in midterm elections that could see Republicans lose control of Congress, endangering US President Donald Trump's legislative agenda. Under the US Constitution, elections are organized by the respective states – but that has not halted US President Donald Trump from trying to wield his influence ahead of the vote.
Trump has a history of challenging unfavorable election results, notably falsely blaming his 2020 defeat by former president Joe Biden on widespread voting fraud.
"The Trump administration has tried to insert the federal government into almost every aspect of the election process” in the lead-up to the 2026 vote, said Jonathan Diaz, director for voting advocacy and partnerships at the Campaign Legal Center.
Read moreGeorgia on Democrats’ minds: Powering up the Black vote to counter Trump's meddling
“The long-term risks I think are very significant, but for these midterms in particular – even if he hasn't been successful in changing the rules or in coercing state and local election officials to do what he wants – it's created an atmosphere of fear and uncertainty,” Diaz added.
In a new poll by the Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs, only 55 percent of Democrats said they are confident the final count after the midterm will be accurate, compared to 38 percent of Republicans.
The following are some examples of how the Trump administration has tried – and in many cases, failed – to interfere in the midterm vote.
The SAVE Act
Trump has repeatedly claimed that large numbers of noncitizens are voting in US elections, despite the actual numbers showing that this is exceedingly rare. Voting in US elections is reserved for citizens and already requires an ID; any non-citizens who attempt to vote can face stiff penalties including fines, prison or deportation.
Even think tanks that support Trump's voting restrictions have failed to find evidence of widespread fraud.
“The Heritage Foundation’s database of documented cases of voter fraud includes 100 cases of noncitizens voting from 1982 to 2025. That is about 0.000008 percent of more than 1.3 billion votes cast in presidential elections during that time,” the New York Times reported in April.
Nevertheless, Trump has been pushing lawmakers to pass the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE) Act, which would require people to present “documentary proof of United States citizenship” to vote.
The United States does not issue a national identity card to its citizens, and under the SAVE Act a driver’s license or other official form of identification would not be sufficient for voting if it does not indicate a place of birth.
Acceptable forms of ID would include a valid US passport, a military ID card, a valid government-issued photo ID showing the person was born in the United States, or a birth certificate – but only if it matches the person’s current name exactly, which could pose a problem for the 69 million women who changed their names after getting married and the trans community.
According to the Campaign Legal Center, more than 21 million Americans, or nearly 10 percent of voting-age Americans, lack access to documentary proof of citizenship, notably young people, those in lower income brackets and people of color. A 2024 report by the Center for Democracy and Civic Engagement found that 3 percent of people of color lack proof of US citizenship like a birth certificate, passport or naturalization documents.
By comparison, only 1 percent of white Americans have no such documentation.
A GOP amendment to the legislation also aimed to curtail the ability to vote by mail or online by overhauling these systems to comply with the stricter ID measures.
The legislation passed the US House of Representatives in February before languishing in the Senate due to a lack of support. Trump allies are still looking to get it passed through the budget reconciliation process.
Controversial database
Last year the Trump administration expanded a controversial federal database, the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (also known as SAVE), which exists to verify whether someone is a citizen and thus qualifies for government benefits. But the expansion allowed states to use it to verify whether someone is eligible to vote.
At least 25 states opted into the voluntary system, and it scanned 67 million registrations before a US district judge blocked it in June over privacy concerns and fears it could remove thousands of eligible voters.
Because SAVE uses historical immigration data its records are often out of date, which results in flagging people who have since become naturalized citizens. In Travis County, Texas, 97 people flagged as noncitizens – 10 percent of them, and possibly up to 21 percent – were actually US nationals, the AP reported.
But the US Supreme Court lifted the judge's block in a September ruling, allowing use of the database to go ahead.
The effects of that ruling on the midterms could be limited, however, as states cannot purge people from electoral rolls less than 90 days before an election.
“SAVE is incredibly unreliable when it comes to verifying the citizenship status of an individual person,” Diaz said, adding that this is especially true for naturalized citizens.
Read moreUS Supreme Court allows Trump to use controversial voter 'verification' system
Charges and arrests
The Trump administration has also used the courts to pursue noncitizen voters. The Justice Department said in mid-October it had charged 113 people across 20 states with either voting or registration offenses in the past seven weeks. It earlier said it had charged some 90 people for election misconduct in 2026, including 50 who are suspected of having voted as noncitizens.
Jose Antonio Banuelos-Diaz, 42, has been living in the United States for 40 years. He was accused of trying to register to vote in 2007, around the time when he applied for a driver's license. California residents are prompted to register to vote at the same time they get their license.
“I have never voted because I know I can’t vote,” he told AP after his arrest, denying he tried to register. “If there was a mistake, they should have called me out right away, not 20 years later.” He has since been released but faces five years in prison if convicted.
The Trump administration also sued California election officials to try to prevent the state from counting some 20,000 mail-in ballots it says were sent by noncitizens. But a federal judge ruled the count should go ahead, saying the administration's request "violates longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states have control over their elections".
Diaz of the Campaign Legal Center said the list was inaccurate. "California looked at the list and said, well, half of these people were born in the United States, so they are citizens," he said. For the other half, "we don't have enough data in this set that you've given us to identify these people, much less verify ... what we're using".
Trump's Department of Justice sent letters to nearly all 50 states demanding unredacted copies of their voter registration rolls. At least 30 states and the District of Columbia were later sued to obtain their voter registration lists; 26 of those lawsuits were subsequently dismissed.
At least 16 states willingly handed over, or promised to provide, their lists.
Restricting mail-in voting
Trump has also been “irrationally” suspicious of mail-in voting, Diaz said, adding that one reason is that many people relied on mail-in voting in 2020 – when he lost the last election – because of Covid-19.
In March, Trump signed an executive order that created new regulations for the US postal system, the USPS, that would have imposed new standards on voter-specific data and ballot envelopes.
The US Supreme Court then blocked the measure in September.
But if it had gone through, this order could have prevented thousands from voting, disproportionately affecting Democrats, who are slightly more likely to use mail-in ballots. According to a report by the MIT Election Data & Science Lab, 37 percent of Democrats reported voting by mail in 2024, compared with 24 percent of Republicans.
Elections in the United States are held on Tuesdays, and many people choose to use mail-in voting instead of going to the polls in person to avoid missing a day of work.
While the Trump administration has appealed the Supreme Court’s decision, the court is unlikely to reinstate it ahead of the midterms.
According to Diaz, he will “certainly continue to try to make mail-in voting more difficult and to add new restrictions to it. I don't think he has much chance of success, but he will keep trying”.

Gerrymandering
The US congressional map looks very different in 2026 than it did in the 2024 election after Trump urged Republicans to redraw dozens of US House of Representatives districts to favor the party, notably in Texas.
This form of political redistricting, known as gerrymandering, has been used to disadvantage voters along class or race lines. Republicans sometimes seek to split up areas with a large Black population to lower their collective voting power since they are statistically more likely to vote Democrat.
“Redistricting is a problem much bigger than these midterm elections,” Diaz said. “It is bad for the long-term health of democracy when a majority of American voters do not have a meaningful choice in who represents them in Congress.”
After Texas lawmakers adopted a new electoral map that would give Republicans five more US House seats in the midterm elections, California held a referendum in which voters overwhelmingly approved a new congressional map that would give Democrats five more seats.
Republicans in Southern states have rushed to follow Texas’s lead.
And in a boost for GOP efforts, the Supreme Court voted in April to narrow the legal grounds for challenging maps that may be racially discriminatory under the Voting Rights Act, potentially opening the door to future redistricting.
Republicans gained an advantage in 16 districts because of this push. But a recent Reuters analysis suggests that nine of them are either too close to call or expected to go to the Democrats on November 3, largely due to Trump’s low approval ratings over the rising cost of living and the unpopular Iran war.
"The thing with gerrymandering is that you're always drawing maps based on data from the last election,” Diaz said. "So if voters change their preferences, the maps that you draw may not be as successful in securing support for your party as you thought.”

The Defence Secretary has called the Scottish National Party’s support for unilateral nuclear disarmament a white flag policy and said the party must explain how it would square that with membership of a nuclear alliance, according to remarks made to reporters in Glasgow.
Wes Streeting was asked about the First Minister’s repeated claim that the government in Westminster is leaving Scotland short of defence.

Senegal hosts Africa’s first ever Youth Olympic Games

Youth Olympics open in Senegal as the first Olympic event in Africa
The 2026 Youth Olympic Games opened Saturday in the Senegalese capital Dakar in the first ever Olympics to be held on African soil. It comes as the continent seeks a bigger role in international sporting competitions.
Issued on: Modified:
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Senegal kicked off the Youth Olympic Games on Saturday, bringing an Olympic event to Africa for the first time as the continent seeks a bigger role in international sporting competitions.
About 2,700 young athletes aged 14 to 17 will compete through Nov. 13 in the capital, Dakar, the nearby city of Diamniadio and the beach resort of Saly.
Hundreds of dancers will join a spectacle celebrating Senegalese and African culture, in line with the Fames motto “Africa welcomes, Dakar celebrates".
“This is a first opportunity for Senegal and, by extension, for Africa, to discover new sports," Thomas Dieme, a Senegalese student said as Dakar prepared to host the games. "It is only natural that we should all be happy to welcome other people, other cultures,” he added.
Among the celebrities expected at Saturday's opening ceremony is French actor Omar Sy, who has Senegalese roots and stars in the Netflix series “Lupin”, as well as Senegalese Italian TikTok star Khaby Lame, both ambassadors for the games.
The mascot, Ayo, is a young lion wearing a traditional Fulani hat. Its name means “joy” in Yoruba, a language spoken in Nigeria and neighboring West African countries.
Watch moreOlympic fever grips Senegal as Dakar hosts Youth Olympic Games
President Bassirou Diomaye Faye is scheduled to declare the games open at 6:30pm local time (0830 GMT) at the Diamniadio stadium where International Olympic Committee President Kirsty Coventry and some heads of state are expected to be present.
The Youth Olympics are a smaller competition than the Summer Olympics. Singapore hosted the first summer edition in 2010. Dakar was initially due to host in 2022, but the coronavirus pandemic delayed the games by four years.
Athletes will compete in 153 medal events across 25 sports, including athletics, swimming and 3-x-3 basketball.
Several sports will make their Youth Olympic debuts. They include Baseball5, a five-on-five version of baseball played without bats and gloves, Wushu, a Chinese martial art, that can be choreography-based or combat sport, and coastal rowing beach sprint, which combines beach runs with a head-to-head rowing race.
Beach wrestling will also feature at the Youth Olympics for the first time, a nod to Senegalese wrestling, the country’s national sport also performed on sand.
The first refugee team at a Youth Olympics will field six athletes based in Kenya and Uganda in track and field, judo and taekwondo.
The games arrive 130 years after the modern Olympics began in Athens. Coventry, a Zimbabwean swimming champion, became the IOC’s first African and first female president last year.
“It is time for Africa, time for Senegal,” Coventry told media upon arriving in Senegal on Tuesday.
South Africa hosted the continent’s first soccer FIFA World Cup in 2010. Morocco will co-host the 2030 tournament with Spain and Portugal. Rwanda hosted Africa’s first road cycling world championships last year and Formula 1 is returning to Africa with a grand prix in Rwanda starting early next decade. Botswana also staged the World Athletics Relays in May.
African countries increasingly see sport as “a weapon in diplomacy and a tool for development”, Dakar-based sports analyst Frédéric Sohoundé said.
He pointed to Morocco’s investment in sports facilities and its ability to attract repeated competitions. Senegal, though, needs reliable maintenance funding and regular events after the games to prevent its venues from becoming expensive, unused facilities, he said.
Russia’s delegation of 13 athletes is competing under its national flag for the first time at an Olympic event since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 led to its suspension. Russians at the Paris Olympics of 2024 and this year’s Winter Olympics competed as neutral athletes without national symbols.
That follows a shift in the IOC’s approach under Coventry, who has said the Olympics shouldn’t “hold athletes accountable for the actions of their governments”.
It could be a trial run for a full Russian return at the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028.
The games come as Senegal grapples with a debt crisis and public frustration over living costs.
Billions of dollars of unreported debt by the previous administration have left Senegalese authorities with little money for public spending, while layoffs and rising living costs have fueled protests in recent months.
Many Senegalese said in interviews that they're prioritizing making ends meet over attending the sporting activities.
A government-led foundation drew criticism after announcing a contribution of 500 million CFA francs (about $854,000) to buy 200,000 tickets for school children. Critics questioned the money’s source, which the president’s political movement said was from donors and benefactors.
President Faye has defended spending on the games, citing renovated sports facilities, training for young people and contracts for Senegalese businesses.
(FRANCE 24 with AP)

Rival US and Russian resolutions on Western Sahara fail at UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
09:35:21 UTC
18:35:21 KST

Rival US and Russian resolutions on Western Sahara fail at UN
The UN Security Council rejected the competing proposals, leaving the peacekeeping mission without an approved extension.
The United Nations peacekeeping mission in the disputed Western Sahara faces an uncertain future after competing United States and Russian resolutions failed at the UN Security Council.
Russia vetoed the US-backed proposal on Friday, despite support from 11 of the 15 council members, including fellow permanent members France and the United Kingdom.
A rival Russian draft then failed to secure the nine votes needed for adoption, receiving two votes in favour, one against and 11 abstentions.
The mandate of the UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO) is due to expire on Saturday unless the council reaches a last-minute agreement.
Western Sahara is a former Spanish colony in northwest Africa. Morocco considers the territory its own while the Algeria-backed Polisario Front seeks to establish an independent state called the Sahrawi Republic.
The UN established MINURSO in 1991 to monitor a ceasefire and prepare a referendum on the territory’s future, but disagreements over who could vote have prevented it from taking place.
The mission has 155 military personnel and is set to cost $62m in the fiscal year that began in June, according to a report by the UN secretary-general.
The US draft would have extended the mission for a year, removed “referendum” from its name and made Morocco’s autonomy proposal the only basis for further talks.
Under that plan, the territory would manage its internal affairs but remain under Moroccan sovereignty.
The council had already made the proposal a basis for negotiations last year and asked UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres to submit a review of the peacekeeping mission.
US Ambassador Mike Waltz told the council in New York on Friday that the referendum had been stalled for decades.
Russia’s UN ambassador, Vassily Nebenzia, said at the same meeting that Moscow opposed the draft because it favoured one side.
“We stress the fact that the Security Council cannot automatically predetermine matters relating to sovereignty,” he said.
Russia instead proposed renewing the existing mission without those changes.
Morocco’s royal palace welcomed the failure to renew MINURSO, saying on Friday that UN personnel and equipment should leave the territory in the coming days, and that the Western Sahara issue should now be withdrawn from the Security Council’s consideration. Morocco said it remained committed to the ceasefire.
Sidi Omar, the Polisario Front’s representative at the UN, told reporters on Friday that he welcomed Russia’s veto because the US proposal would undermine Sahrawi self-determination.
Algeria expressed regret on Saturday over the failure to renew MINURSO’s mandate. Its foreign ministry criticised what it described as the US draft’s excessive bias towards Morocco.
The aid group Oxfam warned that losing MINURSO’s “monitoring and de-escalation functions risks undermining security and stability”.
While most Sahrawis live in Moroccan-ruled Western Sahara, tens of thousands are estimated to live in Polisario-run refugee camps in Algeria. The vetoed US resolution called for a refugee census.
Low-level fighting has continued since Polisario said it was resuming armed struggle in 2020.

Keurig Alta Brewer Review: Brand-New Tech, Classically Good Coffee

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
09:35:00 UTC
18:35:00 KST

Ahead of my virtual taste-test briefing for the new Keurig Alta brewer, it was 9:50 am and I was panicking. Pesky time zones be darned; the meeting I thought was taking place in two hours was actually in 10 minutes. That led to the first of many positive interactions with this machine—I had it fully set up, connected to my Wi-Fi, and ready to brew in less than seven minutes. That's about as intuitive a setup process as one could hope for with a first-of-its-kind coffee machine. (We won't talk about the amount of packaging scattered all over my kitchen floor during the aforementioned meeting.)
The Keurig Alta looks like something straight out of a design convention. It almost looks like spaceship decor with its curved white lines and sleek components (it also comes in black and stainless steel). Whereas some inexpensive Keurigs—the kind that sell for $50 during shopping holidays—can feel cheap and plasticky, this machine feels high-end from top to bottom. The cup holder is metal, the cup and whisk for the steam wand are magnetic, and the reservoir bin is slim and reversible. Both drip trays tuck away seamlessly without adding extra bulk.
The top of the machine has two compartments. On the right side, you'll find the standard Keurig K-Cup basket, with the typical needle at the bottom to pierce the cup. On the left, though, is a new compartment for the brand-new Keurig AltaRounds ($11 for a box of 8). These little pucks are the latest in Keurig's coffee technology and are like nothing I've seen before. The whole package comes at a high price point, but compared to in-home espresso makers, it's not unreasonable.
In Bloom
If you've ever used an espresso machine or watched a barista pull shots, you'll be familiar with the process of filling a portafilter with ground coffee and tamping it down. The Keurig AltaRounds look similar to this puck of coffee. Each puck is coated in a substance derived from seaweed, and that layer of “glue” holding the AltaRounds together allows them to bloom inside the machine. They're available in four varieties right now: dark roast, medium roast, a caramel blend, and double-shot espresso, with light-roast coffee and single-shot espresso varieties coming soon. The AltaRounds are stamped with a QR code that the machine reads in a split second when you insert them into the left touchscreen compartment.

Iran's Khamenei warns US against attacks, orders military buildup
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31

18:35:00 KST

Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has warned that any renewed U.S. or Israeli attack would trigger an immediate and geographically wider Iranian response, ordering the armed forces to expand their target lists, strengthen intelligence capabilities and accelerate weapons production.
In a written message following a meeting with senior military commanders Saturday, Khamenei said Iran would determine the timing and conditions for ending any future conflict if its adversaries resumed military or terrorist attacks.
He ordered the armed forces to prepare an "immediate, impactful and geographically unrestricted response" to any threat, stressing that maintaining a high level of combat readiness was essential to deterring further aggression.
"Intelligent combat readiness for a powerful confrontation with enemies is a fundamental prerequisite for achieving maximum deterrence," he said.
Khamenei also instructed military commanders to update their target database to bring "all U.S. and Israeli assets, tangible and intangible," within striking range, signaling an effort to broaden Iran's potential targeting capabilities in the event of another confrontation.
The directives included strengthening military intelligence, developing domestic defense capabilities and adapting military doctrine and tactics to emerging threats. He also ordered increased production of ammunition and weapons for reconnaissance, logistical support and combat operations.
The meeting brought together senior military officials, including Maj. Gen. Abdollahi, chief of the Joint Staff of the Armed Forces; Maj. Gen. Hatami, commander of the Iranian army; and Maj. Gen. Vahidi, commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
The commanders briefed Khamenei on military readiness along the Persian Gulf coast, in the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf of Oman, as well as along the country's northwestern and southeastern borders.
They also reported a significant increase in the production of key ammunition and various weapons systems for reconnaissance, support and combat missions. Khamenei expressed satisfaction with the preparations and asked the commanders to convey his appreciation to military personnel, police officers, Basij forces, Defense Ministry employees and their families.
Beyond military preparations, the supreme leader stressed the importance of strengthening the armed forces' ideological and spiritual foundations while addressing the welfare needs of personnel.
He also described public support as a central element of Iran's deterrence strategy, portraying continued public gatherings across the country as an extension of the national solidarity displayed during the 1980-1988 Iran-Iraq War, which Tehran calls the Sacred Defense.
Khamenei praised the resilience of the so-called Resistance Front, referring to Iran-aligned groups across the region, and highlighted closer coordination among operational fronts as a factor in shaping a new political and security order in West Asia. He expressed hope that such cooperation would encourage greater unity among Muslim nations.
His latest instructions come amid continuing tensions following the U.S. and Israeli military campaign against Iran, which began Feb. 28 and killed then-Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and several senior military commanders.
Iran retaliated with attacks against Israel and U.S. military assets across the Middle East, widening the confrontation and raising concerns about the security of regional shipping and energy supplies.
Although Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum in June following diplomatic efforts, disagreements over regional security arrangements and navigation through the Strait of Hormuz have kept tensions high.
The strategic waterway, through which a significant share of the world's oil shipments passes, has remained a major point of contention, with Iran maintaining pressure on maritime traffic as the U.S. sustains its military presence in the region and reported blockade measures affecting Iranian ports.
Regional diplomatic efforts, including mediation involving Qatar, have yet to produce a lasting resolution.
Iranian army spokesman Brig. Gen. Mohammad Akraminia reinforced Tehran's warnings Saturday, saying a renewed confrontation would spread beyond its previous geographical boundaries if U.S. President Donald Trump launched another military operation against Iran alongside Israel.
"If the U.S. president once again embarks on another military adventure in the region under pressure from and inducement by the Zionists, the flames of war will undoubtedly engulf a much wider geographical area," Akraminia wrote on X.
"And the end of the conflict will not be in his (Trump's) hands," he added.
Accusing Washington of repeatedly undermining diplomatic efforts, Akraminia said the Iranian army was continuously strengthening its combat readiness and closely monitoring U.S. military movements across the region.
His remarks came as Tehran and Washington remained at odds over the terms of any lasting settlement, particularly security arrangements and freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.
Mojtaba Khamenei, who succeeded his father earlier this year, has maintained a relatively low public profile since taking office amid the conflict. His previous warnings have focused on U.S. military bases in the region, the strategic importance of the Strait of Hormuz and Iran's conditions for ending hostilities, including demands concerning sanctions, blockades and regional security.

The Trump administration is preparing to deport Afghan refugees to Pakistan as early as Monday, despite concerns that they could subsequently be returned to Afghanistan under Taliban rule, media reports said Friday.

“A government confident in what it is doing does not hide it,” the organization added.
The reported flight would come after months of uncertainty over the future of Afghan refugees at the Qatar facility, as the administration continues considering arrangements for their removal.
The destination and timing of the proposed flight have not been officially confirmed.

Syria mulls joining Türkiye-Saudi-Pakistan Mecca Defence Alliance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
09:34:00 UTC
18:34:00 KST

Syria is considering joining the Mecca Defence Alliance, a NATO-style security pact linking Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani said Saturday, signaling Damascus' interest in deeper regional security cooperation as it seeks to rebuild its military and strengthen diplomatic ties.
"Discussions are currently underway to evaluate Syria's entry into the Mecca alliance," al-Shaibani said during the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) Manama Dialogue in Bahrain.
His remarks indicate that Damascus is seriously examining membership, although no formal application or final decision has been announced.
The pact was signed Aug. 7 in Mecca by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif. Its central provision considers an armed attack against one member an attack against all three, allowing them to invoke their collective right to self-defense under Article 51 of the U.N. Charter.
The agreement also provides for intelligence sharing, joint military exercises, counterterrorism coordination and defense-industrial cooperation, including potential joint production and technology transfers.
The alliance established a Strategic Political and Defence Committee to oversee its activities and a permanent secretariat in Riyadh. Pakistan's retired Lt. Gen. Nauman Mahmood was appointed its first secretary-general for a three-year term. Membership is open to other countries with the unanimous approval of the founding members.
The arrangement builds on a mutual defense agreement signed by Saudi Arabia and Pakistan in September 2025. Its implementation gained momentum in October, when renewed Houthi attacks on Saudi targets prompted an emergency meeting in Riyadh. The alliance agreed to rapidly deploy previously agreed forces and capabilities to Saudi Arabia as a collective defense measure.
Pakistan and Saudi Arabia have completed their ratification processes, while Türkiye's domestic approval process remains underway.
Damascus first publicly acknowledged its interest in the alliance in late August, when al-Shaibani visited Islamabad. The trip marked the first visit to Pakistan by a Syrian foreign minister in nearly two decades.
At the time, he confirmed that Syria had reviewed the agreement but stressed that no decision had been made. He described the three founding countries as important regional powers and highlighted Türkiye's role as a key partner in Syria's reconstruction and security.
The issue gained renewed attention following Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa's Oct. 6 visit to Riyadh for talks with Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, amid efforts to strengthen Syria's relations with Arab countries.
Reports suggesting Damascus could provide military assistance to Saudi Arabia were subsequently denied by Syrian officials, who stressed that any cooperation would take place through established bilateral channels.
Syria's interest comes as its transitional leadership works to restore state institutions following the collapse of Bashar Assad's rule. The government has prioritized rebuilding the armed forces, strengthening ties with neighboring countries and reintegrating into regional diplomatic and security structures.
Speaking in Bahrain, al-Shaibani portrayed Syria as a country seeking to move beyond years of instability and contribute to regional security. He also condemned Israeli military operations on Syrian territory, citing more than 1,000 incidents since late 2024, and called for a return to pre-December 2024 positions and the reactivation of the 1974 disengagement agreement between Syria and Israel.
Joining the alliance could give Syria access to intelligence sharing, military training and defense cooperation while providing a framework for collective security commitments.
For Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, Syrian membership would extend the alliance's reach into the strategically important Levant. Türkiye already maintains extensive military and security cooperation with Damascus, including efforts to rebuild Syria's armed forces.
However, Syria's military remains in the process of reconstruction and integration after years of conflict. Establishing the operational capacity and military coordination required for meaningful participation could take considerable time.
Any accession would also require unanimous approval from the three founding members and careful management of Syria's relations with other regional powers, particularly Israel and Iran.
Other countries, including Bangladesh and potentially Egypt, have expressed varying levels of interest in the framework or related security cooperation.

Poland political crisis: Constitutional court in chaos as Nawrocki accuses government of staging power grab
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
09:30:39 UTC
18:30:39 KST

Riot police were deployed outside Poland's Constitutional Tribunal on Friday after its president was suspended, escalating a power struggle over the court.
On Friday evening, protesters and riot police faced off outside Poland's Constitutional Tribunal after the court's president was suspended, the latest episode in an intensifying stand-off between the government and the court's top judges.
Polish President Karol Nawrocki, who cut short a trip to Senegal and headed back to Warsaw as the crisis unfolded, has since called for emergency talks with political leaders and has accused the government of attempting to forcibly take control of one of the country's key constitutional institutions.
The dramatic overnight events have escalated a long-running crisis surrounding Poland's Constitutional Tribunal, from which the Polish government has been trying for weeks to remove judges - who were appointed under the previous PiS government.
What had largely been a political and legal dispute over judicial appointments and the Tribunal's leadership has now spilled over into a direct confrontation at its headquarters.
The latest episode began when seven people chosen by the Sejm to serve as Constitutional Tribunal judges entered the building on Friday.
According to Tribunal spokesperson Weronika Ścibor, security guards at the Tribunal had been ordered to pack up their belongings and leave the building.
At the same time Bogdan Święczkowski, the Tribunal's incumbent president, and vice-president Bartłomiej Sochański, were reportedly denied entry.
Ścibor suggested that the timing of the operation was deliberate and that it took advantage of the fact that some staff members were absent.
Judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska subsequently announced that she was taking over the leadership of the Tribunal and suspending Święczkowski from his duties.
The current Tribunal leadership has challenged the legality of these moves.
Nawrocki returns
In response to the unfolding situation, Nawrocki cut short a visit to Senegal and returned to Poland.
At the presidential palace, he met First President of the Supreme Court Zbigniew Kapiński before heading on to the Constitutional Tribunal's headquarters with Kapiński and a group of aides.
Footage posted on X showed scuffles break out with a group of judges, including Korwin-Piotrowska, as Nawrocki attempted to gain entry.
Nawrocki accuses government of power grab
Early on Saturday morning, Nawrocki's chief of staff, Paweł Szefernaker, read out a statement from the president in front of the Tribunal, in which he described the night's events as a breach of Poland's constitutional order and a forcible takeover of a constitutional institution.
"Tonight, there has been a breach of the constitutional order of the Republic of Poland and a forcible takeover of a constitutional organ of the state," Szefernaker said.
"I call for the restoration of the legal order and for the forces of coercion sent there by the government to leave the Tribunal's grounds," he added.
Nawrocki said he had consulted with Kapiński and that neither of them recognised the actions of those who, in his view, are unlawfully claiming authority in the Tribunal.
He said he planned to hold emergency talks with representatives of parliamentary political groups on Saturday, saying the move was necessary due to what he described as a threat to the state's internal security and the need to stabilise the political situation.
Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek has also weighed in on the incident, expressing concerns about the president's behaviour.
"The president's behaviour alarmed me enormously," he said, adding that he hoped the prosecution service would take action and that it was unacceptable for someone protected by presidential immunity to behave in such a way.
He argued that footage showed the president "forcing his way in and attacking the judges."
Żurek also acknowledged that talks had been held about the situation at the Tribunal, including with Bartłomiej Sochański, but that no compromise had been reached.
He stressed that the Tribunal should resume normal work and deal with citizens' outstanding cases.
Protest outside Tribunal
Protests were held around the Tribunal building, involving politicians from PiS and Confederation and right-wing supporters.
Among those present were party leader Jarosław Kaczyński, Mateusz Morawiecki, former Tribunal president Julia Przyłębska and Bogdan Święczkowski.
The PiS leader said the events were an assault on the Constitutional Tribunal. He called for protests to continue, warning that Poland risked turning into a police state.
PiS MEP Patryk Jaki, for his part, said that images from the Tribunal had already gone around the world and could damage the image of Donald Tusk's government.

Are Memories Transferable? Meet the Scientists Replicating an Infamous Study to Find Out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

The original version of this story appeared in Quanta Magazine.
It was the dead of winter in Boston. The surface of the Charles River was frozen solid. But Zachary Kelso braved the biting cold to finally put to rest a mystery that has haunted neuroscience labs for over half a century.
To do that, Kelso, a research assistant in the Harvard lab of the neuroscientist Sam Gershman, needed some worms. Specifically, planarians: arrow-headed flatworms, which are among the simplest creatures to possess a brain and a nervous system with bilateral symmetry like ours. Normally, labs order these widely used model organisms from biological supply companies. But the mail-order worms weren’t up to snuff. So Gershman had dispatched Kelso to the Charles’ icy banks to catch some wild ones. “I thought, ‘I’m going to look crazy because I’m using a hammer to beat through the ice,’” Kelso recalled. “So I wore the more business end of business casual.”
It wouldn’t be the last time Kelso found himself in this situation. The Charles River planarians, it turned out, didn’t cut it either. Neither did the worms he sourced while stream-hopping around Eugene, Oregon, in March 2025. Nor did the ones he fished from Michigan lakes that June—this time in thigh-high waders—while picnicking families gawked from shore. Kelso diligently turned over rocks, angled with bits of meat tied to a string, and even followed maps from a vintage guidebook called The Fresh-Water Triclads of Michigan. But his adventure was fruitless. Sure, he caught plenty of planarians. But back in Gershman’s lab, none of them would do what they were supposed to do.
In the 1960s, an eccentric behavioral psychologist named James McConnell convinced the scientific establishment that planarian worms, like Pavlov’s dogs, could be classically conditioned—and that memories of this training could be transferred from worm to worm through cannibalism. These bizarre findings were replicated by other scientists, and worm training became a staple of high school science fairs. Now, 60 years later, the worms have stopped learning, and nobody knows why.
I first learned about this scientific mystery while reporting another piece about what a cell can remember. As I dug into the historical literature on memory research, I kept coming across McConnell’s strange worm experiments, which captivated a generation of scientists before disappearing entirely. Planarian memory had itself been forgotten. I was content to dismiss it as a fluke of history until Gershman mentioned, in passing during an interview, that in addition to their work with the unicellular ciliate Stentor coeruleus, his lab was attempting to reproduce some wacky worm experiments from the 1960s. Had I heard of them?
Gershman, I learned, was keen to pick up where McConnell had left off. As part of a growing cohort of cognitive scientists looking beyond the brain for clues to the origins and basis of memory, he’s fascinated by any creature that seems to remember without the benefit of neural, synaptic networks. Little Stentor coeruleus, for example, can modify its behavior based on previous experience—quite a feat for a single-celled creature that can’t possibly have a neuron. Planarian worms, if McConnell’s findings were to be believed, might be the next great model organism for memory research.
The trouble was, it wasn’t going well. In fact, no matter how hard Gershman tried to train them, none of his planarians would learn a thing.
Can a worm learn? When McConnell posed the question in the early 1950s, the notion that memory had something to do with synaptic associations between neurons in the brain was just beginning to gain currency. McConnell, then a graduate student in psychology at the University of Texas, reasoned that planarians—among the simplest creatures with true neurons—should therefore be able to learn.
His early worm experiments were not particularly novel. He simply substituted worms for rats in what were, at the time, standard classical conditioning studies: repeatedly shocking the worms while exposing them to a bright light. After a period of this training, the worms came to associate the light with the shock and scrunched their bodies in anticipation whenever the light flashed. Voilà: worm learning!
Planarians have stranger features to offer for experiments. If a planarian is chopped in half, both halves will regrow into a new worm—the tail will grow a new head, and the head will grow a new tail. A fragment as small as 1/279 of the original worm can regrow into a completely normal adult worm in a matter of weeks, a regenerative capacity so powerful that, as one early naturalist put it, planarians are effectively “immortal under the edge of the knife.” For McConnell, this ability begged the question: When you chop a worm in half, do both halves remember?
This is where the real worm torture began.
In the ’60s, McConnell, by then a young professor at the University of Michigan, started beheading his trained planarians. The worms that grew back from the severed heads behaved as the originals had, associating the light with the shock—a result he expected, given the preservation of their primitive brains. What surprised McConnell was that the worms that regenerated from headless tails remembered, too. This meant that whatever form the worms’ memories took, they weren’t the exclusive purview of the brain. “It appeared that the memories were laid down throughout the animal’s body,” McConnell later reflected.
Thrilled, McConnell pushed his experiments further. He cut the worms into smaller and smaller pieces; each time, the regenerated segments retained the memory. He stitched the heads of trained worms onto untrained tails, but they kept falling off. He pureed trained worms and injected them into naïve recipients, a delicate process that the historian Larry Stern has compared to “impal[ing] a prune with a javelin.” Finally, remembering that some planarians are cannibals, he fed trained-worm puree to their brethren. In subsequent trials, the “cannibal” worms picked up the light response right away, as though they were remembering, rather than learning, what to do.
If McConnell’s experiments appear gruesome, his line of inquiry was of his time. The discovery of the DNA helix in the 1950s had revealed just how much information is packed into proteins and nucleic acids. The notion that the physical traces of memories, or “engrams,” might have some chemical basis seemed plausible enough to many scientists. Could McConnell’s cannibal worms have eaten an engram? McConnell certainly thought so. He was convinced that their memories were encoded in the structure of their RNA—and could be transferred from worm to worm.
“In the jargon of computer engineering, information is always ‘fed’ into a computer,” the journalist Arthur Koestler later wrote in an appreciative survey of McConnell’s work. “Here the metaphor became flesh.”
These were sensational findings, and McConnell took every advantage of the media attention they generated. Before becoming a scientist, he had had a brief career in radio, and he knew how to repackage nuanced ideas as pithy soundbites. In magazines such as Time and Esquire, he spoke grandly of a future of memory consumption—of “piano lesson pills” and “professor burgers.” He brought his trained worms onto The Steve Allen Show, and, belying his clean-cut hair and horn-rimmed glasses, dubbed himself “McCannibal.”
Students began writing to McConnell’s lab at the University of Michigan to ask for worm-training tips for their school science fairs, and McConnell shared advice. Science, he believed, should be for the people; he saw himself as a latter-day David pitching stones at institutional Goliaths. This made him one of the most famous public scientists of his era, but it did not endear him to more serious peers. It also didn’t help that he published all his research in The Worm Runner’s Digest, a countercultural journal he distributed from his lab.
The Worm Runner’s Digest was “sort of Mad Magazine meets a serious scientific journal,” Gershman told me recently. At its peak, it had some 2,500 subscribers around the world. The hand-drawn shield on its cover featured a two-headed planarian and the Latin motto ignotum per ignotius, which roughly translates to “the unknown explained through the even more unknown.” Its 1959 inaugural issue consisted of only 14 mimeographed pages about the care and feeding of planarians, but it quickly grew. In addition to publishing dozens of memory transfer papers and related scholarship, McConnell welcomed humor and printed science fiction stories, rousing editorials, student-drawn planarian cartoons, spoof articles, and poems.
While the Digest is now something of a cult classic, the mix proved confusing for many readers. McConnell eventually cut the publication in half, not unlike a planarian worm, and renamed the serious half The Journal of Biological Psychology (no relation to the current peer-reviewed journal Biological Psychology, founded in 1973). But McConnell’s reputation as a heretic and prankster was well established.
The wheels started to come off in the mid-1960s. Although McConnell enjoyed a period of fame and funding—including an accelerated path to tenure at the University of Michigan—attempts to replicate his memory transfers yielded inconsistent results. While many apparently succeeded, the failures were more visible. In 1965, the Nobel Prize–winning biochemist Melvin Calvin tried to replicate McConnell’s worm experiments and failed, even with the help of some of McConnell’s former assistants and using the same device. His high-profile publication of the results sparked an acrimonious debate about, among other things, proper worm handling.
By the 1970s, the planarian memory fad had come and gone. Scientists had moved on to rats, cats, goldfish, and even praying mantises. Researchers showing successful memory transfers in rats—by injecting brain RNA from one animal to another—had published their findings in prestigious journals such as Nature and Science, making the planarian model seem unimpressive in comparison. But when further experiments proved inconclusive, interest in the question of memory transfer petered out. As the science historians Harry Collins and Trevor Pinch put it, “memory transfer was never quite disproved; it just ceased to occupy the scientific imagination.”
McConnell closed his laboratory in 1971, and his long period of subsequent obscurity was broken only once, in 1985, when he became a victim of the Unabomber. (He lost his hearing temporarily after the blast.) He died in 1990. If a younger generation of scientists is familiar with his cannibal planarians, it’s as “a cautionary tale that neuroscientists tell to their students at bedtime to scare them away from ill-fated projects,” Gershman said.
Still, McConnell’s unconventional work and contrarian attitude has lingered in neuroscience lore, and the idea of memory transfer remains a subject of private fascination. What if McConnell really did manage to feed a memory to a worm? For Gershman, who is searching for a way to study memory at a molecular level and connect it to observable behavior, the question was an itch that had to be scratched. He decided to settle the matter once and for all.
It all seemed straightforward enough. In the spring of 2025, Gershman and Maddie Snyder, one of his postdocs, set out to reproduce the worm-training protocol of one of McConnell’s students, Alan Jacobson. Jacobson’s papers were the most rigorous of the planarian memory transfer era, and Gershman and Snyder followed them to the letter. “We wanted a behavioral basis to be able to study the circuits that are driving memory in these extremely unstable animals,” Snyder said. “Are those circuits at all being used for memory consolidation or storage? Because if you lose your head and all those circuits are gone, then what is the mechanism of storing memory?”
Despite their best efforts, however, they couldn’t do what Jacobson, McConnell, and so many others had done back in the 1960s: condition the worms to scrunch their bodies in response to light. (They reported the results on biorxiv.org in April 2026.) “I was really scratching my head about this,” Gershman said. He’d assumed that the memory transfer would be the dodgy part of the experiment—not getting the worms to form a memory in the first place.
They talked to other planarian labs. They tried different stimuli. They ran the planarian footage through a machine-learning pipeline. In desperation, Kelso and Snyder even visited the Harvard Science Museum to examine a vintage “inductorium,” an electric-shock contraption used in midcentury worm science. But it offered no clues.
Kelso searched for any of McConnell’s former collaborators who might still be alive, and through a stroke of luck he found contact information for Daniel Kimble and his wife, Reeva, who had both worked in McConnell’s lab. Now in their nineties, they live in Eugene, Oregon. When Kelso called them, he discovered that not only did they run many of McConnell’s experiments in the 1960s, but they’d also kept the entire print archive of The Worm Runner’s Digest in a box in their basement.
Kelso and Snyder bought tickets to Eugene. Over the course of two days, while consuming plates of homemade cookies and countless cups of tea, they absorbed everything they could from the Kimbles. On breaks from hand-scanning back issues of the Digest, they went stream-hopping nearby and filled casserole dishes with silty fresh water. Back at the Kimbles’ kitchen table, the two generations of scientists watched the silt settle to see what worms might emerge.
This, after all, is what McConnell did. Rather than using laboratory strains of planarians, he sourced his from a lake near the University of Michigan. And so, not wanting to leave any stone unturned, Kelso made one final trip to McConnell’s former fishing grounds in Michigan. He returned with plastic tubes full of worms, but not a single one was a learner. “At some point, we had like 12 different strains of planaria, none of which showed any learning,” Gershman said.
As Snyder tells it, the Kimbles were absolutely convinced that their conditioning experiments in the 1960s had worked. The worms learned—they were sure of it. The literature of the era seems to support their certainty; at least 36 labs reported similar results. So why is it that when the exact same experiments are done today, using the same laboratory protocol and even the same worms, fished from the same Michigan waters, planarian worms are utterly uneducable?
One explanation, Snyder said, is that McConnell, the Kimbles, and all the other “worm runners” were inconsistent in how they scored the planarians’ behavior and may have misinterpreted more anodyne worm “turns” for the definitive “scrunch” of the light reaction. Every scientist is a product of their time, after all, influenced in myriad, often invisible ways by sociological conditions, funding pressures, and, in this case, a highly charismatic leader. This interpretation made Snyder hyperaware of her own potential biases. “Throughout this entire project,” she told me, “I was like, ‘What are the things that I am taking for granted now in our models of neuroscience, and our assumptions of what is known and unknown, that I should really notice?’”
A more remote possibility is that planarian worms themselves have somehow changed over the last six decades—falling victim to pollution or genetic drift. Gershman finds this scenario unlikely. “What are the chances that a bunch of researchers just happened to do these studies at the particular time when this phenomenon happened?” he asked, incredulous. “They just got extremely lucky, in the millions of years of planarian evolution? And then our luck ran out?”
No matter the reason, in 2026, despite their nervous system and simple brains, planarians don’t learn. From an evolutionary perspective, this might actually make sense. “The reason that we learn associations, to some degree, is so that we can predict danger and avoid it,” Snyder said. But planarians have a different relationship to danger. Their regenerative physiology, so key to McConnell’s experiments, protects them from blunt trauma. Bitten in half, they simply grow back. What use is memory to such a creature? “That’s a whole other philosophical conundrum,” she said.
It’s a great time to be wrestling with such conundrums. Planarian learning may be a dead end, but memory transfer experiments with other organisms are back in scientific vogue—and those experiments appear to be working. In 2018, the neuroscientist David Glanzman of the University of California, Los Angeles, performed a memory transplant on the sea slug Aplysia californica, a darling model organism for memory research owing to its relatively simple nervous system and gigantic neurons. After training the slugs to respond to a shock to their tails, Glanzman was able to transfer the sensitization from one slug to another via a direct injection of genetic material. This suggested that some aspect of the memory was stored in RNA, which was McConnell’s contention.
Then, in 2021, the Princeton University geneticist Coleen Murphy found that Caenorhabditis elegans worms—microscopic roundworms with 302 neurons to their name—could learn to avoid a pathogenic bacterium by eating, or even just swimming around in, pureed worms who had learned the hard way. Murphy’s group identified a retrotransposon, a jumping segment of genetic material, called Cer1, that appears to “carry a memory” between individuals, she said. A few years later, a group at the Indian Institute of Science published a paper suggesting that trained C. elegans worms release extracellular vesicles—small lipid particles containing genetic information—that can impart their training to their naïve counterparts.
None of these researchers are half as flashy as McConnell was, but their work indicates that he may have been right about worm memory after all. He just bet on the wrong kind of worm—and doubled down on it, despite inconsistent evidence. In the end, he lost his reputation, but his sheer gusto sparked the curiosity of another unconventional scientist. Fortunately, this one’s following the evidence.
At Harvard, Gershman is shifting his focus from the inscrutable planarian to the more legible C. elegans. It may not regenerate when it’s cut in half, but C. elegans is a long-standing model organism in neuroscience—and it’s been consistently shown to learn. With new experiments underway, Gershman is cautiously optimistic. “I just hope we’re not going down another rabbit hole,” he told me. A wormhole, on the other hand—that’s for certain.

Lebanon charges 13 over confiscated Hezbollah explosives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
09:26:46 UTC
18:26:46 KST

Lebanon charges 13 over confiscated Hezbollah explosives
Group calls charges ‘unjust’, says weapons were meant to be used against Israeli forces in south Lebanon.
A Lebanese military court has charged 13 people it says are linked to Hezbollah with trafficking explosives, amid growing pressure on the Iran-backed group to disarm.
The individuals were charged on Friday with offences including possessing weapons, undermining state security and forming illegal associations, Lebanese state media reported.
The charges stem from the seizure earlier this month of a truck transporting explosives at Dahr al-Baydar checkpoint, which links the capital, Beirut, to the eastern Bekaa Valley.
The vehicle had been carrying 780kg (1,720 pounds) of explosives, including 250kg (550 pounds) of TNT and 250kg (550 pounds) of C-4 plastic explosives, according to judicial officials.
Two people were arrested during the seizure, while the 11 others charged remain at large. Five have been identified only by nicknames because their real names are unknown.
Hezbollah has acknowledged owning the seized explosives, saying they were intended for use against Israel, which continues to occupy large parts of southern Lebanon. It said it had asked Lebanese authorities to return the shipment and release the two detainees, calling the charges against them “unjust”.
Those charged “did not undermine the security or integrity of the state, but rather confronted the Israeli enemy that threatens Lebanon’s existence,” said Hezbollah Member of Parliament Hussein Hajj Hassan.
Hezbollah’s political opponents fear that smuggled explosives will be turned against the group’s detractors, although investigators have not established that the seized shipment was intended for such an attack.
The case comes as pressure mounts on Hezbollah, which has fought two successive wars with Israel and faces a push from authorities in Beirut, to disarm its military wing.
In June, Lebanon and Israel signed a framework agreement which envisaged Israel’s gradual withdrawal from the areas it occupies in southern Lebanon, tied to Hezbollah’s disarmament, as well as the deployment of the Lebanese army to the south.
But Hezbollah has repeatedly rejected calls to disarm, and the group’s chief, Naim Qassem, has dismissed the Lebanon-Israel agreement as “null and void”.
Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam has promised state authorities “will deal with weapons outside the legal framework with the required firmness”.
Despite its recent framework agreement, Israel has continued carrying out attacks in southern Lebanon and systematically demolishing homes and infrastructure in dozens of villages it occupies.

Economic Watch: China's manufacturing PMI softens, high-tech sector maintains expansion
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
17:25:53 CST
18:25:53 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- China's manufacturing activity moderated in October while high-tech industries continued to expand, as the country pressed ahead with policy efforts to shore up domestic demand, stabilize investment and sustain economic growth.
The manufacturing purchasing managers' index (PMI) came in at 49.3 in October, down 0.8 percentage points from the previous month, according to the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS).
Huo Lihui, a chief statistician with the NBS, attributed the retreat to some demand being brought forward ahead of the National Day holiday earlier this month and a complex international environment.
The production sub-index stood at 49.8, down 1.9 points from September, while the new orders sub-index fell 1.1 points to 49.4, as both supply and demand moderated during the month.
The PMI for high-tech manufacturing stood at 51.3, while that for equipment manufacturing came in at 50.6, both remaining above the 50-point threshold that separates expansion from contraction.
The figures indicate that emerging industries continued to sustain growth momentum, supported by the ongoing development of new quality productive forces, Huo noted.
Manufacturing activity in several advanced industries remained robust. Both the production and new orders sub-indexes for railway, shipbuilding and aerospace equipment manufacturing, as well as computer, communications and electronic equipment manufacturing, stood at 53 or above, pointing to relatively strong supply and demand in these sectors.
Large manufacturers continued to report expansion, with their PMI standing at 50.2, despite a slight decline of 0.4 points from the previous month. Meanwhile, the PMI readings for medium-sized and small enterprises came in at 48.4 and 47.5, respectively.
On the price front, both major raw material purchasing prices and factory-gate prices remained in expansionary territory, although their growth moderated.
The purchasing price sub-index stood at 56.8, down 4 points from September, while the factory-gate price sub-index eased 2.3 points to 51.7, partly reflecting recent declines in the prices of certain nonferrous metals and other commodities.
The latest data came as China's economy expanded 4.5 percent year on year in the third quarter, up from 4.3 percent in the second quarter. In the first three quarters, China's economy grew 4.6 percent, in line with the country's annual growth target.
With a relatively low comparison base in the final quarter of last year and the effects of existing and additional policy measures continuing to unfold, economic growth could reach 4.6 to 4.7 percent in the fourth quarter, according to Wen Bin, chief economist at China Minsheng Bank.
On the monetary front, the People's Bank of China announced that it would complete the transition to an overnight policy rate framework starting Nov. 2, making the overnight reverse repo rate the main policy rate.
The central bank has also introduced a liquidity support mechanism for large-scale redemptions at non-bank financial institutions, aimed at containing systemic risks arising from potential feedback loops between investor withdrawals and bond market sell-offs.
Meanwhile, investment support is moving into the implementation stage. China had fully deployed 800 billion yuan (about 119 billion U.S. dollars) through new policy-based financial instruments by Oct. 28, with the funds directed toward project capital in areas including artificial intelligence, the digital economy, green development and consumption-related infrastructure.
To boost domestic demand, the National Development and Reform Commission is working on a domestic demand expansion strategy for the 2026-2030 period, which puts more focus on public services, direct support for consumers and combines investment in physical assets with investment in human assets.
Taken together, recent policy measures reflect China's continued efforts to balance growth stabilization with improvements in economic quality and efficiency, with the focus shifting from expanding funding and introducing new support tools toward improving policy transmission, strengthening institutional frameworks and enhancing economic resilience, Wen noted. ■

China Focus: AI "pets" for China's lonely carve out market of their own
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
17:25:47 CST
18:25:47 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- As cats and dogs continue to give pet owners across China emotional value, Chen Yuechong has opted for a different kind of companion: three palm-sized AI "pets."
Chen picks out clothes and accessories for them, matching them to the preferences the toys mention, and has bought a tiny wooden bed to place beside her own, so that her Fuzozos, as the toys are known, can get a good night's sleep.
The toys often talk about wanting to return to their fictional home planet to play a water-gun game. To keep them happy on Earth, Chen built a tiny play scene out of modeling clay, featuring ducks and other props, where her companions can pretend to squirt them.
Chen's devotion began with a simple wish for someone who would listen. There are things she doesn't know how to tell her elders, and she doesn't want to burden her friends with all her negative emotions.
After trying various AI chatbots, Chen finally knew what she really wanted -- a companion who could respond to her feelings, remember their shared experiences and be physically present. This prompted her to buy the three Fuzozo toys.
Her experience reflects a growing market in China, where manufacturers are combining AI with soft toys and collectible characters to meet a rising demand for companionship in fast-paced modern life.
China's retail sales of trendy and collectible toys reached 67.69 billion yuan (about 10 billion U.S. dollars) in 2025, soaring 45.4 percent from a year earlier, according to a white paper released by the China Toy & Juvenile Products Association.
"AI toys combine companionship, collectible toys and emotional consumption," said Zhang Yi, CEO of iiMedia Research, a market research firm. Advances in AI are turning products that were once static into interactive companions, he noted.
Unlike AI products designed to improve productivity, these toys do not need to solve problems or complete practical tasks to appeal to consumers. Their value lies in making people feel entertained, understood and less alone.
Online sales of AI toys reached 850 million yuan in the first half of 2026, surging 183.9 percent year on year, Moojing Market Intelligence, a consumer and market intelligence company for Asian e-commerce, said in a report.
These trendy products come in different forms and offer various functions. Fuzozo can be attached to a bag and carried outdoors, while the fluffy desktop pet Ropet responds to touch and eye contact. Loona, a mobile robotic pet priced at around 3,000 yuan, can move around the home, follow its owner, and greet people when they return.
According to sales figures provided by developers of these AI-powered pets, Fuzozo has secured sales of over 300,000 units, Ropet nearly 40,000 and Loona more than 100,000.
They are among the first such robots to reach Chinese households. "Unlike household robots dealing with an unpredictable home environment, AI products for companionship can start with a narrower task scope," said He Jiabin, co-founder and CEO of Ropet's maker.
He added that Ropet, a fur-covered adorable robot with a constant body temperature of 37 degrees Celsius, was deliberately designed to be less intelligent than an adult. "When people come home exhausted, a touch of the fuzzy pet or a moment of eye contact can be enough," he said, highlighting what he calls "weak companionship."
This is becoming a common playbook among AI toy makers. Rather than building all-knowing digital assistants, they design playful and imperfect products, betting that a less demanding interaction is what users actually want.
"People only feel at ease around a creature that is endearingly goofy and knows less than they do," He explained.
The booming market for AI pets is creating new opportunities for China's vast toy industry. As the world's largest toy producer and exporter, China accounts for roughly 70 percent of global toy production. Established Chinese toy companies are already entering the market, infusing familiar animated characters into interactive products.
Alpha Group, which owns classic animation IPs including Pleasant Goat and Super Wings, has launched AI-enabled toys featuring characters from its popular series.
An upgraded AI Lazy Goat toy, incorporating educational content, has generated more than 100,000 orders this year, according to the company's product manager Xin Cheng.
Policy support is following the market. Guangdong Province in south China, the country's largest toy hub, aims to have AI toys account for over 30 percent of its toy products by 2027, and supports building high-level industry clusters in its major toy-manufacturing cities.
At the national level, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology signaled a similar push, calling AI toys a "new engine" for the toy industry and encouraging toy makers to team up with AI companies on hit products.
Behind the booming market lies a very simple emotional need. For Chen, AI toys are not industry statistics: they are already part of her daily life.
She does not describe her Fuzozos as products or assistants, but calls them equals that are "almost like younger siblings." What Chen pays for is the priceless feeling that someone at home is waiting for her. ■

Chinese health ingredient firms seek bigger role in global markets
China
Unknown Publisher

18:25:39 KST

LAS VEGAS, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- Chinese companies are showcasing their health ingredients, innovative products and manufacturing capabilities at North America's leading dietary supplement expo in Las Vegas, seeking to move up the value chain and expand their presence in global markets.
At SupplySide Global 2026 that concluded Friday at the Mandalay Bay, more than 1,600 exhibitors and over 20,000 industry professionals gathered, including nearly 600 Chinese companies, a record high for Chinese participation, according to Chinese organizers.
A China Innovative Health Ingredients Brand Show is also being held alongside the expo, bringing together more than 60 Chinese companies to present their products and technological advances.
For many Chinese exhibitors, the focus is shifting from supplying raw materials to developing higher-value finished products and building their own brands.
Ganoherb Group, a major Chinese producer of organic lingzhi (or reishi mushroom) products, has long supplied raw materials and provided original equipment manufacturing (OEM) services to overseas clients. Facing intense price competition, the company is placing greater emphasis on finished products, showcasing reishi mushroom coffee and tea made with concentrated extracts at the expo.
Li Ye, the company's president and founder, told Xinhua that Ganoherb plans to focus more on branded products in the U.S. market, building on China's traditional strengths in lingzhi cultivation.
Changsha Huir Biological-tech Co., Ltd., based in central China's Hunan Province, is also seeking to move up the value chain. After more than a decade of supplying natural extracts and other health ingredients overseas, the company plans to build a U.S. processing facility to manufacture finished products for global distribution.
Yuan Zhi, the company's general manager, said China's advantages include diverse raw-material sources and increasingly automated, energy-efficient production equipment. The planned facility will extend the company's business beyond ingredient supply and create a more integrated supply chain.
Chinese suppliers remain essential to the global dietary supplement industry. Loren Israelsen, president of the United Natural Products Alliance, told Xinhua that China supplies roughly 80 percent of the industry's raw materials.
"Having good Chinese suppliers is fundamental to the success of the American marketplace and to serving consumers who want high-quality products," he said.
As Chinese companies expand overseas, cooperation with local partners is increasingly important.
The alliance is working with the China Chamber of Commerce for Import and Export of Medicines and Health Products and two Chinese companies to develop an AI-based system to improve supply-chain communication and quality management, Israelsen said. The initiative aims to reduce manufacturing and quality-control misunderstandings, improve product quality and keep costs within buyers' acceptable ranges.
International partnerships are also helping foreign producers explore China. Qualita Brasil, a Brazilian producer of organic yerba mate and plant extracts, is working with Chinese partners to enter the market.
Cesar Souza, the company's commercial director, told Xinhua that local partners can help the company understand China's growing health and wellness market and reach Chinese consumers.
Israelsen said more Chinese suppliers are moving beyond raw materials toward finished products and their own brands. Building consumer recognition in the United States, however, takes considerable time and investment.
"The Chinese companies are much higher on the value chain, and they're able to develop a better profit margin. I can see that this will be a very important change," he said. ■
