When buses stopped running on Brazil election day, 'Lula's Army' grabbed their car keys
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
08:06:41 UTC
17:06:41 KST

When buses stopped running on Brazil election day, 'Lula's Army' grabbed their car keys
SALVADOR, Brazil, Oct 31 - When buses in the northeastern Brazilian city of Salvador inexplicably stopped running last Sunday, history teacher Martins Mafra grabbed his car keys and set off to pick up stranded voters across town.
Mafra's efforts in Salvador, the capital of Bahia state, were part of a massive get-out-the-vote drive across Brazil that helped power leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva to an unprecedented fourth term.
Lula supporters, shocked by right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro's first-round lead, quickly mobilized as the prospect sank in that the Bolsonaro clan could return to power. They used innovative social media initiatives, free taxi rides and grassroots campaigning to secure the incumbent president over 10 million more votes in the runoff.
"I'm a father, and I work in education, so this was an opportunity to teach and show that we can make a difference," said Mafra, who offered rides to supporters of all stripes. "It's one thing to stay home complaining about city hall or posting videos online; it's another thing to get up, walk out the door, and actually do something."
Bolsonaro, son of jailed former President Jair Bolsonaro, fled this week to the US, where he declared himself the legitimate "leader" of Brazil, questioning the credibility of Lula's 10 million-vote leap.
Bolsonaro also questioned a two-hour voting extension, requested by Lula's campaign and granted by a Lula-appointed Supreme Court justice, due to the out-of-service buses in Bahia. Bolsonaro's campaign also sought an extension due to rains in conservative-leaning southern states, and the extension had little bearing on the result, the federal electoral court said.
LULA STRONGHOLD
Bahia, a populous Lula stronghold, was the state with the highest fall in abstention rates between both rounds, with nearly 400,000 more people voting in the runoff.
Almost a quarter of those additional voters came from Salvador, a city of over 2.5 million people where Lula won 73% of runoff votes.
Salvador resident Gabriel Mercury, 41, son of Brazilian pop star Daniela Mercury, was one of those who helped orchestrate the turnaround.
The Lula voter watched with concern as the leftist underperformed in the first round, and decided to do something about it. He began by inviting undecided voters to have coffee with him and talk politics. Later, he offered cash rewards of up to 2,400 reais ($445.67) to anyone who could name a single Bolsonaro legislative proposal that had benefited workers.
Nobody took him up on the offer.
LULA OVERHAULS CAMPAIGN
After the underwhelming first round, Lula's team sought to reboot a campaign marred by infighting, mixed messaging and the complacency of incumbency, aides said.
Aware that no presidential candidate had ever been elected after trailing in the initial vote, the 81-year-old Lula bought his first ever smartphone to reach Brazilians on the platforms that increasingly shape Brazil's political debate.
Meanwhile, lawmaker Andre Janones, who helped Lula beat Jair Bolsonaro in 2022, rapidly expanded a WhatsApp channel he called "Lula's Army."
By instructing followers to recruit friends and amplify Lula content online, he grew the channel from roughly 50,000 people ahead of the first round to over 10 million by the runoff.
Dharma political risk consultant Creomar de Souza said Lula's team, and particularly Janones, successfully pounced on missteps by Bolsonaro to convince voters he would threaten Brazil's democracy, reverse social advances and slash welfare payments on which millions of Brazilians depend.
As the runoff approached, polls showed Lula closing the gap on Bolsonaro. By election day, they were tied.
In Salvador, Mercury began to believe Lula could win. Then, early on Sunday, Salvador's bus network ground to a halt.
BUS FIASCO
In Brazil, public authorities are required to provide free public transport on election day.
But reports from across Salvador, where Mayor Bruno Reis supported Bolsonaro, suggested many buses were not running.
Inspectors from the Bahia consumer protection agency found 944 buses idling in Salvador depots. Jaime Barreiros Neto, the Bahia electoral court's judicial analyst, estimated at least 30% of the fleet was not operating.
Reis blamed the outage on Lula stickers that had been placed on buses in violation of electoral rules. As soon as city hall realized sticker removal efforts were causing a bottleneck, it immediately ordered the fleet released, he said in a press conference on Sunday.
Reis told Reuters he supported Bolsonaro in the runoff in accordance with his party, União Brasil. He denied detaining public transport or hindering voter mobility, saying the stickering of the buses held up the fleet.
Bahia’s electoral court ordered the arrest of Salvador’s transportation chief, Pablo Souza, over the absent buses. It revoked the order once voting had ended the following day, but demanded a probe into the incident.
Souza, who was in Paris on an official visit during the day of the vote, denied wrongdoing. He told Reuters the number of buses was the same as during the first round, and in line with electoral regulations.
MASS MOBILIZATIONS
As news of idling buses rippled through Salvador, Mercury and five friends asked their social media followers to drive people to voting stations. Some people got behind the wheel; others donated to cover fuel costs. Mercury estimated that his team moved around 600 voters on election day.
"Politics isn't just institutional politics," he said. "We make politics through our actions."
Uber drivers also stepped up, with thousands offering free rides worth up to 50 reais ($9.28) throughout the day, said Adriano de Jesus Braga dos Santos, an Uber driver and content creator, who personally offered 36 rides to passengers.
Nicole Soares, 18, waited 40 minutes for a bus, but never considered giving up. "I had the right to vote," she said, casting her ballot for Lula.
Some residents were still unable to vote.
Grecia de Jesus Nunes, a 54-year-old street vendor, said only two buses passed her hotdog stand between 8 a.m. and 2 p.m. No buses were available during her brief break, and when volunteer drivers eventually reached her, she could no longer leave work.
Though unable to vote, Nunes rejoiced at Lula's victory.
"My life is Lula," she said. "I am Lula until I die." REUTERS

China's manufacturing activity moderated in October, with the purchasing managers' index falling to 49.3 as the high-tech and equipment manufacturing sectors maintained expansion, official data showed on Saturday.
The overall reading was down 0.8 percentage points from September, according to the National Bureau of Statistics.
Chief statistician Huo Lihui attributed the retreat to some demand being brought forward ahead of the National Day holiday this month and a complex international environment.
The production subindex stood at 49.8, down 1.9 points from September, while the new-orders subindex fell 1.1 points to 49.4, as both supply and demand moderated during the month.
The PMI for high-tech manufacturing stood at 51.3 while that for equipment manufacturing came in at 50.6, both remaining above the 50-point threshold that separates expansion from contraction.
The figures indicate that emerging industries continued to sustain growth momentum, supported by the ongoing development of new quality productive forces, Huo noted.
Manufacturing activity in several advanced industries remained robust. 
Both the production and new-orders subindexes for railway, shipbuilding and aerospace equipment manufacturing, as well as computer, communications and electronic equipment manufacturing, stood at 53 or above, pointing to relatively strong supply and demand in these sectors.
Large manufacturers continued to report expansion, with their PMI standing at 50.2, despite a slight decline of 0.4 points from the previous month. 
The PMI readings for medium-sized and small enterprises came in at 48.4 and 47.5, respectively.
On the price front, both major raw material purchasing prices and factory-gate prices remained in expansionary territory, although their growth moderated.
The purchasing price subindex stood at 56.8, down four points from September while the factory-gate price subindex eased 2.3 points to 51.7, partly reflecting recent declines in the prices of certain nonferrous metals and other commodities. (Xinhua)

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has praised the US for its "strong decision" to approve the sale of 500 much-coveted Patriot missiles to Ukraine - but he has warned that delivery could take years.
The US State Department announced on Friday that Washington had green-lit a package of Patriot PAC-3 interceptors worth $2.1 billion as Kyiv continues to defend against Russian missile and drone attacks.
"Five hundred PAC-3 interceptors is a substantial number, and very soon – this winter – they COULD make for a highly effective defence package," Zelenskyy wrote in a post on social media in response.
"However, it has been stipulated that deliveries may begin ONLY IN A FEW YEARS," he continued. "We are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3 interceptors."
Earlier this week, Zelenskyy said Kyiv had been waiting for almost a month for US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth to sign off on a batch of missiles for both the Patriot and NASAMS systems.
Kyiv has long called for more interceptors to help its forces fend off Russian attacks, and the rapidly approaching winter is pressing home that need. Russia has repeatedly sought to target Ukraine's power grid over wartime winter periods as Moscow has looked to break the country's resolve.
Dwindling stocks of interceptors have already encouraged Russia to ramp up missile attacks in recent months, and there are fears this trend could lead to an especially brutal winter for Ukrainians.
"The United States, our European partners, and other partners around the world have sufficient stocks of PAC-3 interceptors in their warehouses," Zelenskyy said overnight. "Providing them to Ukraine right now – in the winter of 2026–2027 – and replenishing our partners’ arsenals LATER, in THE FOLLOWING YEARS, through this production already contracted and paid for by Ukraine and our partners would be the right approach."
The Patriot missile platform is one of the world's most advanced air defence systems and can be used to defend against a variety of threats, including incoming aircraft and ballistic missiles.
Ukraine receives the majority of its Patriots through NATO’s Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) initiative, which facilitates the purchase of military equipment and munitions from the US by allies and partners.
As of June 2026, allies had committed to funding more than $6 billion of defence equipment for Ukraine through the scheme, per NATO.

China's marine tourism maintained stable growth in the first three quarters, the ministry said.

"Diversifying the Canon to Recover Humanity’s Past: The Case of Pre-colonial Andean": An Essay by Jorge Sanchez-Perez (Keywords: Erasure; Colonialism;Epistemic injustice;Indigenous Epistemologies)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
07:40:07 UTC
16:40:07 KST

"Diversifying the Canon to Recover Humanity’s Past: The Case of Pre-colonial Andean": An Essay by Jorge Sanchez-Perez (Keywords: Erasure; Colonialism;Epistemic injustice;Indigenous Epistemologies)
From The Philosopher, vol. 114, no. 2 ("Autumn 2026")
You can purchase a physical copy here and a digital copy of this issue and all previous issues here. If you enjoy reading this, please consider becoming a patron or making a small donation. We are unfunded and your support is greatly appreciated.
‘Avila needed the information for indoctrination and
to choose the way to extirpate idolatries.
Who and which were the gods of Huarochirí?
How were they worshipped? When and where?
Everything is spelled out in the manuscript.’
- José María Arguedas
Introduction to Dioses y Hombres de Huarochirí
A brief walk among some of the most prestigious universities in the world will allow anybody to see that demands to expand the philosophical canon beyond Western perspectives have become quite common. This demand – mostly led by students, I have to point out – has created two clear sides in the academic community. On the one hand, we have the large number of academic philosophers who claim to be on board with such an idea, on the other, we have the set of common suspects who claim that something cannot be properly conceived as philosophy unless it is somehow related to European men. For example, it was not too long ago that a reviewer suggested one of my papers be rejected because it made them uncomfortable to engage with philosophical work that does not exclude Indigenous views from philosophy from the beginning. This debate, of course, presupposes that the canon has been somehow limited and shaped by certain perspectives in what the former side might consider unfair ways, and what the latter side might consider consistent with philosophical traditions extending all the way back to Socrates. The presupposition that there might be an unfairness attached to this reality, as many can imagine, does not seem to be far off. Yet for all its rhetorical appeal, if demands to diversify the canon are meant to support real change, first they need some theoretical justification, and second, some awareness of the methodological challenges involved in this demand. I will address both points here, focusing on the colonisation of the Americas as an example of how political structures and actors at different levels develop certain views that end up affecting how something like the philosophical canon looks and what challenges arise when trying to correct that.
A good way to provide theoretical justification to the demand to diversify the canon can come from looking into the work of Peruvian sociologist Anibal Quijano. Throughout his lifetime, Quijano developed an approach known as the colonial matrix of power. This approach can be used to understand colonization, an important historical phenomenon that has shaped the last five hundred years on the planet, in a more comprehensive way. A key element this framework posits is that assuming colonisation as a one-off event is not conducive to understanding the phenomenon. Instead, we are invited to think of colonisation as a set of relations that, even if traced back to an original important historical event, still endure through time and shape different aspects of a society hundreds of years later. As an example of this, we can think of Alexander the Great’s actions in the 4th century BCE, and how they shaped Europe and Asia in a way that would make the Roman Empire possible centuries later. Similarly, we could think of how Tupac Inca Yupanqui, in the 15th century CE, unified South American trading routes in a way that a couple of centuries later would allow the Spanish Empire to control the whole Andean region.
To conceive of a reality where the effects of colonialism are no longer present would be short-sighted.
As those two examples show, although we can study some historical events alone, to conceive of them as detached from other elements would be rather naïve. In the same vein, consider European colonisation, a process which between the 16th and 20th centuries led Europeans to control about 80% of the planet. To conceive of a reality where the effects of colonialism are no longer present would be short-sighted. Another implication of the use of the colonial matrix of power as a framework is that it becomes obvious that certain ways of thinking or certain ideas have indeed been preferred over others due to the role that knowledge plays in the shaping of political projects. Knowledge production, selection, and dissemination are all elements that the colonial matrix of power invites us to reflect upon. Thus, it should not come as a surprise that political projects, such as the one known as the colonisation of the Americas, had epistemic goals or constraints attached to them. Staying with the two examples I provided above, denying that Alexander the Great had a massive impact on the Hellenisation of Europe and other parts of the world, or that Tupac Inca Yupanqui had a role in the expansion of Quechua as the dominant language and culture in South America, would be very hard to defend. Those who think that events that took place in Greece over two thousand years ago can shape the life of contemporary Europe, but events that took place only five hundred years ago in the Americas cannot shape it to this day, can be rightfully called out for suffering from a very clear case of cognitive dissonance.
If we follow that kind of reasoning, a demand to expand the philosophical canon could be framed also as a demand to understand which political choices were made in light of colonial relations of power, and how those choices could have led to the current state of affairs of the set of ideas usually referred to as the philosophical canon. That is, which ideas or ways of thinking were deemed as useful for the different political projects of colonization, and which were deemed as problematic or dangerous. By approaching the topic in this way, it becomes much more obvious that certain ways of engaging with questions around race, gender, class, nature, reality, and so on, benefited certain goals. This approach provides a very plausible explanation of why the canon looks the way it does today.
For the purposes of this essay, I want to focus on the case of the colonisation of the Andean region of South America, and particularly on pre-colonial Andean Philosophy. I consider the relative global lack of awareness of pre-colonial Andean Philosophy a core example of how the colonial matrix of power can be useful to understand how some gaps in the current canon can be explained. To make sense of this, one must first be aware of the existence of the four Alexandrine Bulls, issued in 1493 by Rodrigo Borgia, also known as Pope Alexander VI. They were titled, in order: Inter caetera, Inter caetera II, Eximiae devotionis, and Dudum siquidem. Together, these documents granted the monarchs of Spain and Portugal dominion over large parts of the Americas. The theoretical and legal position that was developed from these documents, among others, would later be known as the infamous Doctrine of Discovery. Under the doctrine of discovery, the kings of Spain and Portugal could claim any discovered land, within certain geographical boundaries, as long as such lands were not ruled by a Christian prince. In practice, this doctrine became the ultimate justification for European colonialism across the planet.
To say that Andean philosophical knowledge was simply sidestepped would be wrong.
As an important sidenote, despite what some readers might think, this doctrine was not explicitly rejected by the Catholic Church until the spring of 2023. Pope Francis rejected it only after his 2022 trip to Canada, where he visited to apologized personally for the historical and contemporary failings of the Catholic Church and its participation in practices such as the implementation and management of the residential school system – a system that effectively promoted the genocide of Indigenous peoples in the country for over a hundred years. While on the trip, Indigenous leaders and scholars demanded the explicit renunciation of the doctrine of discovery. This eventually led to the ultimate abjuration of the doctrine. I consider that this case provides us with one of the most interesting examples of how decisions made in the 15th century with the goal of justifying the seizing of Indigenous land and lives, have a lasting impact reaching our days.
Going back to the case under consideration, the right to rule these ‘new’ lands came with the obligation to exalt and disseminate the Catholic faith among their inhabitants. In this way, an insidious connection between political and religious goals took place; one in which projects to control and dominate an entire continent were intertwined with epistemic goals. The goals were connected to the elimination of local views that could oppose those projects. Since the Inquisition was meant to deal with members of the Catholic faith, and not those outside the Church, new institutions and practices were developed to deal with Indigenous peoples of the Americas – specifically, to facilitate the elimination of Indigenous views which threatened the claims of the Catholic monarchs and the Church. Among those new institutions and practices, the example of the Extirpations of Idolatries needs to be considered as central in understanding why we know so little about pre-colonial Andean Philosophy.
Any individual that claimed the title of Extirpator of Idolatries had a mandate to eradicate any religious or cultural view that could oppose the teachings of the Catholic Church. To do this, they would visit a town, communicate their authority, gather information of ‘sacred’ places or items, and then proceed to destroy them. All this while promoting the abjuration of what they considered idolatries. These views, as one can imagine, were usually held by the local knowledge keepers known in Quechua as amautas. In some cases, extreme measures would be used against Indigenous populations. From physical to psychological violence, extirpators were granted a large degree of autonomy in their pursuit of their goals. These practices took place in the span of three centuries and were, sadly, quite successful. I say successful, because they managed to effectively eradicate large swaths of knowledge that Andean civilisation had carefully accumulated for over five thousand years. Yes, in less than three hundred years, most of the knowledge that had been kept since civilisation started in that part of the world was eradicated. The reason? It was deemed as a threat to the dominant views from both the Catholic Church and the European empires.
Views about time, space, nature, gender, nature, etc., were hunted and eliminated to such a degree that discussions in most philosophical academic circles are either extremely hard or impossible to come by. To say that Andean philosophical knowledge was simply sidestepped would be wrong. At this time, we simply lack the resources to even engage with it in meaningful ways, and that, as I showed before, is by design. A colonial project was implemented in that part of the world and those in command of that project deemed certain ways of knowing the world as competition and as such, those ways had to be eliminated. This is, probably, one of the best examples of how by using the colonial matrix of power we can provide an explanation, in terms of relationships of domination and political goals, of why certain philosophical traditions simply are not part of the canon. With this reality in mind, I want to address my second point: the methodological challenges that diversifying the canon would entail.
It is not uncommon to find the usual suspects who claim that unless something is somehow related to European men, it cannot be properly conceived as philosophy.
Continuing with my example of pre-colonial Andean Philosophy, I want to focus on what demands to diversify the canon would imply. As I mentioned before, most resources that could have informed any discussion of what pre-colonial Andean Philosophy would look like, as well as the views we can attribute to different groups within that part of the world, were actively destroyed. If that is the case, then how can diversification happen? What would it entail to try to diversify the canon by including something like pre-colonial Andean Philosophy? The answer to both questions is simply more work than what many individuals might assume.
My own research is focused on trying to reconstruct pre-colonial Andean philosophy from two sources. The first one is the Huarochirí Manuscript, and the second is a set of legal cases from the 17th and 18th centuries against Indigenous people of the Andes for the crime of idolatry. The first source is, without a doubt, the most important Andean document in existence. This is a manuscript compiled in secret by Choquecasa, a local Indigenous nobleman, at the bequest of the priest Francisco de Ávila, one of the most successful extirpators of his time. In this manuscript, Choquecasa, most likely due to his position as a member of Quechua nobility, was able to secretly record creation stories, practices, and foundational myths of the central Andes region from amautas. Later on, the manuscript was used by de Avila to effectively identify which ideas, places, and individuals had to be eliminated. The manuscript, written in Quechua, was neglected for centuries after the death of de Avila and left in the archives of the Library of Madrid. Luckily for all of us, by the 1930s, Hermann Trimborn, a German expert on American Indigenous cultures, would approach the manuscript with working knowledge of Quechua and properly appreciate its relevance.
While the Huarochirí Manuscript contains a host of wonderful philosophical insights about time, space, nature, human-animal relationships, and more, I also thought it would be useful to rely on alternative sources. For that reason, I engaged with a set of legal cases from the 17th and 18th centuries that are hosted in the archives of the Archbishop of Lima. In those cases, charges of idolatry and sorcery are leveled against Indigenous people. While interesting from a purely historical perspective, the description of the crimes also serves as a relevant tool to put together practices regarding nature, medicine, agriculture, etc., which also show several philosophical views that underlie many of those practices.
I will explain some of the methodological challenges that are connected to working with these sources. First, it is important to be aware of the lack of access to regular philosophical sources like philosophy texts. As I mentioned at the beginning of this essay, it is not uncommon to find the usual suspects who claim that unless something is somehow related to European men, it cannot be properly conceived as philosophy. If we add the reality that the sources people like myself are relying on do not look like the kind of philosophical texts that are common in the Western philosophical canon, then the chances of having one’s work discarded increase as well. For my research, I rely on what philosopher James Maffie, an expert on Mesoamerican pre-colonial thought, calls triangulation, a way of finding philosophically relevant information from sources that do not resemble philosophical texts. This kind of work, however, allows for the challenge of how something like an Indigenous story could count as a philosophical source to be raised. Although I have published on this topic and developed a whole account about how philosophical sources can be identified, these kinds of methodological challenges are not rare and keep happening at every corner.
I am convinced that humanity’s future can benefit from learning from humanity’s past.
Second, it is also important to notice that many of those sources are not going to be written in English, the lingua franca of our times. So, access to “diverse” sources gets even more complex. The number of philosophy PhD holders with training in Indigenous philosophical methodologies is extremely limited, and the number of those who can work on or with an Indigenous language is also quite small. To that, we have to add the difficulties attached to accessing sources like the ones I mentioned above. What I have in mind, based on my personal experience, is the challenge of properly learning palaeography–that is, learning how to read ancient handwritten texts. Finally, and insofar as sometimes those texts are not digitised, accessing those sources involves traveling to the archives in different parts of the world.
None of the points I have raised should be understood as a rejection of the demand to diversify the canon. On the contrary, I am part of the movement of academic philosophers who actively seeks to see this demand come to fruition. I am convinced that humanity’s future can benefit from learning from humanity’s past. If we fail to put the pieces of the worldviews of our predecessors together, we might be limiting our potential to understand how to do better. The drastic loss of much Andean thought is but an example of this sad reality that we need to revert. However, I also think that we need to understand that this demand cannot be materialised unless first, we are able to make sense of why the canon might look how it does nowadays, and second, we are aware of the difficulties that diversification entails. If academic philosophers are serious about this kind of project, and I know many are, we need to do better than provide rhetorical moves and start thinking in terms that address the theoretical and methodological demands that real diversification would demand.
Jorge Sanchez-Perez is an associate professor in the University of Alberta’s Department of Philosophy. He is an academic philosopher and a trained lawyer whose research interests include social epistemology, Indigenous philosophy, early modern philosophy, and moral and legal philosophy. He is the lead researcher of the SSHRC funded project “The Indigenous Stories of Philosophy.” His first manuscript, "Indigeneity and the Mestizo Question: The Limits of Latin American Philosophy," is forthcoming in 2027. He has published in the fields of Indigenous philosophical methodologies, meta philosophical issues surrounding Latin American Philosophy, race in Early Modern Philosophy, the nature of law, and Global Justice.

3 Palestinians killed in Israel's ongoing violations of Gaza ceasefire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
07:38:23 UTC
16:38:23 KST

Ramzi Mahmud, Serdar Dincel, and Rania Abushamala
31 October 2026•Update: 31 October 2026
Two Palestinian were killed and several others injured in Israeli strikes on the Gaza Strip Saturday, while another died of wounds sustained in an earlier attack, medical sources told Anadolu.
The deaths came amid continued Israeli army violations of a ceasefire agreement in the Gaza Strip that has been in effect since October 2025.
In the latest developments, one Palestinian was killed and others were injured in an Israeli strike on a tent sheltering displaced people west of Khan Younis in the southern enclave, a medical source at Nasser Medical Complex said.
Separately, a medical source at Al-Awda Hospital in central Gaza said Diaa Abu al-Rous was killed in an Israeli strike north of the Nuseirat refugee camp.
Four Palestinians were injured in an Israeli strike targeting a group of civilians near the Abu Namous roundabout east of the Maghazi refugee camp, the source added.
Witnesses told Anadolu that an Israeli drone carried out the strike near the headquarters of a power company north of the camp.
Separately, Arafat al-Arair died of serious wounds sustained several days earlier in an Israeli strike targeting a vehicle in the Tel al-Hawa neighborhood, southwest of Gaza City.
A medical source at Al-Shifa Hospital in western Gaza City confirmed his death to Anadolu.
Israeli shelling reported across Gaza
Meanwhile, local sources told Anadolu that Israeli military vehicles and artillery shelled several areas across the Gaza Strip.
The attacks targeted eastern parts of Beit Lahia in northern Gaza, Gaza City, Khan Younis in the south, and Deir al-Balah in central Gaza, according to the sources.
Israeli warships also shelled the Gaza City coastline and opened machine gun fire toward the shore. Israeli military vehicles fired heavily at homes near the al-Sanafour intersection in Gaza City’s eastern Tuffah neighborhood.
In Khan Younis, local sources reported that Israeli military vehicles opened fire toward tents sheltering displaced Palestinians in the al-Iqlimi and Bir 19 areas south of the city.
Several tents were struck by gunfire, but no injuries were reported, according to the sources.
Ceasefire violations leave over 1,500 dead
Israeli violations of the Gaza ceasefire as of Saturday have killed 1,580 Palestinians and wounded 5,711 others, according to figures from Gaza's Health Ministry.
Since October 2023, Israel's war in Gaza has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and wounded over 175,000 others, according to the ministry.
The war has also destroyed around 90% of Gaza’s civilian infrastructure, according to the figures provided.

Iran-Africa trade turnover registers a 66% growth in H1
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

07:37:52 UTC
16:37:52 KST

Speaking in the First Iran-Africa Agricultural Cooperation meeting held in Tehran on Saturday, Iran’s Minister of Agriculture Gholamreza Nouri-Ghezeljeh stated that the $940 million worth of trade with lucrative African countries’ market is insignificant that should be developed to a great extent.
Iran and African countries have high potentials to increase and enhance their trade exchanges to a great extent and this issue must be taken into serious consideration, the minister stressed.
Emphasizing the need for a paradigm shift in economic relations, he called for the transformation of political commitments into operational projects and joint investments.
Pointing to the potential capacities of both sides, Nouri Ghezeljeh emphasized that Iran sees Africa not merely as a sales market, but as a strategic partner in production and development.
Elsewhere in his remarks, the Iranian minister of agriculture pointed to the complementary capabilities of Iran and Africa, highlighting Iran’s strengths in areas such as irrigation management, greenhouse construction, agricultural machinery, seed production, livestock and poultry farming, vaccines, and agro-processing industries/
He emphasized Africa’s immense potential regarding tropical products, fisheries, and its growing markets.
The minister also said Iran has already held technical training courses for delegations from countries such as Ghana and Senegal and had pursued economic cooperation mechanisms with Ghana, Senegal, Tanzania and Kenya. He called for greater involvement of the private sector, saying governments should facilitate cooperation while businesses take the lead in implementing joint projects.

Live: Kangaroos wrap up RLWC group stage against Cook Islands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31

16:36:39 KST

Fri, 11 Sept, 7:50 pm, Final score, Rabbitohs 10, Knights 20
Kangaroos top Rugby League World Cup Pool A with 66-6 win over Cook Islands
The Kangaroos finished the group stage of the Rugby League World Cup undefeated, closing out the Pool A action with a 66-6 win over Cook Islands in Townsville.
On a sweaty night up north, the Australian men were below their best to start and briefly trailed the Islanders 6-4 before asserting their dominance with 10 unanswered tries.
Wingers Tom Trbojevic and Jack Bostock both finished with hat-tricks while Tino Fa'saumaleaui grabbed a double.
Fullback Reece Walsh was named player of the match after a try, five assists and a pair of line breaks, but his fitness is somewhat concerning.
Walsh grabbed at his foot after converting Kotoni Staggs's 27th-minute try and, despite looking untroubled while finishing off a spectacular team try on the half-hour mark, handed over goal-kicking duties.
Cameron Munster kicked goals for the rest of the game and Walsh closed out an impressive performance that will likely quiet calls for him to be replaced by James Tedesco.
The Kangaroos will play their semifinal on Sunday, November 8 at the Sydney Football Stadium, but their opponent will not be known until after the clash between Tonga and Samoa tomorrow night.

Scam centres relocated from Cambodia operate in Madagascar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
07:30:00 UTC
16:30:00 KST

Scam centres relocated from Cambodia operate in Madagascar
ANTANANARIVO, Madagascar – Raids against online scam centres in Madagascar have exposed ties with a criminal group that ran similar operations in Cambodia, also duping African nationals via alleged human trafficking, the authorities told AFP.
Conducting romance, cryptocurrency and investment fraud, the sites were operated mostly by Chinese nationals, 148 of whom have been extradited to China, Madagascar’s Justice Ministry said.
Thirteen Chinese-run scam compounds were taken down in operations in August and September conducted with the US Department of Justice (DOJ), it said.
About US$52 million (S$66.6 million) of cryptocurrency was seized in a single day and more than 3,200 electronic devices were processed, the US authority said in a statement.
The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime had warned in 2025 about the expansion of these networks, particularly into Southern Africa.
Eleven Chinese nationals arrested separately in the online scam crackdown mysteriously walked free from a Madagascar jail in August in a widely publicised scandal allegedly implicating the head of the prison service.
Several African nationals remained in custody, even though initial findings suggested they may have been victims of human trafficking, officials said.
Recruited via social media
As in scam operations in South-east Asia, the Madagascar centres allegedly lured Africans to the Indian Ocean island via social media and with promises of salaries.
In this case, around 20 nationals of Kenya, Rwanda, Uganda and Zimbabwe were in custody, the authorities said.
“According to their statements, they were recruited via Facebook to come work in Madagascar in the commercial sector,” the police crime unit chief Hassan Mouigni told AFP.
“But when they arrived here, most of the passports were confiscated by the boss and they were forced to scam,” he said. “They were victims of deception.”
The man charged with running one romance scam scheme was a Malaysian national, identified as Chui Kok Wa, who had installed himself in a villa in the upscale Ivato neighbourhood near the capital, Antananarivo, the US authorities said.
“From the visa in his passport, we were able to deduce that he arrived here for the first time in 2024. According to the passport, he was previously in Cambodia,” Mouigni said.
The DOJ said it believed his “criminal group with connections to Malaysia and China opened scam compounds in Madagascar in early 2025, likely having moved those operations from Cambodia after law enforcement action in that country”.
The coordinator of the cybercrime unit at Madagascar’s Communications Ministry, Tsitohaina Ralihivao, drew a connection with a 2025 crackdown on scam compounds in Cambodia near the border with Thailand, when their militaries also clashed.
“When the Thais dismantled them, they just relocated the operations. The same organisations came to Madagascar,” Ralihivao told AFP.
Relocating
An FBI court document shared by the DOJ drew a similar conclusion after questioning three Brazilian nationals who worked at a scam compound in Antananarivo.
“These individuals reported that they originally responded to work opportunities posted online, and ended up working at a compound located in Cambodia.
“Later, in part due to an armed conflict between Cambodia and Thailand, and also in response to police activity in Cambodia related to scam compounds, the witnesses were moved to Antananarivo, Madagascar, in early May 2026,” it said.
“Cyber scam centres are increasingly opening in Africa following the closure of such compounds in South-east Asia,” the FBI said.
The US authorities intervened because these centres “primarily targeted English-speaking countries”, including the United States, Canada and Pakistan, Mouigni said.
Hence the “need for nationals from English-speaking African countries”, added Ralihivao.
The arrival of scam centres has not gone unnoticed in the capital of Madagascar.
“Before they occupied villas that were a little discreet. What alerted us was that they started renting entire hotels,” Mouigni said.
The suspected head of one compound installed at the Live Hotel in the city was a Chinese national who was among those extradited to Beijing.
Like all “Chinese nationals identified as leaders”, he could not be questioned by the FBI, a US federal police said in court documents. AFP

Taipei mayor candidates face off in televised debate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
07:24:42 UTC
16:24:42 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — KMT Taipei mayoral candidate Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) and his DPP counterpart Puma Shen (沈伯洋) faced off over housing, childcare, and education in their televised debate Saturday.
CNA reported that the debate, hosted by TVBS and SET News, came ahead of the Nov. 28 mayoral election. Chiang is seeking a second four-year term, while Shen hopes to end KMT rule in the capital.
Chiang cited the opening of the Taipei Dome sports stadium, plans for Nvidia's overseas headquarters in Taipei, and higher birth grants as key achievements. He accused Shen of making promises without clear plans to carry them out.
Shen said voters should judge the candidates on their policies rather than who won the debate. He pledged to plant more trees, tackle child abuse, and improve school meals during his first 100 days in office.
Housing became a major point of dispute, with both candidates questioning how the city should replace aging buildings. About 70% of Taipei's buildings are more than 30 years old, while disputes over ownership, costs, and building rules can hold up rebuilding projects for years.
Chiang said his administration had made progress on several long-delayed urban renewal projects, claiming the number of projects had risen to 2.4 times the previous level. Shen questioned whether the figures showed real progress, arguing that approvals meant little if projects had yet to start or finish construction.
Chiang accused Shen of failing to understand the height limits near Songshan Airport, which restrict how tall nearby buildings can be for flight safety. Shen said the city should explain such rules to residents early and help them work through obstacles to rebuilding.
Childcare was another point of dispute, with Chiang questioning whether Shen could find enough carers to provide four hours of free temporary childcare each week for children under 6. The service would allow parents to leave their children with trained carers for short periods.
Shen said the plan would begin with children under 2 and expand as more staff and childcare places became available. Chiang questioned whether the city could recruit enough carers to meet demand.
The candidates also disagreed over Shen's plan to assign two teachers to each elementary school class to share teaching duties. Chiang cited an existing teacher shortage, while Shen said the scheme could first be tested in selected grades, drawing on a similar program at a school in neighboring New Taipei.
School meals also drew attention, with Chiang highlighting free lunches and milk as ways to ease costs for families. Shen proposed raising meal funding in line with food prices and giving parents the option to pay more for higher-quality meals.
On transport, Chiang pointed to efforts to ease traffic, including the removal of the Gongguan traffic circle, a busy roundabout in southern Taipei. Shen said residents still faced damaged sidewalks and unsafe cycling routes, arguing the city needed to do more to make streets safer.
The debate was the first direct televised meeting between the two candidates after weeks of talks over its date and format. Both camps agreed to let the candidates question each other, giving voters a chance to compare their plans before the election.

Beijing’s Taiwan blockade playbook gets test run in Pakistan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
07:24:34 UTC
16:24:34 KST

Pakistan reportedly barred Taiwanese airlines from its airspace on Oct. 25, forcing China Airlines and EVA Air to reroute Europe-bound flights. However, the restriction was reversed three days later, with Pakistan’s Civil Aviation Authority restoring overflight permissions through March 2027.
Although short-lived, the episode offered Beijing a potential real-world test of how an incremental, legally framed blockade could disrupt Taiwan’s international connectivity and how quickly other countries would respond.
Pakistan’s apparent willingness to risk diplomatic and commercial friction over Taiwan reflects its economic dependence on China. Facing persistent foreign exchange shortages, a heavy debt burden and repeated reliance on International Monetary Fund assistance, Islamabad regards Beijing as a crucial financial backer. China has repeatedly rolled over loans to help the country avoid default.
The political alignment was underscored when Pakistani Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar met Chinese Ambassador Jiang Zaidong in Islamabad to advance the second phase of the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) on the day the reported airspace restriction began. Defense Minister Khawaja Asif subsequently confirmed that Pakistan followed a “one-China” policy.
On Oct. 26, Chinese Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Mao Ning traveled to Islamabad for the third Pakistan-China Spokespersons’ Dialogue, where she joined Pakistani Information Minister Attaullah Tarar in launching the China-Pakistan Information Corridor. Tarar reportedly said: “If CPEC connects our economies, the Information Corridor will connect our minds.”
Administered through the External Publicity Wing Secretariat of Pakistan’s Ministry of Information, the initiative is intended to deepen digital, media and economic cooperation. Its proposed activities include a trade portal to promote Chinese investment in 5G and artificial intelligence, a media coalition involving 18 organizations, including Xinhua, and a northern tourism corridor intended to attract Chinese visitors and foreign exchange.
A coordinated media network could help counter criticism of the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor, including allegations of debt dependency. Meanwhile, the corridor’s supporters have an interest in protecting a project that has attracted tens of billions of dollars in Chinese capital.
Salami-slicing the skies
The Pakistan episode can be viewed as part of a broader pattern of pressure on Taiwan’s international mobility. It offers Beijing an opportunity to assess the consequences of restricting commercial aviation without directly initiating a military confrontation.
The dispute over the M503 flight route illustrates the longer-running pressure. In February 2024, China’s Civil Aviation Administration unilaterally scrapped flight-offset measures for routes near the Taiwan Strait, increasing concerns in Taipei about aircraft operating closer to the median line and potentially reducing its air defense early-warning time.
A second example came earlier this year when President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) faced difficulties arranging overflight clearances for a planned state visit to Eswatini. Taiwan blamed Chinese pressure after several African countries withdrew permissions. Lai eventually traveled to Eswatini in May, following a complicated route across the southern Indian Ocean.
The Pakistan episode potentially took the strategy a step further by targeting commercial aviation networks rather than presidential travel. Deputy Foreign Minister Chen Ming-chi (陳明祺) said China had learned that restricting access to foreign airspace could be an effective way to limit Taiwan’s international connectivity.
For Beijing, the incident offered an opportunity to observe how quickly Taiwan’s diplomatic partners would intervene, what pressure they could bring to bear on Islamabad and whether a temporary restriction could achieve its objectives before an international response gathered momentum.
Legal and systemic fallout
The episode also raises questions about the separation of international aviation from political disputes. Pakistan’s reported decision to condition overflight access on adherence to the “one-China” policy risks undermining the predictable and nondiscriminatory application of international aviation rules.
The Chicago Convention establishes the framework for international civil aviation, while the International Air Services Transit Agreement provides for certain overflight rights among participating states. Using political recognition as a condition for commercial aviation access could weaken confidence in these arrangements.
The restoration of permissions through the International Air Transport Association winter schedule also illustrates how ordinary administrative procedures can become instruments of political pressure. If airlines must repeatedly seek renewed access because of diplomatic disputes, they face uncertainty over routes, costs and operational planning.
Cabinet Spokesperson Michelle Lee (李慧芝) said the government was coordinating with domestic airlines and relevant agencies to address the situation. The transportation ministry would need to consider flight safety, operating costs and alternative routes if access to foreign airspace became unreliable.
The disruption also exposed the country’s potential dependence on Russian airspace. During the reported restriction, China Airlines and EVA Air rerouted some Europe-bound flights through Russian territory. Taiwanese carriers had generally avoided Russian airspace since Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, in line with many Western and Asian airlines.
Such diversions carry financial and strategic risks. Longer routes increase fuel consumption, operating costs and travel times.
They could also leave Taiwanese carriers exposed to political pressure from Moscow, which maintains close relations with Beijing. In a cross-strait crisis, Russia could potentially use its control over its airspace to restrict Taiwanese flights or impose additional conditions on transit.
Also, the episode could have implications elsewhere. If Beijing can persuade a third country to restrict Taiwanese commercial transit, other governments may conclude that similar measures carry limited diplomatic costs. On Thursday, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun dismissed international concerns, saying the “one-China” policy represented an international consensus.
Anticipating the contagion
If the international response remains muted, Beijing could seek to persuade other countries to adopt similar restrictions. Cambodia and Laos are particularly exposed because of their economic dependence on China and their participation in Beijing’s Belt and Road Initiative.
Their financial relationships with China could give Beijing considerable leverage over foreign policy decisions. The strategic picture is further complicated by China’s growing military presence and influence in the region, including its involvement in facilities in Laos and the development of Cambodia’s Ream Naval Base.
The broader diplomatic pattern is also visible in Africa. The African Union endorsed Beijing’s position on Taiwan in the September 2024 Forum on China-Africa Cooperation Beijing Declaration. It reiterated its support for the “one-China” policy during the ninth China-Africa strategic dialogue in Addis Ababa on Jan. 8.
In Central Asia, countries including Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan depend heavily on China for investment, trade and transport connectivity. Their geographic positions could make them important to any effort to restrict Taiwan’s remaining aviation corridors to Europe. Djibouti, which hosts China’s first overseas military base, is another strategically significant country whose position could affect Taiwan’s international access.
The potential implications extend beyond aviation. If Beijing can encourage governments to restrict Taiwanese commercial aircraft from their airspace, it could attempt to apply similar pressure to maritime transport.
Countries hosting Chinese-operated ports, particularly those heavily dependent on Chinese investment, could face pressure to deny access to Taiwanese shipping companies such as Evergreen Marine, Yang Ming and Wan Hai. Restrictions at important ports and maritime bottlenecks in East Africa, Southeast Asia or Central America could disrupt supply chains, increase shipping costs and further isolate Taiwan’s export-dependent economy.
Such a strategy would not necessarily require a formal naval blockade. Administrative restrictions, port access decisions and selective enforcement of regulations could create substantial disruption while allowing Beijing and its partners to argue that they were exercising sovereign authority.
Imposing asymmetric costs
Taiwan cannot easily challenge Pakistan through conventional international institutions because of its exclusion from the UN, the International Civil Aviation Organization and the International Court of Justice. Even so, Chen Ming-chi said several like-minded countries had quietly assisted Taiwan in resolving the airspace dispute.
But diplomatic damage control is not a long-term strategy. Taiwan’s partners need a coordinated diplomatic, financial, economic and legal response designed to deter similar actions before they occur.
The US, Japan and EU members could challenge politically motivated restrictions through diplomatic channels and raise concerns about their compatibility with international civil aviation agreements. Formal complaints would help establish that using commercial overflight rights as a political weapon carries consequences beyond the immediate dispute.
Washington and other Group of Seven members could also consider whether future financial assistance to Islamabad should take account of its willingness to comply with international aviation norms. Pakistan’s dependence on Western-backed financial institutions, including the IMF and World Bank, provides potential leverage, although any conditions would need to be carefully designed and consistent with those institutions’ mandates.
The EU could review Pakistan’s Generalized Scheme of Preferences Plus trade status, which provides preferential access to the European market, as part of a broader discussion about compliance with international commitments. The EU should be cautious about linking trade privileges directly to a bilateral aviation dispute, but the issue could form part of a wider assessment of Pakistan’s obligations.
Regional partners can also help reduce Taiwan’s vulnerability by expanding alternative transport links. India, for example, could explore additional direct flights between the two countries, strengthening commercial connections and reducing reliance on routes vulnerable to political interference.
Pakistan’s reported airspace restriction was more than a brief diplomatic dispute. It exposed how Beijing could potentially use political influence over third countries to undermine Taiwan’s international mobility without resorting to military force.
For Taiwan and its democratic partners, the lesson is clear: allowing politically motivated restrictions to pass without a meaningful response could encourage further attempts to constrain access to international air routes, ports and commercial networks. The pressure may begin in the skies, but its consequences could eventually reach the world’s sea lanes and supply chains.

Taiwan introduces mobile weather radar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
07:24:12 UTC
16:24:12 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – The Central Weather Administration said on Friday that it plans to deploy a mobile weather radar in Hualien next year to track rainfall over the barrier lake near Mataian River, CNA reported.
The CWA commissioned the mobile weather platform alongside its fixed radar station for greater visibility. It said the radar's X/Ka frequencies can observe severe weather, such as typhoons and monsoons.
CWA Deputy Administrator Feng Chin-tzu (馮欽賜) said the fixed radar station can see up to 460 kilometers. He added there were six others across the country and noted that mobile radar can overcome terrain restrictions by covering difficult-to-reach places.
Feng said the mobile platform was previously tested at Yunlin’s Hushan Reservoir and will be redeployed to New Taipei’s Wufenshan to monitor winter low-hanging cloud patterns.
CWA Deputy Administrator Hung Ching-shan (洪景山) explained that fixed radars can see raindrops but not clouds. He noted the mobile weather system can use its Ka-wavelength to see cloud and mist droplets as well as crystals within 20 kilometers, while the X-frequency can detect raindrops and winds within 50 kilometers.
Hung said there were no rainfall measurement stations to record severe rain over Mataian and Wanli barrier lakes until earlier this year. He said the CWA would use AI to compile observation data from both radars to fill information gaps.
Hung added that the system will be redeployed to the upper Mataian River around mid-2027 to monitor rainfall over the barrier lake.

India pulls half a billion people out of poverty – faster than China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
07:22:33 UTC
16:22:33 KST

India pulls half a billion people out of poverty – faster than China
India has pulled nearly half a billion people out of poverty in little more than a decade, the World Bank has said. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government introduced a number of highly effective policies to help channel the benefits of the country’s rapid economic growth to the poor.
The feat is particularly impressive given that its population continued to grow during this period. It is now the most populous country on Earth, having overtaken China in 2023, and achieved poverty reduction much faster than its northern neighbor.
An estimated 496 million Indians were lifted out of poverty between 2011 and 2023, according to the World Bank’s October 2026 Poverty and Equity Brief.
The number of people living in extreme poverty, with an average income of $3 or less per day – declined from 27.1% of the population to as low as 2.6% during the period.
The proportion of Indians living below the lower-middle-income poverty threshold of $4.20 per day, measured at 2021 purchasing power parity (PPP), declined from 57.7% in 2011 to 16.1% in 2023.
A 2022 report, jointly produced by the World Bank and the Chinese Finance Ministry, showed that China had lifted 800 million people out of poverty, although it took four decades to do it. Beijing kickstarted its economic reforms in 1978 and the cited poverty reduction figures are from 2020.
It is not exactly an apples-to-apples comparison, but serves to show New Delhi’s remarkable achievement as India is a much smaller economy. China’s $20.85 trillion economy is now the world’s second-largest, while the Indian economy measures only about a fifth of that, at $4.5 trillion.
Increased employment, particularly among women, and expanded food subsidies and other social benefits boosted consumption growth, which played a key role in India’s achievement.
For much of the period when poverty rates were sharply declining, Modi led the country, having become prime minister in May 2014. His signature policy measure – direct benefit transfers – ensured the money from the government actually reached the bank accounts of the poor, rather than being siphoned off through various intermediaries.
The rapid economic growth under Modi’s stewardship also helped keep job generation far ahead of population growth. In the 2017-2023 period, employment in the South Asian nation increased by about 134 million people, with the job creation rate nearly twice the growth rate of the working-age population.
Much of these gains were driven by rural women entering the paid workforce and raising the number of earners per household.
The World Bank also cited wage disparities in the South Asian nation, as median earnings among the top 10% of workers were about 13 times those of the bottom 10% in 2023. More than 824 million people, about one in ten worldwide, were living in extreme poverty in 2024, as per latest World Bank data.

US, South Korea, Japan call for ‘complete denuclearisation’ of North Korea
The joint statement comes as US President Donald Trump seeks a new meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
The United States, South Korea and Japan have reiterated their longstanding call for North Korea to give up its nuclear weapons, a move Pyongyang has repeatedly ruled out.
The three countries addressed the issue on the sidelines of the Group of 20 (G20) meeting in the US city of Atlanta on Thursday, with their top diplomats reaffirming their “resolute commitment to the complete denuclearisation” of North Korea, according to a readout by the US Department of State.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun and Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi also pledged the “full implementation” of United Nations Security Council resolutions, including a ban on supporting revenue for North Korea’s nuclear and ballistic missile programmes.
The statement comes despite repeated overtures to North Korea by US President Donald Trump, who held a series of historic summits with its leader, Kim Jong Un, during his first term in office and has continued to call Kim a “friend”.
Last year, Trump bucked a long-held US policy by conceding that North Korea was already “sort of a nuclear power”.
More recently, he has played down concerns about North Korea’s nuclear programme and expressed a desire to meet Kim again. Speculation is mounting that the two leaders could reconnect at next month’s APEC summit in China, which Trump is due to attend.
Analysts and South Korea’s spy agency say Kim may have conveyed Pyongyang’s position on potential talks with Trump to Beijing during a recent visit to the Chinese border city of Dandong.
South Korea’s dovish President Lee Jae Myung – who has repeatedly offered Pyongyang talks without preconditions – suggested in September that Washington seek a freeze, rather than the immediate elimination, of the North’s nuclear programme in return for sanctions relief.
Critics have said such an approach risks tacitly accepting North Korea as a nuclear-armed state while allowing Pyongyang to win sanctions relief without giving up its arsenal.
Despite long-running UN sanctions, North Korea, which is backed by Russia and China, has enshrined its status as a nuclear-armed state in law. Pyongyang’s government has declared its atomic arsenal to be permanent and irreversible.
Pyongyang denounced a joint statement on Saturday by a group of nations monitoring sanctions implementation against it, pledging that “the stereotyped sanctions racket of the US and the West can neither influence the position of the DPRK (North Korea) as a nuclear weapons state.”

Louvre heist puts Europe's smaller museums on alert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
07:18:49 UTC
16:18:49 KST

Two men wearing head torches climbed through a forced-open window at the Fondazione Magnani Rocca museum near Parma on the night of March 22 and calmly lifted artworks by Cézanne, Renoir and Matisse from the walls.
Within three minutes, they had passed the works, valued at about €9 million ($10 million), to an accomplice and fled. At the museum's main gate, a fourth man discharged a fire extinguisher when the alarm sounded, distracting the custodian.
"Whatever could go wrong, did," said Stefano Roffi, director of the private foundation that runs the museum.
The raid was one of a string of museum thefts in France, Italy and Spain since last year's heist at the Louvre in Paris, raising concerns that criminals are increasingly targeting smaller institutions with fewer resources to protect valuable collections.
"This is where we see the 'Louvre effect'," said Marc Balcells, a Barcelona-based researcher specialising in crimes against cultural heritage. "If the Louvre was so easy to rob, just imagine a tiny museum in a rural area or a smaller town."
Works by Antonello da Messina vanished from a museum in his Sicilian hometown in August, while two Renoirs were stolen from Cagnes-sur-Mer on the French Riviera the following month.
In Spain, thieves stole hundreds of historic gold coins from museums in Badajoz and Albacete and made off with a Bronze Age treasure in Villena, near Alicante.
A 2024 survey by France's Culture Ministry found only one in four cultural institutions had an emergency and risk-prevention plan, while nearly half lacked video surveillance.
Who checks when the alarm goes off?
A French parliamentary report in May said museums lacked the resources and preparation to adequately protect artworks and artefacts.
In Italy, the challenge is amplified by the way the country's cultural heritage is spread across hundreds of towns and institutions, a legacy of centuries of fragmented rule.
"That is also what makes our system distinctive: works remain in the places where they were created,” said Antonella Pinna, president of the Italian committee of the International Council of Museums. "But we need to make life harder for criminals."
The council worked with Italy's Culture Ministry and the Carabinieri on museum security guidelines published in 2015, but Pinna said technology alone was not enough.
"If an alarm goes off, someone has to make sure it is checked," she said.
In a narrow street in the Tuscan town of Sansepolcro, the civic museum displays four works by Renaissance master Piero della Francesca, born just steps away in the 15th century.
The Louvre theft "affected us deeply because cultural heritage is central to Sansepolcro's identity. It is our soul," culture councillor Francesca Mercati told Reuters.
After the Louvre raid, officers from the Carabinieri's cultural heritage protection unit recommended more cameras, longer retention of CCTV footage and tighter controls on bags and bulky clothing.
"We immediately implemented those recommendations," Mercati said.
A vast network to protect
The scale of the challenge is daunting.
Italy has more than 4,400 museums and similar institutions, according to national statistics agency ISTAT. Spain has about 1,500 museums, while France has more than 1,200 institutions carrying the official "Musees de France" designation, alongside hundreds of smaller collections.
Protecting such a broad network is particularly difficult for smaller institutions that depend on local funding.
Florence Imbert, a Paris-based security consultant for cultural institutions, said 85 percent of small French museums were run by local authorities with limited financial resources.
"The budget is key to winning the war," she said.
France's Culture Ministry announced a 33-point security plan in July, backed by €30 million over three years for local museums.
Recent figures suggest concern is warranted. The Carabinieri art squad recorded 17 thefts from Italian museums and galleries in 2025, up from 14 a year earlier.
Europol said in an August report that museum thefts were becoming more forceful and increasingly focused on precious metals, gemstones and other high-value artefacts.
A fast buck?
Unlike jewellery, stolen famous paintings are difficult to sell openly and are more likely to be hidden, used in ransom attempts or offered privately, art expert Pinna said.
Even recovered works can leave museums facing substantial investigation, recovery and security costs.
Recent thefts have also renewed debate over insurance, with some museums reassessing their coverage.
Insurers are meanwhile exploring AI technology to analyse CCTV footage and help identify suspicious behaviour before thefts occur.
Security vs access
Museum officials face the challenge of improving security while keeping collections accessible to the public.
Julien Volper, a Belgian conservator, said vulnerable treasures should only be displayed when adequate protection is in place.
Italian police recovered three artworks stolen from a Parma museum in August from a cardboard box hidden in an apartment.
Five Moldovan nationals were arrested over the theft. The artworks have since returned to the museum, which now has round-the-clock security funded by a local cheese consortium.

FaceTime while driving costs woman conditional loss of licence in Denmark
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
07:16:49 UTC
16:16:49 KST

A Danish court has ruled that using a correctly mounted phone can still lead to the conditional loss of a driving licence if it distracts the driver from traffic.
A 46-year-old woman has been given a conditional driving ban after using FaceTime while driving on a motorway near Copenhagen.
Although her phone was correctly mounted in the car, Glostrup District Court found that the video call distracted her to such an extent that she failed to pay sufficient attention to the traffic around her.
The case highlights an important distinction for motorists in Denmark: using a mounted or hands-free phone while driving may be legal, but drivers can still be penalised if using it causes dangerous or inattentive driving.
The woman was stopped by police on Motorring 3, Copenhagen’s western ring motorway, in Glostrup on January 13.
Before she was stopped, she had failed to react appropriately to vehicles trying to merge onto the motorway. Several motorists had to brake or accelerate to enter the traffic.
Police found that her attention had been directed towards her phone rather than the road ahead.
Glostrup District Court ruled on Wednesday that she had disregarded essential road-safety considerations.
In addition to the conditional loss of her driving licence, she was fined DKK 2,500.
She must now pass both a new theory test and a practical driving test to retain her licence, according to the prosecution service at Copenhagen Vestegn Police.
“The case emphasises how important it is to keep your focus on traffic when driving a car – even if the phone is correctly mounted,” assistant prosecutor Sabrina Berggren said.
Although the woman was not holding the phone, the FaceTime conversation affected her driving and therefore road safety, Berggren said.
Hands-free does not mean distraction-free
The Danish Road Safety Council (Rådet for Sikker Trafik) also warns motorists that hands-free calls can be distracting.
Jakob Bøving Arendt, CEO of the council, said in a written comment to Ritzau that inattention is one of the major causes of deaths on Danish roads.
Although using a hands-free phone while driving is legal, the council recommends limiting its use because conversations can reduce a driver’s mental attention, he said.
Source: Ritzau
