Breaking Down the Supernatural Ending of Dead-End Job
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
23:19:21 UTC
08:19:21 KST

In Netflix’s latest Korean drama series, Dead-End Job, the economy is literally trying to kill people. Lee Jae-wook (Alchemy of Souls) stars as Byeon Hyeok-jun, a jobless 30-year-old living in contemporary Seoul in this Squid Game-esque fantasy horror. Buried in debt from a landlord scam and subsequent stock-chasing, Hyeok-jun is actively considering dying by suicide. But when a mysterious company called Spider Staffing Agency starts offering him part-time gigs at 50, 100, or even 200 times the minimum wage, he is desperate enough to take them—even when it becomes clear that these jobs are supernaturally deadly.
The series has an anthology-like feel, as Hyeok-jun takes on a new, terrifying part-time job more or less in each episode. Over the course of the eight-episode series, Hyeok-jun’s interest in Spider Staffing Agency’s jobs turns from financial to familial when he realizes that his father, who disappeared 20 years prior after falling into massive debt, was also used the temp agency. With the help of his younger sister, Ji-yoon (Typhoon Family’s Kim Min-ha), and Yeon-joo (Tastefully Yours’ Go Min-si), a mysterious woman investigating the agency, he commits to discovering Spider Staffing’s supernatural secrets.
What is Spider Staffing Agency?
By the end of Dead-End Job’s first season, many questions remain about the true purpose of Spider Staffing Agency. When Hyeok-jun first encounters the organization, it is managed by Mr. S. (Badland Hunters’ Lee Hee-joon), a charismatic middle man who sends part-timers to their probable death without so much as a heads up.
When pressed by Hyeok-jun, Mr. S explains that these worksites exist where the border between the world of humans and the world of supernatural beings is at its thinnest. While humans live in the yang, explains Mr. S., these other beings stay in the yin. People like Hyeok-jun, who are desperate to make a living, emit especially strong yang energy when engaged in acts of paid labor.
Spider Staffing sends workers to these border sites as sacrificial lambs to maintain the division between the two worlds. Surprisingly, Hyeok-jun has a knack for this work—while he may not always get the job done, he survives. But in the process, he watches many of his co-workers die.
Yeon-joo’s secret agenda
At first, Yeon-joo presents herself as an investigator trying to determine if Spider Staffing is facilitating unsafe labor practices. However, we find out in the series’ penultimate episode that Yeon-joo herself is a monster, tied to the other world. She wasn’t born a monster; she was once a young woman trying to make a living as a factory girl in a rapidly modernizing South Korea, roughly 40 years prior to the main events of the series. When Yeon-joo and her co-workers protested against their cruel labor conditions, they were met with violence. Yeon-joo was stuffed in a locker by her older co-worker to avoid the violence, not realizing that it was a doorway to the other world. When Yeon-joo comes out of the locker, it is modern-day Korea, and there is an amusement park where her factory once stood. It’s unclear at what point Yeon-joo turned from human to monster.
The real history related to Go Min-si’s character
Yeon-joo’s backstory ties into the real history of feminist labor organizing in South Korea. In 1970, activist Jeon Tae-il died by self-immolation to protest the treatment of women garment workers, who regularly dealt with sexual harassment, low wages, poor working conditions, and police brutality. The act sparked increased union activity, including the formation of the Garment Makers Union. In 1979, women of the YH Union organized a sit-in at the Seoul headquarters of the New Democratic Party in protest of the closure of the YH Company’s wig factory. Union member Kim Kyoung-sook was killed in the brutal police eviction, provoking widespread public opposition to President Park Chung-hee’s regime.
Yeon-joo is not a specific historic character, but rather a symbol of this period in Korean history and of the role female factory workers and union organizers played in the rapid, painful transformation of the country’s economy and society in the second half of the 20th century.
Hyeok-jun finds his dad, and starts the apocalypse
Hyeok-jun promises his sister that he will not return to Spider Staffing, but he is lured back by Yeon-joo, who tells him she knows how to find his long-lost father. She shows Hyeok-joon the door inside of NeoCity Amusement Park that she came through from the other world, and tells Hyeok-jun that he can find his father through that door. He just has to make it through a shift at the deadly amusement park first.
When Ji-yoon realizes what her brother has done, she confronts Mr. S. about sending Hyeok-jun back on a job. Mr. S. insists that it is not his fault, but rather a direct result of the machinations of Yeon-joo, who is using Hyeok-jun as a pawn to open the door between worlds. When he does so, monsters from the other world will storm into our world, bringing about the apocalypse. From Yeon-joo’s perspective, it is what our world deserves after the way it has treated its most vulnerable workers. It will fully reveal the truth of the bones and blood our cities are built from.
In the end, Hyeok-jun decides to open the door, even after Mr. S. warns him not to. While Hyeok-jun doesn’t understand the magnitude of his decision, he knows that he does not trust Mr. S., who gleefully sends desperate people to their deaths by labor. He watches Mr. S. shoot Yeon-joo several times, and sees no sense in his violence. The unleashed storm of dark energy pulls Yeon-joo and Mr. S. into its void, and tries to take Hyeok-jun too. While it has him in its clutches, he is able to see and talk to his father. A shell of the man he once was, clutching to a meager portion of money he hopes to give to his family, Hyeok-jun’s dad has been claimed by the other side. It is a warning of what Hyeok-jun could become if he allows an obsession with work and debt to take over his life.
Before the darkness can fully claim Hyeok-jun, Ji-yoon pulls her brother from the door’s threshold. Together, they close the door before more of the other world’s entities can escape into ours, stopping—or at least halting—the apocalypse.
Dead-End Job’s ending explained
Following the events of the season, Hyeok-jun is in a much better place than where he started, but his life is far from perfect. He has been able to pay off his debt using the money he earned from Spider Staffing, but he is back to the part-time worker grind. Still, he appreciates the small moments with his mother and sister, and seemingly values his life in a way he did not before. The world is unchanged in its cruelties. When Hyeok-jun meets a woman ready to die by suicide on the same bridge he started the season on, he stops her but cannot give her a good reason why she should live, past that he was like her once. Still, she decides to put her shoes back on and continue living.
In a twist ending, Hyeok-jun gets a text from Spider Staffing and returns to the abandoned office. Once there, he is offered a new job: as Mr. S’s replacement. In a voice message pre-recorded by Mr. S., the manager wonders if Hyeok-jun will make different decisions and come to different conclusions than he did in the role. In Mr. S.’s eyes, the deaths of some people were acceptable for the survival of everyone else.
Reports on the news of unexplained fires and otherworldly remains imply that there may be long-term consequences to Hyeok-jun opening that door. In the series’ final moments, Hyeok-jun opens his mouth to either accept the job or reject it, but the credits roll before we can hear his answer.
In a mid-credits scene, Ji-yoon receives a text about the successful results of a work recruitment from Kyung-il Group. The mysterious company owned both Yeon-joo’s factory, and the amusement park. Could they also be behind Spider Staffing? Either way, both brother and sister are getting pulled back into the ongoing supernatural battle.
Will Dead-End Job have a second season?
Dead-End Job leaves the door open for a second season. Its greenlighting is no doubt dependent on how the first season performs on Netflix. If a second season is greenlit, it will be awhile before it can be filmed, given that main actor Lee Jae-wook is currently performing mandatory military service. He is expected to be discharged in November 2027.

G20 foreign ministers skip 'family' photo amid objections over Russia

G20 foreign ministers skip 'family' photo amid objections over Russia
In short:
Foreign ministers have skipped a traditional group "family" photo ahead of a G20 meeting.
European, Australian and Canadian representatives opposed the idea of being photographed alongside the Russian foreign minister.
A spokesperson for Penny Wong said they support the decision of the United States as G20 host to cancel the photograph.
Foreign ministers from the G20 have skipped a traditional group photo ahead of their meeting after European and Australian representatives objected to the presence of Russia.
A US official said the State Department had taken the family photo off the official agenda on Friday, US time, because Washington did not want it to become a spectacle or distraction.
A third of the participants, including Australia and Canada, made clear they opposed the idea of being photographed alongside Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov.
A spokesperson for Foreign Minister Penny Wong said they support the decision of the United States as G20 host to cancel the photograph.
"Australia has been clear and consistent: we will not normalise Russia's brutal and illegal invasion of Ukraine,"
the statement said.
"Our focus at the G20 remains on the important work before us and addressing the challenges facing the global economy."
European G20 members also back Ukraine, which has objected to US President Donald Trump's recent decisions over Russia, including a deal to buy diesel and waive some sanctions.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Milliband explicitly called out Mr Lavrov, saying that "if we are serious about our values and our interests, we must also work harder to secure just and lasting peace in Ukraine".
"An assault not only on Ukraine but on us all — trampling international law, sovereignty and self determination — core principles on which we all depend," he said.
Polish Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski told reporters in Atlanta that, "I am not the only one who does not want to be photographed with Lavrov."
Consensus looks elusive
Secretary of State Marco Rubio opened the talks with an appeal for unity on the issues that threaten international security and trade.
"We are in a critical moment," Mr Rubio told his colleagues.
"We are facing a series of interconnected economic and geopolitical crises."
Mr Rubio pointed to disruptions to global energy and food supplies, trade and freedom of navigation and said many are posing "severe threats to essential foundations of the global economic order".
Yet there was no sign that the G20 diplomats could come to consensus on many of the most contentious issues they faced.
Among them are the Russia-Ukraine conflict, the US-Israeli war against Iran, US tariffs and Chinese machinations in the South China Sea. All have contributed to spikes in the global cost of fuel as well as uncertainty about trade.
Diplomats who attended the opening session described it as cordial but said Russia's position on Ukraine was unyielding — as was its opposition to Poland's membership in the G20.
Those disagreements, which also cover the Trump administration's not inviting G20 member South Africa over the objections of others, will likely prevent the foreign ministers from producing a joint communique when the meetings wrap up on Saturday, participants said.
Several participants, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorised to discuss the closed-door talks, said all had agreed to try to overcome their differences despite the long odds and to work to make next month's G20 leaders summit hosted by Mr Trump in Florida a success.

US oil companies tripled profits during Iran war – NYT
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30

08:15:45 KST

US oil companies tripled profits during Iran war – NYT
The US’ largest oil companies almost tripled their profits during the US-Israeli war on Iran, the New York Times has reported, at a time when soaring energy costs threaten to wipe out US President Donald Trump’s Republican Party in the upcoming midterm elections.
The American oil giants – including Chevron, Exxon Mobil, and Valero – earned $130 billion in profits between April and September, according to six months worth of financial results covering more than 50 companies, combined by the New York Times. In the same period last year, these companies made less than $47 billion.
This windfall is an almost direct mirror of the extra $147 billion Americans spent on gasoline and diesel since American and Israeli warplanes began striking Iran on February 28.
With the Strait of Hormuz closed to shipping for almost all of the last six months, and Yemen’s Houthis attacking Saudi extraction sites and shipping in the Red Sea, American producers have reaped the benefit of high oil prices, with Chevron and Exxon Mobil recording higher profits than at any point since the Ukraine conflict escalated in 2022.
Exxon’s third-quarter profit more than doubled this year, while Chevron’s almost tripled.
American refiners have taken advantage of the widespread destruction of refining sites in the Gulf region, and the threat of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refineries, leveraging their safe location inside the US. Valero and Phillips 66 both posted all-time record third-quarter profits this year.
Europe’s oil giants have posted similar results, with Shell, TotalEnergies, and Repsol all more than doubling their earnings last quarter over the same timeframe in 2025, as Europeans grapple with record energy bills. Some European finance ministers have demanded that the EU impose windfall taxes on these companies in response.
At $4.29 per gallon as of Monday, US gasoline prices are now higher than they were at any point during former President Joe Biden’s four years in office, with the exception of the first three months after the escalation of the Ukraine conflict. Trump has described the elevated prices as a “small price to pay for” preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon, but voters aren’t convinced.
This week, 72% of respondents told a Gallup poll that gasoline prices are “extremely” important in how they plan to vote in next week’s midterm elections. Most polling organizations show the Republican Party on track to lose one or both houses of Congress next week, with the GOP trailing the Democrats by between eight and nine points nationwide.
Trump has tried to alleviate some of this damage by lifting sanctions on Russian diesel, and at least three diesel tankers have left Russian ports en route to the US. Trump has also pressed Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky to cease attacks on Russian refineries, but Zelensky has apparently ignored these requests.

Why AI could threaten much of the world’s digital infrastructure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
23:13:51 UTC
08:13:51 KST

Why AI could threaten much of the world’s digital infrastructure
Volunteer-led PHP, which powers most websites, is increasingly under threat from cyberattacks leveraging AI capabilities.
Earlier this month, authorities worldwide urged website administrators to execute emergency updates after a nonprofit programming foundation flagged critical security flaws that could allow hackers to breach systems.
Government and corporate websites briefly went offline to patch the vulnerabilities, nicknamed PHP2Shell, which were discovered by independent cybersecurity experts using artificial intelligence (AI).
The vulnerabilities were embedded in the code of a widely used open-source web programming language, PHP, for more than a decade. They had gone unnoticed, however, because it would have been too complicated for humans to exploit them without the use of advanced AI.
But cybersecurity experts, as well as those maintaining important software, say PHP2Shell could be the first in a deluge of security flaws exposed by emerging AI. They say much of the world’s most critical digital infrastructure is maintained by volunteers, who often lack the resources and time to respond to newly discovered threats.
“There’s been a lot of people in the AI safety community that said this is one of the first areas where we are going to see the harmful impact of AI,” said Peter Slattery, a research scientist at MIT’s FutureTech, who studies how cybersecurity experts are dealing with the new technology and tracks real-world incidents involving AI.
A digital world built on volunteer work
PHP got its start in 1995, when Danish-Canadian programmer Rasmus Lerdorf sought to track how many people visited his online resume. Over time, others around the world improved Lerdorf’s software, and it grew in popularity.
As with other open-source coding projects, anyone could download, modify and share improvements. Websites like Facebook and Wikipedia were built using PHP, which runs about 70 percent of the world’s websites.
In 2021, a dedicated nonprofit, the PHP Foundation, was launched to coordinate development. Like many other foundations maintaining open-source software, it operates on a meagre budget.
Most of the digital infrastructure consumers use is powered by open source software. The Mozilla Firefox browser is open source, as are languages like Perl, Python, and JavaScript. The software that lets a computer communicate with others on the internet is often open source, with many servers using products like Apache HTTP Server, maintained by the Apache Software Foundation.
“The world today, including proprietary software vendors, relies on open source software for its digital infrastructure,” said Amanda Brock, CEO of OpenUK, a nonprofit that supports open source software.
The world’s largest corporations, like Meta, Google, OpenAI and Anthropic, depend on that volunteer-built, open-source infrastructure. Now, those companies’ own AI tools are uncovering security flaws in the infrastructure at a pace that needs far more resources for groups like the PHP Foundation to keep up.
“It’s simply not possible with the resources in place to fix all of the known vulnerabilities,” Brock said. “Foundations are attempting to manage these challenges, but the smaller ones don’t have hundreds of millions in funding, and managing this at the pace AI requires is proving impossible.”
A deluge of new bugs to fix
The PHP2Shell vulnerabilities were found through several advanced AI models, which can employ far more complicated attempts to hack past security barriers than humans could.
Developers of other software are also discovering far more security flaws than in the past because AI is being used to probe defences.
Google said it uncovered more than 1,000 security bugs in the last update for its Chrome browser, more than in the last two dozen updates combined. Mozilla, the foundation behind the Firefox browser, found more than 400 security vulnerabilities in April, a significant jump from the previous record of 76 bugs discovered just one month earlier.
“We have maybe 10 times more issues than usual because we are using AI to find them,” said Jarek Potiuk, part of the volunteer security team at the Apache Software Foundation. (In keeping with the foundation’s non-hierarchical ethos, Potiuk said he has no real title).
Potiuk said there is an “industry-wide movement” to conduct scans using AI models and identify security vulnerabilities, much like was done to find the bugs in PHP. But the scans themselves cost money – used to pay for the tokens for AI models – and afterwards, humans must pore over them to weed out false positives.
“Every project, every foundation is doing this right now – spending enormous amounts of time to find these issues,” Potiuk said. “AI helps to find them, but you have to verify things, you have to review them.”
Earlier this year, Anthropic launched Project Glasswing, offering $100m in credits to support its advanced Claude Mythos AI model to search for security vulnerabilities in the world’s critical software. In one month, more than 23,000 vulnerabilities were found across more than 1,000 open source projects.
The Apache Software Foundation has taken advantage of another scheme, the Alpha-Omega project, to scan for security bugs across the 290 software packages it maintains. The project, backed by companies like Anthropic, Amazon, Google, Microsoft and OpenAI, spends about $7m a year helping open-source developers find critical security bugs.
But those working on finding and fixing the security flaws say the corporate world could be doing a lot more, given the trillion-dollar valuation of companies whose products would not work without free software like the packages the Apache Foundation provides.
“They are helping a lot, but we need more active players in this area,” Potiuk said, “because it’s highly disproportional – the impact it has on the corporate world versus the open source world”.
When a major security flaw like PHP2Shell is uncovered, it often comes down to a handful of volunteers to fix it.
Keeping the internet’s infrastructure as decentralised and open-source as possible is crucial, Potiuk said. Instead of buying out something like PHP, major players like Google or Microsoft could, for instance, pay staff to dedicate some of their work hours to maintaining open-source projects they use.
Real-world targets
The 2021 Log4Shell vulnerability, which allowed hackers to remotely run code on millions of devices through a widely used library maintained by the Apache Software Foundation, underscored the critical role open-source software plays in system security. That bug was discovered without the use of AI.
Suddenly, cars, microwaves and a host of electronic devices connected to the internet were vulnerable, Potiuk said.
“That was the moment when the whole ecosystem realised how important it is to take care of open source,” he said.
A bug like that, if found by a malicious hacker and exploited before there is a chance to patch devices, could have caused a major disruption.
Slattery said the database of incidents he and his colleagues maintain shows that an increasing number of vulnerabilities are being detected, and it is a matter of time before some are exploited in the real world.
“We are starting to see both a lot more vulnerabilities detected and addressed in time, but also attacks on a wide range of systems,” Slattery said. “We have been moving in this direction for a long time. There are more and more things now you can attack.”

Türkiye nominates OSCE chief Sinirlioglu as candidate for next UN secretary-general
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
23:08:17 UTC
08:08:17 KST

Merve Aydogan
31 October 2026•Update: 31 October 2026
Türkiye on Friday formally nominated Feridun Sinirlioglu, secretary-general of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE), as a candidate for UN secretary-general, Turkish Foreign Ministry sources said.
The move followed an impasse in the selection process, with the latest straw poll at the UN Security Council on Friday ending inconclusively, the sources said.
In a letter dated Friday to the presidents of the General Assembly and the Security Council, Türkiye's UN envoy Ahmet Yildiz transmitted President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's nomination letter, in line with the UN Charter and a General Assembly resolution.
The nomination letter by Erdogan, addressed to the term president of the Security Council, Aglaia Balta of Greece, referred to a Nov. 25, 2025, letter that launched the selection process.
Erdogan cited Sinirlioglu's more than 40 years in diplomacy, including as foreign minister and UN envoy, and said he was appointed in 2023 to lead an independent assessment on Afghanistan.
"Taking together the strategic vision I have personally witnessed, his deep knowledge of the UN system and his unwavering commitment to the principles of the UN Charter, I believe Ambassador Sinirlioglu possesses the experience and culture of consensus required to lead the United Nations Organization," said the nomination by Türkiye’s president.
A candidate needs at least nine votes in the Security Council to secure the required support, while any of the five permanent members – the US, China, France, Russia and the UK – can block a candidate with a veto.
The eventual nominee must be appointed by the General Assembly, with that step generally considered a formality once the Security Council has reached an agreement.
Current Secretary-General Antonio Guterres' term ends on Dec. 31.
Eight candidates have so far been nominated: Costa Rican diplomat Rebeca Grynspan, International Atomic Energy Agency Director General Rafael Grossi of Argentina, former Senegalese President Macky Sall, Guyana’s UN Ambassador Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett, former UN General Assembly President Maria Fernanda Espinosa of Ecuador, former Chilean President Michelle Bachelet, Ugandan politician and diplomat Olara Otunnu and Ecuadorian diplomat Ivonne A-Baki.

US voters weigh soaring prices as early polls in midterms hit record 48 million
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
23:00:47 UTC
08:00:47 KST

Soaring prices for gas, medicine and other cost-of-living essentials are preoccupying Americans as a record 47.9 million have already voted in next week's US midterm elections, with participation surging in key battleground states.
A whopping 84 percent of voters who have cast their ballots early listed the economy as their biggest concern this election cycle, according to a recent Pew Research Center survey.
Fuel costs have skyrocketed around the world since the United States and Israel launched strikes on Iran in February.
US gas prices rose 9.1 percent in September alone, according to official figures, a headache for residents in a state like Florida, where most people rely on cars to get around.
"It affects transportation, it affects goods, it affects everything," Matthew Moore, a 63-year-old attorney, said after he cast his ballot early.
Is it too late?
US President Donald Trump won reelection in 2024 in part because of his campaign promise to lower prices, which had also increased during the term of his predecessor Joe Biden.
William Galston, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution think tank, said two of Trump's decisions this term have directly contributed to cost pressures: launching the war on Iran and slapping tariffs on trade partners.
"It's within the president's power to remove most of the tariffs that he's imposed. It's within the president's power to end the war that he began," Galston said.
For some voters, however, it's too late.
"My vote was cast based upon my feelings about how they have handled the stewardship that the voters have given them," said Michael Childs, 62.
The White House, for its part, insists that Trump's policies are revitalising the US economy and making life more affordable for Americans.
But millions of households across the United States find it harder than ever to make ends meet.
"The financial hardship is creeping up in America, particularly the middle class," said Symeria Hudson, the CEO of United Way Miami, a non-profit, non-partisan organisation focused on improving the health, education and financial well-being of local communities.
Record early voting
The University of Florida's Election Lab had recorded 47,922,669 early votes nationwide by midday, surpassing the previous midterm record of 45.9 million cast ahead of Election Day in 2022.
The surge is especially pronounced in states with fiercely contested Senate races that could determine control of the chamber during the final two years of President Donald Trump's presidency.
In Texas, more than six million people had voted early by Wednesday, according to official figures, with in-person turnout running around 50 percent ahead of the same stage in 2022.
North Carolina's election board reported early voting up nearly 37 percent on the same point four years ago, while South Carolina surpassed its entire 2022 early vote total on Monday, with five days of early voting still to go.
In Kansas, where Republican Senator Roger Marshall faces a tough re-election fight, advance ballots were running around two-thirds ahead of 2022 last week, according to the secretary of state's office.
In states that record voters' party affiliation, registered Democrats have accounted for a substantially larger share of early ballots than Republicans.
Election Lab figures showed Democrats making up around 44 percent of early voters in those states, compared with 31 percent for Republicans and 25 percent for unaffiliated or minor-party voters.
Not to read too much
University of Florida political scientist Michael McDonald, who oversees the Election Lab, has pointed to rising participation among Black and Hispanic voters in states that report racial and ethnic data, with particularly strong turnout in heavily Hispanic communities along the Texas-Mexico border.
In Georgia, where early in-person voting broke the state's midterm record on Thursday, women accounted for 56 percent of ballots cast by that day, compared with 44 percent for men.
But experts warn against interpreting the figures as a prediction of the election outcome.
A voter's party registration does not reveal which candidates they supported, and tens of millions more Americans are expected to cast ballots on Tuesday.
In recent elections, Republicans have tended to turn out in greater numbers on Election Day, potentially narrowing or reversing the Democrats' early advantage.
And higher early participation does not necessarily translate into higher overall turnout, since some voters may simply be casting ballots sooner than in previous elections.

US judge orders ethics inquiry into Trump lawyers over golf course case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
22:58:38 UTC
07:58:38 KST

US judge orders ethics inquiry into Trump lawyers over golf course case
Judge Ana Reyes calls on US government lawyers to explain contradictory statements about the East Potomac Golf Links.
A United States federal judge has opened a “formal inquiry” into whether US government lawyers misled the court over plans to transform a historic public golf course in Washington, DC.
Friday’s manoeuvre escalates an ongoing legal fight over President Donald Trump’s efforts to reshape the US capital.
Judge Ana Reyes of the US District Court for the District of Columbia announced she would appoint a special master to examine whether government officials withheld information or made misleading assertions concerning the East Potomac Golf Links.
The inquiry will not establish whether government lawyers committed misconduct. It will instead determine whether their conduct breached professional or ethical obligations.
The inquiry follows a series of contradictory statements by administration officials about plans to renovate the course, notably after Trump announced he would proceed with the project on social media.
Reyes questioned Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward Jr for more than two hours during Friday’s hearing, repeatedly comparing his testimony with the president’s online announcements.
She also asked him whether a National Park Service official had been instructed to omit details from a court declaration.
Trump’s posts, which began earlier this month on his Truth Social account, indicated the course would close for 15 months, starting on November 15, to accommodate a major redevelopment.
Yet officials from various government agencies – including the Interior Department, Justice Department and National Park Service – had previously been unable to confirm the existence or scope of any plans when questioned by the judge.
Earlier this year, Reyes had ordered the government to provide advance notice of substantive construction work at the site.
But despite her order, the dispute intensified earlier this month after more than 400 trees were removed from the golf course. Reyes subsequently extended her injunction against the government making any further “irreversible” changes to the site.
On Wednesday, the Justice Department informed the court that the National Park Service would submit a design from golf course architect Tom Fazio to the National Capital Planning Commission on Friday.
But Justice Department lawyers had, up to that point, declined to acknowledge any plans with regards to the golf course.
Even before Wednesday’s submission to the court, Trump had posted about commissioning Fazio “to build a World Class Championship Golf Course” on the park site, which currently includes biking and walking paths.
The DC Preservation League, which filed the lawsuit in February, has argued the redevelopment could violate environmental protections and damage a historically significant public space.
The case marks one of two legal battles unfolding over Trump’s plans for Washington, DC, on Friday.
Another US judge is due to hear a separate challenge to the White House’s proposed construction of a 75-metre (250-foot) memorial arch near Arlington National Cemetery.
The lawsuits raise broader questions about the limits of presidential authority over federal land and public monuments.
David Super, a professor at the Georgetown University Law Center, told The Associated Press news agency that the cases reflect a shift in how the administration approaches legal constraints on executive power.
“There was always the assumption that you would try to do things that were legal,” Super said. “What we’re seeing here now is that if you think the federal courts can’t stop you”, you can break the law.

Alaska Senate election: DOJ wants to 'segregate' all ballots for 2nd Sullivan candidate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
22:57:55 UTC
07:57:55 KST

The Department of Justice wants "to preserve and segregate all ballots ranking" a candidate named Dan Sullivan for a potential investigation of whether voters in Alaska's U.S. Senate election mistakenly ranked him in the belief he was incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, a federal prosecutor told a judge in a court filing late Friday.
The filing came in a lawsuit by the DOJ, which asks District Court Judge Sharon Gleason to block state election officials from immediately certifying the Senate election if Sen. Sullivan loses by a margin that might be attributable to voter confusion from the presence of the other Sullivan on the ballot. The DOJ wants to conduct an investigation to determine voter intent if the incumbent loses.
"Election Day is on November 3, 2026, which poses a substantial risk that the candidacy before us will mislead voters and ultimately result in an electoral process that lacks integrity," U.S. Attorney for Alaska Michael Heyman said in the filing, signed by one of his assistant prosecutors.
"The United States of America contends that the proposed precautionary measures will be impossible after Election Day, showing good cause for expedited consideration," the filing said.
Heyman earlier Friday told reporters at a press conference that there is an "ongoing" criminal investigation into how and why retired school teacher Dan Sullivan decided to run for the Senate for the first time this year.
The DOJ's suit, which President Donald Trump said he had requested, claims the "sole purpose" of the non-incumbent Sullivan running was to benefit the campaign of Democratic nominee Mary Peltola by reducing the number of votes for Sen. Sullivan.
"We will not let anyone or any group undermine this election," said Heyman at a press conference in Anchorage, which was held just four days before Election Day.
"There is both a civil investigation and a criminal investigation that is ongoing," Heyman said. "There is a surge of FBI resources and resources in this office."
"Every Alaskan deserves a fair election, and they're going to get one," the prosecutor said.
He said that the criminal probe has been underway for months. Heyman had previously recused himself from the probe because he was being considered for a judicial nomination, but that recusal was rescinded Thursday because he was no longer under consideration.
Heyman said the criminal investigation has been accelerated because of a New York Times report on Wednesday that said aides Peltola's campaign and senior aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee helped recruit the retired teacher to enter the Senate race with the hope of drawing votes from the incumbent Sullivan.
"When credible information comes out, we are committed to pursuing that information … and we will act on it," Heyman said.
Peltola's campaign and the DSCC deny being involved in the retiree's Senate campaign.
Heyman, when questioned by reporters, would not say what criminal statute might have been violated
Earlier Friday, a federal judge kept on a fast track efforts to dismiss the DOJ's suit.
Judge Sharon Gleason ordered the DOJ to respond by 1 p.m. Alaska Time to the new dismissal motions, which were filed hours after the department amended its suit in U.S. District Court in Anchorage on Thursday to add a new legal claim.
The DOJ's updating of the civil complaint forced Gleason to rule the prior dismissal motions were moot.
Gleason gave state election officials, the campaign of Democratic nominee and other groups until noon Saturday to reply to the DOJ's response.
The judge's order leaves open the possibility that she will rule on the dismissal motions before Tuesday, which is Election Day, as both the state and Peltola's campaign have requested.
The state, the campaign, and other intervenors in the suit argue the DOJ has no legal authority to block certification of an election because two candidates on a four-candidate ballot happen to share the same name.
The winner of Alaska's race could determine which party holds a majority in the Senate starting in January. Republicans currently have 53 seats in the 100-member chamber.
Alaska's election uses ranked-choice voting. If no candidate obtains more than 50% of the vote in the first count, then the fourth-place finisher will be eliminated, and the second choice on that candidate's ballots will be allocated to the remaining candidates.
Only Peltola and Sen. Sullivan are considered likely to draw large shares of the votes.
The DOJ's suit seeks to delay certification of the Senate election if Sen. Sullivan loses by a margin that could be attributable to voter confusion over the presence of the other candidate, who is listed as Daniel J. Sullivan, on the ballot.
The amended complaint, which updates the suit filed Oct. 23, added a claim under the Supremacy Clause of the U.S. Constitution to the first claim, under the National Voter Registration Act.
It also contained added details from the Times article.
Peltola's campaign, in its dismissal motion filed Thursday, said, "Rather than defend its indefensible legal claims as it was ordered to do, the Department of Justice ... has filed an Amended Complaint that does nothing to address the fatal problems that preclude it from bringing this case or obtaining the relief that it seeks."
"The U.S. Constitution leaves the regulation of federal elections exclusively to the States and to Congress, and DOJ has no statutory authority to bring this case," the motion said.
In their own dismissal motion, state election officials said the amended lawsuit "rests on the same meritless theory that the National Voter Registration Act (NVRA) — a voter registration law — governs this case, which has nothing to do with voter registration."
"Because this reading of the NVRA fails, the amended complaint fails," the motion said.

It also reported that an interceptor missile exploded above the town of Taybeh, without providing details.
Separately, contact was lost with a young man from the town of Rub Thalathin after he stopped his vehicle in the Wadi al-Hujeir area and continued on foot toward Qantara, according to the agency.
The developments came after technical military meetings on Oct. 20 and 21 between Beirut and Tel Aviv in Tampa, Florida, under US sponsorship.
The meetings ended without an announced breakthrough or joint statement, although reports said the sides agreed to continue talks amid disputes over Israel’s withdrawal from Lebanon and the disarmament of Hezbollah.
On June 26, Beirut and Tel Aviv reached a Framework Agreement providing for a gradual Israeli withdrawal from occupied Lebanese territory in exchange for the deployment of the Lebanese army and the disarmament of armed groups.
It includes the use of “pilot areas” for implementation but has so far been applied in three towns, while more than 50 towns remain under Israeli occupation.
Despite the agreement, Israel has continued military operations in Lebanon, killing at least 4,386 people and wounding 12,407 since March 2. More than 1 million people have also been displaced.
Israel occupies areas of southern Lebanon, some for decades and others since the 2023-2024 war, while during the latest conflict, its forces advanced up to around 10 kilometers (6 miles) into Lebanese territory.

Who was behind the largest crypto heist in history?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
22:50:12 UTC
07:50:12 KST

Analysts suspect North Korea's TraderTraitor unit behind Binance hack
Almost $9 billion in cryptocurrency has been hacked from exchange company Binance in the largest cyber attack in the cryptocurrency sector's history.
The bulk of the heist unfolded in about 20 minutes, blockchain records show, and 30 or 40 different tokens were affected, including Ethereum, Bitcoin and stablecoins, according to crypto watchers.
So who did it, and where has the money gone?
Who did it and how?
The exact culprit behind the heist is not known, but many analysts have been quick to point the finger at a cyber unit in North Korea, which has previously orchestrated similar hacks.
US blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs said the attack mirrored a 2025 heist at crypto exchange Bybit, which the US Federal Bureau of Investigation attributed to North Korea.
During the attack, hackers manipulated Binance's virtual wallets to empty into hack-controlled ones and from there, move the money.
"TRM attributes the attack to TraderTraitor, North Korea's elite hacking unit, based on robust on and off-chain intelligence," the company said on its website.
"We make this judgement with high confidence."
Blockchain analysis company Chainalysis agreed with TRM's assessment.
An initial investigation suggested the breach may have started with a compromised laptop belonging to one of Binance's engineers, which let an attacker gain access to one of its systems and make unauthorised withdrawals, Binance said.
Later, the company added it had uncovered additional points of breach.
The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has previously warned of the threat TraderTraitor posed, saying it had been targeting cryptocurrency companies since 2020.
"These actors will likely continue exploiting vulnerabilities of cryptocurrency technology firms, gaming companies, and exchanges to generate and launder funds to support the North Korean regime," it said in 2022.
Where is the money?
Binance said customer funds were safe and it was working to recover $4.2 billion of funds it froze following the attack.
"[We have] begun recovering affected assets for users and continue to work with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace, freeze and recover additional funds," it said.
"The company has already publicly committed to cover losses through company funds in the prior announcement."
Binance said it had enough money to "cover this incident", and much of it was in the same type of tokens that were stolen.
These include a variety of different cryptocurrencies, including Bitcoin and stablecoin.
Cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin are a digital asset, which can be bought, sold and transferred online. Most are not issued by a government or central bank, and their value can fluctuate.
The Bank of England describes stablecoin as a cryptocurrency backed by a specified asset or collection of assets, which their creator uses to maintain their value.
Coin value can be pegged to currencies, such as USD.
Roughly half of the stolen coins have been frozen by issuers, but TRM estimated about $3.4 billion worth of crypto was out of reach.
Chainalysis's investigators have traced funds stolen from Binance being laundered and shuffled around in an automated process from different destinations to obscure the trail.
"The investigation remains ongoing and we expect the stolen funds to continue moving in the coming days,"
it said.
What is Binance?
Binance is like a virtual stock exchange crossed with a bank, but for crypto.
There, people can buy, sell and swap coins, as well as make deposits and withdrawals.
It was founded in 2017 and is the largest exchange in the cryptocurrency space by volume.
Issuers using Binance include Tether, Circle, Ripple and World Liberty Financial, the Trump family's crypto venture.
The exchange operates a secure asset fund for users, a $1 billion bitcoin reserve designed to protect customers in the event of a security breach, according to its website.
This is not the first time Binance has been targeted, as hackers stole $US40 million ($56.9 million) worth of bitcoin in 2018 and again in 2022 when $US568 million ($808 million) in coins were affected.
ABC/Reuters

Democratic Republic of Congo Ebola outbreak kills more than 5,000
The death toll from the Ebola outbreak in Democratic Republic of Congo has surpassed 5,000, government data showed on Friday, as authorities had yet to find a way to control the country's deadliest Ebola epidemic on record.
There are no approved treatments or vaccines to combat the rare Bundibugyo species, which is behind the outbreak in the Central African country.
It has infected more than 10,000 people since it was declared in May.
Delayed detection, conflict and strained health services have helped the virus spread more rapidly than in previous outbreaks.
Eight of Congo's 26 provinces have been affected, with many deaths occurring outside treatment centres.
This year's outbreak is the world's second-largest ever, behind only the 2014-2016 one that infected over 28,600 people and killed more than 11,000 across Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone.
Last week Nigeria became the fourth African country to report an Ebola case, extending the outbreak's geographic spread to West Africa. East African countries Kenya and Uganda have also reported cases.

Security Council fails to renew mandate of UN mission for Western Sahara

Representatives vote on a draft resolution during a Security Council meeting at the UN headquarters in New York, Oct. 30, 2026. The Security Council on Friday failed to renew the mandate of the UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO). (Manuel Elias/UN Photo/Handout via Xinhua)
UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- The Security Council on Friday failed to renew the mandate of the UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO).
The Security Council voted on two separate draft resolutions on the renewal of MINURSO's mandate.
A U.S.-drafted resolution, which would make significant changes to the mission's mandate and future presence, won 11 votes in favor, but was vetoed by Russia.
In a subsequent vote on a Russian-drafted resolution for a straightforward one-year renewal of MINURSO's mandate, the draft failed to obtain the nine positive votes needed for adoption. The Russian draft won three votes in favor, one vote against, with 11 abstentions. The United States voted against it.
Following the 1975 Madrid Accords, Spain transferred administrative responsibilities for Western Sahara to Morocco and Mauritania before withdrawing from the territory in 1976. When Mauritania, under pressure from Polisario guerrillas, abandoned all claims to its portion in August 1979, Morocco subsequently took control of the areas vacated by Mauritania and has since controlled most of the territory. Fighting broke out between Morocco and the Polisario Front, which is fighting for the independence of Western Sahara.
A cease-fire was signed in 1991. The UN mission was deployed that year to monitor the cease-fire and to organize, if possible, a referendum on self-determination of the people of Western Sahara. ■

====================================================================================================

Feature: Visiting Kew through lens of biodiversity conservation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
06:48:35 CST
07:48:35 KST

People visit Kew's Palm House in London, Britain, Oct. 17, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhang Feng)
by Zhang Feng and Larry Neild
LONDON, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- Inside the Princess of Wales Conservatory at the Royal Botanic Gardens, also named Kew, a dark blue tile captured the attention of visitors.
In 1985, British naturalist David Attenborough buried a time capsule beneath it, containing seeds of endangered plant species.
According to the plan, the capsule was to be opened in 2085. By then, scientists fear, some of the plants whose seeds lay inside might have disappeared from the wild.
The urgency of biodiversity protection was underscored at the 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17) in the Armenian capital of Yerevan.
How can biodiversity be safeguarded and humanity's relationship with nature restored? And how can the world achieve the goal of halting and reversing biodiversity loss by 2030 and living in harmony with nature by 2050?
Recent visits to Kew offered some clues.
"LIVING RAINFOREST IN LONDON"
Originally the private gardens of King George II, Kew started botanical collections in 1759. Today, Kew is home to some 17,000 plant species and was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2003.
As autumn set in and temperatures began to fall, plants outside Kew's Palm House have been cleared away, making room for species better suited to colder weather.
Yet stepping inside, visitors were greeted by warmth and lush greenery. Nicknamed "living rainforest in London," the Palm House opened in 1848 and housed more than 1,000 tropical and subtropical plant species, including Eastern Cape giant cycad from South Africa and Australia's pandanus tree whose above-ground roots rose to human height.
Staff member Leaf said that to conserve the tropical plants from around the world, the Palm House maintained consistently high temperatures and humidity levels of around 80 percent.
However, the historic structure itself faced considerable challenges. Rust could be seen on the building's framework, with large patches of its surface coating peeling off.
Despite two major restoration projects in the 20th century, the Victorian-era greenhouse continued to suffer from structural deterioration, posing grave challenges to its plant collections.
Leaf said the Palm House was scheduled to close for renovation starting next year, with the project expected to take three to five years.
CONSERVATION BEYOND BORDERS
In 2021, Kew received Guinness World Records recognition for the "largest collection of living plants at a single-site botanic garden."
Alexandre Antonelli, executive director of science at Kew, said that protecting biodiversity called for cross-border efforts. "Kew has a long history of engagement with China," said Antonelli in an exclusive interview with Xinhua.
He noted that Kew maintained long-standing cooperation with the Chinese Academy of Sciences, expanding collaboration in areas such as joint postgraduate training and exchange of scientific research findings.
"Kew supports China's broad goals of ecological civilization, where people and nature thrive together," said Antonelli.
In Kew's Temperate House, sunlight streamed through an enormous glass roof, illuminating elegant architectural curves and towering plants from temperate regions worldwide.
Among them, a Chinese gooseberry, or kiwi fruit plant stood out. The information board nearby unveiled a lesser-known story of the plant's global journey. Contrary to popular belief, kiwifruit did not originate in New Zealand but was native to China, where it has been cultivated for centuries.
In the early 20th century, Mary Fraser, a New Zealand school principal, brought kiwifruit seeds back home after returning from a visit to China's Hubei Province.
Nathan, an exchange student from New Zealand, was much delighted by the discovery. He said that kiwi fruit was commonplace back home, where growers often built fences to support the climbing vines. The English word "kiwi" also became a familiar nickname for New Zealanders.
Learning that the plant was being jointly protected by China and New Zealand, he exclaimed, "That's so cool!"
ENGAGING THE PUBLIC IN CONSERVATION
Antonelli said that preserving biological diversity required not only "world-leading scientific research" but also "public education through exhibitions, interpretation, events, and schools programs."
For many people, the desire to protect biodiversity began with a sense of wonder at the beauty and stunning characteristics of plants.
Inside Kew's the Princess of Wales Conservatory, crowds gather around a pool of giant waterlily, competing to photograph the remarkable plants.
In 2023, Kew took part in the inaugural Giant Waterlily Weigh-Off and claimed first place with a load-bearing capacity of 43.5 kilograms, prompting visitors to reconsider what these seemingly delicate aquatic plants were capable of.
Not far from the pool, curious visitors gravitated towards a cluster of sundews. The slender leaves were covered with countless tiny hairs. At the tips of these hairs, droplets of liquid glistened in the sunlight, resembling morning dew.
But the sparkling droplets concealed an incredible hunting mechanism. Once an insect landed on the leaf, the sundews' trapping mechanism was triggered. Sticky droplets ensnared the prey, while the leaf gradually curled around it, drawing the unfortunate insect into the plant's grasp.
In addition, Kew's annual orchid festival was another important bridge between science and the public. The 30th edition of the festival this year chose China as its theme for the first time. The exhibition area featured a giant dragon made from plant materials, resembling colorful wooden dragons on Kew's Chinese-style Great Pagoda.
Kew Director Richard Deverell said the Orchid Festival was not simply an opportunity to admire beautiful flowers, but also a platform for educating the public about the importance of plant conservation.
China was selected as this year's theme "because it's one of the most biodiverse countries in the world," he explained.
AN INSURANCE POLICY FOR PLANTS
In a report published by Kew in 2020, it was estimated that approximately two-fifths of the world's plant species were at risk of extinction.
To help safeguard plant diversity, Kew established the Millennium Seed Bank around 2000. Located in West Sussex, the facility had stored more than 2.4 billion seeds representing over 40,000 species as of July 1 this year.
Volunteer Simon working there described the seed bank as an "insurance policy" for plants. With global plant diversity facing mounting threats, he said, preserving seeds provided a vital safeguard for restoring species in the future.
In 2020, after months of extreme heat and drought, devastating bushfires swept across Australia, burning more than 10 million hectares of land. Among the plants severely affected was clover glycine, a nationally vulnerable pea endemic to southeast Australia.
Fortunately, more than 1,000 seeds collected in 2007 were safely stored at the Millennium Seed Bank. Some 250 of them were swiftly shipped to Australia for propagation and ecological restoration.
The idea of "insurance policy" resonated with the Germplasm Bank of Wild Species in southwest China's Yunnan Province. The facility conserved a wide range of wild rare and endangered plants, important agricultural crops, and newly discovered species.
Together with the Millennium Seed Bank in Britain and the Svalbard Global Seed Vault in Norway, it formed part of an international network at the forefront of global biodiversity conservation.
In May this year, Attenborough, who placed the time capsule in 1985, celebrated his 100th birthday. Over the decades, he has narrated acclaimed nature documentaries such as The Blue Planet and Planet Earth.
In Kew's documentary Kingdom of Plants, he offered a heartfelt reflection: "Not only do plants give the world much of its beauty, they are indeed the very basis of all life on earth."
For humanity as a whole, ensuring that life in the natural world continues to flourish in all its diversity is a challenge that we must address indefinitely. ■

OTTAWA, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- The two-day 21st Canada-European Union Summit concluded Friday in Montreal, Canada, with the launch of an alliance to bolster collective strength, while Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada is working toward becoming the EU's first "associate member."
According to a joint statement issued Friday, Canada and the EU launched the "Alliance for the Future" aiming to deliver ambitious cooperation in the following areas: trade and regulatory cooperation; digital, research and communications technologies; critical raw materials and energy; financial services and markets; security and preparedness; and people-to-people.
The prime minister's office said in a news release that the alliance is a new partnership of nations that will leverage the strategic capabilities of Canada, the EU, and a variable geometry of like-minded nations to address common issues.
Together, Canada and the EU will deliver more choice and lower costs for families, new export markets for businesses, and greater opportunities for young people to live, work, and study where they want, in Canada or the EU, according to the release.
In closing remarks, Carney said that the two sides are working toward the deepest possible partnership, short of accession, with Canada becoming the EU's first associate member.
"Over the coming months, we will determine the substance, scale and scope of this form of membership," Carney said.
The joint statement noted that the two sides are working to define by the 2027 EU-Canada Summit the concept of an "ever-closer association" of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself.
During the Canada-EU summit, the two sides unveiled more than 20 new initiatives and announced the conclusion of negotiations for the Canada-EU Digital Trade Agreement. As Canada's first agreement dedicated entirely to digital trade, it aims to reduce frictions in online trade and make it easier for businesses to sell goods and services. ■

Meta outlook revised downward by S&P on cash flow and capex concerns
Unknown

07:42:26 KST

Meta's outlook has been revised downward by S&P Global Ratings on concerns surrounding cash flow and AI spending.
The credit agency said Friday that the outlook reflects "uncertainty" about Meta's elevated capex and its negative free cash flow.
Meta's credit rating was revised from AA- stable to AA- negative, S&P said. S&Ps highest credit rating is AAA. Anything below BBB falls into the junk bond category.
The agency questioned "Meta's ability to monetize its AI investments" relative to its peers, which are also spending heavily on data center buildouts and going cash flow negative in the process.
Although Meta has recently debuted its Muse AI agent app and related foundation models, S&P said "it is unclear when these revenue streams will generate material contributions that exceed their rising costs over the next few years."
A Meta spokesperson pushed back on the revision.
"We respectfully disagree with S&P's assertion about Meta's AI monetization capabilities," the spokesperson said in a statement. "We see significant product and business opportunities ahead of us, supporting our very strong credit profile."
Meta said in its third-quarter earnings report last week that it expects full-year capex to come in the range of $135 billion to $145 billion. The company also posted negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion, going in the red for the first time.
Investors sent Meta shares down 7% following the report despite a revenue beat. The stock finished October down 15%, its worst month in four years.
The company said on Monday that it plans to raise $95 billion to help fund its AI initiatives, with plans to first raise $35 billion in underwritten public equity offerings, followed by an additional $60 billion through an at-the-market program.
S&P said that while it expects Meta's capex growth to start "flattening out beginning in 2028," the agency is "less certain that it will curtail its spending as previously anticipated."

China helps dismantle major meth trafficking network in Southeast Asia
Joint operation with Indonesia and Malaysia shuts down what is believed to be Indonesia’s largest methamphetamine laboratory
China has broken up a major transnational drug trafficking network in cooperation with Indonesia and Malaysia, seizing around 1.2 tonnes of liquid methamphetamine, China’s Ministry of Public Security said on Friday.
The operation was carried out on October 21 by Indonesia’s National Narcotics Agency (BNN), which raided and shut down a large-scale drug processing and purification facility in Aceh, Indonesia, and arrested 11 people, with help from China’s National Narcotics Control Commission (NNCC) and Malaysia’s National Anti-Drugs Agency, the ministry said.
The methamphetamine factory, housed in two shops, is believed to be the largest of its kind in Indonesia. Washing machines used to process methamphetamine, liquefied petroleum gas cylinders and other equipment and materials were also found at the site, according to local media reports.

EXPLAINER - Police deployed after head of top court suspended, president cuts trip short: What's happening in Poland?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
22:17:46 UTC
07:17:46 KST

Burak Bir
31 October 2026•Update: 31 October 2026
- 'This is a difficult process, sometimes painful, and it requires decisive action. There is no other way,' says Prime Minister Donald Tusk
- Polish envoy to China resigns following developments, says he 'can no longer serve'
Polish President Karol Nawrocki cut short a trip to Senegal on Friday to return to Warsaw as riot police were deployed to the top court and its president was suspended amid an escalating constitutional crisis.
The crisis surrounding Poland's top court, the Constitutional Tribunal, escalated after the government suspended its two senior justices and moved to bring criminal charges against them.
Prime Minister Donald Tusk's government and Nawrocki have been locked in a dispute over the tribunal's composition.
Judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska issued orders suspending Tribunal President Bogdan Swieczkowski and Vice President Bartlomiej Sochanski from their duties.
Korwin-Piotrowska accused the leadership of obstructing the work of judges elected by the parliamentary majority, violating judicial procedures and preventing the proper functioning of the tribunal.
But the tribunal rejected the orders, saying on its website that Swieczkowski "remains the president of the Constitutional Tribunal and Sochanski remains the vice president."
It wrote on US social media company X: "All persons participating in these actions are committing the crime of a coup d'état."
Following the announcement, protesters gathered outside the tribunal building as tensions escalated, with some reportedly climbing over the fence and throwing objects at police.
Reactions
Following the developments, Nawrocki said he was cutting short his trip to Senegal and returning to Poland.
"At such a moment, the President must be in Poland," he wrote on X.
Tusk said: "Restoring the rule of law is our duty."
"After years of PiS (party)-led lawlessness, this is a difficult process, sometimes painful, and it requires decisive action. There is no other way," he added.
Meanwhile, Polish Ambassador to China Jakub Kumoch resigned following the developments.
"In light of the events in the country, I have concluded that it is no longer possible for me to continue serving as the Ambassador of the Republic of Poland. As of today, I have submitted my resignation and a request for recall," he wrote on X.
Police said they had not entered the court building and denied claims that officers had stormed it.
Law and Justice (PiS) party leader Jaroslaw Kaczynski and other opposition politicians arrived outside the court and accused the government of trying to seize control of the institution.
Kaczynski described the events as a "coup against the Constitutional Tribunal" and urged Nawrocki to intervene.
Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski, in the US city of Atlanta for a G20 meeting, said measures concerning the Constitutional Tribunal aimed to restore the court's functioning after "politicization under the previous government."
Long-running legal dispute
The crisis began after the PiS-led government took office in 2015, as the PiS majority in parliament quickly moved to appoint judges to the court to gain a majority, since the court can decide the legality of legislation.
The European Court of Human Rights and the Court of Justice of the European Union ruled that the PiS majority had improperly elected three judges because they duplicated positions that the previous parliament had validly filled.
The European courts ruled that Poland's Constitutional Tribunal was no longer an "independent and impartial tribunal."
Tusk's government has used the rulings as a basis to stop publishing the tribunal's rulings.
When he took office in 2023, Tusk vowed to depoliticize the judiciary, but he partially failed because Nawrocki and his predecessor, Andrzej Duda, used their presidential vetoes to block the attempts.
PiS and Nawrocki accused the government of using the rule-of-law campaign to remove political opponents from key state institutions.
Nawrocki was expected in Warsaw late Friday evening as the standoff continued and was set to meet the first president of the Supreme Court, Zbigniew Kapinski.

“The world’s becoming more dangerous and divided. Our societies are being shaken by new storms,” Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney told a press conference, mentioning eroding democratic norms and “the weaponisation of trade.”
“Together, Canada and the European Union are anchoring the ground. Anchoring our ground to uphold our values while forming a protective canopy under which our citizens can all thrive,” he said, after talks with EU chiefs Ursula von der Leyen and Antonio Costa.
Nations agree push to get nature goals on track
Nearly 200 nations on Oct 30 adopted hard-fought agreements at a UN biodiversity summit aimed at putting the world back on track in efforts to halt nature’s destruction by 2030.

US midterm early voting hits record 48 million
A record 47.9 million Americans have already voted in next week’s US midterm elections, with participation surging in key battleground states and registered Democrats outpacing Republicans, figures showed Oct 30.
The University of Florida’s Election Lab had recorded 47,922,669 early votes nationwide by midday, surpassing the previous midterm record of 45.9 million cast ahead of Election Day in 2022.

Delayed missile deliveries added to Ukraine’s tensions with the US after President Donald Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia and criticised Zelensky for Ukraine’s unwillingness to stop attacks on Russian refineries.

This early Black Friday sale means you don’t have to wait until the late-November holiday to score the worthwhile discount—and we recommend you don’t. Amazon, Best Buy, and the Google Store are all offering the 25 percent off deal, but I don’t know for how much longer. In other words, now is a great time to score this smartwatch for less.
A Record-Low Price
The Pixel Watch 5 is one of the best smartwatches available for Android users. It’s a refinement of an already brilliant wearable, with double the RAM and storage, plus an upgraded Qualcomm Snapdragon W5 Gen 2 processor that makes this edition 20 percent faster than its predecessor. This is the lowest price I’ve seen for the Pixel Watch 5, so if you’ve been eyeing it, there’s little reason to wait for Black Friday.

People high in neuroticism report sleeping less, but wrist monitors tell a different story
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
22:00:58 UTC
07:00:58 KST

Young adults who scored higher in neuroticism reported sleeping less, but a wrist-worn sleep monitor did not show that they actually slept less, according to a study published in Personality and Individual Differences.
Neuroticism is a personality trait associated with a greater tendency to experience negative emotions, such as worry and distress. Previous research has found that people with higher neuroticism often report shorter sleep. But studies using actigraphy, which relies on a wearable device to estimate sleep from movement, have generally not found the same relationship.
To examine this discrepancy, Derick M. DeCamp and Elizabeth J. Pantesco of Villanova University looked at both kinds of sleep measures in the same group of people. The study included 134 undergraduate students (average age 19; 95 women) without diagnosed sleep disorders.
Participants wore a wrist actigraph for five nights, including two weekend nights, and completed questionnaires about their personality, sleep, and symptoms of depression and anxiety. The researchers measured reported sleep over the past month in two ways: participants directly estimated how many hours of actual sleep they usually got, and the team calculated sleep duration from participants’ usual bedtime, wake time, and time taken to fall asleep.
Higher neuroticism was linked to shorter sleep on both self-report measures, but not to sleep duration as estimated by the actigraph. The differences were modest: each one-point increase in neuroticism on a five-point scale was associated with roughly 15 to 20 fewer minutes of reported sleep. The connection between neuroticism and self-reported sleep remained after the researchers accounted for actigraphy-estimated sleep, demographic characteristics, body mass index, depression and anxiety symptoms, night-to-night sleep regularity, and other personality traits.
The study’s average sleep estimates illustrate how measurement methods can differ. Participants reported 6.74 hours of sleep on the direct question, while the actigraph estimated 6.70 hours, and the calculated self-report estimate was higher, at 7.40 hours. Compared with the actigraph, participants higher in neuroticism tended to underestimate their sleep on the direct question and to overestimate it less on the calculated measure.
Symptoms of depression and anxiety were closely related to neuroticism but were not themselves linked to how long participants slept or reported sleeping, and accounting for them did not weaken the association. The authors suggest this points to a role for the stable personality trait rather than temporary distress.
The authors wrote that their findings are “consistent with the possibility that neuroticism is more strongly related to how individuals perceive, recall, and report their sleep duration than to actigraphy-assessed sleep duration.” They suggested that people higher in neuroticism might recall or interpret their sleep more negatively, or that worry before bed might make it feel as though falling asleep takes longer. These explanations remain speculative, as the researchers did not directly measure recall errors or reporting bias.
The authors also noted other possibilities. People higher in neuroticism might spend more time lying still but awake in bed, which an actigraph can mistake for sleep, and because both neuroticism and habitual sleep were self-reported, part of the association may reflect shared reporting tendencies.
Some limitations should be noted. The questionnaires asked about sleep during the previous month, while the actigraph recorded only five nights, which may not be enough to reliably capture typical sleep; the mismatch also makes direct comparisons harder. Participants may also have altered their sleep because they knew it was being monitored, and the sample consisted of college students, most of them women, from a single private university.
The study, “Neuroticism is associated with self-reported, but not actigraphy-assessed, sleep duration,” was authored by Derick M. DeCamp and Elizabeth J. Pantesco.

2026-10-31

BERLIN, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- Germany's inflation rate eased to 2.8 percent in October after rising for three consecutive months, official data showed Friday, as energy price increases slowed following the introduction of temporary fuel tax cuts.
The decline came after inflation reached 3.3 percent in September, its highest level in nearly three years, driven largely by a sharp rise in energy costs, according to the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis).
Energy prices rose 12.2 percent year-on-year in October, easing from a 14.9-percent surge in September, the sharpest rise since February 2023.
The slowdown in energy price increases followed the introduction of temporary fuel tax cuts by the German government on Oct. 1, with the measures set to expire at the end of the year. Analysts had previously estimated that the tax cuts would lower Germany's October inflation rate by 0.3 percentage points.
Despite the easing in inflation, economists warned that price pressures could intensify again in the coming months as elevated energy costs continued to weigh on Europe's largest economy.
A survey released Friday by the Munich-based ifo Institute showed more German companies were planning to raise prices, with its price expectations index climbing to 25.9 points in October from 23 points in September.
"Companies are responding to the sharp increase in prices for crude oil and natural gas, which reached their highest level in the second half of October since 2022," said Timo Wollmershaeuser, head of forecasts at ifo, who warned both producer and consumer price inflation would rise further in the coming months.
Carsten Brzeski, global head of macro at ING Research, said that the start of the winter heating season, combined with low gas storage levels in Germany, was likely to push up gas prices further in the coming weeks.
Brzeski expected headline inflation to rise again and remain above 3 percent towards the end of this year and in early 2027.
The German government also expects inflationary pressures to persist. In its autumn forecast released earlier this month, it projected an average inflation of 2.7 percent in 2026, up from 2.2 percent in 2025, before rising to 3 percent in 2027. ■

British business confidence drops following Budget 2026: IoD
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
06:00:53 CST
07:00:53 KST

LONDON, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- Confidence of British business leaders fell remarkably after the government unveiled its 2026 budget, according to a poll released Friday by the Institute of Directors (IoD).
Ahead of the budget announcement, entrepreneurs' expectations for business revenue increased from 21 in September to 28 in October, the highest level since July 2024. But the figure plummeted to 8 after the budget release, marking its lowest level since December 2025, the IoD said.
The index of investment intentions also climbed from minus 8 in September to 1 ahead of the budget announcement, hitting the highest level since August 2024, before dropping to minus 9 afterward.
A similar trend was seen in employment expectations, with the index falling from 2, its highest level since April 2025, to minus 6 after the budget announcement.
"Our post-Budget snap poll suggests the budget has done little to encourage business leaders to take their investment and recruitment plans out of mothballs," IoD Chief Economist Anna Leach said. Revenue expectations fell sharply to their weakest in 10 months, while investment and hiring intentions also deteriorated, she added.
Ahead of the budget release, business leaders made clear that they wanted the government to address the deterioration in public finances. In its 2026 budget, the government introduced a package to either freeze in real terms, reduce or cut to zero the business rates for all retail, hospitality and leisure properties in England. It also took around 70,000 more retail, hospitality and leisure businesses out of business rates by increasing the Small Business Rates Relief threshold.
However, Leach said the budget has allowed fiscal headroom to fall substantially, leaving the public finances with relatively little protection against further shocks.
"With difficult decisions on spending still ahead and limited fiscal headroom, businesses will be concerned that the risk of further tax increases has not gone away," she said.
After two years of weak business confidence, the priority remains to provide a more stable and supportive environment for firms to invest, recruit and grow, she added. ■
