====================================================================================================

Feature: Chinese pianist performs Chopin underground in Polish salt mine
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
06:00:43 CST
07:00:43 KST

Chinese pianist Rao Hao performs works by Chopin at the Wieliczka Salt Mine in Wieliczka, Poland, Oct. 27, 2026. (Wieliczka Salt Mine/Handout via Xinhua)
by Xinhua writers Yue Yuanyuan, Du Zhiqian
WIELICZKA, Poland, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- Some 135 meters beneath the surface of the earth, even the softest touch of the piano keys can be clearly heard, resonating through the chamber in the Wieliczka Salt Mine, near Krakow.
For Chinese pianist Rao Hao, the venue was unexpectedly intimate: the audience sat close by while delicate musical details floated through the space. It felt, the pianist said, like a small musical salon.
Rao gave the underground Chopin recital as part of his October concert schedule in Poland. At Wieliczka, Chopin's music was met with a landscape shaped by centuries of mining.
For a musician accustomed to theaters and concert halls, the setting of a subterranean chamber carved from rock salt was inviting.
"It was a very new experience for me," Rao told Xinhua before the performance. "We chose works by Chopin to better express my own feelings and my understanding of Polish musical culture."
Around him was an underground hall connected to chapels in the mine. On the walls of the chambers, sculptures feature generations of miners working to extract salt.
Mining activities here date back to the 13th century and Wieliczka was among the first sites inscribed on UNESCO's World Heritage List in 1978. Its underground spaces preserve both the history of mining and the artistic imagination of those who worked there.
For Rao, however, the main discovery was acoustic. The chamber responded to even the quietest playing, allowing subtle changes in pressure to be heard by the audience, he said.
The short distance between performer and public also made the experience more relaxed, the musician said, providing an ideal setting to convey a powerful Chopin of courage, pride and longing -- qualities he feels can be overlooked in the composer's music.
Chopin was often portrayed as fragile or melancholy, but Rao said: "He was a composer with backbone and courage, and he was full of homesickness."
His program included Chopin's four scherzos and the "Heroic" Polonaise. "This time, I want to bring out his strong side," Rao said.
Rao was 17 when he received an honorable mention at the 2021 International Chopin Piano Competition in Warsaw, an experience that introduced him to a wider international audience.
Now 22, he hopes to demonstrate his growth as a performer. He said his personal connection with the music has deepened, as have his reflections on Polish and Chinese cultures.
For the mine's hosts, the recital also carries special significance.
Barbara Zieba-Godula, president of the management board of the Wieliczka Salt Mine Tourism Company, said Chopin's music is appreciated in both Poland and China, and the concert also showed visitors another way to experience the mine: enjoy an evening listening and explore history at the same time.
Zieba-Godula added that she hoped Rao's visit would encourage more Chinese artists to perform at the mine and create further opportunities for cultural exchange.
For the occasion, the organizers invited representatives of the Chinese embassy, classical music festivals, musical institutions and tourism organizations.
Among the guests was Tomasz Chabowski, who runs a local Chinese kung fu school. With about 30 people in the audience, the concert was "exceptionally intimate," he said, and the setting made it all the more memorable.
"I'm no Chopin expert, but this concert reminded me how moving his music can be," said Chabowski, praising Rao's masterful playing and choice of repertoire. ■
Chinese pianist Rao Hao performs works by Chopin at the Wieliczka Salt Mine in Wieliczka, Poland, Oct. 27, 2026. (Wieliczka Salt Mine/Handout via Xinhua)

Azerbaijan approves draft law to reward corruption whistleblowers
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
06:00:21 CST
07:00:21 KST

BAKU, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- Azerbaijan's parliament on Friday approved a draft law in the first reading that offers financial rewards to individuals who report corruption-related offenses, local media reported.
Under the draft law, whistleblowers whose information is confirmed would be eligible for a tax-exempt reward of up to 25 times the national minimum monthly wage. The reward would be paid within 10 working days and funded from the budget of the organization concerned.
In criminal cases resulting in a conviction or another final ruling, informants would also receive 5 percent of the funds recovered for the state, including through the special confiscation of assets and compensation for damage, after prescribed expenses are deducted.
The reward amount would depend on the nature of the offense, the number of cases involved, the value of the information in exposing the offense, the extent of the damage caused and the value of assets recovered.
In criminal proceedings, decisions on reward payments would be made by an investigator with the prosecutor's consent during the pretrial investigation stage, and by the court during trial.
The draft law also proposes amendments to the Tax Code to exempt such rewards from income tax. ■

====================================================================================================

Explainer: What is Canada's EU "associate member"? Why is it disputed?
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
06:00:15 CST
07:00:15 KST

BRUSSELS, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- The European Union (EU) and Canada on Friday launched "Alliance for the Future" and opted for "ever-closer association" instead of using the name "associate member" in their summit joint statement.
Meeting in Montreal in eastern Canada, the two sides pledged to define the closer relationship, short of full EU membership, by their 2027 summit.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, nevertheless, continued to advocate associate membership, saying after the summit that the idea had been a main point of discussion.
WHAT IS AN "ASSOCIATE MEMBER"?
The proposed status remains undefined. In her statement following the summit, von der Leyen described the idea as "association without accession." She said EU treaties prevented a country outside Europe from joining, but envisaged a partnership closer to membership than any previous arrangement.
The joint statement establishes no new membership category. It provides for closer political engagement through summits, ministerial exchanges and cooperation committees, while leaving the broader concept for further negotiation.
"We will work to define the concept of an ever-closer association of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself, to reflect, through this even closer association, our common endeavour and cooperation towards our shared goals of prosperity, economic security and strategic autonomy," it said.
WHAT COULD CANADA GAIN, AND WHAT WOULD IT CONTRIBUTE?
Von der Leyen outlined closer policy consultations, expanded research cooperation and deeper Canadian participation in EU programs.
The joint statement announced the conclusion of substantive negotiations on a Digital Trade Agreement and welcomed Canada's participation in the European High-Performance Computing Joint Undertaking. Negotiations will also pursue deeper participation in Erasmus+, the EU's education and youth program.
According to the Canadian prime minister's office, Canada intends to participate in the EU's 90 billion euro (100 billion U.S. dollars) Ukraine Support Loan.
WHY HAVE SOME EU COUNTRIES QUESTIONED THE LABEL?
Ahead of the summit, Germany, France, Italy and Greece had objected to mentioning associate membership in the draft declaration, according to a report of POLITICO.
At a government briefing in September, German spokesperson Stefan Kornelius welcomed a particularly close partnership and new models of cooperation, but said the proposed title of "associate member" should be reconsidered.
Analysts said that governments feared the designation could complicate the relations with Ukraine, which seeks full membership of the bloc, and with Norway and Switzerland, which already have special arrangements with the EU.
The Commission acknowledged that member states were making efforts over the wording at a news briefing on Thursday. The final statement leaves the title aside while preserving an extensive cooperation agenda.
WHY ARE THE TWO SIDES MOVING CLOSER NOW?
The joint statement cites geopolitical tensions, economic fragmentation, climate change and technological transformation as reasons for a deeper relationship.
Analysts described the summit as part of efforts by both sides to reduce their dependence on the United States, and to search for new alliances amid international tensions.
The joint statement also expressed regret over U.S. sanctions against the International Criminal Court, illustrating shared differences with Washington.
Von der Leyen argued that acting together would strengthen their ability to respond to a changing world, though she said the partnership was not directed against anyone else.
WHAT'S NEXT?
The joint statement sets the 2027 EU-Canada summit as the target for defining the closer association.
Von der Leyen also announced a meeting between the Canadian government and the full European Commission in spring.
Meanwhile, the two sides will pursue negotiations on deeper Erasmus+ participation and a framework for Canadian access to Galileo services, alongside discussions on mobility and professional qualifications.
These processes will determine how the summit's political commitments translate into practical access responsibilities and opportunities for citizens and businesses. ■

====================================================================================================

UN Security Council holds 7th straw poll on secretary-general candidates
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
06:00:14 CST
07:00:14 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- The UN Security Council on Friday held its seventh straw poll on candidates vying to become the next UN secretary-general.
"The seventh round of straw polls has taken place," said Aglaia Balta, Greece's permanent representative to the United Nations, whose country holds the rotating presidency of the Security Council for the month of October.
Each candidate will be informed of the results through the permanent representatives of nominating member states. The president of the UN General Assembly will also be informed that the poll has been conducted, Balta told reporters after the secret vote.
Security Council straw polls on secretary-general candidates are informal closed-door ballots used to determine the viability of the candidates. Their results are not officially released.
Through the polls, the Security Council selects a candidate to recommend to the General Assembly for appointment as the next UN secretary-general.
Council members are believed to receive one ballot for each candidate, containing the candidate's name followed by three options: "encouraged," "discouraged" and "no opinion expressed."
To win the council's recommendation, a candidate needs at least nine "encouraged" votes and no "discouraged" votes from any of the five permanent members of the council.
In the sixth straw poll held on Oct. 16, ballots were color-coded to distinguish the votes of permanent and non-permanent members. However, in the seventh straw poll, the council members switched back to undifferentiated ballots following the entry of a new candidate into the race.
Lana Nusseibeh, a diplomat from the United Arab Emirates and the country's former permanent representative to the United Nations, entered the race on Oct. 21. Macky Sall, a former president of Senegal, announced his withdrawal on Oct. 17.
In addition to Nusseibeh, six candidates participated in the seventh straw poll: Ivonne A-Baki, a former Ecuadoran minister and diplomat; Maria Fernanda Espinosa, a former president of the UN General Assembly and former foreign minister and defense minister of Ecuador; Rafael Grossi of Argentina, the current director general of the International Atomic Energy Agency; Rebeca Grynspan, a former vice president of Costa Rica and current secretary-general of the UN Conference on Trade and Development; Olara Otunnu of Uganda, a former UN under-secretary-general; and Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett, Guyana's permanent representative to the United Nations.
According to leaked results, Grynspan topped Friday's poll with 11 "encouraged" votes and four "discouraged" votes. She was followed by Grossi, who received nine "encouraged" votes, four "discouraged" votes and two "no opinion expressed" votes.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres' term expires at the end of this year. His successor is scheduled to take office on Jan. 1, 2027. ■

====================================================================================================

'Social Media on Steroids.' Advocates for Children Call for Guardrails Around AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
21:49:22 UTC
06:49:22 KST

“We are living through the greatest transformation that we have seen in our lifetimes, and likely for a significant time before that,” two-time Surgeon General Vivek Murthy told an audience at New York City’s flagship public library on Oct. 28, comparing the advent of artificial intelligence to the advent of nuclear weaponry in terms of the need for carefully thought out safety standards. “We're at a branch point,” he added. “What should the future really look like, what are we trying to protect and preserve?”
Murthy was not alone in sounding the alarm. Jim Steyer, founder and CEO of Common Sense Media, the organizer of the conference, told the mostly supportive crowd that recent history had proved that the industry leaders or, as he called them “tech broligarchs,” could not be relied upon to create digital information systems that were safe or healthy for children. “We did not get out in front of social media in time,” he told the gathering. “This is the moment. AI is a bigger deal. It's basically social media on steroids.”
New York’s governor Kathy Hochul seemed to underscore the point when she made an unscheduled stop at the daylong summit to announce new regulations around chatbots interactions with children. The bill was designed to ensure that AI agents do not impersonate humans or communicate in a way that suggests they have a relationship with a child. “It's happening so quickly,” said Hochul of the technological changes. “It's almost impossible for parents to know what's going on, for elected officials to stay ahead of it, and we certainly have learned the lesson that we can't count on the companies to put out products that are responsible and that put children first.”
Specifically, the new law, which goes into effect in January, will ban chatbots from encouraging suicide, self-harm, secrecy, or isolation and from discouraging children to seek help from other humans. They will also be banned from engaging in sexually explicit interactions and restricted from using a child’s past personal or health information in later conversations.
For the attendees and speakers at the summit, who ranged from Chelsea Clinton and Columbia law professor Tim Wu (onstage) to Uma Thurman (in the audience), the announcement was a good start, although many bemoaned the lack of federal regulation, around both AI and social media. “To this day, 2026, our federal government and Congress has still—nearly a quarter century after the advent of social media—failed to announce anything to protect our kids,” said Murthy, who is now chair of the advisory board of Common Sense Media’s Youth AI Safety Institute, which studies, tests, and rates AI platforms for children.
Panelists called for a range of protective and preventative remedies for what they described as the coming tsunami of AI, including requiring more data transparency from tech companies by enabling regulatory agencies and researchers to get more access to the information they’re holding, using consumer-protection laws to ensure that AI models have been rigorously tested for potential negative outcomes, adopting the European model of not allowing AI companies to deploy their platforms until they have proved they are safe, or even instituting criminal penalties for AI companies who unleash unsafe technologies. “As a former prosecutor, I can tell you one thing,” said New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez, who earlier this month won a $25 billion judgment against Meta. “When you bring out handcuffs, suddenly everything changes.”
Not all the issues around AI can be solved by the law, however. One concern is the socialization of very young children by AI, including via voice-activated assistants like Alexa or very agreeable AI-enabled toys. “What do kids start to learn to expect from social practice? Do they expect someone to always agree with them? Is it always easy? Is it always like a transaction?” asked Dana Suskind, an early-childhood expert and professor at the University of Chicago. Human relationships are a lot messier, she noted. “They're chaotic, and that sort of mess is where a lot of learning happens.” Parents, who were caught off-guard by the influence of social media and digital devices, need to be educated about AI and encouraged that their imperfect parenting, as well as other human interaction, is vastly more beneficial to children than an AI companion, she said.
The summit also touched on the enormous implications AI is having on education and students’ ability to work and learn, when answers are in such ready supply. “MIT just did a report saying every assignment at MIT could be done by generative AI,” said John King, a former U.S. Secretary of Education and current chancellor of State University in New York. King is considering major changes to student assessment. “We have to make sure we are seeing the students do the work, and we have to make sure they're getting those foundational skills,” he said. “It literally means every faculty member reassessing what they assign and how they measure student learning.” And, as Clinton pointed out, this is an equity issue too. “We know that in families with less than $30,000 of household income, teenagers are three times more likely to either largely or entirely do their homework through artificial intelligence than those households with family incomes of $75,000 or more,” she said.
At the same time, students need to be prepared to enter a workforce in which AI skills are not optional. For those who have mastered them, the future is very bright. “The people coming in learn much more rapidly because AI gives them more capacity than they've had before,” said Gene Sykes, chairman of global mergers and acquisitions at Goldman Sachs of the banking giant’s new recruits. “So somebody, within a month, can be doing incredibly productive work.” If good education in AI is distributed unevenly, some graduates will be vastly better prepared for a career than others, further exacerbating wealth inequities.
While there was little consensus on the immediate steps to take as AI arrives, there was no argument that it will be consequential for children, families, and generations to come. “As we go into this age of transformation,” Murthy noted, “the question forced upon us is the following: What aspects of human existence do we want to protect and preserve at all costs?”

The fragile ceasefire – announced by US First Lady Melania Trump last week to pave the way for evacuations and deliveries of humanitarian aid – is due to end on Sunday evening.
Ukrainian and Russian officials visited the town together on Friday, delivering aid and marshalling those who wanted to leave.
After hours there, both sides said they had left with convoys of people – some heading to Russia, others on a journey back to Kyiv-controlled parts of Ukraine via Russia and Belarus.
"The Ukrainian delegation, along with the evacuated residents of Oleshky, set off for Anapa," Ukrainian negotiator David Arakhamia said on Friday, referring to a southern Russian city on the Black Sea coast.
"From there, they will fly to Belarus and then travel home by bus," Arakhamia said.
Moscow said the operation had been completed "without any incidents".
"The humanitarian mission in Oleshky is concluding," Russia's human rights ombudsman Yana Lantratova said in a video post on Telegram.
"Everything went smoothly," she said, saying 25 buses and nine ambulances had been deployed for the evacuations.
Neither side disclosed how many people left.
The pre-war population of Oleshky has dropped from 24,000 to about 2,000.

Russia, US veto rival UN Western Sahara resolutions, leaving peacekeeping mission in limbo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
21:41:24 UTC
06:41:24 KST

Competing US, Russia resolutions on Western Sahara defeated in UN Security Council
UNITED NATIONS, Oct 30 - Russia vetoed a US-drafted resolution on Western Sahara at the Security Council on Friday, leaving the UN peacekeeping mission there without a renewed mandate just a day before it expires.
The resolution would have extended the mission for another year while cementing Morocco's autonomy plan as the only basis for talks to settle the half-century-old conflict and scaling back its military component.
The council then defeated a rival Russian resolution to extend the mission for a year. That draft got 2 votes in favor and 1 against, with 11 abstentions, failing to get the nine affirmative votes needed to pass.
The showdown threatens the future of a mission the council has routinely renewed for decades and deepens a dispute over the territory, most of which is controlled by Morocco but claimed by the Algeria-backed Polisario Front, which seeks an independent state.
Morocco's royal palace welcomed the failure to renew the mission, saying its personnel and equipment should leave Western Sahara in the coming days. Morocco said it remained committed to the ceasefire in the territory. Polisario representative Sidi Omar thanked Russia for vetoing the US-backed resolution, which he said would "torpedo the foundations of the UN peace process" and "threaten regional and international peace".
Unless the Security Council agrees to a last-minute extension, the mandate for the UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara, known as MINURSO, will expire on October 31.
Algeria's foreign ministry expressed regret on Saturday over the failure to renew MINURSO's mandate, criticising what it described as the excessive bias of the US-drafted resolution towards Morocco.
Oxfam warned that losing the mission could put refugees at risk. Hostilities have persisted at low levels since Polisario said in November 2020 that it was resuming "armed struggle".
Last year, the Security Council dealt a blow to Polisario's ambitions when it backed Morocco's autonomy proposal as a basis for resolving the conflict and asked UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres to submit a review of the peacekeeping mission.
The failed US resolution would have gone further, removing the reference to a referendum from the mission's name, renaming it the United Nations Mission in Western Sahara, or MINUSO.
Following the vote, US Ambassador Michael Waltz said a referendum had never taken place because of longstanding disagreements over voter eligibility.
"UN officials have been telling us this reality for 30 years," he said.
"Unfortunately, some members of this Council have used their veto to preserve the letter 'R' for referendum in the mission's name, even though the United Nations has not been preparing to hold such a vote for decades," he added.
France and the UK — the two other permanent Security Council members — along with eight non-permanent members, backed the US resolution and Morocco's autonomy plan.
MISSION AT RISK
Russia said the US draft went too far in endorsing Morocco's position on the disputed territory.
"We stress the fact that the Security Council cannot automatically predetermine matters relating to sovereignty," Russia's UN envoy Vassily Nebenzia said.
"The Security Council must not give a blessing to such a one-sided approach. Therefore we were compelled to block the adoption of the draft," he said.
With 155 military personnel, the mission, tasked with organizing a referendum as part of a UN-brokered ceasefire, is set to cost $62 million in the fiscal year that started in June this year, according to a UN Secretary-General report.
"The loss of MINURSO’s monitoring and de-escalation functions risks undermining security and stability, with serious consequences to civilians and prospects of a peaceful resolution," Oxfam said in reaction to the vote.
While most Sahrawis live in Morocco-ruled Western Sahara, tens of thousands are estimated to be living in Polisario-run refugee camps in Algeria.
The vetoed US resolution called for a census of the refugees.
UNITY DAY
Morocco's royal palace said the non-renewal of the mission was a "significant development" and that it meant the Western Sahara issue should be withdrawn from consideration by the Security Council.
"The non-renewal of MINURSO's mandate clearly means that the presence of the mission in the Kingdom's southern provinces, including its personnel, vehicles, equipment and symbols, should come to an end in the coming days," the palace said in a statement.
In Laayoune, the largest city in Western Sahara, streets were decorated with Moroccan flags and lights to prepare to celebrate “Unity Day”, a holiday the palace declared to commemorate last year’s UN Security Council vote on October 31.
On Wednesday, the Polisario staged a rally at the Smara camp near the town of Tindouf, in southern Algeria.
A couple hundred men and women, waving flags of the Polisario's self-proclaimed Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic, gathered near Polisario fighters in military fatigues, waving signs with slogans such as "No to Morocco's autonomy plan. Yes to the right to self-determination". REUTERS

we drove volvo’s electric EX60 to russel wright’s modernist woodland home at manitoga
from seasonal color studies to an interior that projects leaves onto its seats, volvo’s electric EX60 draws design inspiration from nature.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
an autumn drive into the hudson highlands
Volvo‘s new all-electric EX60 took us from Manhattan to Manitoga, the woodland home of American industrial designer Russel Wright in Garrison, New York. The drive north brought us out of the city and into the tree-lined roads of the Hudson Valley, glowing with autumn color, where the Swedish automaker had organized a design experience around its newest electric SUV.
During the mid-twentieth century, Wright spent decades transforming a former quarry into a 75-acre woodland estate. The experimental and iconic modernist home incorporates the surrounding forest into its architecture, with the resulting space feeling like an architect’s fairytale.
Volvo’s designers have been exploring similar ideas for the EX60, studying natural materials and the changing colors of the landscape to shape the experience inside the car.
the all-electric ex60
The EX60 translates the familiar proportions of Volvo’s popular XC60 into a fully electric SUV. Its low front end and gently sloping roofline contribute to a drag coefficient of just 0.26, while beneath the body sits the company’s new SPA3 electric architecture.
The platform introduces megacasting and cell-to-body battery integration to reduce weight and improve efficiency. For the U.S. market, the P10 AWD offers 503 horsepower and up to 330 miles of EPA-estimated range, with charging from 10 to 80 percent taking as little as 16 minutes under optimal conditions.
material and color choices
Inside, the EX60 introduces a 15-inch curved OLED center display with Google Gemini integrated into the infotainment system. The cabin has a fairly simple layout, with tactile finishes and natural textures softening the presence of its digital technology.
Once we arrived at Manitoga, we met Sara Erichsen Susnjar, Volvo Cars’ Senior Color & Material Design Manager, who has spent twenty years with the company and oversees color and material design for its midsize models.
Presenting a palette of materials, Susnjar drew our attention to the EX60’s available tailored wool-blend upholstery. Wool, she explained, naturally responds to body temperature, remaining comfortable through changes in weather. Its breathability is especially useful when returning to a parked car on a hot day. The material comes with challenges around production costs and customer expectations, although its practical qualities make a compelling case. ‘I think it’s a little bit brave, but also it has a function,‘ she told us.
The conversation soon turned to color. Susnjar explained that developing a new automotive finish can involve an entire year of evaluation, with painted vehicles taken outdoors in different seasons to observe how their colors respond to changing light.
‘We have to check all the light,‘ she explained. This means moving between controlled lighting environments and outdoor settings, from warm summer sunlight to the colder light of winter.
russel wright’s manitoga is a house shaped by the forest
There was an interesting historical parallel waiting inside Manitoga. Wright approached color as something that should respond to the seasons, changing elements of his home’s interior throughout the year. Warmer colors appeared during winter, while cooler tones were introduced for summer. Best known for his American Modern dinnerware, introduced in 1939, Wright had long been interested in how design could make domestic environments more comfortable and enjoyable.
In 1942, Wright and his wife Mary purchased the former quarry and logging property in Garrison. The estate would eventually become home to Dragon Rock, completed in 1961 with architect David Leavitt. Touring the house, we found interiors filled with unusual handmade experiments.
Large boulders extend into the rooms, while actual pine needles are embedded in green plaster walls. Wright even pressed butterfly wings or wildflowers between sheets of translucent plastic to creating decorative screens from materials gathered in nature.
immersed in wild nature
Outside, a waterfall drops into the former quarry pool, while trails wind through the surrounding woodland. Our guide explained how Wright encouraged native moss to spread by removing competing plants to gradually transforming the forest floor.
Today, Manitoga is a National Historic Landmark, designated in 2006, and is maintained by the nonprofit Russel Wright Design Center, which continues to preserve and restore the house and landscape.
bringing the forest into the electric cabin
One of the EX60’s more unusual interior features is its Forest Light ambient lighting system, which projects a pattern of leaves onto the rear seats and center console. Susnjar described the feature during our visit, explaining that the design team wanted to bring some of the experience of nature into the vehicle. As the presentation took place during the day, we could only get a partial impression of the effect, which is designed to be experienced in darkness.
After exploring Dragon Rock, Wright experimented extensively with lighting. Large expanses of glass bring the changing woodland into view from almost every room. His home responds directly to its surroundings, with natural materials appearing throughout the architecture. Volvo takes a different approach, using contemporary technology to introduce an impression of the forest into the enclosed space of a car.

estate: Manitoga / The Russel Wright Design Center | @visitmanitoga
architecture: Russel Wright with David Leavitt, Dragon Rock, completed 1961

‘The killer was never punished’: The forgotten Egypt terror attack and its tragic fifth victim
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
21:35:38 UTC
06:35:38 KST

Mor Shamli, 35, the widow of Alon Shamli, who was murdered before her eyes in Egypt on October 8, 2023, became the fifth victim of the shooting attack Friday, after dying following more than three years of psychological anguish.
The shooting took place in Alexandria one day after the Hamas massacre of October 7, as Israelis were still struggling to comprehend the scale of the atrocities and eliminate the remaining terrorists in communities near the Gaza Strip. An Egyptian police officer opened fire with his weapon at a group of Israeli tourists near Pompey's Pillar, a Roman triumphal column considered one of the best-known tourist attractions in Alexandria, Egypt's second-largest city. 
Alon Shamli and Amnon Bezalel were pronounced dead at the scene, while Hagai Efrat died of his wounds about 10 days later. Egyptian tour guide Sayed Kamel al-Khawalqa was also killed in the attack. Alon's widow later said: "My life ended there in Egypt on October 8, 2023, when they murdered us. The bullet that struck Alon's heart struck mine too."
Alon Shamli, who was 34 when he was killed, coached a youth team at Hapoel Tel Aviv soccer club. He also worked as a physical education teacher at Rishonim School in Bat Yam. Following his death, Hapoel Tel Aviv said Alon "was highly regarded in the youth department. His players said he always devoted himself to them and pushed them to improve."
Amnon Bezalel, 64, of Bat Yam, served in the Israel Police for about 40 years. He was known as a diligent and respected officer and spent much of his career with the Holon police. His final position was technology coordinator in the Ayalon police region.
Hagai Efrat, 83, of Rishon LeZion, whose death was confirmed about 10 days after the attack, played soccer for Hapoel Haifa in his youth and managed Hapoel Jerusalem's soccer club during the 1970s and 1980s.
Friends of Egyptian tour guide Sayed Kamel al-Khawalqa said he was highly educated and possessed extensive knowledge, which helped him in his work as a tour guide. According to Egyptian media reports, he was also accompanying another group of tourists on the day of the attack and was caught in the gunman's line of fire.
But the attack, which received relatively little attention because it occurred so soon after the October 7 massacre, had another victim: Mor Shamli, who never recovered from what happened. In January, she announced to her Instagram followers that she intended to end her life through medically assisted suicide in Switzerland. 
The announcement sparked a wave of false rumors that the procedure had already taken place and that she had died. In Instagram Stories posted that month, she explained the painful decision she had made and the feelings that had accompanied her since the attack, which occurred just one day after the massacre in Israeli communities near the Gaza Strip.
"The pain is unbearable. You wouldn't believe how many tears the heart and eyes can produce," she wrote in January. "I am not alive, but not entirely dead either. I exist as though I am floating above life. Here, but not here. I am sorry that I am hurting everyone, that the suffering is being passed on to you. There are no words that can express how sorry I am. I hope you can understand and forgive me. I wish that every day of your lives could be like the life Alon and I shared together, full of love and happiness. Please try to remember me as I was before that terrible day. And do not hold anger in your hearts. Now I am no longer suffering. Now I am happy and at peace."
Mor's parents, Ilan and Shoshi Cohen, said Friday evening in grief: "Mor was murdered along with Alon in Egypt. She continued living, but she could not bear the pain and the loss of her husband, Alon. She had no desire to live. She was simply living but dead, until today, when she is no longer with us."
Three years without justice
The shooter's name has never been officially released, although several Arabic-language reports identified him as Mohammed Abdel-Magid. Since the October 7 massacre and the war that followed, diplomatic relations with Egypt have deteriorated significantly. Israel has no ambassador stationed in the country, and Israeli diplomats travel to Cairo from time to time for several days but are not permanently based there. 
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi refuses to meet with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Recently, reports emerged that three Israelis, Ahmed al-Dougi, Bilal Salem Abu Aish and Bilal Masoudin, were taken into Egyptian intelligence vehicles in Sharm el-Sheikh and disappeared. Their whereabouts remain unknown.
Against the backdrop of the current diplomatic climate with Egypt, which has hardly distinguished itself by holding accountable terrorists who leave its territory to carry out attacks in Israel, justice has still not been served for those murdered, even three years after the attack. Reports about the gunman are almost impossible to find, and he has yet to stand trial for his actions.
In an interview this past July with Kan's Reshet Bet radio station, Mor Shamli said: "So much time has passed, and every time they give me different answers. The bottom line is that there are no answers. The killer who was caught that day still hasn't been punished. At first, I was told he was awaiting sentencing. Now I've been told his trial will only take place in another three months. It really feels like they're making a mockery of us."
Mor also described her struggle to retrieve Alon's clothes from Egypt. "I kept asking, and at first the Foreign Ministry told me: 'Listen, this takes time.' Then they told me: 'Too much time has passed. They no longer have them. They've already thrown them away.' The Foreign Ministry is basically telling me: 'We're just passing along the Egyptians' answers.' As if they're merely a go-between for me and the Egyptians."
Doubts that the attacker will ever face justice are further heightened by Arabic-language reports published after the shooting that avoided describing it as a terror attack. Al Jazeera, for example, claimed a day after the killings that the shooting had been preceded by "provocations" by the Israeli tourists, who supposedly "insisted on taking photographs with an Israeli flag." 
According to the unsupported account, the police officer asked the Israelis to stop, an argument developed and he eventually opened fire. Israelis who were present at the scene categorically denied the allegations, saying they had actually tried to avoid drawing attention to their Israeli nationality, particularly in light of the October 7 massacre the previous day.
Several months before the Alexandria attack, another deadly attack occurred along the Israel-Egypt border, also carried out by an Egyptian police officer. On June 3, 2023, Egyptian security officer Mohammed Salah infiltrated Israel and killed Staff Sgt. Ori Yitzhak Ilouz and Sgt. Lia Ben-Nun, both serving in the Bardelas Battalion, at a guard post. Later, during searches and an exchange of fire inside Israeli territory, a third soldier, Staff Sgt. Ohad Dahan of the Caracal Battalion, was killed. The terrorist was subsequently shot dead.

The flaw in Australia’s ‘China threat’ thesis

Alex Lo has been an SCMP columnist since 2012, commenting on China and international affairs. 
Australia’s preparations for a possible conflict with China reflect “a relatively superficial understanding”, argues prominent economist John Edwards. Europe, Canada, Indonesia, Malaysia and India, he notes, are not preparing for such a conflict. Why should Australia?
Edwards, a former senior economic adviser to former Labor prime minister Paul Keating, makes the observation in a Lowy Institute paper released in October and in a newspaper interview.
Instead, he sees US-China rivalry as a potential advantage. Sitting between a security partner in Washington and a major economic partner in Beijing can underpin Australian prosperity for 25 years – provided Canberra does not pick sides.

Government asks ministries to identify cases that can be withdrawn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
21:26:42 UTC
06:26:42 KST

Cabinet secretary asks ministries to identify cases for withdrawal after decriminalisation of offences, as Centre moves to reduce over 3.5 lakh pending litigations
NEW DELHI: Cabinet secretary T V Somanathan has directed secretaries of ministries and departments to identify cases that can be withdrawn following decriminalisation of several offences under Jan Vishwas Act and removal of obsolete legal provisions. They have been asked to complete the exercise by the end of this month.The move is part of govt's efforts to reduce its litigation burden and avoid pursuing cases that may have lost their relevance following changes in the legal framework. The review will cover cases affected by amendments under Act and other legal reforms.
Currently, there are over 3.5 lakh litigations involving central govt pending for more than five years, including over one lakh legacy cases across 19 high courts. According to a presentation, the revenue department has the highest number of cases pending for more than five years at 1.27 lakh, followed by railways (45,583), department of military affairs (32,464), labour and employment (28,822) and corporate affairs (27,109).
Officials said some ministries, including road transport, defence and telecommunications, may have fewer pending cases, but the financial implications of these litigations are likely to be substantially higher.
In two rounds under Jan Vishwas legislations, in 2023 and 2026, several sections of different central laws have been decriminalised and rationalised by introducing compliance provisions.TOI has learnt that while chairing a meeting of all secretaries, Somanathan informed them that a dedicated "litigation management portal" will be launched in Nov to monitor the functioning of litigation management cells, review of legacy litigations and appeals, mediation and screening of cases. Ministries and departments will have to regularly update the status of cases.

Census 2027 population enumeration phase to be of record 50 days
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
21:22:14 UTC
06:22:14 KST

Census 2027 population enumeration to span up to 50 days, with 40 questions including caste, Aadhaar and voter ID details
NEW DELHI: The population enumeration phase of Census 2027 will last longer than in past census exercises, with its duration spanning nearly one-and-a-half months from Jan 10 to Feb 28, including the 15-day self-enumeration window, as against the earlier Phase-2 duration of 20 days, conventionally running from Feb 9-28.Sources told TOI that the house-to-house population enumeration schedule announced earlier for poll-bound states of Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Goa and Punjab also spans 35 days. The longer duration may be linked to the increased number of questions at 40, including pertaining to caste, to be asked in Phase-2 of Census 2027, as against 29 in 2011.No census has been declared in Manipur. The census exercise in the state was put on hold after demands from various sections within the state that the National Register of Citizens (NRC) exercise be conducted first.A notification issued by the Union home ministry Friday declared that a nationwide census of population shall be undertaken - except in Manipur (till further declaration); poll-bound states of Goa, UP, Punjab and Uttarakhand, where it was preponed in view of the impending assembly elections early next year; and UT of Ladakh and snow-bound, non-synchronous areas of Himachal Pradesh and UT of Jammu & Kashmir, where it has already been completed - from Jan 25 to Feb 27, 2027.
This shall be preceded by a window of self-enumeration from Jan 10-24. While the reference date for Census 2027 has already been declared as March 1, 2027, a revisional round will be conducted from March 1-5, 2027.The new fields to be captured in Phase-2 of Census include, apart from caste, spouse's name and mother and father's particulars, the respondent's nationality as declared, permanent address, place of Covid-19 vaccination, total number of bank accounts, mobile number, Aadhaar number, voter ID number, passport number and availability of driving licence.While the mobile number, Aadhaar and voter ID may be shared if available, the passport number is required only from an Indian passport holder.

Series set for epic finale as Aussie batters must stand up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
21:21:19 UTC
06:21:19 KST

Although doubts have been expressed in the last few days that the Cape Town speed gun is operating with flawless accuracy, late on day four of the third Test there appeared to be some validity to its claim that Mitchell Starc had breached the 150km/h barrier.
Soon after, one couldn't help thinking of that speedometer figure — illegal in a car, faintly alarming in a sporting arena — and wince. One of Starc's typically brutish bouncers had spat up off the Newlands pitch and was rearing towards a Proteas batsman.
In the split second it took him to realise his gloves would soon be in the ball's path, and having prized his wicket all day, Ryan Rickelton got his hands out of the way on the understanding the ball would cannon into his ribs with that horrifying thud only a rare breed of cricketer accepts as his duty. And boy did it thud.
There was a time not long ago when the done thing in such situations was to grit one's teeth and pretend it hadn't happened. Think David Boon's thousand-yard stare, or Justin Langer grinning sans tooth. Not Rickelton.
He was on 92 by that point, hours into a game-turning innings, and knew that if a nasty bruise was blossoming, there was no point in pretending it wasn't so. Up came his shirt and sure enough, the mark was already ranking high on the Brian Close scale.
Rickelton showed it off to Travis Head at short leg, either for confirmation or possibly approval of its nastiness. Head seemed to offer both.
It is one of those unspoken paradoxes of Test cricket: the more two teams respect each other, the more they try to hurt each other, and vice versa. As they had the previous evening, and for the telling first two-thirds of the fourth day, Australia's bowlers had been throwing everything at Rickelton and none of it was working.
In the end, it took a run-out to remove him — moments after he brought up a century that slowly but surely ruined Australia's hopes of a quick kill. Rickelton already has a Test double century to his name.
He is a world champion. But here was the sort of high-stakes, backs-to-the-wall performance that can define a career.
As a result, from 4-140 at the start of the day, South Africa piled on 387 to convincingly rebut suggestions they'd roll over. For the third time in the series, a Test between these two proud cricket nations will go down to the fifth day.
The pressure is now all on Australia, who will need to chase down 288 runs to win and retain the status of world number one, with Kagiso Rabada, Marco Jansen and Simon Harmer licking their lips at the prospect of series-winning wickets.
That Australia's task is so onerous is mostly a result of Rickelton and Wiaan Mulder's 154-run partnership for the sixth wicket, which stretched across 53 overs after Matthew Breetzke's dismissal for a spiky, counterpunching 43 in the morning.
Mulder was no second fiddle. After Rickelton departed for a brave and controlled 101 from 219 deliveries, Mulder carried on with a faltering tail, scattering fielders and clubbing sixes to reach a superb 115 of his own.
The above numbers should not give the impression the Australian attack misfired, per se, nor that Australia lacked intent. Until the last minute of the day, they fielded with great gusto to create pressure and affect run-outs to make up for the lack of help from the pitch.
All day, Nathan Lyon bowled with guile and control, jagging the ball at right angles.
It was just that for almost as long, Rickelton and Mulder defied him with the disciplined application of a solid plan: put your ego to one side, get back and across, don't hit against the spin, concede Lyon's end in the knowledge that the quicks at the other end would not get as much help from the surface.
Of the latter, Starc, in particular, gave everything of himself and more, and as late as the final half-hour of play was literally bowling himself off his feet to try and take South Africa's final wicket.
His nine dismissals for the game on a pitch that has offered him little represented a superhuman endeavour.
Where Australia can be faulted, perhaps, is for squandering the second new ball. South Africa was 5-222 when it arrived and there was no repeat of Starc's first-innings clean-up job.
In a day of thankless toil, skipper Pat Cummins broke his wicket drought but otherwise rarely threatened, only claiming his second when Mulder holed out in the final over of the day.
Again, there were industrial quantities of interpersonal drama, although nothing that crossed the line. Hyped up and a little uncoordinated between the wickets, Breetzke tangled with Lyon and spoiled for battles with every other bowler, including a prolonged one-way conversation with Starc.
Loading Twitter content
After taking the bails to run out Rickelton, Marnus Labuschagne sprinted down the pitch like a terrier in the Crufts dog show to let Mulder know it was his fault.
Of course, Labuschagne and others will need their bats to do the talking on the final day, and there is a sense that Rabada will not miss out twice in one game, even without his muse Steve Smith around to get his blood boiling.
A week ago, one might have asked: who will be Australia's Rickelton and Mulder? But all of a sudden, there are a few more convincing answers.
So, a gripping Test series — worthy in every way of its billing as a de facto world title — will now get its fitting conclusion.

UK govt announces new ‘safe and legal’ routes for refugees in India to resettle in UK
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
21:15:21 UTC
06:15:21 KST

UK announces three new refugee resettlement routes for people in India and six other countries, allowing sponsorship through charities, employers and universities.
TOI correspondent from London: In a bid to dissuade asylum-seekers from arriving in Britain on the backs of lorries or via small boats, the UK home office has announced three new “safe and legal” sponsorship routes for refugees in India and six other countries to come to the UK and claim asylum.The new routes are initially targeted at refugees who have sought protection in India, Bangladesh, Egypt, Kenya, Malaysia, Pakistan and Uganda.To be eligible, the refugees will need to be outside their country of nationality, to have been verified by the UNHCR as meeting the definition of refugee and to have registered with the UNHCR or relevant authorities in one of these seven countries before Oct 1. So, in India’s case, it could be Tibetans, Sri Lankan Tamils, Afghans, Rohingya and others from Myanmar, who could be eligible for these routes, but not Indian nationals residing in India, nor internally displaced people.
The refugee sponsorship routes, modelled on a similar programme in Canada, allow sponsors in the UK to identify refugees they wish to sponsor. The new routes are named community sponsorship, which enables UK charities to identify refugees they wish to sponsor; refugee work, which enables UK employers to sponsor and provide refugees jobs; and refugee study, which enables UK universities to sponsor refugees to study in the UK.
Once resettled, the refugees will have an immediate right to work, study and to access welfare benefits in Britain and be placed on a five-year path to permanent resettlement.Sponsors will have to finance and provide their accommodation, the aim being to reduce the amount UK’s govt spends on asylum hotels.Applications to be sponsors for the community and study route have opened and the first arrivals are expected in autumn 2027. Applications under the work route will open in spring 2027.Both Reform UK and the Conservatives vowed to shut the scheme if they come to power. Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said until illegal migration is stopped, “we should not be creating new routes into the UK for asylum claimants”.

Bhutan GLOF creates new lake downstream, raises fears of secondary hazards
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
21:11:49 UTC
06:11:49 KST

Bengal spared Bhutan GLOF impact, water of Sankosh recedes
DEHRADUN/KOLKATA/GUWAHATI: A glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) originating in Bhutan, which prompted an alert across parts of Assam and West Bengal on Friday, has led to the formation of a new temporary lake downstream, raising concerns about a possible secondary hazard.Bhutan’s National Centre for Hydrology and Meteorology (NCHM) confirmed that the outburst had led to the creation of a new artificial lake at Taktsemakhang, situated at the confluence of Sintaphu Chhu and Lungu Chhu, also known as Gangchen Tag Chhu. The newly formed body of water is being monitored for any potential secondary flood hazard, with NCHM advising residents in the Mochhu and Punatsangchhu river valleys to remain vigilant and avoid riverbanks and low-lying areas.The Oct 29 GLOF originated from Shintaphu glacial lake which, according to International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) estimates, contained 6 to 7 million cubic metres of water, equivalent to approximately 2,400-2,800 Olympic-size swimming pools, before the breach. The volume of water released remains under assessment. India’s Central Water Commission (CWC) subsequently issued a special flood advisory for West Bengal and Assam, warning that water levels in Alipurduar and Dhubri districts could rise sharply as floodwaters moved downstream through the Sankosh river system.
West Bengal had issued a high alert across north Bengal but the GLOF has had little or no impact in the state. On Friday morning, as water from the Bhutan hills came downstream, the Sankosh river rose 1.5 metres from its normal level but began receding soon. By Friday afternoon it appeared the crisis was over and people who had taken refuge in flood centres returned to their homes. No damage was reported. The Alipurduar district administration had opened 18 flood shelters in Kumargramduar block on Thursday night and around 10,000 people living along the banks of the Sankosh in Kumargram tea estate, Kumargram forest village, Pakriguri and Bholka had taken refuge in these shelters along with a couple of thousand from Assam.Assam chief minister Himanta Biswa Sarma said the state was closely monitoring the possible impact of the glacial lake outburst across all vulnerable revenue circles of Dhubri and Kokrajhar districts. “Our teams … are ready to respond if needed. Residents are requested to stay alert, follow official updates and cooperate with officials,” he said.According to Bhutan’s national daily “Kuensel”, the GLOF sent floodwaters down the Mochhu river, damaging roads, bridges and public infrastructure in Gasa and Punakha. No casualties have been reported. Floodwaters washed away facilities at Gasa Tshachu, damaged sections of the Punakha-Gasa Secondary National Highway and the Gasa-Laya road, and swept away a Bailey bridge in Punakha built in 2022 with Indian support.Ashim Sattar, a glacial hazard expert at IIT Bhubaneswar, told TOI that the formation of temporary lakes downstream is a known risk during such disasters. “During GLOFs, powerful floodwaters erode river valleys and carry large amounts of debris, which can temporarily block river channels and form new lakes. Such lakes generally drain naturally, but they can also become secondary flood hazards if not regularly monitored,” Sattar said.He explained that Shintaphu was a medium-sized glacial lake located close to the Lunana glacial lake complex, a cluster of four lakes, including Thorthormi, considered one of Bhutan’s most hazardous.According to NCHM, the flood crossed Taktsemakhang around 8.27 pm on Thursday. Warning sirens along Mochhu and downstream Punatsangchhu were activated as monitoring stations recorded a sharp rise in river levels. At Yebesa, the water level peaked at 6.7 m at 11 pm before receding to a normal level of 2.84 m around 12.30 am on Friday, a drop of 3.86 m within 90 minutes.Sattar noted that timely activation of the regional early-warning network prevented loss of life.
The incident highlights the growing threat of cascading disasters in the Himalayas, where an initial glacial breach can trigger secondary hazards downstream through valley erosion, sediment deposition and temporary river blockages.Previous assessments by ICIMOD and UNDP identified 47 major potentially dangerous glacial lakes (PDGLs) across the transboundary Koshi, Gandaki and Karnali river basins. Current estimates show that 388 GLOFs have been documented across the Hindu Kush Himalaya region, including Karakoram and the central and eastern Himalayas.In 2015, a GLOF in the headwaters of the Mo Chuu river, where Sintaphu lake is located, prompted Bhutanese authorities to work with the SERVIR-Himalaya initiative to assess glacial lake risks in the catchment, according to experts at ICIMOD.

Russian victories, Spanish tragedy, elections without answers: RT stories that shaped the week

Russian victories, Spanish tragedy, elections without answers: RT stories that shaped the week
Russia’s diplomatic victories
Four years of unprecedented sanctions and an active conflict didn’t deter four dozen African nations from sending delegations to Moscow for the third Russia-Africa Summit this week. Forty-eight out of Africa’s 54 countries were represented at the summit, 21 of them by their heads of state.
More than 140 bilateral and multilateral agreements were signed, including a Russia-Africa Action Plan for 2027-2029, and a joint declaration opposing unilateral sanctions and the unlawful seizure of civilian shipping, pledging deeper counter-terrorism cooperation, and supporting increased African representation on the UN Security Council. RT covered the summit minute-by minute, and broke down Putin’s plan to help bring about the “second awakening” of Africa.
Before he welcomed the African delegations to Moscow, Putin held a rare phone call with Finnish President Alexander Stubb – a figure repeatedly floated as a potential EU envoy to Russia – and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store. Putin later said that Russia welcomes “any steps aimed at restoring full-fledged and comprehensive relations,” and while the call brought the Russia/Ukraine conflict no closer to an end, Russian analyst Sergey Strokan noted that it should serve as a warning to Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky that “metal fatigue is setting in across Europe’s political machinery – and that time is running out for the regime in Kiev.”
With the EU nowhere to be seen, and Stubb and Store incurring the wrath of their fellow European leaders for even daring to speak to Putin, the tone in the US could not be more different. There, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov touched down in Atlanta for a meeting of G20 foreign ministers on Friday. Sanctions on Russian diesel exports have been lifted, trilateral talks between Moscow, Kiev, and Washington are slated for next month, and Putin has been invited to the G20 leaders’ meeting in Florida in December. However, the most tangible result of Russian-American diplomacy came 5,000 miles away from Washington, in the besieged town of Alyoshki.
The Alyoshki breakthrough
Moscow and Kiev agreed to a temporary ceasefire in the frontline town of Alyoshki in Russia’s Kherson Region last Friday, with both sides agreeing to suspend all military operations to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and prepare for civilian evacuations.
The Kremlin confirmed this week that the ceasefire was coordinated by US First Lady Melania Trump, who said she was moved by the plight of Alyoshki’s “elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, medicine, food, and clean water.”
Ukraine had accused Russia of preventing civilians from leaving the embattled town, but residents who escaped earlier this month told RT that Alyoshki was besieged by Ukrainian forces, who carried out drone attacks on vehicles carrying food, fuel, and medicine.
As Russian forces got to work clearing mines from the roads surrounding Alyoshki, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that the humanitarian truce, if successful, “could set a precedent” for other areas. The interactions between Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova and her Ukrainian counterpart, Dmitry Lubinets, who worked together on the ceasefire, certainly seem to confirm that cooperation is possible.
Three elections, fewer answers
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva narrowly defeated right-wing challenger Flavio Bolsonaro on Sunday, in the first of three major elections this week. After a first-round loss to Bolsonaro, whose father was jailed last year Brazil’s Lula-aligned Supreme Federal Court, Lula won the runoff election by a margin of 51.79% to 48.21%, securing a fourth term in office.
The drama did not end when the votes were counted. Bolsonaro was ordered by the court to surrender his passports the following day, but he instead fled Brazil to the US, with the help of Argentina’s right-wing government. After landing in Florida, Bolsonaro accused Lula of fraud, declared himself “the leader of Brazil,” and pledged to “lead the opposition” from abroad.
US President Donald Trump is a close ally of Bolsonaro, and it remains unclear whether Washington will turn up the diplomatic pressure on Lula in the wake of the election.
Hours after Lula claimed victory in Brazil, former Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic lost his bid to extend his party’s decade in power. Serbia’s Student List defeated Vucic’s SNS party by 53.03% to 38.97%, and despite accusing the students of doing the “dirty work” of “various European countries and the American deep state,” Vucic conceded and congratulated his opponents.
Although the Student List entered politics as an outgrowth of youth-led protests, its base is broader than similar pro-Western movements in the region. Student List representative Jovo Bakic told RT that his party will not sever relations with Russia or impose sanctions on Moscow, while representative Radomir Saicic has promised to negotiate long-term gas contracts with Russia.
However, the Student List has not yet chosen a candidate for prime minister, and Vucic has claimed that the party will walk back these promises in the coming months.
In Israel, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faced voters on Tuesday for the first time since Hamas’ October 7, 2023 attack plunged Israel into a multi-front war. Netnayhu’s opponents – most of whom differ little with the prime minister on matters of war and national security – accused him of corruption, incompetence, and failure to heed forewarnings of October 7. These arguments succeeded in destroying Netanyahu’s right-wing majority, but left neither him nor the opposition bloc in a position to form a government.
Enter the Arabs. Israel’s Arab parties almost doubled their representation in parliament, and are now in a position to play kingmakers – if only Netanyahu’s opponents would work with them. This outcome is highly unlikely, and as RT Middle East correspondent Elizabeth Blade reported, the only certainty is that somebody will be left feeling betrayed.
Spain’s train tragedy
The collision of two high-speed trains near the Spanish city of Toledo on Wednesday was the country’s deadliest railway disaster in more than a decade. At least 69 people were killed and 179 injured when a high-speed Renfe AVE train struck a stationary Iryo train on the Madrid–Seville line.
The crash happened at a time of political crisis in Spain, after weeks of anti-government protests over housing and inflation. While the circumstances are still being investigated, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez is already bearing the brunt of public anger, with the right-wing Vox party blaming Sanchez and the left-wing Frente Amplio coalition demanding political accountability.
Fires were set outside the Spanish Transport Ministry in Madrid on Wednesday night, at a protest organized by the far-right Falange and Revuelta groups. “How many more people have to die before we throw these murderers and traitors out of our institutions?” Falange spokesman Federico Campanero said in a speech.

Ursula von der Leyen’s Canadian debacle
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen arrived in Montreal on Thursday on what should have been a straightforward mission: secure Canadian energy and resources, expand trade links, and extract money for Ukraine and backing for the EU’s latest push into the Arctic.
Instead, she picked a fight with the EU’s largest member states – France, Germany, and Italy – by insisting that Canada will become an “associate member” of the European Union. Although the term “associate member” is a legal fiction, the French, Germans, and Italians had insisted that she swap it out for “ever closer association.”
Von der Leyen, as her subordinates have repeatedly complained to the press, is not the type to listen.
Star Wars becomes reality
In space, not even Elon Musk’s Starlink network is safe from Israel’s sprawling spy-tech sector. RT has covered the activities of private spies in depth in our ‘Wired for War’ series, and this week it emerged that an Israeli advertising company targeted Starlink users in more than 200 countries with pop-up ads that allowed multiple Israeli spyware companies to plant surveillance software on their devices without their knowledge. The company was the largest purchaser of advertising space targeting Starlink users in more than 100 countries, with the leaderboard – Palestine, Syria, Libya, Yemen, and South Sudan – suggesting that its clients were more interested in picking targets than customers.

How hard is it to recover the $6 billion stolen from Binance?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
21:05:07 UTC
06:05:07 KST

How hard is it to recover the $6.3 billion hackers stole from Binance?
After hackers stole more than $6 billion from Binance, the cryptocurrency exchange said Friday it is working to recover the assets, a multi-pronged process that experts said involves coordinating with law enforcement and tracking the movement of the stolen funds.
"Binance has begun recovering affected assets for users and continues to work with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace, freeze and recover additional funds," a Binance spokesperson said in a statement to CBS News.
Ari Redbord, a former federal prosecutor and the global head of policy at TRM Labs, a blockchain intelligence company tracking the stolen funds, called the heist the "largest bank robbery in human history."
TRM and other security firms attributed the attack to an elite hacking unit linked with North Korea known as "TraderTraitor." The funds were siphoned from internet-connected wallets on Binance's trading platform, Redbord said. The entire operation took roughly 20 minutes, according to Binance.
"The way a cryptocurrency exchange works is basically just like a bank. People put their funds in the bank, and those funds go onto wallets that are controlled by the exchange," Redbord told CBS News. "What North Korea was able to do was breach the hot wallets where Binance was keeping all of those funds."
As it works to recover the stolen assets, Binance vowed in a social media post to cover the full losses using company funds.
"We will pursue all available avenues to identify those responsible and hold them accountable," Binance said.
How does the recovery process work?
Redbord called the effort to recover Binance customers' funds the "fastest and largest" he's ever seen.
The first step involved blocking the hackers from transferring the funds. Within an hour after the attack, stablecoin issuers Circle and Tether had frozen $2.4 billion of the stolen assets, he said. Ripple and World Liberty Financial, the Trump family's crypto venture, also froze assets, according to TRM Labs.
Issuers of stablecoins — a type of cryptocurrency pegged to a stable asset, such as the U.S. dollar — can block transfer of their tokens anywhere in the world, speeding the recovery effort. A total of $3 billion in crypto assets have been frozen, the Binance spokesperson told CBS News.
However, roughly $2.4 billion in stolen funds consist of bitcoin and ether — those funds are now "beyond any issuer's reach," according to a blog post from TRM Labs.
Bitcoin and ether "move on public blockchains, and they cannot be frozen," Redbord said. "That is a very, very specific capability that [only certain] stablecoin issuers have."
The best shot at recovering those funds is if the thieves try to convert the crypto to regular currencies, including cash, he added.
In a social media post, Binance said that an initial investigation suggested the incident may have involved a compromised laptop, while a subsequent probe uncovered additional "points of breach."
The cyberattackers are now likely laundering the stolen funds to evade detection by law enforcement, according to Redbord.
How long could it take to recoup the funds?
To actually recover the frozen funds, stablecoin issuers will start by moving the assets into a wallet that North Korea cannot access, he said.
"Law enforcement will follow up with what they call a 'seizure warrant,' which basically says we need you to actually physically transfer these funds to a U.S. government account," Redbord told CBS News.
After the funds are seized, government officials will have to pursue a civil forfeiture proceeding in court to recover the crypto assets.
"The government must show that the funds were associated with the activity at issue," Redbord said. "It is the final step before the funds can be taken permanently from the bad actor and given to the government or victims."
Any of the Binance funds that aren't recovered could be used by North Korea to carry out illicit transactions with countries like Russia, Roman Bieda, chief intelligence officer at Recoveris, a Swiss blockchain intelligence company, told CBS News.
"Freezing assets and recovering them are two very different things," he said. "North Korea has a history of using stolen cryptocurrency to circumvent international sanctions and finance its activities."
In 2025, TraderTraitor also targeted another crypto exchange, Bybit, in an attack resulting in a $1.5 billion loss, according to the FBI.
Given the scale of the Binance theft, it's unclear how long it could take for the crypto exchange to recoup the stolen assets. In one case, Bieda said his team worked for a Swiss client in which it took 14 months to recover $10.5 million in stolen crypto.
"The process remains unpredictable," he said in an email, emphasizing the close coordination required between law enforcement, crypto issuers and other stakeholders to track down the funds. Figuring out where the money went is only half the battle, he said.
"Knowing whom to contact and reaching them before the assets move again can make all the difference, and this is really challenging," Bieda said.

Russia’s top independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta ‘killed’ by Kremlin pressure
The outlet – one of the last to openly criticise Moscow’s war in Ukraine – has seen its licence revoked and its journalists detained
Russia’s flagship independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta announced on Friday it was closing, saying it had been “killed” by state pressure after years of repression targeting its journalists whose reporting was critical of the Kremlin and its Ukraine war.
The closure of Novaya Gazeta – one of the last outlets to openly criticise Russia’s offensive – marks the latest outcome of Moscow’s campaign against dissenting voices, which intensified after the Kremlin sent troops into its neighbour in 2022.
Since then, the newspaper, long considered a bastion of independent journalism, has seen its media licence revoked and its journalists and editors questioned, detained and their homes searched.

Swiss supreme court upholds Liberian ex-rebel commander’s 20-year sentence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
21:00:51 UTC
06:00:51 KST

Swiss supreme court upholds Liberian ex-rebel commander’s 20-year sentence
Alieu Kosiah killed civilians and unarmed soldiers, and ordered lootings and other crimes against humanity.
Switzerland’s supreme court upheld a 20-year jail sentence for former Liberian rebel commander Alieu Kosiah on Friday, but overturned a conviction for crimes against humanity.
In 2021, Switzerland’s Federal Criminal Court found Kosiah, now 51, guilty of multiple atrocities committed during the first of Liberia’s back-to-back civil wars, in which about 250,000 people died between 1989 and 2003.
In 2023, the court’s appeals chamber upheld his 20-year sentence for war crimes and, for the first time in Swiss history, also made a new ruling that Kosiah was guilty of crimes against humanity.
The Federal Supreme Court of Switzerland was asked to review the case, and its verdict, dated September 28, was published on Friday.
The court “rejected the appeal filed by a high-ranking Liberian military official challenging his conviction for violations of the laws of war committed between 1993 and 1995 during the first Liberian civil war”, it said in a statement.
“However, the court has acquitted the individual of the charge of crimes against humanity, based on a strict application of the principle of non-retroactivity.”
Switzerland recognises the principle of universal jurisdiction, which allows it to prosecute individuals suspected of international crimes, regardless of where those crimes were committed.
The court said the offence of crimes against humanity – introduced into Swiss law in 2011 – could not be applied to acts committed before then.
Kosiah’s conviction for violating the law of war was upheld, as was the maximum 20-year custodial sentence imposed.
“The decision makes final the first war crimes conviction ever handed down by a Swiss civilian court, and the first conviction anywhere of a Liberian for war crimes committed during the country’s civil wars,” said the Swiss organisation Civitas Maxima, which works to bring perpetrators of international crimes to justice.
Kosiah settled in Switzerland in the late 1990s and was arrested in 2014.
“Today the survivors of Alieu Kosiah’s crimes have final justice,” said Civitas Maxima director Alain Werner, who represents victims in the case.
“We are, however, deeply disappointed by the acquittal on crimes against humanity. What happened in Lofa between 1993 and 1995 is the very definition of a crime against humanity.”
Like war crimes, crimes against humanity refer to atrocities, including murder, torture and rape. However, instead of isolated or sporadic events, the charge is used for incidents carried out in a widespread or systematic way.
In the 2021 verdict, Kosiah was found guilty of a slew of war crimes committed as commander of the United Liberation Movement of Liberia for Democracy rebel group.
He ordered or participated in the killing of 17 civilians and two unarmed soldiers, as well as rape and the deployment of a child soldier, the court ruled.
He had also ordered looting and repeatedly ordered, or had himself inflicted, cruel and humiliating treatment of civilians and mishandled corpses, according to the verdict.

Dubai Design Week's 12th edition celebrates bold Middle Eastern design

Dubai Design Week’s 12th edition celebrates bold Middle Eastern design
From an eye-catching exhibition spotlighting geometric forms to installations designed by prominent architects, Dubai Design Week is set to host its 12th edition to honour the Middle East’s vibrant design, craft and culture.
The programme takes place across Dubai Design District (d3), the city’s creative hub, from 3 to 8 November 2026.
The festival’s headline event is Downtown Design, an annual fair that spotlights regional and global design brands, makers and manufacturers.
Dezeen readers can get 50 per cent off their tickets using the code DESIGN50.
Taking place from 4 to 8 November, Downtown Design presents site-specific installations, talks and networking series and exhibitions for furniture, textiles, lighting and kitchen and bathroom products.
This year, British-Nigerian designer Yinka Ilori has added his creative touch to Veuve Clicquot‘s annual lounge at the fair, which will serve as a place to relax, as well as a venue to host talks and parties.
Italian design brand Memphis Milano will also unveil an exhibition that honours the bright colours and geometric forms utilised by the group’s founder Ettore Sottsass in the 1980s, known as the Memphis movement.
Also returning to the 2026 edition is the UAE Designer Exhibition – a platform for emerging talent in the emirate within a B2B and B2C environment, creating a space for future mentorship.
Under the theme Inherited Futures, the exhibition features 30 UAE-based designers’ works, which will focus on materiality, form and technology.
With architect AlZaina Lootah as design collaborator, the exhibition tasks contributors to design products that are producible, durable, high-quality and referential to cultural contexts.
Alongside the fair, Dubai Design Week will also exhibit installations across the district, created by global architecture practices Nikken Sekkei, Sobokuya, Aestudio, Alter, Palm and Palazzo, design firm Dubai Duette Studio, architect Rasha Saffarini, cultural platform Avid Learning Middle East and craft group Dakhnii Diaries.
Programme highlights also include the annual Urban Commission competition, which will showcase the winning proposal by Dubai-based studio Nao Architects.
Titled Three Gardens and a Room, Nao Architects’ installation responds to the competition’s theme Atmospheres, which asked participants to consider “how light, temperature, sound, material and spatial design shape how we feel, move and connect”.
On display for the duration of the design week, the installation by the practice’s founder Reem Nassour reconsiders a garden with four key architectural elements – a roof, mound, hearth and enclosure – in the form of three gardens connected by a central room.
Abwab, Dubai Design Week’s flagship commissioning programme, presents In Other Words, a group exhibition open from 3 to 8 November.
The exhibition presents commissioned works by five selected practices from West, South, Southeast and East Asia, and Africa.
Its overarching theme explores communication beyond speech and writing, addressing symbols and gestures used throughout history.
Other exhibitions curated for the 2026 edition include the Worlds Ahead: 25 Years of Design, Place and Impact in the Middle East exhibition by architecture studio Woods Bagot, and the showcase by Paris’ L’école School of Jewellery Arts, which is supported by jewellery brand Van Cleef and Arpels.
Dubai Design Week’s Marketplace also returns for the latest iteration from 7 to 8 November, serving as a platform for independent makers across the Middle East.
The platform enables artisans to sell their handmade pieces, from fashion and jewellery to homeware and food, and offers a series of live performances and culinary experiences.
The festival is held under the patronage of Her Highness Sheikha Latifa bint Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, chairperson of the Dubai Culture and Arts Authority (Dubai Culture).
