Trump’s bluff meets Iran’s resolve : Limits of American power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
20:17:09 UTC
05:17:09 KST

Trump’s bluff meets Iran’s resolve : Limits of American power
Goa, India – Donald Trump has been bluffing for far too long. He threatens, he warns, he issues ultimatums, and then he expects the world to believe that he has everything under control. But there comes a point when even the loudest threats begin to lose their effect. Iran may well be that point for Trump. He seems to have underestimated a country whose political instincts, historical memory and civilisational confidence cannot be understood through the narrow lens of American power.
Trump appears to believe that if he raises his voice, threatens military action and keeps the world guessing, Iran will eventually surrender. That might work with some governments. It is unlikely to work with Iran. The Iranian leadership has survived decades of sanctions, isolation, political pressure and military threats. It has learned to live with adversity, and it has developed its own ways of responding to pressure. One may disagree with Iran's government, its policies or its political system, but to dismiss its capacity to think, plan and respond would be a serious mistake.
This is where Trump seems to have got it wrong. He is accustomed to dealing with politics as though it were a business negotiation in which the other party must eventually accept his terms.
But international politics does not work like a real estate deal. Countries have their own histories, their own interests and their own understanding of what they can and cannot concede. Iran is not going to abandon its strategic interests simply because the American President demands it.
The gap between Trump's threats and reality
For months, the world has watched the familiar performance. Trump makes a dramatic announcement, the threat of military action hangs over the region, and then everyone waits to see what happens next. His supporters may interpret this as strength. But there is a difference between strength and the ability to keep making threats without securing a political outcome. At some stage, the threats themselves become a problem. If you repeatedly promise decisive action and the other side refuses to bend, you must either escalate or find a way out. Neither option necessarily makes you look strong.
Iran understands this dilemma. It does not have to respond to every American statement with an equally dramatic announcement. It can wait, calculate and choose its moment. It can also make the costs of escalation sufficiently high to force Washington to think twice. The point is not that Iran is invulnerable or that it can dictate every outcome. It is that the United States cannot assume that its military superiority automatically translates into political victory.
History has repeatedly demonstrated this distinction. A powerful military can destroy targets, damage infrastructure and inflict enormous suffering. But can it compel a country to accept the political future designed for it by a foreign power? That is a different question altogether. The United States has learned this lesson in Vietnam, Iraq and Afghanistan, often at an enormous cost. Yet American presidents continue to behave as though the application of sufficient force will eventually produce the desired political result.
Trump appears determined not to learn from these experiences.
Iran is more than a military challenge: it has a long historical memory
One does not have to romanticise Iran to recognise the depth of its historical consciousness. Persian civilisation stretches back thousands of years. Its political culture has developed through periods of empire, foreign intervention, revolution and war. Modern Iran has also experienced the overthrow of its elected prime minister in the 1953 coup, the restoration and support of the
Shah by the United States, and the revolution of 1979 that transformed the country's political order. The Iran-Iraq War of the 1980s left a deep mark on the national psyche.
These experiences matter. They have helped shape the Iranian leadership's suspicion of American intentions and its determination to resist what it sees as attempts to dictate the country's future. Washington may regard its demands as reasonable or necessary. Tehran may see the same demands as another attempt to impose American will on Iran.
That difference in perception cannot be wished away.
Trump may believe that Iran will eventually calculate that resistance is too costly. But Iranian leaders must also calculate the political cost of surrendering under American pressure. They have to consider not only the immediate military situation but also their standing at home, their credibility with regional partners and the message that capitulation would send to other countries. A government that believes it is fighting for its sovereignty will not necessarily make the choices Washington expects.
This is why the language of ultimatums is so dangerous. It leaves little room for compromise without humiliation. And when leaders begin to see compromise as humiliation, even a sensible settlement can become difficult to achieve.
There is another issue that deserves attention: the reports and speculation surrounding Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei.
Uncertainty surrounding the Iranian leadership has prompted reports about Khamenei’s condition, attracting considerable attention because of his central position in Iran’s political system.
However, Iran’s leadership and institutions cannot be understood simply through speculation about one individual.
Khamenei occupies the country's highest political and religious office, and his influence over its strategic direction has been considerable. But Iran also has a wider political and security establishment, including the presidency, the cabinet, the parliament and powerful security institutions. Their roles and relationships matter when assessing how the country might respond to a crisis.
The assumption that removing one individual would bring Iran to its knees is questionable. Washington would be making a serious miscalculation if it assumed that eliminating Iran’s supreme leader would force the country into submission.
Such an act could escalate the conflict, provoke retaliation and undermine prospects for a negotiated settlement. The consequences would extend beyond Iran, potentially drawing the wider region into a much broader confrontation.
The unanswered question of Trump's endgame
This is the question that needs to be asked more often. Military threats are one thing. Having a clear idea of what comes afterwards is quite another. If the objective is to weaken Iran's military capabilities, what happens next? If the objective is to force political concessions, what concessions are actually achievable? If the aim is regime change, what makes Washington believe that the result would be a stable, friendly government rather than prolonged instability and a more dangerous regional conflict?
These are not academic questions. They concern the lives of millions of people.
Iran is situated in one of the world's most sensitive regions. Any major conflict could affect neighbouring countries, international energy markets, shipping routes and the wider global economy. The consequences would not be limited to Washington and Tehran. Countries that have little influence over the confrontation could find themselves paying a heavy price through rising fuel costs, disrupted trade and regional insecurity.
The Strait of Hormuz is particularly important in this regard. A serious disruption to shipping through this narrow waterway could have consequences for global oil supplies and the economies that depend on them. Iran knows the strategic significance of its geography. Washington knows it too. That is precisely why military escalation cannot be treated as a cost-free exercise in presidential toughness.
Trump may be confident that American military power gives him the upper hand. In conventional terms, the United States possesses formidable advantages. But Iran does not need to match America weapon for weapon to make a conflict costly. It can use its regional relationships, asymmetric capabilities and geographical position to complicate American calculations. Even a militarily superior power must consider what it will have to endure in order to achieve its objectives.
That is the reality behind the bravado.
Ultimately, the question is not whether Trump can sound more threatening than Iran. It is whether he can achieve what he claims to want without plunging the region into a wider war. If his strategy is built on the assumption that Iran will eventually submit, he may discover that the bluff has become a trap of his own making.
The world does not need another war born of presidential arrogance and strategic miscalculation. It needs diplomacy grounded in realism, respect for sovereignty and an honest recognition that American power, however formidable, has limits. Trump may believe that Iran will eventually blink. But if he mistakes Iran’s refusal to surrender for an invitation to escalate, the consequences could extend far beyond Tehran and Washington. The ultimate test of American power will not be how much destruction it can inflict, but whether it possesses the wisdom to know when to stop.

"Because these negotiations were led by the U.S. and Melania Trump, it seems to me that the Russians have agreed to this ceasefire to show that they are a reliable partner for these negotiations and other future peace negotiations with Ukraine," Vadym Ivchenko, a Ukrainian parliament member on its Defense, Intelligence, and National Security Committee, told CBS News.

'Changing of the guard' as fashion retailers return to physical stores
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
20:15:13 UTC
05:15:13 KST

As legacy fashion brands fail, online retailers are moving into physical stores
In short:
A growing number of fashion and beauty brands are moving into physical stores despite a wave of legacy brand collapses.
Brand executives and retail experts say the experience between online and in-store is becoming more integrated.
What's next?
Retail experts expect more e-commerce businesses to move into the physical store space.
Australian retail is experiencing a strange phenomenon: brands with strong online footprints are moving into bricks and mortar.
The wave of legacy Australian fashion brands falling into insolvency has not deterred Princess Polly, which has been opening stores on the Gold Coast and in Brisbane.
"I think there is going to be that bit of a changing of the guards for the brands and retailers that are maybe downsizing or reducing their footprint," chief merchandise officer Courtney Dres said.
"Then the younger, newer brands are coming in and starting to make a little bit of a splash."
In the past few years, Mosaic Brands, the owner of Katies, Millers and Noni B, has collapsed.
On its tail was Cue Clothing Co, Veronika Maine, Betts and Jeanswest, which have entered administration. Country Road Group has downsized its physical presence.
Even 188-year-old department store David Jones is reportedly on life support and weighing cutting store numbers amid the exit of numerous brands.
The outlook for retail is not rosy. Data from CreditorWatch shows the retail insolvency rate has been increasing since June 2022.
Chief executive Patrick Coghlan expects that to increase in the fashion sector due to its reliance on discretionary spending.
"Conditions are likely to get still tougher in the fashion retail space before they improve,"
he said.
Mr Coghlan said moving from online to in-store trade needed "to be carefully managed".
Experiencing the brand
Beauty brands Oz Hair and Beauty, Adore Beauty, activewear brand Kikiva and furniture company Mocka have opened physical stores in the last few years.
When Princess Polly opened in Pacific Fair on the Gold Coast in July, hundreds of customers queued up in the early hours, drawn in by prizes and the chance to be seen at the launch.
"[The customers] are just so excited to be there and so excited to experience the brand in person," Ms Dres said.
"I think that really tells us all we need to know about continuing the rollout of our retail stores."
Princess Polly, which is owned by US-listed A.K.A Brands, opened more than a dozen shops in the US before expanding into Sydney last November, the Gold Coast and, as of this weekend, Brisbane.
Physical space can add value
Queensland University of Technology retail expert Gary Mortimer said moving into omnichannel trade could add value, provided the transition was handled properly.
"You wouldn't expect an online pure-play retailer to suddenly open 64 stores, because it wouldn't be sustainable," he said.
"But they may open three stores, or they may open a bunch of stores, but only temporarily … and that will then create a level of experience and excitement and entertainment which draws people to the online site."
Dr Mortimer said value was not just about price.
"Speed is now becoming the currency of retailers," he said.
"It's not about shopping online because that's convenient — it's consumers' desire for immediate gratification."
Ms Dres said that was part of the Princess Polly strategy.
"Basically, as soon as you buy it online, it almost immediately is packed and shipped out," she said.
"But of course, retail is a way to be able to be instant."
Shifting expectations
VRG GRL co-founder Daniella Dionyssiou says returning to in-store trading feels like a return to the brand's roots.
The business started trading as Verge Girl in 2008 with one Brisbane store and opened a second store in 2014 before moving fully online in 2019.
Ms Dionyssiou says customer expectations have shifted since then.
"It's no longer just about the product, but the experience and value a brand brings beyond the transaction," she said.
"The brands seeing the greatest success are those that understand their customers and have a clear sense of what makes them unique."
An abundance of sales data is available to e-commerce businesses, but social media can also help to inform strategy and create a "brand halo", or the in-store experience leading to online purchases.
"You look at a brand like Mecca … they've done an excellent job in really blending both the social media side of their business, their online business and the physical business together," retail analyst James Stewart said.
Customers shop differently
Ms Dionyssiou, whose business has opened stores in Sydney and plans to open more in Queensland, says the process has its challenges.
"Physical retail brings a different set of considerations, from managing stock across locations to understanding what customers are drawn to when they can see and try on our collections in person," she said.
Ms Dres said every store opening had been a learning experience.
"We can't ignore the fact that obviously retail is a very competitive environment, and customers, of course, will vote with their wallets,"
she said.
Mr Stewart does not believe insolvencies in the sector necessarily mean retailers opening physical stores are putting themselves at risk.
He said the number one reason retail brands failed was because they lost relevance.
"Retailers have been opening and closing for generations," Mr Stearrt said.
"I don't think that just because you're in a physical environment that's necessarily a sign that you might fail, or alternatively, a bad investment. It could be an excellent investment."

Quick hits: Mix-up ends schoolmates' mammoth stand, Breetzke brings the fight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
20:13:35 UTC
05:13:35 KST

Ryan Rickelton was left fuming after a mix-up ended a mammoth partnership with schoolmate Wiaan Mulder, as Matthew Breetzke didn't back down on a day of toil for the Aussies.
Here are the quick hits from day four of the third Test between Australia and South Africa.
1. Schoolmates Rickelton and Mulder break Australia
Ryan Rickelton was enormous on day four.
The wicketkeeper-batter played with supreme confidence and hardly presented an opportunity to the Aussie attack, managing the ebbs and flows of his innings to perfection.
Up the other end, Wiaan Mulder was just as impressive, grinding the Australians into the dirt as he and Rickelton batted for the majority of the day in a mammoth 134-run, 319-ball partnership.
The pair looked completely at home together in the middle, and so they should — Rickelton and Mulder attended secondary school together at Johannesburg's St Stithians College.
After 218 balls and a whopping 12 overs in the 90s, Rickelton pushed the leg-side single that brought up his second Test ton, which he celebrated by embracing his old buddy on a red-letter day for St Stithians.
2. Rickelton fumes after being barbecued
With Pat Cummins seemingly long out of ideas, Rickelton having just brought up his century, and Marnus Labuschagne into his fourth over of the day, Australia was not even threatening to take a wicket.
But there was trouble brewing for the old friends in the middle.
Mulder had nailed his reverse sweep to backward point, where Josh Inglis made a fantastic stop and followed it with a quick release.
From the non-striker's end, Rickelton had raced out of the blocks and found himself all the way up the other end of the pitch.
Unfortunately for the centurion, Mulder was ball watching and completely unmoved, with Rickelton unable to get home as Labuschagne broke the stumps.
Loading Instagram content
Speaking to ABC Sport at stumps, Rickelton was far from impressed — if not overly surprised — by his old schoolmate.
"Wiaan, he grates me sometimes because he drifts away in exactly that moment," Mulder said.
"He hit the shot and he just kind of ball-watched and it was an easy one, but sometimes he isn't really present and he can drift away.
"So it does frustrate me and I'm really irritated about that because we could have got a lot more tonight."
We hadn't seen a run-out all series before day four, but only a matter of minutes after the first, we were treated to a second.
Again, it was Labuschagne at the heart of it, brilliantly throwing down the stumps to have Gerald Coetzee on his way.
3. Breetzke's tongue takes the fight to Australia
After a simmering, tempestuous end to day three, the chat continued as the Proteas looked to fight back on day four.
Matthew Breetzke and Mitchell Starc drew the battlelines early, with the pair sharing a few tense words and Starc providing a mixture of death stares and wry smiles.
And Breetzke, who had provided Labuschagne with a remarkable leaping send-off on day one, was never likely to back down.
With him and Starc a couple overs into their stoush, the quick had the South African ducking underneath a bouncer.
Rising from his haunches, Breetzke cocked his head and poked out his tongue in Starc's direction, before grabbing his box and holding the pose.
Things were heating up — but the chat began to dissipate when Breetzke fell, before almost completely disappearing as Rickelton and Mulder got stuck into their work.
4. Cummins's breakthrough wicket
At the start of South Africa's second innings, Cummins had gone 314 balls without a Test dismissal, with his last wicket coming in the second innings in Durban.
For a man who averages a scalp just about every 22 balls in Test cricket, that's a fair drought.
The Australian captain ran in hard late on day three, and came close to breaking through with a line-ball LBW call, but started day four at Newlands still in search of a pole.
It took over an hour of play, but finally, he broke through.
Bowling back of a length and to a leg-side field, Cummins had the well-set Breetzke (43) out hooking to Starc at backward square leg in.
After 372 wicketless deliveries, Cummins had broken the longest dismissal drought of his Test career, bringing Mulder to the crease.
5. Mulder puts on a show late
With South Africa having lost 4-16 from the Rickelton run-out and No.11 Kagiso Rabada having just joined Mulder at the crease, the start of the Australian run chase loomed large.
But Mulder had other ideas.
The all-rounder farmed the strike smartly, and after batting within himself for the majority of the day, began to take the game to the Australians.
After becoming the day's second St Stithians alumnus to cross three figures, he battered the Aussies, taking Cummins and then Nathan Lyon for massive leg-side sixes in consecutive overs.
With Temba Bavuma opting against a late declaration, Mulder and Rabada extended South Africa's lead by a further 36 runs before the centurion holed out on the final ball of the day.
Australia will begin its fourth innings at the start of the series' deciding day, requiring 288 runs for victory.

FLEX L12 “forest monster” makes autonomous debut with 5-ton load
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
20:13:07 UTC
05:13:07 KST

- UGV Defence’s FLEX L12 drove a 1.7 km off-road course fully autonomously with 5 tons of cargo at Norway’s Camp Rødsmoen on Oct. 29.
- About 100 participants, mainly from the Norwegian and Swedish armed forces, saw the demo alongside partners including Kongsberg and BAE Systems.
Norwegian company UGV Defence has run its FLEX L12 heavy unmanned ground vehicle fully autonomously through a 1.7 km (1.1-mile) off-road course while carrying 5 metric tons (11,000 pounds) of cargo, in a demonstration for Nordic military officers at Camp Rødsmoen in Norway, Chief Executive Carl Ivarsson said on social media.
The tracked vehicle climbed steep inclines and drove through mud, water, large rocks, narrow passages and sharp turns without a driver, Ivarsson said. About 100 people attended the event on Oct. 29, mainly from the Norwegian and Swedish armed forces along with defense industry representatives.
UGV Defence used the day to present what it calls the Nordic Autonomous Mission Platform, a group of companies building equipment around the FLEX L12. The partners include Kongsberg, BAE Systems, Swedish sideloader maker Hammar, Safe-Tec, SKJOLDR and Nordic Shelter. Each company explained how the vehicle could support its products, and several showed their own systems at the event, though Ivarsson did not say which payloads were demonstrated on the vehicle.
“The feedback from defence and industry representatives was very encouraging. More importantly, the day demonstrated what can be achieved when leading Nordic defence companies bring together their expertise around a common autonomous platform,” said Ivarsson.
The FLEX L12 is far larger than most unmanned ground vehicles in service. Its L12-L cargo version is rated for up to 12 tons of payload, and a power-generation variant, the L12-P, carries up to 9 tons with a much larger battery. The vehicle uses a diesel-electric drive, has a top speed of 25 km/h (16 mph) and a stated range of up to 800 km (500 miles), the company said when it showed a civilian version at the DALO Industry Days exhibition in Denmark in August. By comparison, Ukraine’s Protector, one of the largest ground drones in Ukrainian service, weighs about 4 tons in total.
UGV Defence built the FLEX L12 on a civilian tracked carrier and has been reworking it for military use, with a military configuration being prepared for series production. The company has said on its website that deliveries of the FLEX L12-L cargo version are planned from the first quarter of 2027, and it has described possible uses including cargo transport, weapons integration and mobile power generation.
Rødsmoen, near Rena in eastern Norway, is a Norwegian Army camp, and the surrounding training area has hosted earlier unmanned vehicle trials, including a 10-day European Defence Agency test of armed ground robots in February.

World Bank projects India's poverty rate to fall to 12.1% by 2028, from 14.2% in 2026, citing strong consumption growth and rising employment
NEW DELHI: World Bank has said that poverty in India, defined at $4.2 a day, will decline from 14.2% in 2026 to 12.1% by 2028.Between 2011 and 2023, it is estimated that the share of the population living below $4.2 a day declined from 57.7% to 16.1%, lifting an estimated 496 million people out of poverty. It said that extreme poverty ($3 a day) declined from 27.1% to 2.6% during this period."This progress was mainly driven by strong consumption growth; rising employment, especially among women; and expanded social transfers, including food subsidies. As poverty declined, it became increasingly concentrated among households with lower education, fewer assets, limited access to stable employment, and higher dependency ratios. Wage disparities, however, remain pronounced, as median earnings among the top 10% of workers were about 13 times those of the bottom 10% in 2023," World Bank said in its latest Poverty & Equity brief.Finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman cheered the decline in poverty in the country, pointing out that the report recognised India's progress as a country with one of the fastest poverty declines in the world."Under the leadership of PM Narendra Modi, govt's sustained policy efforts are yielding tangible results, strengthening the foundations for inclusive growth and greater economic opportunity.
This is the reason why NDA govt wins people's trust and mandate of our citizens. We remain committed to building on this progress through productive employment, stronger household incomes and effective delivery of public services, so that aspirations of our people are met," she posted on X.
World Bank also noted that between 2017 and 2023, employment increased by about 134 million people, nearly twice the growth of the working-age population, with major gains driven by rural women entering paid work and raising the number of earners in households.
"Labour market conditions continue to be broadly resilient, with labour force participation and employment rates stable between Q1 FY 2026 and Q1 FY 2027. However, youth unemployment rose from 14.6% to 15.9% between the two quarters, particularly among rural young women. Moreover, real earnings remained broadly unchanged with employment growth concentrated in relatively low-productivity activities," it said.

Port Sudan families can barely afford water as shortages persist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
20:10:22 UTC
05:10:22 KST

Port Sudan families can barely afford water as shortages persist
Despite efforts to restore damaged infrastructure, residents face soaring water costs as war, displacement strain supplies.
Port Sudan, Sudan – Every day, Amina Khalafallah spends 10,000 Sudanese pounds ($1 at the parallel market rate) on water for herself and her four children. Over a 30-day month, that amounts to 300,000 pounds ($30) – the equivalent of her entire monthly salary.
Khalafallah lives in the Deim Mayo neighbourhood of Port Sudan, in eastern Sudan, where her home is not connected to a piped water network. Instead, she depends on street vendors, who charge 1,000 pounds ($0.10) for 18 litres.
Khalafallah works in a cafeteria at a private institution, while her husband works in another state and sends money to help her out when he can.
Between them, the family barely scrambles enough money to get by, but Khalafallah says she often has to borrow money. It’s a typical story in Sudan, where, according to the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), the country’s more than three-year-long war has pushed average incomes back to levels last seen in the early 1990s.
The hotter months bring additional challenges, as water prices rise and vendors become harder to find.
“We make sure to set aside money for water in the summer before covering our other household needs, even if that means going without some essentials,” Khalafallah told Al Jazeera.
According to the African Development Bank (AfDB), access to safe water is one of Sudan’s most urgent needs, with millions of children at risk of waterborne diseases.
In Port Sudan, relatively safe from the fighting that has plagued other areas of the country, the arrival of people displaced by the war has put additional pressure on already fragile infrastructure. The AfDB has reported that the city’s water supply was meeting less than 40 percent of demand.
One of the major issues Port Sudan has faced is the collapse of the Arbaat Dam. Located in the Red Sea Hills northwest of Port Sudan, it once supplied half of the coastal city’s daily water needs.
But in August 2024, heavy rainfall and flooding caused the dam to collapse, destroying villages downstream and damaging pipelines and wells.
As a result of the collapse, entire neighbourhoods are dependent on expensive water deliveries by truck.
Rising costs for water vendors
Ahmed Osman, 30, has spent the past three years working at a water distribution station that supplies street vendors who deliver water to households.
When Sudan’s war began in April 2023, Osman said he charged vendors 4,000 Sudanese pounds ($0.40) to fill a donkey-drawn cart carrying at least 250 litres of water.
Those prices have since risen sharply, he said, because of increasing operating costs, particularly the fuel needed to transport water to his distribution station.
“A water tanker carrying 50,000 litres of water now costs 1.5 million Sudanese pounds [$150], compared with about 450,000 pounds before the war,” Osman told Al Jazeera.
Osman keeps the water in storage tanks before pumping it into the vendors’ carts. He charges 16,000 pounds ($1.60) to fill a cart carrying 250 litres.
After his expenses, Osman typically makes a profit of about 70,000 pounds ($7) per day, split between him and his partner.
Repairs yet to end water shortages
Rehabilitation work has restored parts of the damaged water network.
According to the UNDP, the restoration work has included drilling or rehabilitating 15 boreholes, laying 17 kilometres (10.5 miles) of new pipelines, as well as installing solar-powered pumps.
The UNDP said the restored system could supply water to nearly 230,000 people.
However, that would still not be enough to supply water to all of Port Sudan, which the UNDP estimates to now have a population of one million people.
Other projects are therefore necessary to meet the water needs of residents – including one launched in June by the AfDB and UNICEF, which intends to expand access to safe water for up to 750,000 people in the city.
Water shortages threaten public health
Emad Hafez, medical director of the emergency department at Port Sudan Teaching Hospital, told Al Jazeera the water crisis poses serious risks to public health, increasing the risk of waterborne diseases and making it harder for families to maintain basic hygiene.
He warned that disruptions to water supplies can force families to rely on untreated water, increasing the risk of cholera and other diarrhoeal diseases, particularly during the rainy season and in overcrowded displacement camps.
“Water shortages can also make it harder for families to maintain adequate hygiene, increasing the risk of skin infections and other hygiene-related illnesses,” Hafez said. “Meanwhile, storing water in uncovered containers can create breeding sites for mosquitoes, raising the risk of vector-borne diseases such as malaria and dengue fever.”
Water shortages also threaten healthcare services, Hafez said, explaining that hospitals require reliable supplies for infection prevention, cleaning and patient care.
“Beyond its immediate health consequences, water insecurity can worsen food shortages and malnutrition by disrupting agricultural activities and placing additional financial pressure on already vulnerable households,” he said. “Children under five and pregnant women are particularly vulnerable to the effects of inadequate nutrition.”

Promotions for Space Force’s Second-Highest Enlisted Rank Explode

Promotions to the Space Force’s second-highest enlisted grade, senior master sergeant, have surged to the highest level in the young service’s history, bolstering the senior NCO corps. Over the next few years, service officials plan to aggressively expand the force and particularly the enlisted corps.
The Air Force Personnel Center released the 2026 promotion lists and statistics for both chief master sergeant and senior master sergeant in the Space Force on Oct. 29:
- For chief master sergeant, 13 Guardians were selected out of 60 eligible, a 21.67 percent race
- For senior master sergeant, 56 Guardians were selected out of 396 eligible, a 14.14 percent rate
For the higher E-9 grade, those numbers are largely in line with previous cycles; for the last four years, 12-14 senior master sergeants have been selected for promotion, while the rate has hovered around 20 percent in the past three years.
Space Force Chief Master Sergeant Promotions
For E-8, though, the 56 tapped for promotion is far more than the previous Space Force record of 38. It’s also the first time the promotion rate has exceeded 12 percent, much less 14.
Space Force Senior Master Sergeant Promotions
Of note, the time in grade for both lists of selectees was the highest going back to 2021, when the Space Force was still filling out its ranks, while the time in service of those selected for both ranks generally continued a downward trend.
The 56 new senior master sergeants is equivalent to more than a third of the existing Guardians at that rank in the Space Force—there were 147 E-8s according to the most recent data from Air & Space Forces Magazine’s 2026 Almanac.
The 13 new chief master sergeants is equivalent to a little less than a quarter of the 63 chiefs noted in the data.
Both ranks are among the smallest in the Space Force, though the service does have proportionally more than the Active-Duty Air Force. The Space Force also already has a higher ratio of senior master sergeants to chiefs—about 2.33-to-1—something this promotion cycle will likely further.
The increase in E-8 promotions follows a similar uptick in enlisted promotions at lower ranks—the selection rates for new master sergeant (E-7) and technical sergeant (E-6) in 2026 were both the highest they’ve been in five years.
The expansion of the NCO and senior NCO ranks is unfolding as the Space Force prepares to grow dramatically—officials have set a goal of expanding from 10,400 Guardians in fiscal 2026 to 25,000 by fiscal 2031. In fiscal 2027 alone, the service is looking to bolster its end strength by some 2,800 personnel, a 27 percent increase.
Much of that growth will inevitably come at more junior ranks, and the Space Force has shown it has no trouble meeting its recruiting goals, even turning away thousands of interested recruits. But in order for the growth to be “sustainable,” the service will also have to manage its more senior ranks too, Deputy Chief of Space Operations for personnel Katharine Kelley said at September’s Air, Space & Cyber conference.
“It is arguably easier to just say, ‘I need this many new Guardians,’” said Kelley. “It is much harder to say, ‘I need to seed all of that talent inside the service that already exists and not create an imbalance in an up-or-out promotion system.’”
Too many new Guardians with little experience entering at the lowest ranks could wreak havoc on the service’s grade structure, she noted.
The makeup of the force will change, Chief Master Sergeant of the Space Force John F. Bentivegna added—the Space Force has always been unique among the services given its high proportion of officers to enlisted, and while it’s unlikely to approach the ratio of the Air Force or Marine Corps, the coming growth is expected to favor the enlisted side.
“We’re going to grow more enlisted than we are going to grow officer,” Bentivegna said. “I think just a couple years ago it was almost a flat 50/50. Now we’re 53 percent enlisted, and I think that will continue to grow.

19th International Resistance Film Festival kicks off
TEHRAN – The opening ceremony of the 19th International Resistance Film Festival was held on Thursday in Isfahan.
At the beginning of the ceremony, Jalal Ghaffari Ghadir, the secretary of the 19th festival, stated: “In its first 11 editions, the Resistance Film Festival was known as the Sacred Defense Festival. Starting from the 12th edition, two developments occurred: first, the addition of the international section, and second, the semantic evolution and upgrade of ‘Sacred Defense Cinema’ to ‘Resistance Cinema’.”
“Let us not forget that the Resistance Film Festival emerged from the heart of war and the Sacred Defense. An important feature of this current edition is that it is being held amidst active conflict, and the developments we have witnessed in the two recent wars have made its significance even more distinct,” ILNA reported him as saying.
“Understanding resistance cinema stems from understanding the concept of resistance. Before any nation fights, it decides not to be defeated. This is the beginning of resistance. The task of resistance cinema is to reconstruct that very conviction which must be believed and trusted before the bullet and the rifle. The job of resistance cinema is not merely to record memories, but to generate belief,” Ghaffari added.
“A heroic nation loves to see the image of its resistance and might reflected in the mirror of resistance cinema. If cinema speaks solely of defeat, we will fail even if we possess elite military forces. Of course, resistance cinema must distance itself from slogan-driven approaches and, alongside depicting the suffering of war, speak of joy and hope,” he noted.
“In this 19th edition, we have witnessed several special developments. The first indicator is the broad participation of countries from around the world. More than 109 countries submitted works to this festival, and the presence of over 1,900 international works demonstrates the global capacity of resistance cinema. The Resistance Film Festival takes pride in this distinct semantic identity,” the secretary underlined.
During the opening ceremony of the 19th Resistance Film Festival, top works in several sections were honored.
The 19th International Resistance Film Festival is held under the auspices of the Revolution and Sacred Defense Cinema Society.
Resistance Cinema seeks to preserve human dignity by portraying the sacrifices of peoples, defending truth, and standing against oppression and domination, while bringing stories that have been less heard or seen to audiences around the world.
With nearly four decades of history, the Resistance International Film Festival is an artistic and cinematic platform dedicated to promoting a spirit of resistance, awareness, and solidarity among the free peoples of the world.
The festival aims to discover new talents, strengthen the movement of Resistance Cinema, and foster connections among filmmakers and artists from around the world.
The 19th edition of the festival, with an international outlook, focuses on concepts including resistance, freedom, justice, human dignity, peace, hope, and progress. It seeks to present a contemporary, diverse, and vibrant perspective on Resistance Cinema and the human stories associated with it.
In this edition, resistance is not understood solely as resistance on the battlefield or in times of war. Rather, it is viewed as a broader concept encompassing human resistance against oppression, occupation, discrimination, violence, domination, and oblivion; a resistance to preserve truth, identity, freedom, human dignity, and hope for the future.
Beyond being a film festival, the event is a cultural endeavor aimed at fostering dialogue among nations and filmmakers around the world and taking a step toward the realization of justice, freedom, peace, and human dignity.
The screening of festival films began on Friday at Mellat Cineplex in Tehran and will run until November 4.

Iranian army chief of staff: Passive defense key to national resilience against emerging threats

Iranian army chief of staff: Passive defense key to national resilience against emerging threats
TEHRAN –Army Chief of Staff and Deputy Coordinator Rear Admiral Habibollah Sayyari has stressed the strategic importance of passive defense in safeguarding the country’s critical infrastructure, maintaining essential services and strengthening national resilience against emerging and increasingly complex threats.
In a message issued on October 30 to mark Iran’s National Passive Defense Day, Sayyari emphasized that sustainable security depends on anticipating threats, reducing vulnerabilities, and ensuring preparedness before crises emerge.
Sayyari said modern warfare and recent conflicts had shown that threats were no longer limited to conventional military confrontations but were increasingly extending to critical infrastructure, supply chains, communications networks, and the economic and social foundations of countries.
Under such circumstances, he said, passive defense should be regarded not merely as a defensive requirement but as a strategic component of national security, essential to preserving national capabilities, ensuring the continuity of vital services and strengthening the country's ability to withstand multidimensional threats.
Sayyari emphasized that, in contemporary security calculations, national power is measured not only by conventional military capabilities but also by a country's capacity to prevent threats, maintain essential functions, and remain resilient during crises.
He described passive defense as a proactive approach to national security, highlighting the importance of identifying potential vulnerabilities and taking preventive measures before adversaries can exploit them.
Referring to the growing complexity of security challenges, the senior military commander said the experience of recent wars had underscored the need for comprehensive preparedness across different sectors of society.
He noted that disruptions to infrastructure, supply networks and communications systems could have consequences extending well beyond the immediate security sphere, affecting economic activity, public services and social stability.
This, he indicated, makes coordination among relevant institutions and the strengthening of the country's passive defense capabilities essential to maintaining national stability and ensuring the uninterrupted operation of vital systems.

When hanging up is a victory: Inside Israel's hotline for women in prostitution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
20:01:39 UTC
05:01:39 KST

The woman on the other end of the line sounded deeply distressed. "You're not recording me, are you? You won't tell the police, right?" she asked repeatedly. Only after being assured that the conversation was completely confidential did she begin to calm down and describe, in broken sentences, the rape she had experienced at the brothel where she worked.
She had not reported the assault to the police. "How can I file a complaint?" she asked. "If I say anything, they'll throw me out of the brothel. I have to make a living. I have a child."
Anat Sara, the volunteer answering the call, tried to reassure her, offer support and, above all, listen. "I can hear how upset you are," she repeated. "Let's think together about what we can do."
But the anonymous caller was not easily comforted. "Nobody listens to me," she said. "I feel like I'm suffocating. I can't take it anymore." Sara persisted. "What might help you cope?" she asked. "Can you remember other difficult situations you've faced? What helped you get through them?"
By the end of the conversation, the woman sounded somewhat calmer. There was no way of knowing what her situation would be the following day, but one thing had been achieved: Someone had been there to listen. Nothing more, but nothing less.
Except this was not an actual emergency call. The exchange took place during a training exercise in a fluorescent-lit office building in central Israel. The conversation was on speakerphone, allowing everyone in the room to hear it. The distressed caller was an experienced volunteer who had personally answered hundreds of similar calls and was now playing the role of a woman seeking help.
The simulation was part of a training program for approximately 10 prospective volunteers at the Shira Line, a support hotline launched earlier this year by the Israeli nonprofit Lo Omdot Mineged, which assists women involved in prostitution.
The scenario was fictional, but the experiences it portrayed were drawn from the difficult conversations volunteers regularly encounter.
‘The most meaningful thing I've done in my life’
Every evening, the Shira Line receives calls from women involved in prostitution. Some describe abuse by a client, an argument with a pimp or a dispute with another woman at the brothel where they work. Others simply want to talk about their children or a stray cat they have been feeding.
Some callers are very young, while others are considerably older. They include Jewish and Arab women, those who have severed all ties with their families and communities, and others who lead double or even triple lives. Some work on the streets or in brothels, while others entered prostitution through online platforms. Men occasionally call as well.
Some women phone almost every night. Others reach out only when they are experiencing severe distress. For some, the call is the first time they have dared to tell anyone that they are involved in prostitution.
There is a particular intimacy to these conversations, the kind that can develop during a late-night telephone call. There are no witnesses, no demand for identifying information and no expectation that the caller explain herself. Just a woman in distress and another woman trying to help as best she can.
The women volunteering to answer these calls come from strikingly different backgrounds. There are teachers and nurses, lawyers and high-tech professionals. Some have established careers and families, and several are already grandmothers.
Yet something has drawn them to a hotline serving women who are among the most isolated and marginalized members of Israeli society, often at the most difficult moments of their lives.
The commitment is considerable. Volunteers undergo several intensive evening training sessions and are required to continue receiving professional training throughout their time with the hotline.
Still, they are determined to participate. "I feel like this is the most meaningful thing I've done in my life," one volunteer explained.
The hotline is named after Shira, a woman involved in prostitution who had received assistance from the nonprofit and developed close relationships with several staff members and volunteers. She died by suicide four years ago. The organization decided to honor her memory by offering other women something she had desperately needed: Someone willing to listen.
Much of the nonprofit's work focuses on practical assistance, helping women meet urgent needs ranging from emergency dental treatment to housing and educational expenses. But the Shira Line, which began operating in early 2026, is different. Available during evening and nighttime hours, it focuses on emotional support rather than immediate material needs.
"Very often, when you're a woman involved in prostitution, you're outside society, outside your family and outside accepted social norms. You're alone," said Bracha Shapira, the hotline's professional director, who oversees volunteer training.
"We want to be available to these women during their moments of loneliness and difficulty."
Naama Goldberg, the nonprofit's CEO, said the need for this kind of support became evident through the organization's existing services. "Women would call a hotline intended to provide practical assistance, but over time we realized that many of them simply wanted to talk," she explained. "Some women call just to say 'good morning' or 'happy holiday.'"
When traditional support services are out of reach
When the organization tried to understand why these women were not turning to conventional emotional support hotlines, it discovered several obstacles. Many feared that a man might answer the phone. Others worried that the person on the other end would not understand the particular difficulties faced by women involved in prostitution.
Sometimes, the callers did not even recognize that they were experiencing emotional distress. They simply knew that they needed someone to talk to. "It could be something like deciding which client to accept or where to sleep tonight," Shapira explained.
"For most people, it's obvious that when you're going through something difficult, you can call a family member or a close friend. But when you're on the very margins of society, you don't have a friend, a mother or a sister. At the far end of prostitution, there is often an enormous amount of loneliness. And loneliness leads to helplessness."
In recent years, particularly since Israel introduced legislation prohibiting the purchase of sexual services, the Welfare Ministry has developed a range of programs specifically intended to assist people involved in prostitution.
The law, which authorizes police to enforce the ban and fine those who purchase sexual services, also included funding to expand assistance for women and men involved in prostitution.
Shapira, who previously worked in therapeutic programs for young women involved in prostitution, believes the new hotline addresses a need that formal treatment services often struggle to meet.
"Therapeutic programs frequently have difficulty helping women who are still actively involved in prostitution," she said. "They don't wake up, they cancel appointments, they use drugs. They're not in a place where they can undergo a therapeutic process."
Other women cannot seek conventional treatment because their involvement in prostitution is an absolute secret. "Their community would ostracize them," Shapira explained.
She pointed to the particularly painful situation of women from the ultra-Orthodox community, where seeking help could expose a life hidden from everyone around them. A woman dressed in the modest clothing associated with Beit Yaakov, the ultra-Orthodox girls' school system, may be unable to bring herself to enter a treatment center.
For such women, a confidential telephone conversation may be the only way to begin reaching beyond their immediate circumstances and asking for help, however tentative that first step may be.
Some of these conversations take place over WhatsApp rather than by telephone. "I'm afraid I'm failing him," one woman wrote during a simulated chat conversation at a recent training session. Although the participant was a volunteer playing a role, the exchange was modeled on countless similar conversations that had taken place with real callers.
Women contacting the hotline do not have to identify themselves, disclose their location or first register with the welfare authorities.
Why hanging up in anger can be a success
In another training scenario, a caller described sitting on a bench in a public park. She had argued with her pimp, with whom she had recently been living, and did not want to return home. "I'm hungry," she told the volunteer. "Can you send me a pizza?"
Requests like these, Shapira explained to the trainees, can present a difficult dilemma. "Very often, our instinct is to say, 'How can I help you? What do you need from me?'" she said. "But we're not superheroes, and we left our capes at home. We can't help her in a practical way right now."
Even when practical assistance is possible, Shapira reminded the volunteers, it is not the hotline's primary purpose.
The focus is on emotional needs, and the greatest challenge is learning how to address them when the person on the other end is experiencing intense distress. Just as the hotline does not promise material assistance, it does not claim to provide therapy. Nor does it set out to rescue callers from prostitution.
"Many of the women who call us are still a long way from being able to stand on their own two feet," Shapira said.
"Ultimately, if we've helped her just for today, if she goes to sleep tonight without having a panic attack, if because of the conversation she changes the sheets on her bed because a client was on the ones she's using now, that's more than enough. It really is."
Shapira encourages volunteers to recognize even the smallest positive moments during a conversation and reflect them back to the caller.
Sometimes those moments involve something the woman herself has mentioned: her child, a stray cat she cares for or anything else that gives her a sense of strength. Sometimes, the positive moment is simply the decision to pick up the phone and ask for help. And sometimes, remarkably, it is the decision to hang up in anger because something the volunteer said upset her.
For Shapira, that can represent something important: an assertion of control. "One of the biggest difficulties women involved in prostitution face is the ability to say 'no,' to refuse, to have control over their own lives," she explained. "Their lives are controlled by other people's desires."
If a woman chooses to end the conversation on her own terms, Shapira sees that as a possible sign of progress. Perhaps, in the future, she will be able to say "no" to other things as well. "If she manages to say, 'No, this doesn't work for me,' there's enormous value in that," Shapira said.
"A woman involved in prostitution who manages to tell a volunteer, 'I can't stand you, and I'm never speaking to you again,' is, in my eyes, an extraordinarily successful support call. That's a wow moment."

The psychological bias keeping U.S. drug laws out of step with science
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
20:00:57 UTC
05:00:57 KST

Americans tend to support the legality of substances that are already legal and oppose legalizing those that are currently outlawed, more than the drugs’ actual harms would predict. A new study published in Nature Human Behaviour suggests that existing drug laws themselves may shape public attitudes, helping keep regulations out of step with expert assessments of harm. Giving people expert harm ratings reduced their support for legal alcohol and tobacco but did little to change views on less harmful illegal drugs.
The researchers use the term status quo bias in a specific sense: the idea that a substance’s current legal status shapes how the public perceives it. Because most people have little firsthand experience with most drugs, the law itself, along with how media portray a substance, can serve as a cue for what is safe, normal, or morally acceptable. The authors distinguish this from the more familiar psychological concept of the same name, which refers to a general preference for sticking with existing options.
Drug regulations in the United States often clash with medical science. For instance, a 2010 evaluation by addiction experts found that legal substances like alcohol and tobacco cause substantially more physical and social damage than several banned substances, including psychedelics and MDMA (commonly known as ecstasy).
At the same time, politicians are not simply ignoring voters when they maintain these laws. Over the past decade, more than 25 statewide ballot measures on drug regulation have given more than 100 million Americans the chance to vote on these questions. Public sentiment has also been shifting: a 2023 time-series analysis found that Americans’ overall mood toward drugs has grown more liberal since the late 2000s.
That raises a puzzle: if citizens generally want sensible policies that minimize harm, why do they endorse drug laws that contradict expert harm assessments? A 2019 review of criminal justice research argued that public opinion does influence policies such as incarceration rates, which makes the question of how those opinions form all the more pressing.
Bence Hamrak, a research fellow at the European University Institute in Florence, and Gabor Simonovits, an associate professor at Central European University in Vienna and researcher at the ELTE Centre for Social Sciences, set out to explore this puzzle. They argue that criminalizing a drug can concentrate its use among marginalized groups, leaving most people to learn about it mainly through media coverage focused on addiction and crime rather than through firsthand experience. People may then blame the substance or its users for problems partly created by criminalization itself, strengthening support for keeping the ban.
“Drugs with similar harms are regulated very differently: some are available with prescription, while others are punished and might carry prison sentences,” Hamrak and Simonovits told PsyPost. “These regulatory extremes have detrimental effects for society and the individuals, as the opioid epidemic or the mass incarceration show. Experts have long recognized this mismatch, but policies remain largely misaligned. We asked whether public opinion is part of the explanation for bad policies.”
Because more drug policy is now decided directly through ballot measures, the authors reasoned that public opinion could play a direct role in shaping these laws. “Surprisingly, we found that policies largely match public opinion,” the researchers explained. “So, we realized that the real question is how people form their views about drug harms.”
To test this idea, the researchers first conducted a survey of 2,016 American adults recruited through the online panel provider Lucid Theorem, using census quotas to match the national population by age, gender, race, ethnicity, and region. Participants first indicated whether they were familiar with 13 psychoactive substances that vary in legal status: alcohol, aspirin, tobacco, cannabis, codeine, Xanax, Ritalin (a prescription stimulant), cocaine, heroin, LSD, MDMA, methamphetamine, and psilocybin (magic mushrooms). For each familiar substance, respondents stated whether recreational use should be legal or illegal, and if illegal, whether use should be treated as a decriminalized offense, a misdemeanor, or a felony carrying prison time.
The researchers compared these public opinions against a standardized 0 to 100 harm scale derived from addiction medicine experts, which ranks drugs based on physical organ damage, addiction potential, and social consequences. Across the 13 drugs, the negative correlation between expert harm ratings and public support for legalization was not statistically significant (r = −0.54, p = .06). Respondents strongly favored the legality of high-harm legal drugs over low-harm illegal ones; for instance, support for alcohol being legal was 71.1 percentage points higher than support for MDMA, even though experts rate alcohol as more harmful overall.
To measure how people would judge these substances without the baggage of their real-world names and legal histories, the same participants completed an experiment involving hypothetical “off-brand” drugs. Respondents were asked to imagine themselves as regulators evaluating five newly discovered substances, each described with randomly assigned attributes: physical harm (0 to 100), psychological harm (0 to 100), source (natural, semisynthetic, or synthetic), medical utility (existing medical use, ongoing research, or no medical use), and neurological effect (stimulant, depressant, or psychedelic).
Using statistical models based on how participants judged these randomized profiles, the authors calculated the predicted public support for an unnamed, off-brand version of each of the 13 real drugs. The authors treat the gap between support for a real drug and its off-brand twin as a measure of status quo bias.
For substances that are federally legal for recreational or over-the-counter use, support for the real drugs was much higher than for their off-brand profiles, with a median gap of 39.3 percentage points. Specifically, support for the real named substance exceeded its anonymous counterpart by 62.4 percentage points for alcohol, 39.3 percentage points for tobacco, and 23.8 percentage points for aspirin.
A similar positive gap appeared for cannabis (23.0 percentage points), which is legal for recreational use in about half of U.S. states, as well as for prescription drugs like Xanax and Ritalin (ranging from 12.5 to 28.8 percentage points), though codeine was an exception (−8.2 percentage points). For illegal drugs, the pattern reversed: people supported real illegal drugs at a median of 12.6 percentage points less than their unnamed equivalents. Support dropped by between 7.8 and 19.4 percentage points when respondents evaluated real psilocybin, LSD, heroin, cocaine, and MDMA rather than anonymous substances with identical harm profiles, with methamphetamine being the lone exception (+3.1 percentage points).
In an exploratory analysis, the researchers also examined views on prison sentences. For five of the illicit drugs (psilocybin, LSD, MDMA, cocaine, and heroin), participants were 5.5 to 25.5 percentage points more likely to favor felony incarceration when the drug was named than when evaluating its anonymous counterpart. Without the influence of real-world labels, a majority of participants opposed legalizing almost any of the substances apart from low-harm painkillers, yet a majority also opposed felony prison sentences for most of the unnamed illicit drugs.
“When the effect of the status quo is removed in our experiment, citizens seem to be more restrictive about legalization but also more liberal about punishment than current policies,” Hamrak and Simonovits noted. “At the same time, for most experimental substances the majority did not favor prison sentences either, even for harmful drugs. This suggests that without the biasing force of the status quo, the public could correct policy failures in both access and punishment.”
In a further exploratory analysis of how participants evaluated the unnamed hypothetical drugs, the researchers found that people paid close attention to harm. Compared to a hypothetical drug with high physical harm like alcohol, an otherwise identical drug with moderate physical harm received 13.6 percentage points more legalization support, and one with low physical harm received 23.6 percentage points more support. Even with harm held constant, however, participants showed a preference regarding what a drug does to the brain, favoring depressants by 14.5 percentage points over psychedelics.
Because citizens prioritized harm when judging unnamed drugs, the authors conducted a second experiment with 3,037 new American respondents to test whether correcting people’s misconceptions about real drugs would reduce status quo bias. Focusing on seven substances (alcohol, tobacco, Xanax, cannabis, cocaine, MDMA, and LSD), the researchers first measured how dangerous participants thought these drugs were compared to expert ratings. Respondents tended to underestimate the harms of legal drugs, rating alcohol 17.4 points lower on the 100-point scale than experts do, and overestimate the dangers of illegal drugs, rating MDMA 20.6 points higher than the expert score.
The researchers then randomly provided participants with the true expert physical and psychological harm scores for one of the seven drugs before asking whether it should be legal. Receiving accurate harm facts reduced support for the legality of alcohol by 17.7 percentage points and lowered support for tobacco by 12.9 percentage points compared to the uninformed control group. Providing harm facts also lowered support for the prescription drug Xanax to a level below that of its off-brand version.
Correcting misconceptions about illegal drugs, however, had almost no effect. Learning the expert harm ratings for cannabis, cocaine, MDMA, or LSD produced small, statistically non-significant changes in support for legalization. Overall, accurate harm information erased an average of 32 percent of the status quo bias for alcohol and tobacco, but only 18 percent for cocaine, LSD, and MDMA.
The authors suggest that this lopsided reaction occurs because opposition to illegal drugs is anchored in more than just health concerns. Stigma and racial prejudices toward the marginalized groups associated with illicit drug use may play a role as well, though the study did not test this.
“Citizens are probably not gullible or ill-intentioned when they support bad policies,” the researchers said. “Our suggested explanation for the original bias is simple: most people have little direct experience with most substances, so how we regulate drugs, and how we portray them, shapes how people think about them. Furthermore, some narratives are stickier than others, especially those tied to social norms about acceptable drug use.”
“And, in our experiment, people disliked psychedelics more than depressants or stimulants, even when their harms were the same,” Hamrak and Simonovits added. “This suggests that deep-seated prejudices and stereotypes may resist even new information. People rely heavily on the status quo for information and guidance for what is right or wrong, and this makes it harder for the democratic process to correct biased policies.”
“More accurate information moves public preferences closer to what a purely harm-based assessment would suggest,” the authors explained. “But even for legal drugs, where the information effect is clear, two-thirds of the status quo bias survives. This suggests that factors other than a lack of information also drive the difference between how people evaluate real and hypothetical drugs. Future research should focus on the cultural norms that sustain people’s preferences for regulating both legal and illegal substances, above and beyond harm.”
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these results. The study relies on expert harm scores that treat a drug’s danger as a fixed property of the chemical itself, which leaves out how a drug is consumed, the dosage, and the user’s environment. In reality, some harms tied to illegal drugs arise from how they are used and who uses them, factors that are themselves shaped by the drugs’ legal status, so even experts struggle to separate a substance’s pharmacological risk from the consequences of its ban.
“It would go too far to say our experiment revealed the ‘true’ public preferences about real-world drugs,” Hamrak and Simonovits cautioned. “We cannot say with full confidence that our hypothetical drugs matched real drugs in everything except the factors shaped by the status quo. Our experiment may have left out other information that also matters for judging drugs objectively.”
“For example, we did not include substance harms to others or to society, such as crime,” the researchers noted. “We left these out because, for these kinds of harm, the effects of the drug itself may be too entangled with the effects of the status quo, such as who uses the drugs, how they are used, or how users behave under different legal contexts.”
Additionally, to help participants picture the hypothetical drugs’ effects, the researchers attached familiar social purposes to them, describing stimulants, for instance, as making users less tired and enhancing productivity. The authors acknowledge these descriptions reflect socially shaped ideas about drug use, though they argue that, if anything, this would have shrunk the measured gap between real and hypothetical drugs, making their estimate of status quo bias conservative.
The study also relied on quota-matched online opt-in panels rather than true probability samples of the U.S. population, and drew its benchmark harm scores from a ranking by a panel of German addiction medicine experts. Finally, the surveys capture a single snapshot in time, leaving open the question of how status quo bias starts to crack when states gradually decriminalize or legalize substances like cannabis and psilocybin over many years.
The study, “Status quo bias drives public support for drug policy in the USA,” was authored by Bence Hamrak and Gabor Simonovits.

Iran holds US and Israel responsible for disruption of maritime Security
TEHRAN – Iran’s Ambassador and Chargé d’Affaires to the United Nations in New York, Gholamhossein Darzi, has said the United States and the Israeli regime bear direct responsibility for any disruption or obstruction of maritime navigation in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, warning that their continued acts of aggression and maritime restrictions threaten the security of the entire region.
 
Addressing a meeting of the UN Security Council on October 29, Darzi rejected attempts to hold Iran responsible for disruptions to maritime traffic, arguing that the current situation was the direct consequence of military aggression against Iran and measures targeting its civilian and maritime infrastructure.
 
He stressed that Iran had consistently upheld maritime security and freedom of navigation in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz for decades, fulfilling its responsibilities as a coastal state.
However, he said, some participants in the Security Council meeting had once again overlooked the root causes of the current situation.
“The responsibility for any disruption, obstruction, or other interference with maritime navigation in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz lies directly with the aggressors and those who facilitate or assist their acts of aggression against Iran,” Darzi said.
He added that such actions had endangered maritime safety and freedom of navigation throughout the region, describing attempts to shift responsibility onto Iran as unfounded and lacking credibility.
Iran cites attacks on vessels and maritime infrastructure
Darzi said the Strait of Hormuz and the maritime trade route passing through it had remained open until February 28, 2026, when the United States and Israel launched a 'war of aggression against Iran.'
He accused the two sides of continuing their unlawful actions, including deliberate attacks on Iran’s civilian and maritime infrastructure, ports and vessels.
To illustrate the consequences of these actions, the Iranian diplomat cited several incidents involving Iranian naval and commercial vessels.
He said a US submarine sank the Iranian frigate Dena in international waters in the Indian Ocean on March 4, killing more than 100 Iranian sailors.
On April 19, US military forces attacked the Iranian commercial vessel Toska, he added.
Darzi also referred to a statement by the US Central Command (CENTCOM), saying that by May 23, US forces had redirected 100 commercial vessels and disabled four others in enforcing the maritime blockade.
He further said that on July 23, US forces attacked two Iranian search-and-rescue vessels, Naji-15 and Naji-16, in Iranian territorial waters while they were engaged in humanitarian operations.
Tehran denounces US maritime blockade as violation of international law
The Iranian envoy said Washington had imposed a blockade on maritime traffic entering and leaving Iranian ports since April 12, describing the measure and its military enforcement as a flagrant violation of Iran’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.
He argued that the blockade constituted a serious breach of Article 2(4) of the UN Charter, which prohibits the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state.
Darzi also warned that restrictions on maritime traffic threatened civilians’ access to food, medicine, fuel and other essential supplies, potentially depriving the population of necessities indispensable to their survival.
He characterized the consequences of the blockade as a form of collective punishment and called for accountability for the resulting harm to civilians.
Iran invokes its right to self-defence
Rejecting accusations against Tehran, Darzi described Iran’s measures as defensive and lawful, emphasizing the country's right, as a coastal state, to protect its sovereignty, territorial integrity, population and vital national interests.
“As a coastal State, Iran has the legitimate right, under international law, to take all necessary and appropriate measures to protect its sovereign rights, its territorial integrity, its people, and its vital national interests against the US ongoing threat or aggression,” he said.
The diplomat called for full accountability for 'serious violations of international law' and the damage and suffering inflicted on civilians.
He urged the UN Security Council not to remain silent in the face of these developments and called on the body to explicitly demand that Washington immediately end its unlawful actions.
Darzi concluded by reaffirming that Iran would pursue all available legal avenues to ensure that those responsible were held accountable.
A call for the Security Council to address the root causes
At the beginning of his remarks, Darzi also addressed the role of emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, in maritime security.
 
He acknowledged that such technologies could create opportunities to improve maritime safety while simultaneously introducing new vulnerabilities. However, he stressed that the Security
Council should focus on genuine threats within the framework of its mandate under the UN Charter and respect the responsibilities of competent international bodies.
His remarks underscored Tehran’s position that maritime security in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz cannot be separated from the broader security environment and the consequences of military action against Iran.
Iran maintains that ensuring safe and uninterrupted navigation in the strategic waterway requires an end to military aggression, respect for the sovereignty of coastal states and compliance with international law.

EU and Canada seek deeper ties amid worsening global uncertainty
Both sides signed a digital trade deal, as Trump’s trade threats push Washington’s allies to seek closer ties elsewhere.
The European Union and Canada have launched what they described as an Alliance for the Future, as Ottawa prepares to become the bloc’s first so-called “associate member”.
Prime Minister Mark Carney hosted the Canada-EU summit in Montreal and signed a digital trade deal, alongside other agreements. Also at the Friday summit were European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa.
The term “associate member” has no legal basis and is contested by some EU states. However, its use underscores the desire of Canada and the EU to forge closer relations, as United States President Donald Trump continues to threaten Washington’s traditional allies with trade tariffs if they do not play by his rules.
“Canada and the EU are working to establish the closest possible partnership, which will be far from full membership, but which will make Canada the first associate member of the European Union,” Carney posted on X.
“Today in Montreal, we have taken a major step forward by establishing more than twenty measures that will increase affordability, create opportunities and ensure our sovereignty on both sides of the Atlantic.”
In a joint statement following the summit, the two sides announced an agreement under which the European Investment Bank will invest in critical Canadian resources, particularly raw minerals. They also said they would advance cooperation on artificial intelligence security and safety.
“A more dangerous and divided world has fundamentally changed the requirements of sovereignty. It is no longer enough for nations to feed, fuel and defend ourselves,” the statement said.
It added that “true sovereignty” requires secure access to critical minerals, semiconductors, payment systems, energy, vaccines, space-based communications and AI.
Ukraine was also on the meeting agenda, with Carney announcing Canada’s participation in the EU’s 90 billion euro ($103bn) support loan for Kyiv. Carney said Canada would make an initial contribution of 500 million euros ($558m).
Opportunities for students in Canada and the EU were also discussed. Both sides said they would launch negotiations aimed at deepening Ottawa’s participation in Erasmus+, the EU’s flagship student exchange programme.
Carney and Trump are currently engaged in a trade dispute, with talks under way to reach a deal between the two countries.
