Iran reports destruction of US drone and three tanker incidents in Strait of Hormuz
TEHRAN – Iran’s armed forces have reported the destruction of two different American unmanned platforms and incidents involving three oil tankers attempting to navigate unauthorized routes through the Strait of Hormuz, as the country maintains restrictions on maritime traffic through the strategic waterway.
In separate announcements on Thursday and Friday, the Islamic Revolution Guards Corps (IRGC) Navy and the Iranian Army Navy reported the interception of an American MQ-1 unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV), the destruction of an enemy unmanned surface vessel (USV), and incidents involving three oil tankers accused of disregarding Iranian navigation regulations and safety warnings.
The announcements underscore Iran’s continued emphasis on enforcing its maritime security arrangements in the Strait of Hormuz and preventing unauthorized movements through designated shipping routes.
Three oil tankers involved in incidents
In a statement issued on Friday, the IRGC Navy announced that two oil tankers attempting to pass through unauthorized routes in the eastern and western sections of the Strait of Hormuz had encountered incidents and were stopped in the southern waters of the strategic waterway.
According to the statement, both vessels had switched off their navigation and positioning systems and attempted to leave the strait through unauthorized routes with the support of the US military.
The IRGC Navy said the tankers had ignored repeated radio warnings, entered areas designated as unsafe, and subsequently encountered incidents before being halted.
The force attributed the incidents and fires aboard the vessels to 'hostile actions by the US military,' as well as the tankers’ disregard for Iranian regulations governing navigation through the strait.
In a separate announcement, the IRGC Navy reported that a supertanker had exploded after striking a naval mine while attempting to navigate an unauthorized route through the waterway.
The vessel, which was carrying more than two million barrels of oil, was left burning near the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz, according to the statement.
The IRGC Navy described the supertanker as the third oil tanker to have suffered an explosion and caught fire on Friday after attempting to use unauthorized routes.
The announcements did not identify the vessels or disclose their flags, ownership, or the precise circumstances of the incident.
Iranian Navy destroys unmanned surface vessel
Separately, the Iranian Army Navy announced that its forces had destroyed an enemy unmanned surface vessel operating in the eastern Strait of Hormuz in the early hours of Friday.
According to the Navy's public relations office, the remotely operated vessel was struck and destroyed while moving and conducting operations within the area monitored by Iranian naval forces.
The Navy also reported that two enemy oil tankers had sustained damage and caught fire after striking naval mines while navigating restricted and unsafe waters east of the Strait of Hormuz with their tracking systems switched off.
It said the vessels had disregarded previously issued warnings and maritime regulations, adding that their owners would bear full responsibility for the consequences of unauthorized navigation and failure to observe safety instructions.
The Navy warned that any hostile movement, infiltration or provocative action in areas monitored by Iran's armed forces would be met with a firm and proportionate response.
IRGC downs American MQ-1 drone
In a separate development announced on Thursday, the IRGC reported that its Aerospace Division had intercepted and destroyed an American MQ-1 unmanned aerial vehicle over the eastern Strait of Hormuz.
According to a statement published on the IRGC's official website, the drone was brought down by an advanced air defense system operating within Iran's integrated air defense network.
 
The IRGC described the aircraft as the 14th advanced MQ-1 drone intercepted and destroyed.
The aerial drone incident is distinct from the Iranian Army Navy's announcement concerning the destruction of an unmanned surface vessel. The two statements refer to different platforms and separate military operations.
Iran emphasizes control over maritime traffic
Iran has repeatedly warned commercial vessels against using navigation routes that have not been authorized by its maritime authorities, emphasizing that compliance with designated corridors and safety instructions is essential to preventing incidents in the Strait of Hormuz.
Since the US-Israeli war of aggression against Iran began on February 28, 2026, Tehran has introduced new arrangements governing maritime traffic through the strait, citing security considerations and the need to protect its territorial waters and national interests.
The Strait of Hormuz, connecting the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and the wider Indian Ocean, is one of the world's most strategically important maritime passages. A substantial share of internationally traded crude oil and petroleum products passes through this waterway, making maritime security and uninterrupted commercial navigation there a matter of international economic importance.
Iran maintains that safe passage through the strait requires vessels to observe the regulations established by the coastal authorities and refrain from unauthorized movements, particularly amid heightened regional tensions.
The latest announcements by the IRGC Navy and the Iranian Army Navy reinforce Tehran's warning that vessels operating in the area must comply with its maritime security instructions and that unauthorized navigation in designated restricted zones carries serious risks.

U.S. clears sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles to Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
19:48:14 UTC
04:48:14 KST

- The U.S. State Department approved a possible $2.1 billion sale of 500 PAC-3 MSE Patriot interceptors to Ukraine on Oct. 30.
- Canada, Germany and Norway are funding part of the sale through JUMPSTART, with the rest financed by the EU’s Ukraine Support Loan.
The U.S. State Department has approved a possible sale of 500 PAC-3 MSE interceptors to Ukraine for its Patriot air defense systems, a package worth an estimated $2.1 billion that will be paid for entirely by Ukraine’s allies and partners. The department notified Congress of the decision on Oct. 30.
Canada, Germany and Norway are contributing donations through JUMPSTART, a U.S. Foreign Military Sales mechanism for donor-funded Ukraine purchases, and Ukraine will cover the rest with national funds financed by the European Union’s Ukraine Support Loan. No U.S. funds are involved. Besides the missiles, the package includes classified and unclassified PAC-3 MSE spare parts and logistics and program support. Lockheed Martin is the principal contractor.
The notification is not a contract. It opens a congressional review period, after which Ukraine and the U.S. government can sign a letter of offer and acceptance and the U.S. Army can place the order with Lockheed Martin. The State Department gave no delivery schedule, and it did not say how the cost will be split among the three donors and the EU-financed share. Divided evenly, the total comes to about $4.2 million per missile, but that figure also covers spares and support.
The State Department said the missiles will help Ukraine sustain its existing Patriot operations against ongoing aerial threats, and that Ukraine will have no difficulty absorbing them into its armed forces. The sale will not require any additional U.S. government or contractor personnel in Ukraine.
The approval comes days after Ukrainian officials publicly pressed Washington on interceptor supplies. On Oct. 26, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine had waited nearly a month for U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth to sign off on missiles for its Patriot and NASAMS systems, including transfers from allied stocks that require U.S. approval. A day later, he told journalists that Ukraine had received an average of 12 Patriot interceptors a month from the United States in 2026, while Russia launches about 150 ballistic missiles a month that Ukraine needs to intercept.
PAC-3 MSE is the Patriot system’s main weapon against ballistic missiles. Unlike the older PAC-2 interceptors, which detonate a blast-fragmentation warhead near the target, the PAC-3 family destroys targets by direct impact, a method known as hit-to-kill. The Missile Segment Enhancement version adds a larger two-pulse solid rocket motor, with the second pulse firing late in the flight to extend range and altitude against maneuvering threats. That makes it the interceptor Ukraine relies on against Russian Iskander ballistic missiles and Kh-47M2 Kinzhal air-launched missiles. Ukrainian officials have described PAC-3 as their only effective defense against Russian ballistic missiles.
Ukraine received its first Patriot battery in April 2023, and in May of that year Ukrainian crews shot down a Kinzhal over Kyiv, the first publicly confirmed combat interception of the missile. Ukraine has since received further batteries from the United States, Germany, the Netherlands and Romania, and in July 2025 Germany and Norway agreed to pay for three more systems to be bought from the U.S. manufacturer. Interceptor supply has been a tighter constraint than launchers. In February 2026, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius offered five PAC-3 rounds from German stocks if other allies together supplied 30 more, and in July, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry said it was using about $1 billion from the EU loan to buy roughly 100 Patriot missiles.
The financing reflects how Ukraine’s air defense is now paid for. The U.S. Defense Security Cooperation Agency describes JUMPSTART as a channel that lets allies and partners finance Ukraine’s Foreign Military Sales cases with their own donations. Norway reported routing about NOK 10 billion through the mechanism in 2025, much of it for F-16 support. In September 2026, Canada said it would put about C$350 million toward air defense interceptors for Ukraine through JUMPSTART. Separately, NATO allies buy U.S. weapons for Ukraine through the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List, known as PURL.
EU governments agreed in early 2026 on a €90 billion loan for 2026 and 2027, with €60 billion set aside for defense, and the first disbursements went out in June 2026. The loan gives priority to weapons built in Ukraine, the EU and the European Economic Area, but allows purchases elsewhere when no European alternative exists. Patriot interceptors are one case where none does.
Production is the main limit on how fast the missiles can arrive. Lockheed Martin delivered 620 PAC-3 MSE interceptors in 2025, a company record. In January 2026, the company and the U.S. Department of War signed a seven-year framework agreement to raise annual output from about 600 to roughly 2,000. In April, the U.S. Army awarded Lockheed a $4.76 billion PAC-3 MSE contract, most of it funded through Foreign Military Sales customers. Demand has also climbed since the United States drew on its own Patriot inventory during this year’s conflict with Iran.
At 2025 production rates, the 500 missiles approved for Ukraine equal about 10 months of Lockheed’s output. Where Ukraine’s order falls in the production queue, and when the first missiles from this sale will reach Patriot batteries in Ukraine, has not been disclosed.

Border guards deny that "call from Kyiv" enabled Kravchenko to leave Ukraine
Andrii Demchenko, spokesperson for the State Border Guard Service of Ukraine, has denied claims that former prosecutor general Ruslan Kravchenko was allowed to cross the border following a "call from Kyiv".
Source: Demchenko in comments to Ukrinform
Details: According to Ukrainska Pravda sources, Kravchenko, who was prosecutor general at the time, was initially refused permission to enter Poland through the Shehyni checkpoint because of a flag in the database entered by the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) and the Specialised Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO). However, he was later allowed through following a call from Kyiv.
Quote: "Ruslan Kravchenko, who was prosecutor general at the time, crossed the border on the night of 13-14 September 2026. He travelled through the Shehyni checkpoint in Lviv Oblast. During border control procedures, Kravchenko presented documents confirming he was on an official business trip, which entitled him to leave Ukraine."
Details: Demchenko said that during the processing of his documents, an instruction issued by an authorised state body, marked index I (notification), was triggered in the database. According to the spokesperson, this meant that the relevant state authorities had to be informed of the person's departure.
"Under the established procedure, the body that had issued the instruction was immediately notified by telephone that this person had left Ukraine. I would also like to point out that this instruction did not prohibit the person from leaving the country; it merely required the initiating body to be informed. The body that issued the instruction did not raise any objections to Kravchenko's departure. No other instructions restricting this person's departure from Ukraine were issued to the State Border Guard Service by the authorised state bodies," Demchenko explained.
He also said that the authorised state bodies clearly understand the procedures followed by border guards when they receive different types of instructions from the State Border Guard Service. These include travel bans, wanted-person notices and requests for additional checks to establish whether there are legal grounds for someone to cross the state border.
"In this case, there was no ban, and the border guards acted accordingly. When restrictions imposed by authorised bodies are entered into the system, the person is not allowed to leave the country," Demchenko stressed.
Background:
- Kravchenko left Ukraine on the night of 13-14 September. Under an order he had signed himself, he was due to spend five days in Paris, allegedly attending hearings on Ukrainian children under the auspices of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe. However, his name did not appear on the list of participants in the discussion.
- His official business trip ended on 18 September. According to Mariana Haivovska, spokesperson for the Prosecutor General's Office, Kravchenko had not returned to work by 21 September.

What to know about California’s midterm elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
19:38:49 UTC
04:38:49 KST

What to know about California’s midterm elections
Redistricting in California, the most populous US state, could flip control of US House from Republican to Democrat.
As voters across the United States head to the polls for the midterm elections – widely seen as a referendum on President Donald Trump’s second term in office – the state of California is set to play an important role.
Several races across the country’s most populous state could help determine whether the Democratic Party takes control of the US House of Representatives, where Trump’s Republican Party currently holds a slim majority.
California’s ballot initiatives – or policy decisions made by voters – have also received national attention.
Perhaps the biggest difference in this year’s elections, however, is the introduction of new congressional district maps drawn up through a partisan redistricting initiative approved by California voters last year.
That initiative aims to net at least five additional Democratic Party seats in the House, where Republicans have a four-seat majority.
Which California races are competitive, who are the main candidates and how has the state’s redistricting push changed the electoral landscape?
When is election day?
The election will be held on Tuesday, November 3. California polls will be open from 7am (15:00 GMT) to 8pm (04:00 GMT Wednesday). Mail ballots must be postmarked by election day.
What is partisan redistricting?
The House is divided into 435 districts, each represented by one member of Congress elected by their constituents. While congressional districts are populated equally, their boundaries are set by states and can shift.
Partisan redistricting involves states drawing those district maps in a way that advantages candidates from one party over another.
California Governor Gavin Newsom, a Democrat and Trump critic, first proposed a one-time statewide redistricting effort in response to seven Republican-led states redrawing their maps in an attempt to secure seats for Republicans. Although California had banned partisan redistricting, Newsom pitched the idea as an unfortunate but necessary retaliatory measure.
California voters approved the redistricting plan in a 2025 ballot measure – Proposition 50 – that temporarily suspended the state’s nonpartisan redistricting commission until 2030. California then drew new maps to make several Republican strongholds more competitive for Democratic challengers.
As a result, the handful of districts previously seen as favourable terrain for Republicans have instead become hotly-contested races between the two parties.
What races are being watched?
California has 52 members in the House of Representatives – the most of any state – with Republicans holding just eight of the seats. There are several closely watched state races in the Democratic Party’s effort to secure a majority in the House, the lower chamber of the US Congress.
One is the 22nd congressional district, located in California’s agriculture-rich Central Valley. The district map was redrawn under Proposition 50, setting up one of the state’s most contentious races in a former Republican stronghold.
Incumbent Republican Representative David Valadao is locked in a tight race with Democratic challenger Randy Villegas. Valadao has portrayed himself as a moderate, while Villegas has hammered him over issues such as the rising cost of living, healthcare and Trump’s immigration crackdowns – a key issue for the area’s immigrant farm-working communities.
California’s 48th district, a traditionally Republican stronghold which includes parts of San Diego County near the border with Mexico, is also considered highly competitive after its boundaries were redrawn. The district’s longtime representative, Republican Darrell Issa, decided to retire after the redistricting, with two local officials – Republican Jim Desmond and Democratic San Diego Councilmember Marni von Wilpert – now vying for the seat.
While California’s redistricting aimed to make historically reliable Republican districts more competitive for Democrats, the process has also had some unexpected impacts: Two Republican members of Congress, Representatives Ken Calvert and Young Kim, have found themselves locked in a bitter race against each other after redrawn maps put them in the same district.
Who is running for governor?
Vying to replace Governor Newsom are Republican political commentator Steve Hilton and Democrat Xavier Becerra. Becerra is a former California attorney general and secretary of health and human services during former President Joe Biden’s administration.
Hilton has blasted Becerra for rising crime and homelessness as well as high fuel prices in California, where a gallon (3.78 litres) of petrol costs $5.95 compared with $4.22 nationally, according to the American Automobile Association. Heavily favoured in the Democratic stronghold state, Becerra has sought to associate Hilton with Trump, who is deeply unpopular among Californians.
Polls show Becerra with a strong lead over the Republican challenger. A recent Emerson poll suggested that he was ahead by 27 points.
What ballot initiatives are voters deciding on?
California voters will also weigh in on a handful of policy questions, including a tax on billionaires and whether the state should adopt mandatory voter ID.
Perhaps the most contentious is Proposition 40, a one-time tax on billionaires to help fund healthcare and education. The measure is one of three impacting the state’s ultra-wealthy residents, with the referendums dubbed the “billionaire battle”.
The tax would apply to about 200 of the wealthiest people in California, according to the news website CalMatters. The proposition is opposed by powerful industries and tech titans, who have poured more than $152m into fighting the ballot measure compared with $33m raised in support of the tax, a California public radio station KQED reports.
The measure has drawn opposition from figures such as Google cofounder Sergey Brin, who has given more than $102m to defeat the referendum, as well as Hilton, Becerra and Newsom. Despite being supported by the Democratic Party, Proposition 40 is also being fought by some progressive groups opposed to the one-time tax.
Other progressives such as Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Ro Khanna, a wealthy member of Congress from California’s Silicon Valley, support the referendum.
Two other ballot measures, Propositions 41 and 42, would effectively nullify Proposition 40 if approved by voters.
Another measure, Proposition 39, has also been the subject of fierce debate. If passed, it would require Californians to show government-issued IDs in order to vote.
While supporters say mandatory IDs will bolster confidence in elections by countering voter fraud, studies have found that fraudulent voting is nearly nonexistent in the US.
Critics say that voter ID laws add obstacles to voting by requiring government-issued documents, such as a driver’s licence, that not all citizens hold. They argue that strong safeguards ensuring only eligible voters cast ballots are already in place.

Iran condemns Canada, UAE for reiterating territorial claims over three Persian Gulf Islands
TEHRAN– Iran has strongly condemned Canada and the United Arab Emirates for reiterating territorial claims over Abu Musa, the Greater Tunb and the Lesser Tunb, reaffirming that the three islands are inseparable and eternal parts of Iranian territory.
Iranian Foreign Ministry Spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei on Thursday denounced the UAE’s “brazen and interventionist” claims and Canada’s decision to endorse them in a joint statement issued following a meeting between Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan in Ottawa.
Baqaei stressed that the islands’ established geographical, historical and legal status could not be altered by political statements or the repetition of 'baseless territorial claims.'
“The islands of Abu Musa, the Greater Tunb and the Lesser Tunb are inseparable and eternal parts of Iran’s territorial domain, and the repetition of baseless and unfounded claims about them will not change the established geographical, historical and legal realities,” he said.
Tehran denounces Ottawa’s intervention
The Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman particularly criticized Canada's decision to endorse the UAE's position, describing Ottawa's move as short-sighted and contrary to the fundamental principles of the United Nations Charter and international law.
He said Canada's involvement in the territorial dispute was especially objectionable given that the country itself faces territorial assertions by the US administration.
Baqaei stressed that endorsing another country's territorial claims against Iran carries international responsibility for the Canadian government.
He also called on Abu Dhabi to respect the principles of good-neighborliness rather than repeatedly raising territorial claims against a major neighboring country, emphasizing the importance of mutual respect and respect for national sovereignty in relations between regional states.
Canada's position is not new. Ottawa had previously endorsed the UAE's claim in a joint statement issued during Carney's visit to the Emirates in November 2025, in which the two countries likewise called for an end to what they described as the occupation of the three islands.
The latest statement, however, comes as Canada and the UAE move to elevate their bilateral relations to a strategic partnership, expanding cooperation in trade, investment, energy, defence and security, advanced technology and diplomacy.
Iran has consistently maintained that Abu Musa, the Greater Tunb and the Lesser Tunb are integral parts of its national territory and rejects any foreign government's endorsement of competing claims over them.
Tehran has also repeatedly stressed that relations with neighboring countries should be founded on mutual respect, respect for territorial integrity and the principles of good-neighborliness, rather than political alignments with extra-regional powers.

Before captain, a king: The dramatic life of Patrick Stewart
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
19:36:59 UTC
04:36:59 KST

Long before he trekked aboard the USS Enterprise, Sir Patrick Stewart trod the boards on stages across the globe.
"The stage would prove to be a safe space, a refuge from real life in which I could inhabit another person, living in another place and time," Stewart wrote in his memoir.
The Royal Shakespeare Company wrote a tribute to Stewart, who died yesterday aged 86, calling him one of the finest classical Shakespearean actors of his generation.
"Despite being one of the most recognisable Shakespearean performers in the world, Sir Patrick remained deeply connected to Stratford-upon-Avon and the RSC throughout his career," the company said.
The Royal Shakespeare Company said his contribution was "beyond measure", with his knighthood for services to drama and his star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame as markers of a career that spanned 70 years.
But before he was a household name, a young Stewart cut his teeth as an ensemble member touring Australia.
Stewart joined an amateur drama group at 12 and memorised Shakespeare for fun as a teenager.
He would go on to win a scholarship to the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School, launching his career as a character actor.
Theatre programs archived at the National Library of Australia show that a 21-year-old Stewart toured with the Old Vic company across 1961 and 1962.
Stewart had ensemble roles in Twelfth Night and The Lady of the Camellias, both directed by Robert Helpmann and starring Vivien Leigh.
ABC archives show that reporters made sure to capture the moment Leigh and Helpmann landed on the tarmac in Australia to be greeted by adoring fans, but likely didn't know that just out of frame was a star-to-be in young Stewart.
Loading...
From the Young Vic, Stewart went on to join the Royal Shakespeare Company and stayed for 14 years, playing roles including Mark Antony, Henry IV, Shylock and Oberon.
In 1975, he would return to Australia to play Ejlert Løvborg in Hedda Gabler with the company.
From royal crowns to the captain's chair
Although often revered as a classical actor, Stewart denied this title, saying: "I was not a trained classical actor, I just had a training".
"What I did happen to do was spend a huge number of years with the Royal Shakespeare Company, but doing just as much modern drama as I was doing blank verse," he told the ABC in 1995.
After joining Star Trek, he found himself frustrated at the implication from reporters that doing a syndicated television show must have meant he was "slumming it".
Stewart had a very different point of view.
"All of those years with the Royal Shakespeare Company, all of those years sitting in the throne of England, all of those years wearing those crowns and speaking that blank verse was nothing but a preparation for sitting in the captain's chair of the Enterprise," he said.
It was Stewart's understanding of profession that made him so versatile, that every prior piece of work in an artist's portfolio contributes to the next, regardless of the piece being set in futuristic space or written in Elizabethan England.
Always returned to theatre
Star Trek may have been Stewart's launch into the broader global audience, particularly in America, but he continued to return to the stage, often rehearsing shows while filming.
In 1988, Stewart premiered his one-man adaptation of A Christmas Carol.
The performance started as a three-hour rendition, performed in a church in Yorkshire.
Several years later, it would make its Broadway debut.
The revised version would be staged time and time again, nabbing a Laurence Olivier Award for Best Entertainment in 1994.
In 2007, Stewart played the role he'd waited 50 years for — Macbeth.
The Times of London said his performance was "an enthralling creation of frailty, appetite, egotism and grim humour".
"I learned it when I was 14. I memorised all the soliloquies just because I thought they were great," Stewart told The Associated Press.
"And they stuck, so I didn't have to learn those bits of the play, which is a blessing, because learning lines has now become the one curse of this job.
"Nearly 50 years I've waited."
In 2009, Stewart starred with his dear friend Sir Ian McKellen in Waiting for Godot.
McKellen wrote of his friend on social media, retelling the moment Stewart told him about taking a role on Star Trek.
"'But Patrick, think of your stage career in the UK. Do you really want to risk getting lost in Hollywood for years and years?'" McKellen said he asked at the time.
"Well, he took the risk and thank goodness for us all that he did."
Audiences will feel lucky to have seen Patrick Stewart deliver time and time again.
But in his own words, he felt just as lucky to see them too.
"I enjoy what I do so much that I do actually feel sucked into it, particularly the live theatre, the performing side of it," he told the ABC in 1995.
"I'm one of those really fortunate individuals, I do feel blessed in this, who ended up doing as a profession what I would've done for nothing."

Washington’s Midterm Letter Game
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
19:34:49 UTC
04:34:49 KST

Washington’s Midterm Letter Game
From Carter to Vance, US messages have failed to break Iranian resistance
TEHRAN — The disclosure of a letter from US Vice President JD Vance to Secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council Mohsen Rezaei has triggered a wave of contradictory narratives in Washington, speculative reporting in American media, and a calm, conditional response in Tehran.
The story broke on Oct. 28 when The Wall Street Journal, citing US officials and people familiar with the matter, reported that Vance had written to Rezaei, Iran’s top security official and former commander of the Islamic Revolution Guards Corps, to explore a framework for restarting negotiations and averting a new round of US strikes. The report said the outreach was made at President Donald Trump’s direction.
Hours later, Trump himself undercut that account. Asked by reporters whether he had directed Vance to restart peace talks, he said “No,” and claimed the contact was about helping Iran obtain “medical supplies and various things.”
“Basically, it’s getting supplies in to help people that are not well,” Trump said.
The semi-official Tasnim news agency confirmed on Oct. 29 that Tehran had received the letter but had not yet responded. Iran’s Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, one of
Tehran’s negotiators, wrote on X that “Iran’s conditions have been repeatedly and clearly communicated to the mediators” and that “the carrot-and-stick approach has no effect on Iran.”
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi added that while Iran’s Armed Forces are fully prepared to defend the homeland, Iran “continues to give diplomacy a chance.”
Beyond those confirmed facts — a letter was sent via Qatari mediators, delivered on Sunday, acknowledged in Tehran, with no published text and no formal reply — almost everything else published in the past 48 hours is speculation and cannot be verified.
A routine channel, not a breakthrough
Viewed in historical perspective, the letter is anything but unprecedented. Writing to Iranian leaders has been a standard American practice since the victory of the Islamic Revolution in 1979, and at least 20 letters, messages and written contacts have been publicly disclosed so far.
The list begins with President Jimmy Carter’s Nov. 6, 1979 letter to Imam Khomeini carried — but never delivered — by Ramsey Clark and William Miller after the takeover of the US Embassy. It continued with President Ronald Reagan’s signed Bible inscribed on Oct. 3, 1986 with the verse Galatians 3:8, handed to Iranian intermediaries in the Iran-Contra affair, along with the earlier McFarlane mission carrying a key-shaped cake.
President Bill Clinton sent messages through the Swiss ambassador in 1997 proposing direct government-to-government talks after Mohammad Khatami’s election, repeated the offer via Vice President Al Gore through Saudi Crown Prince Abdullah in May 1998, and wrote the detailed June 1999 letter on the Khobar Towers bombing while insisting the US had “no hostile intentions” toward the Islamic Republic.
President Barack Obama wrote at least four letters to Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei — in May 2009, September 2009, January 2012 on the Strait of Hormuz as a “red line,” and mid-October 2014 linking cooperation against ISIS to a nuclear deal — plus the exchange of letters with President Hassan Rouhani in August-September 2013 that led to their historic phone call, not to mention six Nowruz messages.
President Donald Trump sent a letter via late Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe in June 2019, which was publicly rejected, then relied on the Swiss encrypted fax channel in January 2020 after the assassination of General Qassem Soleimani to warn against escalation, and sent the March 5, 2025 letter delivered on March 12 by Emirati diplomat Anwar Gargash, setting a 60-day deadline that led to five rounds of indirect Steve Witkoff-Abbas Araghchi talks in Oman and Rome before the June war.
From this standpoint, a message from a US vice president to the SNSC secretary is a routine and conventional step, not a turning point. Washington writes when pressure fails. Tehran listens, measures, and decides on the basis of interests, not envelopes.
No one knows what is inside
No official text of Vance’s letter has been published by either side, and every claim about its content comes from anonymous “officials familiar with the matter.”
The Journal said it contained “no specific peace plan” but focused on a framework for negotiations. Axios, citing a US official, added that Vance stressed any talks to head off strikes “require discussions on the nuclear issue,” and called it the most senior-level US outreach in months. The New York Times, citing a US official and an Iranian official, claimed the letter proposed an early meeting led by Vance himself, possibly as soon as next week in Qatar or Turkey, technically “without preconditions.”
Washington Post columnist David Ignatius, citing a US official, went further, writing that Vance offered to meet Rezaei personally in Istanbul or Doha, defined America’s interest as ensuring Iran does not obtain a nuclear weapon and Iran’s interest as rebuilding its war-ravaged economy and preserving sovereignty, and demanded “representatives who are empowered to discuss the nuclear issues.” He portrayed Rezaei as “the essential point of contact in Tehran and the only person who could build a consensus.”
None of this has been confirmed by Tehran or by any published document. Iranian media have treated all of it as guesswork. Until a text is released or an official reply is issued, responsible journalism requires treating these versions as competing American leaks aimed at shaping expectations, not as facts.
Midterm panic at the pump
The timing, however, is revealing. The United States is days away from midterm elections on Nov. 3, and all signs point to a very difficult contest for Republicans. The eight-month war with Iran has become the administration’s Achilles’ heel.
Despite repeated threats to “finish the job,” Trump has failed to control domestic gasoline prices, which have surged on the back of disrupted traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, oil prices above $110, damaged tankers, and a US naval blockade that has raised insurance and shipping costs globally rather than forcing Iranian submission.
Washington has tried everything to calm the pump before the vote, from emergency releases and arrangements with Russia to stabilize the fuel market to the highly controversial authorization for the use of cheaper red-dyed diesel, yet prices remain politically toxic. A short, sharp new war would send them even higher; a televised diplomatic “process” would, in the White House calculation, create a positive shock and allow Trump to claim the situation is under control.
That is why the same administration that warns Gulf allies to “prepare” for post-midterm strikes simultaneously leaks a peace letter. The goal is not peace but performance: to stage a show of agreement-seeking before the elections and inject artificial calm into the Republican camp at a moment when it is in no good shape at all.
Seven conditions, no retreat
Tehran’s answer to such theater has been consistent and public. Iran has announced seven conditions for ending the current state of war and reopening the Strait of Hormuz to free navigation, centered on a region-wide ceasefire, lifting the US naval blockade of Iranian ports, lifting sanctions on oil exports, unfreezing Iranian assets abroad, and guarantees against renewed aggression.
Rezaei himself drew the line on Oct. 21: “Not a single ounce of enriched nuclear material will leave Iran,” and negotiations are possible only if Iran’s demands are met. Tasnim stressed on Oct. 29 that “any position that undermines this firm framework is unacceptable.”
This firmness is not rhetorical. It reflects the assessment of Leader of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei, who in his recent meeting with Rezaei described the SNSC and its Secretariat as the “crossroads of policymaking,” stressed safeguarding national and regional security by maintaining control over the Strait of Hormuz, and insisted on pursuing the rights of the Iranian nation and the Resistance Front by ensuring the country’s conditions for ending the war are met and bringing the state of “neither war nor peace” to an end.
Most importantly for the present episode, the Leader said sound and well-grounded decisions require a roadmap based on a comprehensive understanding of each undertaking, from its starting point to its conclusion. In other words, Tehran will not enter a process whose end is pre-scripted in Washington.
Open door, not open eyes
Iran has not closed the doors of diplomacy. The quadrilateral meeting hosted by Tehran on Monday with senior officials from Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia, the continued Qatari mediation — with Qatari envoys returning to Tehran on Friday — and Rezaei’s own statement that security in West Asia must originate from within the region show that Tehran prefers a regional, endogenous order to foreign dictation.
But openness does not mean naivety. Tehran remembers too well the March 2025 Trump letter to Ayatollah Khamenei, the five rounds of Witkoff-Araghchi talks, and then the Israeli attack of June 13 and the 12-day war. It remembers four Obama letters followed by maximum pressure, and a signed JCPOA abandoned unilaterally.
Iran will not walk blindfolded and wishfully into a negotiation so that Trump can exploit the mere image of talks for electoral gain, freeze the battlefield in his favor, pocket a nuclear concession upfront, and postpone sanctions relief, unblocking and guarantees to an indefinite “later.” Sequencing matters: Washington demands nuclear-first, relief-later; Tehran demands simultaneous, verifiable steps. Without that, there is no roadmap from start to finish, only a photo opportunity.
Desperation after failure
Behind the letter is a serious American impasse. Neither eight months of direct strikes and Israeli operations, nor the naval blockade of ports, economic warfare, cyber operations and threats of regime change, have forced Iran to surrender its enrichment, its missile program, or its control over Hormuz. The economy, though wounded, has not collapsed; the Armed Forces have not fractured; regional partners have not defected — they came to Tehran.
A new round of war will not bring Iran to its knees. It will only deepen American costs: higher energy prices before and after the midterms, wider regional escalation that Qatar, Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia openly fear, further exposure of US bases and warships that Leader Khamenei’s commanders have explicitly vowed to target, and a deeper reputational defeat when a superpower cannot dictate terms to a nation it has sanctioned for 47 years.
Washington now acknowledges, in its own leaks, that it must talk to the hard core of Iranian power — the SNSC secretary with direct access to the Leader and the trust of the IRGC — because no imposed settlement is possible. That is an admission of failure, not a gesture of goodwill.
The ball is in the US court. If Washington wants more than an election show, it must trade the logic of imposed agreement for balanced agreement: end the blockade, release Iran’s frozen assets, lift oil sanctions, accept verification in exchange for guarantees, and let West Asia’s security be built within the region. Otherwise, the letter from Vance will join the long archive of American letters since 1979 — received, read, measured against Iran’s roadmap, and answered not with surrender but with resistance.

Time for a trip to New Zealand? Why Australian travellers now have an advantage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
19:30:49 UTC
04:30:49 KST

While the prospect of higher interest rates could leave borrowers with less money to spend, it has come as good news for the Australian dollar.
The Aussie surged above NZ$1.25 this week for the first time in more than 13 years, making holidays across the Tasman more affordable for Australians.
Our currency has gained more than 10 per cent against the New Zealand dollar over the past year, giving Australian travellers greater purchasing power.
Two contrasting economic developments helped drive the latest move.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Wednesday's stronger-than-expected inflation report pushed the market-implied probability of a Melbourne Cup Day interest rate rise by the Reserve Bank of Australia above 80 per cent, supporting the Australian dollar.
Across the Tasman, the Reserve Bank of New Zealand surprised markets by leaving interest rates on hold.
Like Australia, New Zealand is also grappling with inflation above its central bank's target, with annual consumer prices rising 3.7 per cent.
Differences in interest rate expectations between the two countries have helped push the Australian dollar higher, potentially making a New Zealand getaway better value.
Major discounts coming for Australian shoppers
Bigger discounts could be on the way during Black Friday and the Christmas period as many Australian retailers battle for shoppers amid slow sales growth.
The sluggish growth in sales could be a sign that consumers are holding back from spending big during the sales, or that cost of living pressures and the prospect of higher interest rates are weighing on household budgets.
Woolworths CEO Amanda Bardwell told shareholders at the company's annual general meeting (AGM) this week that four in 10 Australians say they often struggle to make ends meet. The supermarket giant estimates groceries account for 10 per cent of household spending among borrowers.
But that hasn't stopped Woolworths from making what its CEO described as a good start to the financial year, with food sales rising nearly 7 per cent in the three months to September. It's doing better than Coles, which reported slower sales growth over the same period at 3.6 per cent, still topping $10 billion in revenue.
It seems that even in tough times, people have to eat — who would have thought?
Betashares investment strategist Hugh Lam told the SBS On the Money podcast that shares in the consumer staples sector have risen about 20 per cent so far this year.
"A lot of companies within there, like Woollies, Coles and even Bega Cheese, are benefiting because these are sectors of the market where people are still going to be spending despite where we are in the economic cycle," Lam said.
For retailers selling more discretionary items, however, the picture isn't as rosy.
This week, Super Retail Group, which owns Rebel, Supercheap Auto, BCF and Macpac, said weaker consumer confidence and pressure on discretionary spending had weighed on its business.
It specifically pointed to higher petrol prices as a factor behind the decline in quarterly like-for-like sales at outdoor retailers BCF and Macpac.
JB Hi-Fi, which also operates The Good Guys and kitchen and bathroom retailer e&s, reported negative comparable sales growth across its Australian businesses.
It highlights the pressures many businesses in the discretionary sector — selling wants rather than needs — are facing in this economic climate.
"I think what this means … is potential discounting from these retailers which is of course going to hit margins," Lam said.
"And that's because higher interest rates mean that there's less discretionary money everyday Australians can spend on."
Even Bunnings, owned by Wesfarmers, has seen sales growth moderate, according to Wesfarmers CEO Rob Scott at the company's AGM.
But he said the group's Kmart business was performing well as shoppers increasingly sought value.
For consumers, that could mean more bargains during Black Friday and Christmas sales, as retailers compete harder for every dollar.
Will you have to pay for Claude and its competitors?
AI chatbot Claude's owner, Anthropic, lodged its prospectus this week as it prepares to list on the US sharemarket.
The filing offered investors a detailed look at the company's extraordinary revenue growth, mounting expenses and the risks associated with developing increasingly powerful artificial intelligence.
Among the most serious risks identified were "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such (AI) systems were misused, replicated, weaponized [sic], or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy".
Loftus Peak chief investment officer Alex Pollack told the SBS On the Money podcast that other potentially catastrophic threats already exist, including nuclear and cyber risks.
"But the question you’ve got to ask yourself is, what is the probability of those risks happening?" Pollack said.
But buried among the warnings was another risk with more immediate implications for the millions of people using AI chatbots for free.
Anthropic warned that its marketing strategies, including free trials and free subscription tiers, might fail to deliver sufficient financial benefits.
"If the costs of supporting free users exceed the value we derive from their eventual conversion or other benefits such as network effects and word-of-mouth referrals, our business, financial condition and results of operations could be adversely affected."
Could that eventually mean an end to free access?
The prospectus doesn't suggest Anthropic has made such a decision, but it does highlight the financial challenge of offering expensive AI services at no cost.
Anthropic reported revenue of US$16.28 billion ($23.12 billion) in the six months to the end of June 2026, compared with US$1.16 billion ($1.65 billion) in the same period a year earlier.
But that extraordinary growth comes with enormous costs.
The company spent nearly US$9 billion ($12.78 billion) on computing and infrastructure over those six months, accounting for more than half its total operating expenses.
It's a reminder that while AI chatbots might be free for many people today, the technology powering them is anything but cheap.

Iran’s nuclear doctrine debate reflects national demand for stronger deterrence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
19:27:55 UTC
04:27:55 KST

Iran’s nuclear doctrine debate reflects national demand for stronger deterrence
TEHRAN — Tehran’s interim Friday prayer leader, Mohammad Javad Haj Ali Akbari, has described calls to review Iran’s nuclear doctrine as a growing national demand rooted in the Iranian people’s experience of Western conduct, heightened security concerns and the need to strengthen the country’s deterrence capabilities.
Addressing worshippers during Friday prayers in the Iranian capital on October 30, Haj Ali Akbari said the debate over a possible revision of the country’s nuclear doctrine should not be dismissed as an emotional reaction or attributed to a particular political faction. Rather, he argued, it reflects a broader public reassessment of the security requirements facing Iran following years of confrontation, unfulfilled commitments and hostile actions by its adversaries.
His remarks come amid renewed public discussion in Iran about the country’s nuclear policy and the relationship between its established positions, national security requirements and the evolving regional and international environment.
A debate shaped by security concerns
Haj Ali Akbari said Iran’s adversaries had crossed the nation’s red lines, pointing to the assassination of the martyred Leader of the Islamic Revolution, Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei, and 'repeated failures' to honor commitments and agreements.
He argued that the Iranian people’s accumulated experience had prompted a more considered debate about the country’s deterrence requirements, including whether its nuclear doctrine should be reviewed in light of the security challenges it faces.
According to the cleric, the proposal is rooted in the Iranian nation’s right to live in dignity and security. He stressed that the discussion should be understood as a matter of national concern rather than an initiative belonging to any single political group or current.
Haj Ali Akbari also said that some people had reacted angrily to the proposal but maintained that the public discussion surrounding it reflected a broader demand that policymakers should examine seriously.
Citing previous surveys, he said more than 70 percent of respondents in some polls had supported reviewing Iran’s nuclear doctrine.
He added that calls for reconsideration had subsequently emerged from a range of social and professional groups, including university students, school students, academics, intellectuals and professional associations.
The cleric urged universities, researchers, security specialists and other experts to contribute to the debate by conducting substantive studies and developing policy proposals. He also called on the relevant authorities to undertake further assessments, with the aim of submitting the resulting recommendations to the Leader of the Islamic Revolution, Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Hosseini Khamenei.
He emphasized that the final decision rested with the Leader and said that any decision he made would be followed.
Negotiations and the question of vigilance
Alongside the nuclear doctrine debate, Haj Ali Akbari cautioned against interpreting US calls for negotiations, diplomatic correspondence, or the involvement of intermediaries as grounds for relaxing Iran’s vigilance.
Drawing on Iran’s experience of dealings with Washington, he argued that diplomatic overtures should be assessed in the context of the other side’s conduct and actions, rather than its statements alone.
He warned that, in some circumstances, US messages and proposals for negotiations could coincide with more serious threats than those conveyed through explicit declarations of hostility. His remarks underscored the importance of maintaining vigilance while assessing diplomatic initiatives.
The comments reflect a central concern in Iranian political and security discourse: that diplomatic engagement must be evaluated alongside practical guarantees, respect for commitments, and the broader security environment.
For Tehran, the question is not simply whether negotiations are proposed, but whether the process can produce credible and lasting commitments while safeguarding Iran’s national interests.
From public debate to policy assessment
Haj Ali Akbari’s remarks place the nuclear doctrine debate within a wider discussion about deterrence, national sovereignty and the country's response to changing security conditions.
 
By calling for contributions from universities, professional bodies and relevant specialists, he presented the issue as one requiring sustained examination rather than a decision driven by immediate political pressures.
The distinction is significant: a public demand for a review does not, in itself, constitute a formal change in national policy. Any revision would require consideration by the competent authorities and a decision through the country's established institutional framework.
Iran's nuclear policy has long been a subject of international debate, particularly in relation to its stated position against nuclear weapons, its nuclear program and the country's security concerns. A discussion about revising the doctrine therefore raises questions that extend beyond technical nuclear policy to include deterrence, strategic calculations and the country's assessment of the international environment.
Haj Ali Akbari called for the debate to be informed by expert analysis and national considerations, while reaffirming that the Leader would make the final decision.
His remarks signal that calls for a reassessment of Iran's nuclear doctrine have become an issue of public and political discussion, with supporters framing the debate around national security, deterrence and the lessons drawn from past confrontations. Whether that discussion results in any change in policy remains a matter for the country's competent decision-making authorities.

Texas grand jury indicts ICE officer accused of running over man in Houston
The officer faces charges after allegedly striking a fleeing construction worker with an SUV during an immigration raid.
A grand jury in Texas has indicted a United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer accused of deliberately running over a Mexican construction worker during an operation in Houston this month.
ICE officer Mario Alberto Morales faces charges of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon for the October 10 incident, Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare announced on Friday.
Criminal charges against federal immigration officers have been rare during President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, although several encounters involving officers have prompted investigations.
Morales is accused of striking 48-year-old Miguel Parra-Hernandez, an immigrant who has lived in Harris County for more than 30 years. Teare said that Parra-Hernandez had no criminal record.
Parra-Hernandez was running away from federal agents when an unmarked black Jeep Cherokee struck him in a car park near Clay Road and Highway 6, according to investigators. He suffered multiple fractures to his right leg and an ankle injury which required surgery.
The indictment follows a dispute between local prosecutors and federal authorities over what happened. ICE has maintained that Parra-Hernandez ran in front of the vehicle, dismissing the allegations that the officer intentionally struck him as “reckless and false.”
But Teare has said surveillance video contradicts the agency’s account.
It shows the SUV crossing a median and pursuing Parra-Hernandez as he runs away. Although another vehicle obscures the moment of impact, the video shows the man on the ground moments later.
Authorities also released body-camera footage on Friday. In the recording, Morales can be heard acknowledging that he struck Parra-Hernandez with his vehicle.
Teare also accused federal authorities of failing to cooperate with the investigation, including by removing the Jeep before local investigators could examine it for potential evidence.
A search warrant obtained by local media shows investigators had not been granted access to the vehicle as of October 23.
The case has also raised questions about the operation’s intended target. ICE said agents were searching for a man identified as Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, whom they believed to be travelling with Parra-Hernandez.
But Mendoza-Cervantes’s daughter told The New York Times that her father died in 2017. Parra-Hernandez’s family has disputed that the two men knew each other.
The Morales indictment comes as the Harris County District Attorney’s Office continues investigating the fatal shooting of another Mexican, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, on July 7.
An ICE officer, Gregory Feathers, has been accused of firing at the vehicle Salgado Araujo was driving on his way to work in Houston.
Federal authorities said the officer acted in self-defence, a claim the surviving passengers in the vehicle dispute.

retro cocktail bar with multi-chrome lighting and curved steel hides behind barcelona focacceria

retro cocktail bar with multi-chrome lighting and curved steel hides behind barcelona focacceria
behind a neighborhood focacceria storefront on barcelona's carrer tuset, designer isern serra completes focacha, a speakeasy cocktail lounge inspired by space age and verner panton's visiona.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
ISERN SERRA CONCEALS RETRO COCKTAIL BAR BEHIND FOCACCERIA
Designed by Isern Serra for hospitality group Grupo La Confitería (led by Lito Baldovinos and Enric Rebordosa), Focacha is a speakeasy cocktail bar situated at Carrer Tuset 17 in Barcelona. The venue pays programmatic and aesthetic homage to the city’s 1960s and 1970s intellectual counterculture, the ‘gauche divine,’ and night-life figure Oriol Regàs, founder of the historic Bocaccio club. Concealed behind a traditional focacceria storefront designed by Pichy Glass, patrons access the venue through an operable refrigerator door, transitioning from a vernacular culinary retail interior into an immersive two-zone lounge modeled after Verner Panton’s 1968 Visiona installation.
CHROMATIC bar interiors PAY HOMAGE TO VERNER PANTON’S VISIONA
The interior layout, developed by designer Isern Serra, divides into two distinct spatial volumes. The initial bar area is wrapped in continuous carpeting across the floor, walls, and ceiling, establishing a monomaterial envelope referencing Verner Panton’s 1968 Visiona installation. At the center of the room, a curved stainless-steel bar features rounded edge profiles that catch and redistribute ambient reflections. Surrounding the counter, seven distinct seating modules transition across a calibrated chromatic gradient from yellow to crimson and deep blue. Along the perimeter, curvilinear niches recessed into the upholstered walls accommodate both functional back-bar bottle shelving and secluded, low-slung banquette seating. Multi-Lite pendants by GUBI suspend directly overhead, illuminating the metallic work surfaces while highlighting the contrast between the reflective steel counter and the dense, sound-dampening textile surfaces.
DOMED DJ LOUNGE INTEGRATES SCENOGRAPHIC LIGHTING design
The second spatial volume hosts the DJ room, creating a Retro-Futuristic setting. A circular portal cuts through the carpeted wall plane, transitioning into the adjoining music and DJ lounge. Centered under an organic vaulted dome, the volume explores Space Age aesthetics through fluid geometry and enveloping surfaces. Scenographic lighting systems are concealed within circular ceiling apertures and perimeter wall openings, allowing the light temperature and color spectrum to shift dynamically in response to musical tempo. Period-specific luminaires anchor the perimeter seating arrangements, including Louis Poulsen Panthella floor lamps, &Tradition Flowerpot VP2 pendants, and Wire Stool VP11 units, while a central Dana lamp by Tacchini acts as a sculptural focal point beneath the plaster canopy.

designer: Isern Serra | @isernserra
team leaders: Aasheen Mittal, Aran Escudero
graphics: Lo Siento Estudio
client: Grup Confiteria | @grupconfiteria
location: Barcelona, Spain

J&K HC asks Rajouri admin to report on Pakistan-born teen's return to Indian father
SRINAGAR: J&K and Ladakh high court sought a compliance report Friday from the Rajouri district administration on its March 25 order to reunite a Pakistan-born teenager deported after the Pahalgam terror attack with his Indian father on grounds of “sacrosanct human values and rights”.Justice MA Chowdhary’s seven-month-old order, iterated by the single-judge bench of Justice Rahul Bharti, equated the boy’s plight with the “human suffering” and estrangement caused by Partition. “The instant case stems out of this tragedy,” the court said, rejecting the Bureau of Immigration’s contention that the boy had been deported because he didn’t have an active visa.Aasim Sajjad, aka Fardin Sajjad, was born to Rajouri-based govt schoolteacher Sajjad Ahmed and a Pakistani woman, Shabnum Kouser of Rawali in Gujranwala. The marriage took place in Pakistan in Dec 2005 and Aasim was born there on Nov 26 the next year.Sajjad’s wife and son visited India in Oct 2007 on a 90-day visa, which was later extended on marital grounds until 2013. When his wife died on June 5, 2013, Ahmed sought an extension of his son’s visa, granted until April 20, 2015. He then purportedly filed repeated applications for Indian citizenship or visa extension on compassionate grounds, none of which was taken up.
Ahmed alleged that J&K Police raided his house on April 29, 2025, took his son away in a van and deported him through the Wagah border without informing him or handing over a deportation order. The deportation came after the Union govt cancelled visas to all Pakistani citizens after the April 22 terrorist attack on tourists in Pahalgam and ordered them to leave.In its objections, the Foreigners Regional Registration Office (FRRO) argued that Ahmed didn’t “come to court with clean hands” and that his son had been staying in India without a valid visa and was legally bound to leave. The FRRO counsel said the status of the teenager’s citizenship application, which Ahmed claims to have filed, remains “not received yet” on the MHA portal.

Ten products that upgrade office interiors
The following products for offices published on our Showroom section allow for streamlined workplaces that don’t compromise on aesthetics.
These include desks, sit-stand tables as well as those with integrated outlets, modular seating systems and ergonomic task chairs.
Global designers and brands aimed to boost productivity through these items, whether that be by reducing desktop clutter, providing spontaneous opportunities for meetings and light work, or correcting posture to make long periods of sitting less taxing on the body.
Read on to find out more about this selection of workplace furniture.
TOT table by Isern Serra for Omelette Editions
A bisected tabletop with electrical outlets tucked neatly inside characterises this co-working desk by Spanish designer Isern Serra for furniture brand Omelette Editions
Supported by cylindrical legs, the TOT table provides a 12-socket power board, allowing wires to be neatly concealed to eliminate excess visual and physical tabletop clutter.
Muku task chair by Foster + Partners for Okamura
Japanese furniture brand Okamura has released a sleek office chair designed by eminent British studio Foster + Partners.
Muku comes in a sober trio of colourways – light grey, dark grey, red and black – all partly made from recycled materials: recycled aluminium for the frames, and recycled fishing nets for the mesh seat upholstery.
Pullman Modular seating system by NaughtOne
Privacy is created for working away from the desk in this seating system by furniture brand NaughtOne.
All three segments in the Pullman Modular system feature high backs, creating visual seclusion, sound-dampening and room division in open plan interiors.
WiChair by Alina Schnizler for Wilkhahn
Dynamism is given to steel and plywood in this task chair by designer Alina Schnizler for German brand Wilkhahn.
WiChair features a thick, strong spring beneath its seat, which gives bounce to the structure and encourages active sitting.
HUB modular system by Lapalma
Indoor landscapes are created via this undulating modular sofa system created by designer Francesco Rota and Italian brand Lapalma.
HUB aims to create islands of activity in open plan spaces, creating space for working, meeting, conversing and waiting.
TNK500 Aurea task chair by Alegre Design for Actiu
Spanish brand Actiu worked with design firm Alegre Design on this task chair, which has a distinctively metallically-finished frame.
TNK500 Aurea supports healthy posture when working, and is made from almost 60 per cent recycled materials.
Konzert office furniture system by Paolo Dell’Elce for Knoll
Complete private office fit-outs are made cohesive with US furniture brand Knoll and Italian designer Paolo Dell’Elce’s new furnishing system.
Konzert comprises configurable wall panels, tables, seating and storage that come in various curated colourways and finishes.
Menssula sit-stand work tables by Actiu
Seated and standing work and meetings alike are made possible by this series of tables by office furniture brand Actiu.
Menssula sit-stand work tables come in various sizes and formats, all containing an electrically-powered height raising mechanism.
HÅG Minu by Flokk
Norwegian designers Andreas Engesvik and Jannicke Grung have created a compact and lighthearted task chair for Flokk-owned furniture brand HÅG
HÅG Minu comes in seven designer-curated curated colourways and aims to bring the comfort and casualness of residential furniture to workplaces.
Eden pods by Boss Design
British furniture brand Boss Design aimed to bring adaptability and personalisation to this range of office booths.
Eden pods can be fitted out with lounge furniture, tactile cladding and finishes, and planters on their roofs to bring the health and wellbeing of plants into workplaces.

IN BRIEF: How humanitarian mission in Alyoshki went
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
18:59:26 UTC
03:59:26 KST

MOSCOW, October 30. /TASS/. Some residents of Alyoshki in the Kherson Region travelled freely towards Russia, while the others travelled to Ukraine, said Russia’s Commissioner for Human Rights Yana Lantratova.
TASS has compiled the key facts about the humanitarian mission.
Lantratova's statements
- Lantratova said that Alyoshki residents thanked all parties for carrying out the humanitarian mission: "It's very important that people waited, they thank both sides."
- According to her, some of the residents travelled "absolutely unhindered" towards Russia, the others to Ukraine: "People gathered, families with children, the elderly, and buses were organized."
- She said that the residents took their pets with them.
- Humanitarian aid was provided to those who were unable to leave the town due to various circumstances.
- Lantratova said that everything was going on normally: "Both offices of the ombudspersons are monitoring the situation."
- She noted the contribution of the First Lady of the United States Melania Trump to the organization of the humanitarian mission: "This is very important to us, and we thank the First Lady for helping people, for saving lives."
Statements by the Ukrainian ombudsman
- Ukraine’s Ombudsman Dmitry Lubinets declared full observance of the silence regime in the Kherson direction and the absence of any violations from the moment of its establishment: "We came to Alyoshki as safely as was possible in the current conditions. The silence regime is fully respected. I emphasize that there have been no violations since the establishment of the silence regime."
- He said that residents of the city who did not have time to submit an evacuation request can still leave the town: " "There are already cases when people who did not sign up came - they were also given the opportunity: ‘Please, come in if you want to leave Alyoshki’."
Lubinets highly appreciated the work of Lantratova's team in Alyoshki, noting high professionalism of the staff: "Yana Valeryevna's staff, together with my staff, have worked out a very systematic approach. And today we are really here, on the ground, seeing how everything works. This is why I rate the organization of the work as very professional, for which I am especially grateful to Yana Valeryevna."
Preparation of the humanitarian corridor
- On the evening of October 29, the Russian military completed the clearance of routes for the humanitarian mission in Alyoshki.
- The Dnepr battlegroup neutralized the roads adjacent to the town from unexploded ordnance, the Russian Defense Ministry said.
- Two people, including a field engineer, were killed while demining to ensure the safe passage of a humanitarian mission, Lantratova said.
- According to the ministry, field engineer of the 98th Guards Airborne Division, Sergeant Andrey Vedernikov was killed.
- Earlier, the Defense Ministry said that Ukraine was remotely mining access roads with drones to prevent the evacuation of civilians and block the delivery of food, medicines and socially important goods to the town.
On conducting a humanitarian operation
- The humanitarian mission in Alyoshki is taking place in full compliance with the agreements between Russia and Ukraine, Melania Trump said.
- In the town, Lantratova and Lubinets coordinated the implementation of the agreements reached with the assistance of the First Lady of the United States.
- The Alyoshki residents who decided to leave the settlement could do so before 2:00 p.m. Moscow time (11:00 a.m. GMT).
- The distribution of humanitarian aid was scheduled for after 2:30 p.m. Moscow time (11:30 a.m. GMT)..
- All security measures were taken.
- According to Lantratova, several dozen tons of humanitarian aid were distributed to the residents of Alyoshki - food, hygiene products, fuel for generators and other necessary things. The list of what is needed was compiled at the request of the residents.
- She noted that it is important for those who decided to stay in the settlement.
- Lantratova said that the ombudspersons of Russia and Ukraine are considering regular delivery of humanitarian aid to Alyoshki.
- Chairman of the Russian Red Cross Pavel Savchuk said that the RCC provided humanitarian aid to the people in Alyoshki. The cargo was delivered by the office of Russia’s ombudsman as part of a humanitarian mission.
Evacuation of the people
- A humanitarian aid convoy was sent to the central district hospital.
- It consisted of 25 buses, Lantratova said.
- Special buses for bedridden people with 30 seats and nine ambulances were also prepared.
- A separate bus was also organized for people with pets.
- On the afternoon of October 30, Lantratova said that all those who expressed the desire to leave Alyoshki were placed on the evacuation buses.
- According to her, people traveled to both Russia and Ukraine.
- On October 26, Lantratova called Kiev's statements about the forced removal of children from Alyoshki unacceptable.
- The ombudswoman called on Ukraine to give the residents of Alyoshki the opportunity to make an informed decision, let them live in peace and order their military to stop the daily shelling of the town and mining roads.
The work of journalists
- According to Lantratova, more than 50 journalists from different countries arrived in the Kherson Region to cover the operation.
- As the ombudswoman noted, all of them will be able to personally communicate with the residents of Alyoshki.
- The humanitarian mission in the city was documented, among others, by Newsmax journalists.
- Melania Trump said they act as neutral observers, will independently film and document the progress of the mission.
- One of the American journalists from the mission, John Chay, said that he was in touch with the first lady of the United States.
Russian Presidential Spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he considers the presence of Russian, not foreign, journalists to be the key to covering the humanitarian mission.
Coordination of the humanitarian operation in Alyoshki
- According to Lantratova, the humanitarian mission in Alyoshki has been prepared since May.
- As previously reported by Russia’s Chief of the General Staff, Army General Valery Gerasimov, Russian troops will introduce a ceasefire regime in the Kherson direction from 4:00 a.m. Moscow time (1:00 a.m. GMT) on October 27 for the humanitarian operation.
- Ukraine’s General Staff also said it was complying with the ceasefire from 4:00 a.m. Moscow time (1:00 a.m. GMT) on October 27.
- Lantratova later said that the temporary ceasefire in the Kherson direction would last until 10:59 p.m. Moscow time (7:59 p.m. GMT) on November 1.
- Since the beginning of the silence regime, she has been reporting daily on its observance by both sides.
Reaction to the announcement of the ceasefire
- Lantratova thanked Melania Trump and all the participants of the negotiating group for their cooperation in organizing a humanitarian mission in Alyoshki.
- UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres welcomed the agreement, his official representative Stephane Dujarric said in a statement.
- White House Communications Director Steven Cheung called the agreements an important step towards resolving the Ukrainian conflict.
The situation in Alyoshki
- On September 21, Peskov called the humanitarian situation in Alyoshki critical.
- It was impossible to bring food or medicines to the town due to shelling and drone attacks from Kiev.
- On September 1, a determined attempt was made to break the blockade of Alyosha to deliver humanitarian aid to the people, but Ukrainian militants fired at a convoy of vehicles and almost completely destroyed the cargo, said Rodion Miroshnik, Ambassador-at-large of the Russian Foreign Ministry for crimes of the Kiev regime.
- A little more than 1,000 people remain in Alyoshki, he informed.
- Miroshnik noted that the situation has worsened in the last four to five months.
- Residents of nearby settlements on the left bank of the Dnepr River tried to deliver food to Alyoshki, but Ukraine prevented this, evacuated resident Svetlana Popova told TASS.
- According to her, the civilian population of the city did not receive humanitarian aid from Ukraine, all reports about this are lies.
