Fire Devastated a Mongolian Nature Reserve. Who’s to Blame?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
18:57:00 UTC
03:57:00 KST

On October 8, a massive fire broke out in Numrug, a nature reserve in Khakhgol soum, Dornod aimag (province), Mongolia. The flames were not completely extinguished until October 16.
According to statistics from the Ministry of Natural Environment and Climate Change of Mongolia released on October 28, the total area burned by the fire amounted to 504,960.4 hectares, approximately 5,050 square kilometers or 1.2 million acres. That’s more than twice the area of Tokyo, Japan’s capital. Nearly all of the damaged land – 448,993.6 hectares – was in the Numrug Strictly Protested Area. Over three-quarters (76.4 percent) of the nature reserve’s total area was affected by the fire.
According to preliminary investigations by Mongolian authorities, the fire was directly caused by a vehicle convoy belonging to Mongolian mobile communication operator Mobicom, which is 98.8 percent controlled by Japanese telecommunications giant KDDI. The chassis of one vehicle became wrapped in dry plants, and prolonged driving caused friction and heat to ignite the grasses. That set off the larger fire.
The fire was located in an area adjacent to the China-Mongolia border, and the issue was compounded by the involvement of a Japanese firm and disputes over border communication infrastructure. Thus it quickly escalated from an ecological event to a geopolitical issue affecting Mongolia, China, and Japan, becoming a landmark sample for observing the logic of cross-border environmental governance and capital regulation in Northeast Asia.
Shortcomings in Ecological Governance
The Numrug Strictly Protected Area is located in the transitional zone between the western foothills of the Greater Khingan Range and the eastern grasslands of Mongolia. It is an important source of biological diversity and an ecological security barrier in Northeast Asia, inhabited by various rare species listed in both the IUCN Red List and Mongolian Red Book, such as the Ussuri moose, black billed capercaillie, and Far Eastern taimen fish, as well as more than 250 species of birds.
The impact of high-intensity burning in autumn on the ecosystem is long-term and irreversible. The organic matter on the surface of the soil is completely carbonized, and the soil’s ability to retain water and nutrients has been greatly diminished. When strong winds arrive in spring and autumn, the risk of regional desertification and sandstorms will significantly increase.
The native vegetation seed bank has also suffered a devastating blow. According to ecological observation data from cold and arid grasslands, it will take at least 20 to 100 years for the native community in this area to fully recover, and permanent species replacement may occur in some areas.
The fire points to an alarming structural failure of environmental governance in Mongolia, even within a protected nature reserve. On the one hand, the government is known for “heavy approval, light supervision” and “heavy firefighting, light prevention.” During autumn, the high-risk period for fires, the core protected areas are still open to commercial vehicles. There is a complete lack of environmental risk assessments and fire prevention verification before human activities.
On the other hand, there is a lack of ecological monitoring and emergency response capabilities. Minister of Natural Environment and Climate Change Sandag-Ochir Tsend admitted that due to the complex terrain and logistical conditions, it is difficult to carry out on-site assessments after disasters. Mongolia’s remote areas have long relied on satellite remote sensing monitoring, and there are obvious shortcomings in the logistics support capabilities for ground verification and emergency response.
Cross-border Ecological Risk and Geopolitical Implications
The fire line approached the Mongolia-China border, directly triggering a cross-border emergency response. According to the 1999 agreement between China and Mongolia on Forest and Grassland Fire Prevention in Border Areas, more than 3,400 professional firefighting and emergency forces were quickly mobilized in Inner Mongolia, China. China was able to keep the fire from crossing the national border, while keeping a passage open for wild animals escaping across the border.
Liu Zhiyan, a researcher at the Institute of Ecological Civilization of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, pointed out that the grasslands in eastern Mongolia are highly interconnected with ecology in northern China. If the fire spreads across borders, it will not only cause huge economic losses, but may also trigger serious diplomatic disputes. Viewed in this light, Mongolia’s passive approach has given it the image of an “ecological risk exporting country.”
The Chinese side invested a large amount of manpower and material resources to intercept the fire. Now China is demanding that it be compensated for the effort – not by Mongolia, but by Japan.
The illegal entry of Japanese companies into the core protected area and the resulting catastrophe have directly undermined Japan’s long-standing image as a responsible green investor in Mongolia.
According to the Japanese embassy in Mongolia, Japan’s official development assistance (ODA) to Mongolia from 1977 to 2021 has accumulated to 364.107 billion yen, covering multiple fields such as infrastructure, energy, and communication. Mobicom was once a benchmark project for Japan Mongolia economic and trade cooperation. Now public anger is running high.
Early on, Mobicom sought to avoid responsibility, saying it had followed “complete legal procedures.” It only publicly apologized and promised to cooperate with the investigation after the public opinion pressure escalated. While Mobicom has now agreed to provide compensation, after a joint working group assesses the loss and damage, the company still insists that it had the proper permits and took necessary precautions.
Mobicom stated that its vehicles entered the protected area to conduct 4G network communication tests, but the project is located adjacent to the Mongolia-China Sumber-Rashaan Border Port, and its technical and economic rationality has been widely questioned by the Mongolian public. According to the 2010 Sino-Mongolian Treaty on the Management of the Border Regime, both sides must give prior notice of major border projects and wireless facilities construction. Thus Mobicom’s presence in the border area also could have an impact on mutual trust in border security between Mongolia and China. Some analysts in Chinese media have raised concerns about information security regarding Japanese communication projects in sensitive border areas, but these claims have not been officially confirmed.
Adding to the discontent, Japanese Chief Cabinet Secretary Kihara Minoru did not make an official statement until October 26, two weeks after the fire broke out. He then only mentioned Japan’s willingness to assist Mongolia in ecological restoration, with no mention of the impact on China. This further exacerbated the geopolitical rift.
On October 29, Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae held 10-minute telephone call with Mongolian Prime Minister Uchral Nyam-Osor, marking the highest‑level bilateral exchange since the disaster. During the call, Takaichi stated that the government of Japan “takes seriously the scale of the damage caused” by the fire, “and extended her heartfelt sympathies to the people of Mongolia.”
She said that Japan “intends to provide a package of cooperation that contributes to the recovery of the affected areas, including the provision of necessary equipment to Mongolia and human resource development in the fields of recovery from the wild fires and environmental restoration.” The package will be based on an on‑site assessment from Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) experts in forestry and natural environment conservation dispatched on October 27. Takaichi pledged “close communication” with the Mongolian government through the assessment and compensation process.
In response, Uchral briefed Takaichi on the full extent of the disaster damage. He expressed deep gratitude for Japan’s sympathy and support offer, and welcomed Japan’s “science‑based approach” to advancing “ecological restoration in a phased and effective manner,” adding that Mongolia stands ready to cooperate closely with Japan on all recovery efforts. The two leaders also agreed to further strengthen bilateral friendly relations and practical cooperation ahead of the 55th anniversary of the establishment of Japan‑Mongolia diplomatic relations in 2027.
According to the official readouts released by both governments, the brief conversation focused exclusively on Japan‑Mongolia bilateral relief and diplomatic agenda. No reference was made to China’s large‑scale firefighting deployment along the border, nor to the cross‑border spillover risks the fire had posed to Chinese territory.
Three Countries, Three Positions
The incident has caused strong reactions in the political, academic, and public opinion circles of Mongolia, China, and Japan, with clear differences in interests and positions among all parties.
In Mongolia, the fire raised questions of sovereignty, accountability, and internal reflection. Uchral classified it as a “serious ecological incident” at a Cabinet meeting. He stated clearly that “foreign investors have no privilege above Mongolian law,” and demanded a thorough investigation of the process of granting access permits to protected areas. He vowed to hold the companies and officials involved accountable according to law, via a comprehensive ecological loss assessment and compensation procedure.
Member of Parliament Altangerel Oyunsaikhan, part of the opposition Democratic Party, has put forward a more radical demand for accountability. He demanded that the judiciary freeze all of Mobicom’s assets and financial accounts in Mongolia as collateral for ecological compensation.
Former sumo wrestler Yokozuna Asashoryu (Dagvadorj Dolgorsuren in Mongolia), who has broad social influence, took a different view. He pointed the finger at Mongolia’s internal governance and bluntly stated that “blindly condemning the Japanese side is one-sided.” He called on the media to thoroughly investigate the officials who issued the permits for Mobicom’s entrance into Numrug, suggesting local regulatory corruption.
Asashoryu’s intervention may have pushed regional border officials and political networks, including Dornod MP Otgonbayar Ukhnaa, brother of President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa, into a fierce media storm over who approved the convoy. However, Otgonbayar firmly denied any involvement in this matter, claiming that the questions were a politically motivated smear campaign.
At the Japanese level, there is anxiety over both corporate responsibility and national image. Shimba Kazuya , the secretary general of Japan’s Democratic Party for the People (DPFP), publicly criticized the incident as far beyond the scope of corporate civil liability. He demanded that the government intervene at the national level to demonstrate the sincerity of Mongolia in assuming responsibility.
Domestic public opinion in Japan generally accuses the government of a slow response and double standards. Japan’s government is highly sensitive to minor environmental damage, while Japanese companies have caused world-class ecological damage. Kihara’s delayed statement has been criticized by opposition parties and the media as diplomatic incompetence and corporate protectionism. Some called the two-week silence from Tokyo a “national shame.”
Voices across Japan’s ruling and opposition camps have converged on the need for accountability, though with differing strategic priorities. Within the ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP), former State Minister for Foreign Affairs Nakayama Yasuhide argued on ABEMA News that while corporate giant KDDI and its subsidiary Mobicom must assume absolute civil, financial, and moral liability, this isolated operational failure must be strictly decoupled from Japan’s sovereign alignment with Mongolia.
Given Ulaanbaatar’s historical value as an irreplaceable diplomatic mediator in resolving the existential national security issue of North Korean abductions, Nakayama stressed that the bilateral strategic bond is far too critical to be compromised by a single corporate incident. He emphasized that the sensitive geographical positioning of this infrastructure along the China-Mongolia and Russia-Mongolia frontiers poses a direct geopolitical signal intelligence risk, meaning that any erosion of Japan’s “third neighbor” status would directly compromise regional security networks.
Concurrently, LDP lawmaker Nagashima Akihisa, chairperson of the Japan-Mongolia Parliamentary Friendship League, fortified the legal defense by highlighting that the Mobicom convoy entered under explicit administrative approval and was actively escorted by Mongolian border port authorities. Consequently, Nagashima condemned premature external judgments. Alongside Nakayama, he flatly rejected Chinese state media demands for a formal apology to Beijing, dismissing them as an unverified cross-border political distortion designed to manufacture leverage.
This unified realist defense has allowed Takaichi to execute her own response. By initiating a direct call with Uchral and deploying a state-backed JICA Environmental Revitalization Expert Group, Takaichi is masterfully deploying sovereign “green diplomacy” to absorb the recovery portfolio, effectively shielding and isolating Japan’s strategic footprint and critical infrastructure map in Mongolia from third-party regional intervention.
Environmental Governance
Beyond the geopolitical implications, the Numrug fire stands as a stark example of the limits of corporate Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) commitments, which too often exist only on paper. KDDI, a leading telecommunications giant in Japan, enforces exceptionally stringent environmental and production safety standards domestically, yet its overseas operations reveal a troubling double standard. By sending a vehicle convoy deep into the core zone of a strictly protected nature reserve during the highest-risk wildfire season, Mobicom exposed a severe discrepancy in risk management. The company’s ability to navigate local regulations via special administrative clearances underscores a systemic exploitation of gaps in host-country environmental oversight.
The lackluster on-site emergency response capabilities further confirmed a catastrophic failure of risk control. Reports indicate that the corporate management team was completely unequipped with professional firefighting tools suitable for open grassland suppression. That’s why the initial fire could not be contained and spread to such a large scale. This critical deficiency pierces the superficial narrative of polished ESG reporting. For many multinational enterprises, complex risk-management and environmental emergency blueprints serve primarily as public relations assets for capital market ratings; when put to a real-world test on the frontlines of a disaster, these theoretical systems fall apart completely.
The ecological cost to Numrug provides a profound warning for cross-border environmental governance in Northeast Asia. To prevent another disaster on this level, there are steps that must be taken by Mongolia specifically and the region collectively.
First, Mongolia should improve the environmental responsibility system for foreign investment. That means promoting the introduction of specialized ecological responsibility regulations for foreign-invested enterprises. High-risk foreign-invested enterprises should be required to set aside environmental safety and quality deposits, as a certain proportion based on their total investment amount, which should be deposited into the central bank’s special account for ecological restoration after accidents.
At the same time, the United Nations ecosystem service valuation standards should be used to calculate the total damages. The U.N. standards include soil carbon sink loss, biodiversity damage, and the costs of managing secondary disasters, thereby significantly increasing the cost of environmental non-compliance.
In terms of technical capabilities, it is necessary to establish an integrated air-ground environmental monitoring network and deploy automated infrared drone patrol systems to enable precise, minute-level early warning of fires during high-risk periods. Furthermore, the equipment and operational authority of the protected area’s law enforcement teams should be upgraded to strengthen the verification of personnel and equipment entering from outside the borders, thereby preventing unauthorized activities conducted under the guise of commercial operations.
Regarding regional cooperation, efforts should be made to upgrade the border fire prevention and control agreement between Mongolia and China, explore the establishment of a green channel for cross-border emergency firefighting within a certain range of the border, and simplify the approval process for cross-border rescue in major fire situations. At the same time, we can promote the establishment of a transnational environmental infringement liability recovery mechanism, and the United Nations Environment Program can promote the establishment of a long-term ecological trust fund supported by the responsible enterprises, specifically for regional ecological restoration and biodiversity protection. This would create a closed-loop system encompassing incident response, compensation, and long-term management.
The ashes that have replaced three-quarters of the Numrug grasslands are a painful reflection of the backwardness of the cross-border environmental governance system in Northeast Asia. In the context of the interweaving of climate change and geopolitical games, environmental governance is no longer the internal affair of a single country, but a core issue related to national sovereignty, regional security, and multilateral trust. Only by constraining the environmental responsibility of transnational capital with rigid systems and filling the blind spots in border governance through multilateral cooperation can we truly build a resilient ecological security barrier for Northeast Asia.

Five children among seven dead in eastern Syria floods
Oct 30 - Seven people, including five children, have died and seven others were injured after torrential rains triggered flash floods in eastern Syria, authorities said on Friday.
Four people remain missing and rescue teams are continuing to search flooded areas, Emergency and Disaster Management Minister Raed al-Saleh said in a statement on X.
The five children drowned in pools of water formed by the floods, while another person died in a traffic accident, Saleh said, without providing details of the seventh death.
Flooding has hit the eastern provinces of Raqqa, Deir al-Zor and Hasakah, as well as parts of Aleppo, damaging infrastructure, cutting off roads and forcing families to leave their homes.
Syria's civil defence teams have carried out more than 550 emergency operations since the storms began, rescuing 60 people trapped by floodwater and responding to more than 900 distress calls, Saleh said.
Emergency crews evacuated more than 350 students from two schools and helped 375 families leave camps in Raqqa province. Teams also responded to flooding at camps in rural Aleppo and Idlib, and pumped water from around 250 homes and public buildings.
In Deir al-Zor, the floods damaged roads and telecommunications infrastructure, disrupting transport and communications, state news agency SANA reported. Heavy rainfall also caused seven culverts to collapse, cutting off access to several areas.
Authorities suspended classes in Raqqa, Hasakah and Deir al-Zor on Thursday, while forecasters warned unsettled weather could continue into Saturday. REUTERS

Berlin student protests: youth demands meet extremist mobilisation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
18:53:30 UTC
03:53:30 KST

According to police, around 5,000 people joined a demonstration by the initiative "Gen Z regelt" at Berlin’s Brandenburg Gate. In the afternoon, organisers claimed some 11,000 participants had taken part.
A protest rally organised by the youth initiative “Gen Z regelt” was held in Berlin on Saturday, with demonstrators calling for more investment in education and an end to rearmament.
Pro-Palestine activists, flags and slogans were prominently visible among the crowd gathered at the Brandenburg Gate.
The rally began at 2 p.m. Its stated demands include more money for schools and climate protection, affordable living costs and no compulsory military service. Organisers promised a peaceful event.
Even so, some shops on Unter den Linden, Friedrichstraße and Kurfürstendamm put up barricades to guard against possible looting.
Pro-Palestine presence across the square
At the entrance to the Brandenburg Gate, a man in a jumper in the colours of the Palestinian flag handed out flyers. Beside him, a representative of the daily newspaper "Junge Welt” offered brochures and copies. The paper is monitored by Germany’s domestic intelligence service, which classifies it as far-left extremist.
Further along, at Platz des 18. März, Palestinian flags flew alongside anarchist and Antifa banners. Some signs focused on military spending, with slogans such as “Flunked the PISA test but passed the military medical” and “Money for social causes instead of war”. Others went further, reading “German weapons kill children in Palestine”, “No money for children’s homes, schools & women’s refuges, but money for war and genocide” and “Stop the genocide in Gaza”.
Many of those present, mostly young men and women, wore the red or black Palestinian scarf known as the kufiya. Some wore it around their necks; others wrapped it around their heads or draped it over their shoulders like a cape.
“Not a single cent left for education”
Euronews spoke to a group of young women who said they were aged 19 to 20 and doing a voluntary social year (FSJ).
They said they had come partly to show solidarity with France and the protests across Europe, but above all to make the point that young people do not feel seen or taken seriously by politicians.
“There is constant militarisation and rearmament, and there is simply not a single cent left for education and social spending,” one of them said.
Two of the women wore a kufiya around their necks. Asked what the conflict in the Middle East has to do with the school student protests, one replied: “It has to do with the fact that we as young people, or as people in Germany in general, also have to take responsibility for the fact that weapons are produced here that are used to kill civilians and children in Palestine, in Gaza and in the West Bank.”
She added: “I do not think I could ever live with myself if I never paid any attention to this.”
“I do not want FU to support a genocide”
A little further away stood a young man with a Palestinian scarf around his neck. He studies chemistry at Freie Universität (FU), where there have repeatedly been pro-Palestine occupations in recent years.
He said he came because universities face ever more cuts, while rents are rising and students have to work on the side. “At some point it simply becomes impossible,” he said. Young people, he added, are also suffering massively from the arms build-up. “I am just angry about what is happening right now.”
He said he wears the scarf because of his university. FU has eleven cooperation projects with Israel, he said, and so indirectly supports research for war. He argued this also affects Germany, because the Federal Republic buys military equipment from Israel.
“I do not want our universities to exist to build war products. I do not want FU to support a genocide,” he said.
Part of a wider European movement
The Berlin rally is part of a wave of youth-led protests across Europe. In France, demonstrations that began last month as a high school student movement have since drawn in labour unions and others angry at President Emmanuel Macron, while rallies were also reported in the Netherlands, Italy and Spain on Saturday.
Critics in Germany, however, say some openly radical groups were represented at the demonstration
Among the demonstrators there are also representatives of radical left-wing groups. Alongside Antifa flags, the youth organisation "Linksjugend ['solid]", the youth wing of the Left Party, is present in smaller numbers. It has long faced criticism over accusations of antisemitism. The Neukölln branch in particular has made headlines recently. The Berlin Linksjugend has also repeatedly come under fire for its anti-Israeli resolutions and its stance on the Middle East conflict.
The "Revolutionäre Linke" was also represented with its own stand. In early 2023 members of the federal working group "Revolutionäre Linke" founded the separate organisation "Jugend für Sozialismus". The background was growing conflicts with the leadership of the youth organisation, which they accused of political adaptation, a lack of class struggle and undemocratic structures.
The organisation criticises the trend of more money for the Bundeswehr and less for hospitals and other social spending. "We see that it is our young generation that will be hit hardest and for the longest time."
Their goal, they say, is to build a better society. That is why they are here. It should be in the interests of every left wing organisation to take part in such events, they argue, because this is where the real power to bring about change lies.
Asked what the issue of Palestine and the conflict in the Middle East have to do with the protests, he replies, "We always put out all our information materials. However, there is also a link here. One of the major problems is that, despite everything that is happening, the Bundeswehr continues to carry out drone tests together with the Israeli army, and weapons are still being sold to Israel. We strongly condemn this. And of course it is also connected with conscription and the expansion of the Bundeswehr here."
Contradictory statements from security authorities
The press office of the Berlin police told Euronews in response to a query two days before the protests that individual groups from the left wing political spectrum were picking up on the protests in France and issuing calls to mobilise. "However, there is currently no reliable evidence of targeted extremist influence or control over this group."
Euronews research paints a different picture. Shortly before the protests in Berlin, serious threats of violence appeared in a private Telegram group. As the "Berliner Zeitung" (B.Z.) reports, one user announced possible violence with the words "I am going out with a machete". Others threatened attacks on synagogues, looting and arson.
The press office of the Berlin Senate Department for the Interior and Sport told Euronews in response to a query beforehand that actors from parts of the left wing extremist and foreign related extremist spectrum were also mobilising for the demonstrations on 31 October.
Their aim in taking part is likely, among other things, to co-opt and radicalise the protests. "Legitimate civil society protest is thereby supposed to be reinterpreted as a struggle against the rule of law and liberal democracy." In the case of individual left-wing extremist actors who are calling for participation, it must also be assumed that they have a basic interest in escalation.
Unclear structures and withdrawal of organisers
Shortly beforehand, several organisers and supporters had distanced themselves from the initiative "Gen Z regelt".
The previous spokesperson Gianni Matheja justified his withdrawal by pointing to differing views within the movement and doubts that the protests would remain peaceful. Berlin supporters Max Schneller and Battal Yali also pulled out of the initiative.
The supporters who stepped down criticised unclear responsibilities and a lack of transparency in the organisation and funding of the protests. According to research by the Tagesspiegel, the Berlin organising team had largely fallen apart for a time. Shortly afterwards, however, new members joined.
The initiative "Gen Z regelt" emphasised the peaceful nature of the nationwide school student protests planned for Saturday 31 October. As the "Münchner Merkur" reported, citing "Die Zeit", 16-year-old co-organiser Konrad Schmitz from Wuppertal said, "We want to fight peacefully for our cause." He said he rejected extremism from both the left and the right.
The 18-year-old co-founder Akram Selo also reported numerous threats in recent days. "They think we want to copy the French; they think we want to destroy the country."
Up to 5 p.m. the protests at the Brandenburg Gate remained peaceful.
Second demonstration at Rosenthaler Platz in the police spotlight
Alongside the rally at the Brandenburg Gate, the Berlin police are also focusing on another demonstration in the capital.
Under the slogan "Gen Z has had enough!", a gathering is due to assemble at Rosenthaler Platz from 5.30 p.m. The police initially expect around 400 to 500 participants, though it cannot be ruled out that significantly more people will join the protest.
The initiative "Gen Z regelt" has clearly distanced itself from this demonstration. Nevertheless, in the afternoon dozens of men and women at the Brandenburg Gate are handing out flyers pointing to the evening event. Neither the press team nor the stewards on site are stopping them.
According to the assessment of the security authorities, the demonstration is being mobilised, among others, from the left wing political spectrum. Participants from the pro Palestine scene are also expected. The event is furthermore being promoted in the far left extremist milieu.
The planned demonstration route leads from Rosenthaler Platz along Kastanienallee, Schönhauser Allee and Danziger Straße to Prenzlauer Allee suburban railway station. Euronews is on site and will report on the demonstration.

London police arrest 48 as hundreds protest Palestine Action ban
Demonstrations in London and Edinburgh come days before a UK Supreme Court appeal challenging the group’s proscription.
Police have arrested at least 48 people after protesters defied a warning not to attend a rally in London against the proscription of Palestine Action, which is classified as a “terrorist” organisation under United Kingdom law.
Hundreds of people gathered outside the United States embassy on Saturday to oppose the ban, which came into effect in July last year under the government of then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer.
The demonstration comes ahead of a Supreme Court appeal on Wednesday challenging the campaign group’s proscription.
“So far this afternoon, officers have arrested 48 people,” London’s Metropolitan Police said in a statement posted on X. “The majority of arrests have been for expressing support for a proscribed organisation. Officers remain at the scene and are continuing to make arrests.”
Responding to the police statement, Labour Party MP John McDonnell posted on X, saying someone protesting against the government’s decision to proscribe an organisation cannot be “automatically interpreted” as them supporting that organisation and “therefore committing an arrestable offence”.
He added that he believes the government “made the wrong decision in proscribing Palestine Action as a terrorist organisation”.
Saturday’s rally is the first mass protest against the proscription since Prime Minister Andy Burnham assumed office in July.
The decision to designate the group a “terrorist” organisation has triggered uproar among sections of British society, with critics arguing that it is part of a wider crackdown aimed at silencing pro-Palestine voices. The proscription means Palestine Action has been added to a list of banned organisations that also includes al-Qaeda and ISIL (ISIS).
UK ‘appeasing Trump and Israeli weapons companies’
Protesters also gathered outside the US consulate in Edinburgh, the Scottish capital. There have been no reports of arrests there.
Demonstrators in both London and Edinburgh could be seen holding placards reading “I oppose genocide. I support Palestine Action”.
Defend Our Juries, which organised the protests, said Saturday’s arrests took the total number of people detained for defying the Palestine Action ban to more than 4,000 since July 2025.
“It is truly dystopian that there have now been over 4,000 arrests under terror laws for peaceful vigils silently expressing opposition to genocide and support for the protest group Palestine Action,” a spokesperson for the group said, as reported by UK news agency Press Association.
“The ban on Palestine Action was straight out of [US President Donald] Trump’s playbook, so it’s fitting that this significant milestone has been reached on Halloween and outside the US embassy,” the spokesperson added, saying the proscription was about the UK government “appeasing Trump and the Israeli weapons companies that Palestine Action disrupted, not about any kind of terrorist threat”.
Felix Jakens, Amnesty International UK’s head of communications and campaigns, also called on the government to reverse Palestine Action’s proscription.
“The sight yet again of grandparents, teenagers and everyone in between being hauled into police vans for peacefully holding placards is a disgraceful attack on freedom of speech,” Jakens said in response to the arrests on Saturday.
“It’s past time for the government to drop the proscription of Palestine Action and reform our laws so that communities have more power to demonstrate on the issues they care about, not less.”

Tension and clashes as hundreds of thousands protest again in France
Authorities say 320,000 march on third consecutive weekend of demonstrations over cost of living and state of schools.
Police have fired tear gas at protesters in Paris and Lyon as hundreds of thousands of mostly young people marched across France over the cost of living and the state of the country’s schools.
Saturday’s rallies were the third consecutive weekend of demonstrations in France.
A coalition of youth organisations and unions representing high school and university students said nearly half a million people took part, including 200,000 in Paris. The authorities put the nationwide turnout at 320,000, including 70,000 in the capital.
Marches in the capital began peacefully, but turned violent as protesters gathered near the point where the main march was due to end on Saturday. Bins and street furniture were set alight, and plumes of smoke could be seen rising over the city.
“What we’ve been seeing … is the police firing a lot of tear gas into this crowd,” said Al Jazeera’s Natacha Butler, reporting from Paris, adding that her team “had to move out of the way because it was simply too much for us to breathe”.
Riot police warned over loudspeakers that they would fire more tear gas if protesters did not clear the street. Medics carried away people who had been injured, while some protesters raised their hands to show police they meant no harm.
Dozens of masked people dressed in black also used hammers to pry up paving stones and hurl them at police on the outskirts of Paris, the AFP news agency reported. At least one incendiary device was also thrown at security forces, who responded with tear gas and baton charges.
France’s Ministry of Interior said at least 290 people nationwide had so far been arrested.
Protesters say ‘trust has gone’
Butler said most protesters condemned the violence, but many blamed the government for failing to listen to them.
“You really get a sense with people who have come into the street again and again over the past few weeks that they simply don’t believe the government any more. That trust has gone,” she said.
The government says it has heard the protesters. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has held several meetings with student unions this week and is looking at measures to ease the cost of living.
About 70,000 police and gendarmes were deployed across the country, and Interior Minister Laurent Nunez warned of a “very high risk” of disorder, especially after dark on Halloween.
The main Paris march was moved to the city’s eastern edge after a last-minute court battle, and unaccompanied minors faced a 9pm (20:00 GMT) curfew around the Champs-Elysees.
The movement began last month with high school students protesting against neglected buildings, teacher shortages and a university admissions system seen as unfair to disadvantaged students. Labour unions have since joined.
Rallies spread across Europe
On October 17, protests drew more than 500,000 people and turned into some of France’s worst rioting in years, according to government estimates, with shops in Paris looted.
Meanwhile, protests have taken place in other cities across Europe.
On Saturday, young people in Germany were the latest to join the fray.
Thousands rallied while police in Cologne used water cannon to break up large crowds protesting against rising costs, education cuts and plans for military conscription. Organisers said 170,000 people had registered for demonstrations in more than 30 cities.
In Barcelona, Spain, regional police prepared their highest alert level after rioting on October 24 led to about 130 arrests, mostly of minors.
Italian police were also on alert after clashes in Milan, Turin and Bologna.

Russia to remain reliable energy, food supplier — Lavrov at G20

MOSCOW, October 31. /TASS/. Russia will remain a leading supplier of energy, food and fertilizers, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said at the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting in Atlanta, according to a Russian Foreign Ministry statement.

'Nearly half a million' flood French streets as protests turn violent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
18:53:32 UTC
03:53:32 KST

Nearly half a million people have demonstrated across France, including 200,000 in Paris, according to a coalition of youth organisations and unions representing high school and university students.
Authorities put Saturday’s nationwide turnout at 320,000, including 70,000 in the French capital. A week earlier, officials counted 410,000 protesters across France, including 110,000 in Paris.
The third consecutive weekend of nationwide protests focused on high living costs and police violence. Demonstrations were largely peaceful before tensions flared at the end of marches in Paris, Marseille, Lyon and other cities.
Some demonstrators wore Halloween costumes and carried placards reading: “No need for tear gas to make our future look bleak” and “Dressed up as an angry citizen for Halloween.”
Clashes in several cities
In Lyon, tensions emerged after some demonstrators tried to leave the authorised route near Place Jean Mace and move towards the city centre, prompting police to use tear gas, according to Franceinfo. Projectiles were also thrown at officers.
In Grenoble, southeastern France, police used tear gas after initial tensions near Place Gustave Rivet, where a march split into two.
In Marseille, clashes broke out at the front of an unauthorised march, with protesters throwing paving stones at riot police blocking Boulevard Chave. Officers responded by charging the crowd, while the march continued towards Saint-Charles railway station.
Police used water cannon against an unauthorised protest involving several thousand people in Toulouse. Scuffles were also reported in Rennes and Nantes.
In Paris, a march that began at Porte de Bagnolet reached Porte de Charenton, the endpoint of the authorised route, where clashes broke out.
Dozens of masked people dressed in black used hammers to pry up paving stones and hurl them at police. At least one incendiary device was also thrown. Officers responded with tear gas and several baton charges.
The Paris police prefecture said “a hard core of several hundred rioters” at the rear of the march attacked officers with projectiles, including a Molotov cocktail.
Arrests decline
Earlier in the afternoon, the Interior Ministry described the situation nationwide as “generally calm, with no notable incidents”.
The number of arrests fell sharply compared with the 217 recorded at the equivalent reporting point on October 24.
The ministry said security arrangements remained adapted to the situation and warned that police would show “the greatest firmness” towards anyone responsible for violence or damage.
Fresh school blockades planned
The protest movement, bringing together Yellow Vest activists, trade unions, and high school and university students, initially focused on rising living costs, inequality and deteriorating learning conditions.
Following a security crackdown and serious injuries to some protesters, its demands broadened to include greater protection of civil liberties and the right to protest.
Student unions vowed to stage fresh blockades of high schools and universities next week, while criticising the decision not to authorise a march through central Paris.
“Starting this Tuesday, we will blockade our universities and high schools, and we will do so again on Thursday before joining the demonstration on November 5 called by workers and trade unions,” said Sabrine Kharbach, spokeswoman for Union Etudiante.

Iran talks ‘have never stopped’, US open to diplomacy: Rubio
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
18:48:34 UTC
03:48:34 KST

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said that diplomatic contacts with Iran have continued despite escalating tensions in the Middle East, stressing that Washington remains open to a peaceful solution provided its core security concerns are addressed.
Speaking to reporters in Atlanta on Saturday, Rubio said there was no set timetable for the ongoing diplomatic efforts, but emphasised that communication channels remained open.
“There are multiple talks. Talks have actually never stopped,” he said, adding that conversations were taking place both directly and, more often, through intermediaries.
“The president’s preference in any challenge around the world is to try to solve it diplomatically and peacefully, if possible,” Rubio said, referring to President Donald Trump’s approach.
Accusing Iran of targeting commercial shipping
Rubio added that Washington would welcome a diplomatic outcome, provided it did not endanger US national security or leave its principal concerns unresolved.
At the centre of those concerns, he said, are Iran’s nuclear programme and what Washington sees as Tehran’s destabilising role across the region.
Rubio accused Iran of targeting commercial shipping in international waters, warning that attacks on vessels carrying oil, natural gas and other cargo threaten not only maritime security but also global energy and food supplies.
He also pointed to Iran’s support for regional groups, including the Houthi militia in Yemen and Hezbollah in Lebanon, arguing that their activities have contributed to instability and security concerns for neighbouring countries.
Addressing Gulf security, Rubio reaffirmed Washington’s defence commitments to Saudi Arabia, saying the US remained in regular contact with Riyadh and intended to honour its agreements.
Possible US-Russia leaders’ encounter
Rubio also said he spoke briefly with Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov on the sidelines of the G20 talks about a possible encounter between their countries’ leaders next month.
“We spoke just briefly about the opportunity for our leaders to potentially interact at APEC next month,” he said, referring to the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the Chinese city of Shenzhen in mid-November.
He stressed, however, that he did not hold a formal meeting with Lavrov during the two-day gathering of G20 foreign ministers in Atlanta, Georgia.
Rubio said Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy could be invited to the December G20 summit in Miami if Trump believes “something positive” could result from his attendance.
“If we can play a role in mediating an end to that conflict, the United States is prepared to play that role,” Rubio said of the war in Ukraine.
“And to play that role, we have to have the ability to communicate with both sides,” he added.
